Stellaris is an entry level real time strategy game with a space setting.
This is a difficult game to review. On the one hand, it is a very addictive blend of 4X and real time strategy, on the other, it is a game lacking a lot of depth.
Paradox's other games like Crusader Kings, Europa Universalis, Victoria, and Hearts of Iron have far more depth than Stellaris does and all have their own niche. A lot of the depth comes from the historical setting in these games that attempts to accurately portray the world's situation at game start, and each game's own take. CK is all about dynasties and plots; EU is a huge game of Risk with actual countries, Vicky can be won through playing the economy, and HoI is obviously all about real time warfar.
But Stellaris? There are no real countries, there are no recognisable situations, and the game isn't sure if it is about diplomacy or warfare in space. Both are very lacking. Diplomacy is almost non-existent and warfare all too often comes down to just spamming immense amounts of ships until you either win or lose.
Even though the recent major patch, Heinlein, introduced much better ship mechanics, all too often it is still just a numbers game.
Does that make Stellaris a bad game? No, absolutely not. If you go in expecting an easier RTS where all players are inherently equal since there are no pre-defined bonuses (other than allowing some AI races to start with a minor advantage), you can have a lot of fun with this game. Each game will be very different since everything in the galaxy will be generated in another way, so where in one game you may find yourself boxed in by stronger empires and lose everything, in another you may be able to control a huge part of the galaxy and eventually conquer it all (until the end game crisis comes).
What elevates Stellaris above just a basic real time strategy game is its events. As you explore the star systems you can encounter many small stories, most of which can turn out different in several ways. One time you find a seemingly abandoned starship and have your scientist explore it, only to lose your entire ship. The next time the same event comes up you get a rare technology instead, etc.
More skilled leaders will usually lead to better results, but everything remains somewhat random.
So, do I recommend Stellaris? Yes, but only for people who already like Paradox games or similar games like Civilization series (bearing in mind Stellaris is real time strategy, not turn based). If you want the next Master of Orion or X, don't go looking here.
Stellaris is the best "oh god, every one of my sci-fi fantasies are fulfilled" simulator.

Dear Paradox developers,
I really tried to like this game, but there has just not been put enough effort into it to make Stellaris a good game. A game like "Europa Universalis IV" in space? Sounded too good.
In terms of game mechanics it feels simpler than Universalis, instead expansion is being slowed down by the sector concept and minimalistic management of colonies.
But the gameplay isn't my main critique, it's the presentation!
Stellaris gets 3/10 points when it comes to graphics, and those 3 points are only for the nice galaxy map and the creative alien races, although there could have been done a lot more with their animations instead of just blinking eyes and wobbling heads.
Fleet battles? I gave up watching that chaotic mess. You just wait for the results.
Another few ugly examples:
When I win a war in this game a text message says "You have won a war". That's basically all.
When I change the weapons on my ship models, different weapons use the same 3D model.
When I upgrade buildings (and I did that a lot), sometimes all that changes in the tiny grapics representing the building is the colour and a number.
When I discover planets of "natural beauty" (special bonus planets), they just have the same background graphics that other planets have too.
All these and other failures make the game boring quickly. And again, the presentation! It's 2016, not 1995! Oh, and don't even think I'll buy a single DLC for this one! Plantoids? More like "greedoids"!
Sincerely,

There are a lot of small bugs, but these seem to be getting ironed out with updates, so I won't mention them.
A couple major issues I have:
1. Sector management:  I wouldn't want to manage 100 planets, but to stuff them all into a poorly-managed 'sector' that you have no control over and get nothing out of seems completely pointless.  And you don't have a choice in the matter, the game punishes you for not using sectors, and also for taking planets out of sectors if you want to reorganize.  It's not very well done in my opinion.
It would be much better if systems and sectors could be managed in the same way planets are, just pooling the resources of the individual planets.  I'm not sure how that would look.  Maybe we need a 'sector map' view, where you can effectively manage the fleets and building and resources of an individual sector: system view < sector view < galaxy view.  I don't really know the answer, but the sector system as it is now doesn't work.
2.  Galaxy size: I appreciate that you can have a huge galaxy, but sometimes I want a short game, and even on the smallest size, I'm stil playing my first game after 40+ hours.  I think a galaxy of <100 stars would be a good option.  This shouldn't be too hard to implement.

I've spent my share of time playing this and got fairly close to beating it before my friends ran out of steam and we decided to pick up something more... fun.
That's the problem with this game. It never even attempts to act as if it was a particularly involving game and this becomes especially apparant when playing with multiple friends, sharing a party together. Perhaps we've all become too impatient with our games, expecting more active battle systems and a gripping story to follow along, but as a review from someone who's put in almost 100 hours into the game, I can, with some authority, say that the game is very, very dull.
Perhaps 20% of the fun of the game came from decisions being made in combat. Another 10% came from the very few decisions you get to make when progressing your character. 0% for story and exploration, and the rest 70% of enjoyment comes from just hanging out for hours with your friends. If you had decided to just talk about random things with 2 of your buddies in a chat room someplace, you'd be having 70% of the enjoyment of this game.
The long hours you spend exploring with friends (no matter how hard you try to keep progressing, it will take very long) are exasperated by slow movement, slow exploration, dull monsters and queststasks; and it quickly becomes a chore to even take your turn in combat. You quickly find that you play this game with a more interesting game in another window playing simultaneously and only return to take your turn because you would feel bad about making your friends wait. That's the sort of chore this game becomes.
As much as I'd have loved to love this game and would have even more liked to say I completed it, I realize that even if I did, I wouldn't be able to say it was worth it at the end. The finale was as boring as the 90-hour road leading up to it. And those were 90 hours each from myself and another 2 of my friends playing together, their experiences so poor that they didn't even feel like finishing it.
I would never wish this experience upon anyone and thus cannot, in good faith, recommend this game to anyone, no matter how patient or enduring they might be. Just because they might be able to play it, doesn't mean they could drag their friends kicking and screaming through such a slog.

Possibly my favourite game of all time. An incredibly deep, immersive FPS/RPG with a rich story, memorable characters and an amazing variation on playstyles. I have completed this game so many times I have lost count, yet each time I discover something new that I hadn't seen before. The games dialogue reacts to everything you do, whether you kill people on sight or simply knock them out, whether you remain hidden or run out in plain view, obey orders or find your own way, how much exploring you do, how much you interact with others. Each time changing the dialogue and story in subtle ways. It's stealth system was one of the most robust for it's day, very much focussing on sticking to the shadows and staying low behind cover. However you may decide to become a literally bulletproof death machine, wielding rifles, swords, rocket launchers and more with equal ferocity.
Definitely worth the purchase. A classic game with a mature, well researched story on the possible future.

Quite simply my personal favorite game. For this title those words have been heard, read, and repeated hundreds of thousands of times over and with good reason. Those looking for a master piece of an experience this is it. Few games understand what elements it wants and how to achieve them quite like the original Deus Ex does.
While graphically the game is somewhat blocky, it still holds up with memorably characters and a strong story ripe to burst with conspiracies mixing in to one another in a cohesive package that will have you curious about what is really going on right until the very last minutes of the game.
Hot off the heels of Thief this title allows for a purely stealth character to the point where characters even acknowledge the use of stealth and lack of a body count in the dialog, and sometimes even reward the player for taking such a route. While its encouraged to not make Duke blush at the amount of corpses and ways to make them, its still an option within the game and a perfectly viable one at that with special abilities known as Augmentations that increase resistence to bullets, or skills that can be trained to perfect aiming. Weapon mods also add to the deadly efficency of guns. Silenced sniper rifles with a laser sight and maxed out accuracy mods in the hands of an expert marksman? Watch the badguys drop to the floor before their friends even figure out what's happening.
How about bypassing security? Get a strength mod and put a dumpster against a wall and simply leap over it, usurping an entire security network of elaborate traps, cameras, and patrols. Perhaps something a little closer down to earth is your style? Then crawl into a vent and ensure you're not caught by guard. Feeling like you want to be a little tricky? Have pepper spray in hand? Spray that in the path of a laser beam and quickly crawl passed it as you block the beam without alerting the guards.
All of this wrapped into a setting so rarely explored, Cyberpunk, and the game is a treat for any tech enthusist to go "what if" with. Those looking for the definitive Ghost in the Shell experience, look no further and enjoy.
On a personal note; this is a game I come back to and play to competion at least once every year and there is almost always something new that I experience in some fashion, be it through gameplay or dialog. I strongly advise against looking up guides or tricks beyond the ones mentioned above that are less intuitive and not an easy few to discover on your own.
Hint: Open the credits and type: "thereisnospoon" without the quotes and enjoy the effects once in game.

The best video game of all time, bar none; the sequels Invisible War (horrible game) and Human Revolution don't even come close.
The game takes place in the year 2052 where the world has become a ghetto ravaged by war, terrorism, and disease. A new plague, known as the Gray Death, is spreading rapidly with no cure; only a vaccine known as Ambrosia can prevent infection, and only if you can keep taking it. Worst of all, production is extremely limited and most of it is rationed out to key government and utility workers. You play as UNATCO (United Nations Anti-Terrorist Coalition) agent J.C. Denton, fresh out of the academy, on his first mission to reacquire a supply of Amrbosia that has been stolen by the terrorist group NSF (National Secessionist Forces). But it doesn't take long to figure out that something much more sinister is going on.
Deus Ex features incorporates conspiracy theries (Illuminati, Trilateral Commission, Knights Templar, Majestic 12, etc) into a well-integrated cyberpunk storyline. It is the most cerebral game I've ever played, which focuses on the ideas of liberty and authority with very intelligent dialogue.
The gameplay is incredible as well. Deus Ex is a FPS/RPG hybrid and the best I've seen in it's genre. You gain skill points that you can invest into different skills, such as Heavy Weaponry, Lockpicking, or Medicine. You also receive nano-augmentations throughout the game that can be toggled on or off at the expense of bioelectrical enegry, such as Quiet Movement or Invisibility.
The only downside to this game, if you want to call it that, is that the graphics are outdated as the game came out in 2000. However, there are lots of mods that improve things like texture quality which make the game more visually pleasing. If you were a PC gamer around the time though (Half Life, Unreal, Tribes, etc) then it shouldn't phase in you the least bit.
Play this game NOW. You're not a real PC gamer if you haven't.

It's about time I wrote a quick review for a game that truly deserves it; Stellaris is amazing!
TLDR; Superbly amazing and surprising game (Especially for a strat-sim), definitely worth more than they are asking for.
I spent a good number of hours building a few different space empires in this game, to get a feel for the different ways to play the pre-built empire types. This game is both forgiving, and challenging at the same time. There is a great in-depth (imo) political system that is fairly easy to grasp and use; This is a very important element for anyone that plays civ-type games.... and this is where the civ and many other civ-type games have fallen very short.
After one of my last half playthroughs, I was finally on my way to conquering more territory by switching over from a very peaceful and diplomatic empire to a war monger. I needed to; The Clixtac empire would never make friends with me, so I needed to conquer them through some other means. My decision to switch my empires goals got me kicked out of the federation I worked so hard to achieve - Rightfully so! This amazed me, and I was a little proud when those weaker liberated empires decided I was no longer a good leader for peace, and booted me out :) This is what makes Stellaris great, the twists and turns, the constant sway of power, the political struggles... the list goes on.
My only gripes are the weapon balances, as there are definitely weapons that seem to not have much benefit other than as a thing to research. The auto-generated ship designs are also lacking... but that's laziness on my part and something to look at doing yourself especially later game.
All in all, a very surprising game that continues to surprise me - Definitely worth the money and Paradox seems to be continually updating it, which on Steam is a very hard thing to come by.
Great job Paradox!

Stellaris isn't a perfect game, but it's also not very deserving of some of the negative feedback I've seen in the reviews.
Yes, it could use a lot of work, and yes there are areas which feel shallow or even meaningless to the gameplay. However; none of that is discouraging nor does it serve to devalue the experience you're provided. If anything, it lets you enjoy what there is rather than overwhelming new players with lots of features and - with many Paradox titles - unnecessary or poorly executed fluff.
If you're a fan of Science Fiction, and enjoy the pace of 4x games, then Stellaris is definitely a good fit. It's every SciFi fan's fantasy, in this man's opinion, and I am sure future updates will continue to improve upon its foundation.

After playing and examining this game, I came to the conclusion that I cannot recommend it in its current form. Stellaris has the potential to be one of the best 4x games out there. The attention to details are amazing storywise, and the game is very addictive. However, there are certain issues that ruin the game completly:
1. There are still to many diplomatic bugs (border closing, opening)
2. The races dont react to large scale events like the unbidden arrival.
3. The game is filled with bugs, for example when you destroy the unbidden portal, it still tracks on the map and says the portal is still there.
4. There are only two ways of victory, both involve war, making it difficult as a peacefull species to win.
5. Its far to difficult to coalese several different alliances of peacefull specias into one, then form a federation
6. In the mid and end game it gets very boring and your after knocking out those last species or colonizing those last planets to win.
7. The fallen empires are boring, they are just there, and do nothing exept waiting to be conquered, which is easy when you reach a certain size of your empire and fleet-strenght.
8. The reward for winning a time consuming game in Stellaris is horrible. You only get a stat overview over the different species. No video, animation, speech or anything that awards you story-wise, you get the option to continue, but whats the point?
9. The game has no piracy function, no trader ship functions, these have to be downloaded as seperate mods.
10. The steam achievements are bugged, they wont work in my steam anyways.
The Paradox team are amazing at creating complex strategy games, and Stellaris can be a very amazing game, but its still not finished. This game in its present form should only be bought on sale, or when they have patched/updated the game which they are good at and Paradox has amazing customer response. I would also wait to buy this game until the mods like Star Trek, Star Gate etc. are fully finished and functional. Wait for around december/january before buying this.

I started playing in 2011, so I actually have a thousand or two more hours played than reported on my steam page. As you might have guessed, it's my favorite game ever. So this review has been a looooong time coming.
As you've already figured out, NEStalgia is truly as if Dragon Warrior was an MORPG, and it does everything right to nail that comparison. If that sounds awesome to you, but the $15 price tag leaves you feeling squeamish, let me assure you, buy the game, man! You're going to love this! There is no other game that takes all of the qualities of beloved 8-bit RPGs and presents them as a MORPG. Skill trees! 8 classes! Gear! Auction House! PvP! For an MORPG, a one-time $15 payment is exceptionally rare. If you're here looking for a great single-player RPG, there are probably better ones than NEStalgia. But the single-player experience is not what this game is about. What makes this game unique and great is the world multiplayer qualities. If you're still thinking about the price, don't forget about that 3-for-the-price-of-2 pack, that's only $10 a person. Or you can wait for a sale that comes around once/twice a year, or ask around for copies that people bought just for the express purpose of supporting the game. personally, I've lost count of how many copies I've accumulated, just because I wanted to help expand the community.
I appreciate that this is one of those games that doesn't hold your hand at all. The Mouse boss at the beginning can be accessed, but can't be defeated at the very moment you take the quest. That doesn't mean the game is brutal, you just lose half the gold you happen to be carrying. It's a very early lesson that there is some necessity for caution, that danger exists, and some discretion is the player's responsibility. It keeps you mindful and present in the game, instead of just unconsciously following arrows, checkpoint to checkpoint. Then you go back, beat the mouse's♥♥♥♥♥♥ and feel like you've accomplished something great. The Shade can also be accessed, but not defeated, early in the game. I think that this teaches you that you can't really metagame your way through this, it discourages thoughts like "I won't encounter something that I couldn't defeat, because this is a game." It adds a sense of realism. It feels like an adventure. It's the mature philosophy that most MORPGs avoid out of fear of losing players to ragequits. And it's certainly not as if the game constantly bombards you with situations completely out of your control.
The world is somewhat small, about on par with most 8-bit RPGs. The play-through time of 30-60 hours is quite standard. After that, there's tons of replayability. You can do daily quests in the Black Sanctum and work your way to the best gear set in the game. If you're 32, you can easily find a veteran willing to carry you almost every day. And even if you can't, there's a 2 or 3 dailies that can be easily solo'd. You can also try out a new class. Each one has a variety of unique, interesting ways to play. Like the soldier! I don't know why everyone rags on him so much lately. He can rip bosses apart with his bleed skills. With counter, he can fulfill his tank duties while still mopping the floor with large groups of trash mobs. Remember to grab those skills that mitigate magic damage - well read, dig deep, shield wall, unstoppable, tenacity, StopSpell, because magic damage will rock your♥♥♥♥♥♥ You might even want to seed up with INT and -ELM seeds.
You could also be that Companion Catch'em all Completionist. There's yet more variety to be found leveling new companions. It will be some crazy faraway date before the game's greatest party compositions are sussed out. Totems have an AOE curse ability, making your cleric's Judgment even more insta-killier. Party with fast, lucky pet, like White Wolf, that learns carnage, so your berzerker soldier doesn't have to use a turn applying bleeds before he can enjoy that sweet damage/crit boost.
To address some common complaints about the game, there is a lot of truth that the leveling portion of the game is wrought with imbalances and screwy things. Mostly a consequence of major patches that significantly altered the game, but didn't go back in detail to make sure everything scaled elegantly with the changes. You'll definitely notice the megamoths in Balzackia, outputting like 9 times the damage of any other monster you've seen so far, and there is no significant choices for magic defense at that point. But you'll learn to accept that it's just the way things are that some monsters are humongous threats, you'll learn which enemies you need to focus down first, and in a level or two, you'll eat them alive. So unfortunately, more often than not, the answer is grinding. This is a valid criticism. On the other hand, grinding done earlier is grinding that you won't have to do later - the Black Sanctum is not an area that requires grinding to participate.
I'm playing on an 8-year old windows XP, and the overworld screen panning is almost perfectly smooth. There is a little stuttering, but after a short while, you get used to it. Besides, it's a turn based game, nothing you do would even slightly benefit from 60fps smoothness. I also barely ever experience server lag. Periods when the game is offline for more than two minutes are also very rare - there is way, waaay, WAAAAY less downtime than World of Warcraft.
The initial cosmetic choices are limited. But there are more dyes and masks than you could ask for all over the world and in the auction house to finalize the appearance you want, so there's nothing to worry about when it comes to finding a unique look.
It's true that there hasn't been a Colosseum tournament in ages, which I agree is unfortunate. But don't think you're missing out on anything. The Colosseum gear is not better than the Sanctum gear, and you can verify that here:
Although the Colosseum set would be easier to get than the Sanctum Set. All the same, you can still be a PvP Pimp by completing your Sanctum set, no Colosseum required.
The combat pacing can feel slow, because you can't skip the text. That's why when I'm grinding, I multitask. I watch videos, check email, do homework, etc, in fact I'm grinding phantom dust while I write this review. I'm up to 5, if you're wondering. :P Honestly, I've never really noticed, because I usually need to read the text anyway, and I read at about the pace the text scrolls, but I can see how when you're new, this can feel like it's slowing you down. I think of it as a balancing mechanism for people who read slower, or for people who need to read to know what's happening, which enemies are within killing range, for example. Characters who can just one-shot enemies without needing to know what's going on shouldn't be able to skip text and thus gain a significant speed advantage over other players. On the other hand, this mechanic also slows down characters that use AOE DOTs, because that text takes foooorrreeeevverrrr, so it's certainly something that could be looked at.
Companion AI is another valid point of frustration. It would be great if my scorcher, who is specced for engulf, but also knows sear, would use engulf, and then follow up with sear, but there is no way to guarantee he will do that, and therefore that strategy is not viable. Usually, he starts with sear, even though he's specced with engulf! Which is nonsensical, and no adjusting of his tactics will change that. With that noted, you will have no problem getting to Arctic having never used any pet other than red slime and blue slime. It's just frustrating when your pets won't follow through with your epic strategy, and you've worked a pet to max level only to find out that your pet won't behave the way you thought he would.
After 1000s of hours, this game is worth $15 to me, no-brainer. I have way more to say, but I'm out of space. Have fun!!!!!!

This has basically no impact on the game, but it's a thing that annoyed me, so I thought I'd share.
Using watts as a unit you amass, like you do in this game, makes no sense. Watts means joules per second, meaning it's an amount of energy (joules) per second. The way the unit is handeled in this game, where you recieve an amount of watts per hour would mean that you have a constant acceleration of energy production (J/s^2).
The correct thing would be to name the unit you amass joules, and the energy per second watts.
All that being said, I love the game ^^

Graphics: the graphics were okish for 2000 when the game released. To bring it this century, follow this guide:
Sound: nice voice overs, decent sound fx. Overall very atmospheric, if a bit low fidelity.
Gameplay: good. The controls and interface are a bit clunky compared to what you may be used to but after 1-2 hours it stops getting in the way. The customization of your character is really meaningful with choices that are not just skin deep. However, there is no way to screw things up, the game can be completed without any items and with any build.
Story: knocks your socks off. This game has real choice and consequence, plot twists, cospiracy theories melded together very smartly and, something that rarely happens nowadays: a great ending. Hard to explain without spoiling anything, but I think this is one of the best game stories of all time and it's the main reason you would want to play this game. There are usually about 3-5 ways to accomplish any objective and combat itself is optional (although sometimes combat is the easiest way to reach objectives).
How to approach: the game doesn't have a compass/objective pointers, doesn't show your position on the map and generally does not hold your hand. Pay attentiona and have a faq at hand if you get stuck (but try to play on your own, it's more fun like that).

A pretty outrageous racing game... Let's go in depth here.
The Good
Open world gameplay is fun. The cars look cool. The idea of being a German highway cop is pretty novel, too, and the city is pretty big, along with the various parts of the autobahn. You can go REALLY fast with nitro and you will find yourself spamming shift/the button on the controller a LOT during missions. The dialouge is so bad, it's good. I promise. You can also pull off some cool stunts and blow up some cars in the process, which is pretty exciting.
The Bad
First of all, be prepared to rage. This game is ridiculously hard and I seriously recommend using a controller if you have one. If you manage to beat all of this with a keyboard, you are either a superhuman or you used some kind of keyboard unknown to man. When you execute a crazy awesome stunt, your car will probably spin out of control and wreck. When you go too fast, you spin out of control and wreck. When you hit a car...
The bad part about the wrecks isn't the damage your car sustains, but the fact that anytime you miss one of the turns or hit something during a mission, you might as well restart the level because that's how hard it is. You'll fail the mission if you don't do *anything* perfectly. Even the tutorial.
Some of the graphics look like they could use a tuneup, but then again this is a game from 2009 and I wouldn't expect it to be looking much better than this. Some of the cars in parking lots just don't show any signs of damage when you hit them, and there are a few weird white cars which are marked as enemies on the map but don't do anything when you hit them.
To sum up the bad, this is where all German game developers go when they die and have done bad things.
Overall, this game is worth $10 if you want a challenge, like Germany, or want Goat Simulator with cars. If you just want a racing game like Need For Speed, this ain't it.

Stellaris is big. Really big. You just won't believe how vastly, hugely, mind-bogglingly big it is. I mean, you may think it's a long way down the road to the chemist, but that's just peanuts to Stellaris.
Adams quotes aside, the game is pretty good. There's fun to be had in creating an empire, in the early-game space exploration, and in most aspects of the game. Unfortunately, an unforunate amount of the mid-late game time is filled with busywork or nothing at all, but speeding up the game can help things along quite a bit. The AI Diplomacy leaves something to be desired, for example some empire might reject your Non-Agression Pact because it's "Not Diplomatically Relevant" which somehow manages to appear in just about every situation, near, far, big, small, worried, peaceful, it will show up and say "No, no diplomacy for you."
tl;dr
Game is pretty good, but overpriced. Wait for a sale if you like this sort of gameplay and don't mind a little bit of busywork between the exciting things that happen. I expect this game will get better with time, the diplomacy will be more intuitive, bugs will be patched out, so the older this review gets, the more likely it is that the issues with the game will become history.

Warning to anyone looking at this game. If you have senstivity to flashing lights or get headaches to flashing, or are just generally annoyed at everything flashing on a frequent basis then avoid this game.
The game currently has a bug which has been stated on the offical forms more than once with the V1.7.0 update and (at writing of this review) hasn't been acknowledged by the dev. The bug is that if you disable either battle or overword flashes  the game corrups and freezes.
Now on to the actuall review:
Summarry incase you didn't want to read the whole thing:
All in all the game is meh. I woudn't say bad but I wouldn't say it is good.
To me it takes nestagia and milks it without regard for advancing anything in a meaningful way.

Full Review:
Mechanics: The mechanics of this game are simple and slightly refined, I would say that simplicity to this game as a throwback to when games didn't need 30 different commads or button presses to do 1 move in battle is what is aluring in this game but the added functions of the skill trees and the companions feel thrown in and unrefined, there is much more potential in thoes systems expecally the companion system. One thing I would change is the ability of actually using the companions in combat instead of setting them on an auto play based on a behavor. Not much else to say here other than the crafting is semi cool but the restriction of dmg based of a particular elemental stat is not needed.
Graphics: Well not much to say here, pixle graphics... if you like that sort of thing.
Game Pace: Here is a rough one. The pace of the game is really really really slow and is horribly dependent on which class you choose which speed you go. I found the game way to grindy for my pace and I was playing with a friend which made it better, but due to the bug mentions before this review he got sick from the flashing and had to quit.
All in all I would say if your looking for some nestagia for the old school games you might be better off waiting on this or playing some of the other old school like games. The creator has an expansion on the horrizon so maybe the game will get better overtime but I would avoid for now but keep on the radar.

Overall, it's definitely a fun incremental game experience.  So fun that you will be wanting more.

I love the idea of summoning elementals prior to casting spells. In theory it adds some immersion and believability to magical systems. Great idea.
As for the execution of that system...not so great. What starts out as a great concept ends up as a data entry job. All you're really doing to implement this concept, is furiously typing away on a keyboard in accordance with a set of data provided by the program's instruction, then pressing a single button to execute the data string. I'm sorry; in the every day world, people get paid to do this sort of rote, mundane work.
And it gets even worse on a controller, where keyboard presses are replaced by terrible quarter circle rotations of the right stick. Try executing that as quickly as key presses. Sorry; dont think so. Which is a pity because the game is built on the idea that you will do just that - use the quarter circle rotations as fast as key presses. And if you dont - you die.
So great ideas...terrible, terrible implementation. Avoid this and the frustration that comes with it.

TL,DR: If you are looking for a way to teach your children about the slave trade. . .maybe buy a book. Playing History 2: The Slave Trade is not a good game, nor is it a particularly effective teaching tool. The gameplay is sparse, lazy and boring. The best thing that could be said about it is that it is not as offensive as it looks.
Which is not saying much.
--------------------
EDIT: Apparently, Slave Tetris was removed. This is good for the obvious reason, but bad because now there is even less to do in this game.
Q: How do you make a game about the horrors of slavery that is also kid-friendly?
Do you:
A. Throw in mini-games like "Spot the Difference," "Memory" or "Tetris"?
B. Put in an anthropomorphic talking mouse and wacky characters like the sailor who loves fishing or the doctor who writes poetry?
C. Mention the horrible conditions and high loss of life involved in the middle passage, but don't really get into it?
D. All of the above.
E. Maybe just don't?
The correct answer is E. The developers chose D.
I am sure Serious Games interactive had nothing but good intentions. Let's teach kids about history, about how awful the process of slave trading is, about the historical aspects of slavery and hint at how it continues today. And, since kids don't necessarily want to learn, let's make it a game. The problem is it fails at everything.
Can kids learn from the game? Sure. Not just about the triangle trace, but there's little facts sprinkled around about other things. Like globes and alcohol. However, the slave trade is horrific. Making it into a kid's game requires the explanation of it to very glib and simplistic. When you give it cutesy graphics and make a game out of it, you lessen the impact of what you're trying to say. Is there a way to explain such things to kids in a way appropriate for them? Sure. A game is not the way.
On top of that, the game itself is not great. Granted, it is meant for children, but the puzzles are ridiculously simple. Most of them are "Get this thing that is right in front of you and go talk to this person on another screen." The mini-games are standard and they're not especially fun or engaging. The memory game is literally just them showing you a color-coded map. The colors stand for the number of slaves imported to that region. Then, they take the colors and key away and quiz on on the numbers. It's short and by the end you haven't done much. There are a few points where you get to make decisions. These decisions seem to effect nothing.There are glitches and lazy programming all around.
There's bugs. Most notably, achievements will not unlock if you've loaded your game. You pretty much have to play everything in one straight shot. This is not too taxing as the game is about 30 minutes long.
Surprisingly, the game is not as offensive as it appears. Yes, slave tetris is the worst thing in the game. Again, it is kind of offensive in how glib, incomplete and shallow it is, but that is a side-effect of the whole mis-guided venture.
Oh, and it has a happy ending. THE HORRORS OF THE SLAVE TRADE!

It's a good game that you can get for cheap frequently.

It's very rare to play an RPG that does not feature a globe trotting, world saving, massive journey taking main character--And it's even rarer to do that twice. Yet here we are with CDPR's incredibly crafted sequel to the legendary Witcher 1, and they have absolutely captured lightning in a bottle once again. Following the events of the previous installment's ending, players find themselves assuming the role of Geralt of Rivia once more as he's tasked with ensuring King Faltest's safety during a major battle to regain heirs to the throne. When an assassin catches the witcher off guard and commits regicide, Geralt sets off on a quest with Dandelion, Triss, Zoltan, and newcomer Roche to capture the kingslayer and the witcher's name. Throughout the three chapters within the Witcher 2, players will encounter sorceresses who are not what they seem, great beasts intent on killing everything in their path, kings who see the witcher as a pawn to do their bidding, and a troll that gets drunk and ignores his bridge duties, among other things.
While the Witcher 1's combat was generally regarded as clunky but servicable, the Witcher 2's combat greatly innovates the concept and improves in nearly every single way. The gameplay could possibly be regarded as a hack and slash, but you absolutely won't get away with simply diving into battle and swinging with wild abandon, lest you want to load your save fifty times in a row--players must tactically dodge, roll, and parry with every strike and use all available resources in order to survive. This simply isn't like previous game in which the player can skirt by without ever coating their blade in oil or drinking only Swallows--the Witcher 2 will kick your♥♥♥♥♥with its difficulty.
Storywise, the Witcher 2 is stronger than ever. The mature themes and writing the Witcher series is known for continue to pervade throughout this sequel, with gritty realism and bleakness factoring into the story's plots and subplots. Choices have to be made, and these choices are never good versus evil, but rather the lesser of two evils or a mixture of gray scaled justice and consequence. Choices you made in the Witcher 1 will come back to bite you or remind you of just who you are, and choices you make here will reveal after effects--some soon, some later. Everything matters.
As for a few short remarks, the music is almost as excellent as the first series' entry, though perhaps not as memorable. The voice acting is leagues ahead of the Witcher 1 as well as the characters' models themselves. Indeed, the graphics and art style of the Witcher 2 look intensely beautiful, and I can only imagine what the Witcher 3 will look like.
Overall, just like its predecessor, the Witcher 2 is an excellent CRPG with a few minor flaws, but otherwise is near perfection in gameplay, story telling, and building a breathing, believable world where the stakes are high and the choices have impact. If you are questioning whether or not you should start your Witcher journey, I wholeheartedly recommend you begin with the Witcher 1 and then make your way here. For those who have finished the Witcher 1 and are wondering if its sequel is just as good, I will tell you this: it is better, and it is incredible.

The price right now is well worth it, plus you'll get a 33% discount on Rebirth.

Stellaris is a real time 4X space strategy game. It is absolutely massive in scale, immensely rich in variety of species and random galactic events, which means you will never ever get bored of it. And if you do, the Steam Workshop community has been working around the clock on new free content available for download at your hearts delight. This game fleshes out the pros of Sword of the Stars (Starship Design), Europa Universalis (Scale, Empire Management) and StarDrive (being a real time strategy game) to create a spectacular galactic experience. Having played 142 hours so far I coulnt stress enough how good Stellaris is. If you are a fun of this genre, buying it is a no brainer.
And for those who dont know which is a better choice between Stellaris and Masters of Orion. Masters of Orion has only Better Graphics and slicker user interface design, not that better per se as an interface, its just prettier... alot prettier. On the other hand, Masters of Orion offers alot less variety compared to Stellaris, meaning less replayability, meaining you will get bored of it alot easier. Also very important, Masters of Orion doesnt have a workshop modding community, therefore kiss free content bye bye. Finally the sense of scale again in Stellaris leaves Masters of Orion wanting.

Where can i start with this game?
Well first off i got it for free so atleast im not annoyed that I payed the steep price of £6.99.
Secondly, Imagine everything you know and love about driving games like stuntman (which IMO this is a poor copy of), now forget it all. The game handles very poorly, from not being able to ue the analog stick in menus to the the car being sluggish to turn one second, to spinning 360 the next.
Continuing with controles, they are so random its not even amusing, (Y) is horn, (X) is siren (on, on silent, off), the right analog stick only has left and right in use and thats only for the respective indicators (im not even joking) and as far as i can tell, the bumpers do nothing at all (atleast in the tutorial anyway).
Interface wise the game is also quite poor, your speedo, map, mission objective and distance to target are all in seperate parts of the screen so you find yourself looking around at everything but the road. The speedo also has this odd feature of telling you what speed you need to hit ramps at, it will do this by taking up 1/4 of your screen and having a huge green mark and arrow at the speed you need to be, this speed is NOT optional, too slow you fall into a gap/dont make the jump, too fast and the game will send you flying into anything that it feels could be in your way.
There is also a replay cam that will replay what you did not 2 seconds ago (that seems about the extent og its record time) whenever it feels you've done something special, this is considered anything from a high speed overtake to a 45 degree turn, a 1080 aileron roll over a building or a 360 backflip over a roundabout? nah thats not replay worth (oh and your leads can get away while the replay is heppening).
Gameplay. The random spawn for cars is so borked that I swear i saw a family car with a caravon on it pull out of an industrial complex, and this wasnt a one off mistake, about 30 cars where queing to get out of a police testing area. The waypoints are another thing that are non-optional, miss one by a smidge and you will find yourself doing a 180 or slamming it into reverse while your lead gets away. Lastly that brings me to the persuit mechanics, it told me to attempt to stop the van with some light taps, instead I got infron of it and forced it to stop. Not good enough. Ok its traiing i can forgive that, so 5 taps it is, then I have to dissable the vehicle, so I flip it on its side with some fancy driving, nope, didnt fill the damage indicator so it de and respawns to carry on.
Overall this game was very poor, it looked ok back in 2010 when it was made im sure, but now its dated, jaded and needs to fade into the background.

It's very rare to play an RPG that does not feature a globe trotting, world saving, massive journey taking main character--And it's even rarer to do that twice. Yet here we are with CDPR's incredibly crafted sequel to the legendary Witcher 1, and they have absolutely captured lightning in a bottle once again. Following the events of the previous installment's ending, players find themselves assuming the role of Geralt of Rivia once more as he's tasked with ensuring King Faltest's safety during a major battle to regain heirs to the throne. When an assassin catches the witcher off guard and commits regicide, Geralt sets off on a quest with Dandelion, Triss, Zoltan, and newcomer Roche to capture the kingslayer and the witcher's name. Throughout the three chapters within the Witcher 2, players will encounter sorceresses who are not what they seem, great beasts intent on killing everything in their path, kings who see the witcher as a pawn to do their bidding, and a troll that gets drunk and ignores his bridge duties, among other things.
While the Witcher 1's combat was generally regarded as clunky but servicable, the Witcher 2's combat greatly innovates the concept and improves in nearly every single way. The gameplay could possibly be regarded as a hack and slash, but you absolutely won't get away with simply diving into battle and swinging with wild abandon, lest you want to load your save fifty times in a row--players must tactically dodge, roll, and parry with every strike and use all available resources in order to survive. This simply isn't like previous game in which the player can skirt by without ever coating their blade in oil or drinking only Swallows--the Witcher 2 will kick your♥♥♥♥♥with its difficulty.
Storywise, the Witcher 2 is stronger than ever. The mature themes and writing the Witcher series is known for continue to pervade throughout this sequel, with gritty realism and bleakness factoring into the story's plots and subplots. Choices have to be made, and these choices are never good versus evil, but rather the lesser of two evils or a mixture of gray scaled justice and consequence. Choices you made in the Witcher 1 will come back to bite you or remind you of just who you are, and choices you make here will reveal after effects--some soon, some later. Everything matters.
As for a few short remarks, the music is almost as excellent as the first series' entry, though perhaps not as memorable. The voice acting is leagues ahead of the Witcher 1 as well as the characters' models themselves. Indeed, the graphics and art style of the Witcher 2 look intensely beautiful, and I can only imagine what the Witcher 3 will look like.
Overall, just like its predecessor, the Witcher 2 is an excellent CRPG with a few minor flaws, but otherwise is near perfection in gameplay, story telling, and building a breathing, believable world where the stakes are high and the choices have impact. If you are questioning whether or not you should start your Witcher journey, I wholeheartedly recommend you begin with the Witcher 1 and then make your way here. For those who have finished the Witcher 1 and are wondering if its sequel is just as good, I will tell you this: it is better, and it is incredible.

Weather Lord is a series of casual time management games, with Victor as a young hero able to manipulate the weather. However, Victor wasn't always the hero there as previous games were showing more humans and less cute animals.
Remember my previous review on the series, which was Following the Princess? Well, The Successor's Path is just the game before it. It's chronicling how Victor came to the throne of his kingdom, by defeating his evil Uncle Wagner. Beginning in your land, you're going to visit different landscapes. I'm currently in the snowed levels, however, given the fact that I've played little of the game in the year, it's no wonder.
The gameplay is simple: you have several objectives per level and you have to fullfill them. To do that, Victor is as any hero of a casual time management game, helped by his allies, the workers and the warriors. The workers are collecting resources (whether they're scattered around or concentrated on one place): food, gold and wood. However, when fields, mines or forests are emptied, you can make them growth again: either by sending a worker (mine) or by using a weather artifact (rain). To help you, you can also build sawmills, mills, forges or houses (this building helps to hire more workers) and upgrade them.
But there are also obstacles and enemies. Some obstacles can be removed thanks to a weather element (sun or wind for example). Enemies can be defeated by warriors or towers. A simple warrior will lose quickly health unless he's powered by the right element when confronting an enemy: sun for goblin, thunder for shaman, wind for ghost, etc.. The towers have to be build but there are only three kinds of them: sun, wind or thunder (needing the weather element to be activated and for a limited time). Enemies can come like that or coming from their lairs that can be destroyed by your workers (but there is always one enemy that will get out in the middle of it, be prepared to see your workers coming back to bases scared).
Altars can also be repaired and give bonus: stop time, faster workers, enemies in the level dying in one click, etc.. They're really useful if you're aiming for a three stars scores. You'll also discover that you can repair buttons, barns, or growth crystals (powered by sun) for the snowed levels, as there are no rain element available.
That's the core of The Successor's Path. But the game is quite difficult as I had to replay level 22 I don't know how many times and to find finally the right strategy to get my three stars score. That's why I quit the game months ago, as there are ingame achievements.
The graphics are nice and the characters are quite cute... I mean Victor and its allies because others are disgusting (like the octopus monster). The soundtrack is also pleasant.
However, what is missing is the achievements: some of the games have them like Royal Holidays and Following the Princess. I don't understand why this one didn't benefit of a little update for Steam achievements. I also prefer the new system of having your elements in a bar to the one in this game which have the elements scattered around: sometimes, it's hard to see them. But given the fact that the Successor's Path is an early game, I will not really whine about it.
Really, the Successor's Path isn't bad, it's just that I've played latter games and find them more appealing that this one because of new mechanics. But it's still nice to follow Victor's life.
Also contrary to some users, I didn't experience crashes at level 12,15 or 20, so I suppose that it's fixed.

The Successor’s Path is a quite fast-paced time management game with strict goal times, repetitive level design, and surprisingly lot of combat for this genre.
Although it is the earliest one on Steam, The Successor’s Path is actually the fourth instalment in the Weather Lord series. This present a mild problem, since the game expects players to know its core mechanics, so it is slim on tutorials.
Luckily, the essence of the game is the same as in most any similar ones: use a set of tireless servants to run around the level collecting resources, which you then spend on clearing obstacles or meeting generic level goals. The devil is in the details, or, in this case, in the series-specific mechanics of using different weather powers to help the servants in different ways—and those may take some time getting used to.
Another problem is that the game works as much as expected, but it doesn’t really offer much of a variety. The only interesting thing in it is that it really loves to use enemies, which turns many levels into tiresome cat and mouse chases, which, combined with the strict goal times, may prove to be too much of a challenge for the casual player.
In the end, I can only recommend this one for those who want their stories without any holes in them, as probably the only reason The Successor’s Path is on Steam is because it starts a new line in the story, which is continued in the much better follow-up game.

A nice time management game.  The graphics are very detailed: swans swim in the pond, chameleons on the rocks in the underground, little bunnies in the snow land.    You have to balance obtaining the items you need for your goal (i.e. 15 food, 20 gold, etc) with defeating random enemies by hiring fighters or building attack towers.  Certain enemies are weak against certain elemental attacks.  So you will have to drag the sun icon onto your fighter or tower to defeat one enemy, then maybe the wind or water element for a different enemy.   However you also need the elemental icons to refresh your crops and trees to gather more stuff.  Or to melt a frozen patch of ground.  It takes a few seconds for an element to refresh after it's been used.
The story is the usual epic of a young man who must prove himself and defeat the evil Uncle who has usurped the throne.  However, this game gives it a twist with the people being humanoid animals rather than just typical humans.   Along the way we meet all kinds of interesting creatures, even a small dragon.   I really like that the characters are not human, it gives the game a unique feel.
The music is more laid back than some time management games (such as the 12 Labours of Hercules games) and it blends into the background nicely.   The gameplay is stil hectic at times, though, especially if you want a gold rating for a fast time.  But you can just sit back and play at a leisurely pace if you want to.
According to Steam my time is at 6 hours and I just finished it on easy.  If they had Steam achievements I would play more, but so far there are just in-game achievements.
Oh, and I actually bought my copy of the game.  I didn't get it free like some of the reviewers.  Make of that what you will.

If you've played time-management games before, you've probably played something really similar to Weather Lord: The Successor's Path. In this game, you help the heir to a kingdom rebuild, and you use weather-related "artifacts" to help your workers complete tasks as you progress through the story. For example, the rain artifact regrows crops or trees, allowing them to be harvested again by your workers to get additional resources needed to complete the level. The sun artifact dries out swampy areas, which will remove obstacles blocking your workers. There are several different artifacts unlocked through gameplay, but they function essentially like the other resources and are on a timer.
In addition to gathering resources, constructing buildings, and clearing obstacles, enemies roam the paths and attack your workers. You can hire guards to protect them, and they essentially patrol the paths or can be directed to attack the enemy.
Completing levels within the fastest time limit gives a gold score (going down to silver and bronze with the longer amount of time you take), but there isn't a penalty for completely exceeding the time limit allowed. Weather Lord is ideal for new gamers, young kids, or anyone without lightning fast reflexes. This makes this game, and others like it, a pretty nice relaxing casual adventure for someone who wants to play something simple and undemanding.
Although the gameplay isn't exactly unique, the weather theme adds a slight twist. Like several other similar games offered by this developer, they are nice quality and have cute graphics and music. The price is pretty low already but you could hold out for sales or bundles. There are a lot of levels, so beating all of them will take several hours at least, and if you want to achieve gold scores you'll likely find yourself replaying quite a few levels.
Unlike many similar time-management style games on social media or mobile platforms, there are no micro-transactions and you don't have to invite all your friends in order to progress. Also, each of the tasks can be completed quickly and each level takes only a short amount of time to play through, so it's good for players who are looking to take their gaming in small bites. However, it's pretty easy for a short session to turn into a long stretch as the "just one more level" drive kicks in.
My only complaint about Weather Lord: The Successor's Path is that the in-game awards aren't tied in to Steam achievements, although the game does have Trading Cards.

A mage is walking through a village and sees a woman standing outside of her house with an exclamation mark over her head, and approaches her to talk.  She asks him to deal with rats in her basement.  And in that moment, RPG veterans would groan from all of the times they were given the same mindless tasks, and these aren't even cranium rats!
But of course, there is a twist here.  Everything in this game takes a comedic dump on RPG conventions, lead by a narrator who is totally not a vampire.  What kind of game is this?  It's the kind of game with a Vietnam expansion where you use a M60 on goblins.  Awkwardness of that expansion aside, this is a rather geeky parody of the RPG genre, in the vein of games like Munchkin that find humor in the genre itself.  It's also in Swedish, which gives it an unusual feel.
The game features a unique magic system, in which eight elements are used in combinations that create spells.  Combining some elements create new elements (such as fire and water making steam), while others cancel each other out.  Learning the combinations that create spells is the key to the game, and it becomes vital to learn to enter them quickly.  While the game can be played with a gamepad, a keyboard and mouse are more effective because they allow faster entry of spells.  Up to four players can play in co-op.

A very different game when compared to the first one, and it vastly improves on most points while taking a couple of steps back..unfortunately i think that the 10% it does worst are some of the most important features that CDPR should have improved on, to the extent that, in the end, i think that overall i prefer the first game..the following are some of the main points of interests i think everybody should know, both the bad and the good.
1) combat wise this is far more enaging, but it's hardly an improvement since the "rythm game" of the first one was easily the worst idea for a combat system, and was luckily made better and engaging by the alchemy system/stat based rpg rules.
That said now there are different issues: it really feels unresponsive, with hitboxes out of this world and a lock on system that feels just wrong: forget ANYTHING you'd expect from Zelda's z-targeting, Devil may cry's dynamic lock on, or the smooth transitioning from the Souls games.
Because of this you're practically required (especially on harder difficulty settings) to take the perk that allows you to absorb partially backstab damages, since most of the times enemies will just flang in the general direction of your back, hitting 2 meters away from you but still dealing 200% extra damage.
Seriously: i've probably seen the game over screen around 10 times during my playthrough, and probably 9 of them were due to my lifebar being completely demolished in a single frame by an enemy that was standing meters away behind me.
Another big part of this serie is the alchemy system and now is...worse...far worse.
While in the first game alchemy was a dynamic tool that you had to strategically apply during combat now you can only drink your potions BEFORE combat happens, and since the effects last a very short time when compared to the first game, you practically have to know beforehand when and what enemy you'll have to fight in advance...aka most of the time save & reload is the only way to properly use the alchemy system.
2) while the controls of the first game worked pretty well but with the only option being mouse+keyboard this one works both with mouse+keyboard AND controllers..but half as good.
Thankfully i play using Playstation controllers instead of Xbox, so i was able to assign to the touchpad of my PS4 controller a lot more functions (like shortcuts for journal, inventory, map ecc) otherwise playing with a controller will feel incredibly clunky when having to use the ingame menus, and you'll have to scroll through 2-3 menus using 7-8 clicks for stuff that, in the first game, was simply done by opening a menu and clicking one thing.
3) These flaws apart be warned: this is a MUCH shorther game when compared to the first one, and that's because it is really focused on replayability (but it still is a Western rpg, so you'll probably need at least 25-30 hours to see just the main quest).
While the first installment had some instances of events the player could choose how to play, here you have entire levels/maps, characters, quests and entire storylines that play out based on not only on your choiches, but also how well you played (for example if you got defeated by an enemy, of if you fail to save someone, or if you got caught during a sneaking mission ecc)
4) Of course the visuals have been vastly made better, but i think that the real star of the show, is the voice acting (i've played with english voices + italian subtitles)
while the first game had some of the most robotic and unexpressive voice acting i've ever heard this time it is at least good...it may not be oscar worthy, but for a mid-market videogame that came out 6 years ago it's pretty good.
5) As Superbunnyhop said in it's essay, however, i consider The witcher games to be more interesting when they feel more like "Shrek" than "Game of thrones", because while the political intrigue is overall very intriguing, to me it was more of an excuse for world building and making it believable, but the most interesting aspects of the world is the mythology rather than it's "history", and the best parts of the first game were the retelling of european folklore-fairy tales being re arranged in a whole new world..which is far less present in this game, with the focus being almost entirely on politics which, again, i tended to consider more of a side argument
Overall i definitely reccomed to whoever is interested in these games to play them all in succession and, possibly, back to back, to really appreciate the improvements and remain completely into the story.
I'm now playing the third chapter, but i won't be able to review it since it is a GOG version, but i easily reccomend this game and it's predecessor..
I'll soon read not only the books, but also it's "rival" (Elric of Melnibornè) which allegedly The Witcher completely ripped off..and i can't wait
PS: edited..now that i've played the third chapter i have to say that the point i still find the most important is number 5...thankfully "the wild hunt" and it's expansions focused a lot more on folklore rather than raw politic, and it is one of the main aspects that made it my favorite game in the serie.

Playing as the United Aerospace Corporation I had the unique ability to deploy all troops and supplies to the field instantly through teleportation. This had worked in my favor until I found myself caught in between a firefight between Black Hand confessors and Combine Elites backed by several Hunters. The instant my forces were on the ground they were incinerated. My stubborness to admit defeat and simply wait for another opportunity to take the site got the best of me and my defenses were spread ridiculously thin. I had ended up taking the cliffsides but it was not even remotely worth the effort. I had an ample supply of brains to reclaim any territory that would be lost to the enemy, but no funds to supply them with backup and the ability to purchase new recruits. At the same time it was plain to see that with the Brotherhood of Nod sweeping across Combine territory and emerging victorious, they had no plans to halt their advance and give me time to save up the cash to produce an army powerful enough to turn the coming red tide. I had no choice but to perform an extremely stupid and desperate attack utilizing all the resources I had at that point against a single stronghold that Nod had dumped most of its cash in. If I could capture this territory I would kill off almost 50% of their units occupying the planet and also maybe gain the use of some Nod units as well.
It was not going well at first, but then I massed a large group of minigunners and rifleman together on a high ground overlooking their main fortress. It was crawling with infantry and surrounded by turrets, but due to the sheer number of rounds I was throwing at them everything above the surface was slowly obliterated by an advancing swarm of lead death.
Finally I was able to send in a modest amount of men armed with shotguns, chainguns and plasma rifles. I was slowly pushing their troops deeper and deeper into a retreat, forcing them to fall further back to the depths of their fortress, bottlenecking them. I had them. My initial strike force was getting weak, so I ordered them to continue onward without my direct interference. I produced another marine, this time armed with a BFG9000 and sent him in to finish the job. My men had managed to corner their brain at the very bottom of the base, but they were missing most of their legs and arms and couldn't land a shot. Their death would not be in vain. I fired the BFG directly at their brain and one second before it reached its target the game crashed.
War is hell.

In the far future, humanity sets out into space.  No longer held back by their fleshy bodies, they transfer their brains into jars, and send out robot clones to fight for territory on newly discovered worlds.  You are one of those brains, and you arrive on a planet in order to harvest it for its plentiful gold.  But you are not the only one searching for riches here.  Welcome to Cortex Command, a side-scrolling real-time strategy game from Data Realms.  This was one of the first games to try the “Early Access” style of development, where the developers sell an unfinished game to the public and allow them to download any updates for free.  Notch has commented that Cortex Command’s strategy was an inspiration for Minecraft’s development, and everyone knows how well that turned out.  Now, Early Access is a major feature of Steam sales and started a huge shift in games development, where the users directly interact with the devs as they create the game.  Cortex Command started all that, so let’s see what came of it.
In each scenario of Cortex Command, you will build an underground bunker to house your delicate brain while simultaneously attacking your enemy to destroy his brain.  You will do this by ordering bodies, weapons, and tools from the store, which are then delivered by dropship from an orbiting space station.  Take control of the bodies to command them directly, or issue them orders to stand lookout, charge forward, or dig for gold to power your economy.  All this takes place in procedurally-generated 2D levels, which look quite gorgeous.  The environment is fully destructible, and the physics are quite complex for an indie project.  Limbs will go flying after a rocket explodes, leaving body parts on the ground intermixed with all the guns and equipment, for the rest of the game.  Flying shrapnel pieces can actually injure or kill your clones and robots.  Jetpacks are difficult to control but can fly your guys across the map in no time.  The controls are comfortable once you get used to them, and you will quickly become adept at managing your little army of expendable bodies.
That is the simple explanation of this game.  It goes so much deeper.  You can take control of the dropship and use its thrusters to kill enemies in a fiery blaze.  You can pick up enemies’ guns off the ground and use them yourself.  You can tunnel beneath the enemy base to get around their carefully constructed defenses.  The situations and strategies you can employ are almost endless.  The store is chock-full of different options, and it can be overwhelming when you try to figure out what combination of stuff to use.  And that’s part of the problem here.  There is a short tutorial that explains basic mechanics, but there is no real learning curve.  The game doesn’t give you a real chance to explore its options slowly.  You are given everything upfront, with no real direction on where to go.  And what’s more, if you do choose a loadout at random and receive a delivery of useless equipment, now you have no money.  You’ll have to restart the mission and try again.  Not the best learning experience.  There are a number of specialized scenarios, which challenge you to survive with just a single unit while a horde of enemies bears down on you, or to defend a large base against waves of well-armed enemies.  These are good fun, and serve as decent ways to test out different equipment, even if none of what is going on is explained to you.
The cartoony visuals are quite entertaining, as bodies will explode violently and parts go flying.  Each faction’s dudes and weapons behave quite differently, but are relatively easy to tell apart once you learn who they are.  Exploring enemy bases and fighting your way through the unknown is a treat.  Every weapon has unique physics and sound effects, making it a neat experience experimenting with a newly discovered weapon to see how it behaves.  The bright colors and loud explosions just make the battles a fun time.
There is a lot of depth in this game, which works both for and against it.  Either you will fall in love with the systems and want to devote dozens of hours to exploring how they work, or you will get frustrated at the lack of direction and quit.  The game has an interesting campaign mode that plays out as a sort of planetary Risk, with you and each enemy brain committing funds to different sites on the planet to explore, attack, or defend, and battles occur when you both go after the same site.  Whoever has the most money at the end of the game wins.  I would have really liked a story mode that slowly introduces the complexity to you, instead of pushing you off the deep end without any guidance.
There is a good game underneath all the complexity!  I just do not have the time it requires to really get the most out of it.  Lively cartoonish graphics combined with fun gameplay give you a decent diversion, but there are better games for short-term enjoyment.  If you are looking for a long-term single-game RTS to play for the next decade, then give Cortex Command a shot.  Encouraging news is that the game is still being updated today, and Data Realms are constantly tweaking balance issues and adding new features.  There is also a strong community dedicated to modding the game.  This is a game you can invest a lot of time into and not run out of things to do!

Note: I've played well over 300 hours in this game offline and off-steam in the 5 years I've been playing.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys fun games with a bit of strategy.
Serving suggestion: This game is best served with a 3 gigabyte helping of mods. These can be found on the workshop.
GAMEPLAY
You play on a 2D sideview map usually with your brain and the enemy's brain having to dig gold and purchase different 'actors' to be delivered from orbit for you to use to attempt to destroy the enemy brain.
The physics in this game are very detailed and very important to winning. However, it may also be the thing that turns some people off. It makes movement feel somewhat 'heavy' and can be frustrating to get the hang of. But once you figure it out you'll be flying (yes everyone gets a jet pack) the body of your recently de-limbed trooper into the face of the enemy, hopefully decapitating them with the force... or maybe knocking the gun out of their hand... or the enemy might just laugh and shoot your face off.
All in all this style is easy to understand and very fun to execute due to the large amount of actors and equipment you can choose from. However some things like the grappling gun and repeller gun are not very useful or practical in normal games.
STORY
Not much here. We're a bunch of space brains with unlimited armies at our backs that are ready and willing to blast each other for gold.
GRAPHICS
The graphical style is wonderfuly done pixel art that isn't to pixely and is pixely enough it doesn't look cheap. It has just the right amount of detail to fantasticaly render every body part and machine piece as they explode and pile up on the map.
CONCLUSION
This is definently THE funnest game I have ever played in my life. The entertainment value is endless due to the active modding community and making mods yourself isn't that hard. It certainly won't disappoint if you can get used to the controls.

Weather Lord: The Successor's Path is Alawar Entertainment's most recent time management simulation game released to Steam and is a welcome entry to their casual game catalog here. Although the game play is very similar to other titles in the genre, I found it just as engaging and fun.
I've only recently gotten into time management games, and for the most part they all play pretty similarly: gather resources, construct buildings, beat the timer, etc. etc. However, Weather Lord feels a little more involved than the rest as there's quite a bit to keep track of between battling monsters, utilizing your weather tools efficiently and assisting NPCs, and that's on top of your standard gathering and building fare. The number of objectives for each stage is also quite high. Not that any of this is bad, but if you're like me and always aiming for perfection, you're going to need at least 2-3 tries on each level to snag gold, and some of those levels can be rather frustrating. One aspect I liked, however, is the ability to chain task your workers, and they'll often go from one job to the next without making a pit stop back at camp. I wish more time management games did this (maybe they do, but I just haven't played enough of them to know).
Presentation is very nice with beautifully drawn maps and character art, although the Prince needs to stop staring at me, it's like he's gazing into my soul with those eyes....::shivers:: Animated wildlife is a nice touch that gives each stage a bit of liveliness. The music is also quite nice, although not particularly memorable.
Once again, my biggest disappointment is the lack of Steam Achievements. In-game achievements are available, all they need is to be linked up to the Steam client. I'm not sure if there is an issue with the game engine being too difficult to program in the hooks, but casual games practically rely on Steam integration to add value on the platform; without them it just doesn't feel like you're getting as much out of the game as you could. And while trading cards are indeed nice, they only go so far.
All said, Weather Lord is a solid entry in the time management genre and definitely worth a look if you're a fan of these type of games. Despite proving a bit more difficult than I was expecting, it's an enjoyable title that will have me toiling hours away until I've snagged that very last gold star! Just don't let the Prince stare at you too long, he might steal your soul with that gaze. ;)
Bottom Line: Recommended for time management fans looking for a solid title to scratch that micro-managing itch.

Weather Lord: The Successor's Path is a casual action puzzle game with a time attack element. Game play is very similar to Rescue Team 1 (by the same publisher "BUKA Entertainment").  Your uncle has lost a sacred heirloom which has the ability to control the weather. You are required to assist with rescue and repair missions across the lands as you build houses, sawmills, lumber mills, foundries and other buildings. Along the way you will train or rescue workers to assist you. You will train brave knights to kill monsters and send workers to destroy monster lairs.
There are treasure chests which require keys, temples that need repair and mechanical devices that need to be repaired before rescuing innocent victims.  Along the way to expanding your search in the kingdom you will meet a variety of beasts and challenges.  You even have to bribe toads to allow you safe passage!
The art style is cartoon like and has a cute factor. The game plays perfectly at full HD 1080p resolutions.
The music is soft rock "laid back" midi sequenced.  Although repetitive sound loops are used the music is unobtrusive and pleasant easy listening. In game sounds are soft clinks and chinks and somewhat understated :)
Game play is fun and simple and gradually eases the player into more complex puzzle scenarios. Players can re-select any previously completed stage should they feel they could improve on their score or time performance.  Completing all the objectives except one and ignoring the time restraint, the player can use workers to collect additional resources or just adopt a lazy sandbox approach but to get a good score players will need to beat the timer bar at the top right of the screen.
This game will appeal to young children and to adults who enjoy casual games. There is only low key cartoon fighting with no blood or gore, so the game is family friendly. This game and "Rescue Team 1" as well as "The Promised Land" would be great first additions to a young players game library.
Weather Lord: The Successor's Path will provide many hours of stress free casual gaming and leave the player feeling relaxed and happy. The game is extremely well thought out and almost bug free (unlike some disappointing AAA titles).  The game did crash and lock up while attempting to take a screenshot as a level was completed, but progress had been saved automatically making it possible to resume play at next start up.
The biggest benefit of this game is the small file size (under 180Mb) which is small even compared to patches or updates of many games. So if you are one of the laptop casual gamers pressed for space this is the game for you!
This game is less complex and less demanding than "The Promised Land" but is fun to play.
Weather Lord: The Successor's Path automatically tracks progress of each player name registered and so there is no need for a Game Save feature. This is a great benefit as a player can easily resume from where they were the next time they open the game without having to remember to save.
Weather Lord: The Successor's Path is a great casual time-waster and at the price is good value for money (especially if it is on discount).  A fun game especially for the younger gamer age 4 to 10 but parents will need to accompany the child if the child's reading skill is not up to scratch yet.
