Deus Ex, how to describe it.  It's been lauded as one of the best games ever made, standing alongside giants such as Ultima 7, XCom, Planescape, Zelda: OOT, Half Life 2, and others.  It sits on many best ever lists alongside whatever interactive media you enjoy.  What is it about this game which makes me and others say, "You must play it."
To start with the bad, the graphics were horrible, even for the standards of 1999 when it was released.  We were playing Unreal Tournament and Tribes II back then and they looked nowhere near as bad as Deus Ex did.  It wasn't even done as an artistic choice as you'd see some Indy projects do nowadays.  I remember it as one of the most terrible looking games of the time period.  The audio was also sometimes choppy.  It all reflects the long development time Ion Storm spent making this game as the technology went out of date and they kept making the game instead of worrying about their graphical engine.  The voice acting was monotone and sometimes phoned in.
The control scheme was an unintuitive mess.  Enemy AI was dumb with next to no field of vision unless they were shooting at you, then the bullets and their insanely good accuracy overcame their stupidity.  Those last two combined together to make this more of a stealth game than a shooting game or at least a shoot people in the back of the head game.
The game still went out of its way to encourage customization, what augmentations you use, what skills you focus on, what upgrades you get on your weapons.  All of this defined your character, poor shooting skill translated into a big aiming reticle and gun sway while aiming, lockpicking and computers determined the level of doors and computers you could break open.  Your augs chose how well you were specced at doing specific things, picking up large objects, running fast, health regeneration, invisibility, you were given two choices and could take one or the other knowing you would lose access to those abilities.  Inventory space was also a premium so you were thinking about your loadout, what weapon upgrades you got on the weapons you liked, how much space it all took up and how much more junk you could hold when you searched through an area.
You could still theoretically spec out to be a front door smashing robo-cop even if it was not the most optimal choice.  You could be an invisible sneaky thief type.  You could be a melee assassin, a sniper, or whatever you liked.  There were always several ways to tackle objectives, you could climb on the roof and go in through a roof access, sneak in a vent shaft, set a bunch of mines outside the front door, blow up the front door, and pick off the guards as they run out.  The areas were big and level of freedom you had to just do whatever was intoxicating.
The story was also something which would grab you.  You may be a new nano-augmented cyber soldier, but you're still a pawn being passed around between factions, until you slowly discover what's going on and what to do about it.  And the way you discover all of this draws you into the game, finding notes, emails, things in desks, on the bodies of people you shoot, until you piece together one conspiracy after another.
There are choices you make and they are meaningful, they also try hard not to present themselves to you as a choice at the time and more as the consequences of an earlier action.  As an example, I didn't know it was even possible to save your brother while he's being attacked by an army of super agents until I tried and succeeded, then something different happened later.
I'm probably missing over a lot of what this game does right to recommend investing your time in playing it.  All I can say is that it was one of the best games I've played and replayed and I can't recommend it enough.

I really wanted to love this game.  I love the other Paradox titles I've played (EU4, CK2, Vicky2).  My love of 4x space games goes back to my first computer (a tsr 80).  You can imagine my excitement when I heard Paradox was doing a 4x game.
I went in knowing and having little problem with the Paradox model: release a fun if feature sparse game, then expand and add depth through dlc.  I think with Stellaris, though, Paradox forgot the "fun" part. I also feel that they took advantage of people willing to be patient for new dlc to expand features, and released something unacceptably incomplete.  It feels more like a proof of concept of a 4x space framework, waiting for the game to be applied.  That may not be completely fair, as the game is polished and stable, but every feature leaves me feeling like they ran out of time before being able to add the fun bits.
Speaking of fun, this is pretty subjective, but for me the galaxy is flavorless.  Alien races and space monsters feel like placeholders.  The alien races especially feel completely randomized and uninteresting. Ship art is also non-distinct or interesting. The spacemonsters feel like research pinatas, waiting for a strong enough fleet to bash them open.
Oh and now we come to my least favorite part of the game, fleets, or as I have come to call them: Giant Stupid Space Blobs (GSSB hereafter).  Gather up all your ships, put them into a single fleet, and run around mushing smaller GSSB's - err fleets.  There is no tactical decision.  Splitting your fleet is just asking for an enemy to use a GSSB and mush your smaller fleets piecemeal.  Also, in addition to lack of tactical depth, the animation of one GSSB fighting another GSSB is so awful that it isn't even accidentally humorous.  A combination of techs and admiral traits and skill should limit the maximum fleet size, and that leads to another problem...
Techs.  I love what they're trying to do here with a treeless system and having rares and super rares, I really do.  For some reason though, it just doesn't work.  I end up getting every tech by the end of the game, and no matter what I choose it really doesn't seem to have a big impact on the feel of the game.  Every empire I play feels pretty much like any other empire I play.  Again, no funsy.
As far as game completeness, I give you: The Sector.  Sectors were an attempt to make large sprawling empires both more controlable and also expand more slowly by limited the number of star systems directly controlable by the player.  I love the idea.  But again, they missed on completeness and funness.  As your empire grows, you will hit a hard coded limit (modable) on the number of stars your empire can directly control.  Once you hit this limit you can transfer control of a star system to one or more sectors that you define. I was hoping these would be semi-autonomous entities similar in scope to EU4 client states. They could automate to manage and defend themselves as an independent vassal, while kicking up a percentage of their labor to the parent empire, maybe based on tax rate, tech, etc.
Unfortunately sectors are nowhere near this automated.  They end up being an arbitrary mechanic with no real gain for the player. You can't even change the color of the sector on the map for easy identification.  It's just a heartbreaking reminder of what could have been if the game were a little more complete.
Unfortunately, the heartbreak of sectors is a pattern that plays out over and over through the game experience.  Early game is fun enough while you do early exploration and expansion, but any sense of fun and wonder disappears by mid-game.
I'll definitely be interested in what new patches and dlc add, but I'll most certainly be taking a look before I leap approach.  I expected better of Paradox, and got let down.

This game is basically Sins of a Solar Empire meets Master of Orion 2.  The ship building tools are greatly simplified in one sense, but there is still plenty of customization.  Deep tech trees, and even though you will eventually see tech again (Unlike MOO2), the uncertainty of when makes the tech system feel very like Orion's to me. Each choice leaves you with that small feeling of loss at those other pretties you couldn't have.  Add in modern sensibilities that clean up the interfaces and streamline play and there you have it, Stellaris.
Diplomacy is something I'm still mastering, and I'm a little sad at the lack of durable trade or science agreements of some sort.  That being said, between the options that exist and the policies you can enable there is a lot you can do with it.  And the war system is far better than the typical 4x smash and grab option.  You can actually fight a defensive war and achieve goals, like embarassing your opponent and weaking their ability to influence events themselves later...not to mention the men and materiel....
Overall, an amazing 4x if you're a fan of the genre, with lots of care and effort put into creating real depth.  And at the time of writing this, the Dev team is very clearly not done releasing content, most of it free.

Nex Machina has earned its place as my favorite bullet hell shmup. It’s an extremely well-crafted game eager to blow your pants off with intense, frantic action. However, I must state that the game can seem overwhelming with the differences between difficulties. In fact, I think anything beyond “Experienced” will be impossible for me, but you can and do improve over time.
This game has a committed arcade design philosophy. You have numerous difficulties, different modes including co-op (with shared lives), and leaderboards for everything. The game’s Arena mode offers credits based on in-game performance used to customize your character and will occasionally throw challengers at you whose score you have to beat in order to continue growing your profile level. I definitely recommend playing some Arena so that you can purchase the bullet color that stands out the most to you if the default isn’t working out. I went with yellow which helped me process the visual information on the screen.
Single World allows you master an area, but Arcade mode is the one that puts you through the entire gauntlet. Each world only takes around 7 minutes for me to complete and there are up to 6 worlds if you play on Experienced. Rookie has 5. What keeps me coming back for me is the desire to achieve mastery due to how the game encourages an incredibly dangerous dance to keep your combo up and the fierce action constantly keeping me on the edge of my seat. You’re a very fragile being. One hit will kill you unless you’re able to collect a shield and you’re doing your best to evade hundreds of enemies and projectiles in every world.
Every world is broken into small levels. Some of those levels contain secrets which involve hidden humans to save, hidden multipliers to help build up your score, extra lives to keep you in the fight instead of using a continue, hidden targets, and secret entrances that take you to another level filled with humans to save and enemies to kill. In addition to the secrets and trying to stay alive against the relentless onslaught, you’re also trying to build up not one, but two combo meters. You have the regular score multiplier that you build up by killing regular enemies, special enemies, or finding them in the level. It doesn’t decay or go down unless you die and use up a life. You also can consider building up the human combo which works by saving a human, waiting for the combo meter to decay, and then saving another human which is very difficult to consistently do since you’re juggling so much information at once. You have to risk it to get the biscuit though and human combos are necessary to racking up huge points to make your friends look bad.
You don’t have to worry about it too much if you’re just trying to beat a higher difficulty and leaving the high score attempts for later. In fact, there are Feats (sorta like in-game achievements) for avoiding all the humans in a world. Don’t feel too overwhelmed and stick with Rookie for a while. Learn the placement of the secrets and enemy patterns before attempting the harder settings, I say.
Oh right, power-ups. They contribute to your overall effectiveness in different ways and dying means dropping one on the ground which you’ll probably want to collect. You’ll frequently encounter Triple Dash, Dash Explosion, Shield, Weapon Range, and Weapon Spread. Having all five at once grants you the 5-projectile spread shot instead of the 3-shot version with 4 out of 5 power-ups. There are also special weapon pick-ups with the Rocket Launcher being my favorite. Your controls involve moving with left stick, shooting with right stick, dashing with LB or L-Trigger, and using your special weapon with RB or R-Trigger. I highly recommend using a controller.
Whew, when you’re not in the zone and super focused on avoiding the cold embrace of death, you might notice the great soundtrack. Every song seems well done and fun to listen to while blasting baddies away. The neon colors also help immerse you in the retro-arcade design of the entire game. It looks good, sounds good (except for weapons which are understated a bit, but is still okay), and plays well.
Again, this game can be extremely difficult on the higher difficulties because faster enemies means faster reflexes are required and sometimes my brain can’t keep up. You can also find yourself in a situation where your run might be over because you’re caught in a death loop against a boss (remember, you lose power-ups on death and continues). It can be weirdly satisfying to take down a boss with just your basic gun and a special weapon, but that did take me around 17 continues which each one having three lives. The 6th boss didn’t even have a weapon to pick up though in its room and I just had to back out at that point. Make Rookie your best friend if you’re new to the genre or aren’t hardcore before making bold difficulty choices.
Still, I love this game very much. It’s my favorite of the genre and I recommend it with two thumbs up. It’s one of the few games that I’ll leave installed indefinitely because I know I’ll be shooting down thousands of more baddies in the future.

I bought this game right after it came out mostly because of the glowing reviews that it received on many of the game review websites plus it was inexpensive. It still has a Very Positive overall ranking here on Steam but buyer beware, you may not be able to play this game.
My system meets all the recommended requirements and then some however the game is basically unplayable for me and for many others. If you check the Community Discussion you will see the main stickied thread plus many others from users like myself who cannot play this game at all or beyond the first level, let alone compete in the arena season. The game will crash immediately on loading a level or after completing the first level every time.
The problem seems to be related to those who still use Windows 7 not any specific hardware. I personally did not refund because immediately after the game was released the developer, Housemarque, was aware of the problem and attempted to fix it with a few hotfixes and one main patch. Unfortunately these quick fixes did not resolve the issue and those of us who waited for them to fix it without refunding were left waiting.
We're still waiting..
Three weeks since release and after a few attempts to fix the problem failed, the developer has apparently stopped supporting the game. Less than a month after release there have been no responses or developer support for the game since July 17, 2017 other than to say they are on holiday and still monitoring the problem. They have not provided any information on their discussion or news page and have apparently stopped trying or are unable to fix their game for Windows 7 users even though it is still listed as a supported OS.
The game (what I have gotten to play of it) is a fast paced, fun twin stick acrade shooter. Perhaps one of the best in a long while but that is also what makes it so frustrating for those who cannot play. I gave them the benefit of the doubt because in the beginning they were making attempts to resolve the problem but that support seemed to end about the same time as the refund period did. If you can play the game on your system then I would recommend it however with the way the situation has played out and the developer ceasing to communicate through Steam in over a month, I can only recommend you buy to try.. and be prepared to refund quickly if you're one of the ones for whom it does not work.
This is definitely a case of Caveat Emptor and a reminder to research the Community Discussion of a game before you purchase.
Update: A new patch was released 8/25/2017 that added a new language and a new leaderboard season but no fixes.

9 Dragons is an oldschool asian MMORPG grinder, where by joining one of the six possible clans and selecting your role inside the clan you try to become a master of Kung-Fu.
Since I played this game back at release on different publishers and invested overall way more than 500 hours into this game, I can surely tell that the story behind Nine Dragons is great. It has been writen by one of the famous chinese novel kung-fu authors. It is quite fun to read the story behind each of the clans, why the game is actually called "Nine Dragons" and how the conflicts between the clans were created. Sadly, besides the story the gameplay part is a bit dull. Playing melee characters you use mostly auto-hit skills where you just have to select a monster. Playing ranged characters you have to be a bit more active training multiple skills. To be able to reach anything in this game you will have to spend hours upon hours grinding, just as in most of the oldschool asian MMORPGs. The dungeons existing in this game have no values besides the absolute last one.
The combat is done by targeting someone with a mouse and then either attacking the person/mob with auto-hit skills or by using some ranged spells for certain classes. Sadly, the gear decides about everything in this game and that gear can be improved a lot by Cash Shop. Yes, you heard right - Cash Shop gives you direct stats and advantage in battles, making this game heavy Pay2Win. The current Publisher RedFox started it well without implementing any unbalancing items, sadly gone down the way of implementing heavy Pay2Win down the road, which made the servers drop most of their activity and population. The community of 9Dragons has just been too many times through Pay2Win Cash Shop publishers and since nowadays there are too many better alternatives, only nostalgia of "brain-afk-grinding" brings some people back from time to time.
The graphic is really aged and has not been graphically updated since 2006. There are some landscapes and dungeons that look still somewhat unique and cool, especially due to the ancient chinese style of the game, but dont expect any eye candies out of a game from beginning of the century.
As explained above, the progress is based on 90% grinding, 9% gearing up and both are heavily connected to the Cash Shop. For better experience you need the so called "Premium Buff" and the "Exp Cards" that increase your experience gain by high multiplicator numbers. For gearing up you need to invest either years of ingame time to grind up enough money to buy Cash Shop items from other players (still Cash Shop involved) or buy them yourself for hundreds of dollars. There are some mini-games on level ups that I always enjoyed and it would be cool to see similar mechanics as "Chi Breathing" in other games.
The audio and the immersion of the game are actually still great. There are multiple different sound tracks that still sound real well in this ancient asian tone, the effects of the game fit the Kung-Fu style of the game while the immersion while traveling the land and your clan is great since clans are totally different from each other.
Nine Dragons has still a core community and a lot of players keep coming back even after a while no matter how heavy Pay2Win the current publisher is, that already speaks that the game is actually good and offers nostalgia for most of players, however judged by modern standards it is aged and not recommended for any new players due to massive amount of much better alternatives. Some oldschool grinders might find its way due to nostalgia feelings, however anyone new should not wasted their time on it.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Deus Ex, how to describe it.  It's been lauded as one of the best games ever made, standing alongside giants such as Ultima 7, XCom, Planescape, Zelda: OOT, Half Life 2, and others.  It sits on many best ever lists alongside whatever interactive media you enjoy.  What is it about this game which makes me and others say, "You must play it."
To start with the bad, the graphics were horrible, even for the standards of 1999 when it was released.  We were playing Unreal Tournament and Tribes II back then and they looked nowhere near as bad as Deus Ex did.  It wasn't even done as an artistic choice as you'd see some Indy projects do nowadays.  I remember it as one of the most terrible looking games of the time period.  The audio was also sometimes choppy.  It all reflects the long development time Ion Storm spent making this game as the technology went out of date and they kept making the game instead of worrying about their graphical engine.  The voice acting was monotone and sometimes phoned in.
The control scheme was an unintuitive mess.  Enemy AI was dumb with next to no field of vision unless they were shooting at you, then the bullets and their insanely good accuracy overcame their stupidity.  Those last two combined together to make this more of a stealth game than a shooting game or at least a shoot people in the back of the head game.
The game still went out of its way to encourage customization, what augmentations you use, what skills you focus on, what upgrades you get on your weapons.  All of this defined your character, poor shooting skill translated into a big aiming reticle and gun sway while aiming, lockpicking and computers determined the level of doors and computers you could break open.  Your augs chose how well you were specced at doing specific things, picking up large objects, running fast, health regeneration, invisibility, you were given two choices and could take one or the other knowing you would lose access to those abilities.  Inventory space was also a premium so you were thinking about your loadout, what weapon upgrades you got on the weapons you liked, how much space it all took up and how much more junk you could hold when you searched through an area.
You could still theoretically spec out to be a front door smashing robo-cop even if it was not the most optimal choice.  You could be an invisible sneaky thief type.  You could be a melee assassin, a sniper, or whatever you liked.  There were always several ways to tackle objectives, you could climb on the roof and go in through a roof access, sneak in a vent shaft, set a bunch of mines outside the front door, blow up the front door, and pick off the guards as they run out.  The areas were big and level of freedom you had to just do whatever was intoxicating.
The story was also something which would grab you.  You may be a new nano-augmented cyber soldier, but you're still a pawn being passed around between factions, until you slowly discover what's going on and what to do about it.  And the way you discover all of this draws you into the game, finding notes, emails, things in desks, on the bodies of people you shoot, until you piece together one conspiracy after another.
There are choices you make and they are meaningful, they also try hard not to present themselves to you as a choice at the time and more as the consequences of an earlier action.  As an example, I didn't know it was even possible to save your brother while he's being attacked by an army of super agents until I tried and succeeded, then something different happened later.
I'm probably missing over a lot of what this game does right to recommend investing your time in playing it.  All I can say is that it was one of the best games I've played and replayed and I can't recommend it enough.

This game could have been something special, but it is clear it was unfinished, rushed to release and then abandoned, so that work could be started with the sequel.  It is a shame when you consider the potential.  The gameplay starts out being fun, but quickly you are forced to notice a deliberate lack of polish.  The cut scenes look like something from a high school class.  Much of the game and the "story" felt uninspired.  The skill tree did not give meaningful choices.  You will notice more if you play the game yourself.  It's all the little things that add up and kill.
The main issue for me was there were tons of bugs and desynchronization issues that soured enjoyment.  Some bugs include characters disappearing from the screen, permanently losing items and weapons that took a while to build, quest tracking issues forcing you to guess the way, and game pausing constantly for lag in the middle of battles.  It leaves you feeling frustrated because you cannot seem to go more than 5-10 minutes without encountering a bug, especially when they impede your progress for the umpteenth time that session.  There was a breaking point that I reached where I just got tired of dealing with it all and just decided to finish the game, forgoing the rest of the DLC and side quests.
I will mention that I played this strictly coop and I wonder if part of the problem we experienced was due to lag from one of us being in Europe and the other in the US.  We have played tons of games together in the past and it is definitely not the norm for connection issues to be as bad as this game.
With the game beaten I feel like I can say that I gave it a fair shot, but I do not recommend it.  I might increase the recommendation to a maybe if you would try it singleplayer or if your coop partner does not live over seas AND the price is around a buck or two.  But I cannot justify encouraging the devs, so I am not recommending the game and I am staying away from purchasing the sequel.

I really wanted to love this game.  I love the other Paradox titles I've played (EU4, CK2, Vicky2).  My love of 4x space games goes back to my first computer (a tsr 80).  You can imagine my excitement when I heard Paradox was doing a 4x game.
I went in knowing and having little problem with the Paradox model: release a fun if feature sparse game, then expand and add depth through dlc.  I think with Stellaris, though, Paradox forgot the "fun" part. I also feel that they took advantage of people willing to be patient for new dlc to expand features, and released something unacceptably incomplete.  It feels more like a proof of concept of a 4x space framework, waiting for the game to be applied.  That may not be completely fair, as the game is polished and stable, but every feature leaves me feeling like they ran out of time before being able to add the fun bits.
Speaking of fun, this is pretty subjective, but for me the galaxy is flavorless.  Alien races and space monsters feel like placeholders.  The alien races especially feel completely randomized and uninteresting. Ship art is also non-distinct or interesting. The spacemonsters feel like research pinatas, waiting for a strong enough fleet to bash them open.
Oh and now we come to my least favorite part of the game, fleets, or as I have come to call them: Giant Stupid Space Blobs (GSSB hereafter).  Gather up all your ships, put them into a single fleet, and run around mushing smaller GSSB's - err fleets.  There is no tactical decision.  Splitting your fleet is just asking for an enemy to use a GSSB and mush your smaller fleets piecemeal.  Also, in addition to lack of tactical depth, the animation of one GSSB fighting another GSSB is so awful that it isn't even accidentally humorous.  A combination of techs and admiral traits and skill should limit the maximum fleet size, and that leads to another problem...
Techs.  I love what they're trying to do here with a treeless system and having rares and super rares, I really do.  For some reason though, it just doesn't work.  I end up getting every tech by the end of the game, and no matter what I choose it really doesn't seem to have a big impact on the feel of the game.  Every empire I play feels pretty much like any other empire I play.  Again, no funsy.
As far as game completeness, I give you: The Sector.  Sectors were an attempt to make large sprawling empires both more controlable and also expand more slowly by limited the number of star systems directly controlable by the player.  I love the idea.  But again, they missed on completeness and funness.  As your empire grows, you will hit a hard coded limit (modable) on the number of stars your empire can directly control.  Once you hit this limit you can transfer control of a star system to one or more sectors that you define. I was hoping these would be semi-autonomous entities similar in scope to EU4 client states. They could automate to manage and defend themselves as an independent vassal, while kicking up a percentage of their labor to the parent empire, maybe based on tax rate, tech, etc.
Unfortunately sectors are nowhere near this automated.  They end up being an arbitrary mechanic with no real gain for the player. You can't even change the color of the sector on the map for easy identification.  It's just a heartbreaking reminder of what could have been if the game were a little more complete.
Unfortunately, the heartbreak of sectors is a pattern that plays out over and over through the game experience.  Early game is fun enough while you do early exploration and expansion, but any sense of fun and wonder disappears by mid-game.
I'll definitely be interested in what new patches and dlc add, but I'll most certainly be taking a look before I leap approach.  I expected better of Paradox, and got let down.

Anyway, I recommend this game to anyone who likes RPGs, humor, and playing with friends. If you like Call of Duty and Horror games, you might not enjoy this one.

They don't make games like this anymore. It is exceptionally well-written in every single detail. At first it's funny how it manages to incorporate all the popular conspiracy theories, and it becomes frightening when
. The way people are kept in line with constant terror alert, the shoot-on-sight cops, and the artificial plague is a very dark vision of the future, but the events since the release of the game suggest that it may be prophetic.
The role-playing elements, and the non-linear and fully interactive environment provide lots of freedom to the player: in every playthrough one can find new ways to complete an objective and discover new details hidden in unexpected places. It is advised to talk to every NPC for several rounds, because almost all of them have something interesting and potentially useful thing to say. Mirrors are rarely found in games for some reason, but, interestingly, in this one they are abundant (check yourself in a mirror to see how bad the character animation is). If you can ignore the outdated graphics and the weak voice acting, you get the best PC gaming experience ever created.
The music is also noteworthy, Straylight Productions composed another perfect soundtrack after their previous work in Unreal. It's interesting to compare the cover image of this game and its sequels: this one shows the moment of enlightenment, while the others show aggressive thugs.
If you liked the game, check out The Nameless Mod as well.

Short and sweet Summary:
The opening is badass and I'd kill to see a mini-cartoon series on it.  This is ONLY a local co-op game, I think the game devs may have misunderstood the steam classification for Multi-player / co-op (online play).
The game has a lot of potential (excellent concept) and looks good, but falls short in game play; specifically around weapon strength and what's randomly given to you as you pick up donuts.  As a single player game, I cannot recommend this.   I wish I could, because the concept and a lot of the level design mechanics are excellent, but ultimately the ineffectivness of the majority of weapons vs. the toughness and number scaling of the enemy really kills the fun factor for me as a player.
The Full Review:
The opening intro was amazing, absolutely blew me away!  Made me excited to play.  Hell, I want to see it come out as a comic or a picture book that I can read to my kid.  The art style is cute, but fits the world and the story perfectly and reminds me of the Worms World Party game or even Bubble Bobble...
...but then I got into the actual menu system and game play.
Game Functions / Menu Issues:
This game doesn't appear to have a true online multiplayer mode to it (which is typically what the steam indicator for Multi-player and co-op means, rather than local co-op).   You have an option to pick one or two player, and when you select two player it asks for you to connect another controller to the computer.
Hitting escape at any point while the game is open will just shut down the game and put you back at your desktop (actually I kinda like this feature, except for the time I manged to bug myself on a level and couldn't die / move / end the level).
Sound controls are either on or off, there's no decreasing unless you simply lower the volume of your computer audio (just a heads up for youtubers, you'll probably have to edit the game audio to be a LOT softer in post production)
Game Play:
There's only 3 levels, which isn't necessarily a bad thing if there's a high replay value to each match, however even after half an hour of learning how to play, I couldn't get past the first level, or even survive past the first minute and a half.
There was one main reasons for this:
The game is steadily increasing the number of bugs that spawn and it increases quickly.  By about 45 seconds in, you have an almost constant line of bugs (and frequently spawning rocket-launching trash cans) that's impossible to dodge, you have to shoot them with the weapons you get from picking up donuts.   This wouldn't be a problem except every time you pick up a donut (which is needed to score) you are given a different weapon.  Frequently this weapon will be a pistol or shotgun which requires multiple shots at that level to kill a single bug and the continual stream makes it impossible to do so, which means you end up getting murdered pretty quick and have to start the level over again.
The dev's tried to offset this by giving you a store where you can buy one-use items such as pipe bombs or shields and such, which costs donuts.  So you use the donuts you collected from grinding through the level to help you try to advance to the next stage.  While I've seen that work in other games, this one it doesn't really go over well because the items cost so much (cheapest item is 15-25 donuts) that it feels more like a grind to get the one use items and then if I don't use them effecitvely I'm back to square one.
You can also unlock new weapons through replaying the level and collecting more donuts and killing more bugs.  By my 14th run through the first level I managed to unlock the rocket launcher which does massive damage and helps manage those hordes of insects that start spawning like mad, but again, the next time I picked up a donut, I was back to being stuck with a shotgun or pistol that sucked so bad that I just get killed.  Two-player is a little more managable, but it still feels more like a grind than that of a really fun game.
I'm disappointed because I really want to like this game.  The premise is awesome and I want to find out more about what happened, but I can't bring myself to play the same level over and over again where I don't feel like I'm really making any progress.  I'm definitely going to keep an eye on this dev, because I think he has some great ideas and with a little more development/balancing of game mechanics he'll make some amazing things.

What an awesome game.
I havent played Metal Gear Solid Games before, so this is just an opinion without a comparison to other games in the franchise.
The GREAT Things:
- Exciting, fast paced combat that makes you feel like the most badass cyborg ninja ever to exist
- Includes very practical and satisfying concept to replenish health and collect bonuses
- Beautifuly rendered cutscenes that are worthy of a Hollywood action blockbuster (comic relief and philosophy included)
- Exhilarating Boss Battles, with rapid techno music, that will push your adrenaline levels to peak
- A story that is as straightforward as it is over the top and has some very well rounded interesting characters (especially Raiden)
- Full controller support (Highly recommended)
The ANNOYING Things:
- When close to walls, the camera tends to spin unnecessary sometimes
- Some boss attacks are occasionally hard to anticipate and react to
- I found one of the characters annoying (my personal opinion)
These thing however were never a deal-breaker and didnt stop me from enjoying the hell out of the game.

EDIT: I realized that this version also inlcudes 2 small DLC stories for 2 different side characters, each with its own new cutscenens and boss battles. While they are not as great as the main game, they are definetly worth checking out, as they add to the story and introduce some interesting new abilities.
This game is the first in a long time to get me heavily invested in the main character and the story, as well as entertaining me with great exciting gameplay along the way. It also made me want to play more Metal Gear Solid games, even though I can imagine none will quite be like this.
Highly recommended.

9 Dragons is a game that has gone through many changes and publishers since 2006. I have followed it from the early days from when it was published by Acclaim to present day where it is now published by RedFox Games. What a journey it has been. I’ve played it off and on since 2007 until I finally quit in early 2014.
Do I recommend this game to new players? No. Stay far away from this.
Not only is this game a grind fest, it also is heavily pay to win. If you look at the item mall, you will quickly see that you need to spend at least a few hundred dollars just to be mildly competitive. I put at least 5,000 hours into this game and I regret a lot of them. It was a fun game back in 2007-08, but it has gone nowhere but downhill since then.
The mechanics in place are designed so that players are compelled to spend money in the item mall if they want to stand a chance against other players or even be strong enough to complete higher level content. This is even further enforced by the strong gambling mechanics built into the game. If you want to refine your clothing or weapons (gives a nice stat boost), then you must risk losing them after refining them to a certain level. The crafting in this game is generally focused on success rate percentages. Some items have a 100% chance to make them. Other items have less than a 1% chance to make.  You can purchase things in the item mall that mitigates the risk of losing your precious gear.
This brings up a pay to win element. Being able to sell item mall items in the game severely disrupts the game economy and favors those who are willing to spend hundreds in the item mall. You would think that the item mall would at least be fairly cheap if the game requires it right? Prepare to spend hundreds of dollars just to have a chance at decent gear. Even the item mall is built around gambling with things like boxes which give you random items when you open them. They aren’t cheap either and you could literally spend thousands and not get anything worthwhile from them.
Even if you look past all of those negatives and see what the game has to offer, you won’t find much. Besides endless grinding; there are a bunch of fetch quests that don’t really give you much for your time. The combat is hot bar based and uses a unique active skill system where your character performs a set of animations depending on the active skill being used.
The story itself is mildly interesting the first time you play through it, but it isn’t much different for each clan in the game. The maps themselves are small and the graphics are extremely dated. The game does has a sort of charm to it though. Something about the whole package is appealing at a first glance. It will be fun and interesting at first, but it quickly grows tiring and you’ll find yourself playing for the next level instead of having fun.
TL;DR? It's just another grind focused Korean MMORPG that reached its peak about 8 years ago. Only play if you are a grind junkie and like old school MMOs.

What is SPACEPLAN?
SPACEPLAN is a story-driven incremental game (also often called Idle or - in my opinion wrongly - Clicker game). The player explores the solar system by using the usual mechanics of incremental games - that is, clicking a bit at the beginning, buying things, buying more things with the money generated, etc.
The storyline is interesting.
There are a few times where waiting for big sums is necessary, following the typical Idle style, while clicking is optional but increases the resources gained, which are measured in Joule - or, if you desire so, in kcal.
After building your armada of potato buildings, you eventually reach a story point, and here the game got my attention. The second half of the game plays almost identical to the first part - i.e. idling or buying things - but the story advances until it reaches a climax, after which the game is over. The final cutscene can be replayed, alternatively the save deleted and started anew. New Game Plus, Resetting for more gains, etc. do not exist here - so after the around three hours long experience there is really no reason to play on, which is kind of sad.
Gameplay wise, there is certainly not much unique - it is almost a typical incremental game - and the most unique thing would be a minor spoiler. There is a kind of building that does something when bought in the second part of the game.
More unique than that gameplay bit is the graphics and storyline. The graphics are to a degree an integral part of the experience, as you probe different planets. Sadly, there is not much of an exploration aspect other than flying from here to there and experiencing the story.
I had the sound and music turned off, as I always do for this kind of games, so I can't say much about it here. The soundtrack is available for purchase on the Steam Store, and it has one positive review without any others, where it is called "incredible", but I haven't heard it yet personally, so I can't vow for it.
Overall, the game was a nice experience to have, and I do not regret playing it. If it justifies the asking price is however left to how much you are willing to invest for a three hours experience that you already know how to play.
Recommended: Neutral, as it is a paid game and even on a sale it is up to you to decide if you are willing to pay for this genre. There apparently is an early browser version, so you might want to find that and check it first. As there is no neutral option, I will click "Yes", as clicking "No" would be completely unjustified, seeing that I enjoyed the game. If there wasn't a plethora of free incremental games, I would recommend it for 1.50€ or less.

In my quest to find a good game to play and spend some quality time on, I’ve gone through several which just haven’t made the cut. I have talked about two of those games (FFXIV and Battlefield: Bad Company 2) and their problems in my past articles in
. However, I am happy to report that I have finally found a game that I can enjoy and really sink some time into. This game is not, as you may think, one of the visually stunning, HD-rendered masterpieces of the modern era (though Driver: San Francisco is pretty good), but instead, is a PC title from the year 2000—a game where you could probably count the polygons in the characters’ faces. This game that I speak of is none other than Deus Ex.
The first thing I noticed when I started playing Deus Ex was how the game played depended heavily on the choices I made. Before the gameplay even started, I was asked to select skills from an array of possible specializations, from lockpicking and hacking to light and heavy arms. Much to my delight, I discovered as I progressed through the game that most objectives could be completed in many different ways, and I was never required to have a certain proficiency in any one skill in order to continue. You could specialize any way you want, and still be able to play the whole game (unless you specialize in Swimming and Environmental Resistance; that’s just dumb).
Deus Ex’s gameplay varies based on how you specialize, so how I experienced it (as a hacking-, lockpicking-, and generally non-confrontationally-specialized player) may differ from how you experience it. I spent most of my time picking locked doors, circumventing security systems, and skirting around guards, rather than running and gunning. When I was forced to disable an enemy, I either took them out from afar (either with a rifle or tranq dart), or knocked them out with a riot prod. However, I spent as much, if not more, time observing the movements of guards or security bots, in order to avoid such confrontations as much as possible.
Another aspect of Deus Ex that I was very happy about was its plot. In this game, the plot is integral to the gameplay—any objective the player is given is directly involved in driving the plot forward. Many times, I found myself thinking, “Even if the game didn’t name that as my next objective, I would probably still be doing it.” This allows the game’s story to take a linear path, even though the game’s environments are generally open. Also, in conjunction with the ability to complete missions in various ways, different characters will treat you differently based on how you play. Certain characters will like you if you take a more covert approach, whereas others might share your fondness of busting in the front door with guns blazing.
Finally, for those of you who plan on playing this game after hearing what I’ve had to say, I’ll just say a few words about the game’s difficulty settings, so you don’t have to scratch your head at them for too long. This game features the three standard difficulty settings, plus a “Realistic” mode. “Realistic” means that the enemies have the same amount of health as you do, and they take the same kind of damage you do (armor and augmentations notwithstanding). This mode works great for stealth players, as you can quickly take out a stray guard if they spot you, but majorly botch an intrusion attempt, and the consequences will be, well, realistic (major injury at best, death most of the time). Players who wish to employ the breaking-down-the-front-door approach will probably find that either Medium or Hard difficulty is necessary in order to provide enough of a challenge.
Overall, Deus Ex is probably the best game I’ve ever had the pleasure of playing (and I don’t say that lightly). If you need a break from the generic, brown FPS console games of late (or if you just want to play a good PC game), give Deus Ex a try.

Fantastic Champions
Paladins is set in a vibrant fantasy world and features a diverse cast of Champions ranging from sharpshooting humans to mech-riding goblins, mystical elves, jetpack-clad dragons, and bomb golems. Each Champion brings a unique set of abilities to the battlefield and new Champions are regularly added to Paladins, keeping the game exciting.
Free-to-Play
Paladins is completely Free-to-Play. Anything that affects gameplay can be unlocked simply by playing, with cosmetic items available for purchase.
Card Mastery
Players collect unique cards for each Champion and build decks that empower their personal play styles. Gamers start with a basic deck of cards and unlock additional cards as they play, opening the door to creative new decks that radically change how Champions play. Players may further tweak their decks in-game with Burn Cards, making themselves stronger or counteracting opponents’ strategies.
Level Up
No matter how players choose to play Paladins, they will gain experience points as they play. As they level up their account, master each Champion, and complete daily quests/achievements players will receive Radiant Chests and Gold which can be used to unlock additional cards, costumes, and weapon skins. The more players play, the more unique their Champions will become.
Accessibility
Paladins is played from a first-person perspective. The controls are simple to grasp for newcomers and shooter veterans alike which makes for an easy pick-up-and-play experience, on either controller or keyboard and mouse.

Growing up, I loved a game called SmashTV, which for me, personified the twin-stick shooter. A room, an avatar with a gun, and more enemies than you can shake a quarter at.
As it turns out, the guy who made SmashTV helmed this game.
Nex Machina brings back the twin-stick shooter and gives it a high gloss sheen, a visually entertaining and colorful affair with very pleasing shifting voxel effects.
There's no story, there's no cut-scenes, you're thrown right into it from the start riding your lightcycle off a small cliff and you start shooting relentlessly until everything is dead. Then you go to the next arena and do it all over again with a slow increase in difficulty.
There is a lot to dodge, a lot to be wary of; you get one hit per life unless you have a shield and then you get two. There is a cornucopia of powerups to help you along the way and when you're maxed out, you feel like a walking god of death dealing a face full of bullets to any sorry mob that gets in your way.
The arcade mode is selecting your difficulty and going forth to destroy all the robots, each increasing difficulty having faster mobs and less continues with easy giving you endless continues at the cost of your ever increasing score.
Arena mode is 1 continue, 5 lives, get as far as you can and get the highest score against a leader board for each difficulty while earning currency you can spend to unlock new levels and cosmetic items.
It's a fantastic game that will get you in a groove and can be played for ten minutes or five hours.
The learning curve is gentle.
A game that's easy to learn and tough to master.

TL;DR: Fun for the first hour or two, but was controversial, and is unoptimized, even after more than 3 years of development.
So this game has been the subject of plenty of controversy for over 3 years. Released multiple times with different names such as Orion: Dino Beatdown and Orion: Dino Horde. Then it was also part of another controversy as far as theft of assets. But let's get off that and into the actual game.
You basically survive wave after wave of killing dinosaurs, while completing the occasional objective or two as the match goes on. You can do this on your own, but it's usually more fun to play with people. It's rather fun, if you like having no challenge, as dinosaurs can easily be unable to get to spots on many of the maps, making it easy to exploit them. This is because of how easy it is to get to some places with the Assault's jetpack, but even then, you wouldn't have too many issues with the normal dinos if you were another class, due to how horrid the AI is. The flying dinosaurs are hardly any issue either, as they don't take too much to kill. This effectively drives any fun in the game extinct unless you like potshotting giant reptiles.
I had some fun with this game, worth the 1 dollar I spent on it, but to be quite honest, I have no faith in the devs at this point, and I doubt this game is going to become much better at all, as much of an unoptimized mess that it is.
But hey, now you can kill derp dinos for free.
You'll get some fun out of it, but don't expect too much more than what you get in perhaps the first hour or two of playing.

For a Hack & Slash, this game is refreshing. I went into it expecting standard mechanics like dodging, countering, an over powered air combo that would be foolish to not over use. However, This game instead replaced some of the basic stuff with some more intresting mechanics, such as healing through slicing enemies apart and grabbing their organs.
The controls are tight and the controller support was good. The fast paced action really makes you feel like their is never a dull moment. The difficulty increases at a steady pace as more enemy types are introduced. The boss battles are very over the top in the best way possible. The game doesn't take itself super seriously and that actually improved it a bit. The checkpoint system may set the player back a bit, but also allows the player to come up with an improved strategy for the next fight. The music is fantastic and really increases the intensity of the battles.
All in all, The game may be a bit short, but the satisfaction in destroying enemies certainly increases it's replay value. I'd recommend it to whoever either enjoys fast-paced gameplay or is just looking for a good single player fighting game.

Spaceplan is a clicker game with a whimsical sci-fi story and an actual ending. The story is very short, but fun to read if you like absurdist humor - the "potato" theme got old very quickly, though.
Gameplay is typical for a clicker: Clicking earns you energy points, with this energy you can buy items that make your clicks worth even more points, or items that produce energy on their own over time. You'll successively unlock more expensive items and will eventually get access to the ones that are required to win the game. You can play the game actively via frantic clicking, or you can put it in the background and let it play itself. Towards the end you'll have to hit moving targets with projectiles, so the game includes a dexterity element as well.
Graphics are very minimalistic. Your spaceship is a dot, other items are also dots, planets are monocolored circles. The music sounds sometimes like a track that a TV broadcaster would use together with a "program will resume soon" screen, and sometimes includes trance or techno elements. I found it mostly boring, and in the techno elements the beat was annoyingly strong, but it's probably a matter of taste, I don't think the music is bad per se.
If you like clicker games, give this one a go - you already know the mechanics, and the story might offer a new and refreshing angle for you.
If, like me, you don't like clicker games, then stay away. I played this game because it had a story, and I wanted to find out whether the story would carry the game despite my dislike for the mechanics. It does not. The story is decent, but not good enough to wait for the next bit while stupidly clicking your mouse.
I suppose it's a matter of "different strokes for different folks". I can't really fathom why anyone would enjoy a game that consists of repeating the same, mindnumbingly simplistic action over and over and over - this is practically the exact opposite of what I'd call fun, to me it feels like working at the worst part of an assembly line, where you have to do the same move for hours while you die inside of sheer boredom. Yet, there are obviously people who like this type of gameplay, and to those, I can recommend this game. Click to your heart's content! :)
Personally though, I just wanted it to end, and I found it particularly annoying that it went on even after completing the first big task. To me, Spaceplan is simply a decent story that's worth 15 minutes of somebody's time, stretched out over 5 hours by implementing a mind- and pointless, repetitive, terribly annoying game mechanic. I've rarely been this happy to uninstall a game. Good golly.

Essentially a cross between EU's real-time gameplay and GalCiv's theme and base-building.  It's a largely competent, good-looking game.  And it's done well with the interface, which is a stumbling block for some other 4x games.
Its biggest shortcoming is the diplomcy system, which leads to idiotic scenarios like you declaring war on a neighbor just so that you can get your ships inside their borders to finish a research mission.
The "blob combat" from other Paradox games returns, complete, with fussy micromanagement of combat units that somehow feels less "grand strategy" and more "herding cats" as you chase (or run from) enemy fleets round and round.
It really is not a bad first effort.  Much better than GalCiv, Endless Space, etc. were when they first appeared.  But it has a lot of problems, and the updates since launch have been hit and miss: diplomcy is worse in some ways than at launch, for example.  I should have stuck with the tried and true "buy Paradox games 2 years after they release when they are finally fixed" strategy.

The Witcher 2 is a game that basically improves on almost every aspect of its predecessor. I will now list some positives and negatives about the game.
POSITIVES
Better technical aspect as a whole, this includes, of course, better graphics, optimization, sound, UI design,etc.

NEGATIVES
Unresponsivenes in controls, sometimes clicks and button presses wont detect or will be registered a bit late during actions like jumping, inventory management, selecting swords/

Without a doubt, you will need to have played the previous game or at least read a summary because this game does NOT hold your hand. Right from the beginning characters will be discussing events that took place at the end of the first game and you’ll be introduced to a huge amount of characters you’re expected to already know. Geralt recovering his memory is a huge plot point this time around that without knowing the events that happened prior, interactions with characters Geralt meets would be confusing if this was your introduction to the Witcher. The good thing is that reading the books is less important here, though having knowledge of the Thanedd Rebellion and Battle of Brenna would help as those events help to understand the political climate as the game doesn’t explain those events quite as well as the books.
Storywise,
puts monster hunting on the backburner and brings political subterfuge to the centre. If you love
and its intriguing politics then you’ll be right at home with this story. With such a vast amount of characters and location playing important roles you’re going to be reading the glossary frequently to keep track of everything. You’ll almost certainly need to have a map of the game world to reference to. Keeping track of all of this is hard, if you’re not going to read the in-game lore books and go through all of a character’s dialogue tree you’re going to have a hard time understanding what’s going on. As someone that loves political conspiracy’s, backstabbing’s and civil wars with a good dose of fantasy involved, this was a story that was right up my alley. The only criticism I have of the story is it feels like its only purpose was to set the stage for
and doesn’t feel quite as epic and the first game.
Another thing that drew me in was that this time around
has characters that are actually interesting. The first game didn’t have a strong cast of characters, but fortunately
solved that problem. Everyone has their own motivations and goals here, very few people you meet won’t be trying to use you in some way. It’s all shades of grey, everyone has something to hide and you’ll never get the feeling you can trust anyone.
One thing that makes
significant is how vastly the game changes based on a single decision you make. Based on one decision at the end of Act 1, the entire rest of the game will play out in a completely different way. Huge plot points that you deal with in one route aren’t even revealed in the other route and major characters that you meet in one you’ll only hear about in the other. It’s one of the few games I’ve played (
being the others) where I’ve really felt that the decisions I made actually changed the story in a significant way, and not just changed the outcome of a quest. Even when you reach the end of the game you’ve still only seen about half of the full story and while it may seem like a downside, that decision to gate off a significant chunk of the game really made it feel like the choices you made had weight to them.
While
has always been about morally grey choices, this game really doubles down on that theme, especially in the side quests. There’s rarely that feeling that you feel like you made the “right” choice and even the choices that seem like the right ones often have ways of backfiring. If you like games with tough decisions, this is one for you.
As far as the combat is concerned it is without a doubt a step up from the previous title, though that wouldn’t have been hard to do to begin with. It still is a little janky though, (side tip; play the ♥♥♥♥ing tutorial because this game just drops you into the heat of things and won’t explain anything.) Attacking feels inconsistent, sometimes when you attack Geralt won’t move forward to strike and will just swipe thin air. Dodge rolling and Quen are completely OP here, nearly every fight will inevitably end up with Quen > dodge > attack > dodge repeat. The combat is still without a doubt a massive improvement over the first game, but can be rough at times.
Adding to combat not reaching its full potential, the potions system was severely flawed. This time the only way to drink potions is through meditation which cannot be done while in combat or in a dangerous area. While in theory this makes sense as preparation for fights is a big focus in The Witcher world, from a gameplay perspective there’ll be fights you’ll have no way of knowing will happen (looking at you end of Act 1 boss.) Since potions can be critical to surviving especially if you make a build around potions, you can end up in situations where you’ll be forced to fight with a huge handicap. Also they don’t last long either, in the first game most potions lasted for 20-30 minutes, here most potions only last 10. It feels like the developers wanted to streamline the process, but missed the mark.
Graphically
has aged well, it was one of the most demanding games on PC when it came out and it shows. The graphics are still extremely good for a 5 year old game, every locale has its own unique feel to it. They didn’t solve the problem of NPC’s though, you’ll be seeing the same recurring NPC faces over and over throughout. Given how dated the first game looked, the graphics here are a big step forward.
The soundtrack here is good, though I never found there were many memorable tunes (apart from the main them in Flotsam) compared to the first game. Also, it’s missing that dope tavern music that was so good in the first.
One of the biggest improvements over the previous title was the voice acting. While the previous games voice acting was outright terrible at times,
is a huge improvement in both voice acting and dialogue. Geralt in particular is especially great here, he has a much stronger personality here and the sarcastic dry humoured witcher he is here suits him better than the blank slate he was in the previous game.
If you’re looking for an RPG with tough choices and
style politics,
has what you’re looking for, with the caveat that you’ll need to have played the previous game or at least read a plot summary to understand the overarching plot.

An innovative game with really fun Co-Op gameplay, tons of spell combinations up to 5 of the 8 individual elements at once, combined with the danger of always-on friendly fire. In addition, there are lots of wizard robes to choose from to further specialize your character to your magick preferences.
What's interesting about this game is you have all the magick at your disposal from the start. Becoming more powerful happens intuitively as you gain more experience with the magick system and learn what spells work best in different scenarios. There is no stats or leveling system. The only form of character customization comes from choosing different wizard robes and equipping different wizard staffs and melee weapons, which each have their own flavour of effects. For example, the Electrorobe makes you be healed by lightning spells, but in turn you become more vulnerable to water and earth damage.
I will give warning: I played this game exclusively with a friend over 40 hours. Throughout this time we experienced
bugs and crashes - while most of these can be considered minor, several times while playing one of us would crash and we would have to restart the campaign. In addition, occasionally while playing latency would become an issue.
For achievement hunters looking to 100% this game, note that 3 particular DLC (Stars are Left, Dungeons and Daemor, Dungeons and Gargoyles) can be challenging to complete on their hard mode without any deaths. They require practice, dedication, and use of specific strategies using a variety of spell combos you'll come to learn.
If you purchase this game, I recommend you purchase Magicka Collection when it is on sale. The collection includes all the DLC which has a fair amount of new content after you complete the main campaign, as well as a variety of robes that really add some cool customization to the game and several pieces of DLC.
I would recommend you purchase this game if you have at least 1 friend to play it with and are a fan of Action RPGs.

Crash Time 2 is an odd mix, but very enjoyable as a driving simulator for cruising around in the depicted german town. I'll preface by saying that I haven't played more than a few missions, but have spent hours cruising around.
You get the brief impression from loading the game that it may have been re-branded from a more conventional german road driving simulator, but it almost liberates the player from taking their time on the road too seriously. The voice actors continue this first impression, causing the gamer to question exactly what subliminal german propaganda is being pumped through their speakers - because clearly, it can't be that superficial..
Yet, for all of its faults, there are plenty of great qualities.
1. The graphics are still nice and shiny on newer directX releases, and it holds up well over the span of 5 years - a virtual eternity, so to speak.
2. The almost apathetic mixture of citizens and police driving around makes for some catastrophic crashes while business as usual goes on around them.
3. The driving itself, while not exactly precise in terms of the on-the-road handling physics, is pretty fun. It maintains a good balance between lively handling and classic arcade driving. The chases are a little easy if we're honest, but the crashes make it worthwhile.
4. The comedy gold. If you start to look at the voice acting less as an actual attempt to create a dramatic environment and more of a strange video game cameo of mystery science theater 3000 post-translation, you'll be able to appreciate the rich social commentary presented between the lines. Bonus points for trying to drive with no front wheels, just a stream of sparks originating from your low-speed collision.
5. The damage contest. While it's not a great idea when you're racing, one of the best parts of the game is seeing just how much property damage you can rack up before "The engine exploded."..
4. Being $2.49 on sale occasionally. Very, very hard to complain about that.
In short, if you come into the game expecting more than flat-out level driving performance, you'll probably be a little underwhelmed. But, if you load it up just to drive around and have a little fun driving like a maniac without the GTA-style shooting, it's a great way to mindlessly pass a few hours!

Of all the Wadjet Eye games I've played, this one's probably the one to skip.
P&C adventure games, as a genre, rely on story and puzzles.  Neither is executed particularly well in this game.  Puzzles and their solutions are more or less laid out in front of you in very small steps, and because of it the pacing of the story that is tied to the puzzles is rushed.
The best examples of this in puzzles are probably in a section where you have to track some moonshiners in the everglades.  This consists of 4 screens, each of which has a metal box with a note in it which tells you to go to one of the others and find another clue of a puzzle.  The way to open the boxes is with the only item you can possible acquire in the chapter (a machete, used to wedge open the lids), sitting on the ground in plain view before you leave the camp that leads to the everglades.  When you get to the moonshiner camp, you block the still to sabotage it using the only interactibles possible, again placed in plain view.  A cup to pour liquid from outside to make mud to block the still pipes and a fire blanket to block the vent.  The same occurs for a lot of NPC dialogue, which is minor fetchquesting and dialogue scenes.  "Your task is to find someone who can do X!"  Someone in the same room, or the same person telling you to do this will say "They might be at place Y!".  You go there, and there they are.  You talk to them, fetch one thing to convince them or play a minigame, and you're done.  This sort of simple-step pacing really messes with the story, because its just so... direct.  There's no nuance to the game, and so no nuance to the characters.
The story itself is also fairly uninteresting, just on its own.  Its supposed to be based on some historical events so I dont know how much of it is fictional or not, but some scenes are just paced so badly for the reasons mentioned above.  Another factor is the time-skips involved.  Years pass between short fetch quest chapters and the character goes from young and eager, to grown but jaded and angry, into aging wistful and grumpy in just a bare few hours.  Events that occur between can be sort of mundane and feel unimportant yet part of a big story.  The ending is a bit anti climactic too and doesn't have any weight to it at all.
About 5 hours of gameplay in total, no technical issues whatsoever.  I got it in a very cheap bundle, and I wouldn't recommend this above $2 or so unless you're fan of the history of Florida in the 1920's and the references of the time period are something you enjoy.  There's a lot of better Wadjet-published games in the genre for you to play that even with their own flaws are much better than this title.  Just pass.

Sadly, I have to give this game a thumbs down, but it has a lot going for it.
The research behind it is meticulous, and the respect for and care given to the people and places is inspiring. It's highly recommend to play with developer commentary on, if only to get more background history. It will include a few spoilers, but I don't see that is a problem (see below), and will also earn you an extra achievement.
The pixelated graphics do a surprisingly good job at capturing the atmosphere, and the voice acting is usually good enough to keep it believable.
Unfortunately the game is very boring.
The story is utterly uninteresting and progresses incredibly slowly. The plot twists lack any real excitement -- this is why I don't think commentary spoilers would affect your enjoyment). Also, the gameplay is dreary. Fans of point-and-click adventures would find the puzzles to be trivial. There are a few innovative mechanics, such as persuading people to do things via conversation, and two chase scenes, but they are poorly exectued and more annoying than fun.
If you're a history buff and are excited by the subject matter of this game, you might be better off treating it as a visual novel and using a walkthrough to just race through the insipid gameplay. Even then, I imagine you'll find it agonizingly slow.
﻿Francisco Gonzalez has exceptional talent and dedication. I hope that in the future he teams up with a developer who knows more about how to make games fun. His passion was wasted here.
I would also like to thank the developer for supporting Linux.

Ah, good old Deus Ex. I hated this game the first time I played it. I hated it the second time. Third time too, but I also chose to stick with it, and it managed to redeem itself in my eyes. The thing that I kept getting snagged on was trying to play the game as it wasn't designed. "It's in first person, you use guns to shoot people, so it's OBVIOUSLY a first-person shooter!" Deus Ex is no mere FPS. It's got an RPG under that disguise.
Deus Ex is the story of one JC Denton, the result of cutting-edge nanotechnology. A superman without any of the unsightly deformations of mechanically-augmented soldiers. The story starts with a hostage situation at the Statue of Liberty, and for all the technology that makes JC great, he can't run and gun. This is where the RPG portion comes into play. It doesn't rely on dice-rolls to hit, but you still need to take a moment to line up your shot...at first. You get your standard skill points based on what you did and how you did those things, and those points can be used to increase JC's skills in weapon types or things like computers, and even swimming and that of course means JC can narrow his crosshair faster for accurate shots, use fewer multitools to hack machines, and swim longer and faster for example. But those are just the skills.
JC's augments are probably the most interesting part about him. Though he starts with some very basic ones, he can find canisters to install new ones to specific portions of his body. The legs have a speed-enhancer or a silent-footsteps aug, or the torso has two different cloak options to make you invisible to two different groups of enemies--but you can only pick one. Deus Ex is a game of choices. And choice a big part of the game. Are you a bloodthirsty maniac? Stealhy and non-combative? A pacifist hacker?
What makes Deus Ex good for me is the customization. You determine which stats to level up as well as what augments to strive for, and even the equipment you carry in your limited inventory. Though enemy placements and such are the same each time you play, you can try completely different player setups with each run to see what's different. You can even slightly customize JC's appearance at the very start of the game. The maps are fairly large and you are rewarded for exploring with items or maybe alternate routes to your destination. And the story's pretty good too: Cyberpunk, with a healthy dose of conspiracy theory. And yes, I know that's barely scratching the surface too. There's a pretty large selection of weapons and items and adversaries. The music's great too--every theme has a normal tune, and then there's one when you're in combat, and another when you're in a conversation with someone, and even a tune when you die.
What makes it bad? The game reacts to your actions, but it also stops caring about whether or not you used lethal force after a point, so that's a big letdown. You can also potentially ruin your game by alloting your skill points and augmentations poorly. The game also has a somewhat broken difficulty balance. JC is pretty heavily reliant on the limited supply of medkits to heal damage, until he gets the regeneration aug, which trivializes the rest of the game. And JC will take a lot of damage too, though the time I went through the game, I did somewhat stealthy but fully-lethal so I might've been able to mitigate a lot of that damage, I don't know. I'd say something about the graphics, but it's an old game, so that's gonna happen.
Deus Ex does deserve a lot of the praise it gets. It just needs an open mind and a little bit of patience, though. You'll probably get frustrated and stop at Liberty Island like I did, but just save often and keep trying. I racked up 400 saves for my first run alone. I uh, had a few instances where I'd save every few feet because I was on death's door and had to make sure everything went perfectly. So yeah.
The game is relatively small in today's world of several gigabyte games, so it would really save you guys the trouble of reinstalling it if you just kept it on your computers.

So how does this game play exactly?
- Imagine you play Smash TV with a flashy graphics
So If I trying to give you some run down for this game...
- No story or narrative. It's straight up arcade game that takes 40~50 minutes to beat a run.
- No precedurally generated levels
- PS4 controller is the best option to play this game (Keyboard and Mouse controls feels counter intuitive due to the fact that you have to move mouse left and right to control the radius of the cursor)
- 5 different types of difficulties that you can choose from.. and all of them are doable depending on your player skills
- Arena mode is basically mission mode that you can earn in game currency to buy customizable items
- There are 6 types of weapon power ups, while the balancing of these weapons still desired, but overall all these weapons encourages to you to play different play style.
- There are 5 types of character power ups. This is more of upgrade items that you can keep until you die.
- The game gives you 3 lives when you start the game, if you ran out of lives you get that the countdown just like the old arcade game
- The credits are differ by the difficulty that you choose. If you ran out of credits, then yes it's game over
- There are 15 levels per each worlds. And there are 6 worlds in the game. So again approximately take 40~50 minutes to beat the run.
- There are a lot of score attacking option, so if you are interested in this type of stuff. You would most likely to enjoy the game more than average player.
- If you just like to beat difficult challenge without much of score attacking, that is fine too. You still have plenty of challenges in the game without much of constant down time or anything.
- You can also make replay video a lot more easier by simply going on your rank and watch replays, you can also watch other people replays as well.
- No online co-op, but it has local co-op.
- If you lose your life you lose your power ups, but you also have to restart the level where you died.
- If you died in the boss battle however, you continue to fight a boss
- If you lost all of your lives during the boss battle, then you have to restart the boss level again.
- That being said some of boss level feels not fair because you lose all of your power ups and you have to restart the boss battle over and over again while you may have hard time dodging all the bullets without your character power ups
- Which means the boss level balancing is still need some balancing (Although it's still doable)
- So overall it's one of the most convinient twin stick shooter game that you can play.
- If you care about genre that you have seen in "Smash TV", "Enter The Gungeon", "Nuclear Throne", "Robotron 2084" It's must buy.
- If you want to see more story based progression, then this is not recommanded.
