Stellaris. Bought this game early. It's really remniscent of Sins of a Solar empire, with some cooler and different features. I've waited a long time before writing this review because I was not sure if I wanted to recommend the game at all.
Stellaris' potential is nearly limitless. The game has enough custimization options that you're able to spend 15 minutes or more just deciding what kind of civilization you wanted to unleash into the galaxy. When that is done, setting up the galaxy will take another 5 minutes. Do I want civilisations that are already advanced in the game? With the chanse that they destroy you on sight? Do I want 20 space-civ's that all start at the same technology?
Next up: starting the game and setting out exploring your surroundings will be your first task. Finding a habitable planet where your species can safely live and expand to. After getting a few colonies you'll quickly end up being surrounded by other empires. Expansion is done, time to develop technology to build stronger fleets. I really love the fact that I can customise my fleets myself. I am able to create several layouts per ship class. I can have cruisers with energy weapons and cruisers with projectile weapons.
However it's at this point that the game gets stale. It's still hard to get access to territory of other empires without being at war with them. When you are at war with enemies, they prefer to use some 'hidden' knowledge of your movements to avoid your fleets, whilst flying directly into your empire and hitting you where you are weakest. To me, the fact that computers avoid confrontation 100% of the time when they are outmatched and rather just go for 'being as annoying as possible' is a major design flaw. I can imagine some species having that natural talent to do that. But there should also be plenty of proud species who would rather risk it all in one massive battle than evading the enemy as long as possible and then just signing a peace offer that makes them lose another couple of planets.
Sadly, where the game gets silly is the difficulty setting. Normal is just too easy by any means, and the hardest difficulty (when all starting at the same tech level) is a fun challenge untill the point in the game where alliances start making all the differences. On this difficulty, it's nearly impossible to get an friendship/alliance going with any of the empires. There is a natural '- to diplomacy' based on the difficulty setting. So when you are a massive empire, but surrounded by 2 federations, both 4 empires strong, it will be nearly impossible staying alive. The larger your empire becomes - the harder they can hit you from all sides. And as said, with the AI having hidden knowledge of your fleet positions and opting to evade direct combat when it's weaker, fighting 4 empires (who individiually are definately weaker than you) at the same time, means you'd have to split your army 4 ways, which in turn will make it nearly impossible for you to come out on top.
Multiplay is what really makes this game worth it. Playing it with 2/3 friends in the galaxy just makes it so much more of a fun game.
Pros and cons:
++ Choice of travel (warp, wormhole and hyperlane) - super awesome feature and makes it a very dynamic game
+ Ship designer - the standard ship models get dull really quickly, but being able to determine their loadout is awesome.
- Alliances and diplomacy are really not anywhere near where they should be. 2 small nations completely dammed in by me and having a +60 or so opinion of me, should be more than willing to join my alliance, based on my allmightyness. Instead they join computer alliances against me, silly.
-- The AI refuses to fight. Where is the honor? Where is the pride? Where are the proud empires that believe in the glory of a battle against the odds? STOP RUNNING AWAYYYYY.

This is the best twin-stick shooter I think I've ever played:  completely slick presentation, perfectly tight gameplay, sick soundtrack and something that's all-too-often-missing: properly implemented competitive stats/leaderboard tracking.
I'll start with the leaderboards:  not only is it cross-platform, showing all players from both console and PC, but for any entry on the same platform as you you're able to easily view the entire run as a replay.  This means access to hundreds of thousands of replays across all the different modes, from the very best in the world to your less-best friends on the friends leaderboard.
On top of this, you have a player-profile with a level and associated currency:  old-school style, this isn't some F2P currency that you can top up with cash, and the only way to make significant gains is through significant accomplishments:  you don't get much for just grinding without any improvement.   For example, you'll be shown individually picked-out rival players on the leaderboards as a short-term targets to beat, and when you do you're rewarded with a bunch of xp.  All this extra engagement between the player and the competition just helps fuel the fire.
There's enough info in other reviews about how incredible the gameplay is, so I won't bother going into that here.  Just wanted to highlight a brilliant part of the game that isn't talked about as much.

I’ve poured in almost 70 hours into Cortex Command with no end in sight.  This may perplex you as Cortex Command was released in 2012 with… mostly negative reception.  However, the developers did not give up this project and have justified the 20 dollar price tag.  I’m usually not one to become obsessed with complicated games, but this game that has consumed me and make hours pass by like minutes.
The story is a great backdrop for a sci-fi sandbox game, and set up the great motives for why you’re doing what you’re and that makes it good. When Earth ends, Cortex Command’s story begins.  Earth had become a viciously dark place, and the only choice the human race had was to leave.  From our evolution we cast aside our insignificant bodies as our brains alone, were capable to control multiple bodies in tandem.  This made it effortless to leave earth as we were literally just brains that could be transported easily.  When reaching the deep edges of space, we as a species learned that we were not alone as well as not important.  After some growing pains, we all adjusted to the alien life.  However, resources were depleting quickly and species started looking towards other systems which will hold the setpiece for a lawless, wild west type gold rush.
The artstyle of Cortex Command is similar to sidescrolling 2D indie games like Terraria, but it leans more on its physics engine to be pleasing on its technical side. The pixel art blossoms, and the physics are heavy and satisfying.  Robots have a similar weight to the B.U.D. in Grow Home, mechs look like controlling hulking metal, and mining in the completely destructable environments beholds an ambitious animation proposition that is executed perfectly.The music is a magically airy chiptune selection.  It sets the atmosphere perfectly, and is a great background to the hundreds of hours you will spend plowing through the wasteland.
Have you ever played StarCraft?  In a sense, Cortex Command is the same idea.  Two bases build themselves up as they slowly try to frame their offensive attack to take out the other player. Instead of controlling multiple units at once, you simultaneously control and give commands to singular units one after another with the flick of a button. You land on a planet and build your base to defend your brain, the juggling and resource management is satisfying and immensely rewarding as you choose whether to attack or defend.  You can allot credits to have more possibilities as you mine for gold and build up your weapons.  Planetary scuffles can either swelter to a grand strike after multiple hours or a swift contest mere seconds into the match.  Jetpacks allow verticality and become weildly after a few hours with it’s amusing physics build. Keep a FAQ in hand however, as the games tutorials can be complicated and enigmatic.
Cortex Command is a Sandbox RTS game crafted by the folks at Data Realms, which is available for 19.99$ on Steam and Data Realms website. I purely suggest that you wait for a Steam sale and order multiple copies to gift to friends, as it’s very pleasant when playing with others.   Data Realm did not give up on their vision, and I applaud them for slowly improving Cortex Command into the game it is today.  Cortex Command is a game, that’s great for those who are looking for that new addicting game that stretches your dollar for hours upon each cent.

Rum is a very enjoyable, if somewhat short experience. My first playthough was about 2h30m in duration.
The game works fine from a technical perspective (I played it on linux using WINE, where it did have some performance problems).
The movement system is servicable, if not a bit "broken". You can stear RUMU by holding in the mouse button (in typical Torchlight/Diablo fashion), which works perfectly well. The game also allows you to single click to auto pathfind to a location. That's where the problems start, since the patthfinding will often drive you into walls or just get stuck. You also have to patfind close to an object, by clicking the ground nearby, in order to interact with the object. Instead of the game just pathfinding you close to objects out of range. I worked around this issue by just never using the pathfinding feature, which is a shame, since I think it fits the style of game better.
The graphics look as good in motion as they do in the still frames on the store page. It's a style i personally love, and the game represents it well.
I liked the story, and although fairly simplistic, it's also engaging. It's mysterious, but provides you with an unequivocal autoritative narrative in the end. While some games in this style choses to leave the story ambigous, RUMU closes the story of in a satisfying and logical way. When you are done playing the game, you feel like you have the complete story, and not just some peices you have to fit together.
The game feels very linear, and although there are places where I could see the game branch out, I haven't investigated that aspect. My gut tells me the story is entirely linear though, with the choices of the player having mininal effect on the major sotry beats.
Overall i recommend it for anyone who likes story driven investigation games. Be aware that it's short though, so the people wanting 8 hours of playtime should probably look elsewhere.

The story itself is quite simple, washed ashore on an unknown island you play one out of four different characters, each having other skills, and try to escape from the island. To do so you have to explore different islands and learn how to survive. Apart from the storymode there are special challenges playable. What I liked most about the game is the possibility to craft lots of different useful things and the fact that you can play the storymode together with a friend!

Here is yet another minimalist puzzle-platformer. Steam has been absolutely flooded with them. It’s because they’re relatively simple to make. But the thing that really bares repeating – and I’m certain that I’ve already said it in summaries about other games – while a game may be simple to make the better they are the generally more time consuming they are to make. Russpuppy have nailed the brief with The Deletion. Simple to make, hard effort to perfect and a great gem of a game that I wish more people would play.
Simple everything. Graphics, sound, game design, etc. Only one thing is complex. The strategy required to defeat some of the levels. Great thing. Addictive too. Everything works entirely as it should. It makes playing the game an enjoyable and arguably addictive experience. Tight controls. It’s cheap enough that most can buy it yet it’s worth the price. Biggest in game negative is the sound. I swear my Commodore 64 had better sound. But you don’t play these games for the sound. You play them for the sense of achievement and satisfaction completing levels and the game gives you.
ARGH! Another game that should have Steam achievements that just does not have them. Frustrating. Annoying. Where is my sense of achievement that I can boast to Steam friend number 97 about how I was able to defeat X level to earn Y achievement and he cannot or at least will not. Why can I not feel as though I need to beat the game to unlock the final achievement and have finally beaten the challenge that your game has offered? This… This is the only negative. I cannot escape The Deletion until I have that sense of satisfaction.
Seriously, a great puzzle game that made my mind work in tangents as I avoid the dreaded red bars, squares and other traps to beat the game. I still want my achievements, damn you!

Although technology enables improvements in games part of me misses the era where games were simple. Simple concepts with simple gameplay that were brilliantly designed. Simple never necessarily implies easy. Some of the most simply designed games offered players enormous challenge. If you were to talk to many gamers today who were raised on the classics you will likely discover that they found the games of yesteryear to be more challenging and difficult.
Some of the classics that I was raised on were 2D side-scrolling shoot 'em ups. The original Duke Nukem games come to mind. It was these games that took hours of my childhood. I lost count how many times I played through those games. Yet this isn't some cry that they don't make them like they used to. Because that isn't true. Bye-Bye, Wacky Planet is testimony to the fact that when developers sit down and consider making one of these games that they are still able to find the magic touch.
Aside from being one of the most promising 2D side-scrolling shoot 'em ups to come along in recent memory, it's a charming space adventure. You play the role of Alan, a green alien who is attempting to escape an enemy facility in order to return to his home planet. So imagine if E.T. were green instead of brown and rather than being sick he had a weapon and shot at all of the murderous enemies that attempt to take him out. It's a fun concept albeit not one that is full of originality.
It is important to note that it is episodic in nature. As of writing the game has three of its six episodes published. Each episode has a varied number of levels. Each tells a different part of the story.
Story
Given that the game is episodic and has a story a key component of the presentation is in fact the story. Eve's dialogue with Alan conveys much of the story. Eve is another alien who is in constant communication. Although the idea behind Eve is well thought out and she does work rather well as a guide - and tutorial - for Alan there are issues with the presentation. Unfortunately, there are a number of grammatical issues that bog down the game.
Checkpoints
The game is set at a medium to higher difficulty. Platform and shoot 'em up experts will probably breeze through most of the available content. However, if you're not an expert some of the game will induce rage. Therefore, I am rather thankful that a checkpoint system has been incorporated into the level design. However, you'll want to be quick on your toes as some of the checkpoints can thrust you immediately back into the action. This becomes a constant battle of the wills and you may die many times over before reaching the subsequent checkpoint.
Graphics
The color palette chosen for the game is largely a bright one. I believe that this should appeal to many. The graphics are relatively pleasing on the eyes but they are not exactly perfect.
I have one issue with the artistic design decisions of the game. Occasionally I find that the game is set too close and not enough of the playing field is visible to the player. I argue that this artificially, and not for the right reasons, increases the difficulty of the game. I'd like to see the game set back a little bit. The result, I believe, would highlight the level design much more than what is currently conveyed. The level design is one of the highlights of the game. Why not show it off?
Visual options also needs to be improved. Although others have reported that they have had FPS issues with the game I have had none whatsoever. However, I easily breeze past the minimum required specs so it would be interesting to see how someone closer to them reports.
Sound
The soundtrack, what there is of it, is easy to listen and has been well chosen for the game. With that said it needs to expand as the rest of the game is released.
Strong AI
The game has some very well designed AI... when playing the game properly (see my next point). There are an onslaught of different enemy types and they amp up in difficulty over time. They are incorporated at well designed intervals giving you just enough time to learn but not become comfortable. AI has always been one of the most important elements of a side scrolling game so it is nice to see the dev nail it this early in development.
Upgrade System
The highlight of the gameplay features is the upgrade system. There are three areas where you can choose to upgrade. These are light attack, heavy attack and a special feature. This is the most strategic element of the gameplay.
However, the upgrade system can be gamed. At the moment when you die and you go back to your checkpoint you can constantly get enemies to respawn from their respawn device. Enemies do not stop spawning nor do they stop dropping coins. If you keep your space from a respawn point there is nothing stopping you from killing over and over again until you have banked enough coins to visit the game shop (generally near a checkpoint) and purchase an upgrade. I hope that this is patched before release.
Intuitive
Perhaps most importantly is that gameplay - certainly with a controller - is very intuitive. I prefer to play with a controller but there are keyboard and mouse controls established. I would argue that the game would play better with a controller but that may just be personal preference. Everything plays and feels as it should control wise.

Bye-Bye, Wacky Planet is a casual early access 2D shoot em up game developed by Rasul Mono and published by Efimov Max. It was released on 16th July 2016. You are Alan, a green coloured alien that wants to escape an enemy facility in order to return to his home planet. He works alongside Eve, another alien that guides his way throughout each level. This review will cover the campaign in reference to design, dialogue, sound, and so forth. It will also cover gameplay, performance and current issues.
Wacky Planet has a very solid campaign that incorporates diverse level designs into various settings. The campaign is split into three episodes with 16 episodes in the first, 15 in the second, and 10 in the third with three more episodes coming out in 2016.  All levels and episodes have disparate objectives and settings. For instance, episode one most levels introduces you to the game and tasks you with finding a key card and finding the exit. Furthermore, all levels and episodes provide different settings such as episode one in a facility to level two featuring various others. These settings have weather effects that I think enhance the atmosphere and enjoyment of levels. Wacky Planet emphasises challenge in complementing the different levels because the game becomes more difficult as it progresses, which climax with very strong bosses. To counter the rage-inducing and repeating nature of some points, the game has checkpoints that occasionally appear and successfully balance difficulty with relief.
Wacky Planet incorporates dialogue via the cute alien characters. All dialogue is simple and is meaningful. For instance, Eve helps Alan discuss how to complete a level and the objectives. In saying that, the dialogue has constant grammar issues that are visible to notice. Lastly, the soundtrack is neat, adding some intrigue into the atmosphere of each level. However, there are not many songs to listen to, but not enough to notice constant repeating of the same. My overall take on both paragraphs is that I enjoyed all three episodes and levels that features new settings, more enemies, often more difficult to beat, disparate objectives, and levels that require more strategies due to the progressively difficult nature of the game. I liked the simple dialogue and the soundtrack that complements the atmosphere. I completed the campaign in 6.5 hours and I feel it had a good length to it.
Wacky Planet has very solid gameplay. As you progress the game adds new gameplay elements into the levels. For instance, a level allows you to play as a tank while another allows you to play as a drone. These spice up and refresh the core gameplay to ensure the game is not stale. There is an upgrade system that is the strategic element of the game. There is three tiers, split into personal abilities, light and heavy weapons. The personal ability has three upgrades and the latter two have four upgrades. You upgrade by collecting in-game currency following killing enemy. I think the upgrade system creates some variety in engaging your enemy and completing levels. Lastly, Wacky Planet features some strong AI that does not feel like an afterthought, rather something crucial that increases the difficulty of the game while not feeling stale and buggy.
Technically, the game needs some polishing. There is no visual options in the game and I do surpass the recommended specs, but I only constantly achieve 50 FPS. I barely notice any stutters while at 50FPS though. However, when I engage multiple enemies my FPS drops to around 35-40 FPS and when I use a machine gun, which is an upgrade in the game, FPS drops to 27-30FPS. In other words, I think the game needs more optimisation.
Wacky Planets store page suggests the game is "absolutely honed and the bugs completely absent". I disagree with this assessment, but I have not noticed many bugs at all. For instance, I have noticed very rarely in some levels of unresponsive AI walking into walls. I noticed another very rare bug of going into steam overlay and exiting out of it and being unable to move the player, but I could shoot. These issues are very minor as stated. Two of my main issues is one through the numerous and very frequent grammar issues. Secondly, I do not like that due to the abundance of enemies you have to beat the screen constantly shakes while shooting. The developer currently seems very committed to fixing and improving the game so I will post my negatives with the game onto the forums for him to review and hopefully fix. If he fixes these little issues he has covered my negatives minus performance. I think some minor features could be of use in the game, particularly load games and a mouse cursor as both are excluded.
Overall, Bye-Bye, Wacky Planet is a very good game. It features three enjoyable episodes with 41 differently designed levels. All levels progress the story of Alan attempting to escape a facility to reach his home planet and incorporate some simple dialogue to nail that point. Furthermore, each episode incorporates diverse environments coupled with increasingly difficult AI to add a wrinkle of strategy and tactics to the game. It features very solid and fluid gameplay and decent performance. At $USD$4.99 I recommend this game because you can complete the game and return regularly as new episodes release to play it before stopping it. Furthermore, the low price allows you to support a developer that has evidently presented a nearly bug-free game, which is not what you usually get in early access.

A Golden Wake is a solid point ‘n’ click adventure title created in Adventure Game Studios, with a realistic setting. Good pick for any fan of the genre– but not at full price.
A Golden Wake is the first commercial game of Grundislav Games, creator of the award-winning freeware Ben Jordan series. Unlike those games though, Golden Wake uses a realistic setting, the 1920s Miami land boom.
The story is a typical rise & fall tale about a real estate agent, who, after feeling being cheated out of his hard-earned rewards, ends up as an enforcer for the mob. It is written in episodes, which in turn use a set of key scenes, but the transitions that are supposed hold them together are not too fleshed out.
The lack of proper plot consistency is evened out with historical details and quality voice acting (except for one main character, whose lines were recorded in two hours, and it shows).
The decline of the protagonists is reflected in the puzzles: the first parts of the game feature a good amount of them with large variety, but as the story goes, eventually everything turns into typical (unrealistic) adventure game scenarios.
The overall difficulty is mild at best, almost on-rails at worst. The good news is that a good number of puzzles can be skipped or solved in more than one ways, giving the players the freedom of choice, and some uniqueness to the game design.

I honestly cannot express how wonderful of a game this is.  I had honestly given up single player games for the past few years in favor of multiplayer games, as they tend to last longer as far as play time goes.  However, sometimes you simply want to sit down and listen to a great story, and a great story this game has.
I cannot express how much I love every character in this game - an interesting point, as at first I found the main character rather cringey.  However, this actually tends to bring out the supporting characters, as you focus on them and their part of the conversation rather than Raiden’s.  (This is great, as I spent a great deal of time just calling my allies and seeing what bits of lore they had to share, an absolute must if you want to get fully immersed in the story).  However, the flaws I had with Raiden’s character ended up being intentional, and the way that plays out… Well, it’s one of those things that depends on the individual’s reception, but I absolutely loved it.
Other than that, the combat is phenomenal - there's a ton of upgrades and skill combos you could unlock and learn.  Although most of the time I was just spamming the same buttons over and over, the fact that there *is* a ton of actual combos I could learn, promises that if I were to play this on hard, I’d have a blast of a different experience than the first time I played.
And then there's the boss fights.  Lord, I was speaking the other day to a friend about the best 5 boss fights I’ve ever played in video games, and I had a hard time thinking of anything in particular - but after this, I have an easy top 2, with phenomenal dialogue and cutscenes leading up to those battles.  And then the music, holy ♥♥♥♥.
TLDR: If you like hack and slash, amazing bosses, philosophy, epic music, memes, and AMERICA, this game is a must - it won’t go easy on you, but who likes easy games anyway?
P.S. Incase you’re reading this in 2017, don’t worry friends; there are no lootboxes.

If your a twinstick fan or score chaser of any sort you will absolutely love Nex Machina.  After purchasing this last night I managed to work my way up to 56th place on the novice forest stage.  Only took me a few hours of dedication and a million retries but this is the sort of challenge I absolutley love.
Scoring in Nex Machina is based on killing enemies/bonus enemies, the finding of secret levels/structures, and the collecting of multipliers/humans.  Timing the collection of humans is paramount in keeping your bonus multiplier going and its quite daunting to do so in a timely manner.
Almost a perfect twinstick, Nex Machinia is a joy once your hands and mind become accustomed to the flow.  With no time to think you will react soley on muscle memory leaving you in an almost zen-like state. It's simply entrancing.  Being a child of the 80's going to the local mall arcade and score chasing games like Robotron used to be the highlight of the week. Thus, I can see Nex Machina not being suitable for a newer generation of gamer.  It's a shame some gamers except more from this type of game such as a story or longer levels but that is just a sign of the times.  What younger folks don't quite understand is that Nex Machinia is offering a updated version of the arcade twinstick score chasers from a time forgotten.  It's pure and simple, nothing more, nothing less.  Zen awaits..

Where to start with this game. This is an odd one. It doesn't really feel like it fits in the franchise. If you take out any reference to metal gear you could call this Samurai sword fight and no one would really know the difference. That's not to say it's necessarily a bad game.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is...pretty lackluster. The sword fighting is a neat concept and they kept the game the perfect length to stop you from getting bored with it (I clocked in at just over 5 hours on normal difficulty). You use your samurai sword to hack up bad guys and if you hold LT you go into "blade mode" (slow-mo). The interesting-ness comes in when you realize that once you hit certain enemies a few times their appendages become blue meaning that they can be severed off. This is the main mechanic for defeating foes and it's utilized well throughout the game. At first though, you don't really feel like you're doing all that much damage, with enemies taking an exhorbitant amount of hits to finish off. Which is understandable in the first few levels. Unfortunately it never really feels improved even after you've upgraded your blade. There are several interesting "secondary" weapons you can unlock by defeating bosses which is a plus. You also have a handful of subweapons like grenades and rocket launchers but keep in mind this is not a standard MG title. Which brings me to my next point. "Stealth gameplay" is...non=existent. There are several times where you can sneak up on enemies and one shot them (the sewer comes to mind) but ultimately, this is not a stealth game. I'm not really sure why the stealth option was implemented as the path you are given for every level is VERY linear and enemies have pretty wide AOEs for spotting you. You'll most likely run through the game as I did..fighting everything head on and as I said, the sword fighting is decent. There are several "special moves" you can buy to help you deal with tougher enemies but nothing is really necessary to help you progress. The game is pretty forgiving when it comes to deaths as you are usually set back before the most recent fight or instance. Boss fights are probably the best part of the acutal gameplay as each one has a unique style that you have to use in order to defeat the boss. Again this is done decently but nothing over the top. There is a fair bit of customization (armor, weapons and weapon upgrades) but it feels like they could've added alot more. All-in-all when the game comes in at around 5 hours on normal though, it's enough.
Characters
UGHHHH... The characters in this game are insufferable. You can tell that many of the character traits were ripped from certain anime characters..mostly the annoying ones. Raiden (the main protagonist) is the worst. His lines are poorly written, and even more poorly delivered. Especially when he is in anger mode/Jack the ripper. It sounds like the voice actor just trying to make his voice as scratchy and "devilish" as possible but when you see it acted out it just looks so stupid and serves to remove you from the game. The other characters aren't any better. The main characters are sterotypes and the villains are all "eccentric". The voice acting is atrocious across the board but that is due mostly to the confusing and boring storyline. Which brings me to my next point..
Story
The story is tied closely enough with the other MG games that if you've played them, you'll understand a bit about what's going on. Overall though, it isn't necessary. It's like the second Thor movie. Ultimately it does nothing for the overall plot, it's just extra content for fans. To be honest, I didn't pay that much attention to the story but it was standard MG stuff. Someone wants take over this (government, world, people group etc...) stop the bad guys. The downside is, it was mixed with the anime style tween drama story telling. Essentially the main character is torn between 2 ideologies and can't make up his mind so he whines about it. And at the end? You end up not really caring because he was so annoying to begin with.
Soundtrack
This is another negative for me. The soundtrack is.....bad. The game is heavily littered with heavy metal guitar solos and plenty of drums a la "what japanese people think of american rock music". If you wanted a modern day guns 'n roses, here it is. Don't get me wrong, it works with the setting. Explosions and gunfire with the over-the-top plotline. I understand it. It just sucks.
Replayability
The game is only replayable if you really like the combat or NEED to collect all of the collectables which essentially amount to concept art. I'm not sure why developers can't think of other worthwhile things to make collectable in games.
Overall
The game is decent. That's it. There isn't really anything memorable about it. It's metal gear the anime. Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad game. It is unnecessary. Unless you are a hardcore MG fan that needs all the content. If you don't, just watch a lets play.

First off, ignore my 9.6 hour play time. The only way I got it that high was because I accidentally shelled out during the credits and forgot about it for 6 hours. In reality, it only took me 3.6 hours to get through. Spoiler warning, by the way.
If you yearn for the Dagger of Amon Ra era of adventure games, this is a very solid presentation of that ouvre. The graphics are good, the animation is good, the voice acting is solid... it's just the subject matter. It's a really curious choice for a game. It's in the curious position of being very well down without actually being good.
I'm sure both members of the Coral Gables Historical Society will find it fascinating, but other people might find it a little hard to get too invested in the tale of the town's founding, boom and bust. Outside of the sporadic namedrop of local-interest historical figures, there really isn't much of a narrative. The main character turns to crime partway through. I thought, "Finally! Something happened!" but nope! It was not to be! Just when the mob story started to be interesting it gets bored and leaves. Then about 20 minutes later the game is over. It's shockingly brief for the asking price and the puzzles are all dead easy since the game is so short, simple and limited you never have more than a tiny handful of places to go, people to talk to or inventory items to try.
I hate to rag on the work of a small group of enthusiasts like this, and I wasn't going to write a review until I saw the $15 asking price (I myself got the game with the humble adventure bundle.) I guess if you simply MUST have an old-school Sierra-style point and click adventure and you've already played the far-superior and FREE Herald of Raganarok and Vohaul Strikes Back and you think $15 is a fair price for 3.5 hours of moderate entertainment then by all means buy this game.

Stellaris is one of those games that any 4x player would enjoy. After playing for sometime solo and with a group of friends it has been a journey of exploration and discovery that continues.
I like 4x games so am a bit biased.  I still think the original Sword of The Stars is one of the best I've played and Stellaris is a good contender for it but not the same.
Stellaris as many have posted has great story lines built in relating to anomolies and historical timelines that randomly pop up and keep you surprised.
Add in pirates, ai races with different goals and always changing stances that keop you on your toes.
The downside is when you first buy the game don't try to play it if you are tired or really not in the mood.  The initial learning curve can be difficult even for those experienced in these types of games.
It took me several starts even with the tutorials and in game help to finally get far enough into the game that I could see more than the micro management and great detail of the game that you need to be aware of.
That being said , once you get that far it becomes much easier to play and understand the concepts of the game and the game becomes a lot more fun.
I am still learning and finding that I missed some of the simple things in the layout as I play so be prepared to keep learning for many games and be surprised.
All in all I would give it an 8 out of 10 based on the built in storylines about artifacts, races and the overall design.   Stellaris somtimes looks a bit spartan at first glance but hides much under that cover.

One of the things I did not like about this game is how ridiculously loud some of the sounds are, I laugh about the lightning strikes at night after they happen, but sometimes they happen IN THE DAY and I find myself ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants before the scary stuff starts happening. To conclude my summary of the game, it is definitely worth buying, and the new update (which will hopefully drop soon) will expand the possibilities with this game, a fantastic game that has amazing potential, and is definitely worth trying.

I'm trying really hard to like this game, because it combines so many elements that I usually love: it's a sandbox (or rather box of toy soldiers) full of cool stuff with crazy physics, ragdoll soldiers, a totally destructible envirnoment... and yet somehow it seems to add up to less than the sum of its parts. Here are a list of some of my grievances:
1) The controls, UI, menus etc are all very ropey and unintuitive. It takes a long time to get a basic grasp on stuff like the RMB command dial and the jetpacks for moving around, and the worst thing is almost nothing is explained to you, so you just have to persevere and figure it out. Now, I'm old enough that I grew up with games that were like this by deafault, but I think most modern gamers would find the lack of a proper tutorial inexcusable and annoying.
2) The load time for the game is ridiculous; it's literally the longest-loading game I own by some distance. This game is a 90Mb download... how can it take longer to load than massive, graphics-intensive games? I feel like I haven't waited this long for a game to load since the days when I owned an Amiga 500!
3) So many crashes, so much lag caused by too much stuff happening on screen. It crashes enough without mods, but with mods I can barely finish a scenario without an unexplained CTD or hang. Given the game's modding community is one of the things people praise about it, this seems prety unforgivable.
4) Absolutely no story, nothing to work for, no progression. It even has a paltry 11 Steam achievements! I know it's a sandbox, but I feel like a structured campaign where you were slowly immersed in the game, unlocking weapons etc as you went, would make it a lot less overwhelming and keep you engaged for longer.
5) Starts to feel very samey very quickly, despite the obvious diversity of units and weapons on offer.
I'm only 7 hours in an debating whether I will put much more time into this, if I'm honest. I got it at 80% off and I guess I've had my £3 worth of entertainment from it already, but there's absolutely no way I could recommend this at full price. Pick it up on sale if you fancy messing around with it for a few hours, but don't expect a game that you'll love. It's a shame, as I really wanted to love it!

Of all the games I've played in 2017, I think Rumu delighted and surprised me the most. Made by a small team in Sydney, Australia, you would expect a simpler game. Something less polished with more lulls, more gaps in the story, more... mistakes. But what you get is a carefully and lovingly crafted little experience. It's the perfect length for playing all at once, and delivers an emotionally moving and clever story.
When you set out, the world of Rumu is shrouded in mystery. If you're anything like me you'll spend the entire time guessing what's going on, and you'd be right for a lot of it, but Rumu still managed to surprise me as it unfolded at a delightful pace. I'm also certain there's more I could've learned and seen and done, so I'm keen to jump back in too. The writing is absolutely stand out, and manages to be clever without being overbearing.
It's beautifully displayed. The art style is gorgeous, and feels adequately futuristic. The music is stellar, and it's easy to fall in love with our plucky protagonist. The controls can be a little clumsy at times, but the game isn't about precision of movement - it's about exploration and intrigue.
This game will stick with me for a while, and there's nothing that frustrated me or tainted my experience. I'd highly recommend this - if for nothing more than I'll have more people to talk to about it!

This game is honestly a pure gem and HIGHLY underrated in my honest opinion. Despite it being an old game (from 11 years ago), and having even older looking graphics, this game honestly delivers a WHOLE LOT. A perfect mix of horror, action, scares, and thrills accompany this masterpiece, with so much attention to detail that the replayability is astoundingly high. I STILL start this wonderful game and it's expansions over and over just to experience them again and again.
By attention to detail, I mean that even with limited graphics, no expense was spared to get things feeling real. When you shoot walls, their decals are accompanied by actual particle effect to make it look like the wall is realistically shattering from bullets (For instance, a shot at concrete makes it look like pieces broke apart and made a nice dent in the wall). When blood is around it drips if it's near a ledge. When explosions go off lights shake, swing, and flicker, doors are flung open, people and body parts go flying. Enemies communicate with each other, and react to things like fellow enemies dying, grenades being thrown at them, their numbers dwindling, or even you going into slow motion. They move into proper firing positions to try and pin you down then flank, and they only use grenades when you're bunkered down tight.
Guns are a bit difficult to control. Sometimes I feel like I'm fighting the game itself just to be accurate, but none-the-less when I kill people it's satisfying as all hell to hear them yell and drop the floor after my attempts. And the scares actually deliver SCARES. Sure there's a few jumpscares, but I would be lying if I said a few times the ATMOSPHERE ITSELF did not set me off to the point a SHADOW would make me jump. Screw limited graphics, this thing STILL makes me crap myself whenever a spook comes up, and I'm begging god to just let me get through safely. I've actually had to quit Extraction Point a few times just to take a breather and relax before continuing. And the expansions are amazing and still deliver as well.
To be informative, Extraction Point and Perceus Mandate seem to be two somewhat seperate games, where Extraction Point focuses on spooking the player and setting their fear off, while Percus Mandate is more about shooting enemies and getting things done. Respectively, they're a "Horror Focused" take and an "Action Focused " take. So choose between them wisely.
All in all, these games are absolutely perfect Shooter/Horror games that I DEFINETLY recommend to anyone who loves to shoot things and be scared.
Final Rating: 10/10 Do Play.
TL;DR Version: Shoots Good, Scares Great, Play It.

This game started off as quite fun. I like the idea behind it, but it definitely suffers from Paradox-Syndrome.
Paradox-Syndrome is a disease in which games are born unfinished, with numerous gaps in content. Whilst pleasing to the eye and imagination, they are ultimately empty or unreplayable unless the player is willing to wait at least a year for patches, or worse to send more money for incremental improvements in the form of DLCs (which I see is the developing pattern here)
I like the game, and my initial thoughts were that it was fun. After a second play through, however, you realise that tech trees are actually rather limited and there are only a few combinations of weapon worth equipping your ships with.
In terms of story line, we were promised more mid-game developments. which have been introduced. Their effects, however, were limited. I had a race-war on one of my planets, but in all honesty, I didn't need to pay any attention to the results.
So although I like this game, and like the "style" of paradox games in general, I really dispute their methods for brining games to market.

I recieved this as a gift and let me tell you, I haven't laughed so hard from a game in years, I had so much fun. Especially when Bigfoot glitched and got stuck on a log and my friend and I went gangster on his hairy♥♥♥♥♥
This game has a lot of potential and I REALLY want to see this game thrive. So as an artist and avid horror fan, I really want to write a contrustive critique on this and I hope the devs will get something out of this.
As of right now, this teeny tiny little game is like a sprout that needs a lot of growing before it becomes something unique. I honestly don't think it has enough content to carry itself, and DEFINITELY doesn't have enough content to carry solo play, and it needs a lot more than just "improved graphics."
The story has a promising start, but there isn't enough of it to carry itself and raises a lot of questions.
Why did the police give up so fast, despite the bodies being so easy to find?
(Maybe they knew about Bigfoot and covered it up)
Is our main characters even looking for these bodies in the first place? Why? From my impression they were looking for Bigfoot only, but the posters in the camper hint that they want to find the bodies as well.
(Maybe they found out about the police covering up this accident somehow, and they wanted to see if it had something to do with Bigfoot)
I noticed Bigfoot might have something to do with aliens, BUILD ON THIS!! This right here was really what intrigued me about the story. It doesn't need little green men in the game, but it is a great explanation for "paranormal" things happening. Think about how far you can push "unexplainable" things happening (without making it too obvious)
As for the horror aspect.
It's got a nice creepy vibe to it, but right now its only got the cliche horror things that probably have been inspired by other games. Keep asking yourselves how you can make this more creepy? Well, the simple answer is unpredictability and inconsistency.
Right now, everything is a bit too predictable and consistent.
For example, lets start with the bodies. I love the creepy sound that plays when a body is discovered, but I don't think it's being used the correct way. Only one time did I ever SEE a body first, and THEN hear the sound. When that sound came up, my friends and I would go "Oh! Body near by somewhere!" So the sound became more of a cue (I definitely don't think that was it's purpose though)
As a fix, I suggest the sound to play only after the camera LOOKS at the body, and to add to that creepiness, I think it would be fun if the camera stayed locked on it for a second or two. (a bit like a gruesome sight that you can't seem to look away from) Any players nearby, maybe the game forces them to look at the body as well for a couple of seconds. Finding a corpse would be unsettling for anyone, so think about how to show it in the most unsettling way.
The bodies right now just feel like objects that the player stumbles upon in the forest. Why keep the bodies all in the same pose and only on the ground?  Why not randomize them, make them harder to find, maybe they are in a tree, or stuffed between huge rocks, in one of those houses or something? Maybe Bigfoot hid the bodies and the player finds clues to hint at where they are?
If you really want to go the extra mile, maybe one of the lost tourests kept a diary and wrote about strange things happening while they were camping. Maybe they even called the police or forest rangers for help and the authorities told them they were on their own.
The cameras, the cameras are such a great idea and you can do so much with this!! Now, when my friend and I returned to the camper, one of the cameras showed a figure that looked an awful lot like one of the players standing in front of it and I honestly couldn't tell if it was a glitch or not which amused me greatly. If it wasn't intended to be a glitch, I think making the figure move around and maybe even examining the camera would really show that something weird was going on out there.
As I mentioned before, if aliens are going to be a factor in this, you can push the weirdness that happens with the cameras. Have more than just figures stand in front of them, maybe animals come to check out the cameras and weird stuff happens to the animals. Maybe the cameras inform the camper's computer when it picks up movement, so you can really take advantage of drawing in the player's attention to show something creepy.
I've read in one of the recent updates that you might add aggresive animals. Be ready to answer the question of why animals are being aggressive and not "because it makes the game more difficult". To be honest, I didn't really think it needed aggresive animals, since realistically if I went out into the forest like that, I probably wouldn't of run into aggresive animals.
However maybe aliens/paranormal factors could make them aggressive. Maybe these animals have some crazed look about them, and even better, what if they were branded and possibly have evidence that aliens messed around with them, kinda like what may have happened to bigfoot?
I hope this really encourages some creative thinking, especially about this game's lore and story and I am definitely staying tuned to watch this game develop.

I bought this game on a personal quest to play all of the first 10 FF games, and I have to say that it is honestly the worst FF game I've ever played. FF8 felt like it was trying to cash in on FF7's popularity the whole way through, while also going too far into experimental territory. The junction system ruined the gameplay because having perfect stats and using magic were mutually exclusive (I ended up going for perfect stats and beat the final boss caveman style), the playable characters were bland nobodies (most of whose character arcs were over by Disc 1), and the plot was a convoluted joke (it was pretty much impossible to tell what the antagonist's primary motivation even was) that culminated in a tasteless modern art film that dragged on far too long. I could not take Squall seriously for a second due to his overwhelming edginess. His credibility as a protagonist went down even more when the game outright revealed that he had an edgy lion OC. The only real enjoyment I got out of this game was from the Laguna segments, since they featured the only enjoyable characters in the entire game. Overall, I'd say that this game is not worth playing unless you have nostalgia for it.

I've beaten FFVIII countless times, and I love the game every time. Being fairly veteran at the game, I can still say the junctioning system broke me at first. It takes a little understanding and practice but you soon find its not a hard concept at all to grasp. There's also plenty of guides that give you indepth instructions and there are tutorials for every new "junction" you learn. Honestly, the cast is what made me love the story as well. Squall and his party were not at all bland characters to me, and I found their interactions with one another both humorous and meaningful. As the game progressed, so too did the complexity of the plot, and it was hard to wrap my head around at first(my second playthrough was revolutionary...I got tny things I never realized before and that made for a better ending). The supporting plot of Laguna and his buddies was always enjoyable to play through, though, and I loved the character progression of Squall and Rinoa, and how ultimately the game is centered around two people falling in love. The game is BEAUTIFUL. It could be easily my nostalgia but this game had taken my full and upmost attention even a decade later with their graphics in cut scenes, I still get hyped when I know one's coming. And so EVEN NOW, the FMV's are still visually stunning and continuously blow me away... You will definitely feel a sense of accomplishment after beating this one.
In my opinion this game takes the cake over most FF games but it could definitely do with some tweeking and minor adjustments to this day and age if they make a remake(please) but its a solid 10/10 in my book. Get this game, give it a go and you won't be disappointed.

Good RPG, nice graphics and a gameplay overhaul of the original game. Probably the weaker game of the series, not that it's a bad thing considering W3 is the best game released in the past 5 years.
Witcher 2: Assassin's of Kings is a direct sequel to the first witcher game, taking place after the uprising in Vizima, when Geralt served as protection to King Foltest. During an assault lead by Foltest himself, Geralt and co. are attacked by a dragon, splitting the King and the Witcher from the rest of the army. Once the battle over, King Foltest is killed by Letho of Gulet, a witcher from the school of the viper. Geralt tries to stop him in vain, and Letho manages to get away, leaving Geralt as the sole suspect in the slaying of the king of Temeria.
The gameplay part is very similar to the original witcher game, with more varied character models, more weapons and a map with alot more ways of getting around, making the ''corridor syndrome'' a bit less annoying. The combat is, as it is in all Witcher games, underwhelming compared to the rest of the game. Various mini-games are playable, very similar to the ones in the first game: Dice and Fist fighting are back, but you can also Arm Wrestle now aswell. The quests are starting to get interesting in W2, with more funny side quests rather than the repeated ''kill all these guys'' or ''collect X number of this'' that W1 had. Choice also has a big impact on what you get to see in the story (by either choosing Roche or Iorveth).
Meditation has been upgraded from the first game, now you're able to use it at will, as long as the area is safe, though you have to be in the meditation position to consume potions now. Potion and oil duration are quite low in this game, but there are ways of prolonging them by choosing a specific path in the skill tree.
In conclusion, W2 is a good improvement in terms of mechanics, graphics and dialogue, but it's rather short (for a Witcher game) and some of the mechanics (such as meditating to drink potions, and quests that aren't explained very well, aswell as a downgrade in terms of the fluidity of the interface.) have led me to consider this game as slightly less good that the original. Still a great game and definitely a good one to play before playing W3.

Wadjet Eye tends to release good aventures but A Golden Wake is a bit lacking. It's a whirlwind tour of Miami from the early 20s to late 30s and full of real-life historic figures from the era, which is pretty cool.
But adventure games live and die on the strength of their puzzles and protagonists. And A Golden Wake's puzzles are a binary between incredibly easy and ridiculously opaque, with many of the Persuasion mini-games effectively demanding repeated trial-and-error. And protagonist Alfie Banks feels like someone out of the Deponia series -- terribly selfish and mean-spirited without any real humanity that makes us want to forgive his flaws. He's out of place in the optimistic wonderland of the 20s or the stoic austerity of the 30s.
I hope the writer keeps improving his craft, but in the meantime, pick up Wadjet Eye titles Resonance, Primordia, or the Blackwell series instead.

A Golden Wake is a strange game because it feels like it has all of the components of what could have been a great game but a lack in execution makes it only decent.
The setting of the roaring 20's was great and I learned quite a bit about Miami, Florida as I was playing. The voice acting was nice and convincing. The mini games were suprisingly fun. The downer in all of this is probably the simplicity in the puzzles and the shortness of the game.
The puzzles were very straight forward. They were essentially go here and do that or fetch these items.  The problem is that while these quests are also prevalent in other adventure games, the ones in A Golden Wake route are like a straight road instead of a twisting but scenic route.  The side effect of this is that I don't learn much about the characters. Puzzles can build up characters because solving puzzles can mean revisiting the same people and learning something new not only about the solving the puzzles but about themselves.
It was only about 3/4 through the game where it feels like the character development was really kicking in but the game soon ends. Either the game had to be longer with more scenes/areas or the puzzles had to be more sophisticated for more character interaction. The game is decent and if you're running low on adventure games to play on Steam, it may be worth a shot.

A Golden Wake is a great little historical adventure game. It tells a great story of the foundation of Coral Gables, Florida without being too heavy-handed.
Pros:
* Story is very rich with accurate history and solid characters
* The lead protagonist, Alfie Banks, is a great, straight guy much like George Stobbart from Broken Sword
* Dialogue is historically sound; much research and care was put into this game
* The persuastion mini-game is a nice change of pace for the genre.
* Some character's voice-acting is top-notch (George Merrick's was my favorite)
Cons:
* There are some holes here and there. For example, we learn during one scene that Alfie has to drive a car for a wingwalker's stunt because her partner has come down with a cold. However, the same sick partner is then in the next scene, in the car, with no apparent signs of illness. Another minor annoyance is characters who do not know Alfie, addressing him as Mr. Banks (or Alfie) as if they are already familiar with who he was (like the train conductor in the last scene).
* Puzzles are easy, and exploration is often stunted with dialoge boxes condemning you from doing certain things off the cuff or going certain places. This is a good adventure game for beginners to the genre.
Overall: 7/10

This game started off as quite fun. I like the idea behind it, but it definitely suffers from Paradox-Syndrome.
Paradox-Syndrome is a disease in which games are born unfinished, with numerous gaps in content. Whilst pleasing to the eye and imagination, they are ultimately empty or unreplayable unless the player is willing to wait at least a year for patches, or worse to send more money for incremental improvements in the form of DLCs (which I see is the developing pattern here)
I like the game, and my initial thoughts were that it was fun. After a second play through, however, you realise that tech trees are actually rather limited and there are only a few combinations of weapon worth equipping your ships with.
In terms of story line, we were promised more mid-game developments. which have been introduced. Their effects, however, were limited. I had a race-war on one of my planets, but in all honesty, I didn't need to pay any attention to the results.
So although I like this game, and like the "style" of paradox games in general, I really dispute their methods for brining games to market.

Deciding on whether to recommend this game or not is difficult for me. I adore WadjetEye games and I love most of their titles. The ones I don't love, I appreciate. I appreciate A Golden Wake. It would not be fair to compare this game to other WE titles. Taken on its own merits, the game is pretty interesting. This is a very light P&C. For a noobie, the puzzles are very easy. For a veteran, they are insultingly easy. You are given only so many locations to visit, but their design is very well done. You can only talk to the characters that will continue the story, making all the other NPC's just decorations. OK, I need to get the positives out of the way. If you are interested in the 1920's, then this game is worth playing. The soundtrack is also very fitting for the game. You are surrounded by popular figures of the 1920's. Like I said, the game looks great. What is new with this is that there are more mini-games than puzzles. You have different dialogue trees, so you can be ruthless or the good guy. Where the game falls flat is that it is over so quickly. I felt the story dragged a little bit. It may seem contradictory to say but it took a long time for the story to get going and once it started to get going, it was soon over. That was my biggest gripe. This was done in a historical context, so the makers had limits as to what they could do. Another strike in my book were the sexual overtones in a couple of places. A villain has a realistic portrait of a nude woman in his office. The protagonist is shown getting out of bed naked with a naked woman lying on the bed. While you only see backsides, I felt this was done in poor taste. Overall, I am glad that I played it. It is definitely a departure from WadjetEye's other works and thats not necessarily a bad thing. The game looks good, sounds good, has some interesting new ideas for a point&click, but was too short for my taste. As I write this review, it occurs to me that I need to recommend it. This game took risks for a P&C. Besides, who makes games about the 1920's?

I really want to like this game, but it's borderline unplayable on OSX. If some of the major issues get addressed, I'd be really excited to play, but at the moment I'm spending most of my time wanting to rip my hair out.  The idea of the game is REALLY cool, and yes, I had fun playing, but mostly it was an exercise in frustration.
These are the major issues that I encountered:
1. Broken 360 controller support. Buttons work, but not the sticks.
2. Godawful frame rate at any resolution.
3. Screen resolution options are terrible with anything other than native screen res. Smaller resolution in a window is very tiny, and going full-screen doesn't actually fill the screen, it just makes the same size "window" in a full-screen. That means lots of black with a still-tiny game in the middle.
4. Fonts - anything smaller than native resolution (1680x1050 in my case) is unreadable.
5. The aiming system is very difficult. Sometimes I get an aiming "reticle" so I can see where I'm aiming across the screen, but other times (even with the same gun) it's not there, which means you can't tell where you're aiming except to carefully watch the bullets.
6. The jet-packs - after 2 hours of play-time, I still can't get my soldiers around using the jet-packs. Most of the time, they seem to barely budge my soldier off the ground. If a soldier gets stuck down a mine-shaft (or whatever), it takes so much time to get them back out that the rest of my squad is usually wiped out. Consequently, I end up leaving many squad members in useless positions and buying more.

Rumu is an adventure game where you play as a sentient roomba, tasked with cleaning the house while your owners are away. ...Yep.
If you like short, slow-paced games with a focus on environmental storytelling, Rumu is definitely worth your time. The admittedly kind of ridiculous premise serves as a perfect way of exploring the story's themes of family and good intentions gone wrong. Things are never too silly or too depressing - it's all balanced out quite nicely.
The game can be completed relatively quickly (~4 hours), so the $20 price tag may be a little bit steep for some. Also, as of the initial release, the game lacks accessibility features such as a colour blind mode. The devs are aware of this, but if you have issues with reading small light blue text on white backgrounds I'd hold off on playing it until a future patch.
Still, I'd highly recommend checking this one out in some form if you can. It's unique, it's heartfelt, and I love it to pieces.

Note: The followings are my first impressions, not a full blown review. I refuse to play this any longer just to write a full review.
This game is a travesty. It's parctically unplayable. It runs on my machine, unlike for some here (probably has to do with the fact that I have a ~10 years old PC with Windows XP), but that just means that I wasted more time on it.
First of all, the game has no tutorial whatsoever. But hey, it shouldn't be that hard, right? Except the very first enemy (a weak, half naked bandit) almost killed me. Whenever I clicked on the enemy, my character just tattered around, doing nothing and only actually attacked for every 2-3rd try. Clearly I am doing something wrong here, right? Okay, let's bring out the manual. Let me quote the supposed solution:
"Click the 'combo' button. Rename the combo from 'Combo1' to
'Brigand Basher' and press 'Enter'. Click the sword icon in the
top-right of the panel to display your knife's combat actions. Then
drag the 'cut' action into the first empty slot at the top of the
combo sequence, and drag the 'cut' action into the second slot.
Finally, click the button to the right of the first slot to make the
combo loop back to the start."
Are you kidding me? Am I suppose to make an auto-repeating attack "combo" for every weapon?! In any decently designed game this is done with repeated clicks or just keeping the attack button pressed.
Here however accomplishing ANYTHING by clicking is a pain. The game is horribly unresponsive and uncomfortable to control. The character always positions himself in the required starting position of the animation VERY tediously. This means that I'll receive 2-3 attacks from an enemy before my character could be bothered to start his own attack animation.
Picking up stuff isn't any better. First of all, I have to find that exact few pixel large area, where I can actually click on the given thing (pixel hunting ahoy...). Then, the character steps closer, tatters around to find the right position for the animation to start. Just to show how tedious this is: I found 3 mushrooms and 2 herbs on the riverbank, near the starting location. I took me over a whole minute to pick them up. As a cherry on top, let's add an absolutelly horrendous pathfinding to this mix. Again, an example: I stood a bit to the right from a door to a building, with nothing blocking the path (tested it). Yet the AI sent my character to the left, went around the entire building, got stuck in a barrel for a while until it finally managed to find the door.
The other main issue is the range of sight. You can see in a distance of, say, 5 meters (~15 feet for ye Americans). Beyond that, everything's pitch black. It's nigh impossible to find anything on the main screen because of this. And there's no minimap. There is a map in your inventory for the starting town, but even that is useless: it shows the entire town as one unit, when in practice it is made up from small chunks, separated by walls. It took me about 40 minutes to find the inn, which was marked on my map, and another 20 to find the uncle's house, where I was supposed to go all along.
The text is painfull to read, since the game uses a bright orange text on a dark backround, and a small font with thick lines, which makes the letters painfully hard to read. The dialogues are even worse, since those are heavily stylised in addition, making them nigh impossible to read, so I relied on the voice acting mostly. Which is amateurish and lifeless for the most part. As for the writing: it's stiff and unnatural, using the oldest cliches under the sun.
The game has some good ideas. Like the balance based magic system (the more you use one of the five, the weaker the other will become) or the freely customisable combos. But the game is so unplayable, that these are meaningless.
I still just absolutely love this game.... even 20 or so years later.

Pretty awesome, will satisfy both fans of the horror genre and action genre. Although throughout the campaign the horror and action aspect is most of the time divided, it just works. The game provides both amazing run and gun action and tactical shooting in the same time, putting you against enemy squads who co-operate surprisingly well. Truly one of the outstanding elements of this game are the firefights against rather great A.I., it’s presentation of weapons is amazing (for example : the SMG just FEELS at least 2x more powerful than a heavy machine gun in any other game), the horror pays homage to some classics and on top with the atmospheric lighting and effects in the game stands out even to this day. The slow-motion  power in this game doesn’t slow down the action like one would expect, but rather it enhances it due to the way the fighting scenes just look like. After a fight once you revisit an area for whatever reason you KNOW you have been there: blood splatter everywhere, majority of furniture destroyed, walls have cracks & bullet holes and you will just recognize your own trial of chaos. As far as the horror aspect goes you either have a nice buildup to it, or it may happen while you look around for scavenging thing like ammo and medic kits. There are also these upgrade syringes which upgrade either your health or slow motion time, but the game will either hide them rather well and fairly or put in in plain sight… where you can see them in an environment comparable to hell. Would recommend it more to high action FPS fans than horror fans (to which I’d also recommend the game).

Oh, boy.  I really wanted to like this, because I've loved every other game from Wadjet Eye so far, but I really had a tough time getting into this one.  I did finish it, more due to the completionist in me, but also in hopes that it would get better.  Parts of it near the end did improve a little, but overall, the game felt very disjointed, and involved a LOT of "To do this, first you have to get this person to do that, but to do THAT, you have to get these three items", rinse and repeat.  A lot of seemingly-arbitrary tasks ahead of you, and not much in the way of an overarching storyline to tie it all together, other than Alfie (the main character) "trying to make it big" and restore his family's name.  That's about it as far as plot.
I looked up reviews to see if I was missing something, and a lot of reviewers said how they really identified with the main character, Alfie Banks, but I honestly felt he was pretty bland... a fairly generic stereotype of a 1920's real estate agent.
The one thing I did like about the game is that it's based on the real "history" (with some artistic liberties taken, of course) of Coral Gables, FL.  Many of the main characters have real life counterparts, with the exception of Alfie.  But other than that, with a plot that couldn't figure out which way it was going and never really tied together, subpar voice acting, a step back in the way of retro-styled graphics that didn't just feel "retro-styled" but more like it actually was made years ago (and not in a good way)... I just wasn't a big fan of the game.  Not awful, but not that good.  A big disappointment compared to Wadjet Eye's other fantastic productions.

Magicka is a game where you are a wizard, trying to conjure spells using elements. The catch is that multiple combinations yield multiple spells, most of which will severely injure yourself and your teammates.
You are given from start, after a quick tutorial on the basics, all the elements. This allows you to beat the game with anything.
Combining elements is the key factor of the game, where you can cast a stone armor to protect yourself and lay healing mines for your teammate who crushes enemies using a steam-electric-arcane beam. Without a mana or cooldown system.
there are some hidden goodies to look for, some only for the sake of it, like the mooses, or magicks, a spell that has to be entered in the right order.
Magicks are unlockable combinations that are far more powerful and/or unique than your normal spells. From slowing time to freezing the entire screen, or as simple as a teleport of flammable oil. They serve the purpose of progression, and one is even a plot point of the game.
The game is also a living pile of references, ranging to movies to games. If you like to see that kind of stuff, it's plenty in this game.
The plot is simple: Your goal is to defeat the main wizard baddie. No heavy plot twists or anything.
The game is also filled with bugs, bust most of them are fixed within seconds. Gamebreaking bugs can be fixed with an easy restart, which will take you a few screens back. The netcode tend to be laggy for the clients, even with low ping.
Most player characters are DLC, but most of them are simple reskins with no unbalanced stats. Some extra content are also DLC-only.

Sometimes the physics are wonky, with the knockback being powerful enough to knock your wizard several meters in the air. You can even reach spots you weren't meant to this way.
Friendly-fire is also a key factor in the game, which can get problematic in certain situations, such as in tight spaces or a miscast. Hilarity can ensue if the wonky physics kick in.
There may or may not be some plot holes around. Not that relevant, since the plot is already an excuse to cast stuff around.
Some bosses can be one-shotted. While some can provide a worthwhile fight, some can be downed in seconds. However, one-shotting a boss requires some skill (and luck), and can be satisfying if you did it right.
Grab this game if you got the coin and friends to play with. I still haven't played through all the chapters and DLC-content, but the fun-factor I had playing with my friend is undeniable. Yes, there will be rage over that single miscast, yes, there will be random deathmatches when someone's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and yes, there will be fooling around whenever there's the chance to. And bugs. And that's it's charm. There's no problem with those, since players can be revived in a matter of seconds.
The fun from this game came from laughing about failures of each other and the good times you spent with them, and when seriousness kicks in when a horde of NPCS appear and you enter a tactical approach to them. If you just care about goofing with your friends in a co-op game, Magicka is there.

A nostalgic adventure game that spans a couple of decades involving real people, locations and events. Like other Wadjet Eye games, A Golden Wake focuses on story, puzzles, pointing and clicking in the style of Monkey Island, and retro style pixel art.
You play as Alfie Banks during the Florida Land Boom of the 1920s. You are a talented real estate agent looking to reach the top while dealing with bootleggers, politicians and shady salesmen. I really enjoyed the story and would not hesitate to say it's the most impressive aspect of the game. It was refreshing to play this type of story and it's the kind of plot that demonstrates the appeal of adventure games.
Unfortunately the game just isn't difficult enough. There is a bit of backtracking and most puzzles are quite obvious. A more seasoned adventure fan will blast through this game in about 4 hours. However, I didn't even mind. I enjoyed the dialoue, the plot and the use of mini persuasion style games. I was interested, and despite only having to think about 1 puzzle in particular, I wanted to play until the end with no hesitation.
A Golden Wake is not very challenging, but offers a good story and is set in an interesting period in history. Any modern point and click game is a blessing and I have no problem recommending this game to veterans of the genre. Do not expect any puzzles to make you pull your hair out, but expect a fresh scenario and setting with a few hours well spent afterwards.  Not as great as Primordia or Resonance, but well worth your time.

Cinematically rediculous cutscenes (in a good way), extremely fun and addictive gameplay unlike any other hack and slash I've played, a non-canon continuum of Metal Gear Solid 4 which is quite plausible to me (I would gladly accept it if it was canon), and an all around fun game to play, beat, replay, and replay again.
Definitely one of my favorite games on Steam, although I've already beat it several times prior to even using Steam like every other game in the Metal Gear series. Still though, that replay value is insane.
The story was well written. They use a lot of themes and a few characters from Metal Gear Solid 4 which is awesome to see, and did really well with the new characters and the development of Raiden himself. Overall I really enjoyed it and personally consider it canon because Kojima Productions held their responsibility for the game's overall plot, and it really seemed like it's the way Hideo Kojima wanted the story to be considering the events and story of MGS4. The story is also packed full of cheesy action cutscenes, but that's something that the Metal Gear series has always incorporated, and something I've always found both funny and enjoyable.
60 VR Missions, mostly quite unique from one another. It's a nice throwback to MGS1, MGS2, and a game simply titled MGS:VR Missions. Great variety of objectives too!
The gameplay is awesome, it's very enjoyable to "cut at will" and "cut what you will". The main purpose of cutting cyborgs/machines in half or into pieces (aside from your own sick pleasure) is to take their "fuel cells" to refill your health and energy.
Combos are very fun, and there are 3 sub weapons, not including your throwable stuff like grenades or launchers. There's definitely a lot to customize and upgrade.
This is
your average hack and slash game. You won't be fighting waves of enemies, in fact it's almost always less than 10 if you actually try to take a whole group on at once. But this is still a Metal Gear game; stealth is often an option, never mandatory. The higher difficulty you go on, the more enemies of course. There are 5 difficulties but you only start with Easy, Medium, and Hard. To get the other two, beat the main story on Hard to get the first locked difficulty, then beat
difficulty to unlock the final one.
Theme of the game:
(CUT, TAKE) or as they say in-game, "Stab & Grab"
The game was originally called Metal Gear Solid: Rising and there is a trailer for it with that title. That's where "cut at will" and "cut what you will" come from.

This game started off as quite fun. I like the idea behind it, but it definitely suffers from Paradox-Syndrome.
Paradox-Syndrome is a disease in which games are born unfinished, with numerous gaps in content. Whilst pleasing to the eye and imagination, they are ultimately empty or unreplayable unless the player is willing to wait at least a year for patches, or worse to send more money for incremental improvements in the form of DLCs (which I see is the developing pattern here)
I like the game, and my initial thoughts were that it was fun. After a second play through, however, you realise that tech trees are actually rather limited and there are only a few combinations of weapon worth equipping your ships with.
In terms of story line, we were promised more mid-game developments. which have been introduced. Their effects, however, were limited. I had a race-war on one of my planets, but in all honesty, I didn't need to pay any attention to the results.
So although I like this game, and like the "style" of paradox games in general, I really dispute their methods for brining games to market.
