Wow, just wow... what a dissapointment this game was. I'm a HUGE fan of the developer. I literally own EVERY SINGLE game made by Housemarque, this is the first one I cannot recommend. I'll explain why below.
1) The game modes are incredibly vague. They dont properly explain the difference between Arcade, Single world, etc. Turns out, you cant unlock other worlds outside of the arcade mode, which is absolutely ridiculous, because THERE IS NO SAVE SYSTEM. You're expected to play through the ENTIRE game in ONE SITTING. If you dont do this, you cant "beat" the game, and you cant unlock new worlds or progress. Say for example, you beat worlds 1 & 2, and you want to call it quits for the night and jump into world 3 tomorrow, you cant. This is not an option, the game would make you start all over again from world 1. Every.Single.Time... Most people don't have the attention span or time to play through all 5 worlds in one sitting. There's no reason to not let players save progress at the beginning of every world.
2) The game is INFURIATINGLY difficult. It might be the hardest and most unfair game I have ever played in my entire life, and this is coming from somone who got a platitum trophy in Resogun, which means I beat that entire game on the hardest difficulty, and without dying once. I also got a platinum on Alienation, which is an absolutely incredible game, also made by this developer. I'm not a stranger when it comes to challenge, but this game is ♥♥♥♥ing IMPOSSIBLE. To make matters worse, there is no way to adjust the difficulty, at all. the only thing you can do is control the number of continues you get, which does nothing to correct the balancing of the game. To give you an idea of how difficult this game is, the DEFAULT setting for continues is 99!!!! Which means they expect you to need up to 100 continues to get through the game, which is insane considering you have to die multiple times in order for the continue screen to trigger, which means you'll die at least 500 times in order to get through the game, and this is assuming you can even make it past world 2, which I could not. Your primary weapon is incredibly slow and weak, and there is no real progression system to even out the odds when it comes to your abilities or weapon selection.
3) Lack of proper controller support. The Xbox One controller is not officially supported, which is ridiculous. The Xbox 360 controller WILL work, but it's a collosal pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to get working, as the game doesnt natively recognize it, you have to go into the settings and force it to switch from keyboard and then enable the xbox 360 controller support as if this were a Steam controller. It's absurd considering this game was designed from the ground up with a controller in mind.
I own over 170 games on Steam. I have never, ever requested a refund for any game, but I'm requesting one for this game. It's a complete and utter waste of money in it's current state.

Edit:
Just a brief note about this, because my original review (below) was positive, but hardly over-the-top glowing. Here is what makes this title so special, after dozens of hours with it:
1) This game has more layers than an onion. Even though you are given all the tools upfront, I was learning significant nuances of the mechanics even at hour 50. I could go on and on, but yeah, it's crazy.
2) If you like twin-stick schmups, this game will spoil you.
has the tightest and most responsive controls I've ever experienced. Ever. It's hard to go to another game at this point - that's how good everything is.
3) There is a metric ton of content. The biggest disservice I see to this game in other reviews is those complaining that it is too short. I'm not sure where the miscommunication happened, but respectfully, those players just aren't informed on how you need to approach this title. If you have questions, friend me and we can chat.
---
While little innovation is brought to the genre,
,
is surely a great go-to schmup to sink your teeth into for tons of quality hours.
For fans of the genre, you'll feel right at home as soon as you drop in. There are well-thought out difficulty levels, and a few good modes to choose from. They trimmed the fat to have content that matters. Even though the levels are not procedurally generated, they play really well. Fortunately, I got over that part pretty quickly.
The only thing I do want to mention is the voxel-built worlds. I know people love this aspect, and while I've enjoyed plenty of voxel-based games before - I'm not sure it works
this game in particular. Yes, it looks nice. Maybe not
, but definitely
. So that's fine, but with this tech comes a fairly high system requirement to run it. I had zero problem running this and everything was great,
I think this 'look' could have been pulled off by much more reasonable/simpler means.
+Super tight gameplay that has a good bit of content; not something you find with many in this genre
+Non-procedural levels (which made me nervous), but they work well and feel fun
+I like the 'quests' or objectives; this adds hours of quality gameplay
=I'm not sure the voxel-based build was worth leaving people out that have toasters; this look could have likely been emulated in another way
If you are a fan of like games, definitely
get this one.

I liked this game, but struggled to play it (don't be fooled by the hours shown, I spent a lot of that time not actually playing, but having paused the game while I browsed the interwebs). I believe this might have had something to do with me nothing feeling so well when playing it, so I had a hard time focusing in general.
Now to the game!
My first impression was that it's a gorgeous looking game and that the combat system sucks. I did the tutorial and failed horribly (because I suck as well) and the game suggested I play on easy. I was cranky and agreed with the game and looking back, it was probably a good decision as otherwise I might not even have made it through the prologue.
I did NOT like the prologue. It was way too linear for me (the same thing happened at the end of chapter 2 and I felt that dampened the favourite chapter for me), but I got through it and in chapter 1 things got better and while it felt quite restricted, it didn't feel like on rails anymore and I had some freedom to move around as I pleased.
I also changed the difficulty to normal (easy was way too easy), and immediately I got my behind handed to me, so here's beef #2 I have with this game; the difficulty scaling. For someone who's mediocre when it comes to playing games, it felt like the gap between easy and normal was too great. Later, it felt like the game went from hard in chapter 1, to pretty much a walk in the park on normal difficulty. I don't know if it was the weapons/armor I bought/found or the way the leveling worked, but it felt unbalanced. While I admit that it was nice going from dying left, right and center to just slaughtering everything, somewhere in between would have been better.
After getting used to the combat system and leveling up a bit more, I liked it much better (so it's not on my gripe-list). Just as in the Witcher 1, it felt like you could do more with it than I did (I only used bombs for quests for example and I never learned to block). While my Witcher 1 combat tactic boiled down to running around in circles and throwing fireballs at everything, my Witcher 2 go to tactic became rolling around in circles and using Aard instead. I do like my circles.
My major issues with the combat system (and partly what made chapter 1 so difficult) was that the enemies did 200% damage when hitting you in the back AND they pretty much never attacked alone. You had to unlock the group fighting which you had from the start in Witcher 1 and that took a while. The other issue I had was that the controls felt unresponsive at times, which got me killed more than once. This might be on my part, I don't know. I'm starting Witcher 3 today, so I guess I'll find out then.
Oh, and I really liked the armor/weapon upgrade system. I never used a single rune in Witcher 1, but slapped them on like mad in Witcher 2.
Some other things I didn't like about the game was that you couldn't use potions while in battle (this really sucked), QTEs (I just don't like QTEs in general) and the UI.
So what did I like then? Well, the graphics for one, the story - although I felt that there was a lot of things unanswered at the end, so either I rushed it or I would have to play the other path to get the rest. I enjoyed a lot of the sidequests and as with Witcher 1, I loved the whole "no good or evil, just choices that will end up hurting someone". I have not read the books, but I love the story/lore in both games so far.
The game felt rather short, but again, that might have to do with me only playing one of the two paths you can choose, and while there were some things I disliked with a passion, the overall experience was good, which is why I recommend it.
Now, on to The Witcher 3.

Paladins. Where do I start.
I have not played this game much in the time of writing this comment (11/28/2017), 82 hours, but I can already tell it's a great game.
The game is well balanced, and not very buggy, because updates come our very often. Of course glitches can be found, a lot in fact because Hi-Rez focuses a lot on pumping out new content, and not so much on polishing the content that already exists.
"Ow mah GAWD Palladicks is a copy of Ovrwuts" Whatever. Overwatch and Paladins are very different games. They might have some similarities, (Actually a lot of them) but it doesn't matter. I enjoy both games, Paladins more, in fact. I think one thing Hi-Rez does better than Blizzard, is the update schedual. Hi-Rez pumps out a new update every two weeks (I think it is?), while Blizzard doesn't update that often. But neither are perfect, in my opinion. With Hi-Rez's high update rate, the content is sometimes unpolished. Blizzard really makes everything polished, but the slow update pace can make the game feel... The same, even boring. The Golden Middle Road (is that a thing in english? At least the "Kultainen Keskitie" is in finnish :P) would be that content comes out so often, that it keeps things interesting, but not so often, that the content would be too unpolished. But, from the two update paces, Hi-Rez's high update rate takes the cake in my opinion. Of course there are more reasons why I prefer Paladins, but this was one that was interesting to mention.
The characters are original and creative, even though a new champion comes out every other update! Because of the great variety and high amount of heroes, it's easy find a champion you like.
I have played with all of the four categories(Damage, Flank, Support and Front Line.), and I enjoy Support and Front Line the most. Actually, my two mains are from these categories, Mal'Damba from Support, and Ash from Front Line.
There is three game modes. Siege, Onslaught and Payload.
In Siege, you and the other team have to first fight for who captures a point, which is in the middle. The side who captures it, gets to push a payload to the other teams base. For every capture, successful push or defending a push your team gets a point. First side to 4 points wins.
Onslaught is a King of the Hill-game mode, where the teams have to fight over controlling a point for a certain amount of time.
Payload is a gamemode, where the attacking team has to push a bomb to the other team's base.
It is good to note that you play against bots until you are level 5.
The Competitive community is fairly friendly, at least in Silver and Gold. Of course there are some black sheeps as in any community, and Russians/other people with different letters can be annoying if they cannot talk english, but for the most part I have had fun playing comp, both with friends and in Solo Queue. I have also met some nice people that made it to my friends list after the match. I definitely recommend trying out comp, you do not have to fear getting hit with a massive wave of salt :P
Edit: OB64 has arrived. Casual is pay2win. Play comp.

Majicka is a game about questions, do you want to set this on fire? Do you want to slap a goblin with an enchanted ice sword as large as a baby skyscraper? Do you want to melt your friend's face, revive him, and melt his face again? These are just a small sampling of soulful questions that Majicka will pose to you, but perhaps you are a busy man with no time for trivia. Majicka can also make full-fledged statements. Ensconcing enemies in ice and flinging a rock at their vulnerable frozen forms will make it Wizard Christmas. Wizard Christmas is just like regular Christmas except Wizard Christmas snow is sometimes red and the only suitable present for a wizard is cheese.
So if you enjoy seeing your enemies driven before you with weeping and gnashing of teeth do not buy this game.
On the other hand if you enjoy helping a friend blow up a golem before using your mighty powers, derived from the deepest depths of Arcana to gently push him off a ledge while cackling madly, then buy this game, and buy a copy for your friend. Then find a new friend once he swears eternal vengeance upon you.

F.E.A.R. is a popular FPS and was released in 2005. While some people consider that a horror FPS, I'd probably call it a FPS with some more or less low-key horror elements. This game has a reputation for offering good gunplay and having a very intelligent AI. Gunplay is very fun and might be the best thing about this game. Although I'm usually no shotgun person, I absolutely loved this weapon in this game. The levels are often very dark and lack some variety since a lot of the fighting happens in offices that look more or less the same. This game comes with two expansion packs that are recommended to play, too. Don't forget that after the release of FEAR 2, the expansion packs for FEAR 1 stopped being canon.
Sadly, I've encountered some problems with the framerate and the FPS was jumping around unexpectedly at some places.
While there might be some fixes for some people, there is no guarantee that they will work 100% for you.
+ Good gunplay
+ intelligent AI
+ graphics still look very nice
+ you can edit your files manually to increase your resolution and your FOV.
- I'm not a fan of Bioshock's background storytelling via ghosts that show what happened nor of  FEARs answering machine messages. You can add it from time to time, but if you want to tell a story, make me a part of the experience and show me what happened. Make me a part of it and not just a mere guy that listens to some messages.
- You can't keep pressing your right mouse button to aim down your sights. Aiming is forced to be toggled on or off, which makes it very awkward to during a gunfight if you are not used to it.
- some FPS problems although it didn't happen all that much.
- some big enemies are annoying to fight against.
Further information:
Resolution and low FOV fix:
1. Go to C:\Users\Public\Documents\Monolith Productions\FEAR\settings.cfg
change the resolution as you wish. I've changed it to
"ScreenWidth" "1920"
[...]
"ScreenHeight" "1080"
2. Add the line "FovYWidescreen" "x.000000"
x = your favourite FOV number.
3. make the file read-only
Bear in mind that this also works for the expansion packs, but since they were made by TimeGate Studios, you have to go to:
C:\Users\Public\Documents\TimeGate Studios\FEARXP\settings.cfg
FEAR 1 is definitely recommended, but you can have a hard time if it's not running as it supposed to do.
Replay value: High since the gunplay is great.
Rating: 8.0 if it works.
Recommendation: Yes.

One of Monolith's best FPS games since Blood. The game pits you as a soldier going against an army of clone troopers led by a commander that is telepathically linked to the clone army. The game stands out on its own through the use of bullet time where you can slow combat down to avoid getting ripped to shreds as you deal with clone troopers that not only have numbers but also some squad tactics and chatter (the latter of which can reflect their situation, be it despair at how much of a threat you are to if you're gone with a response from other squadmates to shut up). Upping the ante is the atmosphere where what would seem like a simple fight against clone troopers becomes intertwined with supernatural elements, from radio static to a little girl in red appearing in places a child shouldn't be.
Overall, FEAR is a fun title to own and play, especially if one is a fan of FPS games.

Stellaris is a great real-time 4x game.
It features great depth, complexity, is comfortably challenging, and features lore from multiple sci-fi franchises. Stellaris’ take on tech research is refreshing, its combat does the job (albeit uninspired), and the political challenges of ruling one’s empire are well thought out.
With that said, some of the planet maintenance is vexing, the NPC AI is shallow, and the game requires a great deal of patience. The UI can be overwhelming at first, but after a couple hours of gameplay it is devoted to memory.
I recommend installing a couple mods including: Auto Build and Improve Buildings, Resource Redux, and Increased Research Window Size. These help with empire/planetary management, resource extraction, and a minor UI annoyance.
All in all, I recommend this game to other lovers of the strategy genre (4x games) and science fiction.

puts an interesting spin on RPG Maker games but it's ultimately superficially and detracts from the interesting parts.
+An interesting take on some RPG conventions, money is earned passively and you can add additional dimensions to your team in the background with the use of books. The finance system is a really cool mechanic.
+Some of the 4th wall breaking humor can be a fun ribbing to RPG tropes.
+Good, basic financial advice for novices.
-The world is quite small. Not a ton of content.
-Since there is little true content, everything is padded with a TON of grinding and random encounters. There were times when I would hit an enemy group every 3 steps or so.
-Much of the humor is super cringe-worthy. Lots of out of place cursing and "lol so random" moments.
-While a unique take by using alternate naming conventions (it's not water magic, it's depression magic!) it ends up making the entire system counter-intuitive to determine effectiveness and weaknesses. Oftentimes you would walk into an area to get one shot by the enemies, reload, try different armor until you find the set optimized for that area. The developer included a small tutorial room at the start explaining some of the game's mechanisms but I suppose they needed to leave room for more jokes instead of mentioning
I could write it down on a post-it but I honestly stopped caring.
-Poor direction and wonky experience curves. Many times you will likely just be wandering around until you find the next area on the map where you don't get wiped immediately.
-For attempting to turn many RPG conventions on their ear, the game seems to use default RPG Maker assets almost exclusively.
-Various minor mapping issues, image overlaps, items on the wrong image level, etc. Nothing horribly jarring but it gets sloppy in the seams.
=WAY too many characters in your party to end up caring about most of them. You end up keeping them around just to cast healing spells on your "main team" between battles.
isn't a BAD game per se, it just doesn't quite deliver on its potential. More content and less grind would probably make this a much more enjoyable experience. That said, I did enjoy it for a while and if you can grab it on sale for 49 cents like I did, you will probably get your money's worth. I would not recommend this at full price.

Game's great. I enjoyed every bit of the shooting action. But there are some design flaws.
1) Game modes are too vague. Arcade? Single world? Took me a while to figure out you need to play arcade mode to unlock other world.
2) Most of us don't have the attention span or time to play through all 5 worlds in one sit. There's no reason to not let player save progress at the beginning of every world.
Games like Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain don't have save/load mainly because the item/skill systems require players to remember what we have got so far in this particular game session. However I can't think of a sole reason why Nex Machina would want this.
3) I clicked 'quit' mid-game wanting to see what the game had to say about that, like, "Your progress in current world will be lost" or "Are you sure you want to lose all progress?". Well guess what, bam, title screen. Why not prompt confirmation like a normal game?
These basically ruined my should-be great experience. I'd be happy to make this review positive once the devs do something to improve it.

I want to love this game. I really do. I've been itching hard for a roguelite with decent combat and actual stuff to do and unlock. This fits into that, but I still cannot find myself enjoying it past the 8 hours I've put into it. The first two hours or so were great. Unlocks came quick, discovering secrets was fun, and the combat wasn't perfectly what I was looking for, but damn did I love it regardless. Quick, heavy, and punishing. The devs really know how to make a weapon feel good and be satisfying to use. Level design is also pretty damn good. For each area, the level design matches very well with the environment and flows naturally. The polished graphics put the cherry on top and elevate the whole presentation to a league of its own. So you might be wondering, why do I recommend against this game despite having all these great things to say about it? They're minor problems that only grow larger the further you get into the game and they add up to make an incredibly frustating experience.
I'll start with the combat. Like I said before, the combat is pretty nice and well designed. It's not perfect, but it does the job well. The problems come when enemies simply do not mesh with the combat. Some areas have enemies that spawn an inch in front of you with no tell that I've seen that they're even there. Those same enemies have poison attacks with very little tell of the attack. Later on, another enemy fires a cannon. There is absolutely no tell for this and no limit on how much they can fire it. So you have a very tough enemy that can fire a rolling projectile at any instant and can spam them as much as it wants. It's so fast, even the attack indicator isn't enough to function as a tell because it's on screen for such a short period of time. Almost any elite enemy with projectile attacks also has this issue and it makes those better left alone. Or to avoid all these problems, you can play the game in an incredibly boring way and just use turret like abilities to whittle the enemies down from a safe spot. This is the safest way in most situations to fight. It's the slowest and most boring, but it's the safest. Standing and throwing turrets is not what this game is good at, it's the exact opposite of what it's good at. But I'm constantly encouraged to use these ad infinitum due to poor enemy design. Don't even get me started on the floating enemies that detect you in a radius and simply damage that entire radius, making any melee that doesn't kill near instantly completely worthless in that situation. Anothing thing that exacerbates this issue with the reliance on turret items is the curses. Curses are fine, they're a staple of the roguelite genre. But so far, the only curse I've seen is dying in one hit. This just does not encourage good play. It encourages safe and boring play with turrets. There is no reason to risk yourself with melee combat when you can just use a turret and save yourself from the curse just the same. All of this adds to make losing feel mostly frustrating. I've had avoidable deaths, yes. Times where I shouldn't have recycled a weapon I swapped out or I failed to effectively use my weapons and items, even just simply getting greedy with my attacks and thinking I can get the last hit in before the enemy does. But those are vastly outnumbered by times I feel I was against a poorly designed enemy or just got locked into a fight I couldn't win.
As a result of the combat being pushed against by the enemy design, every run goes the same. I start the first level, do it as fast as I can to get the timed door, avoid the sewers because it's an objectively inferior area to be in in every way if you want to make progress, go through the promenade, into the ramparts, fight the boss, die at the fjord because of mentioned enemy firing cannonballs. Progress is incredibly slow long term and every run feels exactly the same. This review was spurred by my last play session ending in about 10 minutes because I was just so bored of doing the same thing every time. I know this game is in early access, and maybe this game will turn around for me and become what I know it can be. It can be the best roguelite of its kind. An Early Access game that is already more complete than half the games on Steam.
I can't really say enough great things about this game. It's a rogue-like, so death is inevitable, and heartbreaking.  That being said, the progression is solid, and fairly constant.  I don't think I've died once in this game without making some measure of permanent progress toward a new unlock, so it's not nearly as frustrating as some similar titles may be.
Combat is visceral and very responsive, with absolutely tons of options to fit almost any player style.  I am personally a big fan of using disabling effects like Freeze to control a battlefield and inflict heavy damage on enemies that can't really fight back.  There are tons of other ways to go, though.  You can throw lots of ranged damage, stick up close in melee, deal many different damage over time effects, use a lot of tools like grenades, turrets and traps, or run around as a spellcaster, raining fire and lightning, or any combination of those things (and much more).
I honestly cannot believe this game is Early Access, nor can I believe I waited so long to pick it up.  If you're even remotely on the fence about Deaed Cells, just do it.  It's cheap for the sheer amount of hours of gameplay you'll get out of it, and I can confidently say you'll love it, if you're even considering it.

I liked this game, but struggled to play it (don't be fooled by the hours shown, I spent a lot of that time not actually playing, but having paused the game while I browsed the interwebs). I believe this might have had something to do with me nothing feeling so well when playing it, so I had a hard time focusing in general.
Now to the game!
My first impression was that it's a gorgeous looking game and that the combat system sucks. I did the tutorial and failed horribly (because I suck as well) and the game suggested I play on easy. I was cranky and agreed with the game and looking back, it was probably a good decision as otherwise I might not even have made it through the prologue.
I did NOT like the prologue. It was way too linear for me (the same thing happened at the end of chapter 2 and I felt that dampened the favourite chapter for me), but I got through it and in chapter 1 things got better and while it felt quite restricted, it didn't feel like on rails anymore and I had some freedom to move around as I pleased.
I also changed the difficulty to normal (easy was way too easy), and immediately I got my behind handed to me, so here's beef #2 I have with this game; the difficulty scaling. For someone who's mediocre when it comes to playing games, it felt like the gap between easy and normal was too great. Later, it felt like the game went from hard in chapter 1, to pretty much a walk in the park on normal difficulty. I don't know if it was the weapons/armor I bought/found or the way the leveling worked, but it felt unbalanced. While I admit that it was nice going from dying left, right and center to just slaughtering everything, somewhere in between would have been better.
After getting used to the combat system and leveling up a bit more, I liked it much better (so it's not on my gripe-list). Just as in the Witcher 1, it felt like you could do more with it than I did (I only used bombs for quests for example and I never learned to block). While my Witcher 1 combat tactic boiled down to running around in circles and throwing fireballs at everything, my Witcher 2 go to tactic became rolling around in circles and using Aard instead. I do like my circles.
My major issues with the combat system (and partly what made chapter 1 so difficult) was that the enemies did 200% damage when hitting you in the back AND they pretty much never attacked alone. You had to unlock the group fighting which you had from the start in Witcher 1 and that took a while. The other issue I had was that the controls felt unresponsive at times, which got me killed more than once. This might be on my part, I don't know. I'm starting Witcher 3 today, so I guess I'll find out then.
Oh, and I really liked the armor/weapon upgrade system. I never used a single rune in Witcher 1, but slapped them on like mad in Witcher 2.
Some other things I didn't like about the game was that you couldn't use potions while in battle (this really sucked), QTEs (I just don't like QTEs in general) and the UI.
So what did I like then? Well, the graphics for one, the story - although I felt that there was a lot of things unanswered at the end, so either I rushed it or I would have to play the other path to get the rest. I enjoyed a lot of the sidequests and as with Witcher 1, I loved the whole "no good or evil, just choices that will end up hurting someone". I have not read the books, but I love the story/lore in both games so far.
The game felt rather short, but again, that might have to do with me only playing one of the two paths you can choose, and while there were some things I disliked with a passion, the overall experience was good, which is why I recommend it.
Now, on to The Witcher 3.

Stellaris is by far my favorite game on steam.
A long time ago that honor belonged to Civ 5 (lets not ever speak of Civ 6 which isn’t horrible but nor is it fun, where in lies the rub).
Stellaris can be described as what happens when we wish we could play star trek as the many different beings we encounter over the course of an entire civilization from the perspective of the zeitgeist of an entire species.
I felt noble in one play through for protecting so many lesser evolved beings. In others, a vicious fool hooked on a feeling to conquer all nations whom crossed my path.
It always cames down to the numbers though. You either have what it takes to take someone down or you don’t! This could be raw scientific discovery of better weapons, armor and or technology, or it could be partnering up with so many other species that your combined total is now a gargantuan obstacle for any who oppose your mighty coalition of United Nations.   In one play through, an ancient race awoke and after our UN dominated the stars for countless generations this not so new civ tore as apart like we were simply tissue paper.  Other nations whom we had bullied previously simply watched in a gawk horror as they knew that soon this steady tyrant would soon turn it’s insatiable lust for blood for them too. In the end, it was our petty grievances that kept us from finding peace when needed most.
Iron Man mode, which is present in all Paradox games, is the only way to earn achievements. It also means your only means of saving is auto saved for you, so of course, no going backsies!
Now with the latest tier of updates and DLC, the number of options of what kind of species you get to build, what kind of government your people favor, the kind of natural endowments bestowed upon them by nature and or the powers that be, has only grown more magnificent (otherwise known as “Perks”).
Machine races that carry on a now not so secret mission of its original creator race? Check.
Hive mind singular in purpose in all organics and or machine minds, it controls? Check.
Human beings called anything you like desperately modifying themselves until ascending into a new form that can be achieved whitelist defending against all manner of spectacle that crawls out of the deep dark void of endless space? Check, ckeckedy, check, check.
There is a much longer list that I could place here but it would say as much about me as it would about you if you sat here and read it, this belongs to people whom play the game and not inside this mini review.
Dare to dream to tempt fate, perhaps to kill a few gods along the way whilst making way to become one yourself?
Buy on sale or not, either way, Stellaris is one sexy sci fi beast of a game waiting for no man to chart its’ skies.

- It's less deep than CK2, by which I primarily mean no long-term thinking. Where in CK2 you somethimes had to keep track of 100 family members and plan your strategy for generations to come, in Stellaris it's more 'in the moment'.
- Naming stuff! If you're a fan of naming stuff, including people, planets, empires, ships, you name it (heh) - you can name them all!
- Idle waiting.... I major draw-back for many Stellaris players is that a lot of the game is spent waiting, at a certain point. Luckily for us CK2 players, we're used to waiting until King John the VII'th is finally of age and can marry the Pope's sister.
- Finally, CK2 was all diplomacy. This is a lot less powerful in Stellaris. There are fewer factors that can influence relations with other species/empires. Stellaris is more resource management than people management, so be prepared for that.
Final note: The (in)famous "Can You Run It" website told me that absolutely no way I could run it. That's nonsense: running without lag at high graphics.

What an ingenious game! Start as a young adult with debts up the yin-yang and a low paying job. But you can change all that by leveling and destroying those horrible debt monsters. (Man, I wish you could do that in real life).
Cubicle Quest has many unique aspects. You begin as the ruler of your own kingdom. The Debt Army is outside your castle and threatening to destroy everything so you've got your work cut out for you. As I've already stated, you begin with a low paying job and everytime you sleep in your bed in the castle, a month advances and you receive your salary - minus many expenses. Rent, food, utilities, entertainment, etc. - all these things eat away your money. However, in the basement of your castle, all these expenses are manifested as monsters that you can defeat to either eliminate or lower their cost.
To the north of your castle is the Dungeon of Work where you can get a promotion (which means more money each month!), IF you can defeat the boss. Unfortunately, your main character, Bob, is kind of a doofus and as soon as he begins to earn more money, he begins spending more. Meaning more monsters to defeat in your castle basement.
There are plenty of places where you can level up. There are also many different people who will join you on your quest - you just have to go out there and find them. You can have 4 active party members. Bob is always one so, most of the time, you can choose the other 3 based on your preferences. Luckily, the party members who aren't "active" still receive half of the experience the normal party gets after each fight.
Battles are also unique in the fact that instead of having elements like fire, water, earth, and air, you're working with personal skills, human skills, work skills, and peace skills. Some enemies obviously fit into one of these categories but mostly you'll have to experiment. When you use a skill, you will see in big letters "Resist" or "Weak" (or nothing) on the monster you cast it on so try everything. At the end of a battle you receive experience and BP points. Equip books on your party that boost stats. I began with the History Book on everyone since that increases experience gained. Each book has a certain number (100 - 250). Fill up those books with BP points and you can unequip the book but continue to get the benefit from it! You don't receive gold from enemies - money only comes from your income or..... there's a little trick to getting rich. You can find lots of neat facts in many helpful guides found on Steam.
Equipment in Cubicle Quest is also a bit different. Instead of equipping weapons and armor, you equip goals, communities, and virtues. Many of these things are strong against certain "elements" so if you're getting whooped in a dungeon, try equipment that protects against different things. Equipment with the highest stats aren't always the best choice.
There's so much to explore and experiment with in this game - it's just a ton of fun. Dialog is usually clever and humorous as well. You can see how many hours I put into this and I loved every minute. Well, maybe not the times I was grinding for levels but you don't really have to do that often. I just like to be op. :p
Now I'll list places of interest in the game and what my party was when I beat the "bonus" last boss. There are many secret areas and tons more open up after beating the game the first time. So here goes:
Castle Sanity: Your very own castle. There are 2 basements - one with expense monsters and one that explains different aspects of the game. So both are very important! When you find a roommate to help with rent, they'll begin chilling in your castle. If you get married, your wife will also move here. And this is the place where you can deploy troops against the Debt Army (use your salary to lower your debts) and also advance months.
Port Nostalgia: This is where Mom and Pop kingdom is. You can rest in an inn here for 200g which is something I did often to keep months from advancing. (I wanted to pay off my debts without getting super old - you DO age in Cubicle Quest).
Societyville: Most of the shops are here. There's a library - explore that first to get some free books to equip on your party members and then buy the rest (the ones you're interested in). Get those History books equipped pronto! Societyville is also where you'll meet Jacob who will craft things for you - for free! You just need to find the items he requires. Some you can buy and others drop off certain monsters.
Tower of Self-Improvement: Multiple floors - each containing a dungeon with treasures and bosses.
Dungeon of Work: Where you go to get promoted and increase your monthly salary. Be prepared - it won't be easy!
Financial Mine: Complete the left side of the dungeon to gain access to a bank account. Defeat the right side to open Investment options.
There are many other places to find. I'll let you do the exploring.
By the final end of the game, I managed to pay off all my debts, buy a house and a car, get married, ..... and I was finally able to pay off my mortgage at age 47. My wife helped. There are quite a few marriage options but some girls will add expenses to you. Others, like my choice, will chip in with the bills. And here's my final party:
Bob: Level 83
(weapon) Goal: A Meaningful Life
(armor) Community: Friendships Renewed
(armor) Virtue: Vision
Accessory: Custom Bike
Cecelia: Level 83
(weapon) Goal: Use Time
(armor) Community: Soulmates
(armor) Virtue: Sorrow
Accessory: Shard of Raw Efficiency
Alayna: Level 83
(weapon) Goal: Find Self
(armor) Community: Discussion Group
(armor) Virtue: Self-Sufficiency
Accessory: Feather of Stats
Lisa: Level 83
(weapon) Goal: Analyze Books
(armor) Community: Financial Independents
(armor) Virtue: Self-Awareness
Accessory: Letter of Resignation
In closing..... whew, I'm tired of all the typing. I'll just say if you enjoy RPGs, definitely give this a try. And I bet those who haven't played many RPGs or aren't super fond of them might find a lot to love about this game regardless. Happy debt slaying!

One of the best strategy games I have ever played, if you would call this a strategy game. The unique idea and original story make this game interesting, but it isn't polished enough to be called a finished product.
Start with a moderate amount of funds and take over a mining site on the planet. The amount you invest in an expidition is the amount you will have to purchase troops, upgrades, weapons. A small amount is taken right at the start of the battle in order to cover the cost of the brain and remote body. If you play smart and use the terrain and your troops effectively you will win without spending much. Simply pouring funds and troops into a battle is sure to make you lose in the long run.
Overall the game runs fine. The graphics are almost dated, but they don't look bad. It almost seems like something from the late nineties. Most players will be challenged, but those who enjoy a unique kind of strategy will love it. Try to start a new campaign and learn some of the basics before you form an opinion. There are some bugs, but nothing game breaking. The devs are still working on this game and there's some great add-on content.

SPACEPLAN is - somehow - a story-driven clicker game. It takes the player through a short story involving mostly potatoes and metaphysics, with basic (potato-based) clicker mechanics driving the progression as you generate more and more energy to power your ship through all the root vegetable shenanigans.
The story itself is wonderful and silly, and though it's unlikely to spark any deep philosophical discussions, it's absolutely worth your (small amounts of) time and money to experience it. The game is also aided by a fantastic soundtrack, and the fact that you can continue generating resources with the game closed (for a little while). This means that, when you come to a point where you need to wait for more energy before continuing the story, you can leave the game completely alone while you do so, which keeps the progression from falling too much into the grind inherent to clicker games.
If you have some time and money to spend, and you want to experience something unique, bizarre, and not at all serious, I definitely recommend SPACEPLAN.

The Witcher may make for a fine book, a great story, a tale to remember, but by golly does it also make for a dull game.
Witcher 2 is, after the narrow introductory sequence, set up as a quasi open-world affair, with the player given a bundle of quests and sidequests that rivals some early MMO's. The issue, however, is that the game seems to lack focus and does a rather poor job of explaining what you are supposed to be doing. This is not helped by the fact that majority of characters you interact with are, true to their universe, utterly unpleasant people to deal with, making it a painful affair to slog through their dialogue trees over and over again.
Combat is clunky and neither of my attempts, one with mouse and keyboard, the other with a gamepad, seemed to result in a pleasant playing experience. Magic powers are nonsensical and for some reason the developers felt that blasting an enemy in the face with a fireball should be completely useless, but a gust of wind will allow you to insta-kill basic enemies at will. Make of that what you will.
Credit where credit is due, though: the lore, the visuals and the voice acting are all absolutely amazing, and I can see how people might get attracted into the Witcher based on these factors alone. If you can tolerate the most annoying protagonist of our time, then perhaps you'll delve deeper into the experience than I ever will. As it stands, I cannot recommend the game.

Simply the best twin stick shooter. Nothing is randomly generated or perfunctory, every level and every difficulty setting challenges you in a DIFFERENT way and most are full of secrets. No experience points or ability trees or downtime. Always just a few more things to think about than you can hold in your brain at once. Other games would impress with this game's graphics and music, but they are actually the least of what's great about this game.
Easier modes are not there as a grudging “win the game” mode for casual players, but to lead them to becoming better players, this is harder to design. The player both gets to feel what it’s like to be better at the game while still constantly having encouragement to improve exactly the skills they will need in the harder difficulties.
And the secrets teach you how to play better. They are discoverable and exciting by accident, but in order to find additional layers of more and more subtle secrets you have to make your dodging and shooting of enemies more and more automatic. They get you to always take as much focus as possible away from the immediate threats to put it on longer term goals, and there are many layers of longer term goals that never feel like stuff there just for the obsessive players, but direct extensions and enhancements of the experience you want to have.

[Pros]

- Multiplayer is fun, lot's of time to spend playing this

This is a nice Indie game that could easily be overlooked. Everything about it screams retro side scroller, however I was pleasantly suprized to see alot of interesting gameplay mechanics. It's part castle defense, part RTS, part contra style shootem up. If any of these things sound appealing to you this may just be your game: building the most inpenitrable base, sending waves of units to take out an enemy base, or Running around blowing limbs of scores of baddies, Resourse management and development, or sitting back and letting the computer do it for you.
The game is based in a very distant future where people's brains controll robotic legions to fight over resources. Everything about the game can be found in its opening cutscene (which might i add is freaken awsome) The core gameplay revolves around you Brain... both literally and virturally represented. The brain is either a moving robot or a static part of your defense that controlls all other actors and units. Its pretty simple kill the Brain, win the game. Initially when you occupy a planet at the same time as an opponet your brain will be air assaulted in with a few minor units ( In most cases a mobile sentry with anti arcraft rocket) From there you can call in additional units expending a gold resource that can be mined. Once a plannet is in your controll you can put your gold into building your dream base or have the computer do it for you. In the campain you set the number of factions and faction types along with the number of brains they have. Once all the brains are gone you win... or loose. Lets move on to the actors/units you can rain firery death with.
There are a few tarting factions in the game ( which can be expanded with player made mods) Each faction has a pool of troops (actors) weapons, tools, and aircraft to choose from. In the campaing by selecting a certain faction gives you a discount towards thier troops and gear, however you are not constrained to just that faction type. When your brain calls up troops you'll have a window that you may select the troops and thier eqipment. You start of with how they get thier, what troop type, and eqipment thier carrying. The initial equipment and weapons is expansive, with every weapon and tool verying greatly between eachother. A unit can hold many weapons and tools and freely switch between them on the fly, however if you load up on to much you cant fly... This brings me to another point. All your units are equiped with jet packs. This is both awesome and fustrationg as menuvering your flyboys and girls cand take some practice; and will most likely end up with your trooper splattered against a wall or something. Its almost like Tribes meets Contra.
The combat in this game can be pretty intertaining. All troops have body parts that can be blown off with well aimed shots; can make them beguin to bleed out or not. Another option is shooting the weapons out of enemies hands. The RTS aspect lets you select a groop of actors and set them on a patroll, Guard, Brain hunt mode, or designated points. You can also form a squad and have them move together and/or follow you. This is a pretty interesting aspect and gives the game some depth and versitility. If you feel like being rambo you can,  want to dropp in with an expensive hit team into the heart of the enemy defenses you can, or if You just want to send wave after wave of troops while you mine for gold Terraria style to fund it YOU CAN!
This is a very enjoyable game and has many interesting elements not utilized by other games. It is however not without its faults. The AI can be less desirable at times, as in getting stuck or just flat out non responsive. The game has a tendency to crash when overloaded with actors in the campain feature. The campain is very easy even on hard difficulty and there are many ways of rigging your planet to be niegh impenitrable. It would be a great improvement if you could choose to drop a couple bombs on key locations before your very vulnerable brain drops from the heavens just to get shot down my spammed rocket infantry.
All in all this is a great indi game and well worth a few bucks just to experience an outside the box game. It didnt have the backing of a AAA design team, yet still happens to pack some oomph.

As far as F2P multiplayer experiences go, this is the best I have played. It is very easy to unlock a dozen heroes to their full potential by just playing without spending any money. It is very polished and receives continous updates. I think it is worth trying for everyone, even people that own and enjoy Overwatch.
The resemblance to Overwatch is undeniable, and I think it is fair to say that the developers started out with the idea to make a F2P variant of it. Having played Overwatch during the beta, I feel that Paladins has far surpassed being a mere "poor man's Overwatch" and contains some terrific ideas and design of its own. The resemblance is just in the base concept and the visual style, of both graphics and UI.
I personally like Paladins more than Overwatch. In Paladins the support and tank heroes are less specialized and can deal good damage on their own, also dependent on card loadouts and bought items, while still being hugely important as far as staying power or healing goes. In Overwatch the damage classes were almost always objectively more fun to play than most tanks and all supports, while a solid team composition requires multiple players to play tanks and support. Healers especially have been implemented in a far more enjoyable way.
And thank god, no Mercy full team-revives, *yawn*.

After having played this a bit against humans rather than the bots I went back to edit this review...
Zip around in an arena and try and blast each other. It's good clean fun with friends.
Are there better games of this type? Sure.
Should you buy this? No, I wouldn't recommend doing so.
Why not? While the core gameplay is kinda fun enough, the game has some serious flaws.
In no particular order:
* It's one of those "unlock" games. When you start up you only have access to the basic gear. That means it sucks when you convince your friends to buy this game at the LAN-party, as they won't have the same options as the veteran players. The unlocks are NOT just cosmetic. Some gear is just plain better. Stupid!
* You buy your weapons during a match by collecting coins from critters. While a novel concept, the first player to buy the big guns is at a big advantage. There are no catch-up mechanics.
* Ammo is too limited. Your weapons runs out very fast. Only way to get more ammo is from a pick-up. Which leads to...
* Pick-up points can be scouted. Good luck being out of ammo while the big guns guard the pick-up spawnpoints. It's probably better to just suicide if you are out of ammo...
* Being a barely animated square character I'm in shock you can't customize it besides picking it's color.
* In team-play it's rather hard to see who belongs to which team.
* The big one... Online/LAN doesn't freaking work properly! All players won't see all other players. This makes the game literally unplayable other than local. Did they not test this?
The game has potential if they would fixe some of the issues mentioned above.
Until then, only buy it in a humble bundle or some other deal.

The pixel art of this game is what drew me in, and the addictive combat is why I keep playing.
Maybe I'm just worse than the devs or more blood thirsty in my hunt for cells, but I'm over the intended play time and I keep dying to the first bosses. Even with recent buffs to player HP the bosses feel overly tanky, and it's really easy to get chipped to death and run out of potions no matter how well you dodge. It seems like unless you get really lucky and all of your items synergize you are simply destined to fail until you can afford the final flask upgrade, because I feel like I'm losing each time by about 1 flasks worth of HP (when my gear isn't top tier).
Dodging in platformers is something I do pretty well as I've been playing since Metroid, and have since enjoyed games like Super Meat Boy, but the "Incomplete One" has an attack where he surrounds himself in spikes that are almost too tall to jump over, and then forces you into a corner, while sending shockwaves at you as well. It's just a lot at once, and it feels overly difficult to avoid enough damage. So I went the other way, and while the tenticle boss was a bit easier, the area before it requires better gear than the area before the other boss, otherwise it's a bit of a hit and run grind.
Right now, though fun, it feels a little bit too much like the game is geared towards failing and grinding out cells so that you can buy upgrades so each round is easier, more than it feels like its a game about learning attack patterns, because most of the mobs are a pretty easy to kill even without dodging well, and then the bosses are drastically harder.
To me it feels like the most consistant way to succeed is to get the freeze blast and something that does a lot of crit damage, while attempting to get items that synergize with this. Best round I had I was freezing people using the teleport to get behind people (which also ups crit damage) and then hitting them with a bow that did more damage against close and frozen targets. I was able to beat the incomplete one this way, but running out of arrows meant that I had to do a lot of teleporting just to dodge, while my turret whittled down the boss and arrows slowly popped out of it. (IMO The arrows getting stuck in enemies is super♥♥♥♥♥when you have bosses that suck up all your arrows, but its fine and kinda cool when facing mobs)
Overall I give this game a solid B rating. I'd really like to see it be a bit more skill based and a bit less grind out cells through failing to win based, but I'm also still having fun playing it.

Stellaris is by far my favorite game on steam.
A long time ago that honor belonged to Civ 5 (lets not ever speak of Civ 6 which isn’t horrible but nor is it fun, where in lies the rub).
Stellaris can be described as what happens when we wish we could play star trek as the many different beings we encounter over the course of an entire civilization from the perspective of the zeitgeist of an entire species.
I felt noble in one play through for protecting so many lesser evolved beings. In others, a vicious fool hooked on a feeling to conquer all nations whom crossed my path.
It always cames down to the numbers though. You either have what it takes to take someone down or you don’t! This could be raw scientific discovery of better weapons, armor and or technology, or it could be partnering up with so many other species that your combined total is now a gargantuan obstacle for any who oppose your mighty coalition of United Nations.   In one play through, an ancient race awoke and after our UN dominated the stars for countless generations this not so new civ tore as apart like we were simply tissue paper.  Other nations whom we had bullied previously simply watched in a gawk horror as they knew that soon this steady tyrant would soon turn it’s insatiable lust for blood for them too. In the end, it was our petty grievances that kept us from finding peace when needed most.
Iron Man mode, which is present in all Paradox games, is the only way to earn achievements. It also means your only means of saving is auto saved for you, so of course, no going backsies!
Now with the latest tier of updates and DLC, the number of options of what kind of species you get to build, what kind of government your people favor, the kind of natural endowments bestowed upon them by nature and or the powers that be, has only grown more magnificent (otherwise known as “Perks”).
Machine races that carry on a now not so secret mission of its original creator race? Check.
Hive mind singular in purpose in all organics and or machine minds, it controls? Check.
Human beings called anything you like desperately modifying themselves until ascending into a new form that can be achieved whitelist defending against all manner of spectacle that crawls out of the deep dark void of endless space? Check, ckeckedy, check, check.
There is a much longer list that I could place here but it would say as much about me as it would about you if you sat here and read it, this belongs to people whom play the game and not inside this mini review.
Dare to dream to tempt fate, perhaps to kill a few gods along the way whilst making way to become one yourself?
Buy on sale or not, either way, Stellaris is one sexy sci fi beast of a game waiting for no man to chart its’ skies.
I’d write more but why?

I simply can't get enough of this game. This is a proper early access game! The polish and improvments each major patch have been great, and it just keeps getting better. I feel that rogue likes and rogue lites are one of the few genres that I enjoy even in early access, as the nature of playing through a hard game with perma death means I get to enjoy hopefully amazing game play time and time agian.
And does this game deliver in the game play department. The controls and feel of the game will probably ruin other combat centric platformers forever, your shambling corpse thing handles like a dream, and the combat is fast paced and brutal. It's super addictive.
Down sides?
It's not quite as fair as say Dark Souls or Ninja Gaiden, and you'll occasionally suffer what will feel like cheap deaths.
The game can feel a bit grindy when you're trying to unlock some of the pricier upgrades and options.
The 'metroidvania' aspect of things is a bit over emphasized, It really doesn't have that kind of exploration or progression like metroid or the symphony of the night family. It tries... but it isn't what this game is really trying to do.
And of course it IS still in early access, and the core systems could still change dramatically.
Overall this is an easy recommendation for platformer fans, and fans of challenging 2d content.

I am a big CK2 fan, so let me write this review from the perspective of and for CK2 player(s).
- Many similarities: you start of designing your race, ruler and homeworld much like the Ruler Designer (inc. trait points), the battle system is very similar (but now with space ship design), you will also find event chains much like those in CK2. Plus: blob to your heart's contenct. Also, you won't have many problems with the interface, the buttons are right there where you expect them to be.
- Appoint leaders much like you would appoint chancellors, stewards etc. And succession plays a role in the leadership too! Though not the kill-all-the-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-nephews-and-marry-a-Viking kind of succession issues.
- It's less deep than CK2, by which I primarily mean no long-term thinking. Where in CK2 you somethimes had to keep track of 100 family members and plan your strategy for generations to come, in Stellaris it's more 'in the moment'.
- Naming stuff! If you're a fan of naming stuff, including people, planets, empires, ships, you name it (heh) - you can name them all!
- Idle waiting.... I major draw-back for many Stellaris players is that a lot of the game is spent waiting, at a certain point. Luckily for us CK2 players, we're used to waiting until King John the VII'th is finally of age and can marry the Pope's sister.
- Finally, CK2 was all diplomacy. This is a lot less powerful in Stellaris. There are fewer factors that can influence relations with other species/empires. Stellaris is more resource management than people management, so be prepared for that.
Final note: The (in)famous "Can You Run It" website told me that absolutely no way I could run it. That's nonsense: running without lag at high graphics.

If you like first-person shooters, RPGs, stealthy, or hacker games, you will enjoy Deus Ex.
The story is great. I mean, it's like PFFFSSSSHHHHHHH awesome. It is far from "just another FPS." There are few qualities this game shares with other FPSes. One is the ability to make choices. Not a very ground-breaking addition to a game, but it is when it's a game with guns. There is also a story-line, unlike your Call of Duty games, which doesn't have a real story. You can't just take a rapid-fire weapon and run into battle holding M1 and win. No. You need to hack your way through security panels, manipulate sentry guns to fire at the enemy, sneak around large groups of terrorists... There is nothing this game deosn't have (with the exception of graphics and physics, but hey, this is from 2000, what do you expect?).
As for the multiplayer, it is fun if you have friends to play with. It's hard to find a public server with people on it. But it is still playable. Just go download Hamachi, host a server, and have your friends join through LAN using your Hamachi ip. But this really isn't a game for multiplayer.
The music is excelent. I'd love to be able to take them and put them on my MP3 player to listen to them at all times. This game probably has some of the best music ever made for video games.
Overall, you should get this game. It's great. And don't bother to get Invisible War. Humanity is in an agreement that that game never happened. Right guys? RIGHT?

Deus Ex is a sort of classic that I have a hard time commenting on, as everything has been said about it multiple times. For the uninitiated, Deus Ex is a first person action-rpg. That is to say, it's an rpg with guns. But guns aren't the only option. You can rely on stealth, a variety of lethal and non-lethal weapons, and even, occasionally, automated security systems. To aid this, you have several powers you can use and upgrade throughout the game, often to a superhuman extent.  While these options are becoming more-and-more frequent in current games, Deus Ex is still sort of a pioneer in how open your options are, and still provides more depth than many games today. My own character ended up relying on his wits, speed, an a bit of stealth camo, unless he was cornered, in which case he was suddenly a character from the Matrix, weaving around rockets as they were fired at me and dispatching what was essentially a SWAT team with a sword.
Honestly, however, what brought me through about 3 dozen hours of gameplay was not the gameplay itself, but the story. Deus Ex is a facinating medley of every conspiracy theory you have heard of forced to interact with each other in a world that is quite literally dying. One can spend a lot of time simply wading through e-mails and newspapers, gaining a better understanding of an increasingly bleak culture. Presented with questions of the role of government of society, the rights of the individual, and man's relationship with technology, leaving you as the player to determine your own beliefs. The works of Thomas Aquinas, Voltaire, and other philosophers and futurists are brought up. The story is wonderfully unapologetic about how reflective it seeks to be.
The game has its flaws, notably AI that gives up on chases far too quickly and some bad voice acting in some unfortunate areas, but I'd be hard pressed to suggest anyone should skip something so unique. Ultimately, however, if someone appreciates games with story, there's a beautiful little sci-fi novel packed into this massive game.

Enter Defragmented At face value it might look like a Hotline Miami knockoff, but what ended up in play was a much different story. The futurewave has hit, and hard, sending us out games like Far Cry: Blood Dragon, dripping in neon thumping music that matches the atmosphere of wetwork involved. It's a trend that I'm glad to be on board with, the nostalgia of the 80's a welcome place in my gaming heart.
You play as a newcomer to a cyber-esque future city called Entropolis, working your way up a chain of involvement that mirrors your talent trees. The player can choose from three different unique classes - Cyberzerker, Railrunner and Ascended. This allows for the malleable gameplay, and shapes your end game accordingly. Each class has it's own specific special ability to tailor what kind of destruction you wish to cause. And with the top down view, you feel like your a rat in a maze, fighting the next for your cut of the cheese.
The gameplay was fast, hard and unforgiving. But with the right planning for each small job, you can make your way through quite smoothly. A very satisfying win to each level also--when the last enemy hits the pavement, and the stats of the day's work roll in with a sigh of relief and exhilaration. They don't forget to shower you in credits and Deal-EO tokens to upgrade though, making the feeling of a lost level not entirely impossible to overcome by any means. It feels good to win at this game...and I would certainly say that's what keeps you coming back for more pain each time.
The build of the objects and their surroundings might come off as simple at first, but are actually quite ingenious. Everything is made into geometric shapes, causing you to concentrate on how you're moving through each level. The pacing causing you to skip stopping off and smelling the flowers. Not to say you can't do this though--after each last blow, the level officially ends, giving you the score, but also leaving it open to explore before you calmly exit the premises. Lockers and dumpsters full of goodies--that room you might have missed when you were dodging a mounted machine gun...it doesn't rob you of the chance of a neat cleanup. This also adds to the replayability of the levels, as after you officially beat them, the items don't ghost out. It's an easy touch, one that makes me think the developers were quite in tune with how they wanted us to have fun.
If the playing bit doesn't entice you enough, there's always the soundtrack. A gorgeous mixture of what's widely called the 'retro wave' genre...it effectively gets a blood flow going at all the right moments, and reels you back in for an interesting dystopic storyline. A stand alone buy on its own.
In all, this game comes highly recommended on my end, something you won't regret having in your library. It's unique and challenging for the seasoned gaming vet, and easy enough for a casual gamer to enjoy as well. You don't want to miss out on this one!

As a huge fan of cyberpunk work and shooters I was drawn to
, and that is what made it hard to come to a conclusion about this game for I really wanted to like it buut ultimately it feels like it still needs a lot of work and polish.
describes itself as
but I disagree, I prefer to say it is a shooter with some minor RPG elements. I’ll first adress the things I like about the game and which kept me playing as well as giving a general insight on what the game has to offer.
The game focuses heavily on fast-paced shooting in which characters can die in a split second, weapons with various different stats that you can loot and leveling up 1 out of 3 available characters, each with their own unique set of abilities and starting weapon. When starting a new game you can select 1 out of 2 modes,
, which is described as “the way the game was meant to be played”, and
in which the characters can soak a lot more damage. Besides the shooting part of the game, you have this kind of visual novel style of dialogue which happens between levels and fills you in on the story. The game also offers a couple of bonus stories, which are basically sets of dialogue expanding on some characters from the main game.
I like the fact that the game has 3 difficulty options to choose from, the variety of weapons that you have at your disposal and the ability to approach any level the way I want, go in stealthy using melee attacks or going in guns blazing. The game gets progressively harder and harder and, in a way, I thank the devs for not making the levels procedural generated. The fact that each of the levels are hand crafted lets you learn your way around and improve yourself, as well as develop different tactics, the more you play it.
One thing I can’t stress enough is how good the music is. All those times I was getting slightly annoyed by some of the problems the game has, it was one of the things that managed to keep me in line for it is so good to listen to (considering you’re into this type of music). The other thing that kept me going was the story. At first it felt okay but around half way through the game things get more interesting, if somewhat predictable.
Now for the sad part. First of all, the game is a shooter and as such it allows you to choose between a top down view camera (default) and some sort of isometric camera. The latter feels wonky and I can’t imagine why you’d use this over the other, especially when you can “look ahead” of you to see your surroundings. Also, having to spam E to loot things is kind of bothersome, at least to me, why don’t you pick up credits and ammo automatically by walking over them?
The biggest problem I have with the game are the enemies. While playing in the same difficulty setting, on the same level, they can either be extremely deadly or real dummies. Sometimes enemies would start shooting the wall when I was on the opposite side. There were numerous in which my shots missed the target but, even though they were crossing the enemy field of vision, they just stood there doing nothing. There were also times in which 2 enemies were facing each other and if I killed one of them the other wouldn’t react. That said, seeing their fellow comrades on the floor, dead, didn’t seem to bother them either.
Another nuisance I have is related to the visual side of the game but not the graphics themselves. For instance, the fact that the UI looks very odd and it isn’t very appealing, it feels like a placeholder. The fact that the game reuses the same backgrounds during the dialogue sections a lot of times, a bit of variety would be nice there to keep things interesting. In addition, the main character has no portrait and never speaks directly but you act sort of as the game’s narrator.
I really wanted to like this game but due to all the tech side of things I don’t feel comfortable in recommending it. Besides what I’ve mentioned, it’s worth pointing out that it takes about 6 hours to complete the story mode, and then you have NG+. For the asking price of 15€, I’m not really sure I can say it is worth it.

I’m only recommending this game with a caveat in mind which is explained below. For a more in-depth review, please check out the video below:
Otherwise, here’s a summarized pros and cons list after a primer on the game.
Nex Machina is a twinstick shooter that often delves into bullet hell territory. Using a normal blaster, a dash mechanic and some special weapons, the objective is to clear each room of enemies and defeat the boss and the end of the level, all while trying to get as high a score as possible. You can play all worlds in succession (via arcade mode), a score attack of one world (via Arena mode) or any world individually at your discretion (via Single World mode). There’s also local coop for Arcade and Single World mode, though there is no support for online coop whatsoever.
1) Good performance
Runs at around 150 ish region with all settings at max with a gtx 980ti. Does not stutter even when screen is filled with the many many particle effects flying around everywhere.
2)  Decent Shooter Trance
The game’s mechanics are rather simple. Analogs to control movement and shooting respectively while shoulder button is used to dash (with I-frames). As you continue through the rooms, you pick up powerups in the form of special weapons and upgrades, the former of which is the more interesting. Special weapons range from things like lasers, remote bombs, smartbombs, rocket launchers, etc and their low cooldown incentivizes you to use them as much as possible, thereby changing up your playstyle as well since they each have their own optimal use case.
Enemies will try to overwhelm you with numbers and since the game has such a low margin of error (you die in one hit), especially on the higher difficulties where more and faster enemies are introduced, it challenges you to be responsive, have smart judgement and manage your resources (in terms of your available dodges) well. The dynamic between you and the enemies is only further enhanced when robots that do things like shoot projectile and lazers get introduced, thereby adding an aura of bullet hell into the mix. Ultimately, I find this part of the core gameplay loop, regardless of its repetitiveness and lack of progression, a compelling experience. To be able to best overwhelming odds with my full arsenal makes it easy to just sink time into this game. As unforgiving as the game can be, deaths themselves never feel unfair, though what they lead to can be an unfair circumstance, but more on that in the cons. For now, if you like twin sticks, this one doesn’t do anything too original but it does well for what it offers.
3)  Functional presentation
Games that try to be flashy often do it at the expense of unnecessary visual fluff and the abundance of particle effects in Nex Machina is bound to garner mixed reception, I’d like to bring your attention to their functional visual designs as well. Useful information like how much time is left for a temporary score multiplier (since this is also a score attack game) to be in effect is implemented in the game zone itself in the form of a circle that’s closing in on itself. The same can also be said about the audio since there is a narrator that passes you rather useful information about your arsenal, such as when you’ve lost your shield or when you’ve gotten all the upgrades. It might seem like a trivial thing, after all you can see what upgrades you have, but once you get used to how little the margin of error there is in this game, you start to realize how detrimental it can be to take your eyes off the centre of the screen for even the slightest of moments, especially given the fact that you die in one hit.
1) The implementation of the death mechanic
Remember when I said we’d get back to how deaths can lead to unfair situations? Well to understand that, you should know that Nex Machina uses a simple retry/ continue system that arcades use. X number of lives per retry and if you waste them you gotta use a credit to have another go. While you’re still able to retain your gear after losing lives, a retry or continue forces you to abandon your loadout completely, causing you to continue from that point on with the base (and rather weak) equipment. Normally, this wouldn’t be a problem since it doesn’t take long for these upgrades to randomly drop again but when you take into account the fact that you’ll normally have to use the retry or continue function during the boss which resides in the last stage of a level, then you’ll notice how common it is to fight the hardest encounters with the least amount of equipment. This seems like an unnecessarily harsh punishment since some of the upgrades we lose are almost crucial to our survival (the triple dash brings with it 3 times the amount of I-frames). While you could argue that every boss is beatable without any upgrades, it still doesn’t get away from the fact that the main appeal of the game lies in using the upgraded equipment, so creating a situation where you don’t have said equipment when you probably need it will end with the user feeling more frustrated than challenged.
This game gets a circumstantial recommendation because of the way it’s built. It’s designed to be replayed over and over again, whether to get a higher score on the same difficulty setting, or to try to complete all the worlds again on a harder preset. If you’re into either of these things, then you’re likely able to find the value in your 20 dollar investment. However, if you’re someone who wants to just picked this up to experience the twin stick shooting from start to end a single time, then content wise I’d only recommend getting it at 12 dollars instead.

This has always been my favorite Final Fantasy, and while that may be because of the nostalgia from playing it when I was little, I enjoyed it much more replaying it in recent years. Unfortunately, the Steam port is inferior to the PS1 version, but with a couple of mods and some tweaks it makes it far more enjoyable. Overall the story, characters, and gameplay are great and the graphics really are amazing considering the year it came out. Its hard for me to write anything negative about this game for the simple reason that I've enjoyed it so much and played it multiple times. The junction system takes some time to figure out, but it adds to the unique qualities that FFVIII has along with an awesome story that any SciFi/Romance fan would love. The soundtrack is also noteworthy for one of the best in the series.
However, everyone formulates their own opinion, and while myself and many other loves this game, there are those who probably hate it and would not recommend it as well. All I can say is play it and see for yourself. In my opinion FFVIII is a solid 9/10. This is a game that I think is worthy of a modern remake for the PS4 after the FFVII remake is finished and released.
