In this review, I will try to help you answer two questions:
1. Should you play Final Fantasy VIII?
2. Should you play the Steam version as opposed to some other release?
=== SHOULD YOU PLAY FINAL FANTASY VIII ===
If you're even considering Final Fantasy VIII, I assume you're a fan of JRPGs; I'm not gonna try to convince someone who doesn't like JRPGs to play this game. Even if you're looking to get into the genre, FF8 is by no means an entry-level JRPG. For that, I would probably recommend Final Fantasy VI instead (note: do NOT get the Steam or Mobile version of that; play it on SNES or GBA.)
- Gameplay -
FF8 is a slow game with a lot of parts that drag, so queue up hours of YouTube videos, podcasts, audiobooks, or whatever to put on in the background while you do some of the more tedious parts of the game. I played recently FF8 for two reasons. The first is because I never beat it as a kid because of how broken and stupid it is, and I wanted to go back to it and finally check it off on a mental checklist as "a game I beat" instead of "a game I gave up on." The second and more important reason is because I had a pretty long backlog of YouTube videos in Watch Later I wanted to clear out, and I wanted a mindless game to play in the background while I did so. FF8 served that function very well.
I will give it to you straight: FF8 is a badly designed game. FF8 punishes you for trying to play it like a normal JRPG. FF8 almost demands that you exploit it. I would honestly suggest playing the game with a guide open and following it start to finish. If you're a completionist, the game will drive you absolutely mad if you don't. This is quite possibly the worst designed Final Fantasy game with the possible exception of Final Fantasy II (that's the one starring Firion, for those of you who still insist on calling Final Fantasy IV by the wrong name.) It honestly baffles me how they made such a broken, unfun, unsatisfying battle system hot on the heels of the massively successful Final Fantasy VII; it's almost like they wanted to drive people away from the genre. FF8 feels rushed, like they were trying to get the successor to FF7 out as fast as possible. It is technically finished, but could have used a lot of work on the balance, and on developing the junction system more.
The root of the problem is the fact that the game has level scaling. As you level up, so do the enemies. However, the enemies get stronger faster than you, so leveling up is actually counter-productive! The main way to get stronger is through Junctioning magic to your stats. If you're at a low level with all of the strongest magic Junctioned to your stats, you'll steamroll almost any enemy in the game. At a high level, you can still win, but it's more difficult. Therefore, you should learn the Enc-None ability which disables random encounters as early as you can, and equip it pretty much throughout the whole game to keep your levels low. This alleviates a lot of the tedium of constant random encounters as well. At the very end of the game, you can equip abilities that grant you stat boosts as you level up, and grind up to level 100 then (which takes almost no time, surprisingly.)
Although you want to avoid EXP, you still need AP. You can gain AP by grinding Fastitocalons on the Balamb beach early in the game (this grants some EXP, but is the best AP to EXP ratio early in the game), and Cactuars later in the game (which grants tons of AP and almost no EXP.) You can use Card to kill enemies without getting EXP if you want to be a perfectionist about keeping your levels low, but I'll tell you right now, straight up, don't do this. It takes forever and isn't worth it. You'll probably get to level 20-30 from grinding Fastitocalons, but don't worry about it. You'll still do very well against enemies at this level.
Unless you deliberately kill off Squall while grinding, or take one of the rare few opportunities to grind while Squall is not in your party, he will wind up being about twice the level of everyone else. This isn't actually a big deal, because you hardly get stronger as you level up anyway, but it's one of those little frustrations that point to the game being not-so-well-designed. Many other FF games have this same setup where you have many party members rotating in and out and the main character rarely if ever leaves the party, but none of them have this issue where the main character breaks ahead of everyone else by dozens of levels. I don't get why it happens here.
The game's main "character customization" system comes in the form of Junctioning, which I mentioned before but didn't go into detail on. I will now. Junctioning is not very fun or satisfying, and doesn't offer you very many options for how to develop your characters. It makes each character a blank slate that you can swap different configurations onto instantly, which causes each character to lose any kind of unique identity, minus Limit Breaks. Contrast this to, say, Final Fantasy IV where each character is unique. Or contrast it to Final Fantasy V or Bravely Default, where each character is a blank slate at the start, but you give them their own unique identity by developing them in different directions. The Job System in those games is also very thematically interesting and it makes character growth satisfying. The way you make character stronger in this game is by Junctioning magic to your stats. Greater quantities of magic, and more powerful spells, give you greater boosts. Each character can stock at most 100 of each spell. The two ways you get magic are to draw them from enemies (which is pretty tedious) or by refining cards and items into magic. High-level magic is only available from high-level monsters, so if you're keeping your levels low like you should be, the only way to get it is to refine cards and items. One annoyance I'll touch on here is that each character can only hold 32 spells, and there are significantly more spells than that in the game.
The card game is technically optional, but the rewards you get from it are too good to ignore. If you keep your levels low like you should, the card game will be the earliest available source of a lot of powerful items and magic. I'm not gonna lie, the card game will be a significant time investment, but it will pay off. You'll spend a few hours doing it at Balamb Garden early in the game to build up a nice stock of cards from Level 1-5. This goes much faster if you use the Queen of Cards to set the regional trade rule to All. Your first few games will be difficult because your starting cards suck, but once you start winning a few games you won't ever face that much difficulty with it. From there, you'll only have to play cards every once in a while to get all the rare cards you need. However, you will have to invest a few hours into moving the Queen of Cards around and setting the rules in each region to the ones you want. I'm not gonna pretend this is fun; honestly, it sucks pretty hard. However, apart from these annoying chores, the card game is decently fun; less tedious than random encounters, that's for sure.

Final Fantasy VIII is one of the best Final Fantasy games, if not of all games, of all time. I'll make a quick list of pros and cons of the game that won't spoil any storyline:
Pros:
1. Open World - The map is completely open world, and can be freely traveled and explored (aside from some missions that do not allow exiting to the world map).
2. Large World - The open world is large enough that you can find something entertaining and fun to do each time you play, well after you've beaten the main storyline. Great great great replay and continous play fator.
3. Deep and Interesting Story - The storyline is rich and keeps you drawn in and wanting to know what's going to happen.
4. Character Development - There is good character development, and you get to grow with the main storyline characters
5. GF System - I LOVE, LOVE, LOVE the Gaurdian Force system. One of the best fighting concepts of any of the Final Fantasy games, in my opinion.
Some of the Cons:
1. No way to skip cutscenes - It would be great to be able to skip these on replays.
2. Drags on - Some of the storyline, while a great story, seems to drag on a little bit too much, enough to take way from the enjoyment of the game. I won't say what parts as to not spoil it, but after playing it should be obvious what parts I've referring to.
3. No voice - It would be amazing to have voice acting for this game. To hear some of the interactions instead of reading the sub-titles would be awesome!
That's really it. This game is well rounded and a staple in any game library. It will forever be one of my all time favorite games and to me, one of the best games in the Final Fantasy series.

I recommend this game, because I absolutely love the world, cutscenes, characters, and story. Where I find most of the problems lie are in the systems/combat.
-Most of your combat will have to be done through Guardian Forces (GF's), which every time you use/activate plays a fairly lengthy cutscene attack, and while they can be impressive it makes battles extremely long.
-There is a junctioning system to upgrade your character by equipping magic to attributes, but it requires a lot of tedious farming of magic.
Having beat the original the hard way, I can say I was able to enjoy this game so much more because of the "cheats" they added to the PC version. Yes I'll admit I'm not playing the game as it was originally intended anymore, and not getting the full challenge, but for someone that really enjoys the story, world, and characters it was simply the most efficient, and enjoyable way for me to experience this content.
So point being, if you don't use the cheats I'd just recommend doing some reading ahead of time for tips on junctioning/weapons/GF and draw locations to make the experience smoother.
Only other note is that while the game is on PC, the backgrounds still appear extremely low resolution, as if they never had anything but the PS1 assets.

Take a good game and make it even better. That's basically what CD PROJECT RED did.
The Witcher 2 is a sequel to The Witcher 1. You continue your journey as Geralt of Rivia, a professional monsterslayer, aka a witcher. A month has passed since The Witcher 1's ending. After Geralt saved king Foltest from the mysterious assassin, Foltest kept Geralt as a personal bodyguard. In the beginning of this game Foltest's army is attacking the La Valette's castle to save Foltest's children. After long attack they finally get his children but another assassin murders Foltest and escapes. There starts a new journey to find the kingslayer.
This game really fixed many of the weak points the first game had. Bad graphics and poor optimization? Well they made them better. Boring combat system? That is also made better. The developers like literally took The Witcher 1, figured out what was bad about it and made it better. That's the way how all sequels should be done.
The graphics are very good. Even for a game that was released in 2011. Sometimes you may notice yourself just looking at the beautiful landscapes. The optimization is also much better. It ran on my pc just fine. On high settings 60fps like 95% of the time. Framerate only dropped sometimes during rain and storms.
The combat system really got the biggest change. Not anymore that point and click style. Now it's more like, kinda like Dark Souls stylish combat. You dodge and roll alot and make couple quick hits and so on. Much better than in The Witcher 1.
I've heard people saying that the combat is really hard. I just got to say that they play it wrong way. You don't just dive into combat and start spamming the attack button, because that is the way to die. You need to prepare for combat, drink some potions, make bombs and blade oils. And during combat you really need to use those your magic spells called Signs. Use Axii to make one enemy your ally, use Quen to make you magical shield, use Yrden to trap the enemy, use Igni to burn the enemy and use Aard to knock 'em back. Also you don't just stand still, you need to roll around to not to get hit.
The world is petty cool too. There are three main areas that you can explore during your journey. The maps aren't superbig, but since your only choice is to travel on foot, the world may seem to be big. No fast traveling. The world also seems to be quite realistic. It's not like your typical fantasy world that your mom told you stories about before you went to bed. Like there are wars and conflicts going on, political matters and racism. Also if you want to get a tattoo removed, it costs you quite alot to buy the ingredients for it. I was like ''Wow, that's pretty damn realistic''
The RPG-elements are good in this game. You can upgrade Geralt's skills, have a lot of conversations with characters and make your own choices that impact how the story plays on. There are plenty of side quests. They usually have couple of different ways how you can play them. Minor spoiler but it's only a side quest: You get a contract where you have to kill a troll that lives under a bridge. So you can just go there and kill it and get your reward. But then one villagers tells you not to kill it because it takes care of the bridge. It just started drinking and wont do anything else. So you have two options, to kill the troll or not to kill it and try to help. It's your choice how you want to play it.
This game is improved from The Witcher 1 on many ways. So I can recommend this to more people. If you like good story driven action adventure RPGs, this is a game for you. But if you hate RPGs then you probably wont like this. If you buy this on sale for like under 2€ I can say it is worth it.

This one has me scratching my head.  I know so many people that love this game, and there is always two or three thousand people playing it.  The best thing this game has going for it is the sound track. The game-play is beyond repetitive, the player has to start from scratch every time with no load-out options, the enemies have so many advantages over the player, and there is no description for any of the items the player can find.

To bad the first of each item that is found will have to be wasted, seeing that there is no explanation to what any of them do.  A lot of these items will get the  player killed the first time around, not knowing that it gives a de-buff.
I'm perfectly fine with the grotesque humor and art style.  It makes the game stand apart -- not the game-play.  A big emphasis was put on the random dungeon generation, which is all well and good; unfortunately, the game turns into a game of chance rather than skill.  On multiple occasions I walked through a  door only to find myself surrounded by enemies before having the chance to get two steps.
I wont call The Binding of Isaac a bad game, but I will say that it is not worth all the hype.  Get it when it's less than a dollar.

This game is supposed to be 4X but often feels more like 2X due to how strangely it handles the eXpansion part and lacks eXtermination. It is also fairly dumbed down in terms of research and combat.
Pros:
+Awesome Star Trek style events and anomolies to make it more interesting.
+Very stylish species and artwork.
+Has multiplayer mode.
+Can play across a large galaxy with systems in the 1000+ range.
+Science vessels play a huge role in exploration.
+Can play on Earth with accurately named planets and nearby stars.
Maybes:
~Real Time game. Makes little or no sense that ships are fighting in real time while the clock is going 1 day per second, but who really cares? One month is one turn, so it's fake real time as well.
~Research is 3-4 randomly selected research items that you can choose. Eventually, you can get them all, but it makes a huge difference which ones become available first adding to luck factor.
~Planets cannot be conquered, only occupied. Unless the AI surrenders the planet, it stays theirs regardless of how many troops you land on it.
~War is non-intuitive. Can only declare based on surrender conditions and cannot ask for too much thanks to a "warscore" mechanic making it mostly impossible to exterminate.
~Policy is ridiculously inflexible. Unless you have the right government type, you are restricted in everything from bombardments to colonizing planets with animals present. Seriously, even pre-sentient ones block you from settling.
~Sectors. Game penalizes anyone trying to expand with research penalties and restricting to only 5 controllable systems(10 max with the right government type). Everything else must be in an AI sector.
Cons:
-Cannot start out as a team in multiplayer mode. You're often stuck on opposite sides of the galaxy forever.
-Ship battles are the worst of any 4X game I have ever played. You have 2 options: continue to let the AI fight or flee. There is no control of anything else, not even choosing a target.
-Most weapons are useless. Missiles and strike craft can't make it past the point defenses and mass drivers aren't as good as laser/disrupter combos. Ship customization might as well not exist.
Summary:
Initially fun but restrictive game that feels like a casual version of MOO3 meets Civilization and SOASE with some Star Trek styling to make it interesting. How you like this game will almost certainly rest on whether you think the "maybes" make the game better or worse.

Stellaris is a game that will on the first playthrough engage and challenge you. Subsequent playthroughs become less engaging as you come to grasp how the different knobs and levers of governance work. The main issue is the mid-game- there is little to no content in terms of narrative or challenge. You are not facing financial ruin due to a sudden inflation rate, You are not quelling an uprising, or straight up secession apropos of sudden political change too quick to respond to, you are not dealing with terrorists, funded either by malcontents within or without of your borders, you do not have to deal with the continuous challenge of holding your empire together because of competing political blocks (irregardless of whether or not they have any say within your political system). There are no sudden disasters that require delicate bipartisan co-operation between uneasy borders. There is, in short, little to nothing to add more flavour to the game beyond altering the difficulty.
Fleet combat is a numbers game, technological research means nothing in terms of specialisation. There is no subterfuge. Nothing that really gives the 'strat' element to a 'grand strategy'. Even the win conditions are vague at best.
In short, its a game that has a lot of potential and I'm holding out for more, I recommend the game, because at its core, even with all my complaints, I still find myself looking at the clock and wondering where the hell the hours went.

Thie Review Originally Appeared on
on 2/29/16 -  For the full review;
When I first heard the announcement that Glass Knuckle Games, creators of the fabulous Thief Town (seriously, Thief Town comes in a VERY close second behind Knight Squad in my list of “Greatest Indie Party Games of all time”) were doing a Cyberpunk RPG. I was excited. It gets said a lot, but Cyberpunk is an often underrepresented genre in media and in gaming. I think that we could see Cyberpunk dethrone Steampunk from its places as the most popular geek sub-culture in the near future, but currently, seeing a good Cyberpunk game release is a relatively rare thing, particularly if you discount Shadowrun.
Defragmeneted is here to help scratch that Cyberpunk itch.
Defragmented knows what it is aiming for, and it hits the mark. It’s a fast paced, loot-based top down Run-and-Gun RPG, and while it is not without a few missteps, the mechanics are tight, and lend themselves to hours of mixing and matching guns and abilities, trying to nail down a combination of stats that’ll let you run and gun your way through the bright neon levels as long as your reflexes are fast enough.
The RPG elements of Defragmented are well implemented, if basic. When you begin the game, you have the choice of one of three classes, and have two trees of abilities into which you pump skill points as you level up. My main play through was as an Ascendant, and all my abilities felt powerful, if situational. I was able to use Fracture, a short range psychic melee attack, Ascension, which was a sort of stacking damage buff earned through kills, and Intervention, a psychic shield that drained my energy over time. However, once I got a couple good guns in my loadout, I didn’t end up using my abilities all that often. They simply didn’t feel as important while I was toting around a shotgun that could obliterate anyone I pointed it in the direction of. This very well may be a case of mismatched play style and class though, so take this critique with a grain of cyber-salt.
The best part of Defragmented’s gameplay however, is the random loot. Loot drops aren’t super common in the game, but happen often enough to keep you excited for the next one. Since weapon stats are randomized in both drops and at the in-game DEAL-EO shops, you’re on a constant hunt for a great new shotgun or SMG to use. And boy, is it a good feeling when you get a good gun. I almost think that gun power is tuned a little bit too high in Defragmented, as getting one legendary gun with the perfect stats can change the course of your gameplay. Yet,  your so squishy to enemy attacks that I think this isn’t a substantial issue, and doesn’t break the game or your enjoyment of it.
However, somewhat frustratingly and somewhat brilliantly, this sword cuts both ways in Defragmented. Enemies also have their weapon type and qualities randomized in each level. On your first attempt in a new level, you might go up against a standard rapid fire turret, only for it to become an epic shotgun turret death-machine in the next run. This can feel a bit unfair at times, creating situations in certain levels where you don’t really have a chance, but I like it. It keeps you on your toes, forces you to pay attention, and helps levels remain fresh when playing them over and over again.
Which you will do. Because you will die. A lot.
Defragmented is a tough game, and after the first couple introductory levels there is a MASSIVE ramp up in difficulty (the game actually warns you about this, which I laughed at like a fool the first time I saw the PSA). I like this kind of challenge, but I’m sure there are many gamers that will find this a bit too harsh. And that’s okay; different strokes for different folks!
In regards to the look and feel of the game, Defragmented NAILS the cyberpunk aesthetic when you are inside the levels. Each level is a mix of bright neon lights, angular lines, and cold futuristic hallways. The pulsing synth soundtrack is one of the best electronic game soundtracks I’ve ever heard, and perfectly sets the stage for running and gunning in the Cyberpunk world that Glass Knuckle Games has created. I could go on, but I really don’t think I have to: the aesthetic of Defragmented’s levels speaks for itself.
However, in between these levels of run-and-gun madness are short narrative sequences. These felt very jarring to me from an artistic standpoint.  I liked the story of Defragmented, which was full of conspiracy and terrorism, and a wonderfully imaginative cyber death cult,but the art style used in these scenes is vastly different from the art style you see when you are inside the gameplay levels. Inside these levels, there is a Tron feel to everything; bright neon lights, lots of angles, and low poly models. However, in these narrative sequences, the art style is done in a much more classically animated style; bright primary colors, crisp lines and plenty of detail. Both, individually, are done very well. However, side-by-side, they are so radically different that it takes me out of my immersion in the cyberpunk world of Defragmented.
When all is said and done, I’d recommend Defragmented to anyone looking for a fast paced, if at times punishing, game. Any fan of the Cyberpunk genre should certainly check the game out, if at a bare minimum for the soundtrack, and the few very minor missteps in design don’t in any way effect your enjoyment of the story, or of the absolutely fantastic gameplay. Glass Knuckle has delivered a very solid loot based RPG that promises hours of enjoyment and a great deal of replayability.

I like this game. It has many tropes common to arpg's: loot, leveling up, abilities etc..., but its combat is refreshingly different than most arpg's. I have not gotten too far into the story yet, but wanted to give it a positive review because the combat is so different.
Missions are brief, usually kill everyone or retrieve data. There are usually between 3-6 enemies per mission (so far). Just like in real life, no one in this game survives more than one or two shots. Instead of facing down hordes of foes spamming heal potions, the goal of every enemy encounter is to ambush the enemy, picking the approach that gives the best odds of surviving quick, brutal gunfights where even just one bullet can put you down. In fact, it is best to never take any opponent head on.  Flanking, waiting for patrolling guards to turn around, and the element of surprise are essential for success.
It can be frustrating at first, but there seems to be no penalty for dying. Once I got used to the pace of the gunfights, I learned to approach each enemy tactically, using the environment to maximize my odds, and the game became quite fun.

This is a pretty divisive game in the series due to its battle system. Final Fantasy VIII is overall a pretty good RPG with memorable characters, lots of unique monsters, great summons, and a fairly large world. It's a little shorter than some of the other final fantasy games and the battle system revolves around "junctioning" guardian forces (summons/eidolons) to your characters and then junctioning magic to stats such as junctioning fira to your strength to make you stronger. In addition you have limited ability slots with basic ones like GF (summon), draw, magic, item, etc. You also get others later on such as Mug, Darkside and Recover. You also have secondary ability slots for passives, such as Luck +50% or Initiative. The main issue with this system is that you spend a lot of time during combat drawing over and over to fill up your characters stock of magic, and in many cases you won't want to use said magic during battle because you're using it to increase your overall stats. The system isn't really as bad as people make it out to be, but it can get tedious and it's certainly not as good as materia or any of the older games.
In terms of visuals, the game has aged a "little" better than FF7, but this version did not update them at all and they're still pretty ugly. That being said, there's a number of mods that do a good job of making the game look much nicer than it originally did, so I'd recommend checking those out. Audio is a sore spot for this port as the sound and music are actually lower quality than the PSX original release, but again there's mods to fix that. I personally used Roses and Wine and it sounds fantastic.
Overall, it's a fun game still. The story gets a bit weird later on and the ending is basically nonsensical but I still think if you can get past the draw system that it's an enjoyable game. On that note this game has built in cheats that do not block achievements. If you want to save yourself some annoyance with the draw system, they help a lot. They do make the game a lot easier (obviously), but if you just want to see the story or you've already done this all before like I have, they're a nice option to speed things along.

Zup 3 is the third installment of the Zup franchise by Quiet River. With it's simple and easy-to-understand objective, it gets addictive quickly as the game requires you to use your brain with more complex layouts for the ball to land on the designated area.
The visuals are a bit meh...Don't get me wrong. Just because a game has great (and/or realistic) graphics, doesn't mean it's a great game to play in terms of gameplay and replayablity. But the game looks like a flash game. Not to say that's a bad thing, it's just...meh... The background looks pretty plain as well with some random white shapes and a green door to advance the next stage once you've completed a puzzle. Overall, visuals not bad but some may not find it appealing to look at.
The game has a very simple objective. You click the red blocks to make force for the yellow blocks which makes the white ball move to the area that will clear the stage. Very simple. But as you advance to the higher stages, you'll need to be quicker mentally to get the timing right. It's easy to understand but can get challenging to master.
There's none. I'm not joking. As far as I'm aware, there's no offficial soundtrack in the game. For those who play music for the soundtrack, there is none, so you're better off listen to your own music.
It's a game that I reccommend for those who are into puzzles and those who are good into speed puzzles. Plus, it comes with nice achievements and Steam trading cards to spice up your profile, if you want to become a fancy and stylish player on Steam. Otherwise if you're not into puzzles, this isn't a reccommendation.
+Addictive gameplay that requires you to use your brain to think and do quick reactions.
+Easy to understand objective.
+Nice achievements and Steam trading cards for your profile.
+Nice colours to look at.
+Becomes challenging later on.
-Somewhat bland visuals.
-No music whatsoever besides sound effects.
-Not for those that aren't into puzzle games.
-No story.
-All of the above (especially the second dotpoint) can get you to be bored.

Final Fantasy VIII is one of those games you either liked or hated in the series. Coming off of Final Fantasy VII and how (over)hyped that game was at the time, it would be expected. Everyone had different expectations for FF8. Admittedly, it's my favorite game in the series. Do I think it's the best in the series? No. I hold that regard for FF6/FF3. I've put a lot of time into the game as a kid and even more into the PC version. So I feel comfortable giving a review of all the positives and negatives this port has to offer and compare it to it's PSX counterpart.
Graphics: That's one of the good things I can say about this port. The game holds up pretty well and with higher resolution options, can definitely see more detail in the characters and fields.
Sound: This is subjective. A lot of people are okay with the midi tracks. If you played on the PSX before (like me), you probably won't be. The difference is night and day. You can mod back in the PSX soundtrack and I recommend it if midi isn't your jam. But on a plus side, the sound effects are much better on this port.
Story: Again, you'll either like it or hate it. It starts out slow and can even get overly complicated... But I enjoyed my time with it. And if you stick with it, you might think the same as I do. Character development I think was done well with Squall and the gang. Rinoa...has her moments. But screw it, I love her anyway. And yes, love story elements are in this game.
Gameplay: I'm going to keep this brief... You'll probably fall into two groups with the GFs and junctioning/draw system. It's either going to confuse you and you'll give up. Which makes the game a lot tougher. Or...you'll master/exploit it and become so OP early in the game that the rest is a cakewalk. The rest of the combat is your typical turn-based. Like FF7.
Extra Plus: Triple Triad. Now that is a fun minigame/card game and one of the shining points for this game, in my opinion.
PC Port: This is where things get sketchy. I already touched on the music. And outside of graphics and (mostly) good performance, there isn't very much I can say is good about this port. Controller support is iffy with it's directional input or recognizing your controller. Not to mention no button icons to speak of. (Good luck with the Forrest Owl's mission!) Some sound effects do not work properly. The UV in this game is terrible. Trust me, look at the world map in this port and then look at the PSX version. It's bad. A few texture problems. Like the instruments at the concert. Battles are locked at 15FPS. The PSX version is 30FPS. So the game isn't near as responsive in battle as it should be. A Square Enix account is needed just to play. But...you have to do this with almost all their games on here. Dumb, but tolerable. You may already have an account. And that about covers all of the PC port itself.
Mods: There are mods for this game that can really make the game pretty and even fix certain issues. Those being music, the UV on the world map, and lack of controller icons. If you know what you're doing, you can pretty much tweak the game to your liking with all the graphical mods and sound mods offered on the Qhimm Forums. And yes, I've made a few of those mods. Feel like I need to point that out for some reason... The choice is yours. The game is still pretty good on it's own.
Do I recommend this game? Sure. At full price? Eh... Maybe not. On sale? For sure. It's not the best port and there are a number of things SE should've fixed before releasing it. And we all know they most likely never will. But if you haven't played FF8 and are curious, then I say go for it. Or if you have a PSX, get it for that.

is insanely fun, very responsive and fast. The controls are simple and easy to get into, but you can really master them and there is a fair learning curve.
You run through a series of "randomly generated" versions of the same levels, which are somewhat different, but never too much and you will at some point notice patterns. However this does not really bother me. More randomness would be great, but it isn't hindering the game.
While going from level to level, you pick up weapons, skills, amulets and such, creating a set of gear. This gear will usually differ, as there is great variety of weapons, playstyles, ways to skill your character and so on. It invites you to try things out, theorycraft a build and see how it works. Very satisfying when you find something working in great synergy. These levels usually have 1-2 options of where to go next, so you can mix your chosen path up.
The game does have permadeath, so once you die, you start from level 1 again. However, you collect cells in each level and in between the levels, you can use these cells to unlock new weapons, more potions and such. This makes for some
which is very motivating. I often find roguelike games to kinda crush motivation, not with Dead Cells though.
Advancing through the levels fast is encouraged and rewarded with timed doors, only staying open for a while in your run. The loot in there is great. So more experienced players have an incentive to go faster and not get bored.
You will also unlock abilities/runes which let you grow a vine or teleport between statues. This will open up more paths over the time, letting you get more loot in levels, opening new areas and even open up new paths to take. This also keeps the game interesting and fresh.
There is only very little
, most of it is cryptic. You won't meet many characters, but things do happen and I am still wondering, what the game holds in store for me, cause I am far from finished. I can't say I dislike the storytelling, but that can be very subjective. Some people don't like the wonderful way of storytelling in Dark Souls for all I know.
are outstanding, just as

Dead Cells is very polished already and I usually don't like to buy into unfinished early access titles, but this doesn't even feel unfinished to me. I am just glad there will be even more content to come.

For a series of games as complex and intimidating as Paradox creates, Stellaris aims to make an easier system to understand in a sci-fi setting.  You create a race of people, deciding how they live, their physical traits and attitudes, and types of government, and guide them from the earliest beginnings of space travel, to waging interstellar war thousands of light years away.
Along this path, you have to decide which planets you will colonize, judging wealth of resources and territory against the habitibility of that planet sustaining your people.  Your military force needs to be continually increased to prevent predation by the more established empires, and the openly hostile "nuetral" entities that float freely in space.
As your researchers roam the stars finding new resources to utilize, primitive civilizations to monitor, and all sorts of other galactic weirdness to investigate, evants will occur that give you some interesting decisions to make.  This is one of thse games where the flavor text truly creates the story.  Such a case is deciding to aggresivly monitor a developing species and getting busted. The scientest claimed to the primitives that he was their true god.  Do I fire him,and sort out the technological contamination, or select "this will be the greatest prank in our history," and watch as civil war erupts over a terrible scientist sparking a crusade?  Or watching a firetorm rage across a planet as a species you were preparing to uplift into an ally erases themselves in a nuclear exchange, destroying the planet's ecosystem in the process.  An allegory to the future, perhaps?
For all the interesting moments that the game provides, it does fall flat as the time passes.  You run out of things to explore. The decisions of where to go are much less weighty as resources grow in abundance.  Your AI neighbors will refuse to conduct mutually beneficial trade for no reason other than "He is the PC, screw that guy."  Players of Civilization will recognize this.
Wars are highly exciting initially, as everyone moves their fleets around, prepares their armies for invasions, and lines up their demands to their opponents.  Sadly, these wars are often decided by a single key battle as massive deathball fleets smash into eachother, where the victor of that brawl has free reign for months as the opponenet can no longer muster a reasonable challenge.  As with most of Paradox's other games, numbers generally win the fights, as you have no tactical control over how it plays out, other than the initial positioning of your forces.  Around the mid-game, the Tachyon Lance comes out, and is unquestionably the strongest weapon in the game.  This is never a good thing, as whichever side is not utlizing it will likely lose half of their fleet before even being able to fire back.  Having more viable playstyles would be nice, rather than everyone being forced into the same OP loadouts.
For it's faults, Stellaris is not a fantastic game.  But I believe for it's positives, it is quite good.  Since it's release, Paradox has been making design choices that I can mostly agree with to continually improve the gameplay.  I will definitly recommend this game to others, with the caveats that it has some questionable features and definitly falls off in the late game.

This game is an exquisite example of Grand Strategy done right, having had said that it isn't perfect. The actual combat portion of the game is completely hands off, meaning that simple orders that could save your fleet from destruction cannot be given. The ship designer, while quite basic, can allow for a large amount of variation in how exactly your starships function in combat or other roles. The management of your empire is grand and awesome, allowing you to control a certain amount of direct systems and then assign sectors in space that will be ruled over by your designated sector governors. The diplomacy could use some work but it works out well the majority of the time and the galaxy wide crisis events are fun and challenging, even if their are too few of them. Overall, this game will devour your free time in a rewarding, ever changing, easy to learn difficult to master experience that makes you truly feel like the ruler of the galaxy. 8.5/10

You may find the conversation options with the NPCs a little stale after you exhaust them throughout the game, but you'll still be pleasantly surprised by the change of conversation lines every now and then which occur based on your actions / time elapsed.
As a parody of life, Cubicle Quest actually offers a lot of food for thought. For example, defeating the extra expenses in the game made me think about how I could cut costs in my own life and waiting for a promotion in the game made me think about how sometimes you just need time to get things done.
In the game, some of the things you thought were important end up totally useless in the grand scheme of things;

Some things just don't work out, just like in real life: you'll never
no matter how hard you try.
This applies even to NPCs: no matter how much
loves the main character, her limited skills and low effectiveness in combat (which can be implied as emotional support in real life) ultimately make her a poor choice for a partner compared to the other NPCs, mirroring the fact that no matter how much you love someone, you may never be the right one for him/her.
Most RPGs follow the concept of grinding, followed by buying weapons and armor and then min-maxing your stats.
Cubicle Quest takes a slightly different approach by only selling consumables and giving you equipment as you progress through the story. Not only that, enemies have different types of attacks and can afflict different types of ailments, which can be countered by equipping the appropriate accessories; meanwhile, they have their various weaknesses which you can exploit with your skills and different characters.
This keeps the game remarkably fresh as you're constantly figuring out and building your strategy to counter the enemies in the different dungeons.
Most games are kind of linear and generally have some sort of order in which you have to complete the game. Cubicle Quest doesn't really enforce that; you can get married first and then buy a house, or get yourself promoted first etc, so long as you reach your goals in the end.
It is actually quite good.
That said, the game is not flawless and it can feel a little rough around the edges with a few trivial bugs and occasional crashes.
Most of the game is quite intuitive but some things can always be more clearly elaborated on (for example, one doesn't know how effective an accessory with "Reduces damage" is).
This can be written off with "life is sometimes vague", but frankly speaking the game forces you to do a lot of trial and error whether you like it or not. Fortunately, there's a pretty comprehensive guide for those who hate to experiment too much.
Freedom is a double-edged sword, especially in RPGs since you don't know where is the best place to go next for your level. You're very likely to wander into somewhere that's way beyond your skill level and get yourself slaughtered.
There's actually quite a number of hidden gems in the game which make you wonder if there's more to be done, which can trick you into looking for secrets that were never there in the first place.
After you struggled so hard to reach the end, there isn't much incentive for the player to start all over again.

Defragmented is a difficult game with the similar mechanic to Hotline Miami - work your way through a level murdering everyone, mindful that if they see you they'll probably kill you. And when you die, you get rapid restarts so you get straight back to the murdering.
You need to be stealthy, you need to work out their movement patterns, and when things go south you need to be deadly accurate.
Your first weapon will not be accurate, so you'll die over and over. But every level is full of random loot placed in lockers, bins and on the bodies of the people you murder. Eventually you'll find a weapon (or two) whose stats you are happy with - maybe a sniper, maybe a full-on assault rifle. You'll start to feel more confident.
Most importantly, you keep everything when you die. You even keep your XP, so the more you play, the more of a beating your character can take.
Post-tutorial gameplay from chapter one [pre-release build]:
Crucially, it never becomes easy. You'll always need quick reactions, you'll still need to figure out the cleverly constructed levels, and if you murder somebody in earshot of other enemies, you'll still be chased by a mob and almost certainly get wiped out. So you can't grind your way to success, although it does help.
Some neat additional skills give you extra tactical possibilities. Possibly the most useful is a decoy that marches forwards and draws enemy fire for a few shots, useful if there's a heavily armed guard facing the direction you want to go and who you can't get behind.
The game camera takes a bit of getting used to. The top-down view goes a long way but for precision shooting (and working out fields of vision) you'll need to use the temporary 3D views. In a tight spot, predicting which way the camera will point when you press the camera button isn't easy. And using these views while actively moving around isn't usually a good idea. A few times I fell off the level into a chasm because the camera did a sudden 180.
The story happens between levels and adds context to the game, is well-written and skippable. It does feel a bit separate from the action, though; it feels like you could rewrite the story completely and the game itself would be identical.
Complaints? I didn't like the menu system. In going for an 80s cyberpunk terminal feel (to fit in with the rest of the game) it ends up being confusing and hard to read, particularly at first. The grinding aspect can be off-putting when you start to worry you can't complete a level until you've raided the same locker 50 times. And yeah, I shouted a lot at the aforementioned camera.
That's it. Defragmented is unforgiving at first, but rewards you for persistence (and repetition). If you can get past that, dig the neon cyberpunk aesthetic and enjoy rummaging through bins for loot, you'll get a lot out of this game. It's satisfyingly frustrating all round.

This game is funny, good RPG Maker variation on the theme of life with a special emphasis on money management. I'd really want to recommend but two things prevent me.
1. The "final" boss is op. The instructions states the game is not grindy but I'm level ~30 and I see in comments elsewhere it's better to tackle at level ~60. That's a lot of missing levels. I've done everything else, even looked at a walkthrough to ensure I didn't miss anything. I *believe* it's doable around level 30, but you need serious luck on your side. The problem here is that the final boss is really a sequence of 8 fights. Fights #2-#6 are straightforward, but they take time and a bad RNG streak will result in a party wipe. After trying this sequence 5 times, I'm done. No way I'm spending time grinding 30 levels for a small RPG Maker game.
2. Various monsters are weak against specific damage types and inflict ailments of a specific type. So far so good, staple of old school RPGs. However, this is not well explained in the game and there are no ways to "analyze" monsters. Trial and error ensues and I guarantee you'll not remember these combinations. The way to find if your character is protected against a type is via a "resist" popup when the damage is applied. Given each character has different equipment protecting against various types and the damage type is not specified, you need to scour your inventory post-battle and proceed by elimination: "Character A was resistant to monster B's attacks. They have gear resistant to laziness and aggression. This means monster A does either laziness or aggression attacks." And so on and so forth. On top of this, some monsters have nonsensical resistances. For instance, a work-related monster that is resistant to work attacks. It didn't take me long to stop bothering and the whole scheme fell flat.
Overall, very interesting idea but I can't recommend in good conscience.

I stumbled upon this game on Reddit and was very impressed with the quick progression of its development over 18 months with a mainly two-man team. I received a review copy and was excited to play because it reminded me of Hotline Miami (HM), but with a sleek cyberpunk feel. Despite dying countless times, I was pleasantly satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like overhead shooters in the vein of Hotline Miami, lots of loot, cyberpunk themes, role-playing elements, and great electronic music (particularly synth), then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are great - the amount of detail in the environment is good, and the artstyle during cutscenes is very nice; the world feels vibrant and alive. Running on max settings is not too intensive on your rig, and the flashiness of everything can be quite entertaining and pretty to look at. With a upbeat electronic soundtrack supplemented by visualization in the game world (the black areas of the level pulse different colors in tune with the beat), the music adds immensely to the cyberpunk, action-intensive atmosphere. The story is interesting and well-written - I like the conflict of clones vs. naturalism in a previously-struggling society. You can skip cutscenes and fast-forward through them (also includes the option to toggle them off), which is something small, but still very appreciated.
The controls are easy to learn and the tutorial is very helpful at orienting you to the game mechanics, however, I would strongly suggest you use a controller. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, and the most challenging part of the game will probably be either managing the camera and/or accepting the amount of caution and planning required to complete each level. On a keyboard and mouse setup, the camera switching did not feel as smooth compared to when I used a controller - and quick orientation is essential to success because if you fall off the stage you will die and have to restart. Similar to Hotline Miami, the enemy AI can be very brutal, discouraging a guns blazing strategy (at least initially). Scouting the area and learning enemy movement patterns is critical to beating each level. It is easy for you to be killed, however, the game is much more forgiving than HM because when you die you restart, but also keep any experience and money gained - I've actually levelled up a few times by repeatedly dying in a level that I was stuck on.
Gameplay involves you entering an area and killing everyone found within. Every character has a laser pointer that shows current aiming direction, however, other elements to consider when firing are distance, weapon accuracy, and bullet spread. There are three classes to choose from, each with two unique skill trees and abilities - like creating a ghost decoy, manifesting a small bullet-negating shield, and healing yourself based on stacks accumulated. Guns are categorized into heavy, light, and energy - each having upgradeable ammo capacity. Furthermore, you can increase your weapon mastery with pistols, submachineguns, rifles, shotguns, and energy arms (adding 2% damage per mastery level) by killing a certain number of enemies. Equipment is further varied by rarity, with orange-colored items being extremely high-valued. When you are in the pre-mission setup interface, you can also go to a store, however, there are different storekeepers in a number of the stages.
During each level, you will have to assess the situation carefully - unless you enjoy dying and restarting numerous times. Enemies will chase you if spotted and investigate weapon fire if nearby. One tactic I favored in HM - shooting at things to lure enemies into my killing zone - remains very effective at thinning down the enemy count. You can change up your equipment and have 3 slots for different active weapons (you can still keep others in your inventory). Included in your equipment are 1 grenade and 2 program core (passive abilities like increased dodge chance) slots. I found that both the variety in weapon types and class skill trees made each playthrough unique enough to enjoy. To encourage multiple playthroughs, you have access to a storage container accessible by every character you have.
I really enjoyed the brutality and unforgiving nature of HM, however, that savagery is missing from Defragmented because you still retain your experience points and loot. That being said, you will still die quite frequently and each level is highly entertaining. My favorite element of the game is the fantastic soundtrack, followed closely by the flashy presentation of everything. I really do feel like I am in a cyberpunk world whenever I play a stage.
Overall, the game plays really well and is a lot of fun if you are interested in intense action in a cyberpunk world. I do not know if there is an item/weapon that addresses this, but one thing I would like is a way to scan enemy health because it is exceedingly easy to die if you do not double-tap (continue firing/attacking) when an enemy has more health than the damage you dealt. One ability I like using teleports you to a nearby enemy (very short casting range) and unleashes a melee attack, however, performing such an action on a shotgun-wielding and/or high-levelled opponent will usually cause you to instantly be killed. With a 30 level cap (more of a soft cap because you still gain experience points) and three different classes to try, replayability is fairly high. If you enjoy top-down action shooters with rpg elements, then definitely give this game a try.
Recommend!

A few years back I remember saying "I wish someone would make a new Smash TV or Total Carnage! That'd be awesome!" Well clearly Housemarque and the creator of those games, Eugene Jarvis were somehow listening and decided to follow up with a spiritual successor called "Nex Machina". In typical fashion this is a twin stick shoot 'em up that I'd say feels more like Total Carnage than Smash TV (which is a good thing as all these games are awesome). It's pure arcade excellence, and runs smoother than butter (on my 5 year old machine). The plot is super simple you are a hero sent to destroy machines and save humans that are scattered through levels. So basically Kill robots, kill the bosses but don't get killed. The art style is really enjoyable, with neon blasting around the arenas, cables bursting out of the almost organic worlds and voxels flying everywhere when you destroy the enemies. The enemies are quite varied both visually and mentally as each has different styles to fight (much like you'd expect from this genre of games). Nex Machina also includes yet another incredible soundtrack which many of Housemarque's games are well known for, this time adopting a Retro Synthwave style to go with the retro arcade gameplay (I am looking forward to Housemarque releasing the soundtrack alone, as it's just that good). So what about gameplay? Well much of it was covered it's a twin stick shoot 'em up, where you progress through levels and fight an end level boss whilst surviving hordes of robots. There's secrets to find which can contribute to your high score and there's power-ups to make you ultimate hero and bane of machines! As of right now there is 3 different modes Arcade; classic get from the beginning to end. Arena; earn unlockables and rank up with modifiers changing the gameplay, also this mode updates. And finally Single World; where you pick a level (must be unlocked via Arcade play) and play through just that world. Knowing Housemarque they will likely release a Season Pass (which is usally quite cheap) and it will expand gameplay options further and with Arena constantly updating things are looking really good for Nex Machina. Just prepare to rage, because this genre can be rage inducing.

F.E.A.R. isn't a game about running away from a scary girl that died. F.E.A.R. is about taking on an army of highly coordinated clone soldiers by using experimental weaponry and your legs. The AI is the stuff of legends nowadays, and while it's not the most advanced system of all time, it's possibly the best designed. Enemies have so many different vocal callouts and interactions with the environment that it really does feel like you're taking on squads of highly trained soldiers and not just a collection of bumbling grunts in a room. They'll flush you out with nades and send a guy out to flank, retreat over a wall if the going gets rough, knock over certain objects for cover, crawl under physics objects, etc.
While it gets a little slow toward the middle and the horror elements can be a bit ham-fisted, the lighting is great and really keeps the game feeling atmospheric despite its age. Seriously, dynamic shadows on all objects including yourself is not only cool, it affects gameplay by letting you know where the AI is and letting the AI know where your flashlight is coming from. It makes for a seriously fun combat sandbox. Also the midpoint of the game starts introducing some crazy weapons to play with like the Particle Lance. Shotgun is also nuts for the entire game.
TL;DR: Want a shooter that requires you to legitimately out-play your enemies instead of just casually gunning them down from cover? Get F.E.A.R. And if you're having FPS problems, make sure to visit PCGamingWiki and get the fixes for the game. Have fun.

The art and graphics are quite simplistic, but doesn't detract at all from the gameplay.
One complaint is that when introducing a concept, such as bullet time, the button you need to press should be displayed on the screen.  I didn't realize until after a couple of tries that it was only displayed right when you start the level, but not when you actually needed to use the ability.  MInor nitpicking, but the script needs some editing.  There are a couple of grammatical errors and spelling mistakes that should be fixed.
Overall, I would not hesitate to recommend this game.

Often touted as the black sheep of the Final Fantasy games, Final Fantasy VIII tried a lot of new things to the franchise, and many of those things it tried.... didn't really work for a lot of people. I strongly warn that it's a 'YMMV' game. If you liked it on the PS, you'll like it here. There haven't been many changes made. If you haven't tried it, I highly recommend either waiting until it's on sale, or buying it *after* you have tried it and seen how it holds up for you.
With that in mind, I am not one of those people. Yes, it has a lot of aspects that even I can barely stand, but while it does bring down the game's grade for me, I still consider it a classic, and a perfect example of Square's exploration and willingness to try new things, even if some of them fell flat.
The characters are amazing. The junction system, while combined with the magic system is 'problematic', is fantastic for customizing characters as you see fit. The scaling enemies, while a *huge* strike against it for me, is a great way to preserve a game's challenge, and to keep things from simply becoming a case of 'level enough and you'll get there'; you actually have to decide a balance between leveling/grinding, sidequests, and storyline. Plus, Triple Triad as a 'side game' is just about untouchable in the Final Fantasies I have played; I have actual physical decks of TT cards I enjoy it so much.
Now, my one huge problem: the port. If you play with a Logitech or X-Box controller (potentially others), be warned that the port's button detection is exceedingly poor, and the way it maps the buttons is absolutely *abysmal*. If there was anything that would make me put a massive black mark on the game, it would be this. Fortunately it's playable with a keyboard, but I don't think I can stress enough how huge an oversight and issue the mapping features are.
All in all, while I do recommend it, I do so with a 7/10; 5/10 if you're trying to use a game controller thanks to the potential mapping difficulties. Nostalgia keeps me loving the game. Story and good parts keep me coming back, and I want to recommend that people try it and see for themselves. I would hesitate to call it 'An Underrated Gem' (see my Final Fantasy IX review for that!), but I will say that it is a game worth playing. One you can skip if you dislike, but one that any Final Fantasy fan should at least try, to see just how large the leaps Square was willing to take in order to explore the boundaries and to try out new things.

Never played a Castlevania-esque game that felt this good. You can rip and tear through the levels (and are encouraged to do so with stuff like timed gates,) and it's just about the most satisfying thing I've done in a game. The controls are on-point, the animation is fluid, and the atmosphere is good. This is a stellar game.
There's a nice balance between difficulty and fairness. Some games nail it, some fail, and yet some others don't strive for it. This game strikes the correct balance that I feel is missing from some of the other games I've played recently. Cuphead, for example, is a game that is difficult for the sake of being difficult, where this game is simply demanding of the skills you learn while playing it. It's not a fair comparison, and I'm not knocking on the beautiful but miserable game that is Cuphead, but this game I found to be much more enjoyable to play, and around the same price point (as of the winter sale 2017/2018), but not entirely similar from a gameplay perspective. This is a roguelite Castlevania on speed, and Cuphead is a Contra or Gradius game on mushrooms.
That being said, it is in Early Access, and they warn you up front about potential bugs and other problems. I haven't really encountered any of these, but I'm sure they're there. I really like the direction this game is going so far, and I haven't enjoyed bashing my head against a roguelite this much since the Binding of Isaac or Rogue Legacy. If you liked Rogue Legacy, this game is similar in some ways but vastly different in others. The level design here has a lot of verticality like Rogue Legacy. It goes for a vaguely Castlevania-esque or Dark Soulsian vibe without giving up it's own style, similar to Rogue Legacy. It controls incredibly well, and feels very satisfying to play, which is a big improvement on the somewhat clunky Rogue Legacy. It doesn't focus at all on genetics, instead focusing on permenantly unlocking abilities and unlocking weapons that will randomly appear. Most of the weapons and items are pretty fun and powerful if used at opportune times.
So, if you like roguelites, this is one of the best for sure. Give it a go!

Things Stellaris is not:
Europa Universalis
Victoria
Crusader Kings
Hearts of Iron
Things Stellaris IS:
An awesome and well fleshed out space empire sim that delves into the ethical standpoint and racial attributes of space-fairing empires. It has a very Star Trek and Mass Effect feel to it, where one race is a "warrior race", and another is a collectivist hive with no individuality.
Stellaris supports any sci-fi space opera dream you could come up with. Want the Arachnid Collective to finally put an end to that pesky fascist Human Federation? Now you can.
You want to build the Borg, ingratiate yourself to them, and assist them on a machine crusade throughout the galaxy? Go for it.
You want to rip holes in space and time, and accidentally let the things that live between the folds of reality through? Sure.
You want to be a pacifistic, peacable empire spreading a grand federation across the galaxy? You want to blow up space whales to learn their secrets? You want to genetically toy with a primitive species?
All are available.
Some say that Stellaris is a mile wide, and an inch deep. I disagree with this. Stellaris is still an extremely deep and enjoyable game with a wide variety of playstyles. What Stellaris does different is an elegence and efficiency of design that cuts out the fluff, and leaves the meat.

Textual Summary:
Defragmented starts you off with some of my favorite game music in ages, bringing me straight back to Kung Fury and my adrenaline pumping like only hotline miami could. It's unique art style for both menu and cut scenes takes my attention, even if the options menu is a bit confusing to navigate.
The art in the cutscenes is clean and stylized, with tons of character and little details being put into place to draw the attention to the entire scene. Though there is no spoken dialogue, and the cutscenes play like those you'd expect in a dating sim, the art style really sells it here.
Following you get dropped in the game proper... and there my issues start and don't really end.
The graphics are a very stylized polygon based ..something. I cant put any reason behind it, as the best i can describe them is "unfinished". the textures are poor, the models are very simple and frankly, quite ugly and the character animations are clunky and don't translate well to the 3D medium. On top of some levels just not having a backdrop at all and only displaying a rotation number of colors while the level floats in the air...
This weird top-down-3d creates a lot of problems that needlessly make the game harder than it should be with line of sight not being blocked (or enemy bullets) but your player bullets are. Where certain objects are static and non movable, but others are... somewhat. The entire render & art mostly just leaves me sad, because I've been taken in by a well styled and themed introduction and then thrown into a pile of manure.
And i could probably get past all that for the enjoyable implementation of the leveling, character progression and loot mechanics... were it not that the main "strategy" of the game is surviving the RNG of your weapons accuracy. Yes, in a tactical shooter... the game has accuracy that is a random weaponstat. Which means all your planning in a level is thrown out the window in the vain hope "maybe that mob wont dodge my lazergun this time and shotgun me to the face 5 times"
The levels are pretty varied in terms of layout, but all aspects of enemy types (gun/etc..) and unit models (or lack thereof) and graphical aspects are simply... not.
For a game that sounds absolutely phenomenal, it is heavily let down by it's graphics & randomized hit-chance. Creating frustration, annoyance and confusion where it should create adrenaline, satisfaction and tension.
buy this game if you don't hate fun.

Most of the time it doesn't take much to gain my interest in an action-rpg. It's easy to be seduced by the promise of phat loot, leveling, and those lovely rare drops. Unfortunately, it takes me a few hours before I realize that a lot of these games don't offer any other compelling aspects. Defragmented is a welcome surprise. It has the elements of a typical action-rpg, but its unique game-design and appropriate pacing, really help it stand out.
Let's start with a subject I normally don't consider: the graphics. In the age of youtube long-plays and 4K screenshots, there's hardly any reason to comment on something anyone can see for themselves. Still, I want to take a moment to discuss just how well Defragmented's graphics work. This is a lo-fi game, but it's also an intense shooter with elements of stealth. It's visually consistent, so you can focus on determining routes, making shots, and dodging bullets. The look of everything is very slick and refined, and you'll never be distracted by bloated and unnecessary details.
Now just because I mentioned "stealth elements" does not make this a core part of the game. It's something to consider, depending on your play-style, but... let's take a step back and determine what your play-style is. There are three classes in the game. The Cyberzerker is a bruiser. Their starting weapon is a shotgun, and their talents include a powerful area of effect blast, and a temporary strength buff. The Railrunner relies on decoys to draw the attention of enemies. Their ability to enhance their speed and dodging ability for several seconds is also massively useful. The Ascended uses a shield and a couple other techniques to carefully pick apart their foes.
Each mission consists of rooms and hall-ways with armed guards patrolling them. Your missions involves killing everyone or accessing a data-terminal. The catch is that even a Cyberzerker can't just rush blindly into battle. The only real advantage you have is your own agency. You decide the route and you have all of the time in the world to plan your attack. As is typical of AI opponents, everyone has better aim and reaction time than you. A lot of the early-game is going to be spent understanding your abilities, finding some decent weaponry, and getting overly familiar with the (r)etry key.
Due to the myriad of circumstances that can occur in every mission, the best advice is to never stick with just one type of gun. A sniper rifle is perfectly fine when you have the opportunity to make an accurate shot, but a shotgun is necessary for a frontal assault. It's important to adapt your movements to your weapon. Trying to counterbalance the inaccuracy of a SMG by standing still is going to get you killed. The speed of a bullet is a factor to consider as well. Laser pistols are extremely slow, but you can time your shots so that enemies run into them as they're rounding corners.
If all else fails, you can grind until your numbers are just that much better than the enemy's, but this becomes increasingly less viable as the game progresses. Once you hit new game+, your progress is going to be halted if you don't reconsider your strategies and your gear. Aside from tougher enemies, NG+ also adds to their numbers. This adds new depth and forces players into situations they hadn't considered earlier. The best part is that these missions never really become frustrating. They're all very short. If you're that good (or that over-leveled) you'll clear almost all of them in 30 seconds each. Granted, these same missions can also take well over 30 minutes apiece to figure out. There are a few difficulty settings for players who are having trouble, or for those craving a little more danger.
While this game is on the lean side, it also doesn't make any attempts to overstay its welcome. The story is functionally adept, the action is fulfilling, and you hardly ever get the feeling that you're merely grinding the hours away. This is what I mean about when I talk about appropriate pacing. All too often, an action-rpg is compared to the likes of Diablo, Marvel Heroes 2016, or another title that practically requires a huge time investment. Defragmented shares similarities with these games, but also has the good sense not to extend far beyond its means. This game could use a handful of additional missions, and maybe even a way for players to build and upload their own levels. At the same time, I respect that it doesn't try to pad itself out. There are three classes with a few abilities between them, a handful of weapon-types, and really only two kinds of enemies. Basically, this game takes what it has, uses everything to its fullest extent, and that's perfect.
Speaking of, the soundtrack to this game is also perfect. There's isn't a weak link anywhere to be found. The songs always fit the mission, and the developer made sure that the music doesn't restart everytime the player dies. Yes, it is a minor detail, but I really appreciate it.
Honestly, I wasn't sure what I was getting into when I started this game. Aside from Defragmented looking like something from the earliest 3D games, I also wasn't exactly floored with its tutorial missions. However, as soon as it clicks, everything comes together quite wonderfully. All in all, I think that this is a quality title; one worth setting aside a weekend or two for.

For a series of games as complex and intimidating as Paradox creates, Stellaris aims to make an easier system to understand in a sci-fi setting.  You create a race of people, deciding how they live, their physical traits and attitudes, and types of government, and guide them from the earliest beginnings of space travel, to waging interstellar war thousands of light years away.
Along this path, you have to decide which planets you will colonize, judging wealth of resources and territory against the habitibility of that planet sustaining your people.  Your military force needs to be continually increased to prevent predation by the more established empires, and the openly hostile "nuetral" entities that float freely in space.
As your researchers roam the stars finding new resources to utilize, primitive civilizations to monitor, and all sorts of other galactic weirdness to investigate, evants will occur that give you some interesting decisions to make.  This is one of thse games where the flavor text truly creates the story.  Such a case is deciding to aggresivly monitor a developing species and getting busted. The scientest claimed to the primitives that he was their true god.  Do I fire him,and sort out the technological contamination, or select "this will be the greatest prank in our history," and watch as civil war erupts over a terrible scientist sparking a crusade?  Or watching a firetorm rage across a planet as a species you were preparing to uplift into an ally erases themselves in a nuclear exchange, destroying the planet's ecosystem in the process.  An allegory to the future, perhaps?
For all the interesting moments that the game provides, it does fall flat as the time passes.  You run out of things to explore. The decisions of where to go are much less weighty as resources grow in abundance.  Your AI neighbors will refuse to conduct mutually beneficial trade for no reason other than "He is the PC, screw that guy."  Players of Civilization will recognize this.
Wars are highly exciting initially, as everyone moves their fleets around, prepares their armies for invasions, and lines up their demands to their opponents.  Sadly, these wars are often decided by a single key battle as massive deathball fleets smash into eachother, where the victor of that brawl has free reign for months as the opponenet can no longer muster a reasonable challenge.  As with most of Paradox's other games, numbers generally win the fights, as you have no tactical control over how it plays out, other than the initial positioning of your forces.  Around the mid-game, the Tachyon Lance comes out, and is unquestionably the strongest weapon in the game.  This is never a good thing, as whichever side is not utlizing it will likely lose half of their fleet before even being able to fire back.  Having more viable playstyles would be nice, rather than everyone being forced into the same OP loadouts.
For it's faults, Stellaris is not a fantastic game.  But I believe for it's positives, it is quite good.  Since it's release, Paradox has been making design choices that I can mostly agree with to continually improve the gameplay.  I will definitly recommend this game to others, with the caveats that it has some questionable features and definitly falls off in the late game.

Ah, Cubicle Quest. A game that, despite it's plain exterior, has been an obsession of mine for the last while. Will it be yours?
First off, ignore the negative reviews. They mostly make referenced to one of two things; first, the fact this game uses generic RPGMaker assets, which honestly doesn't really matter since the built in assets are there for a reason. Does every RPGMaker game need to have customized assets? Nope. Anyway, the second complaint is that things in the game are poorly explained. Well, in the area called "Castle Sanity" where you start the game and spend a great deal of time in, there is a staircase that leads to a basement with references on all of the mechanics of the game. So yeah, not really a complaint when everything is right there.
Now then, why is this game great and why would it be an obsession? Honestly it comes from the theme. It is laid out as a traditional fantasy RPG, but the skin on it reflects, well, any of us really. Your protagonist Bob (or whatever you decide to call him) decides to leave the safety of Mom'n'Pop Kingdom (he moves out on his own) and forms the Kingdom of Bob (gets his own place). Your job is to guide him through the process of defeating the Debt Alliance, consisting of the First & Second Credit Card Legions along with the College Loan Army (pay off all your debt).
You do this by sending your soldiers to defeat enemy soldiers (pay your bills dammit!) You also go the Dungeon of Work and enter the Promotion Dungeon (get promoted at work and get paid more), enter your basement and defeat monsters representing your various expenses like food, hydro, etc (quit spending so much!) and even recruit a roomate to split your rent (acquire your first party member). Oh, and of course marry and buy a house (or not, as there are a lot of options in the game)
This theme proceeds throughout the whole game and it's wonderful. While appearing as generic monsters, you battle against things like fear of commitment, facebook comparisons, false hopes, depression, panic, broken utilities, etc. Your boss battles are against things such as the Spectre of Loneliness, The Road Less Travelled, Fear of Change, True Hardship, etc.
Eventually once you get your bills paid off, you're confronted by everyone's greatest fear; an empty life. The physical representation of just working for years at a job you're not happy with; of just working all the time and not really living. Once you conquer that, there's some post game content to deal with. All in all, I've put in 24 hours of time into the game and I've completed about 98% of the game, with a couple of the brutal post game bosses being too much for me to handle.
As said earlier, the game has generic sprites, portraits, music, etc, but it is done very well to the point where the actual gameplay overshadows the graphical part. With a total of 8 recruitable party members, several candidates for marriage, multiple dungeons and bosses, and the fact that the game is very open ended after you get your first promotion, there's a lot to like here. I highly recommend this game as it helped me out personally by making me chuckle at some of life's difficulties, and I think it'll do the same for you.
