The Witcher 2 by CD Projeckt Red review.
I will start off by saying that I was late to the Witcher series. (Still haven't played Wild Hunt) With that being said, they are games that should not be overlooked by RPG fans, even though the first 2 are 5+ years old. I played The Witcher about 3 years ago and I wish I would of played it alot closer to my Witcher 2 playthrough because I had forgotten details about some of the previous characters and locations. A quick trip to google cleared up all my confusion and my gameplay experience was great.
Story -> 9/10
I was fully immersed in the story once I cleared up a few things I had forgotten from the first one. It moves along a steady pace and ramps up to a good finale by Act III. I imported my character from the original which added a few weapons and armour (as far as I could tell) as well as a few references and minor story alterations. There are some very tough decisions to make which can alter the course of the game. The voice acting (English) was a little wooden from some of the characters (Dandelion, Triss and to some extent, Geralt himself) but it didn't diminish my experience any. The dwarves in particuliar were great as they are vulagar as f*** and are always good for a laugh. I am also happy to report not a single character took an arrow to the knee.
Sound -> 8/10 [Creative SB X-FI Platinum]
The sound effects were very well done, especially in combat. Ambience while walking around really pulls you in. From the idle chatter in towns to the various sounds while out for a stroll in the wild. I found the music score to be great but there was not as many tracks and got a bit repetitive. The music in the taverns is burned into my memory probably forever now.
Graphics/Performance -> 9/10 [Asus Maximus VII - 4790K - 16GB 1600MHZ - R9290X Crossfire - Freesync]
From a 2011 point of view, the graphics are amazing, from a 2017 point of view.....I still thought the graphics looked great.(Looked better and ran better than Skyrim all modded up) The enviroments were extremely detailed, in particular the forest in Act I. Textures were fairly hi-res and the lighting was very nice. Character models look good and the clothes/armour all looked great. Some minor clipping and characters teleporting around abit but nothing major.
From a performance standpoint everything was top notch. The game scaled amazing with multi-gpu, I had no problem maintaining 144 fps. (Dips down to 115-120fps in some places) With that being said I played alot of the game with a single gpu with the framerate locked to 90 fps because my monitor only can run Freesync up to 90hz. If I ran Freesync on with multi-gpu, the framerate would just rocket out of control (sometimes to 200fps) turning my room into a sauna. I ran all settings on max except the Uber setting, which just tanked performance, at 2560x1440 resolution. I experienced about 5 crashes in 45 hours of gameplay which is exponentially lower than the Bethesda games I've played on the same system.
Gameplay -> 7/10 [Normal Difficulty]
The Good: The overall feel of the game was generally good. I was able to map the keys in a way that I was not fumbling around like some games. The combat was improved from the first one. It feels rewarding as you start to accumulate better talents and equipment. By the end cutting down 6+ enemies at once was easy using a combination of weapons and signs. I didn't use alchemy much as I couldn't be bothered to meditate everytime I wanted to drink a potion. Also it is nice you don't need to be near a fire to meditate anymore.
The Bad: The quicktime events are horrible and whoever puts these in the game and continues to use them to this day should be shot. I was kind of let down by some of the mini games, especially the dice, you can't win!!! The economy is sort of crappy. I found a rare elven sword and I went to sell it and I was given enough money to buy 5 apples from another vendor. WTF? If you are a completionist and need every book and every crafting diagram (which I will do on another playthrough) you better enjoy killing harpies for hours on end. Money is scarce. I believe there is a mod for it which I may use on my second playthrough.
Conclusion -> 8.5/10
I would recommend this game to anyone that even had their eye on it in the slightest. You can always pick it up for cheap. Halfway through the first act I realized I should had the difficulty alot higher since normal was a leisurely stroll. I put 45 hours in one playthrough and like I said I never went through it with a fine toothed comb. I see myself putting one maybe two more playthroughs so I could easily have over 100hours in it before I never look at it again. I recommend play the first Witcher prior to playing this one because it sets up the world and events happening. I felt that this game felt smaller in scale compared to the first Witcher. I felt that way about Mass Effect 2 & 3 as well. But still, 45 hours for a game I probably paid 5 bucks for on a Steam sale is great value. Now on to The Wild Hunt!!!

PSA: I'm also friends with the developer. He's awesome, and made it solo (as far as I know).
Ride the Bullet is a rather simple arcadey game, where you go through orange boosters to speed up your bullet, blue boosters to keep your bullet off the ground, use slo-mo in trying times, and assassinate people along the way.
The story is quite interesting, with a basic introduction of the character and the world, in just a few slides. Characters speak to you before each mission, and have a small portrait displaying their emotional state as they talk. Their portraits actually look surprisingly convincing, given that they are photos (of Radjor and friends) that were edited slightly, and hair or other accessories drawn on, giving them an interesting character for dang cheap development time.
As you play through the game, new mechanics are introduced pretty smoothly (although they tend to be some variant of "HIT THING WITH BOOOOOOOLET"), and even some difficult concepts are explained with hardly a word from the narrative. It starts pretty easy, but you'll be surprised how difficult it gets, so quickly you won't notice until you've retried that dang vase-smash level 20+ times. The soundtrack is pretty decent (I for one LOVE the theme) especially if you consider the constraints under which it was made. A lot of time is put into establishing locations and characters, and it felt great to finally finish the game, killing a certain baddy.
The art style is pretty simple, but I think it really works for the game. I think the characters really breath life into the world, while the cartoony levels challenge you to work for the next snippet of narrative. I played through the game to completion on both Android and PC (It works on both!), and it ran very smooth on both. When I (just barely) installed the steam(PC) version, I was getting 200+ FPS stable on 1280x720 and ran through a couple levels smooth as butter on my rather sub-par PC.
Seriously, try this game. I am a big fan of noir-mafia esque settings, so I unsurprisingly loved the writing.
P.S: My playtime is very low since I played it mainly through Itch.io.
P.S.S: If you haven't watched it, check out the trailer. It's great.

While I had thought about getting the Steam Release of this game for a while, it was the reacent KIM JUSTICE Videos on YouTube that convinced me to give it another shot...
EDIT: Frankly I wasnot happy with the original format of my Review so here is a better effort.
LEGEND: Sqaull Leonheart is a Studant at a Merceanary academy that with his friends must prevent the end of the world from an Evil Sorceress while also finding out about his past...
The games page gives you enough of a backstory, you don't realy need me to repeat it - Though it can be quite disturbing when you take a deeper look... These Students are being trained as Mercenaries... And Squall is only 18... So they have been trained since THEY WERE BABIES?
Japanese RPG's will give you some seriusly disturbing thoughts if you think about them too deeply!!
But yeah - Its a JRPG... Prepare for a story that spans extremes - Sometimes Romantic, sometimes scary, sometimes disheartening, sometimes just plain BAT S**T MENTAL (And trust me it does go that direction!!!)
GRAPHICS: Anyone who played Final Fantasy VII - The epic that bought almost everyone to JRPG's - There is no denying that this game is a MASSIVE graphical upgrade. Loking more realistic can put some off who prefer the more Anime Style of FFVII but there is no contest when it comes to how well everything has been upscaled.
The STEAM Port is more or less a direct port of the original PC release - As such, this game does not look its best on more modern machines and it is sort of sad that not more effort was put in for a re-release... But making upgrades can be very expensive.
The great news is that there is a dedictaed fan base making mods which I have now tried - The Tonberry Graphical Upgrade System you can find on STEAM Froums can help you choose between numerous user created Upgrades that vastly clean up teh gamne without going so far as to ruin the games original feel.
Worth noting - BE CAUTIOUS WITH THE MODS!!! They are not perfect... It is often recommended you turn off teh Steam Overlay - and when playing, if you should Alt-Tab back to desktop... Often you will be stuffed!!! It crashes the game!!
Even without Mods, The game is beautiful - Especially for the Nostalgic among us, A great Port of the PS1.
SOUND: While the sound Quality is exactly what you would expect and serves well - THE MUSIC IS AWFUL! I am sorry but JESUS they really dropped the ball on this one... It is TINNY AND GRATING AS ALL HELL!!! OK - It does not detract from tyeh gameplay and it is a port... You kind of expect it, but it feels like it has lost so much and teh amazing tunes from teh PS1 are totally lost...
Or would be but again - We have a fantastic Modding Community who released the 'Roses and Wine' Music Upgrade - and ... HOLY GOD!!!! Even SQUARE ENIX must be kicking themselves as this mod is SO DAMN GOOD it makes the PS1 and its CD Quality Audio sound like it was recorded by a bunch of Ametuers!
The PS1 Music was great - The Steam Port - BLOODY AWFUL! The Roses and Wine Mod... GET OUT YOUR IPODS as you are going to want to replace all your Lady Gaga and Eminem for this!!! YES ITS THAT GOOD!
GAMEPLAY: Its a JRPG in the standrd style that FFVII madse so popular, an expansive open world that you actually access very early on. But compared to other releases, the dungeons can be very bland and samey... Still, the story should keep you going...
But thats not to say the game is not without Issues... Most complain about the new Magic System called 'Junction' - Far from as intuitive as its predecessor, the new system requires you use your summons - Guardian Forces or GF's - as an equip item and 'Draw Spells' from enemies and Draw Points...
This limits you on the number of spells you can carry which should add extra challange... But the System is BROKEN BEYOND BELIEF!!!
Speed Runners will lhave a field day - Without teh Cut Scenes which take up most of the game - This 80 Hour game CAN be completed in as little as an hour!!! Thats how BROKEN the junction system is!!! Find the right spells and the game is a walk in the park!!!
But that funnily adds to the fun... Seeing just how many different ways you can break the game and how you can turn a near impossible boss fight into a one hit kill every time is HILARIOUS!
The most serious downside to the Junction System though is Exchange... Playing properly you can have every spell you need for a very hard battle only to realise too late that youleft all teh spells you needed on another character!!!
And Exchanging spells is ANNOYING!!!! It really is!!!
That aside, teh game is actually very good in playability - If you liked FFVII - Then pretty much you have more of the same... The Junction System takes some getting used to but other than that its what youhave come to expect of SQUARE ENIX.
CONTROLS: Being an Early port... Controls are NOT great. You can of course add a controller if you have one - But sadly the game in its original form lacks support for PS3 Controllers (Manages X-Box... But I have not been able to get my PS3 Controller to work AT ALL regardless of what Third Party Software I have tried...), so if you have not got a controller... You are stuck with keyboard.
And... Keyboard controls are somewhat a pain - Yes you can redefine them which is a major bonus (Sorry but X.C.V and G for the trigger on the gunblade? As a default these seriously gave me hand cramp!!!) but as a Port from Console - We all know the best way to go is a Controller... Its far more comfortable and easy to use.
That said, Its responsive, Smooth and not a major downside except for cramp!
LIFESPAN: The addition of Steam Achievements may seem liek a great way of keeping you coming back for multiple playthroughs... And I have to admit I have found myself wanting them all... BUT - Many are SERIOUSLY LACKLUSTRE!!!
While its not unusual to see Story Mode Achievements in a game - Sadly, the largest majority of the Completion tragets are actually story driven... As such they offer little challange.
With that being said - 100% on this game is NOT easy... Its a JRPG staple now top have so many Sidequests you will have to work HARD to get that KUDOS that says I AM A COMPLETIONIST!!!!
From Sub Games to Sub Quests... There is a lot to keep you going - But its also NOT the most inetresting thing to do... Bearing in mind it has been 4 years since I last played this game but only 6 Months since I went back to its predecessor... Yeah - Its far from as compelling as its Elder sibling.
OVERALL:
GRAPHICS: (Without Mod) - 9
SOUND: (Without Mod) - 4
GAMEPLAY: 7
CONTROLS: 6
LONGEVITY: 6
OVERALL: 7/10

In a world where humans have transferred their brains into robot husks and an interplanetary gold rush begins, players must make the choice of either flying a rocket filled with bombs into the enemy brain or simply rush in with a dude with a very large gun.
Cortex Command is one of those oddly unique games that are just meant for modding. 80% of the game's content is stuff you'll find in the workshop and on the data realms forums. As for gameplay, it's interesting to say the least. The game is definitely not a realistic combat simulation, but it definitely uses jetpacks in ways they've never been used before. Keep the throttle on for too long and you'll find yourself zooming across the map at the speed of sound. As for actual combat, it's thought out and entertaining. Things such as bullet weight and velocity play a good part in battle; a pistol's bullets will literally bounce off enemies if they're too far away, while a sniper rifle is heavy to carry but can penetrate armor from a good distance. You'll soon find that when you build your base you'll be putting down heavily armored juggernauts with rocket launchers and LMGs since you don't need them to move much (you'll also find weight is a real hinderance since jetpacks are the only real way to move) while your assault troops will probably just have that one remote-detonation-grenade launcher you think is really cool. While most battles have the simple objective "kill the enemy brain", there are alternative game modes available in the base game, like surviving with one troop for a set amount of time or holding down a base being attacked by dummies.
Cortex Command isn't for everyone, but if you don't mind a random decapitation becuase you hit the roof from time to time and you're not super serious about realism then this game will be worth the money.

I usually don't review games which I haven't played that long (currently ~9 hours), but this game surprised me.
The controls are incredibly fluid and in my humble opinion, despite the dev's recommendation, best enjoyed with mouse and keyboard. The game feels more responsive than anything else I have played before, the combat is insanely well-made. The level design seems logical and rewards exploration, but punishes it if it takes too long.
The first thing I always wanna know in roguelike games is how you can progress - this game has some good answers to that question and those solutions seem well-designed and make the game even more fun... and more challenging once you progress a certain point ;)
Now for the part that really surprised me - Most of the modern pixel-like games don't put effort into their graphics. They just implement those graphics because of """nostalgia-feeling""" and just basically expect you to like those pixel designs because they might appeal to you due to nostalgia. This game, on the other hand, just has amazing animations, really pretty effects and overall looks beatiful, considering it's a game where you can see every pixel.
The graphics and effects could still be improved and the animations could be made better working. Content-wise the game is unfinished and some of the mechanics still need balancing, but other than that, the game already is worth even the full price. This is one of the most interesting Early Access games I played.
Definetly looking forward to where the road leads this game and I really hope I don't have to change this review to negative one day.

The diplomacy could use some work but it works out well the majority of the time and the galaxy wide crisis events are fun and challenging, even if their are too few of them. Overall, this game will devour your free time in a rewarding, ever changing, easy to learn difficult to master experience that makes you truly feel like the ruler of the galaxy. 8.5/10

100 hours and I finally feel I can write a review that will be meaningful.
This game is almost great. There are some very interesting ideas available. The opening of the game might be the most engaging of any 4x I have played. There is a real sense of exploration, and discovery.
Shortly after you have colonized a few planets, you will likely lose all of that. Once the free space is gone and all the stars, or most of them are claimed, this game stops being about exploration and becomes all about the politics, and war.
Given that you would think the politics and war systems would be a major focus. Sadly, they are not. Each war must be declared, and don't position your ships in their empire, you'll have to fly out and then back in, yes, your ships will literally leave the contested space under AI control and you won't be able to issue orders until they get back.
Wars have goals, it might be to conquer a few planets, or make the empire you are fighting become a tributary or vassel. What is nearly impossible is to conquer another empire outright, as each war goal has a cost associated and there is a cap of 100 points able to be spent.
After you win, there is an enforced 10 years of game time peace. You are not allowed to attack, the buttons do not work.
Politics is a number match up game, if you are nice, the AI will be friendly back, but there isn't much to gain in friendship. There are no trade treaties, technology can not be directly traded. Minerals and Energy can be exchanged, but it is not hard to make enough of these without trade in most instances.
The game limits player action with reasource, and none more precious than Influence. If you are low on influence you can not hire leaders, or colonize planets, or claim space, or even take basic diplomatic actions. The game regularly shuts off player access to its most engaging parts.
Combat is horrible. There is a ship designer, and you can research improvments to various weapons. However the fights are in real time, on the main map. The player has no control, at all, of ships once they are engaged. You can set a basic strategy, get close or keep range, but only if you research technology that allows you to preset your ships for this ability. If you don't have it, your fast ships will leave your slow ships behind and fling themselves suicidally at the enemy.
It gets worse.
Ships do not focus fire, at all. They will ignore critical targets to spread their fire over noncritical targets and all the player can tell them is to retreat, or not. There is no manuver, no strategy, there are weapons that are not well balanced, but the basic idea is to have more ships than the empire you are fighting.
The endgame?
There are two types of difficulty in the game, 1 is the random "gotcha" events where you are offered a decision, and very little information, and then it might turn out to harm you, sometimes significantly. Some of these are plesant surprises. The other difficulty comes from the AI controlled empires.
The AI cannot build or maintain an empire. It is very, very bad at it. So the AI gets some empires that are absurdly more powerful than the player's empire. They may or may not be agressive. At the end game the AI gets attackers who come from outside the galexy.
They do not follow the rules of construction, ship limits, or any other limiter the player must deal with. They just spawn in, and either you are ready, or you lose the game. Surprise, build a big fleet.
There are things to like about this game, the real time game play, pausable and with multiple fast and slow settings, is not one of them. It is yet another mechanic designed to cover for a weak AI. By forcing a player to multitask.
Armies, are well done. If you can get to one planatary invasions are cool.
The tech research is interesting. The advancments a player is offered are random, though some can not be lost, and will sit waiting for you to take them, or not. As an empire grows it becomes harder and harder to research technologies, but if the empire prooritized tech it's managable.
A player is only allowd to directly control 5 star systems. This could be as many as 5 or as few as 1 planet in each.
No tech is gained from conquest, only by researching the wrecks of enemy ships with a science ship.
I enjoy playing, multiplayer. Two humans working togeather can offset a lot of the randomness, and the "gotcha" moments. I would not enjoy multiplayer if I had to pay for it.
That is why I give this game a negative review. It's not worth money yet. It was released early, and there is no espionage system, at all. The political and treaty interaction is limited, and the AI has more options than the player. It can ask you not to colonize near it, you can not ask it the same.
Galaxies are so large that individual systems lose their meaning.
Species looks can be quite varried, but you won't see your image much. Its just a 2d flat image that twitches a bit. The systems for governments and ethics are genuinely interesting. I wish the interaction with other species was as deep as the space offered for back stories, language and other flavor bits.
If you want this game, wait until it is on sale. In a few years it might be worth the buy, and if you like random events fustrating you, heck this may be your thing.
If you want to feel like you won because you have skill, and not you beat RNGesus, this is not the game for you.
Multiplayer is fun, it eliminates a lot of the horror, however games take weeks to resolve, so limit the number of people playing and hope you have some regular time to play.

I'm probably pretty far from beating the game but I think I've experienced enough story and stuff to write a preliminary review. I'll update this when I finally beat the game.
Bottom line: Cubicle Quest is a ramshackle mashup of life simulation and RPG. Worse-than-average system saved by good writing. A thought-provoking interactive prophecy of your own life. Grinding required.
The life simulation part is... I shouldn't describe the story as fun or cheesy because it's not intended to be that way, save for the constant sarcastic reference of video game traditions and tropes; I'd rather say the story is something young adults like me can relate to, and (to a degree) learn from. Consumerism, drudgery, social convention, peer pressure, red herrings... The original author has many aspects of modern human experience covered. Sort of gives me a sense of actually living the main character's life.
Throughout the game NPCs keep reminding me that the in-game world is constructed as nothing but a metaphor. As a part of gameplay this feature is rather distractive, but for this game it's not too inappropriate.
It's because the RPG part is really just meh, just like what you see and hear in the official trailer. It's made up almost entirely of RPGMaker standard assets, quite unattractive. Graphics are passable, but maybe this game would be more enjoyable without any graphic overworld; a pure-text presentation should connect to the players just as well. The same goes for music. Some tracks feel too pumped-up and percussive for the scene while some could've been more uplifting or emotional. Game balance doesn't feel like it's been fine tuned. As someone else has pointed out, either we one-shot the monsters or they one-shot us. Yet the game's tutorial says no grinding is required. Maybe there's a certain route which I can just push through without grinding, but this game is heavily nonlinear, and as a result I run into overpowered monsters and get screwed now and then, here and there. For a game, this kind of experience really sucks.
But as I mentioned, NPCs keep reminding me of the metaphor which is the entirety of Cubicle Quest's fantasy setting. Maybe this is life. You don't know where you're heading for, you don't know what's ahead, you don't know if you can deal with it. This realism has motivated me to keep playing, as I believe this game knows my future - or futures.

I've really had to think about my time in stellaris, limited it may be, whether it has been good or bad. To start with, the diplomacy in this game is beautiful and is honestly the reason I got it in the first place (Pretty stupid reason, giant 4x paradox space game and I like it for diplomacy?) it's really well thought out and is easily far more realistic in relation to the species ethos than in even victoria 2. Research is also a good part of this as it is far more different to any other paradox game I have played before, not to say it is bad just to say it is interesting. War is where I feel this game lacks, though what I suppose you could class as 'naval' combat is pretty great especially to watch when it comes to land battles it is far more dissapointing especially for a paradox game. colonisation too is somewhat boring, comparing it again to victoria 2 when world wide conflicts could start of some more than useless african state, seeing so many nations just roll over and give in when you settle on their borders is a mechanic evident in even civ that this game really lacks. I also feel like the early and late game is fairly boring (*SPOILER ALERT* Unless you count the various extinctions that can come about in the end) leaving the mid game, which mind you ends up looking not to different to many other paradox games at this point, really comes into its own. Galactic politics flares up, empires rise and fall much like the federations that try to prevent them from even existing, this is really what saves the game in my opinion and though I wish that paradox would put us on rails like so many of their other games, being left to create your own empire like in civ is a still wonderful experience, one that could not be rivaled if you were given a nation by force. Ultimately you'll find this game can surprise you and when it does it will be then that you are thankfull for buying the game.
TLDR: Give it a shot, you'll be surprised.

In Devilry, you play an irresponsible, paranoid, quite possibly alcoholic father (well, I assume it's a dude) whose chosen method of "protecting" his family against a marauding ghost is to run directionlessly about a house with very few working light switches, scary pictures on the walls, terrifyingly huge teddy bears, "broken" cameras which emit UV signals by sheer accident and radios which only seem to emit a signal from the very depths of Hell itself...while said family members attempt to sleep in separate rooms with THEIR EYES WIDE OPEN IN ABJECT TERROR.  Maybe I beat on them during the daytime or something, and frankly, I'm not sure the encounters with the "ghost" aren't just in my own booze-addled head.

Perhaps this was influenced by the Kubrick version of The Shining?  Only set in a "regular" suburban house with epic fountains out in the garden and what-not (like we all have).  Perhaps this is intended as a biting social commentary on the peculiar, first world-y madness which only upper middle-class families can generate for themselves, in a world where status creates stresses we neither need nor benefit from?  Or perhaps it's just another example of a horror "game" which serves as little more than an admittedly impressive "showcase" for the programming - if not exactly STORYTELLING - talents of its alleged "developers"?!  I mean, it's atmospheric and spooky and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but WHAT EXACTLY AM I SUPPOSED TO BE DOING?!?

Let me put it another way:  Have a look at all the "positive" reviews for this game on the Store page - including mine! - and see how short all the playing times actually are.  If you find it on super-sale and fancy a quick, creepy ♥♥♥♥-around inside a small-but-spooky map, then go for it.  Just don't expect a proper "game" for your hard-earned cash.  Oh, what ambivalent times we live in:  So many horror games for those of us who covet such things, yet so few with anything one could describe as quality "gameplay".  Still, it is a great feckin' era for SHOWCASES, ennit?  Here's to the next generation of horror game designers progressing past the "tech demo" stage...character, story and gameplay, anyone?  Ooh, I'm so old-fashioned...

When I first heard of Black Ops, I was afraid that it would be a shoddy MW2 ripoff. While it retains much of the MW2 formula, the changes are a fresh breath of air.
PROS:
+One of the best stories in Call of Duty history, with plausible realism.
+A great single-player campaign full of intrigue, questions, answers, and glorious setpieces.
+Collected intel can be viewed to learn more about the story, as well as provide a prologue and epilogue to the story.
+Damn fine score.
+Refined multiplayer with a level-cap closer to CoD 4, so less grinding to prestige.
+Highly balanced multiplayer. There's maybe one or two over-powered guns.
+Customizable emblems!
+Bots! (Only for Team Deathmatch and Free for All, though)
+Nazi Zombies!
+Self-reviving in SP zombies.
+New and fun Nazi Zombies maps in some setpieces quite a bit cooler than WaW's locations.
+DLC for WaW zombies maps in Black Ops.
+Feels similar to MW2 without going over-the-top.
+Dedicated servers!
+Zork!
CONS:
-A number of mediocre to downright terrible maps in multiplayer and zombies (Shangri-La comes to mind).
-In multiplayer, those few overpowered guns are nearly everywhere. It's hard to find a game without less than three players using said guns.
-Worse graphics than in MW2.
-Killstreaks don't count towards further killstreaks.
-Multiplayer uses "CODpoints," a currency used to buy everything you want to unlock, even if you have the level cap for it. So you won't be able to feasably build a half-decent custom emblem until the late part of multiplayer.
A really fine game, and a welcome addition to the Call of Duty lineup.

(TL:DR at the bottom)
The base game has a nice balance of action and surrealist horror. I wouldn't consider this game a survival horror as you are given a generous amount of ammo and health. Coupled with the leaning and slow-mo ability, the player is encouraged to play less conservatively and take risks which I found very fun.
I'm torn on the level design. On one hand there is a lot of repetitive, dimly lit hallways. On the other are areas that clearly had thought put into them. How the player, and enemies, navigate and utilize these environments is why the AI in F.E.A.R. is perceived as intelligent and combat doesn't get stale quickly.
The horror is mostly scripted events - as it plays an ambiguous but important role in the story - so while your first playthrough may be pretty terrifying, subsequent playthroughs won't have as much of an impact.
One thing to note is that the PC version lacks the instant action mode as well as a couple of console-exclusive weapons (machine pistol and automatic shotgun). This brings the amount of unique weapons down to 9 (not including the 3 grenade types). Some weapons are satisfying to use but don't expect much variety there.
Overall, I left F.E.A.R. with optimism that despite recently having its twelfth birthday, it still holds up really well gameplay-wise and at an asking price of under $10 USD, it is a fully fledged bargain.
The first in Vivendi's two non-canon expansions, Extraction Point follows what happened to the Pointman after the events of the main game. Gameplay is much the same although there were some differences I spotted. For starters power weapon ammunition - such as for the ASP rifle and rocket launcher - seems to be more abundant. The three new weapons (minigun, laser rifle and grenade turret) are all welcome additions. The AI also seems to be more aggressive and so I found myself peeking and waiting for enemies to come within range more often than rushing them.
Horror is ramped up in quantity and quality which I really liked. Although just with the original, since these events are scripted, they won't have much lasting replay value. This is only worsened by the considerable amount of reused assets, textures, and music so you may find you've exhausted most of what there is to do and the story is the only motivator to keep you going.

Despite this, I still enjoyed my time playing Extraction Point. At a campaign length of around 5 hours, I would recommend it for anyone who's completed the main game and is itching for a bit more story content and some extra spooks.
Released two years after the original game, Perseus Mandate takes place about midway through F.E.A.R.'s story from the perspective of a Sergeant from a secondary team of operatives. Once again, gameplay is essentially the same albeit a few additional weapons and enemy types. Also included is three bonus missions which are reminiscent of the Xbox 360's instant action missions. Nice addition but it seems like expanding on these was a missed opportunity.
Like Extraction Point there is a lot of repetition. However now there is more emphasis on the combat which overstays its welcome about a third of the way through the campaign. The last two intervals in particular are very monotonous and follow the basic pattern of: enter room > music starts playing > shoot 4/5 baddies > kill the last guy > music stops, confirming they're all gone > move to the next room > rinse/repeat. Occasionally a small horror moment will provide some respite but by this point most players would have probably lost too much interest to be engaged. Game time clocked in again at around 5 hours.
I also experienced the most bugs within Perseus Mandate (listed below) so in retrospect, I think this expansion was of a lower quality when compared to the other two games. If you are a fan of the series and would like it for completion's sake, give it a go. But otherwise I would recommend stopping after Extraction Point.

The Witcher 2 is a great game. The plot is great and has more story about Geralt's past in it than the previous game.
Combat is a step up from the first game, but its nothing to write home about. Alchemy got a slight rework too, however I prefer the alchemy in the first game. A good crafting mechanic has been added that helps you get better gear cheaply as long as you have the crafting diagrams and the required components.
What I really liked about this game (and what many people dislike) is the preparation aspect. You have to drink the potions before fights instead of using them as consumables on the go. The potions last much longer than they do in the first game. There are also blade oils that you have to apply beforehand. Although, I must admit, certain fights that you don't expect to happen catch you off-guard because of this.
The 3 skill trees allow for different playstyles, but don't expect different classes like common rpgs - you use your swords, potions and signs in conjunction with each other, regardless of your build.
The sidequests are interesting and sometimes deep, only a very few of them are simple fetch quests.
The game also has some flaws, like the UI is pretty bad and breaks immersion. Doors in the game are pretty bad. Many of the fights can be won by just rolling around till you have enough vigour to use quen (a spell that negates the damage from one attack) making you wonder why you even bothered to use potions or craft better gear. It is also extremely evident that the minigames and the quick time events have been designed favoring a controller, which is really a shame because this really is a game you'd want to play with kb+m.
All in all, The Witcher 2 is a very enjoyable game. I suggest playing the first Witcher game and this before starting The Witcher 3.

This game has also one of the best romance scenes in the gaming history (yes, I mean the one with the Triss Merigold :-)) ) and the choices you make throughout your adventure makes you feel like they really have impact on the story (which they really do!).
If you played Witcher 3 but haven't tried previous two titles, I highly recommend you to go for it - you will have ton of fun! And if you haven't play Witcher 3 yet and you are thinking if you should start with the previous games first - hell yes! It feels great to go through the lore from the very beggining, absorb the story, the characters and all the things that will come back at every corner in the Witcher 3.

Nex Machina... wow wow WOW.... Housemarque has done it again! This is an extremely well done arcade style game and you can definetely tell where it's inspiration is from, considering the creator of Smash TV and Robotron 2084 (both games I loved as a kid) helped make this game. The twin-stick shooter genre has always been a staple for me in games since I was a kid. I've been a fan of Housemarque's games all the way back to Super Stardust, a little game that was kind of like Asteroids in the late 90s. This was later remastered for the PSP and PS3 and spawned many more Super Stardust games.  Housemarque's previous title, Resogun, is one of my current favorite games to play on my PSVITA and I wish it would come to PC, but sadly that doesn't seem to be happening, but that's ok! Nex Machina MORE than makes up for it! It's fast, frenetic, and keeps you on your toes with constant action, from dodging enemy fire, lasers, dashing around to save humans for that sweet score multiplier, and collecting several different weapon power-ups to blow the baddies to literal bits of cubes. The voxel driven look of this game is very similar to what was used in Resogun, but seems to be cranked up even higher than before! At the time of this review, there is currently only single player, and local co-op, and I'd like to see online multi-player added at some point. If you're a huge fan of arcade games or twin-stick shooter/bullet hell style games, I totally recommend this!

A shockingly competent and overlooked shooter that made the unfortunate mistake of being released at the same time as Quake 2. Graphically, it cannot hold a candle to that game. But its charmingly old-school, yet functional, gameplay make it perfectly palatable to retro FPS fans like myself.
This feels like a combination of Duke Nukem 3D and Doom 64. There are three characters to choose from with slight stat variations like speed, health, etc. and while they do speak from time to time it's mostly to comment on the current puzzle or the nature of the situation in general to keep the player tuned in; players hoping for wise-cracks about bubble gum might be disappointed. The horror element comes from the perpetually dim environments and the haunting ambient soundtrack, which suggests trepidation on the part of the player rather than going in guns-blazing (though you are free to play that way if you so desire).
As one would expect from a BUILD engine game, there is a degree of environmental interaction, such as explosive objects and floating / moving platforms. Enemies die in fiery explosions with gibs flying this way and that. There is an inventory full of the usual plethora of deployable powerups. But Eradicator has some features that set it apart from the likes of Duke, Blood and Shadow Warrior; air and ground mechs that can be controlled remotely to attack the enemy and solve puzzles, deployable remote-controlled bombs, non-linear missions with multiple objectives, and a METRIC ****-TON OF WEAPONS.
This game has honestly the largest arsenal of any game from that time period that I know of. They are pretty creative, too-- triple barrelled explosive dart launchers, energy shotguns, boomerangs (that actually return to you!), bouncing pellet cluster bombs, support drones, so on and so forth.
My only complaints would be the sensitivity of certain functions. You have to tap the key that controls run / always run very quickly or else it will switch right back. Same goes for the map, which will shoot the camera into the floor and back out into outer space if you tap the +/-zoom keys with anything more than a feather. The lack of a QUICK quick save really bugged me as well-- F6 works, but it takes you to the save screen, where you have to spend precious seconds tapping ENTER once or twice before you can get back into the action. I refunded Duke Nukem 20th Anniversary World Tour after 30 seconds for this oversight alone.

The gameplay is just as compelling today as it must have been a decade ago, and I often found myself wanting to play one more level. Admittedly, it does have some pacing issues, and I feel like it suffers a bit from lack of an autosave feature. The level design is great, with each area presenting several means of progressing, and you rarely feel like you're forced to choose a specific play style or set of powers or weapons. However, in some respects, the game hasn't aged well. The graphics are painfully dated, but in Deus Ex's defense, its ridiculous plot and cheesy dialogue provides more than enough charm to overlook its faults. It's impressive to see a game that was made 10 years ago contains more choices (and perhaps more importantly, consequences) than many games made today. If there's any game in need of a remake, it's Deus Ex.

The first two hours had me traveling the same path numerous times while fighting the same respawns.  It can be maddening.
Compared to a far superior ARPG like Torchlight that came out a year earlier, Hazen: The Dark Whispers just can't compete.

Eradicator is quite typical of the late 90s. A sci-fi plot with 'x-tr33m badassitude' bordering on Image Comics silliness (Dan with his metal skullcap is a good example), dark and brooding ambience with cyborgs and explosions, but at the same times interesting mechanics (with secrets to find, interactive environments and multi-layered levels). The controls are simple but fine, there is a staggering 15 weapons (easily a year before the Turok games went overboard with it) each character has a personal gun and their own plot. The graphics, being sprite-based, did not age that well (also because they're based on low-res GC render), but it's nothing eye searing. Sounds are a mixed bag, while the guns, alarm voices and explosions work quite well, the characters' banter is lifeless and add nothing in the end. The music is nice, mixing basic ambient industrial and basic industrial rock, and the CD version offers redbook music, which is very pleasant. Unfortunately multiplayer will be hard to use, being restricted to modem or serial play according to 1996 DOS stardards. Levels are built around the idea of searching everywhere for hidden stashes of ammo and power-ups, and function on an objective-based script rather than a key hunt structure, which might mean a bit more backtracking in later stages and much more experimentation (for example, in the third level of Eleena's story you can explore the whole stage by hacking a security drone) than DooM or Heretic's labyrinths. The controls are fairly responsive, but the camera focus is a bit close, making jumps a bit tedious.

This game is closing in on 18 years now, and it's still one of the best games I know. The dialogue, the variety in choices to complete missions and the alternative endings... So many of later games have, knowingly or not, borrowed plot points from Deus Ex. It's more than nostalgia, it's an epic within the genre.

It's like Endless Space and Crusaders Kings had wild, mechanically complicated sex and spawned this little bundle of timesinky joy.
Stand Out Features: Realtime 4x gameplay that doesn't overwhelm those more accustomed to turn based affairs.  Beautiful art and music that matches the alien atmosphere.  Crazy levels of depth in the management of your space empire (manage your colonies, edicts, government leaders, policies, ship design, ground armies, naval fleets, diplomatic relations with primitive and rival alien species, technology and I'm pretty sure I'm missing at least 3 other aspects to micromanage).  Narrative elements jazz up the traditional 4x gameplay, turning every new game into a miniature story.
Pros:  Aforementioned depth (Cannot be oversold.  Compared to many other 4x games, there's just so much more to do in this one).  Variety in the leaders allow for different gameplay experiences.  Has that "one more turn" allure of similar 4x titles.  Solid and clever writing.
Cons: Volume of different mechanics to internalize might be overwhelming.  Tutorial leaves out several mechanics that you'll quickly learn are quintessential to your success.  Some mechanics are a bit soft and may leave you scratching your head to figure out why certain things played out the way they did (looking at you fleet combat score).  Game will require hours of your time and probably some independent research to fully immerse into.
Would Recommend To: Fans of the Endless 4x franchise games, Crusader Kings 2 players looking for a little more gameplay, Civ 4 fans who felt Civ 5 was too much of a streamlined experience.  Fans of Sci-Fi games who are not intimidated by a steep learning curve.

Eradicator is a mostly forgotten shooter from 1996. I recently played it, and decided that it's understandable why it was forgotten. It's murky, monotonous, and frustrating, and it doesn't really do anything to stand out in any way.
It looks and plays a hell of a lot like Duke Nukem 3D, to the point that I wouldn't be surprised if the code was mostly Build Engine. The palette's the same, the gib physics are the same, there are security cameras you can look at, and overall it just seems like a Duke Nukem mod. This isn't a bad thing, necessarily, but it's very noticeable if you've played any Duke Nukem.
Eradicator's main aesthetic difference from DN3D is that it's really ♥♥♥♥ing dark. Most of the colors are brown and gray, and everything is in so much shadow that a lot of the time you can't even tell what's going on. This even extends to the minimap, so often it's nigh-impossible to navigate. I'm not sure why this choice was made, but it makes the game unpleasant and confusing to play and really detracts from the overall experience.
There are three different characters (plus a secret fourth one once you beat the game), like in HeXen, but unlike HeXen they don't seem to have entirely different playstyles, so I just wouldn't bother.
The level design is really screwy and often difficult to navigate, a concern only exacerbated by the omnipresent shadow and darkened minimap.
The game's really bad at telling you if what you're looking at is an objective, or if you're making any progress at all. Eventually you get the hang of what sorts of things are interactible and which aren't, but it's an uphill battle getting to that point.
You don't seem to obtain guns in this game; rather, your character seems to start out with all the guns already and simply collects different types of ammunition to gain use of them.
The default controls are pretty dumb, and require some rebinding.
The various "Buddy" powerups are pretty fun. They just summon a little robot friend who floats next to you and shoots whatever you shoot for a short period of time.
The jumping controls/physics are ♥♥♥♥ing terrible, which sucks because there's a lot of platforming in this game.
Sometimes the gameplay attempts to vary itself with sections where you remotely control a robot (tedious) or do something with a time limit (egregious).
Eradicator's main problem besides the murkiness, however, are its enemies. They're just annoying and poorly concieved. There are not one but two kinds of erratic flying suicide bomber enemies, which are really frustrating to fight. Quake also had an enemy like that, but Quake also made that enemy a big target and gave you a really inaccurate shotgun to hit it with; Eradicator does neither of these things. Also, I thought Dark Forces taught us that a water-based enemy who occasionally pops up and fires a projectile at you is a really bad idea, but apparently the developers of this game didn't get that message. These are only the worst examples of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ enemy design; there are certainly many others.
Overall, Eradicator is just frustrating and unfun; not enough to make it offensively bad, but enough that it becomes a chore to play. If you're on the fence about getting it, normally I'd recommend it because playing more games is always good; however, I just can't see anyone getting anything out of playing this. It won't broaden any horizons or teach you new things. It just exists, pointless and bad. Unless you're an FPS completionist like me, I recommend saving your money for something better.

Probably the best real-time 4x game I've ever played. Suffers from trying to do too many things at once, ending feeling a bit shallow. The lack of actual end-game objectives feels very restrictive, as the only ways to win the game are either to fight everyone else and win, or to spread to a ludicrous amount of planets that makes the game a laggy nightmare to manage. Lacks any sort of peaceful victory conditions, religions, minor factions and singular planet states. Also the lack of neutral aliens (total of 4 races and 3 end-game horrors) makes the universe pretty boring.
That said, the huge game-changing patches have improved on almost every important aspect of the game, and knowing Paradox, they will keep on improving and adding content. The fact that the lead writer of Sunless Sea has recently joined the team gives me a lot of hope for the galaxy to become a lot more interesting place.

Here is my work around for Cossacks after much finagling. I hope this helps you guys.
1. You need the C2_Patch_v1_2.exe (google that exact thing and download it)
2. Download Universal Extractor (google it and download it
3. Use Universal Extractor to extract the C2_Patch_v1_2.exe patch into any file you want on your desktop
4. Copy and paste extracted patch into the root folder for Cossacks 2 c:/programfiles(x86)-Steam-steamapps-common-Cossacks II Napoleonic Wars
5. Run game using startengine.exe button in root folder
This may be all you need to get it to work. However if you get the error
'Engine.exe has detected, that video memory is not configured properly. Please restart computer and set AGP Aperture size-256 Mb or more in BIOS configuration program."
you need to do another couple of steps
6. Download the c2-hoae-3d-patch.zip and copy and paste its contents into the same root folder the first patch went in and run the game using the startengine.exe button
O.k. now the game works but I can't save a file (smh why would steam allow this to be sold when its so broken?)
1. Go to the root folder.
c:/programfiles(x86)-Steam-steamapps-common-Cossacks II Napoleonic Wars
2. If there is no folder named 'Save' then create a folder named 'Save'
3. If there is a folder named 'Save' open it and delete any folders inside it (possibly says 'camp' not sure)
4. Remove the "Read-only" status from the Cossacks II Napoleonic Wars folder
-Do this by right clicking on the folder, select properties, deselect 'read-only' and hit apply (may need to do this every time you play the game...I have for some reason.)

Cubicle Quest is a turn based RPG Maker game which combines itself with real life concepts. You just graduated from college with tons of debt, mainly college loan, and you'll have to do anything to pay them off and succeed in life. You can get married, fight tons of internal and external conflicts which are wrapped as monsters, and so on. This game reminds me with Harvest Moon with its non linear timeline in real life setting.
Most (if not all) of this game's musics are using default assets. Some musics are not appropriate although most of them are okay. The music is forgettable though. This is probably because of the default assets.
Similar to the musics, most (if not all) of this game's graphics are using default assets. The town mappings are quite bland with houses placed everywhere and the dungeon designs are just okay. The dungeons itself are quite short and some of them has puzzles, although it's quite easy and not that interesting.
There is also an overlapping enemies in Key of the Soul. If there are two big sized enemies, one of them will have their face covered with the others.
There isn't much story to the game except for how our MC pay the debt and kill the last boss. However, there are lack of informations in the game; There is a sign with no text in Port Nostalgia, Boss Complacency and Hedonic Treadmill which has their dialogue swapped, and an equipment, "Me, Myself, and I", which isn't written that it has counterattack chance although it does.
First of all, there are 9 playable characters although you can only choose 3 person (the MC is a must have) as your party members. They will join your party after you either help or talk to them. Although you can't raise your party member's stats, their stats will be increased automatically each levels which will help them determine their role. Some party members are healers, and some are dps. Because the non active party member will receive half exp from battle, you can switch some party members if you're not quite satisfied with them.
Each character has its own skills. Although there are a lot of party members, their skills distribution are unbalanced. Most bosses weak against personal attacks and most multi damaging skills (the strongest type) are personal type. Party healing skill can only be learned by the glass cannon (Alayna) and there is even a party member which has 2 skills which can only be used outside the battle with a high MP cost despite of its weak skill effect (Gina).
Speaking of attack types, this game has different elements from your usual RPG. This game introduces 4 main elements: personal, work, human, and mental. The only way to know the enemy type is by attacking them with each skill type. However, mental element is divided into several other elements such as stress, depression, and delusion and each of them have their own skill weaknesses which make them looks like a separate element although it can be reduced easily with equipments. The status effects are also spelled differently from normal RPG. However, if you play a lot of RPG Maker games, you'll know what they do based on their symbol.
The equipments are also spelled differently in this game. "Goal" is your weapon, "Community" is your armor, and "Virtue" is your shield. The shield mostly is used either to reduce damage from various mental element damage or status resist (not nullify). There is also a book which can give you passive and active boost. You'll receive the active boost when you're equipping the book while you'll receive the passive boost after you gather enough BP which can be obtained by killing enemies. Although that there are a lot of statuses which can be obtained from the books, you can't see all of your party member's status (such as eva and special eva). Lastly, there is also an accessory which can give additional status boost.
In this game, you'll mostly explore short dungeons and defeat their bosses in the end. Although the dungeons are short, they have high damaging enemies which can drain your MP quickly. Because there is no way to restore MP in dungeon except by using MP restoring items, you have to finish the dungeon quickly (you even have to save and load often) and the short dungeon works in our favor. However, some bosses in the game have an unforgiving one hit ko skill (for single and all party members) which have like 50% chance of succeeding.
Pros:
- 9 playable characters
- Marriage
- Lots of dungeons to explore
- Learnable stat boost (books)
Cons:
- Unbalanced party members
- Unusual and nonsensical element type (mental elements)
- Enemies are quite strong (and drain tons of MP to beat)

Terrifying...the best looking ghost I've seen in an indie horror game. The ambient sounds, and the visual effects all play with your mind. Your goal is to "kill" the ghost. Now just know that you cannot run up and simply kill it when you see it, you must track it using radios and wtching for visual queues as well. You get quite a few tools but you must search the house to find them first. IR and UV cameras, candles, flour, (yes, flour) poison, and bear traps are among the many things you'll find lying about at your disposal.
There are a number of different modifiers to play the game, like a timed mode, no candles, one hit, and so on, giving this game a fair amount of replayability. The gameplay can at times be quiet and slow and at other times, fast and frantic. I really recommend this game, especially for the price.
The menu and options menu could use a little work, adding more customizable graphics options and so on, maybe an FOV slider. Also when you die, it just automatically restarts the game. I'd like the option to quit or restart, so you for sure know you've failed, also a "You've Died" type screen would be a nice addition as well. Its only day one for this game so hopefully the dev will read this and consider adding some or all of these things. Other than these few small gripes an overall terrifying and fun game.

I loved Witcher 1, and dived directly into W2. When starting, I found the new controls really clunky, and the manner in which they replaced the (admittedly rather simple) W1 combat was overly full of useless trinkets (did anyone ever use the caltrops?) and annoying button mashing. Someone in testing must have stopped at some point in the first chapter and said "I'm just rolling around the whole time". The difficulty curve is backwards, the fights in the endgame were against less enemies, and simpler patterns. The nekkers in the first chapter were borderline impossible because of how many of them you encountered at once. In the late game, you would rarely run into more than two enemies at the same time. You also fought a lot more human enemies in the later game, who were easier to dodge and parry, as opposed to the plants (forget the name) in the first chapter who can spit acid, break your block and charge.
Second, the dice and arm wrestling minigames were hardly interactive enough to make them fun diversions from the rest of the game. I understand that it would be unfair to compare it to Gwent in W3, but even the brawling in W2 at least had some fun to it, and not just a luck roll every time.
The cities were poorly laid out, which is completely possible, but the awful maps made the experience go from authentic feeling to generally frustrating.
My biggest issue with the Witcher 2, however, is the storytelling. I understand that the world of the Witcher is intended to be a grimdark or generally depressing place to be. However, while the Witcher 1 allowed small moments of success or levity, Witcher 2 seemed to make every decision a dilemma of worst-case scenarios. Oh, do I let innocent people burn to death, or the bad guy I've been chasing for hours get away for good? Hmm. You can rely on nearly every character in the entire game stabbing Geralt in the back at some point (sorry for spoilers) and it gets to the extent where you wonder how this NEW person is going to try and sell out, imprison or poison Geralt. Your main quest seems to be generally a moot point, because he is hoping to clear his name by blaming another Witcher, but everyone already hates Witchers in general and shifting the blame from one to another isn't likely to make a huge difference. Unlike Witcher 3, your actions never seem to actually create an impact on the world you're living in.
Overall, when I replay the series, I will play W1, read a plotline synopsis of W2, and then play W3. The game just isn't worth playing through again.

This is great game, but overshadowed by contemporary 3D action releases.
Should Duke Nukem3D and Quake be released later, this game would have claimed the throne.
Why? Imagine:
- destructable environment elements
- shootable switches
- more than 10 different weapons with upgrades
- usable remote cameras
- 1st / 3rd person view switch, 3rd person view has changable camera angle
- remotely controlled weapons and objects
- hi-res environmental audio with really artistic soundtracks
- characters are talking and soliloquizing
- atmospheric level design and art
- night vision system
- normal mouselook is on just from the start (!)
- diverse inventory, which is not just to boost your stats, but to interact with enemies (turret gun or forcefiled)
- enemies are really different in their features and behavior making the game properly challenging
- game is more or less replayable due to different characters (1 is hidden!) who can somehow make shortcuts or can go slightly another way because of their diffferent stats and slightly varying weapons.
- fairly good physics for that dated title and no glitches
Use your brain to combine weapons and inventory items according to situation and you will have a strong taste of tactical shooter. Look how much break-through features had this game. And this all came years ago!
Drawbacks? Probably just 2:
- As many games of that period the story is slightly bland and generic (but still explains what, where and why are you doing). But this was where lot of games fall short back to these days.
-There is only one thing I can really complain about considering the age of the game: this is low resolution (seems to be VGA) which was not a top notch than already.
Summary:
If you've haven't played any retro shooters and don't know what to expect, probably you won't be satisfied with Eradicator.
If you are sure that you feel good about playing retro and you have fair expectations for the title of that age - go ahead and buy it. You will be pleased with what you will get.

This is not a great game.  In fact, it's really barely a mediocre game.  There are some problems with the AI, a lot of the weapons are situational at best, and fairly useless at worst, ammo is too limited, and there's a lot of hunting for buttons to press to advance.
But it's not a strictly bad game.  Particularly compared to other 90's FPS games.  The engine is comparable to Build (Duke Nukem, Shadow Warrior, Blood), or Jedi (Dark Forces), and there are some neat features, such as some picture-in-picture weapons that let you remote control them.  The game does have inventory with some neat ideas in there.  And, while there's only a few you will be trying to use most of the game, there's a pretty wide selection of weapons actually available.
Overall, the game is serviceable, if a bit short.  The plot is threadbare.  But there's plenty of things to shoot, and plenty of secrets to find, like any good 90's FPS should have.  As a note, it has native mouse look, and it works fairly well, once you tweak the sensitivity enough.

The released game is barebone and buggy : you will spend your time accelerating time and waiting for whatever new meaningless research you have to go throuh.
There is pretty much no visual feedback to your progression and tech advances. None.
The only way to have any meaningfull enjoyable with the game is if you add a lot of mods to it.

Game mechanics that should work simply don't because they are bugs and once again you will need mods to correct those as there is no clear indication from the devs what is working and what is not.
Maybe in 2 years with some DLC will this be any good.
Right now it is just shiny and giving a good enough illusion of depth for most people to be happy, begin 10 games, finish 1 eventually, or maybe rather just giving up in the end when the victory conditions are just impossible to reach in any interesting manner.

It is unbelieveable how gullible people are and how companies can get away releasing such an unfinished product hidden behind a bit of graphical niceties. Such a game and its hype and broken mechanics is a pretty good reason not to buy games anynore.

Update - April 16th, 2017:
The game has improved enormously, and whilst some of its original flaws are still present, enough changes have been made to change my review to a cautious recommendation. It's still not for everyone, but with the addition of Utopia (which I would consider a must-have at this particular moment in time) the game is very enjoyable.
The new faction system is a big improvement and the rework of government, ethics, addition of civics and ascension perks just make for a far more rounded game.
If you are still unsure or a cautious buyer, wait one or two expansions further, otherwise if the game is on sale it is at this point worth picking up.
Old Review:
Stellaris could and should have been my absolute number one favourite game of all time.
It combines the concept of Paradox Grand Strategy with my absolute favourite genre, how could you not love this? Unfortunately the actual game falls flat. After the initial novelty wears off, there's nothing new to discover and exploration becomes a mundane and tedious chore.
The tech tree is incredibly shallow and extremely predictable, which leads to every single race feeling the same. There are game which came out a long time ago which have deeper tech trees and this is a hugely missed opportunity.
The worst part perhaps is that the game completely lacks any incentive in multiplayer to go to war with one another, due to the way war mechanics work and wars become an all-or-nothing thing. EU4 handles this in a much, much more enjoyable manner and the fact we can't go to war in Stellaris over a single system completely ruins everything.
The mid and late game need an enormous amount of work. I can't help but think that the game simply wasn't finish or that they've build a framework to expand on - but I personally don't feel like beta testing a game for Paradox. I know they will eventually turn this game into something that's probably going to be incredibly enjoyable, but for me they really dropped the ball on Stellaris. It's not anywhere near as fun as it could and should have been and it needs a lot of work to get it to a place that would make us want to play it again in our regular multiplayer group. For now, we will stick to EU4.

It's a vastly superior upgrade to the first Witcher game in almost every way.  Almost.  Since Witcher games are entrenched in a narrative, you would only be looking at reviews for the second game to wonder if it's better than the first while possibly being on your way (or way back) to the third game.  It is, so go ahead and get it.
The graphics are a huge upgrade, whereas the sound design is more of a side-grade.  It's not much of an issue since the sound in the first game wasn't bad, but it's only a slight upgrade here.  I did have crashing issues, but I might have to attribute that to Windows 8.1 since the game as designed for Windows 7.
The story is largely the same for any choices of Act 1, but a decision at the beginning of Act 2 splits the game down the center with different areas, quests, story, and cutscenes.  There are 16 "endings" to the game which pertain mostly to which people live (lol).  Something I give the game credit for is that if you choose one of the primary paths, it's a little more high fantasy and involved with monster hunting (which the series still doesn't have enough of).  The other path with your first ally is much more politically-charged, and I was glad to have a way out of it.  That's right, I've gone through 7 books and 2 games and medieval politics still bore the absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me, and although everyone seems to agree that both primary paths are interesting and informative, I was glad to have a side door to go through and have a different experience.
Leveling has been overhauled as well, with a tree for alchemy, swordplay, and magic.  You might be able to maximize one tree in all of your 35 levels.  Most of the upgrades aren't particularly fascinating, and only a few have one-time mutagen slots you can use to add other stats.  There is a respec available, but only if you discovered the item early on in the game.
Combat got a significant overhaul.  The signs are all still there, but sword styles are limited to light and heavy attacks with beautiful, inefficient flourishes.  They've also added a block and counterstrike system which can occasionally instantly kill enemies.  Something I disagree with is no longer being able to use potions in combat.  I understand that in the Witcher universe these are presented as toxic substances with benefits, and are supposed to contribute to an overall methodology of preparation before battle, but the outcome isn't handled all that well here.  You either fight in a surprise battle (like every battle), and if you die, you reload and shoot up, or you're relegated to boss fights reminiscent of Dark Souls.  I will say that these bosses ARE cheap, there's no question about that, but you CAN overcome them by simply playing better or learning patterns.  My complaint is that this mechanic and its compensatory factor are completely contrived for one sole reason - the absence of potions during combat.  I'm happy the game is tougher than the first, but unhappy that the challenge came about from such a lazy design choice.  Blade oils can still be used mid-fight - how the hell is the careful process of oiling your blade permitted but taking a quick swig from a tiny bottle not?
Money still has the same strange dichotomy here as it does in the first game - too little early, too much later on.  However, grinding still doesn't feel necessary.  I did it anyway because I wanted cash for all the crafting diagrams, but in retrospect I didn't need to.  Dice poker is chump change, 20-30 orens a pop, but at least it isn't badly rigged against the player this time around.
Some things are a little rough around the edges.  A crafting recipe MUST be in your inventory to make the item, you can't stash it in storage afterwards.  Upgrades and runes are permanent, no way to remove them.  Monster knowledge is enigmatically split into two menus, one in your journal, and the practical knowledge only when you meditate, so it can't be accessed during battle.  Normal mode, in spite of cheap deaths due to the potion mechanic, still didn't seem to make use of the "prepatory" mindset you're supposed to play the game with.  In spite of a profound number of oils, potions, and traps, I only used the basic healing potion and two or three blade oils the entire game, and even that much was unnecessary.
Game should last you at least 40 hours, tack on another 40 if you feel like seeing at least the other primary questline.  Worth it, on sale or not.

The game is a simple, yet fun arena.
The game modi are: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Gnome Hunt (you have to control a zone for a short time), Team Gnome Hunt, Survival (coop) and Kingslayer (coop)
It can be played multiplayer via internet, lan or local or singleplayer versus bots. The bots come in different difficulty levels, but are never as smart as a human.
The game also includes different hats and weapons that are unlocked via achievements or leveling, although the basic gear is just fine, so you are never at a high disadvantage towards high levels.
Basically, you are shooting small aliens to gain gold, which unlocks higher tier weapons in this round. In coop, these aliens attack you, in the other modes they are harmless.
The singleplayer consists of a short tutorial and then several matches against bots with different maps, settings and rules, and finally the match against the Alien King. It's really more a preparation for the MP or a way to gain levels, although you can easier gain levels by just creating an offline match to your rules.
What I really liked was the response of the devs to the problems I reported. It never took long to fix them and they always answered me.
The downside of this game is that it's player base is small, so you either bring your friends or you take the high ping problems. Or just do it with bots.
I had my 10 hours fun out of the game so far and I still play it with my friends.
TL;DR: Nothing special, cheap, casual fun, but recommended.

I don't think I've ever been so in love with a video game before...
It's buggy, horribly optimized, and suffers from such bad models and animations that they make a joke of it (traveling through landscapes that showcase herds of sheep-facades propped up in the pastures, or riding upon noble steeds who seem to be from the finest wooden toy horse stock), and you won't give a damn about any of it.  The multiplayer is nearly impossible to set up and laggy almost to the point of unplayability once you do, but it's such vibrant, stupid and chaotic fun that you'll ignore such minor negatives in favor of the grander scheme of bumbling wizards.
The innovative magic system is profoundly complex and joyously destructive to experiment with, and there's a very scientific glee involved with working out your trademark spell(s) or finding the coolest combinations to solve a particular problem.
You'll also learn to develop a newfound respect for such veterans of the wizardry craft as Gandalf or Dumbledore...  When you recognize just how much obscenely destructive force you have at your unwitting fingertips, it's always impressive when you DON'T manage to disintegrate/melt yourself and everyone in a 4-mile radius when attempting to do something.
While the game is fun enough on its own and the writing is of absolutely stellar class, with actually funny wit and some really quite unexpectedly subtle jokes and twists, this game excels at multiplayer.  Yes, the horribly-irritating-to-get-started multiplayer.
My deepest recommendation is to play this game with 3 friends, preferably with none of you knowing your wizard staves from your rump bristles.  Idiocy and a vast array of destructive weaponry often lead to the best of times, and ignorance of your own strength is the perfect excuse for "accidentally" slaughtering everyone on your team.
The game starts you off with a resurrection spell, and as with all spells and magic in this game there is neither a mana cost nor a cooldown of any sort...  And you'll be very happy that it is this way, as roughly 98% of player deaths are either self-induced or from friendly fire.  Or some wonderfully flashy combination of the two.
Indeed, the greatest danger you face is not the foe in front of you, but rather your overeagerness to simultaneously shock, burn, freeze and meltingly explode the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ into his primary colors.  Positively philsophical, really.
I have never for a moment regretted purchasing this game.  Indeed, my saddest moment was when it finally ended...  for the second or third time.  Along with all the DLC missions.

Great game. I really like the combat and AI. The environments were a little bland and repetetive, but I understand why it was done so (to accomodate the AI and technical limitations due to those awesome particle and shader effects). The texture work (mostly) is very well done and the dynamic light system is phenomenal. The level design is mostly combat centric (accomodating the AI behaviours) which is a very unique thing and adds a different type of exploration system.
The game has a bit of problems with newer hardware but that is due to the old engine. My only major complaint is that, some sections of the game drags on for a bit too long, hence making the pacing a bit bad. And some enemy types weren't really necessary and for them alternate ways to take them down would have been better. But for a product of its time, the game is way ahead of it. Completed the game in the hardest difficulty and I am glad to do so.
Also, the story is somewhat touching (towards the end), and making me feel sympathatic for the antagonist was a great deal. But some subtleities, like the morality behind cloning human beings and using them as expendable soldiers and stuff like that wasn't really explored, as it could have added a whole new layer of depth to the already good game.
As an aspiring level designer, it was awesome to see that every place I quick saved was the exact spots where the checkpoints were placed. In the mean time I will be attemting the sequels. Hope they are somewhat good and not as bad as what I have read in some reviews. A big thumbs up from me on this one. Good job and have a nice day devs!

This is one of my favourite but sadly underrated shooters from the 90's. Having played a demo of it at a young age I always longed to play the full version and bought the big box of it a couple of years ago. Now it seems the game is finally on Steam and so you might want to know a thing or two about it.
Eradicator is an oldschool shooter in the veins of Doom and Duke Nukem 3D, to which it shares most of its similarities though it is rather unique for its time. For one, it features multiple characters, each with their own personality. The weapons are also all rather interesting and serve different purposes. Another groundbreaking feature for this game was the ability to use RC cars and other remote controlled devices thanks to something called PIP (picture-in-picture) view. Another enjoyable thing about the game is the ability to switch between third person and first person perspectives at will (or automatically if you so choose) which helps immensely with the platforming sections, of which there are plentiful. The graphics are also really good for their time and give the game a gritty and dirty sci-fi atmosphere I enjoy a lot.
My only gripe with the game is the level design which does show its age. It is confusing and relies heavily on hunting down switches to push and it's not always obvious where to go. The maze-like design also makes it difficult to navigate the levels and using the map is something you will get used to quickly. The music also doesn't really do much and stays in the background most of the time, adding to the ambience of the game. I'd much rather turn it off and turn on some good old 90's rock.
But all in all this is one of the more underrated shooters from the 90's and fell under the shadow of Quake and other more successfull games. It's nice to see it on Steam and back in action for those who missed it and those who love it. If you're a fan of shooters like Doom, Duke 3D, Blood etc. I highly recommend picking it up.
