This game is good, no doubt, but it suffers so much that at times its not enjoyable. The combat is very clunky and at times just doesn't work right and theres very little differentiation in how to defeat enemies besides block/parry/dodge/spam. Theres almost nothing to do with all of the crafting items that you get, items from merchants are way too overpriced, armor except for the chest pieces are virtually the same things The voice acting is super off in some parts and is pretty bad at times. The bosses are by far the absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wrost boss fights I have ever encoutered in a video game. The first fight with the Kingslayer is unfair and boring, the fight with the Draug is monotonous and dumb because he'll spam a ranged attack over and over, and the fight with the dragon is literally just a roll back->roll forward->attack->repeat. The signs except for Quen, Igni, and Yren (or however you spell it) are absolutely useless in my opinion. The skill tree is far too big for such a short game, as I ended up being around level 35 when I beat the game. The potion system is very poorly done, because on your first playthrough you have no idea what is going to be up ahead, and therefore you don't know what potions to have used and probably die as a result.
Despite all the negatives, the game also does have its good parts as well. The soundtrack is very well done, it has beautiful tunes, but they're overused at times and I probably didn't even hear half of them. The graphics are beautiful for the time, even though I wasn't able to run it on max settings it still looked good and held a very stable FPS. There's a good story, but it is easy to get lost quickly if you don't pay attention or didn't play the first game (like me). I do like that they added a toxicity to the potions so you can't just chug everything at once and become a sterioded mess.
Overall, I'd have to give it a 6/10. I have high hopes for The Witcher 3 whenever I get to playing it, but I'd say to skip out on this entry on the series unless you're looking for backstory.

I feel like I have to clear up somethings on this game since recently there have been many bad comments on this game. Overall I really enjoyed the game and would play it many times to come. Now I have played Crusader Kings 2 and EU4, and I can say this game is not like them....but that's the point. This is a game based off of the syfi universe movies and modern culture have created. All of it is open to change, new features, etc. However, when it comes to CK2 and EU4, they  both are made off of real time periods and events. When Paradox is making a game off of a real event, they can add in the many complicated and complex features of running and maintaining a kingdom/empire. With sifi you can not do the same to it. There is so much variety and difference in not just the time period or the technology but in everything! You can not make every alien race act like humans because they are not human. You can not give them the flaws humans have because they are not human. The path Paradox took in this game made sense and is fun. What other game is there where you have so much control over an empire in a vast galaxy? If there are other games that are out there who try to accomplish that goal, they have a lot to compete with. A player can create his own faction from scratch. Deside from the start if this empire should be a warhungry empire or a peaceful city state in a waring galaxy. If you want it to be like eu4 then give yourself restrictions, make enemy empires that have all the flaws and assets of a human society. If you are too lazy to do that then simply open your mind to the many possibilities that come from being able to make an empire as large as a galaxy and embracing the lifestyle you want not what is programmed into the system.

Honestly, I was pretty excited about this game after watching some Youtubers play it.
I convinced my friend to get it with me, and we played for about an hour and a half and nearly killed Bigfoot on our first try.
That's when we realised that the game just isn't that fun. The janky placeholder (hopefully temporary) animations and models aside, there just isn't much to do. Either  you place a trap and watch it on your cameras, then rush to the site and hopefully get a tracker on Bigfoot so you can chase him for 5 minutes while doing almost no damage to him whenever you shoot; or you just go out and search for him without the use of traps. That's all you can do, really, and I don't see any other mechanics being added anytime soon. If you see how The Rake turned out, it's not really expected there'll be much more in terms of mechanics, and I don't count the soon*tm* to be released snow map + Yeti to be much different other than a re-skin of the default map.
Eventually Bigfoot will become a bit more aggressive and start attacking your trailer, but as long as you are there to shoot him he'll usually start running away after 2-3 shots. My friend and I repeated this (trapping, then chasing for 5-10 minutes until out of trackers) for over an hour and a half, until my friend died and was unable to respawn (because that isn't added yet) and I got bored being on my own, because there's nothing to do except endlessly chasing Bigfoot around in circles.
On top of this, the gameplay just isn't good. The mouse sensitivity was way too high, with no way to change it in the settings. You can't aim down sights, shooting feels incredibly lackluster, and the lack of any sort of shooting or reloading animations is more offputting than Bigfoot itself.
Oh, and to finish off, there is a random "jump scare" of lightning striking nearby, setting a tree ablaze. The lightning sound effect is maxed out volume wise, and is incredibly (realistically) loud. The issue is, it'll happen completely randomly. During the day, during the nighttime, during a storm, and during a clear morning with no clouds. And it happens frequently, once every 5 minutes maybe.
Anyway, I can't recommend this game to anyone until they introduce more mechanics and polish to the game, which, as I said before, probably won't happen as we've seen with The Rake. My bets are the devs will "finish" the snow map, add a save feature and respawn feature (yeah, no saving in a game that takes easily 2 hours to actually kill Bigfoot alone,) and then will move on to a new monster game with a familiar lack of polish.
Prove me wrong, devs.

This has been probably one of the best gaming adventures I've ever had. It's hard to compare its weight, story, dialogue, character and mood with any other.
It's choices are the of the weightiest I've ever had to make. The world, script and atmosphere made several of these major choices nerve-wracking for a variety of different reasons. There is no "good" path or "bad" path, it's just choice and consequence, and it's not always 100% clear what those consequences are, but the reactions and effects are fantastic to see unfold.
It's improved over the Witcher 1 in every single way, and even now, years after it's release, the graphics are still downright great, the combat challenging but fun, and it still feels humble, well-acted and a solid adventure title. I would extremely recommend this to anyone looking for a good story that isn't squeamish. It's very adult, and it treats you like and adult.
My cons with it would be perhaps a better tutorial, and a few other specifics like certain abilities better explained. As well as fast travel wouldn't hurt a few times. I played using keyboard+mouse and found the controls decent, though it seems to be well-made for controllers too. Overall, I had a total blast and definitely will be playing it again in the future, using a different path and different choices.
Very few games I've ever played could match this for quality writing, content, script and atmosphere.

I started up the game switched the controls to joystick and tried again.  After loading up the tutorial I was met with being told to do things with [][]  with no buttons inside to let me know what to do.  So Knowing I was trying to select a bot I hit every button on the controller including pushing down the movement sticks, yet none of the buttons slected the bots.  So with all my dreams crushed and the inability to deal with the horrendous controls, I step back and write this review to warn others.

This is an Indie game that has it's own standards and priorities that diverge, tremendously, from that of AAA titles. There are so many games that seek to limit the player into a narrow and limited vision that a couple developers had. This game is not like that.
I think if all you play is the currently popular games then this game will be an empowering experience for you. This is a game that is wide open for you to change. Play this game. With that said, though, I absolutely recommend it for those out there that enjoy a game that encourages a balance of creativity, quick thinking and fast reflexes but want to avoid any excessively steep learning curves and/or extreme demand for pure twitch skill that can come with trying to enjoy similarly difficult and fast-paced action games.

Nice story and character moments, and the visuals hold up surprisingly well. Aside from modding potential, this release has 2 specific advantages to simply emulating the original, getting in on PSN, etc.
1) Hi-speed mode. This is like unlocking the FPS limit on an emulator, but the music doesn't get warped. Since you will spend a lot of time either in the field or an unskippable cutscene, this could save you multiple hours in a single playthrough. Also, during certain timed segments the timer will not be sped up - this is kinda cheating, but arguably justified since you're dealing with some annoyingly long battle animations. I think you can use this hotkey (F1), avoid the rest (F2-F5, which are unquestionably cheating) and still feel like you are playing legitimately.
2) Magic Booster. This is a built-in hack that gives you 100 copies of every spell in your inventory, for each character. But it does not give you spells you don't have. This is definitely cheating, but if you've played the game before, you might see this cheat as acceptable compared to max Gil/damage/etc... you can easily farm 100 copies of most spells, but it is very time-consuming.
That said, this game has some design issues regardless of what platform you're on. The Junction system is kinda broken, and the game ends up becoming very easy once you've obtained enough spells (which takes time and/or effort, but not skill). For me, one particular character could completely demolish every boss with little to no strategy involved. It's not awful, but it's not great either, which is why I think stuff like the magic booster isn't a big deal. Overall, this is one you'll enjoy for the story over the gameplay.

The game still has a LOT of things that need to be fixed. For a lot of people, the game DOESN'T WORK AT ALL. Stellaris is an interesting, long and mostly absorbing game of grand strategy. It is not, imo, a game for those that like quick results, snappy gameplay or to be continuously entertained. It requires patience and some degree of bloody-mindedness to persevere with.
In the beginning it seems relatively quick, stuff happens a lot and you need to pay attention. As the game progresses you take more time preparing and planning and accumulating resources, ships, etc for your next move.
In essence the game stops giving you things to do and you need to take over the universe, or die trying! There is really not much else to do, and here I think is the issue. The end game is not handed to you, you have to work for it.
Overall I think it is a great game, but I can see how others do not care for it.
Note: this review was largely written after playing against the AI (which is decent, but not awesome) on a medium map with standard settings (600 systems, 17 opponents, 4 advanced).

This game is the thinking man's space strategy game. It really does make you think about real-life society, because you get complete control over how your in-game society looks, behaves, and performs. The various government forms, the way you can choose to enslave your people for extra mineral and food output, but most of all the ethics system. There are 8 ethics, each of them with an opposite (e.g. individualist vs collectivist). Some might seem plain evil at the outset, but when you read the short paragraph about each of them by mousing over them, you start to wonder. What do I choose if I want to be a "good guy"? The game even makes it unclear what to choose to be a "bad guy". There simply are no such things. You can be a warlike race who hates aliens with a passion, but really all you want is to keep your citizens safe from the dangers of the galaxy. And yes, there are dangers. Some alien races will hate you. And if you've managed to break away from the rest of the pack and become one of the big powers, as usually happens with skilled players, you have to decide who lives and who dies, because allies will be seeking your help against enemies that you know they can't possibly beat. And you'll have to choose.
Oh, one more thing. The weapons are quite nice too. Even if you want to be all peaceful, sometimes you'll find yourself giddy at the prospect of a particle lance, or a neutron torpedo.

Stellaris is, at heart, Sword of the Stars III. Given that the original SotS was excellent and that SotS II was almost as good as Master of Orion III (snark intended), it's hard to guess how it turned out until you play it for a while.
The early game is solid, with interesting choices for Xploitation, Xpansion, and Xploration.
However, after the initial XXX phase is over, the game settles into a long, drawn-out death rattle of tedium from which you cannot avert your eyes and let the game progress in real-time because the developers removed almost all of the user-configurable auto-pause triggers from the game (they are just not there, an issue that also plagues the more recent Hearts of Iron IV). The recent "Asimov" patch does not cure the boredom-inducing real-time zombification of being forced to remain glued to the screen while you wait an interminably long time for things to happen or for your influence resource to creep high enough to allow you to make further progress.
That missing feature is enough for me to tip this review from generally positive to generally negative.

F.E.A.R. is one of the best FPS games of its generation. It still holds-up fantastically over a decade later, not just in its gameplay, but its graphics. It's not hard to run the game with max settings and it looks excellent, like something from 2010, not 2005.
The single-player is a solid length, especially for how cheap it is now and how often it goes on sale. The Max Payne-ish bullet-time shooting is excellent and satisfying. The A.I. is good, though I recommend people who like a high difficulty to play on Veteran instead of Hard, as the game gives you lots of healing and ammunition to keep you going as long as you make it out of combat alive.
The horror elements of the game are fun, but not particularly frigtening. It is an FPS first and a horror-game second, so if you want it to be really scary, you'll likely be disappointed. However, it does have a decent atmosphere, and I did get jump-scared a couple times in my playthrough.
The only complaint I have is that whenever I would exit the game, my computer would be black-screened until I manually restarted it. I couldn't windows-key or ctrl+alt+delete out of it, so I had to really commit to playing it in long sessions.
Overall, it's a 5/5 in 2017, and I implore you to buy this game.

This has been probably one of the best gaming adventures I've ever had. It's hard to compare its weight, story, dialogue, character and mood with any other.
It's choices are the of the weightiest I've ever had to make. The world, script and atmosphere made several of these major choices nerve-wracking for a variety of different reasons. It's improved over the Witcher 1 in every single way, and even now, years after it's release, the graphics are still downright great, the combat challenging but fun, and it still feels humble, well-acted and a solid adventure title. I would extremely recommend this to anyone looking for a good story that isn't squeamish. It's very adult, and it treats you like and adult.
My cons with it would be perhaps a better tutorial, and a few other specifics like certain abilities better explained. As well as fast travel wouldn't hurt a few times. I played using keyboard+mouse and found the controls decent, though it seems to be well-made for controllers too. Overall, I had a total blast and definitely will be playing it again in the future, using a different path and different choices.
Very few games I've ever played could match this for quality writing, content, script and atmosphere.

One of my first Paradox strategy games was Victoria 2; and I absolutely loved it. I'm not as experienced as many of the players of strategy games due to my late introduction to the genre at the age of about 16. But from the Paradox Grand Strategy games I have played, I have enjoyed every minute. There are definitely many times where I think of the ways in which the games can be improved, and Stellaris is no exception to this rule. If I want to be specific, I have a large problem with the military system in this game due to the inability to fight a defensive war. Much of the time when I have been at war with another space empire, I feel like one of the only engaging strategies implemented is that of ship upgrades. When I send my ships to fight, I find myself winning all the time just as long as I have more ships. I feel like such a stratgey (More ships + Effective Upgrades = Instant Win) doesn't engage the player in warfare as much as I would like. Considering Stellaris is a game about space conquest, warfare should be very well developed and strategic. But I digress from that of what I enjoy about this game. What really brings me back to playing this game is immersion. As silly as my opinion may sound to some, creating your own species, managing your planets, gathering resources, etc. makes me feel like I built something from nothing; A feeling that is something I really enjoy in any strategy game. Stellaris implements that very effectively. Despite questionable but pragmatic developer decisions (such as greater popualtion and colonies creating research penalties), Stellaris is a game that I would recommend to anyone looking to experience a sense of the unknown. To those looking for a war-based strategy game, I would look to the Hearts of Iron series instead. But simply because Stellaris brings out the inner astrobiologist in me, I can't rate this game down. This game employs the same simple and easy-to-play turn-based tactical singleplayer game system as HexWar's other releases in their TANK BATTLE and CIVIL WAR series, with novelties like amphibious landings, bridge-laying, mine-clearing, parachute-drops, a "historical" combat option, etc.  Ranged combat with line-of-sight implementation and some unit facing considerations.  Each unit has a maximum strength of 10, with attack capability diminished as strength is reduced.  The scale is tactical but unspecified with no unit stacking.  The combat system is odds-based with some variability in outcome, better than similar games which are entirely dice-based.  No headquarters or command-and-control implementation.  Many mini-campaigns included allowing you to play the U.S., British and Germans for many hours.  Some scenarios are tough nuts to crack.  Competent AI with three difficulty options.  High playability, low technicality.  If you like HexWar's other games, this won't disappoint.  Just beware that no multiplayer option is available.  Recommended.

Final Fantasy 8 is one of the first games that I remember playing, and I got hooked and it currently sits as my second favorite game I've ever played (behind Baldur's Gate 2). I've played it many times, read all of the criticism, and just recently completed all of the quests, so I'll attempt to address the main points on every side, bad stuff first.
What this leaves us with is a fantastic junction system that is built on the power and versatility of GFs, but is crippled by the forced grinding that is inherent in the broken Magic stock system. A small handful of characters shine, while the side characters prop them up and then fall to the wayside.
Final Fantasy is a deeply flawed game, and is not very forgiving to newcomers, but has some deep complexity with several rewarding points, both in combat and side quests.
The biggest complaint I've seen for FF8 is how your power level progresses, specifically the Draw + Junction systems as well as level scaling. The Draw system is the magic system in the game; each character has 32 total slots for magic and can "draw" magic from enemies or draw points, or have magic refined through a variety of abilities, with a maximum cap of 100 total stock of each spell. The Junction system works in conjunction with GFs (Guardian Forces, equipable summons that give you a bunch of skills and such) and is reliant on the Draw system in that you junction magic to your stats (HP, strength, magic, vitality, spirit for health, physical attack power, magical attack power, physical defense, magic defense), as well as more rare junctions like hit %, speed (how quick your turn comes up), evasion, status and elemental attack and defense junctions. Sounds all great and dandy with tons of customization right? And it is!
is that the effect of junctioned magic is directly related to how much of said magic you have stocked. 100 fires will give a lot more health than 10 fires, and the system very much encourages sitting in a super boring battle for 10 minutes to fully stock up on magic.
is that using magic will deplete your stock, therefore reducing their effectiveness as junctions, and thus meaning that there is never a good reason to use good spells, which is sad considering all of the crazy interesting spells, from Maelstrom (reduces physical defense to 0), to Double or Triple (allows you to cast 2 or 3 spells in a turn, respectively) to more traditional stuff like haste, regen, meteor, etc etc.
The other problem that arises where power levels are concerned is level scaling. Every enemy in the game (with a handful of exceptions) has a scaling set of stats, skills, and draws that corresponds to what level your characters are, and they scale much faster than your characters do respective to their levels. That's right, you're better off never leveling up anybody, as using the roundabout ways to acquire junctioning magic will make you much stronger relatively speaking than gaining EXP.
As far as the story goes, the problem here is that the side characters have little to no character progression. Outside of the main ~3 characters in the story, the side characters just don't have much going story wise to flesh out their personalities, introduce conflict, or provide any meaningful way for them to grow as characters. Personally, I like Squall (the main character), but the fact that there are so few developed characters means that 1) seemingly interesting characters are mostly wasted and 2) there is less of a chance for the player to bond with any of the characters (see: FF9 with its varied cast of characters), so unless you like Squall, Rinoa, or Laguna you probably won’t like the game from a story perspective.
*Note* I’m not touching the plot, as I feel like it is good not great, with several somewhat questionable choices throughout, but it neither makes nor breaks the game in and of itself.
Woohoo, stuff that makes the game worth playing! First up, Guardian Forces! Guardian Forces (or GFs) are summons that give you command abilities, let you junction magic, and refine stuff from stuff to give you more stuff! And you can summon them in battles to fight if you want, but that’s far from their most useful function (with the possible exception of the coolest of them all, Doomtrain). Why are GFs so cool? Because they tie everything together! They can help you in battle in a pinch, can be mixed and matched to get the right junctions, command skills, and support buffs you need, and can learn refining skills that will turn the useless junk you find into stupidly awesome magic and weapons! On top of that, many of them are new. Quezacotl takes Ramuh’s place as the lightning summon, while mainstays Shiva, Leviathan, Ifrit, Carbuncle, and Bahamut, in his best form of the entire series, all make appearances. New characters like Diablos, Pandemona, and Eden, and recurring characters that get their first appearance as summons in Cactuar, Tonberry, and Gilgamesh, all provide unique skill sets, as well as interesting ways to hunt them down (good luck with Ultima Weapon, Bahamut, Eden, and Tonberry without guides).
Next up, Triple Triad! Yes, it’s a mini game. Yes, it’s the easiest (and frankly, only realistic) way to become a God, but it’s much more than that. It’s a simple game with a 3x3 grid where each player has 5 cards with 4 numbers on them, one for each cardinal direction, and you flip cards but having a higher number than the one you place a card next to. Simple, right? But that doesn’t include a rule like Plus, where you have to calculate what they can do with their cards so you don’t get your super cards flipped. But then there’s the Elemental rule which turns your only safe play into a losing play. Triple Triad is fantastic fun, working on the winning formula of easy to learn, hard to master (until you hit the Queen of Cards quest or random rule, screw that garbage).

Although this is a local multiplayer game there are bots that make up for the lack of numbers. Initially Ainslie (my girlfriend) demonstrated some interest in challenging me. Unfortunately, real life events got in the way of the two of us playing and I held off writing this review. When she continued to be busy I decided to try my luck against the AI. I’m thankful that I did. This review will purely focus on the single-player experience.
Variety of vehicle types: There are a total of six. vehicle types. Each plays and performs differently from the other. Each has their own distinct advantages and disadvantages. One of the keys to being successful at the game will be discovering which vehicle you perform best with. Vehicle types include tank, Humvee, APC, artillery and hovercraft. Players also have the choice of choosing at random and having one.
A ton of game modes: More game modes have been included in the game than you can poke a stick at. Game modes include: Death match, war spoils, bullet hell, future tech, bombshell, spare parts, tour of duty, arms race, experimental weapon, blitzkrieg and limited resources.  Although some play very similarly there are enough differences to provide a broad enough arrangement of game styles to appease most players.
Great tutorial system: There is a great tutorial system which can be played through multiple times for each different vehicle type. I highly recommend that you play through with each type.
In summary, thanks to a good variety of vehicle types, game modes and a very well designed tutorial system that can be - and should be - replayed Toys of War's strengths make the game a ton of fun.
Mouse play: The biggest actual weakness in the game is the mouse play. The game has been designed with a controller in mind and with twin stick shooting mechanics at its heart. Therefore, unfortunately, the mouse play is vastly inferior to controller play.
Marketing: Unfortunately, when a game has been released for over a week, as of writing, and the game has just the sole review on steam marketing is to blame. In this respect the failure to mark the game as a single-player game is a significant hindrance. I understand that the developers have not wanted to market a game intended for local multiplayer unfairly. However, players such as myself enjoy the single-player options that the game has. Yes, I’m missing fun with friends but I do get joy from the game.
Slow loading time at the beginning: The original loading screen took my computer quite some time to process. This is a little disappointing given that there doesn’t appear to be a lot of content loading. However, the menu screens are quite well detailed and polished. Therefore, if this is the reason why then I can and will deal with it.
Toys of War already has a number of Steam achievements for the hunters out there. However, unfortunately, it currently lacks trading cards. The developers know that adding them will spur sales so I hope that they do so.
Although, Toys of War, would make for a highly entertaining party game I don’t feel as though I missed out on the experience as a single-player game. Unfortunately, because the game is marked as a local multiplayer game and not as a single-player the game has been ignored by most on Steam. Those who love action games and arena games would find this highly enjoyable.
As a single player, I recommend this if you’re looking for an arena shooter and are looking for some solidly designed AI. The great thing about this game is that it will never be dead and you’ll always be able to play it with or without other players around.

A totally unscientific look at the Science behind shooting potatoes into the sun, Spaceplan has you clicking a button to launch spudniks into orbit. With a clean, humorous interface, with self-effacing generic titles, the narrative becomes the focus of the game. As you add to your potato arsenal from the items on the left, and upgrade with research ideas on the right, more spud power is generated to propel your starchy voyage to return a dead earth to its former glory.
What I liked most about Spaceplan was that it left out the drag of hand-numbing clicking. There are no set number of clicks required to complete the game. And, the ability to upgrade means that the power continues to generate even while you have the game closed. Clicking speeds up the generation rate. Of course, macros work here too if you really want to speed things up. So, you are totally in control of the narrative.
Most importantly, it is a clicker that you really can’t stop playing until the end… or is there an end? The story is circular, and could keep going. So, theoretically you could keep playing forever. Seriously though, I see absolutely no replay value once you’ve reached the beautiful ending. That ending is fantastic enough to make you close the game with a happy feeling until you realize there is not another clicker like it to fill the new black hole you’ve created.

F.E.A.R. is one of the best FPS games of its generation. It still holds-up fantastically over a decade later, not just in its gameplay, but its graphics. It's not hard to run the game with max settings and it looks excellent, like something from 2010, not 2005.
The single-player is a solid length, especially for how cheap it is now and how often it goes on sale. The Max Payne-ish bullet-time shooting is excellent and satisfying. The A.I. is good, though I recommend people who like a high difficulty to play on Veteran instead of Hard, as the game gives you lots of healing and ammunition to keep you going as long as you make it out of combat alive.
The horror elements of the game are fun, but not particularly frigtening. It is an FPS first and a horror-game second, so if you want it to be really scary, you'll likely be disappointed. However, it does have a decent atmosphere, and I did get jump-scared a couple times in my playthrough.
The only complaint I have is that whenever I would exit the game, my computer would be black-screened until I manually restarted it. I couldn't windows-key or ctrl+alt+delete out of it, so I had to really commit to playing it in long sessions.
Overall, it's a 5/5 in 2017, and I implore you to buy this game.

This game is truly one of a kind and its not even finished. The general summarization of what you do is you hunt bigfoot and attempt to find the missing crew and thats alot more fun than it sounds. Every game is a striaght shot no saving or reloading here just you play till you complete the story or die or play for hours on end till you need to sleep. You can "hunt" Bigfoot luring him with deer meat, trapping him in hidden traps and looking for him with cameras. Unfortatley all of these are hit or miss and he will be the one hunting you most likely. You start with a set amount of supplies and from there on out your on your own so use your items sparingly. Your ultimate goal is to hunt Bigfoot and trap him and yes it is indeed as hard as it sounds so goodluck, other than that your sub goal if you will is to find the missing crew and looking for the clues and piecing the story together like a striaght X-Files episode and its my favorite part of the game.
Now with all that amazing stuff being said there are some problems with the game but like I said before its not finished so you cant really hold it at fault
1. You cannot talk to your friends on the game. This is a big problem because its based on teamwork, Im hoping for long range communication you need walkie talkies and you could find them aswell and not just be handed them.
2. Its the same thing everytime you start a level. Although the game does NOT suffer from replayability issues it could deeply benifit it to change up where a house is or where a post is things like that, maybe start with different items everytime as well?
3. There is no stance other than standing up. I think the game would benifit alot from having crouching and crawling which could allow you to hide a bit easier from Bigfoot it just seems unrealistic that you would never couch or crawl in a situation like that
Thats really all my big issues with it however there are alot of things that im hoping for in the future considering its not finished and there is alot to come.
1. Customization options! Specifically I would like you to be able to customize your character in the way they look to be honest the base skins are kind of ugly and I think being able to edit the looks of your guy would be awsome. Another aspect iv heard talk of is perks? But I dont know where I stand on this one it seems like it COULD be good but it also might completely ruin the game, maybe a gamemode where its disabled or just none at all.
2. Crafting. The game doesnt really suffer from not having crafting its one of those ideas that might be cool but the ability to build a camp fire and basic survival things like that would be a nice touch.
3. More ways to track Bigfoot. I was really excited to see tracking bullets on the table as I started and I also think its really cool he can rip them out, but thats the only way to track him I thought you could be able to find footprints or track his blood after you shot him alot like have him leave some kind of trace behind that stays for a bit.
4. 4 player. This one seems so natural to have a 4 player game but its only 3 and its weird to me maybe have Bigfoots dificulty scale with how many players there are but we need 4 players. With this being said the camper could use a little more room if threes a crowd in there 4 is unimagineable
5. Splitscreen. I didnt expect it to have this but its always a bounus to have split screen on a co op game if you ask me.
6. Limitations. This game is super grounded well more less but you have unlimited flashlight and stamina and I think there should simply be batteries for the flashlight maybe different ones from the nightvision and have a stamina bar to recharge.
7. Better AI. Although Bigfoots AI isnt bad I feel like all he does is walk around and scream I mean it definetly works but having him sore through the trees and crawl around sneakily and maybe even stalk you for awhile like a Bigfoot would would be an amazing update.

This game is the thinking man's space strategy game. It really does make you think about real-life society, because you get complete control over how your in-game society looks, behaves, and performs. The various government forms, the way you can choose to enslave your people for extra mineral and food output, but most of all the ethics system. There are 8 ethics, each of them with an opposite (e.g. individualist vs collectivist). Some might seem plain evil at the outset, but when you read the short paragraph about each of them by mousing over them, you start to wonder. What do I choose if I want to be a "good guy"? The game even makes it unclear what to choose to be a "bad guy". There simply are no such things. You can be a warlike race who hates aliens with a passion, but really all you want is to keep your citizens safe from the dangers of the galaxy. And yes, there are dangers. Some alien races will hate you. And if you've managed to break away from the rest of the pack and become one of the big powers, as usually happens with skilled players, you have to decide who lives and who dies, because allies will be seeking your help against enemies that you know they can't possibly beat. And you'll have to choose.
Oh, one more thing. The weapons are quite nice too. Even if you want to be all peaceful, sometimes you'll find yourself giddy at the prospect of a particle lance, or a neutron torpedo.

I have found this to be a solid tower defense game that is well balanced, imaginative, and fun. Getting to play as the "villian" is a neat touch. Some reviews complain of having to grind missions for exp, but I only find that to be partially true. They are correct, you will pretty much never 3 star a mission the first time around. Expect it, accept it, and move on. After doing two to three later missions (and leveling up after each), come back, and it will be much easier. Move on again, then come back a bit later and try the night missions. When progressing that way, I reached max level without having to replay any missions (unless, of course, I messed up, but that's on me, not the game).
It's also true you can find the game free other places. That's how I first played it. However, again in contrast to other reviews, I have not had any crashing problems or lag with many monsters (and I have a very cheap laptop); it plays far better than online version I've tried. For a few bucks, I'm happy to support the developer, and getting Steam achievements is always fun.

However, after the initial XXX phase is over, the game settles into a long, drawn-out death rattle of tedium from which you cannot avert your eyes and let the game progress in real-time because the developers removed almost all of the user-configurable auto-pause triggers from the game (they are just not there, an issue that also plagues the more recent Hearts of Iron IV). The recent "Asimov" patch does not cure the boredom-inducing real-time zombification of being forced to remain glued to the screen while you wait an interminably long time for things to happen or for your influence resource to creep high enough to allow you to make further progress.
That missing feature is enough for me to tip this review from generally positive to generally negative.

One of my first Paradox strategy games was Victoria 2; and I absolutely loved it. I'm not as experienced as many of the players of strategy games due to my late introduction to the genre at the age of about 16. But from the Paradox Grand Strategy games I have played, I have enjoyed every minute. There are definitely many times where I think of the ways in which the games can be improved, and Stellaris is no exception to this rule. If I want to be specific, I have a large problem with the military system in this game due to the inability to fight a defensive war. Much of the time when I have been at war with another space empire, I feel like one of the only engaging strategies implemented is that of ship upgrades. When I send my ships to fight, I find myself winning all the time just as long as I have more ships. I feel like such a stratgey (More ships + Effective Upgrades = Instant Win) doesn't engage the player in warfare as much as I would like. Considering Stellaris is a game about space conquest, warfare should be very well developed and strategic. But I digress from that of what I enjoy about this game. What really brings me back to playing this game is immersion. As silly as my opinion may sound to some, creating your own species, managing your planets, gathering resources, etc. makes me feel like I built something from nothing; A feeling that is something I really enjoy in any strategy game. Stellaris implements that very effectively. Despite questionable but pragmatic developer decisions (such as greater popualtion and colonies creating research penalties), Stellaris is a game that I would recommend to anyone looking to experience a sense of the unknown. To those looking for a war-based strategy game, I would look to the Hearts of Iron series instead. But simply because Stellaris brings out the inner astrobiologist in me, I can't rate this game down. I can definitely talk about what's wrong with this game for hours at a time, but if games such as Endless Space can be so bland and boring, yet Stellaris can maintain my interest... Something somewhere must have been done right.

Cursed Treasure 2 is a tower defense game where you play as the dark lord - master of orcs, undead, and demons - who must defend your cursed gemstones from greedy humans who want to steal them. Developed by Iriy Soft, the game was originally published on Armor Games before recieving this updated rerelease. In fact, if you're at all interested in tower defense games you've probably already played this game before on Armor Games.
Approaching this review, I found myself feeling like there are two big questions to answer.
Obviously on some level this is going to depend on your opinion of tower defense games, which seems to be a love-it-or-hate-it kind of genre. If you hate tower defense, this game isn't going to change your opinion.
If you love tower defense? Well, the game is at least competently made. Abilities and upgrades are well thought out and the game controls pretty well.
Compared to other tower defense games, the level of strategy here is... rather simplistic. Each type of tower can only go on a single type of terrain so there's no real decision making in choosing what to place where. (What should I put on this green tile? Duh, an orc tower, the only thing that CAN go there.) There are multiple upgrade paths; for example, orc towers can become either snipers or explosive ballista dens, but there's still not much to decide there. You want snipers in the front, mortars in the back. You want terror crypts in the back to scare enemies and make them run back through your gauntlet again, and frost crypts in the front to slow them down as they make their way through.
The game isn't the best tower defense there is, but it isn't terrible. It's competent and fun. In fact...
My Rating: [3/5] MEDIOCRE
So, on to question number two...
That's a bit of a hard question. There are some thing that I like about this new version and some things I really don't.
The graphics have improved, and now each region of the game has its own distinct theme. The starting region, Meadowshire, is fairly generic forest and dirt roads, the Holy Mountain is snowy, Tanglewood is green and swampy, and so on. It's a nice touch.
Some of the gameplay mechanics have changed. There are now special spells that require skulls - a new resource and the only resource that carries over between missions - to cast, and which give strong effects like giving you 1,000 free gold or instantly returning all your gems to the caves.
There's also three new missions set in "The Deep", the land of the dwarves.
On the other hand, difficulty has also been increased, and I'm not sure if I'd say it's been done in a good way. For one, gold mines  have been removed from most of the missions and you'll be seriously money-starved. (And before you ask, villages and castles and the like no longer give gold income when captured; instead they just spit out coins that you can grab when you first hit them.)
Also, some enemies have been made more difficult. Wizards now have a very powerful mass heal, and the Dendrologists will summon their little tree friends much faster, to the point of actual swarming.
And this leads us to the biggest problem... those three new missions against the dwarves? They're just plain broken, to the point of being borderline impossible. This isn't just me talking, either. The official strategy for how to beat them is to save up your skulls over the course of the entire game and just cheese the @#%$ out of them. It's generally considered you'll need to spend 2,000 or so skulls (to put that in perspective, you might get 50 skulls in one mission and the spells themselves cost arund 100-350 skulls to cast) in order to have a real chance.
The best I can say is, at least it's not just a completely ridiculous cash grab. I was actually surprised to find that the skull-based super spells weren't actually a cash shop and instead a legit in-game thing.
+ Nicely drawn, cute graphics.
+ Did at least entertain me for several hours.
- Not a lot of deep, strategic decision making.
- Can be kind of difficult.
- The last three missions are laughably unbalanced and not really fun at all.
In the end, I have to ask myself, would I really want to recommend this game to people? If one of my friends came up to me and said "hey, man, what new game do you think I should play?" would I name this one?
No, not really.
It's not terrible and if you want to spend five bucks on it, hey, go right ahead. But I'm afraid I just really don't feel like I can honestly recommend it.

You've probably played parts of Dead Cells before. Its DNA is familiar, a patchwork assembly of recognizable influences. There are echoes of Symphony of the Night and Super Metroid in the 2D action platformer. It is a fast-paced combat.
It'd be easy to look at the borrowed bits and reworked ideas mentioned above and write Dead Cells off as a weird Frankenstein's monster title, full of copied mechanics and gameplay systems. On paper, it sure reads like that. But to play Dead Cells and see how its pieces come together; to feel how it adopts elements and twists them together to create something different. It looks great and plays even better. It's an electric mix of polish and challenge that's all the more impressive considering the metroidvania/rogue-lite/whatever we're calling them these days only just released on Early Access.
Most of your time is spent navigating the labyrinthian corridors of underground prisons and destroyed castle ramparts. The protagonist, a green blob who's commandeered a decapitated corpse, cannot die. Every death starts the same cycle over again: fuse with the body, find some weapons, and move through the randomly generated halls of a decaying kingdom. There's not much by way of a story, but that's alright, considering that Dead Cells' actions speak louder than its vague words.
Combat, then, becomes and intricate dance. It's fast and fluid, but challenging enough that players will have to watch each enemy's attack pattern. Despite his long-dead body, the Prisoner is a capable fighter in the right hands. Players can double jump, perform aerial attacks, roll past enemies, and switch between their two primary weapons and utility skills to perform powerful combos. If, and when you take damage, landing a few quick strikes earns some of the Prisoner's health back, further adding to the game's core focus on risks and rewards. Dead Cells does an exceptional job of making combat look super flashy, with smooth animations to complement its pixel art, while also making each strike feel as though it has weight behind it.
I could go on and on about Dead Cells. Despite the fact that it's not fully released, it's already one of my favorite games of 2017. I'm a sucker for tight platforming and roguelike exploration, both of which Dead Cells delivers. Much like the Prisoner's inability to stay dead for good, I'm sure I'll keep coming back to this game time and time again.

Final Fantasy VIII is a game that was an experimental shift from the traditional Final Fantasy series. This is a game where you do not need to level and grind in order to beat the game. For that reason alone, someone can beat this game in under 12 hours if they truly wanted to. To fully embrace the characters, that is a whole different situation.
To sum up the mechanics and key differences, FF8 focuses around enemies that will scale to your highest level hero. You will be allowed to have up to 3 heroes at any given time. Your main source of power comes from your summons, which act as something you can equipt in a new system called Junctioning. In Junctioning, you must attach summons and pick their respective abilities. They act as stat boosters and provide unique skills.
Through this new system, you must "Draw" unique magic. These are much like your traditional spells/magic such as Fira, Cure, Esuna, only with Junctioning, you attach these limited spells like equipment and can potentially attach one spell to each attribute stat to boost them. In fact... this is your main method of powering up, not traditional grinding.
Drawing magic is possible through almost every monster you encounter, or "Draw-Points" that are located throughout the game. These magic spells you "draw" are expendable and limited. If you run out, even if you have the best spells, Ultima, Holy, Demi, you must re-draw them from key locations, monsters, or through a craft system called "Refinement."
A lot of people will miss the point, but this series adds a bonus method of Crafting or Refinement by means of a card game, Triple Triad. It's a simple game where you have 4 numbers for each direction, top, right, left, bottom, and you must play your strategy to beat the numbers of the previous set cards. There will be additional rules that come into play to make this much more challenging. Using these cards, you can potentially refine powerful items, some of which may make you immortal for a short duration, which is needed for the dreadful final boss.
Now for the plot...
You start off as Squall, who aims to pass his SeeD exam to become an official member of the most prestigious honor in the Garden. Squall and his companions take on various assigned missions, acting as mercenaries. Eventually, they are assigned a special task by Master Cid. The one who gives this task is Rinoa, our main heroine. Together, this sparks the start of a long, treacherous fight against the ambitious Galbadian Dictatorship that plans to use the Sorceress Edea to take over the world.
The story will be a hit or miss for most people. Squall is your typical lazy teenager who doesn't have any plans in his life. He has a very "Why should I do this...?" attitude and does not want the burden of responsibility to rest on his shoulders.
Later on, you will discover Rinoa is actually a spoiled girl from a powerful family, and everyone has a negative impression of her cause of it. She will learn to become fearful of loss as well after her first confrontation with the Sorceress. As for Squall... because Squall's "older sister" left him at an early age, he isolated himself from the world to prevent himself from being hurt. In essence, you could say these two are the most paranoid heroes you will ever come across in the FF series. But because of this, the heroes in FF8 are also the most human you will ever meet. It makes them relate-able to the average person and requires a rather mature audience to play.
By the end of the game, you will discover that majority of the characters will have something personal that they struggle through. Learning about their insecurities and pasts will, without a doubt, draw you closer to loving the characters. Several parts of Final Fantasy VIII will have your heart tugged.

Quite simply one of the greatest games ever made.
I could spend hours talking about Deux Ex, and what makes it so, so good. There are elements that modern games fail to even partially emulate - but Deux Ex not only implements them masterfully, but blends them together into something amazing.
Where to start? Probably one of the single biggest plus points on this game is the sheer size and scale of it. Not in the size of the maps, but rather in the level of depth and thought that has been put into every single scenario. The game challenges you to do things your own way, and to find your own solutions to the problems it presents you - and every eventuality has been foreseen and planned for by the devs. The characters and the world react to you and the choices you have made, in a way that no other game that I have played as achieved, but again it is the attention to detail that really ascends it.
To give a light hearted example and avoid any sort of spoilers - there is a point where you (as JC Denton - a male) may decide that in your quest to explore an area, you have a stroll into the ladies toilets. The angry lady in there yells for you to leave, and as the obnoxious player you of course stay. And then an hour later when having your mission debriefing - your boss may casually remark to you about trying to stay out of the womens toilets.
The game remembers decisions and actions - no matter how small and innocuous they may seem at the time, and uses them. Similarly, there are times (which I will not detail in order to avoid spoiling any of the story) where the game basically tells you that you are "meant" to do something. In my second playthrough, I decided to do the opposite, and was staggered to realise that my decision there affected the entire rest of the storyline in a pretty big way. Every thing you want to do - even the choices that you dont realise that you are making - are all planned for by the devs, and this creates a living and believable world that very few "proper" RPGs have managed to replicate - not bad considering that Deux Ex isnt even a true RPG.
This brings me onto my second point - Deux Ex blurs the lines when it comes to game genres. It takes some of the best bits out of stealthers like Thief, RPGs, and FPS games, and blends them together immaculately. The skill point system allows you to really differentiate your character every bit as much as in The Elder Scrolls (for instance). If you are untrained with pistols, your crosshairs will be wide and you will be wildly inaccurate - but train up to master level and you can shoot with pinpoint accuracy whilst moving.
But combat is only one part of it - the game allows you to take the stealthy approach, with lockpicking, hacking and stealth all key parts of the game - and importantly, all are equally viable throughout. I have played other games where my approach as a stealther was not rewarded, and I ended up going back and killing the enemies that I had bypassed, just to get the extra XP and loot. In Deux Ex however, you will be rewarded (through skillpoints, hidden areas, loot etc) for whichever path you take. And with ammunition being quite limited, it becomes very relevant whether you want to enter into a firefight when not truly necessary.
As I hinted before - the game also reacts to your playstyle. In your very first mission, if you create a bloodbath and clear out the entire zone, you may feel quite proud as a "completionist" - but you are quickly brought back down to earth when your older brother (in game) scolds you for your use of excessive force. This can even affect how you are rewarded (or not) for certain missions and side quests.
At this point, I would say something like "It is easy to forget that this is a 15 year old game" - but it isnt, unfortuntaely. The graphics are rather dated, and some of the mechanics and interfaces feel a little clunky compared to what is currently available. These are small sacrifices to make however, and are vastly outweighed by the good points. Also, when you are remembering that this is a 15 year old game - consider the depth and detail of the world, and try to think of which games (if any) have managed to match it. This is a game in which it references the World Trade Centre being destroyed by a terrorist attack - but was created a year before this actually happened in real life, such was the level of realism and believability of it.
As I said at the start of this review, I could go on for hours - but honestly the best thing I can say is that this is a game almost universally acclaimed as one of the finest ever made - and it is with good reason. Pick the game up and see for yourself. It is a game that requires some investment, but will repay your dedication a hundredfold. The amount of choices and different approaches offer incredible replay value, and every play through you will no doubt discover new things - even from just listening to the NPC conversations.
I dont use the term lightly, but for anyone who considers themself to be a proper gamer - Deux Ex is a must-have.

It kind of sucks to me that F.E.A.R. is like a lost masterpiece to the modern gaming generation.
For a 2005 game, it has surprisingly amazing dynamic shaders & shadows. The game's stylized feeling and its graphics engine are just right enough to put you on edge in dimly lit rooms.
The game itself was developed with influence from eastern, specifically Asian horror, and its antagonists are mostly non-cliche. The way its horror is designed industrially and in an urban setting, always fighting in dimly-lit buildings and walkways, maintenance shafts and other miscellaneous locations. There are subtle mental cues that put you on edge. Its horror was designed in a specific way, leaving the player to their own thoughts and devices. There is little to no music in the game at all, leaving you to walk in silence in its industrial complexes, only the quiet, eerie ambience of its buildings enough to keep you sane. It leaves the player emotionally exhausted. The jumpscares are few and far between, but they are present. Most of the "jumpscares" you'll encounter in this game are solely sudden; no screaming noises.. just an omnipresent piece of terror. I'll give you one hint: LADDERS.
As put in a quote from one of its creative directors, "Sure, in all these games, you have nothing, you gotta hide from it all. But when a little girl takes out an entire squad of professionally trained Delta guys, what then?"
Its shooter aspect is so amazing compared to modern games I still can't get over it. It has a full-blown melee system with martial arts and other sick moves for when you get up close to your enemy, almost like a first-person fighting game. Melee is not redundant in this game; it is a beautiful addition. The guns feel beefy and meaty, with heavy recoil but satisfying pay-off when you land a blow on a Replica. Its weapon variety is massive, including the 10mm HV Penetrator, essentially a weaponized nail gun, instead firing large metal stakes straight into your opponents, which of course dynamically paints the walls with their blood and pins their limp corpses to said walls. Firefights are majestically done, your character having a supernatural ability that activates bullet time for a managed amount of time. It is surprisingly not overpowered and you will find yourself using it a lot in fights inside the game. When bullets fly through the room, dust clouds it, particles and sparks flying off of drywall and metal objects respectively. Its grenades are terrifying in the greatest way, each detonation making the lights in the room flicker as paper scraps and dust particles fog the room, the entirety of it shaking with shockwave from the blast.
And on to its artificial intelligence.. it is still the best AI in any first person shooter to date that I have seen. Its entirely badass Replicas, the clone soldiers under Paxton Fettel's psychic command, are a serious threat to you and your health. They will pull off their own martial arts in close quarters if you are to try and get close to them, leading you to counter their atttacks with your own melee abilities. Their AI is constantly aware, searching for the player vehemently as you hear them communicating with eachother (dynamically, in engine, may I add!), about your whereabouts and their positions. As you enter a firefight, they react quickly, tossing down things like tables and other various furniture and environmental aids for cover. Screaming your position in their comms, they notice you jump over their hastily arranged fortification, reacting with a loud "♥♥♥♥!!" as you blast them to pieces mid-bullet time with your shotgun. The other replicas react quickly as well, tossing grenades in your direction and communicating your combat effectiveness to their allies. As you near a fire extinguisher, one of them takes note and screams "BY THE FIRE EXTINGUISHER!!" as he takes a precision shot at it, dazing you as it explodes in a puff of white powder. As they rush you, you head for cover, only to toss a grenade into their general direction as the room shakes from the blast, the only remains of the Replicas now a limp ragdoll and various bloody pieces.. that is, until the door busts down and you see a Heavy Replica with that 10mm Stake-gun.. uh oh.
All in all, F.E.A.R. is a wonderfully crafted masterpiece for the ages, taking place as one of my few favorite games from my childhood. With spendid AI mechanics, that match almost no games to date, an amazing and beefy shooter mechanic with eerie, edge-of-your-seat horror, the segments in this game will leave you both craving more and feeling exhausted, emotionally.

GAMEPLAY
Cursed Treasures 2 is the sequel/enhancement for the great Cursed Treasure game. On Cursed Treasures 2 you need to defend your precious gems from getting stolen building powerful towers to defeat the enemies.We have 3 types of towers on the game:Den,Crypt and the Temple each one with a speciality. Also we have a lot of things that can help us on our quest,like the super powers and some special bulidings that can give us items like coins for buying new towers. We can use to destroy some terrain to build new towers too.As the game advances,it gets more challenging with the coming of the bosses,that are very strong and call reinforcements,so,you will need to think on a strategy and upgrade the towers to the max. You play the game like a traditional Tower-Defense Game:Using the mouse to make almost everything here,but the game also features some keyboard shortcuts for you too. The main game has 24 levels,but when you defeat the bosses you unlock the night mode that is the same level,but you can build only where the light reaches.Also you have a lot of skills and achievements to unlock as you progress in the game.
GRAPHICS
Cursed Treasure 2 features beautiful and colorful graphics,that can run almost in any computer.
SOUNDTRACK
A great soundtrack that makes the game more addictive than it is.
SUMMARY
Cursed Treasures 2 is a game for people that want a challenging and fun tower defense game to play and also for newbies that wants to be introduced on this genre too.The game has a lot of explanations to help you and it's also easy to learn. The game also have a lot of content for it's price and certainly will entertain anyone that buys for a lot of time trying to beat every level with 3 stars.

Dead Cells is best described as a roller coaster ride that when you die throws you back to the beginning. Dying is the tutorial. It's entertaining , I wish I could save my progress through some of the maps but progress in this game is measured differently than it is in traditional 2D  side scrolling games that are similar to it. There are upgrades you can take back to the start with you and a subtle progression, unlocks and such but you are penalized for dying in a run thru. You have to keep the flow , evade , strike fluidly with precision and timing which you learn because you die over and over and over again. Dying is the tutorial. it trains you to get better at the game so you can go further in the game, just when you think you're getting good at it, the game challenges you again, if you fail , you die and go back to the start with some 'Cells' taken away , which are like experience points you use to upgrade buffs and unlock starting weapons and abilities for the next run through. It's an interesting and cleverly made game. It has a familar old school feel to it but it's definitely different and refreshing.

While it may not be the best in the Final Fantasy series, FF8 holds a big place in my heart. This is the first time I've played the game, so I'm not speaking with feelings of nostalgia here.
Gameplay: Initially, I was turned off. The Junction system wasn't something I was used to. MP doesn't exist here with magic being a consumeable item. It's just something you draw from enemies or synthesize. I rarely casted magic against monsters and used it as a stat upgrade, which left a bad taste in my mouth. Eventually though, I learned to like the system. Once you get the hang of it, it's like a fact of life that you don't put much thought on. It's also easy to power up your party, making this one of the easier FF games.
Sidequests: Not a lot. Plus most of the sidequests are not difficult to accomplish. They are just time-consuming. To note a few challenges, there's a Steam achievement called "Contrived Victory"; you may have to play through the game a second time. Card collecting is also a big hassle.
Story: I really enjoyed the story even if it was presented in a confusing manner. For a game that had schools training teen soldiers, warring factions, and a time compression scheme by a corrupt sorceress, I didn't feel the gravity of the world's situation until the middle of Disc 3. That's just something funny to observe. You could tell that the game's theme was about friendship and love being the most precious thing that surpasses past, present, and future. Cheesy but endearing. (Squall and the gang are #squadgoals; Laguna and the gang are #squadgoals)
Music: Memorable. There are strong pieces in the game that you will download and listen to on repeat. They go very well with the various places scattered in the world. My favorite scene was when "Compression of Time" started playing. To me, that will always be an iconic moment in the game.
(Just make sure to replace the bad steam port music with the orginal PS1 version!!! It makes the gaming experience significantly better!)
All in all it is highly-reccommended you play FF8. The whole game plays like a sentimental memory because time is what brings this whole game together. There's a lot to be had in FF8 that will give you a great experience despite its' imperfections.

After becoming a Final Fantasy fan after playing the seventh game, the junction system that had been implemented into Final Fantasy VIII had me extremely confused, where was the MP bar that was so prevelent in other RPGs? After putting 15 hours of restarting the beginning section of the main game I fell in love with the new junction system. The fact that you could draw magic from mobs and stock them to create a devestating elemental or a status attack, (Or defense instead.) People who say that the junctioning system is confusing, ignore the fact that it played a vital key in developing future Final Fantasy games, like Final Fantasy X where they implemented a simplified version of this.
The Guardian Force, or GF mechanic, however, is exclusive to Final Fantasy VIII and acts as a form of progression for the party member who is junctioned to the GF. Many people were disappointed that EXP doesn't level your party up, ignoring the fact that the GF mechanic lets them switch abilities that makes Final Fantasy VIII far more refined than VII.
Technically the game hasn't aged well, but there are various mods out there to fix any issues, otherwise this is a game that has been obscured by the main stream crowd of 1999, still give it a shot for it's personal twist of generic fantasy RPG mechanics.
(Personally this game is better than Final Fantasy IXs generic fantasy world and basic gameplay.)

This is a great example of the risk you take when you buy indie games. Don't worry, the game is completely functional (as far as I know).
RS:TFR (does an acronym go within another acronym?) was one of the relatively few games I voted for on Greenlight. It looked really interesting and I was excited for it to possibly be released. And then it was Greenlit, and came out soon after! Neat! However, it seemed rather bare-bones. It didn't have controller support. It didn't have a lot of enemies. The classes weren't balanced. The game didn't even seem balanced! Surely they'd add more classes, enemies, controller support, weapons, etc. later on, right?
They didn't, and they won't. The game has had technical patches, so it works. It's just not as much as I expected it to be, going in.
As for the game itself, it plays like Duke 3D in that you're only allowed to look left and right, not up or down. The levels are randomly generated hallways (with scenery and a theme). Enemies are two-dimensional. Walls are two-dimensional. The creatures and weapons are creative, both in design and strategy. It is a true roguelike in which you go through floor and floor until you reach the 100th (which I haven't achieved). Intel, a rare drop from any enemy, accumulates to unlock more classes, more perks, and more monster bios, which detail their strengths and weaknesses.
I'm not so thrilled about everything being two-dimensional and being locked into horizontal aiming. Sure, it's "old-school," but it's not really fun today. Controller support would be great for this title, but I guess it's just too much for the devs to implement. Also, the game was made to run at a much smaller resolution than 1920x1080 and just won't look well if you stretch it out. You can see this with the screenshots - your Steam screenshots end up as a tiny screenshot in the upper left corner of a black canvas. Also, well, you can see it in the art assets. Two-dimensional and low-res.
The game is fun, but it needs more love from the devs in terms of controller support, content, and maybe better resolution options. Since they're indie, I doubt this game will ever see another update - they've moved on. A good price to pay for this title would be $5.

Quite simply one of the greatest games ever made.
I could spend hours talking about Deux Ex, and what makes it so, so good. There are elements that modern games fail to even partially emulate - but Deux Ex not only implements them masterfully, but blends them together into something amazing.
Where to start? Probably one of the single biggest plus points on this game is the sheer size and scale of it. Not in the size of the maps, but rather in the level of depth and thought that has been put into every single scenario. The game challenges you to do things your own way, and to find your own solutions to the problems it presents you - and every eventuality has been foreseen and planned for by the devs. The characters and the world react to you and the choices you have made, in a way that no other game that I have played as achieved, but again it is the attention to detail that really ascends it.
To give a light hearted example and avoid any sort of spoilers - there is a point where you (as JC Denton - a male) may decide that in your quest to explore an area, you have a stroll into the ladies toilets. The angry lady in there yells for you to leave, and as the obnoxious player you of course stay. And then an hour later when having your mission debriefing - your boss may casually remark to you about trying to stay out of the womens toilets.
The game remembers decisions and actions - no matter how small and innocuous they may seem at the time, and uses them. Similarly, there are times (which I will not detail in order to avoid spoiling any of the story) where the game basically tells you that you are "meant" to do something. In my second playthrough, I decided to do the opposite, and was staggered to realise that my decision there affected the entire rest of the storyline in a pretty big way. Every thing you want to do - even the choices that you dont realise that you are making - are all planned for by the devs, and this creates a living and believable world that very few "proper" RPGs have managed to replicate - not bad considering that Deux Ex isnt even a true RPG.
This brings me onto my second point - Deux Ex blurs the lines when it comes to game genres. It takes some of the best bits out of stealthers like Thief, RPGs, and FPS games, and blends them together immaculately. The skill point system allows you to really differentiate your character every bit as much as in The Elder Scrolls (for instance). If you are untrained with pistols, your crosshairs will be wide and you will be wildly inaccurate - but train up to master level and you can shoot with pinpoint accuracy whilst moving.
But combat is only one part of it - the game allows you to take the stealthy approach, with lockpicking, hacking and stealth all key parts of the game - and importantly, all are equally viable throughout. I have played other games where my approach as a stealther was not rewarded, and I ended up going back and killing the enemies that I had bypassed, just to get the extra XP and loot. In Deux Ex however, you will be rewarded (through skillpoints, hidden areas, loot etc) for whichever path you take. And with ammunition being quite limited, it becomes very relevant whether you want to enter into a firefight when not truly necessary.
As I hinted before - the game also reacts to your playstyle. In your very first mission, if you create a bloodbath and clear out the entire zone, you may feel quite proud as a "completionist" - but you are quickly brought back down to earth when your older brother (in game) scolds you for your use of excessive force. This can even affect how you are rewarded (or not) for certain missions and side quests.
At this point, I would say something like "It is easy to forget that this is a 15 year old game" - but it isnt, unfortuntaely. The graphics are rather dated, and some of the mechanics and interfaces feel a little clunky compared to what is currently available. These are small sacrifices to make however, and are vastly outweighed by the good points. Also, when you are remembering that this is a 15 year old game - consider the depth and detail of the world, and try to think of which games (if any) have managed to match it. This is a game in which it references the World Trade Centre being destroyed by a terrorist attack - but was created a year before this actually happened in real life, such was the level of realism and believability of it.
As I said at the start of this review, I could go on for hours - but honestly the best thing I can say is that this is a game almost universally acclaimed as one of the finest ever made - and it is with good reason. Pick the game up and see for yourself. It is a game that requires some investment, but will repay your dedication a hundredfold. The amount of choices and different approaches offer incredible replay value, and every play through you will no doubt discover new things - even from just listening to the NPC conversations.
I dont use the term lightly, but for anyone who considers themself to be a proper gamer - Deux Ex is a must-have.

As a fan of Gun Rocket I definitely wanted to try this game and can say I didn't regret finishing it the first time...
While starting a New Game+ I was positively surprised by some of the ideas implemented to make the levels a lot harder. I kept playing till I got stuck here:
I tried and tried, but had to contact the developer. He decided to the change the level and I finally got an update:
I was still excited and continued playing past the 1st boss in New Game+. At a certain moment - while at this level 'Detour' - I came to the conclusion that the games wasn't a fun experience anymore; there was just too little room for error (again), and with that in mind, you were forced to move very slowly a lot of the time. Not a problem in case of a short level experience, but that wasn't the case a lot of the time. That aside, it's not possible to move backwards nor use a 'handbrake' or similar to completely park the triangle/rocket, making it only harder (especially with your 'Luv', where you sometimes need 4 eyes); not only unforgiven, also unfair I had to conclude, partially caused by slowness = annoyance. Checkpoints are recommended in some levels, but there are none.
A few recommendations for an update:
- 'Reverse gear' = moving backwards; only being able to make turns and rotate, often means dying through 1/3 edges of the triangle, because there's little room for error (in New Game+);
- The possibility to completely park the triangle, not moving a pixel;
- Level tests in New Game+...the progression in difficulty didn't always make sense,
;
- Level screen! Could have motivated me to continue or maybe I could have skipped a few levels first, if that would have been an option. I didn't have any insight regarding my progress, I could only find some numbers in the game data...
That being said, I can actually still recommend playing this game, because there's enough fun before you start a New Game+ - which I don't expect everyone to start anyway. I just have mixed feelings about the New Game+ Mode and actually regret having started it...I could eventually finish it, but when something's not entertaining anymore, it's better to stop. I left the game with a bad taste in my mouth.
7/10 - If you like Gun Rocket and are good at it, definitely try this, but think twice prior starting a playthrough in New Game+.
