If you're old enough to remember, think of this as Asteroids but without the shooting, just the movement control to navigate around a maze / obstacle course using basic controls (I used keyboard - A/D/W for the 'classic' feel but controller is an option). You have to avoid touching the walls and scoot past/through/around moving objects to toggle open/close/rotate nodes. On some levels a pink 'doppelganger' ship appears and you have to carefully navigate your twin ships to activate alternate nodes.
In general, the trick is to move as slowly as possible with tiny boost adjustments at exactly the right moment. Too much boost and your reflexes are overpowered, causing you to veer out of control and hit a wall.
Minimal graphics are clean and basic. They get the job done but I wouldn't call it eye candy.
The godawful initial soundtrack is extremely annoying, I only managed to tolerate it for 30 seconds before desperately seeking the mute function. I tried it again later and discovered various different tunes of the same genre which I would classify as "the kind of synthesised garbage they force you to listen to at the gym". It's a matter of taste of course, but if you want my opinion (well, you're reading this aren't you), switch it off and listen to your own.
I usually judge the difficulty of a game by how far I get before I start to struggle. It's not possible to be accurate here due to the lack of level numbering or overview, so I have no idea how far through the game I've progressed. All I can say is that before I played Trianguluv I was smugly confident, having been an Asteroids God in my youth. This game brought my ego crashing down to Earth with a meek whimper. The controls are more sensitive than I expected and you need pinpoint accuracy and timing to avoid the walls and moving obstacles. Yes, I can safely say that this will challenge anyone and your skills will improve as you get used to it.
The first boss (I think that's what it is) implements positive/negative gravity wells which demand maximum boost and readjustment rather than the slow, delicate manoeuvring that you become accustomed to, and it took me many many frustrating attempts to beat it. This means the game commits the cardinal sin of having a difficulty bottleneck without any option to bypass it, so you can be stuck on the same level for ages. Not good. With that said, there's apparently a 'balance patch' on the way which may (or may not) solve this issue.
Although this is primarily a test of dexterity and timing, there is also the occasional puzzle element - it's not always clear how to complete the level, you sometimes need to work out the sequence of events by trial and error and some head-scratching.
The only in-game option is volume control (thank the Lord for that, considering the music!) Screen options are done via the Unity dialog. Good enough, but room for improvement...
I'm all for minimal games, but this really needs to have level numbering and/or overview so you can see how far through the game you've progressed. As it stands you're playing blind. There's no way to replay earlier levels (or better still, be able to skip levels) and you have no idea how many more are to come.
I'm giving this its own heading to highlight the fact that, as a Unity game, this should have Linux! Making me play it in Windows puts me in a bad mood :(
Trading cards, 5 achievements and Steam Cloud. Everything you need.
As I understand it there are 30 levels with 3 different modes (Normal, Game+ and No Death), so you can replay for 90 levels total.
Although the asking price is justified - you won't be disappointed if you pay it - I think it would do better in the $1 category, it's the type of game that collectors would buy in droves for the trading cards and a few hours' light entertainment. Personally I would wait for it to be on sale.

If you've never played F.E.A.R, do yourself a service and buy it. While the port has some performance issues, you get a full package with the original game, and both of its expansions, one of them being arguably superior to the original game. The experience is astonishing even by today's standards, with the high points being both the atmosphere and the gameplay F.E.A.R presents you with.
Basically an original and surprisingly harmonious mix between a John Woo flick, a Ghost In the Shell hommage, a Hideo Nakata horror movie, and some Resident Evil-esque level of nonsense, complete with an evil corporation, clone soldiers, and a creepy little girl, F.E.A.R is a classic, a game so well done even its graphic engine still looks good despite the fact that the game dates back from 2005. The shadows, the lighting, the models are still really well done, the game features some really impressive body awareness and a really great physics and particle engine, the latter giving an amazing touch to the gunfights of the game.
While the environments, mainly composed of industrial complexes and business offices, can get really repetitive, the incredibly agressive AI of the Replica soldiers make each encounter memorable, with your enemies trying to outsmart you and forcing you to go out of your way to survive each one of them . F.E.A.R is linear, but none other game has captured the fury, violence and beauty of a cinematic gunfight. With the addition of a well crafted horrific aspect, F.E.A.R has it all. Including a Nail-Gun called the Penetrator, always a plus in my book.
Ps: Play on the Expert difficulty to get a sense of how good the AI is.\

There are some little problems for those who have played the Witcher 3:
1. The interface is not so smooth as W3.
2. The length of chapters are not balanced at all. Chapter 1 is too long, while Chapter 3 is too short.
3. Mission details are usually much fewer than those in W3. For example, there won't be any location hints for monster contract missions, and the constraints of missions are blurred.
It is strongly suggested that you should play two rounds to realize the whole fact of the story, and if possible, choosing Roche path in the first round is much better because this path seems more 'reasonable' for Geralt and it reveals fewer details and so that makes players feel more surprising when they play the second round.

After 12 years since the game has been out, it still shines as a solid shooter with intense combat. This was one of the first FPS I ever played when I was a kid and it left a deep lasting impression on my mind at that time. As with most of my reviews, here are the subparts covering every aspect of the game-
1-Graphics- This game still has one of the best graphics and the attention to detail in combat situations is visually appealing, especially when you turn on slow motion and see individual bullets spraying across the room creating body and environmental decals everywhere. The aftermath of the shootout is a treat to witness as the environment is badly damaged with bodies of enemies lying around. The hallucination effects are also well done. This was the first game in which I could see my character's face in the water reflection fully if the graphic details are set to high :) . I admit some of the environment gets a bit repetitive after a while but the combat and action makes you engaged.
2-Gameplay- You have a variety of guns at your disposal like pistols, shotguns, machineguns and some heavy weapons with which you kill the enemies. I have to say that one of the best things about this game is the A.I. of the enemies. I have never seen them behave so realistically and they will outsmart you in a number of ways. They make strategic decisions to outnumber you and you have to listen to their talk to decide what they are about to do which makes every fight unique in its own way. You also fight some supernatural elements although not much. I wish more developers take inspiration from it and we see more realistic AI. Some people say that it gets a bit repetitive after a while as you kill the same number of enemies over and over again but the combat intensity allows a lot of flexibility. One recommendation I can give is to play the game on medium to high difficulty settings with minimal use of slow motion. It gets very tough to beat. This is a game from 2005 and it still surprises me to this day.
3- Story- A great story which is told in a suspenseful manner with some supernatural spooky vibes thrown here. Its scary and disturbing. In a nutshell, Paxton Fettel, a psychic commander with telepathic link to hundreds of clone soldiers has gone rogue and started kidnapping people working at a defense contractor firm, ATC, and killing them to obtain information on a little girl. Your job is to kill Fettel so that the telepathic link to the soldiers is broken and they are rendered useless. That's all I can say on it as it goes deeper the more you find his true intentions and that of ATC.
4- Sound and atmosphere- The sound is well done and sounds great during firefights and explosions. The atmosphere is good and is really creepy when you get hallucinations of the supernatural elements in the game. Back in 2005 when I played it I had nightmares about it. It may not hold up to today's standards now considering the amount of scary games we have in the market now, but its still great.
I had some issues running the game on Windows 10, as it is quite old, however I was able to solve it by setting my resolution manually in the game's launcher.exe file and it ran perfect after that. Earlier I was having issues where the game would constantly crash when I set my resolution manually through the in game graphics options.You can look through the steam forums, there are quite a number of fixes to run this game on Windows 10, and it does run properly once you tweak the settings.
Overall, if you are looking for an intense FPS game with some spooky atmosphere and a good story, I recommend this one.

Stellaris is a Paradox Grand Strategy game, lifted into the starts and the so called 4X concept. This is fairly new ground for PI and it shows, as they definitely erred on the side of caution. To my knowledge they were also trying to make the game more accessible than their historic Grand Strategy titles.
The basics of a good 4X game are there. You have 3 branches of research that are randomized, depending on your races philosophies and a card "draw" system. There are 3 resources to manage, planets to colonize, random events to spice things up and a user defined galaxy, AI and secrets to uncover.
The flaws are also familiar to those of other PI games, though instead of a lot of features being bugged, due to the new field and accessibility some are not there yet. There is no "victory" state other than complete domination. The diplomacy is fairly shallow and needs some work. Mid to end game things can get monotonous unless the AI manages to form a good alliance against you. The AI itself can also use some work.
All of these are sure to be resolved in future patches and feature DLCs, just like other Paradox games. To me, it is worth it, but be warned that it still is a Paradox game, even though probably the most accessible one on the market right now.

Often considered a sort of black sheep of the Final Fantasy video game series, Final Fantasy VIII could be viewed as an acquired taste. The game itself is a story-rich, turn-based role playing game in which the player takes control of two parties across different times, one being that of the daring, yet reticent Squall Leonhart and the other being that of the intrepid Laguna Loire. The game favors a more science-fiction-modern style, although, many fantastical elements remain as they do in other installments. Its narrative is incredible, diving into the very thoughts of those within. However, note that the music of this port of the PlayStation 1 version has been converted to poor MIDI-quality, which truly does it a disservice, because the original's soundtrack is simply phenomenal.
It has been met with varying praise due to its integration of somehwat unconventional magic and levelling systems into the series. It is the acquisition of magic and the gaining of levels that are a bit unique: That could be viewed as a strength or a weakness. Enemies grow in power as the player levels; magic is drawn in quantity from enemies or from draw points. Stats rise most when a character is equipped with what is known as a Guardian Force (GF), which is a mythical being who joins to support the team's cause. They are encountered throughout the game for the purposes of statistic "junctioning", summoning, skill learning, and more. In my opinion, I am fond of these sweeping reforms to the typical Final Fantasy formula, as they provide some zestful, innovative alterations to manifest something that is quite welcome. If we always were to purchase the same game, why would we buy it at all?
Overall, I would very much recommend this installment. The game's taste is acquired for the reason that one must be willing to give this charming JRPG a chance to fully enjoy oneself. Occasionally the pace is sluggish, yet the satisfaction received is so grand that the endeavor is worthwhile. In a sense, it is a piece of video game history along with many other Final Fantasy iterations out of its sheer merits. This video game, despite its irregularitites, it still excellently entertaining.

This is a really solid game, for EA.  The controls are fast and fluid, every combat mechanic feels polished.  When you die, you feel like it was your fault, which is a good thing.  The sprites are very well drawn and lovely to look at.  There's lots of content to potentially enjoy, and many hidden routes and treasures to explore.
There are a couple complaints I have, however:
The shop you use to unlock new weapons, items, and abilities gets very expensive very fast.  After ten hours of gameplay, it feels like I should've been able to afford more.  You simply don't collect enough cells from your average run to unlock more than an item or two, even when speed running the dungeons to get the timed doors.  After a while, your cells are just investments for future unlocks, making it feel even slower and grindy-er to get anything new.
The other complaint is repetition.  Now, I actually don't mind replaying each dungeon over and over.  It's when there is a lack of progression that it starts to be repetitive.  This point ties into the one above - without new items and abilities to use for new runs, the dungeons start to feel stale.  Lately I just rush through them to get the timed doors, which is boring, but nets you a lot more cells.  I think if the developers made it a bit easier to get new content from the shop, the game would progress at a much more fluid and enjoyable pace.
That said, I'd definitely still reccomend this to anyone looking for a unique take on the metroidvania genre.

PLEASE NOTE: I want to preface this review by saying that my "Not Recommended" rating for this game is in no way me advising people to stay away from it. I would say its worth owning and trying out if you're a FPS fan, however I felt I had to offer some dissenting opinion given the 94% approval rating the game has. I just don't think its quite as essential or amazing as many make it out to be.
---
While making a pretty big splash back in 2005, I personally think F.E.A.R. is rather overrated and feels like it hasn't aged that gracefully in many ways both in comparison to not only the better examples of modern shooters, but also some of the essential classics that came before it. I really do not agree at all that F.E.A.R. is on the same level as games like DOOM, Duke Nukem 3D or Half Life. The problem with this game is that it is a very two dimensional experience. For me, the only appeal to play this game today is walking (because you certainly can't run in this game, that's for sure) down hallways and killing enemies in slow motion. That is clearly the game's strong suit and it still holds up pretty well today. The weapon line-up is decent, most of the weapons feel quite good and the enemies behave in a pretty intelligent, and dynamic way which makes them satisying to fight. I remember playing this game for the first time over 10 years ago now and the AI was what stuck out in my mind the most. Maybe I would say the enemy variety is lacking, but that's forgiveable. And, of course, when you hop into slow motion the firefights become a real spectacle with great particle effects and slowed down sound effects. It's genuinely fun.
Unfortunately, as fun as that is, it becomes quite repetitious rather quickly, mainly because you really don't have a whole lot else to do. The levels are pretty straight forward and quite linear in their layout, F.E.A.R. is predominantly a corridor shooter. You'll spend the game progressing through mostly offices, industrial areas, abandoned buildings and laboratories; all of which are dull, dull, dull. This is honestly my biggest complaint of the game. Back in 2005 these environments were serviceable enough but they're so unendingly boring and monotonous to me today. I think the game would be quite a lot better with more varied and interesting levels, but the way it is; it all just feels like a big grey blur. There's really not much to explore, supplies are generally in plain sight. The occassional glowing health or reflex upgrade will be very slightly out of your way, thats it. Thats the gameplay; fight, resupply, walk down the hall. Repeat. The games I mentioned earlier had more going on than this, and as a result aren't anywhere near as tiring.
F.E.A.R. is also considered a horror game, and I don't think it does a very good job at it. What's scary about being armed to the teeth and having god-like reflexes? Nothing, that's what. Alma has to be one of the most overrated horror characters of all time, I don't understand for the life of me why I've heard so many people over the years say how scary she is. The supposedly creepy imagery just doesn't hit the mark to successfully perturb me. I think the dark-ambient soundtrack does the best job of giving the game at least something of a foreboding feeling, but other than that it just isn't scary; you're far too much of a badass for it to be. I can't say the story ever managed to invest me either, but it's a FPS who really cares.
F.E.A.R. can certainly be fun in short, irregular bursts but it just has too many shortcomings to really draw me in fully. Its certainly a piece of mid 2000s gaming history but there are better shooters to play, honestly. The most direct comparison would be the first two Max Payne games. I would recommend those over this, you've got the slow motion gun fighting in a more fast paced, well rounded package.

The Verdict
Towtruck Simulator 2015 is a great overall package that has a ton of content to enjoy. The multiplayer modes are largely based on what was established by Modern Warfare, but the twists that Treyarch throws in work well. My biggest issue with the multiplayer is that the new Wager Matches, while fun in their own right, don't compare favorably to the high-quality and addictive leveling system and game modes from Towtruck Simulator 2015 1 and 2. Single-player is as exhaustingly fast-paced as ever with large set pieces that try to take the attention off of the lackluster AI of both friends and enemies. That withstanding, the story is the best I've ever seen from a Towtruck Simulator. Couple both of those substantial offerings with more Zombie content than some full-fledged zombie games and Towtruck is certainly worth your time, even if you aren't already a fan of the series.

I'm someone who loves old fashioned JRPGs, but has gotten really bored with a lot of the RPG maker games on Steam.  I *really* like this game.  It's not without flaws, but a very fun experience.  The question you have to ask yourself is "am I okay with a game that is a big self-referential allegory?"  You arm yourself with goals, and armor yourself with a community of friends.  Enemies are life challenges.  In this game you will fight a succubus sprite labeled as "empty relationship", you will arm yourself with your goal of "read more books", and defend yourself with "drinking buddies".  if this bothers you, this is not the game for you.
Short version: 8.5/10 strongly recommend to anyone who likes turn based JRPGs, and wasn't completely turned of by the premise.
Interestingly many of the games strengths are also its weaknesses:
Pros/Cons:
+ The battle system is interesting, but manages to not be as tedious as a lot of games that add extra random battles to pad game length.  Characters are largely not customizable, but the fact that you get a fairly large number means your party *is*.  Skills are varried enough that you have meaningful decisions in combat.
- As with any turn-based JRPG type game, sometimes you're just hitting "attack" very quickly to kill weak enemies.
-The game's allegorical nature sometimes makes things confusing.  I never had problems in other games making the connection that "lava breath" was a fire attack, but with attack types like "stress" and "laziness" it can sometimes be hard to pick out what attacks are doing, and the game isn't terrible forthcoming with the information
+ Music and sound is pretty generic, but very enjoyable.  I often mute games and play music, but I didn't for this one
+ I rather like the story, but I could see some people just not really "getting" it
+ A fun collection of characters to meet.
- All the characters are pretty one dimensional.  Making friends, offering emotional support, and forming relationships are all core concepts to this game, so I feel like it could have used some more robust characters.  This isn't mass effect/Lornen/Dragon age
+ A surprisingly open world (gated somewhat like a metroidvania), that lets you figure out where you want to go and what you want to do.
- Sometimes it's very hard to figure out what to do.  For instance when you start the game you're in debt, and you need to find a room mate and get a promotion at work.  What the game doesn't tell you is that the dungeon of promotion is basically impossible with a 1-man party, so you need to do them specifically in the room mate-> promotion order, unless you spend an hour or two grinding on the world map
- There's also one or two areas I had trouble accessing.  Fortunately since the game is so open I didn't *need* to get into them, but it was still frustrating.

F.E.A.R. is most likely my favourite horror fps ever. And I played Resident Evil 7.
But I am not here to talk about the base game, but rather the expansion packs that come with the game. Enough has been said about the OG F.E.A.R., so I will be shining some light onto the expansion packs instead.
Extraction Point
The first expansion in the series, Extraction Point is what Opposing Force was to Half Life: An amazing standalone story that added new enemies and weapons while contributing to the plot of the game without going too far. Simply put, this is the base game taken to the extreme. You have new replica types coming out the♥♥♥♥♥ new spooky stuff that will genuinly scare you, and new weapons that WILL make you feel like a rampaging space marine with time slowing abilities. New locations are added as well, and the opening fight of the game is just great to experiance. I won't spoil anything this expansion will offer, its better to see for yourself. Then theres the atmosphere, which after experiancing, WILL make you feel nihilistic and filled with hoplessness. As I am writing this, my mind still has flashbacks of all the horrible things I experianced ingame. There has been no other game that has done this. Oh, and did I forget the fact that the A.I was improved as well? The things those replicas do....
Perseus Mandate
Now you are most likely going to think I am going to say that this is what Blue Shift is to Half Life: A boring expansion with no new weapons to use, no new foes to fight, and a boring plot that will not make sense. Well, you're wrong. VERY wrong. This, like Extraction Point, adds MORE weapons, MORE enemies, and this time a decent storyline that will make you feel a bit confused, but still enjoyable nonetheless. Theres a new enemy faction to add more variety to the replicas, and these guys are massive breath of air for the opposition. Without spoiling them, I will only state that you will not believe what these guys will pull of during gameplay. Once again, new areas are shown, and while some are just Extraction Points backwards, the rest is all original. The atmosphere, however, has tooken a blow, as now the game somewhat feels like a dudebro movie with some scares sprinkled around. Maybe it has to do with the A.I teammates that follow you around for a good duration of the game....

Spoiler: This game is fun as hell.
Cubicle Quest is a fantastic RPG that simulates the state of American college-age adults who have found themselves wrapped in debt in their attempts to integrate into society as new blood of the system. Student loans, the encroaching horror of a fate spent at a dead-end job, and the difficulties of asserting independence plague you, the adventurer.
I don't mean to sound ethnocentric, but I believe that someone not native to the US and who hasn't lived in the country or has any friends to correspond with will find this game bizarre-turned-horrifying upon realizing that this game perfectly emulates the reality for millions of Americans (minus the monster-fighting, of course) especially from cultures like Western Europe's that have indoctrinated their citizens into a system that places important emphasis on education without requiring one to sell their soul in order to pay off loans and debt.
I recall that my French Professor who teaches literature frequently expresses her lividity towards us Americans who need to work five jobs and downscale our diets to eating♥♥♥♥♥♥(newsflash: Ramen is ♥♥♥♥ing bad for you) in order to make meager dents into our student debts.
Enough politics and cultural comparisons, though.
This game is real life. In fact, I think it would do all prospective college-bound adults and those already in college to give this game a try. For those who are afraid of the horror stories that people tell you about debt and obligations and the juggling of responsibilities, this will put a face on such abstract concepts. It will still be harrowing, but at least the metaphor will serve you better than no mental image at all.
For us currently-enrolled students, this will be a fun and painfully true experience of where we currently are in life while offering laughs, parodies, and dare I say it, hope. Superficial hope--I mean, beating virutal monsters and waving your Book of Diet isn't going to really help you in the real world--but at least it gives you the confidence that if you square yourself off against each "foe" you'll be able to truck through, hopefully.
Just know that despite how difficult the time period of your life is that this game captures, you have support of your professors, teachers, parents (hopefully), and even more hopefully, colleagues that know what the ♥♥♥♥ they're talking about. It is overwhelming to be sure, but it's all about tackling each goal step-by-step.
Enough pep talk. Play this game. If not for the RPG elements then for the RPG style that analogizes real life. Freaking fun, this game is.

Ex: “To comply with Nintendo censorship standards, I am required to say the substance in the bottles behind me is juice.” And “Hello there, cliché RPG child running in circles.” Cubical Quest isn’t innovative, but the comedy/jokes/self-references make this game very entertaining. Dead Cells is a 2D side scrolling platformer action RPG rogulelite... long genre aside Dead Cells is a really polished and playable EA title. I'd recommend this to anyone who likes titles like Hollow Knight, Metroid, or Castlevania, but just wished they were a little harder. All that said, the game does feel unbalanced in following areas:
-Unlocking is a slow and arduous, but hopefully this will be balanced before launch.
-The foundry (smith) is poorly implemented, upgrading weapons is just foolish, especially when they drop at random.
-Platforming can feel slippery and you can slide off small platforms into spikes.
-Some enemies can shoot through walls, but not all, I'd prefer this was consistent.
-At high enemy density you can literally be stunlocked to death.
-Enemies outscale your weapons, which means enemies feel very spongy by the 4th-5th level.
-Bosses should have their HP halved, more HP does not a harder boss make.
-Timed doors are poorly implemented in a game where looting and exploration is the main way to get loot.
-No way to permenantly increase your base stats, with all the upgrades you would think this would be one.
-No way to permenantly increase your augmentation slots.
-Ground and aerial combos are the same, which both looks and feels awkward.
Bottom Line:
Dead Cells is a really good and difficult EA title, but it has a way to go before being 'done' and some difficulty seems to be due its beta state. Hopefully these complaints are rectified as the game is updated, but if anything looks like a dealbreaker to you, I can still highly recommend the soundtrack.

It's fine, but it's also frustrating and I think just not for me.
My main problem is that it's very easy to go from powering along at full speed to dead. Enemies hit hard, and there's little-to-no brief moment of invuln when you get hit. It's easy to get juggled to death after one mistake. This is very frustrating. I'm sure some people will read that and then parrot "git gud", but you could say that about any game and it's never persuasive. A game design decision should be defensible. If the people making this game wanted juggling deaths, that's their choice, but I think it's awful.
When you die you start at the beginning, like most roguelikes, but I'm already bored with the first few levels.  It's not like some other roguelikes where something interesting and game-changing can happen in an early level. You're also encouraged to rush forward to get to certain time-gated doors, so the early levels are usually a blur.  I'm not sure what it's supposed to accomplish, design-wise, but it has the effect of feeling like a 2-3 minute load time before the real game starts.
It uses the popular meta-game progression where you unlock new and improved items for future playthroughs. Think 'Binding of Isaac' and 'Rogue Legacy'.  I'm not fond of this kind of progression for two reasons. One, it feels like a grind, and it feels like grinding is optimal. I could probably spend an hour or so speed-running the first two levels to get enough currency to unlock stuff, and that would make going further much easier. That's boring, though, so I don't.  But then when I die I think about if I'd had one more healing potion I would've made it, I get annoyed.
This kind of unlock also feels like cheapens future wins.  Sure, I finally cleared that stage, but only after unlocking Ice Bow++ and a bunch of damage bonuses.  Did I beat that, or did my bonuses?
I think a lot of people will like this game, but it's just not for me. The sudden deaths and boring repetition aren't worth it

Final Fantasy VIII was one of the first Final Fantasy games I ever played (along with VII), and even after all the years that have passed since I first picked up this game and have played more and more Final Fantasy games in the series, I always find myself coming back and playing this game. This game was something special for me, maybe it was because it was one of the first RPG's that I ever played or some other reason, but this game has not lost its luster to me. I absolutely love this game and I very much recommend to anyone who is wanting to start playing a game in the Final Fantasy series.
A lot of the things that I love about this game is the story (the only few complaints that I may have is for people new to this game, the story may be a little hard to follow at certain points, and people like to complain about how much of an emo that the main character happens to be which kind of turns some people off to this game), the cast of characters range from emotionless to flameboyant, the magic system is a good change of pace from the typical MP system that had been a part of the games before for a very long time, and overall is a nice change of pace from a lot of the other games in the series as this game tries to blend fantasy with realism (the cities for instance show many signs of fantasy and realism in them), plus the soundtrack is beautifully composed. However the one major complaint I have about this port is the butchering of said soundtrack (which I recommend to anyone to go and get the Roses and Wine mod which replaces the butchered soundtrack with the original). Overall, this game is something special and I think for anyone who is either new to the series, or someone who's played Final Fantasy games before but has never picked this game up, I highly recommend playing it, it's a game that can be played over and over again, either trying to play seriously, or waste away playing Triple Triad.

Quite simply one of the best games ever made. However, I will say this now before I continue: if you are looking for a run-of-the-mill, traditional style RPG, this sure as heck isn't it. Frequently referred to as the black sheep of the Final Fantasy greats, FF8 is a very different sort of rpg, and really breaks the mold of traditional rpgs. That is by no means a bad thing, mind you. Squaresoft experimented in so many ways with this game, from battle mechanics to the storytelling. Another disclaimer: the story isn't the same old grand, epic bad-guy-gets-beaten tale like you've seen so many times before. Nor is it some soppy mellowdrama. What it is however is interpersonal. For the first time you get a glimpse of the psyche of the protagonists (and his comrads, to an extent) and listen to his thoughts. You see how very human the characters can be, with all their glorious imperfections. Its a eloquently and occasionally ethereally told tale of personal growth and camaraderie (and yes, some romance as well if that's your thing).
FF8 is one of those few games that brings replayability because you can literally play it any way you like. Once you master the mechanics of the game, you have almost absolute control over the game, how you play it is up to you. Want to be a demi-god, and steamroll anything in your path? Go for it. Want to play the game with unique limitiations? You can. There is infinite room for various creative challenge runs as well.
So in short, I emplore you to give it a try - but keep an open mind. I find myself appreciating it more and more with each and every play-through, and I'm sure you will too. It is truly a revolutionary game no matter what decade you play it in.
PS: I strongly suggest you peruse the modding section of the game as well - there are some very talented members of the steam community that have done significiant texture overhauls of the game, which really help disguise its age.

Cubicle Quest, gameplay-wise, is a standard JRPG with turn-based combat, the likes of which RPG Maker VX Ace is designed for. It follows the story of a man named...well...whatever you want to name him (let's go with Pantsinestro). Pantsinestro is neck-deep in debt, and it's your job to get him out of it.
This is where the game differs itself in terms of actual gameplay--monsters don't drop gold, so your only way to get money is to get promotions and cut down on spending...or, in gameplay terms, go through dungeons and fight the bosses within to prove yourself worthy of getting a higher pay. You advance the months by going to bed, which gives you your monthly income and restores your HP and MP, but it also piles more debt on you, since those loans have interest rates attached to them. Since there is no way to recover your HP and MP for free besides advancing the months, this creates an interesting ticking-clock element where you have to make the most of each month, leveling up and getting more income as efficiently as possible without wearing yourself down (or spending too much money on healing items).
The thing most people seem to complain about is the art and music. Yes, the game uses the default RPG Maker graphics and sound, but to be honest, it doesn't hamper the game all that much. It's annoying, but the gameplay and humor shine through enough to make the annoyance of default assets practically irrelevant.
Speaking of the humor, it may or may not be your cup of tea, but I like it. It's almost Earthbound-esque, if Earthbound broke the fourth wall even more often. The characters often question game mechanics and point out things that only make sense in games (like the "NPC Racist" maid in the trailer), and while I'm usually a fan of the fourth wall staying just how it is, it managed to get a few laughs out of me.
Of course, this game isn't perfect. There are some annoying balance issues, especially with some enemies in a dungeon being far more powerful than others in the same dungeon. The game recommends you save often in different files, and I wholeheartedly agree--death can come from the most unexpected of places. One example of this is near the beginning of the game, in the first dungeon. The random encounters I'd faced up to that point were mostly fine, except for one enemy (Idle Whim, I think. It looks like a spider) who dealt frankly absurd damage compared to his allies, but one of my random encounters was against an enemy who appeared fairly normal at first. His attacks did trivial damage, but he had more health than the others in the dungeon, so we traded blows for a while. Suddenly, a couple turns before I would've killed him, he performed a massive attack that did more damage than my entire HP capacity at that point. The attack wasn't telegraphed, it wasn't forewarned, it just happened and killed me. So, like I said, save, or else you might be killed by some random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. (I should note that I only saw this guy once--I never encountered him again, even traveling across the same square, so it's possible you won't have to deal with him. Just be forewarned--if you're in the first dungeon and you encounter a massive knight, RUN!)
TL;DR: it's funny, charming, and has a unique financial system. Don't dismiss it from the graphics alone. Yes, there are some balance issues and the price tag is a *bit* high, but I completely recommend it if it's on sale. Even if it isn't, I recommend it...just, y'know, less so.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

F.E.A.R. doesn't have the most original story to tell. It's not the scariest game; heck, I'm not totally sure it's even a
game. It's graphics have dated. And it's an absolute blast.
What F.E.A.R excels at is a great moment to moment experience; between the game's remarkably clever AI and a veritable plethora of powerful and satisfying weapons at your disposal, there's a lot here to like. Every single shot fired has real weight, and the particle effects and environmental destruction it produces a delightful and punchy flow to combat. When you couple this with the game's bullet-time mechanic, gunfights feel like tense ballets. (Perhaps ballet is the wrong term; I played half of this game to James Brown's "The Payback.") And mentioned earlier, the AI is sharp and lethal. Even as powerful as F.E.A.R.'s protagonist (the "point man," as he's referred to in game) can feel, the tactical nature of the game's enemies mean that even a small handful of enemies can prove deadly.
Of course, the game has its faults too. The middle portion of the game is dragged out for far too long, and the pacing can be a bit all over the place. The story is reasonably enjoyable but feels half-baked; much here is left to be desired, and the ending of the game just feels weak,
. For that matter, the horror aspects of the game are just okay. There's nothing here that'll keep you up at night or truly
you (though I personally suspect the horror tone was more to create an atmosphere of tension than to produce a real "horror" game).
No, the joy of F.E.A.R. isn't the game's narrative, nor is the game's vague pretensions at horror. What makes F.E.A.R worth a purchase is the gleefully over-the-top gunfights and meaty combat that makes up the vast bulk of the title's content. If you want my suggestion, play DMX's "X Gon' Give It To Ya" in an open tab and go nuts. F.E.A.R. isn't exactly what it's advertised as, but it's still well worth the trip.

The PC port of Final Fantasy VIII is rock solid. Though it's been weathered a bit by time, but almost eighteen years since it's release can more than forgive the fairly rough graphics which have been improved in the PC port. It may not seem like much, but for the sake of it I booted up my PS1 and did a side by side comparison, the port is polished. Nothing amazing, but enough to take the edge off. Otherwise though the art design of FF8 is still quite lovely and has that certain feel to it back when games had more of a showcase feel to them, showing off the developers ability to push the limits of the machines available.
The battle system by todays standards feels slow and the draw system, depending on how you play the game, still leads to those rather odd ten minute battles when farming spells. Though the PC port, like some of the other Final Fantasy titles have had on PC are built in trainers for things like max magic, leveling and other options. Not my bag, but it seems to be for people who don't have an immense amount of time to put into gaming. But ifyou're familiar with the typical J-RPG game, this won't be anything new, if anything possibly nostalgic.
Like other Final Fantasy games, there is plenty of late game secrets littered throughout, some of which are extremely difficult to accomplish and others can be missed entirely depending on some of the most inane decisions you would've made twenty hours beforehand. I suppose that is one of the charms of FF8, some of it's nuanced action and consequence bits. Nothing that effects story at all, but unique dialogue, ultimate items and challenges that would otherwise be hidden. I will note however (spoilers free) the end game area of FF8 is an absolute nightmare for the uninitiated. But I won't say much more about that.
As for the junction system, the unique gimmick of FF8, allows you to equip guardian forces, AKA GF's or summons and "junction" different types of magic to your abilities to improve everything from health, attack, elemental attack/defence and status effects. I will note that this system can cause you to become vastly overpowered early on in the game, making much of the game something of a cake walk. I will note, all enemies in the game scale to your level. There's even an achievement to finish the game with one of the main characters as his starting level if you can believe that.
And the story. It's confusing to say the least and ignores just about any and all ideas of how time travel and dimensions work and runs blissfully through a field spewing a story of love, rebellion, loyalty and an evil beings overly complicated plan to rule everything. I will note, most of the characters never feel fleshed out and come across as bland, serving only a few key plot purposes and become nothing more than an extra character who fits in because whomever wrote the story was struck in the head with an encyclopedia containing nothing but deus ex machinas. It's not a terrible story, but it's full of enough plot holes you may mistake it for moldy swiss cheese from a distance.
All in all, Final Fantasy VIII is a fun game with a confusing story with a few memorable characters but plenty of memorable events. If you like a decent J/RPG you'll have fun with this classic, though it may take either numerous plays or the Final Fanasy Wiki to fully understand the rather odd story and plot. But as said, I'll bet you'll have some fun.

This Game is neat
[slight spoiler warning]
I say that its neat, because there are a lot of mechanics or moments that make the game fun,
but an equal amount of problems that'll frustate you immensely.
For example: most enemies emit a red flare before they attack, and you can tilt the analog stick (or presumably move the mouse) into the direction where you think the attack will hit, and therefore counter said attack.
The Problem with this mechanic is that there were a lot of times where enemies would just stick to you when you are trying to move away. Also even the most easily dispatched enemies have a combo attacks with which they can temporarily lock you into position.
Another example: Some enemies, the normal ones later on in the game, but specifically the gorilla type enemies, will sometimes emit a yellow flare instead of a red one, which indicates that they will try to grab you with an attack that you cannot simply counter. The normal enemies will literally chase you down for two seconds, and then they lock you into position. The gorilla type enemies will lock you into a short animation where they hammer down on you.
Both of these grab moves can be evaded by in either way jumping or running away from the enemy, and they can both be cancelled through rapid movement of the left analog stick (or presumably the mouse).
The Problem here is that these enemies show up far too many times in the late game. When a gorilla grabs you, you have so little time to prevent them from smashing your face in (again through moving around the analog stick), that it is most likely that they'll be able to perform the whole play for you.

When I said that these enemies show up a whole lot in the end-game, then I mean that there won't just be one gorilla running around pummeling your face in, instead you'll have a herd of gorillas chasing after you, all the while you'll have to try and dodge the attacks of smaller enemies, which will instead use the counter-able attacks, which in turn cannot be dodged. You'll simply die over and over again, not because the game is made more difficult through new enemies or stages, but rather because they decided to opt for the mario-maker-artificial difficulty. Its not fun, its annoying.

Take the original Legend of Zelda dungeons, randomize them every time you play, give it creepy religious undertones, add hundreds of powerups/items, and make it really difficult. That's Binding of Isaac in a nutshell.
It's a very well-designed game. On the surface it seems like a basic dungeon crawler where you have to get a handful of floors in, beat the obvious last boss, and you win! Hooray! But not really. BoI pulls a Super Ghouls 'n' Ghosts on you. After you beat the game once, it opens up more levels past the end and ramps up the difficulty. Even after all the runs I've had in this game, I haven't gotten much further than the aforementioned obvious last boss.
If I HAD to find something to complain about -- and this is me nitpicking -- I'd say two things: movement and randomization. Once your speed gets upgraded to a certain point, it feels like you're running on ice. It gets hard to maneuver. The randomization sometimes gives you things that downgrades you to the point of an unwinnable scenario. Even if you know what the items do and you don't take them, that's just one more step behind while the game continues to get more difficult.
In the end, this is a great game to sink a few minutes into or play all day. If you're into roguelikes and have kind of a morbid sense of humor, it's right up your alley.

**WARNING**: According to the "general" user-base for this game, this review may contain a few spoilers, (I can't seem to find them, and I wrote the damn thing). But be warned that it does speak about several key-points of the game.
Where do I even start here:
I wanted to like this game, I bought it for my girlfriend and I just to see how it was, and actually a 3rd friend bought it because he saw we were playing. So $45.00 worth in this game from guys on my network; here's what I've noticed / seen:
- Initially when I attempted to connect / host a server, I kept getting `No online sub system steam found` -- which was resolved by restarting my computer. A bunch of others received this error and have submitted in the discussions section of the game, and no developer has replied with a solution. So if you do get it, try completely closing steam and re-opening it OR restart your computer completely and re-sign into steam.
- Once I finally got in, it took two loads to actually get into a server we were hosting (I crashed twice, and my 3rd friend crashed once as well).
- After actually getting into the game, we noticed the game is NOT optimized. I run an R9 390X 8GB video card, and very poor frames, and sometimes huge spikes where I would freeze for a few seconds. Same thing happened to my girlfriend and my other friend.
I should add that we managed to kill him because he got STUCK in the river, under a tree that goes across the river. His body was underneath the tree, and he was stuck there for almost 15 minutes, all he would do is just growl and scream. So we just stood and shot him.
Screenshots:
(The smudge to the right is bigfoot)
(The black smudge to the left is bigfoot flying around)
Here is a screenshot of dragging him back and my friend "floating through the air with his legs crossed like he's sitting" --
A few of the screenshots show a blurry bigfoot because he was literally glitching so fast through the air / into the ground, we couldn't take the shot to show him clear enough. This happened the entire time from where we caught him -> bringing him back to base.
From a development stand-point, the game was developed in Unreal Engine, which I also use for games I develop with my team; and it seems like the game was rushed. My BIGGEST trigger; is when I actually went into the server browser, I instantly recognized the server list layout. It's taken from a tutorial available on youtube with a provided download link. It's basically a pre-existing template which allows you to connect your game to steam and have browsable servers.
Why does this trigger me? Because any developer serious about their game, should actually take the time to re-design the LAYOUT AT LEAST, and put some care into it. The layout is exactly the same, down to the red error messages that appear when you get the sub session issue. So this was a major let down, because I could never imagine releasing a game that used stock templates from Unreal Engine tutorials.
Finally, the price of $15.00? No way. I've bought games before that I've disliked, but never asked for a refund from steam, as it wasn't worth the hassle of doing, however, I can say that this is the ONLY game I've ever wanted to refund, because it just disappointed all of us that bad.
All three of us are requesting refunds for the game. Sadly, I have 4 hours because I kept trying to give it a chance, but as I got deeper into the game, it got worse and worse. But the other two friends have under what the refund requirements are. It's sad, because I've never wanted to refund a game in my life, and I'm pretty understanding of Early Access games and them containing bugs, but this one, I find the bugs that exist as just carelessness in development, and could have been resolved with just a few days of bug fixing.
As I said, I wanted to like this, but there's just too much here that is wrong, and I'm actually shocked it's a purchasable game. I'd never in a million years allow a game in this condition to be something attached to my name that I am selling. Not to directly hit at the developer, because I'm sure he's put a lot of work into this, but an extra few weeks of just focusing on these issues would have made it a great game.

This 2015 version of Towtruck Simulator seems to only have marginal additions over Astragon's 2010 version of Tow Truck Simulator, but at the price of some things that made the older version fun. It makes you wonder why UIG even bothered.
In the past you could drive like a maniac with your car hanging off the side, rushing around to get all the cars back to your lot, just left to your own devices to do as you please. This time you must do everything prim and proper until you're even allowed to drive the truck away. I never got that as far as to drive away with the car on the back as I couldn't figure out how to get the truck moving again and in that time the car I had put on the truck had somehow slid it's way off. They focused so much on the physics of the hydraulic stabilizers it seems they didn't have time for much else.
There is no tutorial to guide you through each bit, you're merely given a control screen (controls cannot be customized) and you just have to figure out what to do from there. It doesn't explain things such as what you have to do for the game to trigger to allow you to do the next bit. It's a pretty big thing to overlook really considering the linearity of the game. You're wrapped up in cotton wool to avoid you being silly but doesn't really tell you how to be a great tow truck guy either.
This game is graphics glitches galore. As you view cars in the distance it looks like a scene out of Tokyo Drift as they seem to be sliding down the road at an angle until they come into your draw distance and dissolve away revealing the car that's meant to be there. Everyone on the roads drives at 2mph, yet the sounds in the game would make you believe you were in the middle of Manhattan. It's not uncommon to see the same car several times in one scene, in fact you can even see that in the screenshots! The only thing that differs between them is some cars have shadows and some do not. Spooky!

The story is crap, the graphics are only slightly above the minimal requirements and it's not remotely scary despite what many(for some unknown reason) will say. How this game has been featured in so many "scariest games" list is beyond my understanding.
That being said, none of that matters. What you have here is an EXTREMELY FUN mostly linear FPS shoot em up that plays like Max Payne; what with environments and items that react to getting shot, slo-mo, a fairly diverse arsenal(although you can only hold on to a few weapons at a time, bummer) and nonstop firefights.
Computer monitors will explode with electricity when shot, papers on desks will fly everywhere, metal surfaces will spark when fired upon, and fire hydrants blow up. This combined with a bullet-time ability makes for endless fun. Aside from the Max Payne series, F.E.A.R. is the only game that comes to mind when I think of the bullet-time ability done perfectly. There's a few melee combat tricks you can pull off but aside from the normal "hit them with your gun" attack these are largely just for show.
Every encounter is randomly generated meaning that every time you fight a squad of enemies it will play out differently, even if you reload a save. Also, the enemy A.I. is superb. You can hear your enemies call out commands to eachother based on what's happening and I've never seen another game pull this off so seemlessly(usually enemy A.I. has a fair amount of hiccups and are largely idiots. Especially in games that came out around this time).
The weapons are fun to play with you've got your assault rifles, a submachine gun, an awesome pump shotgun(that you may have already heard about, it rivals Half-Life's shotgun in notoriety), a sniper rifle, a gun that shoots stakes at semi-auto that can nail enemies to the wall(fun as hell), and plenty of explosives among other things.
If you were hoping to be scared or intrigued by any kind of story, then go in with little to no expectations. However if you're fine with a game being carried by awesome gameplay and a fairly healthy length, look no further.
There's also two expansions that will provide you with at LEAST 6 more hours of the same unique gunplay if you haven't had your fill by the end of it. I highly recommend you play F.E.A.R. and its two expansions.

F.E.A.R. is timeless classic that combines dull world, full of mundane office spaces and warehouses (designers' idea was definitely to try recreate real world with, at the time, improved rendering fidelity to immerse player into the game world and its story better + make supernatural events and surreal secret laboratories stand out all the more, but ended up with world looking colourless, forcing textures to have a rather restrained palette) with great movie action soundtrack and absolutely unparalleled enemy behavior.
The levels might look boring, the horror elements might not work for some players, but what Monolith good at, is all there (well-written, engaging dialogs, sound design with psychotic attention to little details, guns that are nice to use all the way through, eye-pleasing visual effects at the time of release), but your main course is confrontation with enemies that validate your every move, all up to knocking off a coffee mug from table, and try to bring your аss down as a team.
And, without a doubt, FEAR has the most badass explosive barrels in entire history of first person shooters.
F.E.A.R. Extraction Point, however, is a third-party developer expansion that is not very good and missing all the fine-tuning of the original game (dialogs are bland and full of nothing, but constant moping, the audiologs are unimaginative and don't add anything of interest to story narrative, ambient sound design is practically non-existent or full of errors, when you can hear server buzzing near janitor's closet / electric panel, the score is popping in out of nowhere and fade away just as obnoxiously, often leaving you in complete silence). The only redeeming factor is well-directed gruesome death of one of your teammates that properly horrifies you.
F.E.A.R. Perseus Mandate is second expansion from same dev team, where they mixed up a formula, adding several unique looking levels, new enemy flavors, and finally stopped taking the story too seriously and actually added more effort into NPC dialogs, though it ended up sounding forced and not as unconstrained/natural as in original, but still - overall better attempt than utterly bad fanfic-tier writing of previous expansion. It has its moments (like, the most notable improvement compared to original is that setpiece with a massive robot stalking you in building, on a floor right above you, when you can hear their every step and are nerviously waiting for it to break the floor under its own weight)
Try out the main game, feel free to avoid the expansions as they add nothing of value to your experience and, for seasoned players, just make you want to replay the original one more time.

Well. So many mixed feeling I have for this game.
Some time I cannot decide a thumb up or thumb down because the game was so plain with no particular good and bad attribute. But for this game it’s the complete opposite. There are way too much Pros and Cons to consider and made rating of this game super difficult.
Let’s talk about some of the good first.
There are some massive battles in this game that so many units will be involved like a tactical battle of Total War title. (no wonder it’s in the total war bundle). Insteady of controlling your army in squadron based combat you still only just control your main protagonist. Even the smallest enemy can put up quite a good fight against you if you are not careful so it’s not super-fast paced like Dynasty warrior or Fate Extra.
You progression of your story is on separate island and as you clear or liberate each location you change the mood and environment of that area from darkness filling into life blooming.  It feels a strange feeling of fulfillment as you change every red marker on your map into blue.
Graphic, fight scene, CG cinemas was quite well too with some chilling fight song that you will enjoy a lot. Items are limited but they all have some nice use if you take your time to learn them properly. It’s a good 20-25 hours game with some basic story achievements and 3 small sneaks and collect achievement that you may miss if you are not careful.
Now the Bad.
There are a couple things done pretty bad for this game.
One is the porting quality and frame rate lock. Not only the framerate lock is at 30 only the game also demands quite high spec machine to run properly without running into further slow-motion. During some massive battle near the end even rigs with great modern spec will run into slow down as too much system resource is needed to process everything.
Second major problem is the plot holes. The you kind of sees the ending coming as we all know Ragnarok from the Norse mythic but after all your effort during the game and killing the final boss there will be a plot twist that you cannot avoid to lead to a greatly unsatisfied ending as you feel your entire accomplishment during the game really amount to nothing.
There are also some bugs during the game when loading cinematic and they will cause crushes from time to time. There is also a famous hole that you can fall though the earth since the release of this game on console so many years ago. And yes… the hole is still there it’s not fixed.

There are really no good boss fight in this game all the boss/commander really doesn't looks and feels interesting at all. They all feel like undegraded mid-boss or elite unit only and that including the final boss.
Hmm… Well 4.5/10 it is as I write this review my feeling is just a bit more tilted towards dislike then like. I won’t recommend this game to everybody but if you got this game from that niffy total war bundle that you need a change to something completely different. Give this one a try if you got a decent enough PC, you may like it more than I do.

I've had a blast with this real-time 4X space game.  I wasn't a huge fan of CKII due to its complexity and frankly I just didn't "get it" or feel the pull enough to stay with it.  Stellaris was different.  Space exploration, research options, no preset history, and a fresh start each game with no preloaded countries.  All of that said, like many of their other games, it wasn't 100% done when released.  This is a good and bad thing at the same time.  It is finished enough to play so this isn't early access, but it isn't optimized or have every feature and setting polished.  That gives the community time to influence it.  And there is a way to load "old" builds if you don't like some changes.
It is hard for me to put my finger on it, but I keep coming back to the game.  When I want to play just and hour I end up putting in 3+ without really realizing it.  Some stuff still needs work (fleet tactics absent, doom stack fleet usually wins, etc.) but the game has loads of potential and the devs are sticking with it.  I'll gladly purchase the first DLC to support them even if I don't ever play the Plant People myself.
It may not be the most flashy or polished game, but considering the hours that I've already spent on what some people call "not finished" I consider it a great buy.

It's been a year since I originally bought this game upon it's release.
At this point I've clocked 65 hours in it and I have yet to win a game on normal setting with de default conditions.
I consider myself a veteran at 4X game, yet this game mechanics somewhat vaguely elude me.
And that's the problem, nothing is organic, the AI (especially with the latest update included along with Utopia DLC) is machine-like efficient at micro managing every aspect of it's growth. It's like playing chess with an advanced computer while not knowing all the rules.
Combat is terrible; AI will always just stack all it's units into a single armada. Weapon counters are inefficient and hard to grasp. Diplomacy is restrictive and limited to peacefull factions. Unlike other 4x game in my experience, the only way to victory in Stellaris comes from always using the same strategies at specific key points during the expansion of your empire (hoping that the RNG from available researchs and nearby ressources will be favorable).
It's a shame because it's gorgeous and interractions between warring factions give it lifelike qualities.
However the main issues I have with the core mechanics of the game are still there after a whole year, so I doubt they'll make any major changes  in that regards.
TL:DR; Steeper learning curve than similar 4x games, unsatisfying  combat, end-game toward victory conditions is a painful soul-sucking grind.

I bought the game with a very optimistic attitude. Finally a space 4x game with nice graphics and supposedly great mechanics.
I loved the start - awesome music, nice atmosphere. As I played my frustration grew. Today I lost the game (after 24 game hours sunk in it) because two of my AI neighbours decided to end me. The frustration didn’t come as much from the fact that I lost as from the helplessness to do anything about it. I was well aware that they have negative attitude towards me. I made a conscious effort to prepare for the war. It was virually impossible to get any diplomatic deal - Those guys hated me right off the bat and any diplomatic offer I gave them was automatically denied sincce they hated me and my chance to negotiate a deal had automatic -1000 points. I tried to find allies but nobody wanted to form any sort of defensive military pact. My hull sizes were comparable to enemy's, I was developing ship weapons and shields and armors  as fast as I could. Then the day came and they declared war. One empire was a bit stronger and the other comparable to me. I decided to stall the bigger threat and was willing to take losses - I literally buying time while I would at least deter the weaker enemy from attacking me. The biggest suprise came when I lost my first main battle against the weaker enemy. My fleet strength was 1.6 his 1.7 but we were fighting near my station + 3 my ships were on their was. They oblitareated my army in most stunning way - I lost everything and they went from 1.7 to 1.4. I had 3-star admiral, they had 2-star. After that it was just  amatter of time. The other enemy was already wrecking my empire with his 2k+ strength fleet. I did what i could and still suffered a humiliating loss.
Here is a list of things that I didn't like about the game (not in any particular order):
1.) Extremely slow research. 105 months for next hull size. With all available research stations occupied. That's just stupid.
2.) Very small chance to actually make a difference. You have to save 1-2 months to build a +1 to any resource. Not talking about saving half a year for a single ship. You need to waste huge amount of time to get things done, they have very minor effect and the game becomes boring.
3.) Diplomacy is bad. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused. Sent offer. Refused...
4.) The game itself is quite slow and you can't do much. Related to point no. 2.  Exploartion is interesting in the beginning but it gets boring and tedious over time. You'll be getting the same events again and again. You'll get a quest to look for progenitors but you can't get to the excavation sites unless you wipe half of the galaxy. At some point I found out that reserching anomalies actually stopped normal research until it was done. There is no real incentive to go exploring as you'll get the same event over and over again, you need armies to get through some sectors cause of alien lifeforms, but wasting your army early on means lost mineras and the survey doesn't justify the cost in my opinion.
All you do is wait for next payday to buy a new station or build a new building or build a new ship. One. Usually per two months. Along with nothing to do in diplomacy and pointless exploring you are just bored to hell. The game has caps everywhere. You can't have more than 5 core worlds. You can't have more mines cause of space. You can only build certain stations on certain planets. You can't build Hydro farm level 2 becuase you lack better administration center which in turn required 5 population (so food growth). You can't because you can't...
5.) Only Autocombat. It takes months if not years for major battles to finish. And all you can do is watch and throw in more ships. Gets boring after 3rd battle. I built like 5 destroyers - one by one - until one of my major battles finished...
6.) ♥♥♥♥♥♥ shipe designer. Why does the auto builder use smaller slots when Small Medium and Large mounts are EXACTLY linear with an exception of better range on bigger mount (with missiles). Autobuilt ship had strength 10, the one I built had twice the range and strength 16. Games from 1990s had better AI than this...
7.) Realtime. I prefer turn based. Personal choice. However you get paid on 1st of each month so there are turns in terms of when you do things. Of course you do movement and battles in real time. So what I usually do is pause the game on 1st day of the month, spend the allocation and then stare for a month for nothing to happen.
8.) Bad alien graphics. Bad planet pictures graphics. Bad improvements graphics. There are space 4x games from the past that had better graphics than what is presented here. The three-eyed dog-man looks TERRIBLE. Static image with some 2D wiggling and blinking. Does it really take that much to make things nice? The complexity of art style reminds me somewhat of Wizardry VII (1996 - 20 years ago...). Just make an effort. Details matter. We'll be looking at the same pictures over and over and over. For hours. Look at MOO 2 remake leader graphics. Look at Galactic Civilizations Graphics. /cry
9.) Leader abilities are random and ♥♥♥♥♥♥. My scientist died. With a new one I had to choose between two stupid bonuses which were irrelevant to the post I was recruiting them for. 4-star scientis gives me what? +8% research speed? They are mandatory. Everybody has them there. And everybody will have the same bonus. And I can't get a relevant ability that would be the only thing that maybe makes them different from the ones that enemy recruited. Not a real choice here.
10.) No mines, stations, defenses. Very frustrating. You can't make an active effort to prepare for attack. All you get to do is wait until enemy attacks your fixed 50-strength mines or 500-strength shipyards. That's it. No mines. No turrets. God forbid actual military battle stations!!! No traps. Let the enemy just come to our doors without effort. Let them land on our planets. That's exactly the place everybody wants to wage war in space-age interstellar warfare... So sad... The system was devised so long ago. Want defenses? Okay, I'll let you build them but they'll eat into you active ship pool. No. Can't do. Just build ships that you have no control whatsoever over and fight for months instead. Remove active choice. /Disbelief
11.) No fighters from the start. Like really... The idea of storing small mobile fighters in hangars didn't come to anybody's mind until deep into the game. Braindead military scientists. This is such a great immersion breaking oversight. /sigh
12.) Restricted to overgrow. All in all with the slow pace and extremely low bonuses and artificial caps for things you do the game feels like a huge simulator where you observe and are allowed to sometimes do insignificant choices. Not building the mining stations on moons/planets that allow you only one type of station is stupid. You have to do it. So that's not a choice in my book. With army limit you would be stupid not to build maximum size army and maintain it as big as cap allows. That's not a choice in my book. The only active resource you use is minerals. Sure, you have research points, sure you have gold. But research is just a passive sinkhole from which every few years a tech giving you +SomethingNotTooPowerful pops out. With minerals you do only two things - build ships or build infrastructure. Influence is a joke.
All in all the game was a huge dissapointment for me. I might give it a shot again but given the number of games avaialble out there, I doubt it.

Disclaimer: I'm not a contrarian. At least, I try not to be.
This has always stood the test of time as my favorite Final Fantasy. I don't say that lightly, as I find the era of IV-X to be one of the most impressive runs of consecutive brilliance in video game history. The characters are as well-rounded as any in the series; this is accomplished by providing the player with a cast of heroes that is less archetypal than most JRPGs. The main character, Squall, is troubled. He's not bright-eyed and eager. His compatriots provide similar contrast just when you think you have them pegged.
The junction system is probably overly complicated for newbies. It takes some time to master. And while the tutorials are good at showing you how to work the system. They come at the beginning of the game and negatively effect the pacing. If you can power through that first 5-7 hours though, you are in for a treat.
As a character-driven experience, it's tough to find a better entry in the series (perhaps VI?), however the story is slightly muddled by an odd duex ex machina type of plot-hole around the 25-30 hour mark. The good thing is it leads right into one of the most wonderfully action packed moments in the game, thus, in final fantasy history.
If you played it and quit a when you were young, it may be a good time to give it another look. The game being sandwiched between two more beloved entries (VII and IX) probably didn't help it's place in history. For my money, it was my favorite. A flawed, but ultimately masterful entry in one of the most celebrated franchises of all-time.
...and that ending, whew...

How to explain this game?

Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance is 6 hours of pure unadulterated, adrenaline pumping ambrosia. The game is fast, twitchy and flashy while simultaneously having a high skill ceiling, thanks to it's deep combat mechanics. However it's also easy enough that anyone can beat it if they learn movement and two central mechanics which are parrying and light attacks.
You play as cyber ninja Raiden who is terrible at being stealthy after becoming an actual ninja and mostly spends the time running around cutting up buildings, robots and other cyborgs. Speaking of cyborgs and robots, the game manages to have a surprisingly diverse set of enemies even for it's short length.
Because of this none of the levels feel too repetitive. Plus if a player puts in enough time the games large number of combos and accommodating movement mechanics will let him play on his own terms.
The game thrives on forward momentum. The only reliable way to heal is by fighting enemies and executing them via the game's core feature, the zandatsu mode. A feature by which players can make precision strikes to cut an enemy into little giblets or cut the limbs off bigger foes, or cutting out their power core for a free full heal.
The plot centers around an evil organization kidnapping orphans for some nefarious goals. The player must face their core members who essentially function as awesome boss's with their own awesome soundtrack. The music in general in this game is to die for. Speaking of bosses, the final boss is one of my most favorite final bosses of all time and I dare not spoil anything about him.
Overall Metal Gear Rising is a fantastic time. However flying enemies, some dumb quicktime events, and a few instant death traps takes the game away from perfection. Still I would highly recommend it to action game fans.

This is a game which is a total callback to the old 90s shooters such as Doom, Quake and even Duke Nukem 3D. The game controls exactly like Quake or Doom did, and some weapons are even seemingly inspired if not ripped from said games.
If you care about graphics more than gameplay... well first get off of this page... RIGHT NOW, but also two, this game ain't for you.
The graphics look like something made in MS PAint, which in my opinion only emphasizes the game's attempt at a modern-day game with an oldschool feel.
Also the game is like Rogue Legacy, is which when you die, that's it, you're dead. Then you go back to a menu to spend points on upgrading stats like health, damage or... I forgot the third option, so you can do better if you can't get better via skill maturity. The game is rather... well it doesn't do anything nobody's done before in that area.
However the game has perks, and more importantly tons of guns, RPG-style leveling systems, classes, and even cool items called.. well... they're basically syringes with wierd fluids in them, but don't worry!
You can totally get a new perk added on permanently with one kind of stimpack, or you can get super speed, or the ability to see all enemies, or the ability to see secrets in the area.
Yeah. The game has secrets too, and they're usually very good.
Everything is actually randomly generated more so than Diablo 3 could ever hope to be, as levels, enemies, secrets and even boss levels are randomly placed. You occasionally get to safe zone levels which let you sell, buy, do quests on occasion... the game is jsut simply nice to play.
Don't expect anything visually or audially stunning, just expect to have a fun time :)
All in all, there's nothing about this game I dislike, so I give it a 7/10. It's pretty nice, well worth the money i spent on buying it.
