Back in the old days - mid 90s - I was introduced to Master Of Orion II. I loved the game and kept playing it off and on until this year, 2016.
Enter Stellaris; In many ways the game feels like MOO2 refurbished and upgraded to a 2016 version. Stellaris is what I wish the new MOO could have been: The galaxy is large, the tech tree is laid out in a very nice manner, being more random than the traditional fixed tech trees - and also being dependent on your civilizations' ethics and biology. For example if you start with a scientific materialist ethic and a biology evolved for a tropical world your research options will mirror this: You are more likely to get options to research robotics than spiritually inclined civilizations and you are unlikely to get the opportunity to research colonization of planets with a climate far removed from your own. You are for example unlikely to quickly learn how to colonize tundra planets but more likely to colonize e.g. continental or ocean worlds.
What I do miss are:
A more intricate diplomacy system. It is quite good as it is, but it doesn`t fit with the complexity of the game in other respects.
Spying and tech theft would be nice. For example when integrating a vassal empire into your own it would make sense for you to also acquire their technology. Some technology should also be acquired upon conquest of another empire.
There is very little control over what happens in battles. You send your fleet in to duke it out and control appears to be taken over by the AI. You control troop movements on the galactic or solar system levels, but not in a battle.
Still, the game is excellent and I would warmly recommend it to anyone who is fond of 4X games.

The Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF):
There is a solid core of a game here, and recent updates have patched most of the content holes that were in the game at launch. Buy now if you're eager, but recommended for all to buy when on sale.
Review:
This game is a hybrid of a grand strategy game and a space 4X game. I've played my fair share, and I have read a lot of reviews from both Paradox veterans and also those new to Paradox games. Initially, I agreed with many of the concerns raised with how the game was first launched, but now with 2 updates under their belt, the gaps from before have been minimized, with more promised. I've updated my "cons" from launch with my current view on things.
Pros:
Very visual setting. Avatars with movement.
For the most part, a pretty easy to learn interface.
Excellent soundtrack.
Customizable factions & detailed ethics systems.
Planetary population (or "Pop") system.
Three varied weapons systems.
Multiplayer (have not tested it myself yet)
Cons:
AI and Diplomacy is flat. (Partially fixed from launch)
Mid-game gets boring, and end-game can be so-so depending on how AI empires respond. (Partially fixed)
An empire can feel a little empty, graphically. (Partially fixed)
No layers view to tell who's in which Federation. (Still not fixed?)
Little replay value at present. (I have found more replay value playing as different empires with different traits and ethics.)
I'm sure it's a great game for multiplayer, but most people play single player, and I think that experience has gotten better.  For the moment I would still recommend a Paradox game that's been out for over a year, like Crusader Kings 2 or Europa Universalis IV. There, the gameplay has been improved with updates and dlc's. But now, with the updates, this game gets my thumbs up. I'm sure Paradox will make the game even better over the next couple months.

An Analysis of Lavapools
Recommendation for people who like rage games/games that require skill and have lots of player death: 10/10
Recommendation for people who aren't into that stuff: 5/10
Overview: Lavapools is a top-down rage game. You are a crab, trying to get your son back who has been stolen by an octopus who is designing traps for you.
Lavapools has 3 gamemodes on several levels:
1. Procedural
The most common gamemode. You collect gems from gem spawn points, and as you get more gems the world gets more hazardous. At 25 gems the door opens to end your progress and save your score, but you can keep collecting gems. When you die, you drop about half of your gems in one little pile and can pick them back up when you respawn (with 0 gems, of course). The hazard level/rank/music also resets when you die. The levels in this gamemode are the smallest compared to other gamemodes.
2. Maze
Gems are already spawned in and do not respawn at special spawn points. There are several banks located around the map, and walking over one stores any gems you may have collected so you don't lose them if you die, and it also becomes your spawn. The banks are not separate, they all add to one total count displayed on the bank. If you die but have collected gems, the gems return to their original positions and no gem pile is dropped. 25 gems opens the door, but there are more located around the map - you may want to try and collect all of them for an extra challenge.
3. Vertical
There are no gems in this gamemode. Instead, the screen scrolls and a lava wall is at the bottom of the screen. You have to keep up with the moving level, at the same time dodging hazards. There are several paths to take in this level, which will lead you to a checkpoint mark. If you die, you respawn either at the beginning or at the checkpoint, if you have passed it. After the checkpoint, there is another stretch until the end of the level.
There is a bug - the octopus talks about finding 25 gems at the beginning of the vertical levels, even though no gems are involved.
Some of the many hazards you will encounter:
-Lava pools (of course)
-Sawblades moving across fixed paths, and sometimes switching directions
-damn bats moving in fixed directions that you have to observe on your own
-spinning arms in different arrangements: 180 degrees, 90 degrees, T formation, cross formation, and half-arm (center on end of arm instead of middle)
-spike-shooters aimed at one or multiple directions along the x and y axes
-lava wall in vertical levels
Maybe I am missing some hazards, but I got the most common ones
Good luck!

The first time I heard about this game, the friend who mentioned it to me described it as a cross between Worms and Terraria.  While I don't know if that's the bast analogy, this game certainly brings the best of both genres to the table.  There is a constantly changing battlefield that doesn't reset all the holes and debris just because the fight ends for the day.  There's also an element of creating a safe shelter to direct the operation from, as the whole fight hinges on success or failure in keeping safe one particular member of your forces.
I should also point out that in my opinion, CC is not a game about tactical fighting.  Yes, you did just read me deny the majority of standing opinion.  AI can be used for most battle functions that the player can direct, granted not as efficiently as a skilled cortex operator - but no AI can manage your funds.  This game is about war economy.  Deciding what's necessary for an attack and implementing those choices, while keeping back enough money to create a defense.  Bring your management skills: all transactions may just be gold dust but you have to operate a stable system of income and expense to dominate the resource race.

This is a game I wanted to like, but the game simply would not let me.
I can deal with the unpolished visuals.  I expected it to look like a mobile game.
The controls are slow and clunky.  You are often waiting for whatever time cycle to pass before you can enter another command.  Sure, the pauses are generally small, but the frustration adds up.  Plus, the default swipe movements are always there, so you can end up accidentally moving while trying to activate levers or pick up objects.
You can use the 1-4 keys to make attacks, an improvement on Legend of Grimrock which is click only, but half of the default party are spell casters and there are no keyboard shortcuts for spells.
And if you accidentally cast a spell with no possible target?  You're still stuck waiting for everyone to return to "idle" state so you can move again.
You also start with almost no equipment.  You can pick up a few items laying around an intro area, but when the first fight arrived only half my party had weapons.  By the time everyone was wiped out by some golem thing, my shaman had yet to find a weapon and so all they could do was cast Heal and twiddle their thumbs.
There is also the inane conversation between the party members.  It's better than talking to the two crazy ladies who run an inn and a shop in a dungeon, but that isn't really saying much.
Yet despite all the time spent on text and conversation, there are other areas that are blatantly ignored when it comes to prose.  For instance, the areas you enter and teleport to/from are things like "2a" and "1".  It just struck me as odd.  There is also no real explanation of what game items are and how they work.  Why do I have rations?  No idea.  Why can't the shaman wield a staff?  No clue.
All in all, this game just isn't worth $5.

Fighting in first-person seemed like a potentially huge turn-on to me. I quickly found out that this would not the case here.
My sessions in this game lasted no more than half-an-hour at a time. The sound of the strikes and bullets hitting flesh, while not exactly realistic, made me recoil in "pain" often. I never realized how the intensity would push my comfort level, since most of the combat takes place within a tiny radius of the protagonist. Zeno Clash caused me to feel damage more than any other game I've ever played.
The artwork leaves me feeling disappointed... about the majority of games. I admit that I'm picky when choosing a game based on aesthetics, but even the amazing-looking ones could stand to be a tad more bizarre or goofy. Zeno Clash is the zenith of imaginative design, yet coherent and believable in an unbelievable universe.
The combat system is quite basic, but it works alright. I only wish it was easier to lock-off and flee in tight quarters, but I suppose that forced me to be aware of my map position and strategize accordingly. The key to success is finding the appropriate approach for every encounter, and that may require a failure or two to understand.
With all that being said, Zeno Clash was an unforgettable experience, even though I didn't become horny. Maybe boxing gloves and no projectiles would have done the job, but that's not the case. I'll look elsewhere.

I absolutely loved Mini Ghost, so I was waiting for a sale to give this game a shot, and unfortunately, it's not doing it for me. Mini Ghost's gameplay was perfect for what it was. Controls were simple and tight. In Ghost 1.0, everything feels kind of wrong.
Everything feels a bit slow, but then some things feel too fast. Some enemies lock on and shoot you really fast, and some of the shots go almost too fast to react to without dodge rolling, but my biggest problem IS the dodge roll. It's pretty useless. After playing most other games with a dodge roll, I'm constantly expecting the dodge to actually act like a dodge. Some of the level design and enemy placement makes you feel like you want to be dodging through shots with the roll, or dodging through enemies to avoid getting hit so you can kite them back and forth. It doesn't work like that. From what I can tell, the dodge just shrinks your hitbox a little and maybe speeds you up very slightly. In my less than two hours with the game, I've gotten stuck in spots where I'm basically waiting for shots to hit me, and it feels bad.
There are some other mechanics that feel out of place. The loss of accuracy while running and the need to wait for your basic shots to charge ammo really slow things down and made me feel frustrated. Being able to dash around and make skill shots without having to stop for accuracy or ever wait for ammo would serve the game much better, in my opinion. I want to feel like I'm controlling something similar to Samus in Super Metroid, but instead I feel like I'm playing more of a slower paced strategy game, where the enemies aren't giving me time to take my turn.
The voice acting and writing aren't amazing, but I think they're overstated as a negative. It's not a big deal. There's maybe a bit too much of it at first. Lots of flavor dialogue that slows stuff down during the tutorial. I thought Ghost was voiced and written a bit better than the others though.
Ultimately, there's enough that feels wrong to make me want to stop playing before I'm unable to refund, which is a real bummer, because there's a lot of potential here, and Mini Ghost was such a gem, but it just feels too unnatural compared to other games like it. I'd definitely pick it up again if some of these things were changed, but for now, it's no for me.
That said, I'd like to recommend Mini Ghost again. Everyone play Mini Ghost.

Although you have basically the same abilities throughout the game, it expects you to get better at using them as the difficulty increases, and you will, going from casting basic fire spells constantly to being lightning fast at both blowing up and reviving your friends.
I recommend a keyboard and mouse because of the number of buttons that are needed for spellcasting, but the game does support 4 person local multiplayer, and playing with a gamepad is more challenging, but for couch coop, is still very doable.
All in all, only get this game is you will play with friends, but it is a rip roaring good time.

I'm so sad about it, but I cannot recommend the game. It has a cool story, good game mechanics, decent graphics and sound and the combat feels satisfying. However, it has one major problem: exploration just does not work well.
The map is broken into small, self-contained pieces connected with elevators and doors:
Elevators would be fine, except that you cannot use shift to look-ahead vertically, only horizontally, which is a really crippling limitation IMHO.
Doors are the main reason I do not recommend the game. If you want real exploration, you need to be able to orient yourself in the space. In Ghost 1.0 it's simply impossible because the map is broken into numerous short corridors connected with doors. It's way too easy to lose any direction and get lost. You feel like you're just walking down the same corridor over and over again. The map does wrap back at some points, but it's almost impossible to tell because there are no distinct landmarks.
The game has a "map", but it only shows you rectangles, not the actual shapes of the corridors. Pretty much useless, because you can't see how they are connected. So, it's more like a compass, not a real map.
The only way to play the game would be to take out a piece of paper and a pen and draw my own map. I might do that at some point if I run out of other games to play.
Take a look at some great metroidvanias like Guacamelee or Axiom Verge to see how the map should be done.

It's a fun little game that is reasonably priced.  The graphics made me think of the old arcade game "Tapper" and the gameplay is satisfying for what it is.  It's ridiculous, silly, crude, simple, but all in the best way possible.  Essentially your battery power is draining, and to keep yourself alive you need to lure people using certain items that appeal to them, and while they are distracted you rip their hearts out and replace your battery with their heart to keep on going, and repeat this to get a high enough score to advance to the next level.  The catch being however that different types of characters have better hearts than others, so a wealthy businessman might give you 30 seconds of life to work with to find a new heart, while some fat slob might only give you 10 seconds.  There's also hazards and the likes to try and avoid that will shave off valuable time on your battery/heart.  The plus side is your battery can be picked back up again at any time to replace a heart, and it keeps its energy with it so there is a bit of strategy involved for when to use your battery and when to use a heart.  The gameplay is very reminiscent of oldschool arcades where the focus was a high score.

Wanted to like this game and gave it a fair try, but the controls are so bad, so so incredibly bad, that I just ended up deleting it out of frustration because I couldn't even get past a relatively simple miniboss somewhere after the intro. The biggest issue is the camera combined with the fact that it doesn't have a normal dodge/roll mechanic (like other Platinum games do have) - you have to press the left stick towards an enemy and press light attack. That's 2 buttons instead of one to make sure you don't get hit. This doesn't seem to work 100% of the time and gets even more trying considering you can get attacked by multiple enemies at once AND the camera flies all over the place, preferring to look at walls rather than the enemies you're fighting. Then you also need to be pretty precise with the timing so you need to learn all the enemy telegraphs in order to successfully parry.
So to sum up: you have no idea where attacks are coming from because the camera is all over the place, and if you do manage to catch an enemy attacking you probably mistime the parry due to weird telegraphs and if you DO time it well the parry just randomly seems to fail anyway. Now, since you're pressing light attack the character attacks instead of parries, then obviously gets hit, knocked all over the place making the camera have an even bigger spaz attack accumulating in the controller taking an unscheduled flight to the other side of the room.
Oh but there's a sidestep/dodge you can buy at the start of the game! That would be great if it didn't suffer from the same issues - it just doesn't work 30% of the time. You can literally do the dodge 50 times in a row and quite often it will just not work. And that's just out of combat, when it gets hectic there's no way to get it working reliably.
Other than that there's probably a lot to like which is why it's such a shame the controls make it unplayable.

I played Witcher 2 without having played the first one. I understand the point of the game was about political struggles and as such there are a lot of key players in the story, and it gets confusing sometimes. I think a more streamlined narrative in terms of the politics would have helped the game, but that's just my opinion. The game looks very good for a somewhat older title, and I only experienced minor frame drops in a few areas, and no hard crashes the whole game. Overall the Witcher 2 is a wonderful, if somewhat confusing game (read EVERYTHING), but I am very glad I played it and now I can play Witcher 3, having gained a good grasp on a lot of characters and lore of the world. If I had to rate it, I would give it an 8.5/10, with the combat mechanics and at times very confusing story bringing it down from a 10, if I replay it with the combat overhaul and it fixes a lot of my concerns, I might raise that to a 9.25.

It's Chex Quest with more corridors.
It's a fun and charming distraction. The randomly generated content lies primarily in the map layout, the level of weapons and armor you pick up, and which enemies you will be facing on each floor. There are some weapons with status effects, and a varity of alternative items like stims, shields, and explosives. It's just enough to allow for a bit of experimentation.
As you play more you can choose to start with different perks and items, but by floor 20, your loadout will reflect your playstyle rather than the "background" you chose to start with.
The more you play, the more intel you get, which can be spent on permanent stat upgrades, more backgrounds, and enemy strengths and data. You also unlock story logs which carry on the odd humor of the game. You can play the game fully without touching them though.
Besides each floor being made entirely of corridors and rectangle rooms with texture swaps for the walls, the big flaw with this game are some odd bugs. I haven't encountered any game breaking bugs or crashing, but sometimes you will see a few enemies who have spawned outside the map that you can't shoot, or the music will stop and not start playing until you reach the next floor, and how strange the game window acts, as it if its moved away from the screen's center, strange things happen. Screenshots suck to.
Playing the demo though shows off quite a bit of what the full games provides for only a couple of the easiest floors. It should expose any bugs that there may be on your system, or if this type of gameplay is your thing.
If you are craving Chex Quest: The Roguelike. This is the game for you. Just enough content and variety at a $5 price point that allows for cheap, quick, fast-paced, tactical gameplay. What it may lack in the variety of items you may be used to from Binding of Isaac, it's quirky humor, lively enemies, and plenty of opportunity for thoughtful experimentation, it holds its own, if you keep in mind what kind of games its drawing inspiration from, classic old-school shooters.
Like I said, it's pretty much Chex Quest with more corridors.

Two words coming to mind are wasted potential. One might thing EA released this, because it's horrendously buggy and unbalanced. As it is right now, it ends up unplayable sooner or later along the game always. Maybe, with some serious patching, it'll become better.
There is hope. Much of the engine is clear and usable, the groundwork is generally well done, you get a cozy environment in your galaxy with a lot to tweak, options to do more or less of that yourself, many ways to go. The UI gives mixed feelings, some things are very clear but others are just catastrophically stupid, causing dozens of extra clicks for simple matters. A number of bugs will cause a lot of game restarts, with blank windows filling the screen or clicks stopping to register every now and then. The balance of resources feels mostly good, and I'm guessing constantly running out of energy is more due to lack of my gameplay skills. It makes sense to have some lack of resources, so you'll actually need to balance it. Strategy games tend to be too easy in this regard, so I consider this a better option.
The AI. That's where it all falls down. Even if you set the AI to passive, what it means is excessively aggressive. If you get a late game event with really bad guys taking over the galaxy, the AI empires just ignore them and try to fight you twice as hard when you're supposed to be saving the galaxy on your own. There's a lot of other illogicals in the AI behaviour, which simply make the gameplay extremely frustrating. And when I say extremely, I mean "this monitor's going out the window" level of frustrating. There's just no balance and no sense. It's hard to make it perfect, I've seen that with way too many thousands of hours in strategy games, but this is not "slightly untweaked", it's a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job. Unfortunately.
Give us an easier way to manage all spaceports, give us a more balanced AI and wouldn't be a bad idea to add a beginner friendly difficulty level to get you started at first. The first gameplays ended way too quickly with a massively overwhelming attack by... well, everyone. Make love not war, you know?
To sum it up: close to unplayable now due to bugs, UI frustration and mostly AI problems, but with a LOT of hard work, that might change. I dearly hope that happens. I would like to play this game. Should further patches change it, I will gladly change my opinion.

So, originally, I wasnt going to recommend this game. I tried it, liked it, bought it... but there was no save function.
That, however has been added in, removing the one and only real problem I had with this game.  And that's great, because I really like this one alot.
This game is exactly what the title says: A combination of an FPS and a Roguelike.   When it says "FPS", it generally means those done in the Doom/Duke3D/Wolfenstein style... older FPS games where the combat was fast, you had to actually dodge enemy projectiles (no cover systems here!), and there were maze-like levels to explore full of goodies to pick up, and a large variety of unique enemies.
This takes all of those elements, and replicates them well.  I particularly like some of the enemy design/behavior... there's some creative ones in here, in terms of what they do and how they attack (a couple can attack by hugging you and sticking to your screen.  No, really.), and I really like that some of them will actively try to dodge your attacks, leaping quickly to the side, or even firing at you a couple of times, and then running off down some random corridor, only to come at you from a different angle later.  That's pretty neat to see.
The roguelike elements are done well also.  You've got your typical permadeath, as well as the full randomization and murderous difficulty that you'd expect.  There's alot of different items and weapons to find, randomized with all sorts of different stats and special effects, with all equippable items being breakable, as they lose durability when you get hit, though you can fix them with tools once you reach a safe room.  You also have the ability to craft various things, there's alot of special items to find like grenades that triple the damage you do to the enemy after hitting them with it, or holographic decoys, and all sorts of other stuff.  There's various other mechanics to the game as well.
As in most roguelikes though you're gonna be hard-pressed to keep a good supply of stuff going.  Ammo isnt always so easy to come by, so you need to be careful, aim well, and conserve your shots to make the best of it and be efficient.
That being said, this game isnt for everyone.  If you dont like Doom-style games, you wont like this one.  Same for roguelikes in general.... all levels are *completely* randomized, and just like with basically all roguelikes, the game as a whole is repetetive.  Which is fine if you're used to that sort of game (seriously, most roguelikes really do get quite repetetive).  And you've gotta be able to handle the difficulty and the dying over and over.
And if you're the sort that considers graphics and such to be important... yeah, this isnt for you.  Dont get me wrong.  I dont think this is a bad looking game.  The artstyle entertains me and I like the overall aesthetic.  But like a great many indie titles, the graphics are quite limited overall.  But this doesnt affect the gameplay one bit, so.... like it or leave it, up to you.
Overall, yeah, I recommend this one.  I'm having a blast with it, and it's going to get alot of play time from me.  It's exactly my sort of thing.  Hopefully, it might be yours as well.

Ah at last, a game that scratches the itch Galactic Civilizations II left in my little gamer heart. If you love micromanaging an empire, customize an entire alien race (in a more intuative and detailed way than GalCivII), and really feel like you're exploring a living Galaxy, this is the game for you.
Pro's
-Intuative controls (for me at least)
-Multitude of options for governing your empire
-No fleet-size cap. Only number of total ships are limited
-Interesting races that you can discover/create. (I myself made the Chozo and am loving it)
-You can easily keep track of everything in your empire (once you learn the layout)
-Vast number of options for creating a race, including multiple (up to 8) different species within a phenotype. (Avain, fungus, ect)
-Research 3 tech at once instead of a (very slow and useless) single tech research
-Beautiful music and atmosphere (or lack of one)
-Not possible to simply "steamroll" the Galaxy once the player desires (they still have to use their brain with the Warscore system)
-Random events that feel real and keep the player's attention
Con's
-Nonsensical solar system control limit
+Can only control 5 systems
+Must automize systems beyond that with ai controlled sectors
+Ai controlled races still control every system despite your own cap. (In big empires at war this is a huge handicap for the player, beyond a fair fight for them)
-Steep learning curve to capturing worlds (I'm peaceful till I get crowded)
-Research options change in between selections. Unclear how they are unlocked
+Almost feels like the lottery at some points
+This part is unexplained and leaves the player confused
-Unusual negotiations between races
Going back to my 8/10 rating. This game is spectacular, fun, and engaging, but has some issues that do ruin the experience at times. (to the point that I had to get mods to rectify the situation, like the system control cap and the research lottery)
Remember that this review was my own personal opinion, so some things that I like might make/break the game for others.

I've best read this game described as "stonepunk." The atmosphere is alieniating to an extreme and doesn't always make a lot of sense. It's a first-person brawler that may seem complicated at first, but is actually very simple in both intuitive and shallow ways. Some moves like the charged punch (Backward + RMB) don't feel like they really serve any purpose due to how much setup needs to go into making it land successfully, whereas just holding LMB to to a flurry of punches or two elbow charges (Sprint + LMB) to stun enemies will work just as good. If the game was any longer than it is (I took about 5-6 hours to beat the story) then its combat would be a much more glaring flaw. But it does the job well for entertaining you on the ride, alongside some firearm segments (gun models are stylish as all hell for the "stonepunk" vibe) and heavy-type enemies, strange beasts, and boss fights to help break up the pace.
You move through extremely linear levels very quickly -- maybe even too quickly -- from one brawl to the next between cutscenes while
is being shoved down your throat. It gave me the impression that the development team really wanted to show off an estranged and novel setting but didn't quite have the time or budget to make it shine as much as it could have.
If the weirdness of the trailer and screenshots have you fascinated, pick it up on a sale.

Now having finished both titles, I can strongly recommend them to anyone who likes an unusual visual experience. The world of Zeno Clash is so absurdly creative, it's a delight to travel through it and fight all the strange creature that inhabit Zenozoik.
The fighting system was unique and unusual enough to match the strangeness of the world, but if the game hadn't sucked me into its atmospheric world, I probably wouldn't have given the fight mechanics any second thought. I have to say though that the fighting system of Zeno Clash II has a very clever game mechnic that gives the brawling action another dimension in the second half of the game. Compared to that, Zeno Clash's fight system almost felt a bit too basic. But I can't really be mad at a game as mad as this, so I take it as it is, warts and all.
Highly recommended to anyone who is looking for a different experience and doesn't mind a few snags along the way.

Many times I found myself punching someone other than my intended target. The weapons were nice and few, forcing the player to rely upon their melee skills much of the time. I enjoyed the imagination which went into the rather well done characters (for the most part), though the number of character models seemed limited and I was either fighting the same characters most of the time or there were are number of twins and triplets. Sometimes the AI seemed confused and fought amongst itself or simply waited for the one in front of it to die before attacking. These are all rather small gripes in the grand scope of the game. My only real gripes were the short game play (3 hours) and the story was decently predictable and could have used some polishing. The voice acting felt a bit strange in the beginning but I warmed to it by the end. Not a bad game at $15 but I'd wait for it to go on sale to feel like you are getting your money's worth.
I had to buy it for my friends too, even though it's a single player game.  Phenominal game.

A great game? YES, definitely. The story is awesome, deep and make yourself a favor: don't spoil yourself. The game mechanics are very interesting. And it's also a mix between Metroidvania and linear action platformer. But... this game has a lot of small issues. A unique experience you shouldn't miss though.
In details:
It took me a lot of time to think deeply about how this game succeeds at so many levels and somehow managed to fail at so many little things. I'm still highly recommending this game to both: players looking for an action game and metroidvania players.
It's uniqueness is it somehow managed to mix two different play style: classic and survival.
The classic mode is more like a metroidvania, focused on exploration, some actions, some bosses, a lot of power ups and items to collect and it has also some RPG elements like a skill tree.
The survival mode on the other hand puts some rogue like elements: when you die, you lose all your items and most of your power ups, some power ups are permanent though and you never loose points in your skill tree. You will receive power ups a lot faster than the classic mode but you will die a lot more. Overall it's more challenging and intense.
The story line:
I usually prefer games with a very small story line but I have a few exceptions in my list like Metal Gear Solid (1st one on PS). To me Ghost 1.0 has a story line reaching that level. Just like MGS you're really going to watch a movie that will question you on your beliefs: what's life, how humans differs from machines, etc... This is exactly the right epoch to start questioning yourself on this with all the technological progress we are currently going through in the real life.
One of the greatest and unique feature of this game is that when you resume your game you will get a typical "Previously on Ghost 1.0" movie sequence that will remind you what happened in the story line the last time you played, just like a TV show.
Game play:
The whole adventure mode is pretty linear, you go from point A to B but you're allowed to take some variations on your way. I would compare it to Super Metroid where you can't do the objectives in a different order (I'm lying here, you can definitely do the objectives in a different order but it's really complicated). In Ghost 1.0 you need to do some objectives that can be done in a different order but will ultimately put you back on the main track.
The map is not randomly generated and the kind of enemies you will find at every room will stay the same. With experience, you can anticipate the alarms and the type of enemies you will get and be able to survive 20 alarms or more.
The "alarms" is also part of the unique aspects of this game: roughly 30% of the rooms have alarms you can or are forced to trigger. During the alarm, the door closes and a lot of enemies will spawn in the room and try to kill you. It's up to you to find the best strategy to survive with the equipment you have. The more alarms you trigger, the more difficult it becomes until you die. In survival dying will reset all the alarms of all the rooms and you can trigger whichever alarm in whatever order you want.
Graphics:
Beautiful in general. I reproach though the main character to be not more cooler. Her way of running is far from a secret agent style. Her face in the game lacks expressions. She looks much cooler on the title picture here.
The music:
They're not as awesome as in Super Metroid of Metroid: Zero Mission or special as in Hollow Knight. They're unique and suit the game perfectly. The music of the central area is stuck in my head which means I suppose this one in particular is awesome.
The humor:
This game is filled with geek humor and easter eggs. If you're a fan of sci fi movies and video games you will certainly love it. I don't have a particular example in mind except the easter egg with Metal Gear Solid where when you die you can hear one of your mates saying "Ghost, what happened? Ghost? Ghooooost!". Or the one with Terminator where when you teleport to another room the animation is replaced by the electric bubble and you see Ghost on her knees slowly rising up. This game is certainly a lot of fun to play.
Now the FLAWS. I'm sure that's the first thing some people want to know.
First of all and the biggest one in my opinion:
The controls:
The controls are tight, you don't feel that you die because you're character is not responding or something. That is not the problem with the controls. The problem is the logic. Seriously lacking of logic.
You evolve in a 2D environment similar to the Wonder Boy / Monster World serie. In Wonder Body, you enter or exit a door with Up or Down. In Ghost 1.0 they found cool to add an extra button almost exclusively used to enter doors and activate panels. Things that could have been done so naturally with the Up and Down keys. There is no point of having an extra button and if you plan to play with a game pad you're gonna need to assign a button dedicated to this "action button".
You can get out of you're mechanical body with a button (fine) but why on earth did the put a different button to get back to your mechanical body?? With a keyboard and mouse you press R to leave the body but you need to press right click to get back to it. Why not R? They use R instead to do an action: getting into a different mechanical body. Why not left click? Anyway, I just keep pressing the wrong button at the wrong time even after having played for 20 hours.
You want to play with a game pad? Forget it. I love gamepads too but the game mechanics doesn't really allow you to do so. You need a mouse to shoot in the right direction with the right angle and a keyboard to move the character. Some weapons don't even work at all with a joystick because they need you to click on the screen to get an area effect on this specific location. I recently saw there is some kind of cheat code to have automatic aiming. I believe this could solve part of the problem.
You character can run, shoot, crouch, make a fast roll on the ground to escape projectiles BUT you can't run, shoot and roll on the ground at the same time. So you can't enter a room while running, shooting at enemies and trying to avoid projectiles by rolling on the ground at the same time. But why? You may thing this is a maybe due to keyboard ghosting but the button for shooting is on the mouse so a different device and there is no problem to run and make a roll on the ground at the same time.
No "hold" button on the gamepad controls. If you really want to play with the game pad you have to realize that you're going to play like Contra to shoot in the diagonal directions: by jumping, then using the D-pad/analog stick, then firing. There is not button to tell the character to not move while you're shooting (like in Super Metroid, Zero Misson, Contra: Hard Corps, Super Cyborg, etc...).
You character doesn't hold on ropes automatically. Also the button to hold a rope is not E but Up for some reason. (Up is better in my opinion, E should not even exist.) Fortunately there are maybe 3-4 ropes in the entire adventure but when you try to do the rope mission you realize how much it's annoying to have to press Up all the time to grab a rope.
The puzzles:
If like me you don't like puzzle elements but love action, this kills the replayability of the game. After finishing the game once I wanted to play again in hard mode to get a few more achievements. When I reached the labs I just gave up: the lazer rooms are fine when you do it once the first time but going over it again was too painful. I wish the survival mode would have removed all the laser rooms because this requires a lot of patience and become easily frustrating.
The end of the adventure:
When you reach a certain point in the game most game will warn you that there is no way to come back. Ghost 1.0 unfortunately doesn't give you this warning. The gold card is basically the point of no return.

On the surface Ghost 1.0 appears to be a fairly standard sci-fi "metroidvania" game. However there us much more to it than that.
Owing in no small part to the excellent soundtrack, beautiful graphics, and solid gameplay; the game draws you in further with an interesting story, and ensnares you with replayability in its Survival mode and NewGame+.
In Survival mode the available weapons and upgrades in the shops are randomized, making each run- each death, a different challenge. In Classic mode, weapons and upgrades are limited and static, however the game still offers enough variety to give the player choice of preference.
There are also Challenge missions which both teach the player some new techniques, and force the player to come up with interesting solutions to different situations.
Ghost 1.0 is a bit of a hidden gem that I would recommend to anyone, but is still best enjoyed if the player already likes the "metroidvania" genre.

I bought Bigfoot after seeing a few videos on Youtube that appeared to show a solid game with interesting mechanics and a large world to explore in. After the first hour I played on my own however I found that without other players this game just does not deliver a fun experiance because of several reasons. The first issue I noted is that the day cycle is far too short for a single player to accomplish any exploring since most of your time has to be spent setting up traps and cameras which I felt took away one of this games strongest assets. Another issue that I found as a single player is that actually hunting bigfoot once you spot him is just plain annoying because his model isn't representitive of his range or hitbox and he can easily kill you in two hits. Other than this I noted that there was just a general lack of interesting events on my own and after finding extra guns, traps, and ammo scattered around the map I reached the conclusion that this game just is not designed for single player. I guess in a way this makes sense because if bigfoot was real and you were alone in the woods with him he would probably kick your a$$ and it wouldn't be very fun at all.
Fortunately I had some money to burn and I gifted a copy of this game to a friend, and once I had another player with me the experiance I had with this game vastly improved. This game was incredibly fun with a friend because exploration felt more possible, traps and cameras were less tedious, and bigfoot was no longer a death machine but he still felt powerful.  Multiplayer is definately what this game excels at but I am disappointed that it delivers a subpar single player experiance.

It took me a little while to warm up to Ghost 1.0, because the game dumps a ton of options on you. There are six ways to play the game because of the three difficulty settings and two fairly different modes to try. Eventually I found one that felt right and moved forward, but it took starting over a few times to get there. While this game is heavily advertised as a Metroidvania, it balks a lot of conventions and level design, proving that within the genre there are a myriad of experiences. If you're looking for something very similar to Metroid (or Castlevania) this might not be the best choice for you, but if you like the Metroidvania map and want something different, I can give this a recommendation as a solid title to try.
Ghost 1.0 takes place in the great space station "Nakamura" that serves as a computer server for Robot AI around the world. You play Ghost - a specialized infiltration agent - who inhabits robots including the main chassis you control throughout the game. As you work to uncover the secrets of the Nakamura AI, the game has a lot of variety, but there are two types of play that it emphasizes the most: Puzzles using the Robot Possession mechanic, and Wave-Based Enemy challenge rooms.
At any point in time you can leave your chassis and possess other intelligent robots, but your body is left vulnerable during this process - and if your body is destroyed you suffer the consequences of death. While you can use the possession mechanic offensively by sending your thralls to their doom as they do as much damage as possible, this is basically suicide in the game's challenge rooms. So its primary purpose is to solve puzzles, which generally consist of hitting switches that are out of your reach. As you progress these puzzles get complex enough to make this more than just a gimmick. It's a fun way to break up the gameplay - though because of the amount of time you spend in the challenge rooms I occasionally forgot about the ability entirely.
On the challenge rooms; as you wander around the space station you come across rooms with motion sensors that often cannot be avoided. Once the sensors are triggered, you're locked in that room until your client can hack the doors open again - which time varies based on how you've selected your skill points. During this time enemies spawn in waves and attempt to destroy your chassis. These rooms clearly pad the game, but it's in an enjoyable way. It's a little like random encounters in an RPG - they CAN be tedious, but as long as you have new things to try it remains mostly engaging. If you're playing on survival mode you're also always given a nice skinner box reward for doing them.
Because this game uses a Twin-Stick system with 360 degree aiming, Ghost moves a little sluggish, and the enemies are slow as well to compensate. You have a dodge roll, but by default it doesn't offer any defensive benefit other than very slight movement speed boost to get out of the way. It all controls very well, but as these challenge rooms get more chaotic your lack of movement options starts to become more frustrating as more enemies fill the screen. With the right weapons this is a non-issue, but this becomes a minor problem with survival mode since the weapons you receive are random.
The loot is the primary difference between Classic and Survival Mode. In both modes, you receive money that you can use to buy upgrades, but on Survival mode you get a random secondary weapon or power-up with each alarm. The alarm has a difficulty level that make all the enemies on Nakamura harder, and with Survival the alarm level goes up by one with each successful challenge complete. If you die, you lose all of your powerups and secondary weapons (except 3 random ones), but the alarm is set back to 1, so the difficulty scales back to match your lack of gear.
Classic lets you save your gear at the checkpoints, but if you die you still lose all your money, and because you rarely receive upgrades from alarm rooms money is the primary means of powering up. This means - as the Classic Mode description warns - to level up you need to farm money. While it might be fun to accumulate inseparable power throughout the game, I personally found this tedious. I'd be a little more forgiving of the system if in death you had the opportunity to retrieve your money, because as-is if you're saving up for an expensive upgrade death represents a very frustrating setback. Ideally I would have liked Classic Mode to have you find upgrades through exploration (Metroidvania Style), but I feel like the mode was an afterthought for players with a hording mentality. I personally liked Survival mode more, but I can understand the appeal of not needing to worry if your current build is suddenly going to be reset.
Overall I think the gameplay is "Good enough". Good enough that I was amused until the end, and good enough that I might come back to it again just to try and get to that level 20 Alarm on New Game + (And I might try Classic Mode on Hard at some point.) For the first play through though, I actually felt like the story was a great motivating factor. After I got past the initial cringe of the voicework, the characters really grew on me (I'm a big fan of Boogan.) They make a lot of references to other sci-fi fiction, but with the context of a couple of Geeks breaking into an expensive space station just to see what they can find, it actually made the characters seem more real to me. The Science Fiction aspect of the story is also well-constructed, and it creates a world I would be happy to see in a sequel.
So while I don't think Ghost 1.0 is a GREAT game, I definitely think it's worth checking out. I've tried to be as descriptive as possible in this review so you know what you're getting into, but if anything I've said appeals to you I encourage you to support these devs. There's a real passion in this work, and you can feel it when you play it.

Ahhh Viking, what a absolute chore you are to play.
Viking: Battle for Asgard (Midgard really) is CA's next installment of the Total Warrior - not to be confused with Total War - series and is a *spiritual* successor to Spartan: Total Warrior.
This is going to be a straightforward review where I will talk briefly about each factor of the game. Let's begin:
VISUALS:
This games visuals are not its selling point, nor its strong point. They are sharp enough to clearly outline and create a believable world, but the textures are extremely flat, and lack detail. Most character models are poor with only the main character looking capable of taking the podium. This is quite obvious when the dragons are revealed. This game, visually, feels akin to Fable II, yet somehow worse. Let's move on.
STORY:
This games story is honestly quite half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Basically Hel, Goddess of the Underworld has rebelled against Asgard and launched an assault on Midgard, after successfully taking most of Midgard, you lead the counter attack. The story takes place over 3 isles, with each consecutive isle being larger than the previous. Each isle has its own distinct feel but personally I felt the 2nd, Niflberg, to be the spotlight of the game. Don't expect anything too in depth here, as the game evidently doesn't entirely care to explain much of anything nor do a good job of it. The story can pretty much be summed up as you need to kill Hel's forces because she's evil, and that's literally what the game is all about. Voice acting is pretty bad to average at best, especially for the 2 main gods presented within the game, Hel and Freya. The game also sports and extremely underwhelming and unsatisfactory ending/boss fight which feels entirely rushed and poorly paced.
GAMEPLAY:
The most important aspect, of this game anyway. The gameplay is both the saving grace, and the silent killer of the game. It is absolutely riddled with poor design choices and hazardly implementations. Skarin moves painfully slow as he trudges around the isles at a breakneck speed, IF you consider jogging equivalent to lightspeed for a Viking warrior. Paired with map size, though the scope and scale of these isles is admirable, they are empty and devoid of life. The scenery is decent at best, and the lack of any observable wildlife only serves to emphasise the extremely shallow and overall lousy effort present in the game.
The single, most, frustrating aspect of this game comes in the form of quick time events, which quite literally plague the game. The amount of button mashing for the most mundane of tasks is nothing short of infuriating. Mash B to open the chest, mash B to teleport, mash B to unlock the door, mash X,Y, A to kill every boss in the whole game, Msh B to release Vikings. Rinse, repeat, the formula grows tired and old only minutes into the game, and when you become aware of just how many times you are required to perform these actions, you will come to begin pulverising and smashing your controller in a fit of rage. Rage worthy of the fabled Vikings mind you. The isles are littered with Waystones to allow 'quick travel', but again, the requirement to run hundreds if not thousands of meters just to travel from them, and to your point of interest is tedious. You will find yourself jumping off the nearest cliff simply to respawn at the main town.
The combat is by far the only redeemable factor in the whole game, but this is not saying much. Combat, whilst somewhat fluid in its hack and slash button mash fest, does become tiring and repetetive too. This only serves to fuel negativity regarding the game when you only have access to 4-5 'finisher' animations and bugger all diversity in the default attack animations. You unlock moves by going to an Arena and using your hard earned cash to purchase them. These are the most expensive thing in game and are only partially available as you unlock them by progressing to the new isles. Sneaking around lopping arms off of rogue Legion is all good and fine, but the combat really shines in the huge battles at key points in the game, mostly in taking towns, where hundreds of NPC's are engulfed in the turmoil that is battle, and these battles are genuinely entertaining, if not, again, simply a repeating formula. Actual axe hits and sword strokes are meaty, but only a few feel genuinely powerful. Compare the actual gameplay to the trailer released back in 2006-2007 (Yes, the original game for console released in 2008), and you will see more fluid and impactful animations that really convey the weight and power behind Skarin's heavy hits.
You earn currency for spending in stores through exploration of the isles, be careful however as there is a limit to how much you can find, I won't say spend it wisely, but I will say be conservative in item use, as costs do add up. You can unlock combat runes to upgrade your capabilities, I suggest only going for lightning or ice, as both of these will absolutely decimate any and all foes, a bit too easily if you ask me. Questing is tedious and enraging, as most of the quests are either fetch, or kill certain enemies. They hardly deviate and none of legitimately interesting in the slightest, you will complete these only because you are forced to.
SOUND AND TECHNOLOGY:
The game luckily is rife with plentiful sound, from birds whistling, wind howling, to zombie grunting and battlecries. Soft squelchy footfalls and solid stone cracking. The game isn't rich in this department by any means, but is satisfying enough. However, most sounds, particularly from dragons, sound quite compressed and muffled, a true shame as this really breaks the immersion and reminds you that you are playing such an average yet timid game. The music is a nice accompaniment, from soft ambience to powerful choirs, there's some nice pieces here, but the official soundtrack released differs somewhat from the actual music in game. The engine does its job well enough to provide a game to play, but frequent glitches to audio loss, clunky controls, locked fps of 30 (Unlocking this forces the game to speed up, 45 fps through a mod is the most desirable), really hammer the nail in the coffin for this one, even if the large scale battles are somewhat impressive for a 360/PS3 title.
OVERALL VERDICT:
I really cannot recommend this game. It is average at best, and after completing it 3-4 times (Xbox 360 counts too), I fully realise what an absolute chore it is to play and complete this game. If by any means you MUST play this, pick it up when it's drastically reduced. The gameplay is mediocre, the story abysmal, there's really no incentive to play this game, and I will gladly uninstall it, for the last time ever. This game literally underlines the definition of repetition. You have been warned, purchase at your own risk!

Cortex Command is a game I have been following for a long time. It has always been a fun toy to play around with but has gotten a lot better recently. Gameplay is fast paced, entertaining and often leads to hilarious moments such as shooting a dropship down only for its engine to shoot off across the map and brain one of your actors.
Now to be honest its a bit of tricky game to deal with sometimes. Controls are strange and not always very responsive. It can be very hard to get your actor to go exactly where you want to go. Shooting on the other hand feels good and has satisfying results.
The campaign is a bit of a mix bag. It is nice as a framework to play the individual matches but has some curious game design decisions. If a player doesn't get a base straight away they will usually get left behind permanently in the game. Building up the bases themselves can be tedious, impossible or completely hands off, depending. You can have the computer design the base for you at which point you will have to deal with a base layour you don't know. Or you can design the base yourself which can be fun the first few times but after the tenth base can get very tedious. And sometimes the last isn't possible because the fog of war wont have lifted on the map so you wouldn't be able to see where you are placing the base modules (Although this might have been fixed now).
One of the best things about this game though are the mods. This is a game that is very easy and fun to mod. It is quick and easy to come up with new guns and troops to make your own faction in the game. Not to mention the plathora of great factions and maps already out there.

Metal Gear Rising is a polarizing game among Metal Gear fans, and most noticeably so for one reason: the gameplay is entirely different from every other game in the series. But that’s the point. Even if it wasn’t a spin-off made by the hack-and-slash Gods over at Platinum Games it would never be a Solid game. It was always designed to be an action game, even when it was originally going to be directed by Kojima’s team. Gameplay demos and trailers of the game before being handed off to Platinum from development hell showed this, while it clearly looked less flashy and slower than the game we got, stealth wasn’t going to be the main focus. Hell, look at the scene where we first see Raiden be the cyborg ninja of MGS4 -- he’s jumping around killing Gekkos in one slice from his HF blade, an enemy which you had been running and stealthing from the entire game so far.
Another complaint, and this is one I share myself, is that Revengeance is a slap in the face to the series most tragic character since The Boss, from MGS2 Raiden being a medium for the player and a metaphor for the nature of sequels and thus subverting players expectations of said sequels by ripping Solid Snake from our hands and forcing us to play as a pathetic, baby faced soldier who will never live up to the legend we all saw in MGS1 -- all the way to MG4 where he is lied to by the person he loves and views himself as a failure, but is redeemed throughout the course of the game and given one of the best character arcs in the entire game, being my personal favorite and only surpassed by the Epilogue scene.
With Revengeance carrying on from what was a fantastic closure to one of the greatest gaming series of all time appears to be a far greater slap in the face to MGS fans than 5 was. But Platinum, with the help of a little codec retconning that every MGS fan is used to by now, miraculously makes a great game and story for Raiden, letting him be a complete and utter badass just like Snake.
I had fun all throughout the game, the gameplay is crisp and sweet in the manner everyone now expects from Platinum, with a nicely sized list of combos and a neat mechanic based around parrying, which if you are terrible at video games like me will be the most difficult yet rewarding thing in the entire game, instead of the dodging seen in Bayonetta. The story also follows many of the points we have all come to love about MGS. Everything from the spectacular political and social critiques, amazing boss battles, and even dealing with the same theme of MGS2, which in itself is a fantastic tribute to all of us who played and loved MGS2.
This game is now four years old and I’m a bit late to the party of reviewing it, but if you are for some reason still holding out on buying this game, a Metal Gear fan or not, you will love it. Trust me.
Metal Gear Rising is Solid/10

tl;dr I said the exact same thing a year ago and I (as many others) will say this: Wait until there's more, or it's on sale.
Stellaris launched bare bones and broken, it's been slowly improving over time with the typical and divisive Paradox approach of mixing improvements, and much-needed additions, in a mix of paid DLC and free updates. Utopia thus far has added the greatest amount of desirable new content, but the game is still shallow in all areas, and requires more to everything.
The ship and empire customization are the best aspects of the game. Few strategy games allow you to create and customize both the civilization you play as, but also feature a unit customization system. On the face of it, there is a good deal of diversity in playstyles granted to you by customizing your empire and by adopting different equipment types for your fleets. However, every empire, no matter it's type, will expand, fight, and manage in exactly the same manner. Empire customization is solely percentage changes and perhaps some aspects of gameplay (eg slavery) restricted.
Research is the worst feature of the game, there exists no tech tree or web of any sort, the game will randomly assign you tech to research in the 3 different categories with a slight bias based upon your previous research and current scientist type. You also need to get lucky enough to get the right type of scientist you need for tech you may desperately need. I've lost games because the tech I've been given is useless for the situation, not because of poor skill on my part.
Both space and ground combat are pitifully shallow. Space combat is like 2 individual units in a traditional RTS fighting each other until 1 dies, this is the level of depth we're talking about. You can barely control your fleets, eg you're unable to control which enemies your fleet fights. Battles boil down solely to whichever fleet is biggest, no tactics or strategy involved. Ground battles are exactly the same in principle, although you don't see them happen.
The economy is incredibly shallow, and boils down to two resources: energy credits and minerals. There is a single luxury resource but you need to research it, it's also rare, meaning it's almost never used in trade due to low quantities. There is no marketplace where you can buy/sell resources, heroes, or ships, like in say, Endless Space 2. Energy credits are used to maintain buildings and units, and minerals are used to build said buildings and units.
As you see from screenshots in game, the galaxy is huge. How do you micromanage all those planets? You don't, you instead turn over swathes of territory to a sector AI which will manage it for you. This feature is broken. It will terraform planets into the wrong type. It will put robots (which have a penalty when used in research labs) onto tiles with research labs. I know many players who have simply modded this feature out because it is broken. This is a bizarre game design flaw, the galaxy is so huge that the devs deem it impossible for players to manage, so rather than scaling the game down and making management easier (or simply possible in this case) they instead add AI to try and manage territory for you.
NPC empire AI is a cheating mess. After conquering some I have seen AI manage utter slums of empires and yet they are able to maintain a vast powerful fleet. They can also upgrade their ships to the newest designs in the field, when they should be only able to upgrade at space stations. You will see AI fleets invade your territory and gradually increase in power as they do so. I understand that it's difficult to make good AI, and making them cheat bypasses a lot of issues, but this is a joke.
I do enjoy playing this game with friends, much like in Civ and other strategy games I enjoy the politics and debates, the threats and arguments, it's only possible in a few genres of video games. However, this game is too shallow in all areas for me to recommend. I know the legion of Paradox fans will mass-downvote anything which speaks against their beloved devs and franchises, but Stellaris is just not a very good game.
The economy is shallow, diplomacy options are shallow, combat is shallow, empire management is shallow, the AI is broken, research RNG will sabotage your games, the mid game is boring and lacks content, the soundtrack is forgettable, and the graphics and audio are extremely dated.
4/10, wait until it's on sale or has more content.

The flying directions after a major hit need to be more predictable/deterministic; I never felt like I truly got a good grip on the mechanics because of its seemingly random nature. When a bunch of tougher enemies were on-screen and I had full meter, I just used it all up on the nearest enemy, insta-killed them, and then watched as my most recent victim's corpse bounced around and increased my body count by proxy.
That's another REALLY annoying thing: While the difficulty does increase over time, a good chunk of it is due to higher defense values amongst enemies. It seems like the devs couldn't find another way to raise the stakes than to make enemies eat more hits before being able to actually be stunned. This is especially a shame, because some of my favorite moments involved beating out opponent parries with my own, an event that could've manifested itself as its own boss.
Also, there REALLY needs to be SOME sort of progression/higher amount of content: All characters and levels are available from the word "Go", and you don't get any upgrades. This is pretty unfortunate, because the game could benefit from a larger player arsenal, which would allow for more combos and, in a few cases after a major reworking, better control of the enemies' flying directions (Particularly by way of having player upgrade attacks move the player in a certain direction, like an Akuma-esque dropkick, that also moves the enemy upon contact).
All in all, an ok game with pretty good challenge and a fair amount of skill involved, but to say it needs more work and more in general is an understatement.

FULL YET BRIEF REVIEW (PROS/CONS):
This is an open world survival horror game in which the player (alone or with friends) attempts to find and capture bigfoot. The feeling of roaming around an open world not know where he is and knowing that he can attack at any moment is horrifying yet thrilling for me. As a big fan of open world and survival horror games, this definitely is a must own.
PROS:
- Live CCTV camera monitoring
- Additional objectives (finding lost tourists)
- Surplus of equipment that's fun to use
- Advanced mechanics like covering traps in leaves to hide them
- Brilliant sounds
- Large map with several waypoints
- The game requires strategy as Bigfoot is a strong enemy
MAJOR CONS:
- No instructions (there are some tips hidden in the corner of the screen, but the controls are slightly confusing and hard to figure out initially.)
- Poor "Guide" (we are left with a two page guide explaing who Bigfoot is. The objective is simple but offers no insight onto how it might be achieved.)
- Night vision (it just sucks...it's harder to see with it than without it due to the saturated green color.)
- Bigfoot's reach (even if in the camper, he can attack you through walls...you're basically always at risk even in your supposedly "safe spot". It's frustrating if you die because you are attacked through a wall.)
MINOR NOTES DUE TO EARLY ACCESS RELEASE:
- Graphics issues (60FPS is doable if shadows are disabled; things need to be optimized.)
- Small Location Issues (the way some objects in the camper are set up makes it hard to look out windows optimally.)
- Batteries (plenty of them, but you can't carry them with you. The way batteries work seems inefficient.)
- Certain Supplies (Plenty of supplies we don't always need.)
- Language (the language in this book is mostly written in a slightly awkward broken English.)
-Bigfoot's neon green blood
Overall, this game kicks♥♥♥♥♥ It runs very vell for me and the gameplay is good. There are very few cons that are easily outweighed by the pros. Some of the smaller notes will be fixed with time due to the game currently being in early access. Once the game is figured out, it becomes a very fun yet difficult challenge that forces you to use your resources wisely and try to capture Bigfoot. If this sounds even remotely cool to anybody reading, then I think you will enjoy this game (especially if you like survival horror games). I think with the addition of new maps, fixed gameplay mechanics, and other new features and tweaks being added soon, this game will become very popular. I would recommend this game.

This game is incredibly fun with a cooperating team of players. Taking up roles, and working out strategies put a lot of emphasis on the tiniest detail such as who should stay and man the cameras, and which two should seek out the Squatch.
Survival: There is a finite amount of resources to distribute amongst your party. Between the hunters, you need to quickly establish who is preparing traps/cameras, looking for lost campers, and finding resources. There are plenty of flares, but ammo for your rifles can be quickly depleted. Unfortunately there is no looting, or trade aspect in the game. While in a way I like this for encouraging the team to work together, so everyone can defend themselves, on the other-hand it's easy for another player to horde all the ammo for themselves. Since there is no loot system, if that player dies, there is no way to retrieve anything off their corpse.
Horror: Bigfoot does provide for a good jump scare. There is no safe place, and if you think you can just lock the door and hide in the camper, think again. I find the green blood out of place, but it does help when trying to track him down at night. Lighting strikes are sudden and random, so headphone users be prepared.
Communication/multilayer: The fun factor is much greater amongst a group of friends than the single player can offer. The role playing, and teamwork add a real nice extra layer of depth. If you lack friends that play the game you're missing out on a good portion of the fun. Thankfully you can just set an obvious password for anyone can join your match, however this creates a whole new problem; no communication. There is no way to chat with your fellow hunters, and you're left to communicating with your tools like you're some sort of caveman. Trying to tell someone how to track the tagged Bigfoot, or help a new player find ammo is very frustrating that can be solved with a text chat system. Adding more public match support is essential for those who have trouble getting a group of friends together.
Bigfoot: Again, I'm not much of a fan of the green blood, but overall I was impressed with the creatures AI. Hearing his calling roar in the distance, for the first time got me quite nervous of what was awaiting me out in the woods. Possibly adding more distant grunts, or having the squatch maybe throw something at you can help increase the early game tension imo. From the impression I got though, I'm greatly looking forward to the expansion, and I hope the team is willing to explore other North American Cryptids!

I still remember when one of my old PC rigs really struggled to play this game.  When it was released, these graphics were very close to being state of the art, especially with the shadows and real time lighting.  Fast forward to today, and the graphics actually hold up fairly well, although the low resolution on the textures and awkward facial animations stand out a bit.
The AI, on the other hand, is still one of the best AI's in the business.  Its quick to react to what you're trying to do, and its pretty aggressive in trying to force you out into the open.  Don't be too surprised to find the AI maneuvering to outflank you, using cover fire to keep you hunkered down, and well placed grenades to flush you out.  A lot of modern games could really learn some lessons from this AI system.
Of course, the biggest draw to this game is the thrills and chills.  The horror elements aren't hurt too much by the graphics quality, and the game design goes a long way to amp up the forboding elements that make a great horror game.  Granted, the story is a bit difficult to follow, but it never lets off the gas, either.
At the end of the day, this is one of those gems thats a bit forgotten about.  Coming out in the same era as other heavy hitters like Half Life 2, DOOM 3, FarCry, and the original Call of Duty, this game is left out of the discussions of great FPS games far too often.  The muliplayer probably had something to do with that since it wasn't really all that memorable, but the single player portion was definitely a cut above.
Classic Score: 9/10
Modern Score: 7/10

Grabbed this since I was looking for something more casual. I wanted something I could easily put down and pick up. Well...i managed to clock in over 8 hours within a 24 hour span. This game is good! Every play through is different. And it's hard, like really really ball breaking hard.  I fought for about 6 hours to beat Easycore (50 levels or so).
Weapons - There are so many weapons it's hard to chose favorites. The weapon drop system is similar to Boarderlands in that its random and they scale with your level. You get explosives, miniguns, shotguns, rifles, pistols, plasma weapons and even thors hammer. Just remember to fix your weapons. 10/10
Graphics - I really like the lo fi look. It reminds me of the days of playing DOS games. The baddies look pretty cool even through they are cartoony. It runs well on my system. 8/10
Audio - This is where it gets a bit crappy (at least for me). The mixing on this is pretty bad. The game music seems to be super quiet (though it's really not that great.) You're better off muting the music and throwing on some Sonic Mayhem instead. Also the elvator sound between levels is so freakin loud and bassy. It's actually annoying. The gun sounds are alright and the bad guys sort of make sounds. Don't expect too much here. 5/10
Controls - Simple, very very simple. WASD, Space, Q, E, R, 1,2,3,. + mouse. That's it. It's has a bit of a learning curve with the mouse since you can't look up and down. Once you wrap your brain around that it's smooth sailing. 10/10
Overall - Get this if you want a time killer or a mindless killing game. The challenge will keep you busy for a while. It would be cool to see a co op mode in this at some point. Also turn your subwoofer down between levels.

Rating - 60/100
Recommendation - Play Legend of Grimrock instead
By all outwards appearances, this is a pretty decent game. However, it greatly annoys me for one big reason: It's a quintessential mobile game, in every way.
I have nothing against mobile games in general, but the entire mobile game market is FLOODED with carbon-copies and even copy-pasted games. Try to count all the match-3 Bejeweled clones in the App Store, and you will go insane. Try to find all the Flappy Bird clones in the Google Play Store, and your family/friends will have to stage an intervention.
This game is no exception. It is nothing but a slightly-dumbed-down mobile version of Legend of Grimrock, full-stop.
The graphics are good-looking (not within a stone's throw of LoG though), and the character art is pretty fantastic, but movement feels like LoG (albeit clunky and restrictive), secret buttons feel like LoG (with far less imagination), puzzles are similar to LoG (albeit not clever, and RIDICULOUSLY simple), and combat feels like LoG (albeit stripped to its most basic).
Now, to be fair, Legend of Grimrock was far from groundbreaking in the dungeon-crawling genre to begin with, but in a world where Legend of Grimrock exists (and has workshop support!), why would you play a game that is almost exactly the same (or worse) in every way?
Legend of Grimrock felt mysterious, and alive, and it had a distinctive dark and brooding atmosphere. The puzzles were incredibly clever, bordering on diabolical, and combat was tough but rewarding. This game, however, feels bright, friendly, and... I hate to say it... casual. Combat is slow and boring, puzzles are insultingly easy, and the whole thing feels like it's catering to 15 minute playsessions.
I've barely put any time into this one, and I can't see myself putting more in. With LoG, rather, I got in trouble for putting off work to play it.
If you ABSOLUTELY LOVED Grimrock, have played all the high-quality workshop content, and are utterly dying for more dungeon-crawling, it might be worth waiting for this to go on sale. Myself, however? I'm deleting it and moving on. There are far too many excellent games in my backlog for me to spend time replaying a detuned version of one I already beat.

Hospitalize is an interesting game. I will point out I have only played a small amount so far. It is a game I intend to come back to and invest more time in. I will admit I am a sucker for simulation and building games. You can see a first look video here of the game
On to the review
Hospitalize is a fun little game with some interesting elements and a few flaws that don’t impede it to much. Any memories of Theme Hospital are quickly removed as its set up as a “serious” building management Sim. The building element is simple and the icon to show where the user would stand to use equipment is something missing in a lot of other games in the genre. Hiring / firing staff is pretty much as expected as is managing the budget. Where Hospitalize is different is the mircomanagment you could diagnose a patient before your Dr if you feel like it. However you will need to expand the facilites available in the hospital to really get to the bottom of an illness. You do this buy unlocking levels and which each level new equipment.
I will say the UI can often make or break a game like this, however in this case it has its flaws, but its functional. It wasn’t so frustrating that I could not deal with it but it could do with some tweaking to make it a little more user friendly.
All in all I enjoyed my brief time with the game and I will re visit and replay soon.
