Aces Wild: Manic Brawling Action is a side scrolling beat em' up. This game focuses on maneuverability and the featured "Wild" meter. You will be battling your way through 8 levels of enemies, each stage different from the last. You can play through it with a friend, or go alone. The “Wild” Meter is a familiar Gimmick. It allows you to deal more damage based on how full it is, but you will also take more damage. While we’ve seen this used before in JRPGs and such, I’ve never seen it used in a beat em’ up.
Let’s start of on a bad note, the controls in this game aren’t so hot if you are using a keyboard. You will use wasd to move, and a few keys in the right to attack. Its meh, you lose a lot of mobility when you play this way, and it’s really not the best way to play. It’s even worse trying to play co-op on one keyboard. You and your partner will be crammed around one keyboard, with your hands mashing against theirs. Lucky, the game supports Xbox controllers and other gamepads. It even managed to pick up the NVidia shield controller fine, which was a nice surprise. An additional note, it allows one keyboard player, and one Controller player. If your just on a keyboard, you’re not going to have near as much fun as the controller alternative. I’m going to give this 2 scores, because it completely depends on what control scheme your using. 3/10 for keyboards, but 10/10 for most gamepads
The games sound track is pretty good. Perhaps a tad small of a selection, and it would be better if the music intensified with your "Wild" meter, but it does the job well. 8/10
The game takes a Saturday morning cartoon style.it looks great in most all resolutions, but the FOV could be a tad larger in my opinion. 9/10
This game has some difficulty issues. There were parts where I would fly through enemies, but then there are moments where the level design is made to hurt you, or a boss is overpowered. one of the toughest parts of my play through was when I died at a boss, and was unable to fill up my wild meter, because there were no minions to kill. I was unable to fill my "wild" meter, so I couldn’t dish any real damage to the boss. It just makes the game seem very unfair, if not hateful to the player. 5/10
The only story you’re going to get out of this game is the opening cut seen. Its real just an excuse to fight people, but it’s a decent enough plot. I feel that there is much room for improvement, as some of the boss designs are quite unique. I would have liked back story on each playable characters. At this point, it’s just lost potential. It passes, but it doesn’t come near to excelling. 6.5/10
While it is simply and optional added feature, it’s the way I enjoyed the game most. This is probably one of the best couch co-op games I’ve ever played. Its rather worthless on one keyboard, but if you have 2 input methods and a spare friend, this is the way to go. 10/10
Aces Wild is a very strange game, it’s one of the indie genre's organized messes of a game. The best part about this one, is that all it needed was a bit more polish and it would’ve been near perfect. Sadly, this is not the case, we simply have what we have, and what we have is something pretty damn fun if you have the correct setup. For $10 and a spare controller, you can’t go wrong with this one, but go in knowing that it has a few ups and downs, and is not the most polished or perfect game in the world.

Metal Gear Rising Revengeance is a fast paced hack and slash developed by Platinum Games, who are well known for their over the top and games with intricate battle systems such as Bayonetta, Vanquish and the recently released Nier:Automata.
The story follows the tradition of Platinum Games so don't expect any masterpiece, but the story is just good fun. Starting with Raiden
he then receives many cybernetiic enhancements turning him into a badass cyborg ninja. Equipped with his trusty HF blad he takes of in revengeance against the group who took his
eventually turning into a story about child brain harvesting and a metaphor for american evil.
Unlike the games mentioned above Metal Gear Rising: REVENGEANCE does not feature an intricate combo list so if you are looking for a fast paced hack and slash with a intricate and long combo list this game is not for you. But don't let that hinder your choice to buy it, the game completely makes up for it. The game has two basic attack functions a fast light attack and a slightly slower heavy attack. The game is fairly short totalling around 5-6 hours long giving you a boss around every hour or so, and enemy types are introduced fairly reguarly each having their own unique moves and attack patterns. On regular difficulties the game is a rather easy only posing a challenge to those not understanding the game, but at the higher difficulties the game can be rather difficult with a few bullets removing most of your health. Apart from the two attack buttons raiden can also "ninja run" in which raiden runs at supersonic speed and deflects bullets with his sword at the same time is quite spectacle. One of the problems most people have with the game is with the parry mechanic as it is not explained very well, in short if you move the left stick towards the enemy and press the light attack button before the enemy hit you will block it, do it when the attack is even closer and Raiden will unleash a very powerful counter attack which is almost neccesary to know at higher difficulties as the amount of damage depends on the difficulty. The main gimmic and feature of this game is "blade mode" Raiden slows down time to a crawl and you can carefully disect enemies positioning where to slice with you're blade. Every enemy has a spot containing a big blue energy cell which raiden rips out of his enemies and crushes them while shouting a cheesy one liner. After every boss raiden recieves their weapon which adds more variety to the combat. The weapons are all interesting and unique but using a weapon discards the heavy attack limiting you're combo's with the normal katana. The animations do not flow as smoothly between the sword and and the extra weapons which feels very clunky and odd.
The level design is unique each level has it's own feel and atmosphere. From a sewer level to climbing a giant skyscraper the game is not short on interesting ideas.
Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance is a flawed game, the combat is fairly simple, the story has plotholes unless you listen to hours of codec calls. But this is by no means a bad game. This game is so much fun and the things it does right. It does flawlessly. The story is hillarious, the combat feels good and is very fun. The action sequences within the game are amazing and physics defying. If you are looking for a fun game this is for you.

Zeno Clash is a weird game, everyone seem to agree with that. Most criticism this melee oriented FPS gets is how nonsensical the plot is. Well, there are indeed strange things in the story - the end especially - will probably leave you perplexed, but it is coherent and makes sense, more than Half-Life 2 for example (speaking of which, Zeno Clash uses the same Source engine). The game is unique in more than one way, mainly because of its style not just in apparence and gameplay, but also in storytelling.
The game takes place in the fictional world of Zenozoik and we play as Ghat, a brawler fleeing from his clan (simply referred to as 'family') for killing the chief, Father-Mother. The only person who sympathizes with him is Deadra, his soulmate/girlfriend, who also accompanies him on the perilous journey. As they flee and travel (the sceney gets darker along with the story), reaching the end of the world eventually and meeting a powerful being, they realize they can't run away from their home and must face their pursuers and fate.
The storytelling is similar to a Tarantino movie: the segments are mixed up, but if we pay attention we can easily put them into chronological order. Therefore we get to play through the events of the past as well: when Ghat lived amongst the Corwids (insane woodland people) or when he attacked Father-Mother. These flashbacks are inserted inbetween present actions and unfold as stories told to Deadra (for whom all of these count as new, just like as they do for us).
It's not the narrative however that makes the game strange primarily, but the graphic design: surreal or outright bizarre are mild terms to describe the game. It looks like the work of the famous Dutch painter Hieronymus Bosch infused with some weird asian elements: the architecture (and the landscapes altogether) seem crudely natural yet otherworldly and most of the characters show birdlike features. The corwids are straight-out disturbing looking, but even friendly beings, such as Golem can look menacing. If this wasn't enough there's a blind (!) assassin who tries to kill us by throwing and shooting squirrels with exploding barrels tied onto their backs... It might be surprising but even our protagonist doesn't look completely normal (I mean he likes hanging around creepy lunatics who tend to eat each other from time to time), Deadra is the only sane person in the entire universe of Zeno Clash.
So I can safely say without exaggeration that this is the craziest looking game I've ever played.
The gameplay consists of first-person hand-to-hand combat, altough we can use weapons from time to time. Our fist are going to be our primary weapons with some combinations we can perform with them. The most important one is the haymaker for which we have to press back and hold (then release) the right mouse button. With this alone we can successfully finish off even the strongest opponents (the aforementioned assassin). We can also kick combatants lying on the ground or when they are stunned, but these are basically automatic moves. There's an option to dodge attacks, but it's just easier to strafe and block (not to mention we can counterattack after successfully deflecting a strike). All in all the combos aren't too complicated nor are there too many of them and most of the time it's just about running around and attacking at the right moment, so we can end up smashing buttons with little tactics whatsoever.
There are various large, armored enemies against whom our fists do next to no damage. For these situations there are melee weapons around which are slower, but they can be swinged from a distance and deal serious damage. Unfortunately they break after a few hits, so make sure to use them against bosses only. In some segments we can also use ranged weapons and while they are quite powerful as well, it takes a long time to reload them during which our enemies will probably catch up to us and beat the weapon out of our hand, pick it up  and use it against us (yes it is possible, but we can and should do the same against armed opponents). Needless to say these weapons are also not ordinary looking, just like everything else in the game.
The level design is simple, basically there are peaceful areas (in which dialogues occur) and arenas where we have to beat a fair number of opponens in order to progress (in these segments a splash screen is shown where our enemies are listed). These enemies usually come in waves and in groups. The first problem comes here: we have to lock onto our opponent we want to focus on. While this is a relatively fast process, it is bothersome and it occassionly makes us turning our back to another enemy who can (and will) hit us from behind. If we don't use the select button, the game will do it automatically for us, resulting in some undeserved hits, we could have easily avoided had it been not for this weird feature. The solution is to try and avoid contact with the enemies until they split up and there's a fair distance between them.
Another strange thing is: we fight the same enemies over and over again, so apparently we never kill any of them, just knock them out (they all have names too). In the case of the assassin and our clan bratohers/sisters it may be understandable, but with the corwids or the street scum who attack us it isn't and it just seems like a cheap way to use the same models over and over again.
Besides the 'story mode' there's also an arena mode (called Tower Challenge), it's still single player though, where we have to fight the same well-known creatures. It does require more skills to prevail, but otherwise it's forgettable.
The music is something I liked and while there aren't many, I found almost all of them great and fitting that exact scene, representing the current mood of our heroes. The voices were outstanding, altough some of the monstrosities sounded awful (but that was the point I guess).
Despite its shortcomings Zeno Clash is not a bad game at all and nearly not as incomprehensible as it may seem at first. The ending is somewhat predictable (foreshadowing a
), but the story is told in a rather enjoyable way that will probably make the player finish this 3-4 hour long adventure in one sitting, with some symbolism and sagacity along the way (some are obvious, some are subtle). Give this game a chance as it is certainly a unique (in a good way) one and is worth a playthrough for the overall atmosphere and storytelling alone.

This is a twitch-action combat puzzle game akin to Bangai-O. The focus is on watching enemy AI and trying to figure out the best way to take them down. Combat is fast and feels great - which is good, because that's the basis for the entire game. The game revolves around its Wild meter - you build it with weak attacks and use it to do a heavy one, heal, or fly.
Herein lies Aces Wild's biggest problem - the fly mechanic, which is used to chase enemies and generally travel around every stage, drains your Wild. It drains the longer you hold it, which is an issue because -
A) bosses LOVE to run away and (with the exception of the Guile-type enemy) have ranged attacks that can combo, doing tons of damage -
and B) the latter 2/3rds of the game feature instant death pits. You can air jump infinitely, or tap fly so it uses barely any  meter, but that's a timing window so it's inadvisable - you'll lose focus on enemies and they'll just push you into the pit anyway. I played through this without using the fly mechanic, once I lost to a boss because I drained my meter trying to avoid her floor filling attack that stays until the battle is over. Let me tell you, it was much easier since I wasn't wasting it on foolish endeavors like avoiding damage. It actually becomes unuseable on boss fights like VS Gene.
There's no interim save either, so if you're trying to get a high score run, well, better put some time aside for it. For the rest of us who just want to see the game, you can stage skip, which is nice.
However, the game runs out of unique enemies pretty fast. This wouldn't be an issue if all the screens had interesting or unique solutions, but unfortunately many of them are just "here's a million dudes, don't die." Don't get me wrong, some battles are fantastic BECAUSE they have tons of enemies in it - but there's just too much sameness everywhere that you start going through the motions.
The boss rush section near the end is completely unsatisfying - there's no power growth so they're just nerfed versions of ealier bosses. More fodder to extend playtime. The final boss has somewhere around 4 health bars,
Ultimately, the game is challenging and feels good, but the flying mechanic is a wasted opportunity. The saving grace is the utility of dodging, but even then the game just feels too long - mostly due to lack of enemy variation.

This game is so frustrating. The thing I didn't understand when writing my first review (see at the end of this review) was that you cannot go full melee unless you're a really, really good player (and I'm not). Having understood that, I was able to go a bit further in the game by playing more cautiously.
But it's frustrating to play cautiously. You have all those melee weapons but you can't use them on most enemies because you'll get killed. So instead you immobilize them with a bear trap and shoot them from distance, and if somehow they teleport near you you hit them once with your melee weapon and run until your beartrap cooldown resets and you can immobilize them again.
So yeah, you have more chance of surviving this way.
But where is the fun?
I've just been killed by an Elite in the Ossuary level. I had a good gear, a bear trap, a melee weapon and a ranged weapon. I was running waiting for my beartrap cooldown. He teleported on me, hit me 3 times in one second (stunning me each time) and killed me. I was full life. Game over.
So right now I'm wondering why I keep playing. This is not "fun". This is not rewarding. When I end a session of gameplay, I don't feel better, I just feel frustrated. I don't know what mental mecanism is at play here but it's like a hard drug that got you hooked, you can't stop taking it and it's slowly destroying you.
This is why I don't recommend this game.

Plot/Overview:  Breaking Fast is a fast-paced side-scrolling racing game about breakfast foods.  There are power ups and attacks to help you win the mad dash to the finish line.  The game is super easy to pick up and play, supports 4 player local multiplayer as well as 8 player online.  There are 16 total breakfast foods for you to play as, all with different strengths/weaknesses and are unlocked as you earn expierence playing the game.
Music/Sound:  The music and sound effects are very playful and simple.  The songs fit the levels and the only thing I found wrong was the warning noise for an incoming special attack, it tends to drown out all the other sounds, and gets chaotic when playing with 7 other people.
Gameplay:  The game play is stupid simple, run, jump, roll and attack your way through the level, avoiding obstalces such as spoons, mixers, picnic baskets, toasters, and various other level specific food items.  There are power-ups such as confusion, freezing, and power attack.  Race over time or to the finish, depending on well you do, you earn experience which will unlock more breakfast foods to play as well as more levels.
Controls:  The controls are serviceable.  When playing with an X-Box One controller, there was a lack of responsiveness and at the beginning of levels, if you move the thumbstick for movement, you won't move until you return it to neutral.  The controls are rebindable for both keyboard and controller.  There isn't any mouse support.

+Quirky concept.
+Simple Gameplay loop.

Cons:
-Controls aren't responsive enough.
-Unlocking characters and levels is a grind.
-No AI difficulty settings.
-Difficulty finding multiplayer games.

A great action-platformer experience within the "metroidvania" family, Ghost 1.0 is a solid delivery on what makes the genre great, while also introducing several innovative features I haven't seen in others like it.
The features I've loved (so far!) include:
+ There is an in-narrative reason for virtually every game mechanic that exists. While this is never a requirement, it always helps to know "the devs thought of everything", and it helps with immersion and suspension of disbelief.
+ A "Previously on..." feature, akin to the best recaps done in your favorite TV shows, has been used here to great effect. Start up the game at any time, choose "Continue" and you'll get a quick update on what was happening and what main objectives you were trying to accomplish when last you played. This is a fantastic approach, and a HUGE positive contribution to a genre where any time away from the game can make it difficult to jump back in. This game solves that problem with elegance and genius.
+ The map includes indicators for players on what obstacle blocks progress along any path, as well as extended information on hover for any area such as shops, which will tell you what they still have available for purchase. A common frustration with "metroidvania" lies in the memory game aspects of having to remember a lot of information, and to backtrack too much to determine whether that latest unlock might be helpful throughout the extensive map you've explored. The developers must have understood this, because they took steps to eradicate that annoyance and make exploring and item unlocking painless and all the more fun!
+ A robust level-up system offered by virtue of spending discovered ability points to unlock new benefits/abilities, combined very well with...
+ Finding new abilities/items through exploring.
+ Forethought in laying out the map to make traversal always fun without the repetitiveness of excessive backtracking, unlocking new shortcuts and interesting quick-travel points.
+ Fully customizable controls. This seems like a given, but too often it's not.
+ Full controller and Steam Link support! Again this should be a given for a lot of similar games, especially of the genre, but it's not.
These features are FANTASTIC, and other developers would do well to learn from what @unepic_fran has done here, and not just for games of the same genre.
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED, both for the experience and seeing what CAN be done to improve games in general!

An extremely fun shooting game!
Positives:
- Enemies are split into squads instead of coming at you in waves. This is more fun in my opinion because each encounter can become unique instead of just sitting at one spot while each brain dead enemy appears.
- Slow motion is really fun, especially with how the physics engine shows every detail of your destruction. You can see a grenade distort the surroundings before exploding. You can see the enemies fly back after blasting them. Particle effects everywhere while you kick an enemy's face in mid air.
- Each gun feels great to use, especially the shotgun!
- Enemies are actually pretty smart and react accordingly to what you're doing.
- The game's spooky feeling is so much better than being barraged with jumpscares,
- The dark and gritty atmosphere crawls into your skin.
Negatives:
- Too short in my opinion.
- The environments can get repetitive.
- You can't aim down sight. Minor thing,
- If you have Logitech, you have to disable a few things in your devices for it to run at a proper frame rate. Don't know why this happens.
Overall definitely worth checking out, although the other games in the series aren't that great,,,

Ghost 1.0 is a metroidvania 2D platform shooter with a very interesting science fiction story, lot's of action and great humour.
You are Ghost, and you are literally a ghost, well sort of. It's unclear exactly what you are at first and it's part of the game to unveil Ghosts story. As a ghost you have the ability to take control of androids. Switching between different androids is part of the game and makes up for some very nice puzzles.
Of course, the emphasis of the game is action and fighting. But the story also plays a huge part which is quite unusual for a 2D platformer.
Pros:
- simple but nice graphics
- very good story
- great voice acting
- often very funny
- addictive
- different weapons
- lots of upgrades
- collectables
- very good puzzles
- good sound effects
- different environments
- a long game, took me about 25 hours to finish it in classic mode. I started survival mode after finishing the game and it seemed much easier and therefore probably shorter.
- different game modes (survival, classic)
- extra missions (that are extremely challenging)
- option to replay the game while keeping all your upgrades
- several save slots
Cons:
- annoying music (I turned it off)
- many extremely difficult achievements
- tearing (no v-sync)
- no option to activate v-sync (I activated v-sync via the graphics driver, overriding the game settings, which worked)
- in order to use ladders and air lifts you need to place Ghost exactly at the right position. In the heat of the action where you quickly need to escape this often is a huge problem.
- alarm level is reduced if you die
- alarm levels have a temporary cool-down phase
- the difficulty of the extra missions is insane
- at least one broken achievement

This game was interesting. Did I get scared? Not at all really, a few jumps, that's it. So, not nescessarily a horror game even though there are horror elements incorporated into the game, it's more of an fps in a way. The level design first of all was very linear, not much exploration at all, apart from a few rooms with supplies here and there, and maybe 2 routes if you need to go around an obsticle of some sort, but for the most part pretty linear. I did see some cool A.I behaviour, not 100% sure if scripted or not, but at one point, an enemy NPC knocked over a fridge for cover, but this only happened once, that was pretty cool. The A.I can be silly at times, for example if a sall portion of their body is not covered by a wall, they'll just stand there and take shots from me, not even moving. And also, it would be nice if they investigated sounds more, if they come across dead comrades, they will scout out the area, and if there's another route to your position, they attempt to flank you, which is great. The enemy ai work together allot, constantly calling out commands to each other and doing different tactics depending on the situation. So the ai, really impressive for an old game. There was quite a few weapons in the game as well, not that much, but you encounter the big guns later on in the game. The gunplay works great, I enjoyed the experience however, hoenstly I never used the reflex ability as well as melee oftn because I didn't really get situations to use them in, of course mostly because I was playing on the default difficulty, and I died quite allot, so the game is still challenging on the preset, which is nice. There were honestly no real memerable characters in the game, maybe apart from the commander on the radio, and the stupid individual you come across, can't even remember their names honestly, not much interaction between the characters, and you're just really a generic soldier for the most part. The story is certainly interesting however, as you get to find you mor about Project Origin and Alma by getting intel from laptops which you encounter throughout the game and learn how sick the people behind it were. The voicemails were a nice touch, but nothing of real interest, just the callers talking to people in the office, so I didn't really pay much attention as it wasn't really interesting. I enjoyed my experience with the game but honestly, it isn't my cup of tea, wheather you will like it or not, is for you to decide. unfortunatly, no real replay value (anymore) as they multiplier is discontinued due to Gamespy servers shutting down and the linear level design and no choices to make. Not the greatest game out there, but it was something. Oh and as for bugs, I got a bug whihc happened twice in a row after my first encounter with Alma, and once the cutscene played, it didn't end and my character was locked in position, worked after 2 reloads though. Also got stuck inside doors a few times, only once where I had to reload though. That was about it.
DLC Thoughts
The DLC's also offer something new, new enemies, new weapons, new situations, new horror scenes etc etc. And I really can't say anything more about them other than the main points in the review.

The biggest argument against this game that I see the most is that it is not a true Rogue-like. To those of you who think that, let me add one thing. To most avid gamers, the only true Rogue-like... is the original Rogue. Gamers will never be satisfied by a game that dissapoints them by not living up to its expectations (which few games are able to do). We need to accept that in games and recognize them for their true positive qualities and mechanics. In the case of this game, a game marketed as "Rogue-like" will never be a true FPS, and a game marketed as "FPS" will never be a true Rogue-like. However, this game accomplishes both Rogue-like and FPS qualities and mechanics. This game is able to beautifully combine a "Doom"-esque FPS and a slightly humorous and enjoyably difficult Rogue-like. I would recomend this game to anyone willing to try something different, and I ensure you, you will be amazed.

Yes, I was hoping for a more modernised 90s Theme Hospital type game, and was excited that this game seemed to offer a more realistic (no bloaty head syndrome - actual routine and critical conditions that you get to aid in the diagnostic process!) take on that old classic. Regrettably, I can't see it developing into something remotely as entertaining as that any time soon. Given that it's almost a year since release, I would have expected to see a more established game with far fewer negatives.
My primary initial thoughts on this game were:
- Very basic interface in some ways, then other text-rich features that make jumping into the game quite complex/more so than it needs to be. WAY too easy to quit out of the game accidentally when you're just starting and cant navigate the controls/buttons.
- Frustrating user controls, edge scrolling/zoom features unsophisticated and laggy.
- For me, the graphics are just a little bit too unrefined. Not entirely down to the devs, obviously I had screenshots/previews prior to purchasing so I was aware of the style but in action it just lacked... the charm of traditional modern era pixel type games. A bit 'bleh' in terms of graphics quality and appeal as it's neither old-school cheery little pixel people, or edgy stylish characters. Additionaly the building process, staff actions and overall feel to the game is just rather slapdash. I dislike the building structure, the walls are hugely thick, obscure a lot of the visibility and don't make me feel like I'm building a hospital but a blocky square featuring a few bits of crammed furniture.
- DELETING things! Confusing, long and drawn out, menus all over the place clogging up my screen and my mind with their unwanted presence. Too much clicking...
- Sandbox?? I belived this was a sandbox game but either thats not an established feature or its way too hard to find. Either way, as soon as something requires me to follow (somewhat glitchy) tutorials, be reliant on before I've even started money, and unable to create as my heart desires, points are immediately deducted. As a lover of Theme Hospital, or virtually every tycoon game, a sandbox mode or money cheat is a vital part of my gameplaying experience. Without it, exploring is too much of a chore until I am ready to go campaign mode.
- £11.99 was not really worth my expense for what hasn't turned out to be endless hours of fun as I had hoped.
Don't mistake my criticism for idle dismissal of what is clearly a promising WIP from the developers and it is clearly satisfactory to some, or those who are willing to hang around for the gradual improvement, however I shall not be returning to playing this game for some time/if at all. Knowing that my review has been largely critical I do want to commend the following feature:
- YAY for some realistic medical things! Proper conditions, symptoms, diagnoses and diagnostic protocols. Having some realism should make for interesting gameplay for those who arent bothered by my other concerns or who can overlook them. I especially love the features such as an emergency room, a vital feature of a hospital that distinguishes it from what otherwise might be a glorified doctors surgery. Its great to see games acknowledge the tiers of medicine can range from routine to life-threatening and offer facilities to accomodate those needs. It shows real depth of thought into the challenges associated with healthcare and I hope the Devs continue to expand on the ERs role and use within the game.
- There are other features that ought to be credited given that this isnt exactly a huge developer franchise that we expect a loooot from, they've done a good job with many aspects, unfortunately its just not for me. Which is fine.
I hope for those who continue to play, the updates continue to be consistent and beneficial, and that the improvement results in a successful and well-rounded game. My final statement on it will just be that if you've got high expectations, expect the diversity and freedom of something like Theme hospital, want to go big or go home, maybe this isnt for you.

tl;dr I said the exact same thing a year ago and I (as many others) will say this: Wait until there's more, or it's on sale.
Stellaris launched bare bones and broken, it's been slowly improving over time with the typical and divisive Paradox approach of mixing improvements, and much-needed additions, in a mix of paid DLC and free updates. Utopia thus far has added the greatest amount of desirable new content, but the game is still shallow in all areas, and requires more to everything.
The ship and empire customization are the best aspects of the game. Few strategy games allow you to create and customize both the civilization you play as, but also feature a unit customization system. On the face of it, there is a good deal of diversity in playstyles granted to you by customizing your empire and by adopting different equipment types for your fleets. However, every empire, no matter it's type, will expand, fight, and manage in exactly the same manner. Empire customization is solely percentage changes and perhaps some aspects of gameplay (eg slavery) restricted.
Research is the worst feature of the game, there exists no tech tree or web of any sort, the game will randomly assign you tech to research in the 3 different categories with a slight bias based upon your previous research and current scientist type. You also need to get lucky enough to get the right type of scientist you need for tech you may desperately need. I've lost games because the tech I've been given is useless for the situation, not because of poor skill on my part.
Both space and ground combat are pitifully shallow. Space combat is like 2 individual units in a traditional RTS fighting each other until 1 dies, this is the level of depth we're talking about. You can barely control your fleets, eg you're unable to control which enemies your fleet fights. Battles boil down solely to whichever fleet is biggest, no tactics or strategy involved. Ground battles are exactly the same in principle, although you don't see them happen.
The economy is incredibly shallow, and boils down to two resources: energy credits and minerals. There is a single luxury resource but you need to research it, it's also rare, meaning it's almost never used in trade due to low quantities. There is no marketplace where you can buy/sell resources, heroes, or ships, like in say, Endless Space 2. Energy credits are used to maintain buildings and units, and minerals are used to build said buildings and units.
As you see from screenshots in game, the galaxy is huge. How do you micromanage all those planets? You don't, you instead turn over swathes of territory to a sector AI which will manage it for you. This feature is broken. It will terraform planets into the wrong type. It will put robots (which have a penalty when used in research labs) onto tiles with research labs. I know many players who have simply modded this feature out because it is broken. This is a bizarre game design flaw, the galaxy is so huge that the devs deem it impossible for players to manage, so rather than scaling the game down and making management easier (or simply possible in this case) they instead add AI to try and manage territory for you.
NPC empire AI is a cheating mess. After conquering some I have seen AI manage utter slums of empires and yet they are able to maintain a vast powerful fleet. They can also upgrade their ships to the newest designs in the field, when they should be only able to upgrade at space stations. You will see AI fleets invade your territory and gradually increase in power as they do so. I understand that it's difficult to make good AI, and making them cheat bypasses a lot of issues, but this is a joke.
I do enjoy playing this game with friends, much like in Civ and other strategy games I enjoy the politics and debates, the threats and arguments, it's only possible in a few genres of video games. However, this game is too shallow in all areas for me to recommend. I know the legion of Paradox fans will mass-downvote anything which speaks against their beloved devs and franchises, but Stellaris is just not a very good game.
The economy is shallow, diplomacy options are shallow, combat is shallow, empire management is shallow, the AI is broken, research RNG will sabotage your games, the mid game is boring and lacks content, the soundtrack is forgettable, and the graphics and audio are extremely dated.
4/10, wait until it's on sale or has more content.

Ok, after playing for a bit. My impression is this is a "dungeon crawl (beyond incredibly) lite" for mobile.
It is not for a hardcore RPGer. It is definitely not for a PC gamer who is expecting the depth (whether story or mechanics) that comes from real PC RPGs.
IF I played games on my phone (and I dont- I'm VERY anti mobile game, esp those ported to PC - See thread "i hope this is as good as it sounds" for why), and IF I was looking for an RPG to while away some time on the train or whatever, It'd be ok for that.
Definitely not a "suck away an entire weekend in dungeon crawling bliss" game though.
Ok for starters, yeah. The textures are really uninspired basic texture packs as Gwion noticed and Angelo pointed out. You could probably find the exact same pack on the web for purchase with a few words on google.
The story is...Meh. Thats not really surprising. The dungeon crawl genre isnt known for its stories, but for its intricate dungeons full of monsters and traps.
Yes theres 2 NPCS Ive met so far, an "innkeeper and a "shop". The story of why theyre there is beyond weak. And as far as I can tell, you cant buy or sell anything but arrows, rations, and fishing gear at the shop. Why even have a shop? Why not an arrow and rations vending machine?
It would have been served better to just have very little story, as Dungeon Master and LoG did. Just a "a big evil dungeon and you have to defeat the big evil at the end of it". That worked for the old games.
But in this one, your characters actually talk to each other sometimes. And the writing is bland and not really worth being there. The screenshots are misleading, as they show the charcaters talking to an NPC and each other.
The NPCs are dispensers, the writing of the charcater's speech sounds like it was written by a junior high schooler. NOT needed.
The thing that gets me more than anything is beyond a few screens of basic instruction (that any RPGer pretty much knows automatically) there is NO ingame helpfiles. NO tutorial, no nothing. And the ones you do get are impossible to look at once they're gone.
So you get basic self explanatory introduction (Minus what the "gestures" are - I still cant figure out how to strafe and it was only through experimentation that I figured out how to work them at all), and NOTHING about unique aspects of the game that you need to know.
Like for instance in the character screen there is a yellow bar next to my health. Whats that? Experience? Fatigue? Food? No idea. Suppose Ive got to fiddle around with it till I figure it out.
I'm all for not hand holding, but this game doesnt even tell you basic stuff you need to know.
That and theres no options screen. So I hope the resolution, graphics, keymap and sounds are to your liking. Cuz you CANT CHANGE THEM.
That might be OK for mobile, but on a PC it is an absolute necessity. Not everyone has the same configuration. Not everyone has hands that can use a keyboard to steer. (I have partial paralysis.)
The "gestures" are a good thing. I really like that as an alternate movement. But theres no tutorial of what to do to work them! It took an "aha" moment and 10 minutes of experimentation to figure out why my mouseclicks were spinning the PCs around.
So, in summary. This is a PC port of a mobile dungeon crawler. For mobile games that Ive seem, its pretty good. By the standards of the PC, no.
Go play Legend of Grimrock or even the old Dungeon Master. If you like dungeon crawls and have an iWhatever, get this game on there. Then you can while away time in the waiting room or on the bus.
But I'd recommend actually playing real dungeon crawlers on the PC.
FINAL VERDICT:
Uninspired, run of the mill mobile dungeon crawler with non unique textures. Will not in any way shape or form impress a PC RPGer, but its worth poking at a bit if its on sale for $2 and youre really really hard up for a dungeon crawler. Way overpriced here though.
The lack of any sort of re-readable helpfiles, and not giving basic information about the game's mechanics really sucks. That and THERE IS NO OPTION MENU. That might fly on mobile. Not here.
If you have an iThing and want a dungeon crawl to waste time while waiting for the bus or whatever, get it on there. Its ok by the standards of mobile. Not by the standards of the PC.

A heartfelt retro-arcade recommendation!
Mutants and aliens are rampaging a space station. You're the one-man-army to kill them all. Each game of Rogue Shooter is a 100-level tour-de-force tasking you to clean at least 50% of a floor's enemies, and not get killed by them. As is custom for any game with "roguel" in the title the levels are randomly generated, and there are some light RPG mechanics in place. Your base equipment is determined by your "background training" (soldier, scientist... ninja, MUSICIAN), and as you gain experience you are able to get "perks"- small useful skills. All of this is useful because at the core there's really just a lot of speedy gunfighting against increasingly powerful and tough enemies.
For Rogue Shooter this all works really well. The levels are small enough to be cleared within a few minutes; the absolutely random grid layout quickly gets old but then again, you're not here to enjoy the scenery. While there aren't really that many different enemy types each has at least something that makes them unique. Some grab onto you, slowing you down, some throw flash grenades, some explode after death, you get the idea. The classes are a nice touch; even nicer are the perk that really allow you to buff strengths or cover weaknesses: Often out of ammo? Get a perk that makes you find more. Good at shooting already? Pick a perk to add critical hits to the mix.
As you kill enemies you also gain "intel", an odd in-game currency that unlocks more perks, backgrounds, enemy infos and crafting recipes. Clearly designed to give the player some extra incentive to play, it's also used to buy permanent upgrades- similar to Borderlands 2 you can opt to spend intel on bonus health et al that affects all future characters. It's a nice gimmick.
Now, two things must be mentioned: This game is a love-letter to old shooters. As in, really old shooters. If you remember games like Wolfenstein 3D, Blake Stone and probably the first Doom, you know what I am talking about: This game is so intentially ugly that it's approaching "nice looks" from the other side. Add to that some oddly catchy 80s game tunes and you're almost there.
Also your tutor is, for some reason, a mime lady. Best not to ask.
If you like to just shoot at stuff a bit- with often very outlandish weapons (Puppy Launcher... it launches puppies!) - and don't mind the cheerful goofy looks this may very well be a great addition to your library. I mean that: It's charming, it's fast, it's intentionally silly and that's really a major source of it's charme. But it's also a downright decent arcade shooter.
The latest update removed my only complaint- initially there was no way to ever safe your game, so a full playthrough would have to be made in one session (100 levels, remember!). Now you can at any time "save and exit"; this keeps the risk of permadeath but allows you to take a break.
Alsol, there's a good DEMO that allows you to play the tutorial and a few levels on the easiest difficulty. Due to the fully random nature of the game you'll see a lot in that demo and seriously, you need to see this in action.

The Witcher 2 continues Geralt's quest of recovering his memory and unlike the first game, it dives right in to reveal his lost memories. Already this is a huge jumpstart on what I had thought about the original which left Geralt's history a mystery and suddenly ending which gave an unsatisfying conclusion. Whether CDPR also thought the same is up to anyones' opinion, but I think it was a subject taken to heart. Another gaping flaw in the original which was also redeemed was the villain, in the first game Azar Javed (who was the villain until the epilogue) had very unclear motivations and besides stealing the Witcher secrets had no real relationship to Geralt. Thinking from the perspective of someone with no knowledge in the Witcher world, how could someone care about a villain who had stolen secrets for hidden reasons and fled every chance he got? (The hidden villain of the game was even more lackluster.) The Witcher 2 has a villain who from the start gets the player's attention from the prologue but also has a mystery surrounding his character. It's like CDPR took the two biggest flaws of the first and reversed them here in the sequel. The plot I felt was the strongest part of this game and at the end my only question was: What is going to happen from here?
In fact after finishing this game I started questioning why the first game even existed as part of the trilogy, it probably would've been better to just call it Witcher: Assassins of Kings rather than naming it as a sequel since the original game has so little to do with the main plot aside from being a story of when Geralt was an amnesiac the entire time. (I'd rather him just be smashed throughout the whole ordeal instead.)
I'd heard coming into this game many people complaining about the length, which stems from the original game which is supposedly longer.
The Witcher 2 fully expects you to play through the game a second time as there's absolutely no possible way for you to figure everything out without having done both routes (in a way I have a problem with this, but it was a design choice).
The Witcher 1 has problems starting from the third of five chapters (not counting the epilogue). The first two chapters were well-crafted, no areas were worthless and everything was placed with precision. The third chapter repeated all of the content of the second and even refilled the Noticeboard with more "go collect blood/bones/scales" quests, and this was problematic because it's a shoddy way of elongating the game. The main plot of the third chapter can be done within an hour but if you decide to do all of the side quests it can take much longer (hours) since the materials you'll need can't be farmed in a single run. If you don't have the perk to obtain twice the ingredients from monsters it can take literally ages. The fourth chapter is even shorter than that if not for all the time spent sprinting from one side of the map to the other with acres of blank space between. The fifth chapter is even worse than that consisting of going to a crypt and then to the old manor and proceeding to end the game in the epilogue.
Which begs the question: Did CDPR need to repeat a map like they did in Witcher 1 with a bunch of bollox MMO-like quests to extend length? It was straight to the point and CDPR understood where the priorities lie. The game can only last as long as the story and if you wanted to continue the game it'd mean hurting the plot overall (a point I praised this sequel for, in criticism of the original). This is why I think the Witcher 2 does it better, the three chapters are all more consistent and give off equal amounts of content but does so without harming the plot.
The gameplay is... well it's an Action RPG alright. You got traits, weapons/armor, upgrades to weapons/armor, signs, mutations (passive buffs in trait trees), etc. The game essentially consists of hacking at enemies while using signs to assist fighting. The problem I've seen with the game through a Dark playthrough is that regardless of the choices of all the things listed, the playstyle of the player differs slightly. With a more tanky approach you can play more brazenly but with a magical glass canon approach you'd be more cautious, a pure sign set would still have to swing a sword around unless they want to sit down and wait for charge times on Vigor (probably less so in easier difficulties). The fighting isn't bug free however as you'll find your sword slicing emptily through enemies as the game fails to register a clean hit, Igni (essentially a fireball) will fail to contact enemies if you are slightly angled up or down from the target. The game is also CLEARLY not designed to deal with group combat, something the first game had no issue with by having multiple styles. By removing the styles and simply giving a fast or strong attack, enemies that clump in hordes are now an issue. Sometimes you can hit two enemies at once but at insane difficulty you can get ♥♥♥♥ed quickly, which resorts to bombs. Ah bombs, the most overpowered thing in the game, they're an infinite resource you can use since materials are thrown at you in heaps (which can have a 100% damage buff through perks). Mentioning perks brings me to I think a large part of the problem I had with gameplay: SIGNS.
In the first game the only really good signs were Aard (it locked an opponent for an instant kill) and Igni (if you got to the real late game to buff the ever living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of). Anyways the point is that only two signs were viable and they were broken as all hell. In the Witcher 2 they nerfed Igni and buffed Quen. Aard stayed the same except no instakilling, Igni is now trashcan status even fully buffed (no damage), but now Quen comes into play being a damage absorbing shield that you can fight with (the first game you couldn't attack while active). The problem is that upgrading into signs is pretty worthless, there's no huge gains in damage or utility. Yrden is only useful for one boss fight and Axii is bad because the AI are scripted poorly.
The most broken build in this game
One of the bigger flaws to me was the voice acting in this game. Witcher 1 had it's fair share of: 'I can't believe they thought that line was good enough in one take' - moments. Witcher 2 seems to continue the trend but it felt wrong in a different sense, like the voice actors didn't understand the scene they were supposed to voice out. When Saskia goes out to inspire the troops to repel an invading army she's supposed to give a speech to a large audience, but instead she speaks perfectly normally instead of shouting. It's as though she was giving a speech to herself in private akin to prepping an actual speech. Then there was another moment with a small side-character who is supposed to be shouting down questions to a prisoner they've captured but again the vocals don't match the scene. This character nearly whispers questions like "what is your name?" instead of shouting them, as she's almost a good two building-lengths above the other character.
I'd recommend the game overall just for the plot alone, the rest is icing on the cake.

F.E.A.R. - First Encounter Assault Recon is a horror first-person shooter that was released in Oct 17, 2005. For those unaware of this game, this game at the time of release was praised for its good graphics, game mechanics, storyline, and AI system - which to this day still blows out other FPS AI's out of the water.
Here's the story:
You work in a government military, employed under the name "F.E.A.R." - abbreviated for "First Encounter Assault Recon", to handle extreme paranormal activities that pose a threat. Your name is only known as "Pointman" - which is an indivdual who leads the way and tries to handle the threat firsthand. You are tasked to handle a situation that resulted in unusual paranormal activity that caused casaulties, only to realize that Paxton Fettel is behind these deaths and that he is controlling a battalion of elite soldiers who can only be commanded by indivduals who have psychic powers. As you continue, you soon realize that the main cause for this sudden threat is Alma - a girl with dangerous psychic powers that was tested and experimented on by a company - where she is trying to set herself free and Fettel is there to help. You are to eliminate Fettel and prevent the release of Alma, but you must fight the elite soldiers that stand in your way and the hallucations Alma places on you that provide some good scares.
The game mechanics in this game are simple, but provide a great gameplay experience that is satisifying to witness - even for a 12 year old game(at the time of this review). You can lean to help take gun battles with the battles, melee the enemies with style (whether you bicycle kick them, whack them with your gun, or slide kick). If that isn't much to you, you have the ability to slow down time and quickly take on multiple enemies.
However, the enemies will try their best to "eliminate the threat". The AI in this game will work with each other to outplay and take down the player - whether that is flanking you when you're not paying attention, throwing grenades to get you out of a area, or grouping together to take you down. If you were to compare some FPS title's AI to F.E.A.R.'s AI, you'd see that F.E.A.R.'s AI is vastly superior than those few titles (and yes, there are titles where the AI is veeeeery bad and playing this game will show you a whole world difference with good and bad AI's).
For the graphics, it's a 2005 game and it still looks okay. At the time, it was pretty good looking game and that you needed a decent system to play this game on all Max settings. Hopefully, you should be able to MAX out the settings of the game if you were to pick this up. (A side note: Look up "FEAR FPS issue" and look for a Steam guide that involves replacing a .dll file with a patched .dll that deals with your FPS being really low despite having a good system and not having anything hog resources).
As for the OST, it's solid and does its job to giving the player a unique experience.
All in all, this game is incredibly fun to play and gives you a good scare time to time. The story is solid and if you're looking for a game that can offer some challenge, this is a title for you. Maybe after a first normal mode playthrough, play on the "Extreme" difficulty setting - that's where you can see the AI in work.

I am not a drug culture guy. More specifically I'm was not into the psychedelic punk art/music culture of the 70's and early 80's. I find some of that art interesting but I was never draw to it. Zeno Clash has made me reconsider that and maybe I need to take a closer look.
Zeno Clash was a game I first heard talked about when it came out back in 2008, getting a lot of press for just being real weird in a way games had taken a break from for a while. Not since the early 2000's with games like MDK and Giant Citizen Kabuto had the flat out strangeness of a game like this been seen. The combination of FPS, fighting game and a psychedelic punk fantasy world came almost out of nowhere.
In Zeno Clash you take on the role of Ghat, a skinny but determined protagonist (maybe?), and work your way through a crazy story. I often had zero idea what was going on in anything but the most basic sense but that was okay. The world is intriguing all on its own and the bits of story that drip out were more than enough to keep me pushing forwards to see what was next. I was consistently thinking "what can Zeno Clash show me next???"
The game is controlled just like a first person shooter, and even has a number of guns, from piranha shaped pistols to the most bizarre crossbowy-thing I've even seen in a game. The guns are strong but need to be reloaded often (again with some of the most unique reload animations in a game) and if they aren't available or convenient you fall back to fighting with your fists. And this isn't just a basic "punch guys when you are out of ammo" FPS style melee combat, no sir, it has the full range of punches, kicks, holds, stuns and throws. All this is taught to you via these fever dream sequences at the start of the game. Each fight takes place in more or less a cordoned off area and begins much like a standard fighting game where Ghat (and any companions that are with him at the time) are pitched VS the enemies in a splash screen, and at the end of the fight the story moves on.
Zeno Clash is a treat for the eyes with a huge array of characters and landscapes, very few repeated over the course of the game. Unlike a lot of FPS games there is not push for length here, no level or area out stays its welcome - sometimes I actually felt a little rushed, wanting the game to show me more of the place I was in. And it should be mentioned that this game has aged very well graphically and because of the unique art style avoided the problem of looking dated on a more modern PC.
Zeno Clash is a short(ish) game that banks on oddity, strangeness, mystery and a unique mix of game mechanics - pulling it off wonderfully. If you are comfortable with the combat concepts (it has difficulty settings) and dig the style I recommend it for anyone looking to take a break from the abundant same-old-same-old games.

My overall rating for Stellaris: 90/100
Paradox Development Studio and Paradox Entertainment shine in the genre of grand-strategy games. Their last step lead into space and amazing galaxy conquest. Stellaris is not the first or most complicated game among others grand stategies and 4X space-set games, but surely, it is the finest. Lets see in detail, what were positives and negatives of this title.
GAMEPLAY
+ Transparent and smooth design
+ Challenges and changing nature of playthrough
+ Simple combats
+ Great impact of strategy
+ Each choice has pros and cons
+ End-game crisis element
- Confusing tutorial
- Late game might get repetetive and boring
Gameplay might be a bit confusing from the beginning (I spent six hours with creation of my empire :-D), but after a while, it is easy to get used to it. The course of the game is changing and bringing new challenges and goals to fulfill, what is good and I somehow miss it in other similar titles.
Combat is simply looking, basically it is a simulator of numbers with graphical addition as you see ships cruising and firing, what gives the player impression of direct control. Yet you can intervene with strategical moves, e. g. one fleet serves as a bait and second flanks the enemy resulting into total destruction of enemy fleets, even with own fleets outnumbered.
There are no only positive or negative decisions. You can gain greater control over your subjects, but they will protest, that they have no voting rights. In case of allowing them, they might be more satisfied, but a totally disastrous candidate might get elected during elections. Military contra economy, trust against power and so on.
Mid and late game can get repetetive and boring and as a countermeasure, we have here an end-game crisis. It is a unique challenge, that is a little bit overpowered in design to change the course in the galaxy and it can end game efficiently, if left uncontested. Designs of extradimensional invaders (The Unbidden), Prethoryn Plague (hive, swarm civilisation) or AI uprising are perfectly done, even hive civilisation is made so perfectly, that many scifi novels should take a lecture from the developers.
Here we are getting also to negatives. The timing of the end-game crisis might not be always fair, they might spawn too early, what may be frustrating for players, or too late, when the empires are so strong, that the crisis is beaten very swiftly.
Also tutorial is a very confusing, I suggest turning it off and view instructions from YouTubers, which are far easier to understand.
Also the management of planets in late game should get some improvements, it is horrible to watch over two hundred planets and seek the one, which you forgot to develop. Not to mention, that after the crisis, you just conquer, negotiate and rule.
CHARACTERS
+ Variety of state parameters
+ Wide doplomacy possibilities
+ Moding possibilities
- AI behaviour might be illogical and not corresponding the situation
The creation of own state is something amazing, with wide racial, state, government factors and much more, you are guaranteed, that each playthrough will be unique. Also, as you cannot explore everything in one game (e. g. materialists have almost a zero chance, that they will get psionics), it motivates to replay the game with different setup.
Also diplomay is great, after the last patch (1.2), you can conquer, liberate, or just humiliate another empire, form alliancies, threaten, insult, the possibilities here are borderless.
I also admit, that Paradox let their players to modify the game and add own content, which may make the game even more challenging. This is a great step towards the community, what brings more joy to this great game.
AI behaviour, although, has to be critized here, because sometimes it behaves irrationally. Empire threatened with and end-game crisis is ignoring it completely, though after the 1.2 update, things got a bit better. But, if the crisis spawns in the opposite corner of the galaxy, you might get there too late to win the fight. Also, I understand, that it is more difficult to implement new technologies to big empire than to small country. But small country cannot keep the pace of research capabilities of a huge empire!
VISUALS
+ Nicely stylised graphics
+ Reasonable hardware/software demands
- Few glitches
Visuals are stylised and it gives an impression of controlling something, that contains several worlds, solar systems or a part of the galaxy. Also modification of this races, genetic intervention, everything is detailed, even the ships and stations.
Addition to this point is, that Stellaris has relatively fair demands on hardware and software, so also players with integrated graphic card may play it with only slight difficulties.
Only few glitches were encountered, they did not affected the gameplay, so I did not count them into evaluation.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Atmospherical
+ Corresponding to the game and its situations
Composed by Andreas Waldetoft and recorded by Brandenburg State Orchestra is well performed and suits the atmosphere and situations during the game. Transitions are not being felt, music plays smoothly and accordingly. Great addition to this impressions are Mia Stegmar's vocals.
MULTIPLAYER
+ Well balanced (after 1.2 Patch)
- Only one goal (domination)
Multiplayer was the weakest part of the game and many players end up complaining against corvette-spam. Things got better after the last patch (1.2), so players are forced to find various tactics, because it is easy to build corvettes, but also with proper ships easy to destroy.
However, there is still only domination victory possible, with diplomatic possibilities players may decide, whether they will dominate the galaxy together or end up in a desperate fight with only one winner.
SUMMARY
To sum it up, if the grand-strategy games would be stones, differing from silica to emerald or ruby, Stellaris is definitely a sapphire. It can give much also to players outside the genre and if somebody is considering starting playing this kind of games, Stellaris is a great start.
Changing gameplay, new goals and opponents, various strategies, all of this outweights the few negatives, that the game has. With my evaluation I remained at the sapphire metaphore (90/100) and Stellaris can calmly claim to be one of best titles in this genre.

I usually don't give bad reviews because I try to see what the game has to offer rather than what it fell short of.
That said, Viking: Battle for Asgard was a complete mess.
Not only is it terribly optimized so even a GTX 1070 can't play this 2012 game, it is also rife with unintuitive controls ported from console by people who've obviously never played on PC before.
Also, when you turn the camera with your mouse, the everything besides your character tears and frame-rate experiences dips. I had to avoid moving the mouse too much to avoid migraines.
Worst of all, you cannot change graphics settings IN-GAME - you have to close the program, run a config, and then reopen it, get into the game, playtest, see if you like the changes, and then change again if something's off, which takes forever to set up.
We're not done yet. Besides all that jarring crap ^, the gameplay itself isn't well thought out either.
The game is supposed to be about combat. What if I told you they tried so hard to make things flashy that half the time you die because you're locked in long animation sequences whenever you perform moves?
Case in point; Round-house-dragon-penes-odin-love-juices-stab move sprinkled with ice rune magic feels clumsy rather than bad♥♥♥♥♥ especially when a noob minion with just cleaner attacks knock you out of animation every time. What's the point in learning new moves when it's more effective to just left-click your way to victory?
How do you progress you wonder? By buying everything in a store. Want an Odin-love-juice move? Pay gold. I'm serious. Whereas there's plot, trials, and a journey of some kind to obtain great power in other games, here there's just a shopkeeper. If these shop owners are so strong, why doesn't he lead the Vikings? Disgusting - the developers didn't even try.
I stopped after 1.1 hrs of gameplay and gave up because my index finger got tired and I needed something for my headache.
Would NOT EVER recommend. Not even if I received this for free. Not even if someone paid me and my medical bills to play this - because I'll never get my 1.1 hrs back.

In Viking: Battle for Asgard you fill the boots of Skarin, a young Viking Warrior who takes it upon himself to turn the tide against the evil forces of the Underworld and stop the plans of Hel, Goddess of said forces. With the help and guidance of Freya, Skarin will unite the Viking Clans and wage war.
Plot wise, I believe Viking is on the weak side. The story, although it's rather simple, it's executed in a weird way and how it progresses further, just leave you either wanting for more or just trying to figure out what the hell happened. The combat however is quite fun and you can be versatile with the various combos you have and although repetitive after a while, it still is fun! Especially the Skirmish Battles are simply epic: it really feels like a battle between armies.
Although it's quite old now as a game, it has aged well. However, there are some things that are just terrible, such as the camera is quite unsupportive of your cause and the map is rather hard to use. While there is Fast Travel available, if you miss your queue of spamming the button to enable it, you have to redo it and that is simply annoying. The kill, sneak attack and dodge animations are suburb, but some things, like the blood on Skarin's sword all the time feel a bit unnatural.
All in all, Viking is a game that it delivers to do what it set out to do as a game: able to entertain you long enough until you finish that campaign, but I am afraid it leaves no room for replaybility, unless you are hunting down the achievements, although it is possible to do them in one run and be done with it!
I would give it a 6/10 rating (Better Than Average Game)
----------------
PROS
- Fun combat mechanics with various combos
- Battle Arena, where you learn skills and how to utilize them
- Skirmish Battles! You need that army, you can't solo it!
- Soundtrack, especially the Skirmish Battle Soundtrack!
- Challenging combat when it needs to be
- Rune Magic is quite fun and powerful
- Good graphics
- A few details such as the changing terrain when you free an area or uphill and downhill running!
CONS
- Story is kinda weak
- Skarin never talks and doesn't really leave an impression to you
- Repetitive combat
- Generic quests and no sidequests (unless you count the Beer Delivery Service!)
- Map is hard to use
- Slow switching from attack to defence
- Camera screws up more often than not
- Bloody mashing button

A very tight platforming beat-em-up. The game is geared toward over-the-top Dragonball-esque mid-air combat, so the feel of the gameplay sets itself far apart from any other beat-em-ups that I know of.
A lot of things are really well thought out in this game. While you aren't actually FLYING in this gmae, you have an omni-directional dash button that can be infinitely chained with your jump in midair for unlited airtime, plus a dodge button that can...well dodge BUT also give you a little extra distance in a certain direction to fine-tune your trajectory. You also have a Panic! Meter, which can be used to recover most/all of your health, but only with a certain minimum amount on the gauge - first at about 25% full, then an extra 25% every other heal, up to every heal requiring 100% Panic! after 3 heals. You'll need them for sure sometimes, but you'll need to weigh this against all of the other things you can do with your Panic! Gauge, as you can also use it to dash longer distances, charge up your Heavy attack to absolutely stupid levels of damage (although Panic! is still consumed if you miss), and not using it even gives you a passive damage bonus to all your attacks as the gauge fills. So you'll need to juggle your options, especially when your health starts dropping.
The enemies are pretty clever too. Since you have so much maneuverability within the game, the developers compensated by making sure you cannot simply single out your enemies and just stun-lock them to death. Both your light finisher and your heavy attack send your opponents flying away at breakneck speeds, and they'll often return already seconds from performing a counterattack, making it extremely difficult to consistently chain attacks together.
Not only that, but a lot of enemies can dodge out of your light combo on some occasions and perform an un-telegraphed counter on you. But cleverest of all is how they designed the elite enemies and bosses. These enemies are special - not only in being more powerful than your average fist fodder, but also in that they each have a shield bar. It doesn't reccharge (unless you go a really long time without hitting them) but while they have Shield, they have absolutely zero reaction to your attacks. Your hits don't knock them back, stun them, or interrupt their attacks WHATSOEVER, which is why you want that shield down quick so you can catch them up in a combo without worrying about a retaliation.
The way the developers designed the difficulty around this fresh mid-air beat-em-up was smart, but it's unfortunately still far from flawless. One problem I ran into on more than a few occasions was too much visual noise. It's barely noticeable against one or two enemies, but you'll often find yourself fighting roughly six enemies at a time. Because of ho0w big and flashy all of the effects are - especially the hit effects - it's easy to lose track of enemies and end up getting hit before you even realized the guy was rearing up to swing.
And while we're on the subject of getting overwhelmed, the enemies don't show you much of any mercy in their attack patterns. It doesn't matter if an enemy is telegraphing his attack from two feet away or from off the screen - if you aren't ready to dodge, he's going to swoop in and nail you. As such, there's really no way to kite enemies away from eachother; you'll be fighting them all at once, with almost no exceptions. I understand why they went this route, but the enemies often home in on you in a way where the only truly reliable way of evading their attack is the dodge button...which you will be hammerring mercilessly in the later levels. And if it's not homing melee attacks, it's bullet attacks that cover the screen. Even the earliest enemies have a kunai spray that has a ludicrous radius of effect. You can hit most of these to deflect them, but this is very unreliable and often gets you hurt. Again, dodging is almost exclusively the only option to deal with these. It would be nice if some of these homing attacks had a more deliberate trajectory that could better encourage use of the air dash in combat, or if the bullet attacks had more openings that encouraged maneuvering around them rather than just dodging through them. Overall, I'm disappointed with this game on that front. It gives you all this space to move around in, but does very little to encourage you to use it, as it seems too wrapped up in its dodge mechanic instead.
These issues are far from game-breaking. I still greatly enjoy this game. However, if a sequel were ever in the works, I would love to see the developers go back and take a second look at how these mechanics function, and hopefully fine-tune them to really bring out the game's full potential.

While many of the Metal Gear games bear the submoniker "Tactical Espionage Action", Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance drops this style of gameplay in favour of the kind of action Platinum is known for- more akin to Bayonetta than any of the core Metal Gear games.
Combat involves stringing together long combos of light and heavy attacks with a High Frequency blade, lacerating opponents. If Raiden's Electrolyte count is high enough, he can slow down time when entering Blade Mode and hack many enemies apart. Some stronger enemies such as the Mastiffs require a certain amount of damage to be given before Raiden can mince them, but many of the enemies are ordinary Cyborgs, and can be chopped into little pieces from the get go. Blade Mode can also be used to pull off the Xandatsu Technique, which allows Raiden to completely restore both his health and his electrolytes. In place of a dodge, as you would find in many action games such as Bayonetta or Devil May Cry, Raiden must parry enemies attacks at the right time, with a perfectly timed parry resulting in Raiden performing a powerful counterattack. While a dodge technique can be bought from the game's shop, it's unclear how to perform this technique, and you can get through the game without it. Players can also equip "Unique Weapons" after obtaining them from the bosses, but these weapons replace Raiden's High Frequency Blade using the heavy attack button, and can make combat seem a little more disjointed. However, if players wish to expand their knowledge of the game's combat, this is a good place to start.
Bosses are the obvious highlight of the game, and while Metal Gear Ray and Metal Gear Exelcus aren't well suited to the combat system, the more human bosses allow the game's combat to shine, many ending with a gory Blade Mode finisher. Sundowner seems to be the clear highlight, alongside the game's final boss, who won't be spoilt here. These bosses test the player not only on their ability to parry, but also on their mastery of Blade Mode, which may be easier on a controller such as an XBox controller with joysticks, but can be difficult to perform using a Steam Controller. This is not necessarily a negative, but something players should be aware of, whether or not they wish to give themselves a little extra challenge.
Stealth does occur in the game, but is largely unnecessary, and if failed, most players will easily be able to fight their way out of the situation, seeming as though it was put in as an afterthought to appeal to fans of the core series. It's an option at times, but many players will have more fun simply engaging with the excellent combat.
The game's story, involving cyborgs, Private Militaries, human trafficking, and philosophy, is as ludicrous as is to be expected, switching wildly between deadly serious and hilariously over the top, fitting the game's playful mechanics well, and offering an entertaining, if far fetched, tale.
Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance is a creative and expertly made action game that's well worth anyone's time, though fans of the core series shouldn't go in expecting another stealthy romp.

Though I have yet to play the game myself (due to the game crashing on the menu screen) I can't properly review it the way I'd like to. BUT from what I've seen by many youtubers, the game looks very interesting and seems to be a lot of fun, unlike 'The Rake' which was cancelled in a very un-polished state.
The game looks visually appealing and rather nice, the lighting is extremely well done, as well as the models and textures, with high poly models with proper hair physics and high-res textures giving off a somewhat realistic feel to the game.
Some downsides about the current state (in my opinion) are:
1: the game's menus are uninteresting in it's released state, with no real representation of what the game is like, I mean sure, there's a forest in t he background, but even 'The Rake' had an interesting, nice looking menu. But the devs appear to be changing the menu right now anyway.
2: current character models are all the same, with 'interesting' walking animations that look rather odd, they look like some of my very first walk cycles right now. The character models are well done, but need more variation for multiplayer games, so the players aren't all clones of each other. This is also being fixed.
3: the current price for the game $15.99 USD, around $16. For the quality of the game so far, I don't believe this price is low enough for the state of the game, yes there is lots of stuff being added as we speak, but at least $10.00 at the most, I've told my friends (who also have seen the game, but haven't bought it) about the game and what is being added, I then told them the price and most of them thought it was too much money right now. Like I said, $10 at least, it would probably get more customers if it had a lower price.
Overall I think it's a nice game, and there's soo much to be added in the next version. But I'd wait until more content is added (when the next update is released). There'll be a nicer menu, revamped Bigfoot AI, another level, remote control drones, other animals like wolves and deers (even racoons) and probably much more, and Nvidia hairworks is getting dumped so more people can play the game at a more consistant framerate. Once I can play the game I'll be updating my review.
Now for all you people who can't get the game to run past the loading screen (me included) I think I have some idea of why. Nvidia hairworks is an advanced software.. A REALLY advanced software, it was even used in games like Witcher 3. However, it is not well optimized for low-quality PCs and/or laptops. When the loading screen is done loading the game shows up, and instantly loads in Bigfoot, then applies Nvidia hairworks to him, causing lower end PCs to crash, due to the almost zero optimization of hairworks, your laptop can't handle Bigfoot being loaded in along with the hair he uses, so it crashes. This also explains why you can hear the game sounds before it crashes: it loads the game, then Bigfoot, then crashes because it can't handle it.
I have emailed the Devs (cyberlight) about this and am awaiting a reply. Until then, I'd recommend not downvoting the game constantly because it crashes for you, the next update is removing Nvidia hairworks, due to poor optimization ok?
