Back in my young college days there was a downloaded version of this game going around amongst my friends (I really wanted to buy it but couldn't spare even the small amount of money required). At the time it was an unfinished sandbox where you basically downloaded mods and shoot crazy guns and stuff at terrible AI that practically just stood there.
Now there's actually a game here. The campaign consists of taking and defending territories while competing with up to 3 othere AI players. You pick a place and if anyone challenges you for it you fight for it. Once you take it you can either design your own base within it, or pick a budget and let the game build one for you.
I found designing things to be a little unfriendly because i wasn't sure what everything was, and it can take a lot of time depending on how crazy you want to get. Considering that at the moment the campaign doesn't usually last a long time depending on how good you are and the settings you choose I didn't feel compelled to do it. Additionally you'll be taking over several bases over the course of the game and it would be insane to manually build each one unless you were really quick. However, the autobuilding feature of the game tends to build some pretty decent looking bases. The problem is that each day you give the computer a budget for your base and then it decides how to spend the money and in what order. This means over time the base will get better but at the beginning you might have a pretty incomplete base. When you get attacked and you have an incomplete base, it can be nearly impossible to protect.
The actual battles are where the game shines. You start with a brainbot or if you have a base he might just be a brain in a jar. He's basically your commander and if his fragile brain jar gets destroyed then its game over. I usually send him down to dig for gold while i let my other units guard him.
This game is a physics based game where each pixel acually has its own properties. Units are actually made up of connected parts that move and interact based on their physics. This means that every part of a character can be blown off and every spec of dirt or other material has its own properties that can be deformed. Bullets go through softer objects and ricochet off harder ones. Rockets all have their own forces and when they explode they shred into pieces that can effect characters around the environment.
This game is run by gold and every unit is bought and dropped into your scene through the buy menu that will let you customize the unit and what it's carrying. generally they all have jetpacks, and weight matters so you dont want to bog a guy down too much otherwise he'll get stuck a lot and won't be able to jetpack too high.
Once a unit is called down you can take control of him and use his arsenal to take out other units and hopefully their brain. This is the part thats both amazingly fun, hilarious, and sometimes frustrating. The AI has gotten pretty smart at navigating around the levels and everyone is so fragile it can get pretty difficult, but in a good way. Especially when you're outnumbered and units are getting close to your brain. Having to fend off guys while simultaneously trying to buy and call down more units can be really tense. Especially because you're always working within a changing budget. Juggling shooting things, buying things, and budgetting can be pretty crazy at times.
But the real craziness comes from the Cortex Command moments you'll experience. Blowing up dropships and having them rollover and land on top of the guys they just dropped off, then exploding is always awesome. Jetpacking out of control and then smashing into 3 enemy NPCs and watching everyone explode is hilarious. Sniping a guy from long range and watching his parts just fly off is super satifying, and if you get your hands on a rocket launcher, you're in for some serious entertainment. These moments almost never get old, and will keep you playing this game for hours on end. Even when you totally fail the simplest task and all these things happen to you, its still hilarious.
And when you get bored? There are a bunch of great secenarios and community made mods on the steam workshop that will keep the game fresh. weegee's unmapped lands 2 mod is a really great conversion of the campaign and probably more fun than the vanilla game itself. He even has his own interpretation of FTL in the CC world that's worth checking out.
I'll be honest, this game has a bit of a learning curve. In the current state I'm reviewing this game it's unfinished. The developer has admitted that all the features are in the game, they just arent polished, and thats true. There is a tutorial that does an okay job of teaching you the basics of combat and mining gold, but as far as the campaign part of the game goes, there's basically no guidance at all. The community has made up for this though.
In it's current state it's a game you can sit down and play for 15mins or 5 hours. However, you can really see the potential of the game, and it can really only get better from here on out. It's a great game to add to your collection, play until your burnt out, forget about it for a year or two, and then play it until your burnt out again. It's that solid and that evergreen. You'll never get tired of blowing things up.

The message here is, don't believe the major reviews or metacritic score. Read the reviews on steam. Everyone is recommending it, just like myself.

Given the upcoming release of Binding of Issac: Rebirth, I have decided to update my review of The Binding of Issac + The Wrath of Lamb. Having doubled my playtime in the past couple of weeks i have come to the conclusion that my initial response to the game was premature.
For those unfamiliar with Issac, the game is a Rougelike Dual Analogue Shooter. this means you controll Issac (or one of his unlocakble alternates) who fights randomly spawned monsters in a procedurely generated dungeon using his own tears as bullets. Issac is heavially inspired by retro titles, especially the original Legend of Zelda, as can be seen in the way each room is a seperate yet in many ways similar mirror of each other with some room s designated as treasure or boss rooms, and the heart based life meter.
The presentation of Issac is that of a Newgrounds flash game on steriods. To be fair that description is fairly apt. the game is built on the flash engine and if it hadn't had the time, creativity, and vision applied to it that is what it would likely have ended up as. That flash comment is not meant in the derrogative though, the game looks and sounds beautiful (Mostly thanks to Danny Baranowsky). Because it sticks to the limitations of the engine rather than attempt more realistic graphics the game looks perfect for what it is.
Gameplay is where Issac truly shines. The controls are simple and tight, keeping the already difficult gameplay from becoming frustrating. The best part of the gameplay though is the items. The randomly generated items ensure that no two runs are the same. These items are most awesome when they work together (Protip-Polyphimus+Technology =Awesome.). The enemies have unique attack and movement patterns that are easy to learn but will always be able to throw you for a loop.
The only problem I have with the game is the same as it was before. The random nature of the item drops and boss spawns can make some playthroughs almost instant throwaways. This is aliviated by the sortness of the game and the rapidity of the respawn but if a few games in a row with a bad start and even I get frustrated.
8/10. Worthy of a checkout before Rebirth comes out.

i really wanted to like this game, but took me 45 minutes of play to unlock the basic 'possess other robots' mechanism in favor of some painfully unfunny dialogue that added nothing to the experience. some tips for developers:
• if you're going to put in interruptions for the game to add to the story, t should probably be more than just audio and subtitles while your character idles. even the aggravating codec interruptions in Metal Gear Solid were more dynamic than this, and that was almost 2 decades ago.
• even if you do the above, you probably don't want to put cut scene interruptions every other room. Even if they were well-written and added to the game (these fall far short of that), you're not letting someone actually play the game. you're taking away the biggest thing about games as a playable narrative: making them playable. At best you're wasting my time because you love your own writing, at worst you're wasting my time because you really hope i'll stick around past the 2 hour steam refund window.
• if you're going to put gameplay tips in that require a keypress to dismiss, you might want to put them in the center of the screen and pause the game. it's really not helpful to remove all control from the player during their first alarm by putting up a tip in the upper right corner. If you have a big monitor, this might as well be invisible.
there's tons of positive reviews for this game, so you can probably safely ignore mine; there may be a good game in here somewhere. but if you'd like to actually play the game right away instead of watching poorly written jokes about a hacker stereotype, you can skip this one.

If you've lived in the era of DOS shareware shooters, this game is custom made for you! Don't let the quirky graphics and humour fool you, this title's gameplay is deeper than you'd expect. Numerous enemy and weapon types keep you on your toes, changing your tactics constantly. Gadgets, grenades and stims provide supporting temporary solutions while unlockable perks have a more stable effect.
Initially I wrote that Rogue Shooter is an enjoyable laid-back game, now I would say: Yes and No. With its style it's a perfect title for picking up for a brief relaxing shooting sprees, but it gets more and more hardcore as you press on to further levels: enemies become more numerous and tougher (as do the guns you find and buy, luckily) and you're forced to do some extremely quick thinking on your feet to come out alive.
Easily recommended for the initial price of 4.99, if it's at full price you should propably check out the trailer and the demo to see if this game hits a nerve for you. After 4 hours of playing and feeling like I've only scratched the surface I would recommend it even then, but not everyone gets the nostalgia factor from this game.
When considering purchase, it's also worth noting that some other reviews still claim there is no save function in the game. This was the case at the release, forcing you to either uninterrupted play sessions or to leave the game running in the background as you do something else. This changed five days later, when the developers gave you a save file for when you exit the game. You still only get one and it's erased at death, so game difficulty hasn't been altered.
Splendid first work from the Hippomancer studio, I'm glad to have lots of free time in this new golden age of gaming.

If you've ever wanted the spectacle of a curtain-fire shoot-em-up mixed with the hack and slash / brawler action of Dynasty Warriors, Streets of Rage, Fairy Bloom Freesia, or Scott Pilgrim VS the World the Game, this is a strong execution of the concept.
Pros:
+ Easy to learn battle controls, difficult to master scenarios.
+ Spectacular particle effects when using Crash Attacks to slam enemies bouncing around the screen into obstacles and each other.
+ You can jump forever! In theory, you could complete the game without ever touching the ground again after the first jump in any given level.
+ Silly sense of humor.
+ Energetic catchy soundtrack which brings to mind the likes of Mega Man.
+ Arcade-style Score Attack setup minimizes the time to get back in the brawl after a failed attempt to clear a room.
+ Boss Rush included and available from the start!
+ GIANT ROBOT THAT SHOOTS MINI ROBOTS. YES.
Cons:
- Brief tutorial. It's easy to skip a portion while experimenting with controls and miss important details. And the weaker up/down Crash attacks are not mentioned.
- Wild mechanic is a bit counter-intuitive
- Repetitive. Especially if you have trouble figuring out how to deal with any specific room of enemies.
MANIC BRAWLING ACTION. A very apt description of the gameplay.
Casual Tumblr Note from the first time I beat the game:
"This game. <3 I had fun. Took me a bit to learn how the Wild gauge worked though. Wild boosts YOUR damage of all attacks significantly, but ALSO boosts the damage you take. Crash is the best way to break through shields, but charging it drains Wild. So it’s often more advantageous to NOT charge it at all. And Panic restores HP and reduces the damage you take, but it does not clear the enemies already on screen. And you lose ALL Wild, so most of your damage potential is out the door. A lot less intuitive than Fairy Bloom Freesia, but similar gameplay at the core. Though Freesia’s quite a bit more technical."

The 2D beat-up genre was a giant during the 8 and 16 bit generations, as well as dominating arcades with their quarter munching gameplay and cooperative game design. With the decline of arcades and the birth of new genres in 3d, the popularity of beat 'em ups waned, making way for new gaming zeitgeists. In recent years the 2D beat-em up has settled for reboots of classics with little success, luckily the love for the genre burns in the hearts of indie developers and with this, Aces Wild Manic Brawling Action comes to life. Does this beat 'em up deliver a first round knock out punch or does it feel like being roughed up and having your lunch money taken away by a bully?

Taking control of the title character Aces Wild, who must participate in this year's Maximus Circuit in an attempt to preserve the lands held by the Wilder Family. His brother Rex has struck a deal with key entrants of the tournament to ensure his victory so he can sell the lands for a hefty sum. In classic beat 'em up tradition, the story stops there allowing you to pummel your way through the games stages without narrative interruption.

Aces Wild's obvious key focus is it's stylized fast paced aerial combat. The controls consist of a light and heavy attack which are linked to the wild meter located at the top left corner of the screen. The meter is filled with every light attack landed increasing the potency of all your attacks. It's also used for health recovery, and charged attacks. These simple mechanics create a system in which managing your wild meter becomes crucial. You'll find yourself debating on whether to use it for a quick heal, full on charge attack or conserving it just a bit longer for an array of potent light attacks. The three selectable characters also bring a distinct combat style to the table, each with their unique skill set. If you find yourself in a bind consider a new route by selecting another character.

The combat is a bitter sweet. While it is mechanically solid, the level design and enemy encounters undermine it's strengths. One minute you will feel like you are a part of a knuckle sandwich catering service and the next you will find yourself beaten, battered and tossed out on your @$$ like an unruly patron at a biker bar. This often becomes a one sided affair in the later stages when the screen is cluttered with enemies, and one missed dodge results in ten enemy hits. A handful of sword, fists and draggers to the face is a high price to pay for missing one dodge in a cluttered an chaotic melee where sometimes the greatest challenge is keeping track of where your character is at among the action. Enemy's moves don't necessarily evolve either, spamming becomes their default strategy and it becomes extremely irritating when the difficulty is ramped up by cluttering the screen with enemies instead of providing a clever mix of foes that complement one another's attacks and patterns.

Boss battles continue the trend of being frustrating. Like their lesser counterparts, they have a bit of a penchant for spamming the same attacks again and again creating very narrow windows in which to land attacks. Small mistakes and missed dodges are also punished severely. Earlier bosses are formidable at first but quickly become a joke as you learn their patterns. Later encounters ramp up completely taking much of the fun away as they become tedious and annoying. Knowing what to do is one thing, but succeeding is another when everything consuming the screen seems to be at the right spot to put a hurting on you. All is slightly remedied though, as you can select any stage whenever, infinite lives, and the instant respawn with full health after a loss. Still, place fragile valuables in a safe place while playing to ensure their safety.

Leaderboards have recently been added for those looking to ascend them and local mutiplayer is available if you and friend want to tackle the challenge as a team. Co-op play isn't all that exciting though, other then adding a second player on screen the game is exactly the same. If played on a small screen the zooming in and out of the screen can be a pain, making it even more difficult to keep up with what is going on. Unless you have a large monitor and two controllers at hand consider passing on this feature.

Aces Wild channels the style of late 90's Capcom fighting games and side scrolling titles with the UI design and the character animations but is a bit lacking when it comes to detail. Many of the environments feel lifeless and static. There are few interactive objects nor props. Generally, stages are constructed with a photographic backdrop layered with platforms that are crisp and clean but lacking in personality or style. A more dynamic environment could easily add another layer to the static world of Aces Wild and payed better homage to a genre where using objects in the environment as weapons has been a long standing staple. There's also a dearth of detail missing throughout all the characters with little to no animation involved. Fortunately, the soundtrack is well done delivering some fantastic 16bit tracks and sounds.

If Aces Wild Manic Brawling Action gets a sequel a more polished experienced shouldn't be too hard to achieve. The foundation of a great game is present but the overall experience becomes a bit repetitive as the variation in enemies and environment do little to evolve along the way. Manic Brawling Action is a tough game with some infuriating segments, there is no escaping the anger along the ride, but in some ways, that's inherent to the genre. Aces Wild is large dose of nostalgia for a low price, if you're itching for a beat-em up and have run out of other options pick it up. It might just be enough to scratch you right where you need it.

I played Witcher 2 after playing Witcher 3. If you are considering buying 3 you should play 2 first, both because it's a fun game on its own, and because it makes for a much richer experience knowing more of the context and references. But know that you might love 3 even if its prequel isn't the game for you. That's because Witcher 2 is:
- Much harder. The combat system is very unforgiving, and every fight must be planned out and prepared for. Boss fights may have you throwing your controller at the screen. The sequel has similar combat elements, and battles are not simply button-mashing affairs, but it's a lot more balanced and the learning curve is less steep. (3 also provides the courtesy of suggesting which fights you ought to run from because you're under-leveled.)
- Far more focused on item crafting. Both games feature a potion-crafting mechanism that plays a core function in the game, but whereas 2 makes you gather and use ingredients every time you want to replenish your items, 3 only makes you craft a recipe once, with a much simpler, grind-free mechanic to replace them after that.
- Short. Witcher 3 offers easily over 100 hours of gameplay, with DLC adding 20-30. Expect Witcher 2 to run maybe 20-25% as long.
- Small. Again, perhaps this isn't true compared to many other games, especially those released at the same time. But the three primary maps of Witcher 2 combined are 3% the size of the map of its sequel.
Again, Witcher 2 is fun and I do recommend it, especially if you're considering 3. But if you do and find any of the above limiting your enjoyment, know that these issues have been ironed out in the Game of the Decade-level sequel.

I'm not sure how to feel about this game. It's clearly trying to be like something made by Treasure and for a while, it really feels like it succeeds in doing this. The core parts of the game feel great, but there's just too many things letting it down.
Those core parts work really well - the movement and combat are simple while having a decent amount of depth. Rapid attacks build up the 'Wild' meter, which is used for both charged attacks and restoring health. It provides an interesting balance that adds a nice risk/reward element. The combat is fun and satisfying when it works out.
Unfortunately, there's a lot dragging this game down. There are only about five types of enemies, with a couple variations on each. This might not be a big deal if the fights felt like they were carefully designed, but later levels usually throw more enemies in at once. One missed dodge can lead to taking a string of hits and losing a large chunk of health. Boss battles have similar issues. Plenty of things simply feel too unforgiving or even unfair. If there was more variety in enemies along with more carefully designed fights, it could be a great game. It just ends up being difficult for dumb reasons, which is a shame because it has a lot of potential.

How Paradox tricked me into wasting a month fighting an unwinnable war.
First game, built a small civ, was boxed-in by hostile nighbors, gaps between galaxy arms, and limited wormhole range. Finally through working what I had to advance drive tech, and careful placement of a new wormhole generator, got a toe-hold on my first planet outside that.
For daring to venture outside my little box, the Shabtak decided I should be punished. A LOT.
You do not know the Shabtak Continuum, (all randomly generated races, not like civ with its historical figures), so imagine this. Ancient advanced race. Very creepy insects, ships like flying shields. Spiritual extremist alignment.
I was going to just stay away from the ancients, and never bother them. The Shabtak wouldn't let me. Said my first colony outside The Box was a holy planet.
For immediately apologizing and removing the colony as-asked, the Shabtak... destroyed my ENTIRE navy, every ship, EVERY spaceport around every planet, EVERY little mining station, then invaded a major colony and broke its defense force with genetically-engineered monsters. Only then, having beat me within an inch of extinction, did they offer a cease-fire, IF I accepted a Humiliation Penalty, which made ALL my surviving citizens unhappy, and drained my civilization's political influence.
Accepting the Humiliation, at the peace treaty signing ceremony, they ASSASSINATED MY LEADER. (What they didn't seem to get was my Republic changed leaders so frequently I barely remember which character is in which slot half the time, lol)
Wars have been started over less, but I was completely at their mercy, so I had to bear whatever they did to me.
Ordinary races in this game are less aggressive than AIs in Civ, which was a nice change of pace, but, these Ancients are bullies. Beat you down, then kick you while you curl into a fetal-position type bullies.
AFTER that, since I'd shown submission, the Shabtak spoke to me condensceningly, all the time, as they were wise sensei and I was their little adopted child. Just pouring salt in the psychological wound, grinding it in, grinding it in...
"Why hello there,  child." "What do you want, little one?" "We warn you, foolish child..."
Something snapped.
There was, against all odds, a couple patches of debris from damaged Shabtak ships. I scanned it, unlocked their core technologies. They had all apex weapons, shields, armor, and reactors. I still had to do the hard work of researching them myself. It took 50 simulated years.
An alliance of half the Galaxy decided I was easy pickings since I had nothing (the AIs were blissfully ignorant WHY all fleets were space dust now) and I fought them off. They had superior numbers and good tactics, but, I was building up for a higher-caliber opponent, and snagged half their territory to discourage them. I had the cruellest teachers imaginable, after all, and I needed the planets for the resources to support a large enough fleet to kill those teachers.
It took 100 simulated years. My Republic now had 6 different races working together in mixed planets of every type and a mix of leaders, (Star Trek) and spanned half the Galaxy with an amphibian admiral commanding the grand fleet of 150 vessels (Star Wars). My poor PC could barely render it, and the CPU core temp shot up whenever it was on-screen. If I advance any further I'm in-danger of not being able to get revenge on the Shabtak BECAUSE OF WINNING THE GAME AND ENDING IT.
At H-Hour, without warning, wormholes opened in every system of the Shabtak Continuum. I remembered from the first war what they had, how strong it was, where it was based in peacetime. I didn't even need to scout and tip my hand.
I was right, and I was also misled. The combat strengths stated BY THE GAME ENGINE were a lie. 20k fleets were shredded by 10k fleets. Each individual turret fired 3 shots for every 1 of mine. The Shabtak versions of the apex technologies were cheat-level good. Maybe they had rediculously high levels in generic technologies, say, Flash Coolant 30 for their beam weapons, and Shield Harmonics 25, and so on, IF they weren't cheating.
They were.
I saw "reinforcements" jump-in that weren't there before. If I'd seen them frantically construct out of starbases, I'd buy that, but no, the Ancients can just "beam in" cheating-good ships at will, by hack.
I fell for it, fake combat strengths, goading into rage, and all.
Good one, Paradox.

Stellaris, in a nutshell, is a hybrid between the sci-fi 4X and grand strategy genres.
When Stellaris launched last year, it was (to be brutally honest) an unfinished, unpolished mess. I ultimately came away from the game with a sour taste in my mouth, and I gave the game as it was in July 2016 (the 1.2 "Asimov" patch) a thumbs-down. The release of the expansion Utopia, with its accompanying free patch (1.5/"Banks") prompted me to return to the game again.
Having played about a hundred hours of the game with this latest patch, I think I can now give Stellaris a recommendation. Many of the problems that plagued the release version have been greatly improved on, if not entirely solved.
The AI is less braindead. Internal politics makes some sense. Ship combat feels much more balanced, where every ship class has a useful role to play. An actually functional sector AI makes the mid-game micromanagement slump much, much more bearable. A number of small but critical UI improvements (like being able to fully upgrade a building in one click, or manage sectors from the outliner) makes the moment-to-moment gameplay much less frustrating. Empire customization is also a bit more flexible. The new civics system allows for more unique empires and playstyles.
As of this patch, it's not a game that is devoid of flaws, yet. Certain aspects of the game still badly need a rebalance/rework - slavery, for example, or certain ascension paths, or ground combat, or the warscore system. It's still lacking major things like civilian trade or espionage. Diplomacy still tends towards ossification - as a campaign progresses, everyone gets locked into permanent pacts/federations. Federation mechanics are still total garbage. And on bigger galaxies, the tech tree tends to run out way before you actually achieve galactic dominance.
But finally the implementation of the gameplay in general have improved to a point where they do not impede the greatest strength of Paradox games - their ability to create an immersive world in which you can tell the story of a civilization.
The megastructures and ascension paths gated behind the Utopia paid expansion are cool, but honestly they're not strictly essential, more like late-game toys for the dedicated player. The meat of the improvements are available to owners of the base game. If the rest of Stellaris' expansions maintain this solid ratio of free to paid content, I feel comfortable recommending Stellaris, to both 4X players at large and fans of Paradox games.

Let's get this out of the way first: this game isn't for everyone. If you don't like old school (and I mean, Doom/Quake era) gameplay and hardcore randomization, then you shouldn't buy this game. That being said, if you enjoy either/both or are open minded, this could be right up your alley.
Rogue Shooter blends rogue-like elements (permadeath, random levels/items) with gunplay from the shooters of yore. It does have a couple of technical limitations (the lack of a volume slider, locked resolution, and oddball fullscreen modes), but the gameplay more than makes up for it. Weapons feel satisfying and varied, enemies are diverse, and levels (while basic) are never quite the same. Furthermore, the higher difficulties are challenging and give you a good space to grow into as you graduate from noob to veteran.
If you're a fan of modern roguelike hybrids, classic shooters, or just plain old innovative games, then Rogue Shooter is worth a shot. Don't take my word for it-check out the demo and see for yourself.

Edited: Now it's more of a proper review.
Initial impressions after 2 hours:
So far Rogue Shooter has actually been very fun. It's silly, colourful and fun. Anyone who remembers PC gaming in the early Nineties will likely approve. It's a Roguelike/Roguelite/I'm-not-going-to-be-drawn-into-an-internet-squabble-over-semantics FPS, Doom meets Rogue Legacy is the most common comparison I've been hearing, and with good reason. So far the only issue I can place on this game is the Steam Overlay is absolutely unusable, but this is patchable. I'll definitely be playing more of this when I don't need to be sociable.
Side note to the devs; Having a playthrough trailer was a very smart idea; it gave me a good idea of what I was getting into and it was that which earned a sale from me. Doubly important in this day and age when any old pap is coming onto Steam. I am glad my money went to a properly good game and not the next Earth: Year 2066
Now that I've played more:
Some more time later I can say the initial impressions held up but there are some things that I do need to address. Firstly, at this time is is seriously buggy. The music doesn't loop and I've had mooks appear outside of the map (though thankfully close enough for me to boot to death through the wall). I've not had a game breaker so far though a good mate of mine has come across a splintered map with unattached sections. Of course if this game's been patched then ignore this paragraph.
Another is the graphics and presentation. Personally I am fine with the cheesy cartoon style as not only does it invoke a Blake Stone esque vibe but it is a welcome change from the overly pixelled sprites of similar low-resource games. Still, it's not to everyone's style and if the screenshots bug you, seeing it in action won't win you over.
Once all is said and done, I can see myself returning to this game fairly regularily and giving it a bash. The numerous classes and the randomisation definitely have lasting appeal, like other such games.

It's very difficult for me to recommend this game.
Don't get me wrong, it's a fantastic excellent game, and one of the best of its kind in my Opinion.
However... as a Metal Gear game, it feels like it's trying to be Metal Gear rather than actually being Metal Gear.
And as a hack and slash, it's far to focus on it simple story for it so I'm good, hence the trying to be a Metal Gear part.
The stealth combat is difficult to get used to it first, mainly because you don't have a traditional block button, but instead a very unconventional Perry Technique, which at first is difficult to use; but become second nature sooner than you would think. Other than that it's pretty standard; just more aggressive.
Stealth is "technically" in the game... but not really. If anything it just gets in the way of the Focus of the game, and slows everything down.
One of these games biggest show pieces are the boss fights, which do everything but fail to disappoint! They're all very doing unique, all with different styles of attack in their own method for you to counter.
Not to mention the music for this game is absolutely brilliant. Every boss fight track fills you with energy, while still fitting the moment just right.
Overall, I would say it's a great game. But something Metal Gear fans should look more consciously into before picking up, and as an action game, expect someone a little bit more seasoned in the typical game of the genre.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a gem of a game. It ticks all the right boxes you wish for in a game. It's a Metroidvania game in which you have to revisit places as you earn more abilities, with a growing and original story, very good voice acting with characters that feel very alive and real, and a peculiar companion who gave me a few good laughs and grew fond of. The combat is simple and straight forward with an AI who is smart but not too hard, however for the ones who like a challenge there are 2 higher difficulties above normal and an achievement for passing it on one of those 2 difficulties. I never got bored in this game and I enjoyed every minute of it as the story, the quests and the general progression of the game are very balanced. The only criticisms I could make are that the story could have been a bit more developped at the end and that I could have easily played the game for twice as long. So I just wish for more games like this!
Dust: An Elysian Tail is just a fun, moving game that you will remember for how unique it is. For your sake, I hope you have the opportunity to buy it and enjoy it.

F.E.A.R. is one of those games, which was 90000% better when you were a child, but now that you've grown up, and so has the gaming industry, it's aged really poorly.
Fyi, some spoilers (ish, you're really not missing anything)
The story gets worse as the series progressed. Having two timelines because WB sold the rights to vivendi first then monolith produces two different "cannons" meaning that what happens in the first game means little anyway. The combat is fun at first but after about an hour it becomes grating to say the least. Given that the only other element is "story" the game really just ends up being in a crisis as to what it wants to be.
F.E.A.R. First Encounter Assault Recon (this one) is the best of all the games, and you will get some enjoyment out of it, but no matter which expansion/sequel you play after the series just gets dull. You can pick from vivendi's "Everything you did in this game didn't matter and everyone dies" which comes in the form of two mediocre "expansions". You could also pick  monoliths timeline which starts a bit more promisingly with F.E.A.R. 2,  but then shoots it's own foot off when it kills the protagonist we spent the whole game getting attached to in F.E.A.R. 3. which is a sorry excuse for a game if ever I saw one.
Enviroments are boring to say the least. Once you get past the whole "decayed urban centre" you get "slightly futuristic office" and then back to a mix of the two. Guns are fairly bland, you get various types of machine gun ranging from pop-gun pew, heavy pew, lots of pew and long range pew. They have names apparently but somehow it really didn't seem important. One thing I did like is that, your starting weapon, the pistol is one of the best weapons throughout the whole game.
Characters are really poorly done, there's very little fleshing out, your own character you only really get any developments much later/at the end of the game. The there's a team mate who goes missing who no one really gives a toss about, some scientists who die, a scientist daughter who dies, evil cannibal guy who dies (and thanks to both cannons annoyingly comes back anyway) , kick♥♥♥♥♥black guy who dies in one of the cannons and a hot asian who also dies in one of the cannons. My favourite was the nice asian lady because she hits on you at one point. Overall it doesn't really leave much room for attachments or immersion though.
The cover mechanics are interesting in the way of you poke your head out you get shot, but that's alright because armour is literally everywhere as well as the same generic medic box, ammunition isn't too much of a problem - rough conservation means you can use your favourite gun 70% of the time, and the slow motion feature is to be honest, boringly repetitive.
The enemy varies from several types "grunt" "stronger grunt" "tough cyborg" "mech robot" "flying mech robot" and some nasty ghost fellows. For it's time? Great! Nowadays?♥♥♥♥♥♥poor and boring. Not to mention the fact they conveniently shout literally everything they're doing before they do it handly giving you the perfect 3 seconds to jump out and rain bullets on their day.
This all being said, it's a good game. I remember watching my dad when I was younger playing it and often I'd be sent away because it was that scary. Now I'm older of course, the scary bits are just rather inconveinient.
The series really needs a reboot. A remake of the first game, and an entirely new set of sequels with a storyline that will actually make me show interest and concern for the characters. It needs to foccus more on immersion and storyline than combat and gameplay. Multiplayer and Co-op kill off almost totally the horror/terror element to the game so that simply needs to stop. Killing off every character within the space of a game also is a pretty big no if you want people to get attached to them or care about your series. The fact that the first game spends almost it's entirety making you scared of the evil cannibal guy and then F.E.A.R. 3 lets you play as him totally kills any vibes it might have had as a horror title.
If I had to describe the whole series and this game in one word it'd just be dull or bland. The most interesting part of the whole F.E.A.R story, is when in F.E.A.R. 2 the main protagonist gets sexually used against his will. And that's purely out of the fact that it's the first time I've seen that conecpt in gaming; that such a thing happens to a guy, and not because it's actually interesting.
I think the biggest let down of all is that the game starts off with a pretty tactical theme, and as it progresses, the whole operational feel just goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ which rather than immerses you, just makes you feel the developers needed an excuse to make the game way too simplistic. Everyone conveiniently seems to die ¬_¬
Tl;DR; dull game, ruined series, too many cannons, and everyone dies before you can care.

This game is bad. Now I know this is a controversal opinion here but here are my points.
The humor is hit or miss for me, personally I found the humor in Unepic to be good, and it is obvious that they are trying to go for the same feel, but I do not think it works.
It tries to come off philosophical like Ghost in the Shell (one of the main inspirations), Bladerunner, or the Matirx on commenting on robotic and AI and the philosophy of the future, but adds nothing new to the topic, just the same old "robots are people too" schtick.
Combat is fun, but I think they try and flood the screen with too many enemies in a game where mobility is simplified making it so there is often times a ridiculous amount of unavoidable damage and too many things on the screen to properly account for everything. The boss battles are too simple, sometimes they are good and requier some work, but other times they are a DPS race where I need to deal more damage than I take and that is how I dealt with every boss up until the point I am at.
The puzzles are a mix of monotonous and infuriating. They are punishing, but requier repetition of having your AI ghost move between them. Don't even get me started on the lab missions.
Before I am labled a hater by anyone I will say that the voice acting is not half bad. The upgrade system is unique and enjoyable, and I do find the combat fun most times.

A good game that could have been a fantastic game.
If you ever wanted to play a 2d version of a game like DMC or Bayonetta, this is probably the exact game you’re looking for, but have never heard of. Aces wild is an interesting mix up between crazy action beat um up, and old school side scrolling beat um up, That does the former much better than it does the latter.

It’s crazy to think that an Indy made game like this, could have out classed so many games made by major publishers, if it weren’t for a few key features missing from it’s incredibly fluid, over the top play style. The games basic controls consist of two main attacks, a dash, and a guard, The light attack button is your standard combo attack, and the other is the heavy crash attack button. The game also has an extremely interesting mechanic that holds it all together, called wild meter. The wild meter fills up as you preform combos. The fun thing about it is that it has a large variety of uses, wild can be used for preforming crash attacks, for charging  crash attacks, crash counters, extended dashing, and activating “panic”. Not only this, but the more wild you have the more base damage your combos do, which constantly keeps you thinking about how much wild you spend as opposed to keeping it in to do more combo damage to your enemy’s. Also unlike a lot of other games, all of these skills are essential to master, and none of them feel pointless. The game has a great deal of enemy variety, all of which demand a different way of fighting. The weaker foes in the game can be mowed down with basic combos, but it gets really tricky when you have to fight enemies who are not affected by hit stun because of their shields, or enemy’s that spam projectiles, and others that counter. The game makes you think about what enemy’s you want to prioritize, as well as what you want to use your wild on. Sometimes it will be more beneficial to fight a good long fight while dogging all incoming attacks mixing up your basic, and crash attacks to gain wild faster. Or sometimes it will be better rolling into the part of the level, and destroying everything with one fully charged crash attack, causing all your enemy’s to knock into each other at full force. Or you just might want to play it safe till you get enough wild to use a panic, which restores a great deal of health depending on how much wild you have.
Another huge part of the games great combat, is how the dashing and dogging work so well, it never gets old watching your enemy’s fly to the other side of the screen, and catching right up to them, in a split second just to keep the beat down going, then sending the body whirling into the rest of the enemy’s. It also serves as a great tool to catch, and pummel many of the bosses before they are able to perform an attack, if they don’t have a guard up. It’s also nice to see that dogging has an extended window of invincibility which makes it easier to preform counters which comes in handy to beating most of the games earlier foes. The game does a fantastic job at keeping the action going even at some of its more chaotic points, dashing around preforming a combo, finishing a guy of and diving right into the rest of the group with a fully charged crash attack is satisfying. The game is a complete joy to play, and delivers on making the player feel like a badass, as the action never breaks, till the last few stages.
Unfortunately as much as I want to gush about the games combat it has some extremely large draw backs as the game moves on. Now it should be said that these games are difficult by nature, but towards the end of the game, you can be punished with death for the slightest mistakes. It’s all fun and games till you have around one hundred enemies on screen, and twenty of them are throwing projectiles at you, making it look more like a smup than a beat um up. At this stage one missed dodge will open you up to a fifty or more hit combo taking half your life away, only to wind up in the same position less than a second later because you failed to take out any enemies, because they were too busy styling all over your face. It’s also not fun to run into twenty or so enemy’s that all have shields, and aren’t affected by hit stun, and are essentially invulnerable, while they mercilessly hack away at you. In fights like these, the games mechanics begin to break down. Counters become worthless; with only limited invincibility leaving you open to punishment after only killing a few guys. And crash attacks become almost unusable, as you may never get even the one second it takes to charge them up to guard break. And even if you do, it’s easy to wiff, and wastes your entire wild meter on noting, while you put your controller down, and get styled on into oblivion. Just whiffing a crash attack at certain times can spell instant death, because you may not get a good chance to gain enough wild back to guard break. The games main problem is that it doesn’t include any kind of upgrade system that is seen in any of the games 3d counter parts. The game makes itself into a perfect example of, why such things are needed in a manic brawler. Being able to customize how you fight keeps it so you can keep playing the game the way you want to play, instead of the game playing you, as you are forced to conform to enemy patterns, or die. It would have been fantastic to put points into the counter mechanic so that you could remain invincible while you perform a crash counter, so you know you’re not going to burn your entire wild meter for nothing. Being able to upgrade key mechanics is a must for games like this, 3d or 2d. It just can’t stay true to its old school arcade street brawler roots, where you don’t get any kind of upgrades, and you have to rely on basic mechanics. If things stay to basic, the enemy verity begins to cap out at a point, and you end up with a game that just poor’s on the hurt to artificially extend its length.
Another one of the games sore spots is its presentation it’s environments are clean, but dull, character animation’s outside of aces, are very poor, and aces are very lacking, and enemy designs are very hit or miss. You only get two playable characters with only minor differences. The game is only about seven to eight hours long, and the game has no reliability, or online play at all. Despite the name, F.E.A.R. is not primarily a horror game.  It is a fast paced FPS with horror elements, and its best attributes are not horror related.  What F.E.A.R. does best, and what it does better than any other game I've played to this day, is make shooting people an art.  Seriously.  This is accomplished by a combination of things, namely:
- The best, most advanced AI of any action game to date.  AI utilizes cover and various teamwork tactics better than in any other shooter, as well as flanking, and their understanding of the environment is great.  RPS has a good writeup on this:
Moving on...
- Perhaps the best ragdoll physics/animations I have ever seen.  They are not entirely realistic, but are entirely awesome.
- Everything not bolted down is a physics object, and bullets and explosions send them flying.  Great physics, well above average by today's standards (better than most modern shooters).
- More and better quality particle effects demonstrating greater realism than most other shooters (yes, even the vast majority of today's).  From dust to sparks and other debris, bullets send them all flying, bullet decals are most believable and don't just disappear.
- Outstanding sound effects, better than what we get today since 3D sound processing and hardware acceleration is essentially dead, and EAX Advanced HD (aka EAX 3, which this game uses) goes many steps further than what today's games attempt with regards to dynamic environmental sound effects (e.g. multiple simultaneous sound environments, more realistic dynamic echoes/reverb).
- Top tier blood and gore, and body physics + blood splatter don't disappear when an NPC dies.  Few games can compete with this game in this regard.
- Cool, unique guns, such as a militarized nail gun that can nail people to walls, and a particle rifle that vaporizes enemies leaving behind only a blackened skeleton.  It also has multiple kinds of melee attacks (regular grounded one, aerial one, slide, and more), a testament to the game's greater attention to detail with movement.  Other examples of this include a first person player mesh, more movement sounds than most FPS games bother to include, and leaning which was once a standard in PC games (it was during its time period).
- Slow motion of course.  This allows you to shoot down thrown grenades and rockets, and be the ultimate badass.
Notice how Steam's official screenshots all capture shootouts and particles.  This is why.
You see, F.E.A.R. actually utilizes advanced technology (much of which is still advanced and superior by today's standards, like those specified above) to improve gameplay drastically, not just for eye candy.  Compare that to the majority of AAA shooters, in which everything is static and the AI is dumber than a bag of rocks and totally dysfunctional even in the simplest of scenarios... atrocious.  Because of the dynamic nature of F.E.A.R., every shootout can be its own unique experience and its own work of art.
It is both funny and sad how F.E.A.R., a 2005 game, is more technologically advanced in many ways than AAA games coming 10 years later.  Not just the elements listed above, but others such as the number of dynamic lights and dynamic shadows (almost every light source is dynamic and casts dynamic shadows, rare in AAA games even today), reflections, water.  Make sure you download the dynamic flashlight mod, it really adds to the atmosphere.
F.E.A.R.'s storytelling is awful, but hardly anyone will care when playing it because it's not really the point.  This game is about shooting people, and no game does it better.  For this reason, playing F.E.A.R. might make you appreciate all other shooters a bit less... that is, the actual act of shooting people, because F.E.A.R. does the best job.
F.E.A.R.'s multiplayer can be downloaded separately for free.
Also beware of compatibility issues with Logitech peripherals.  If you use a Logitech mouse and/or keyboard, disable all "HID-compliant devices" under Human Interface Devices within your Device Manager, or else your performance will tank regardless of your system (I was getting 40 FPS on a GTX 1080 at 2560 x 1440 before I did this).
For those who want more F.E.A.R. and hate the sequels (that describes everyone who played the sequels), play Underhell.  It is a Source mod that only requires Source SDK Base 2007 to be installed, no game required.  It is inspired by F.E.A.R., it is similarly good as a shooter in all respects (AI, ragdolls, blood/gore, and particles are not as good but still very good), but it is a far creepier horror game, it actually has good storytelling, and it is just a better game in every way besides shooting people.

The early-game of Stellaris is easily some of the most fun I've ever had in a 4X game. There's always stuff to do, with quests leading you along, systems to explore, races to meet, etc etc. It really makes you feel like you're leading your fledgling civilization on the path to galactic dominance. The customization options for your empire are incredible, allowing you to create a race that suits your playstyle and role-playing preferences.
However, that being said, I find the mid-game is generally quite stale. The quest-events are few and far between, the majority of the systems in your neck of the galaxy have been explored, and there's a lot of sitting and waiting for research and buildings to complete. It's stagnant. I think one of the main issues that causes this is the lack of meaningful diplomacy. The other civilizations you encounter are IMPOSSIBLE to work with, refusing to give you anything unless you're completely dominant in terms of naval power, fleet capacity, and technology, and even then it's a chore to make them cooperate. This, as you might imagine, is detrimental if you choose to play as a pacifist race as you inevitably fall behind the militarized civilizations and you have no diplomatic avenues to pursue other than complete subservience.
All that being said though, the early-game almost makes it worth it because it gives you an idea of the immense potential this game has. If Paradox can fix the diplomacy system and make the mid- and late-game as enjoyable as the beginning, I have no doubt Stellaris will go down as one of the most legendary Space 4X's of all time.

The talented people at CD Projekt deliver another outstanding game with the second chapter in the Witcher series, inspired by and following Polish writer Sapkowski's narrative.
The Witcher 2 is a direct sequel to the first one, improved in many ways, but not without its flaws.
What I felt as I started the game and played through it was that the developers really aimed for something bigger, different and entirely original. A new graphic engine, combat system and overall look were the things they aimed for, in my opinion. Despite this, it was difficult for me to consider this chapter a complete game on its own, as all of the returning characters, protagonist included, carried many plot elements from the first game into this one, and many of these were left unfinished. It constantly reminded me that this was not as much a story in its own, but more a setup for the third chapter.
The combat system was a great improvement, completely replacing the different styles from the first game with a normal hack&slash mode, very easy to understand, but difficult to master. Playing just normal difficulty meant you would get killed pretty easily, unless you understand the mechanics, and prepare accordingly using every tool at your disposal (potions became really a must-have now, with the nice addition of bombs and traps), forcing you to think as a professional monster-slayer. Boss-battles were also improved from the first game, making them different and interesting (altough quite small in number).
Inventory management is still a mess. The game now included a crafting system for mostly everything, pushing you to collect every little item you find scattered around the map. This proves wortwhile in some occasions, and completely useless in others, as you would sometimes find better weapons and armor that easily surpassed the ones you craft. The best armor in the game is something that you have to craft, but you only get to use it for the last thirty minutes...
As the game is quite short, the plot is probably the best and worst thing about it, for a number of reasons. It is certainly filled with many interesting characters, well defined and designed (as an artist myself, I could not help but appreciate the work put into the character models - absolutely stunning); but many of these can be quite confusing to someone who is not familiar with the world's lore and previous backstory. Too many elements are borrowed from the books storyline, making it worthwhile to someone who is familiar with them, but very confusing for newcomers. As an example, there is one questline that can be completed in different ways, but one way requires the player to be quite familiar with some historical data from a very important battle that occured in the last book.
The plot is very deep, complex and political. It requires you to pay attention to every detail in order to fully understand it, and even then many of the branching plots are left unfinished, probably to be continued in the third chapter. As this is a very linear game, I would not reccomend it to someone who is not in it for the story. The advantage in this are obviously the quests: varied, complex and interesting, easily superior to many other RPGs.
As for the soundtrack and atmosphere, I felt like this time they were aiming for something different. Both are still very high quality, but they lacked the gloomy witcheresque feeling from the first game that I loved, and felt more like a high fantasy ambience.
Overall, The Witcher2 is a very good game, but unlike the first one, it did not feel like a story that you can enjoy on its own. It was clearly a major setup for the third game, and aimed in some occasions at book readers.
PROS: Story-Quests-Characters-Combat System-It makes you feel like a true Witcher-Choices-Design and Art Style-
CONS: Lenght-Inventory Management-

TL;DR It is fun but used to be better, If you like RP you will be right at home.

A difficult game, to say the least, but it's so worth it. The depth of this game, not to mention the unlockables and the pure challenge of it creates an addictive rogue-like game with infinite replayability.

For those of you who enjoyed classic shooters, this is a treat. It has retro-borderlands style graphics and the loot mechanics are comparable to that of your basic roguelike game.
Pick your background (prisoner, scientist etc., and there are a LOT!) which essentially defines what you start with in your inventory. You move up randomly generated floors and find loot and kill monsters for exp. When you level, you can unlock a perk (and there are quite a bit to choose from). You can combine materials that you find to create anything from useful items to experimental syringes that yield random buffs/debuffs.
Movement is different than most first person games, whereas you cannot look up or down, but only left and right. You manage your inventory in real time (you'll be doing this quite a bit considering all the items you'll be picking up). You'll also be hacking (mouse cursor dodging mini-game) datapads in real time too so best to clear the floor of enemies before attempting this. You get a random amount of credits (possibly other rewards) for successful hacking attempts.
When you die, you start over, but the 'intel' acquired is persistent. You acquire more and more intel as you replay the game more and more, and with more intel comes more unlockables whether that's more available perks, backgrounds and enemies.
My only gripe is that there are many dead ends, but because you move quite fast (what with the fast paced gameplay), it's negligible.
[Edit] The music also does not loop, so if you're on a floor for some time clearing enemies or hacking datapads, then you'll notice the music will eventually cut out and you'll be left alone in silence.
For the current sale price ($4.99) this game is more than worth it. If you're a fan of roguelike games and enjoyed classic shooters like Duke Nukem and Quake, you'll definitely be getting your money's worth.

One of the best games you will ever play.  If you want a surprisingly believable story involving government and global conspiracies with a multitude of characters & a wide variety of skills to upgrade, buy this, you will not be let down.  The soundtrack  is phenomenal, the music matches exactly what the level and setting feels like.  There are lots of skills in which you can put skill points into to make yourself a deadlier close range fighter, a pinpoint sniper, a more proficient hacker, and more.  The augmentations are awesome, you can give yourself the ability to cloak, to see through walls, to run as quiet as amouse, and much more.  There's an abundance of weapons which you can upgrade to give it a laser, a scope, make it more accurate, and more.  There's really just more of everything.  You get to go to Hong Kong, Paris, and even Area 51, the places are very memorable, with the amazing soundtrack to accompany them.  One thing that people would argue as being a flaw of this game, is the voice acting, and while I do agree it's mediocre, it's that voice acting that gives the game even more charm to it.  Fighting with enemies isn't really that much fun though, it's a standard 'click until dead' combat system.
+ Believable and gripping story with lots of twists
+ Best video game soundtrack ever
+ Many skills and augmentations
+ Many weapons with modifications to boot
+ Memorable levels and great level design
+/- Off-kilter voice acting can be a turn-off
- Battles could be done much better

The first Black Ops in the game series, it is not much different from the rest of the previous games before it. Only the settings and story is different.
The story takes place in the 1960's, playing as Alex Mason, an american operative who is interrogated by unknown captors.
They question his previous missions, which take place in various countries. The story heavily focuses on the Cold War Era, and there are several famous people during the Cold War who appear in this game, such as Kennedy and Castro.
You can expect all kinds of classic CoD cliché's from previous games in this one, aswell as a twist.
The gameplay is very, very much the same as previous Call of Duty titles. Despite this, the multiplayer feels different from previous and newer CoD MP games. It feels more "grittier" with turning, shooting and especially reloading. Not even Black ops 2 MP has this. Overall the animations feel more focused when firing and reloading.
The MP of this game is no different from previous games, there are tons of different game modes, a fair amount of maps, lots of weapons and the usual killstreaks. Being a first (This was in 2010 again), you can customize your characters with face paints, and there are quite alot to unlock.
Unlike previous MP's, you get "CoD" points each match that you can use to unlock everything with.
The game also includes a Zombies mode, having up to 4 co-op players team up against waves upon waves of zombies. The aiming in this feels abit stiff, and sometimes when firing at a zombies head despite aiming perfectly well, the shots may miss.
The settings and story in zombies mode is of a supernatural theme, with anything from zombies, ghosts and hounds from hell.
The graphics, for a 2010 game, are very good. Back then, it was of course something really well made, graphics wise.
Though if you are looking for something amazing for todays standards, you are going to be abit dissapointed.
Yes, I would, but only for the hardcore CoD fans. The MP side is great and what most buyers back in 2010 went for. Today, 2015, I'd say you have to see the story and zombies mode as a bonus when buying the game. The MP side of the game is still very active and has players on servers 24/7, even late night. There are also alot of achievements, both story mode and in zombies. MP there are only 3 achievements.
This game is not worth its price tag of 39,99 though. It is 5 years old, and strangely the devs haven't lowered the price. Get it on a sale instead, but even then, you're lucky if you get it for 10.
I really enjoyed the twist in the story mode.
I was impressed by the menu, having not seen this style in any other game.
I was not impressed by the DLC map packs, and it is very known these days that not many play the map packs anymore, leaving you with a waste of money, so keep this in mind.
You can't review the DLC Map packs individually like other games have on steam. While there are some reviews on them, they are few, and simple, and no doubt done by the devs/friends of the devs, raising the question as to why the reviewing has been disabled for these map packs.
TL:DR: DONT BUY THIS DLC, ITS OVER 4 YEARS OLD AND CANT BE PLAYED ANYMORE DUE TO LIMITED PLAYERBASE.
One of the steep priced DLC's I've ever bought and regretted. It's surprising how this has so many positive reviews, but they are all funnily enough extremely short. No doubt some fanboys or devs decided to boost this dlc's rep by making such a short review.
This dlc comes at full price, 13,99 euro, way to much for something that's over 4 years old by now from this review. A typical marketing strategy from the devs and their publisher, simply leave the price tag at full since launch, with very few sales.
This dlc has 5 different maps, nothing more, nothing less. No bonus weapons and such.
4 multiplayer maps and 1 zombie mode map.
Now I bought this dlc simply for MP maps, not the zombie one, but I saw that as an extra bonus.
Today I defently regret this, and this is no way worth its full price. It's a downright scam if you press to buy it for 13,99 euro, there is alot of other stuff you can spend your money on.
So why the negative review? Because, all CoD games have this dlc problem pattern. When a new CoD game comes out, the playerbase moves on to the next new thing and abandons (75% of the players atleast) the previous game/s. This leaves a very little, staggering playerbase left, and thus the amount of players who own the dlcs can't find any new games to play these dlc maps. This is why there should never have been dlc map packs in the first place. I admit I fell for the trap. Not once or twice, but thrice, having bought a beautifull map pack in MW3 and BO2. Don't take me wrong, these maps are fun to play on, and are stunningly beautiful. The issue here is not being able to play the dlc anymore. You have to either find friends to start a game and play with, or simply try and hit daytime in hope there just might be a server or two. The chances are extremely low.
The Maps are detailed, entertaining to play on.
A map based on the Berlin Wall, fighting in the snow covered streets of the german capital, the map features a "restricted zone" in the middle among the walls. Running through it will cause automated turrets in towers to kill you. Two parts of the walls have been blown apart and players are able to run between safely from the towers.
A map set in the Antartica, an abandoned german base with thin cliff bridges that can be shot or exploded to cause humiliating deaths to players. Perfect for any snow/ice lovers, contains the Southern Lights.
A map set in Hong Kong on building rooftops (You better believe it). Players clash with eachother throughout these large buildings filled with the classic stuff that every major, packed city has (signs, chimneys, antenna's etc). Surprisingly, the buildings still stand after the matches end and a good amount of airstrikes have been used. A good old CoD logic.
A map set at a  hockey stadium in New York, the fights focuses around the outside of the stadium aswell as inside where the ticket booths are. You can't enter into the hockey arena. The map lives up to its name though, the feeling of being at a stadium is well received in this map. Has a large 'Earth' statue fountain in the middle of it.
The only zombie map in this pack, Ascension takes place in an abandoned Soviet Cosmodome. Instead of Hellhounds, zombified monkeys appear instead, straight from space! The WWII characters make their apperance in this map from the World at War Zombie cast.
The maps are great, but for the price, it's simply too steep, counting the age of this dlc aswell. Not only that, but the chances of playing the 4 MP maps with other random players are slim.

The witcher 2 continues the story from where the last game ended, where an assassin attempted to murder the king of Temeria, king Foltest. The assassin was unsuccessful, he was killed before he could reach Foltest. When Geralt unmasked the assassin he is revealed to be a witcher.
Some time after the events from the first game, another assassin kills Demavend III, the ruler of Aedrin. Some More time go by, Foltest with his army and Geralt at his side, attacks La Valette castle. They are successful in taking over the castle. King Foltest reunites with his two children, Anais and Boussy locked up in a tower, with help from Geralt. In the tower with Foltest's children is a blind monk. As Anais and Boussy leaves the room, the monk throws off his cape to Murder king Foltest. This time the assassination on Foltest was a success. The assassin is reavealed to be yet another witcher. He flees and jump out of the castle tower. Two soildiers enter the tower only to find Geralt with king Foltest's corpse lying on the ground, Geralt is framed for the murder of the king of Temeria. He is taken to the castle dungeons for interrogation, this is how he meets Vernon Roche, a commander of the Blue Stripes, a special force in the Temerian military. He trusts Geralt and thus he decides to help Geralt find the real murderer. Geralt is still trying to recover his memory which he lost in the beginning of the first game.
The dialogue and voice acting has also been upgraded, the conversations feel way more real and alive.
The graphics have Been upgraded a lot from the first game, it actually looks quite amazing for the time it came out. Characters also look much more unique. They have also added more cutscenes and the new animations look very good. The UI has also been changed, The UI in the first game could be a mess at times, but it looks a lot better in witcher 2.
Something i miss with the UI from the original witcher game however, is the 3D witcher medallion in the top left corner.
The sound quality is much better than it was in the first game, and of course the music is still amazing, the soundtrack has become one of my favorite soundtracks of all time. The soundtrack is epic and it fits the theme of the game.
Perhaps one of the biggest changes to the witcher 2 is the new action combat system, the group fighting mode is gone now you can use either fast attacks or strong attacks in battle. They have added rolling and blocking to the combat, the combat is much more fast phased. I have to say i really like the new combat system, its not as frustrating as the combat from the first game. You still have your magical witcher signs, and this time you have every sign unlocked from the start of the game.
There is also a brand new alchemy system, now you can only create and drink potions while meditating, and you can only have three potions active at a time. The potions also last very short, in the first game they lasted for several in-game hours, now they only last 10 minutes. A big problem with this is that potions and other buffs last over cutscenes which means that some potions wear off before a fight, and you can't drink a new one since you're in fight.
The character building is not as good in the witcher 2 as it was in the first game in my opinion. You can however get some quite satisfying finishers. The alchemy tree is not very good, and thats due to the bad alchemy system, so if you're planning to play this game i wouldn't recommend to do an alchemy build as it might not work out so well.
The game runs pretty good on my computer, but I have heard of people having optimization issues. I have however experienced a couple of hard crashes and freezes, which is pretty annoying if you haven't saved your game in a while.
The game has its flaws but it's still an amazing game. I'll give an 8/10 to the whole game as I didn't really like the alchemy system nor do I think that the story can match up with the first game, but the combat is definitely a big upgrade to the games gameplay and a kick in the right direction

Just imagine a 2D version of Devil May Cry. It has the same fast, over the top fighting action in a full-screen environment, filled with colorful backgrounds, a pumped up electro-pop soundtrack and a wacky, yet interesting amalgam of martial arts, samurais, ninja clans and military technology. The "Wild" mechanic adds a new layer of depth and strategy to the game, requiring you to manage your resources to go either for high damage, high stakes fights with huge waves of enemies, or a more slow paced, defensive approach. Beware of this game though, as this one is not begineer friendly in any way, not even in the "easiest" difficulty. Lots of touch-of-death beatdowns, cheap enemies, and deceitful stages wait for you to get frustrated and consumed in gaming rage. This title required a lot of patience, trial and error, rinse and repeat gameplay, and of course, practice, for me to get at least decent. But once I did, it was incredibly satisfying and one of the most unique experiences I've ever had with the genre. Definitely recommended for the hardcore beat 'em up enthusiast who is looking for new challenges to conquer.

Ever since Master of Orion 2 I've waited for a worthy successor to the 4x genre, and after numerous failures and utter dissapointments (from MoO3 up until Beyond Earth) the candidate was finally released and in the different genre altogether - grand strategy and not a turn based game at all.
The game absolutly shines; exploration is terrific, quest-based scripting works well, empire managment is easy and satisfying, graphics are gorgeous, music is haunting and I am always left wanting for more.
Where the game lacks is the (current) lack of more detailed combat and inter-species diplomacy, but we are reassured by Paradox these will be addressed shortly in the 1.3 patch. Furthermore there is no spying at all, however I'm certain this aspect will also whow up sooner than later in a form of a DLC (which is a shame since spying should have been in there since day 1).
After all is said and done, over 300hours in game have left me with a feeling that I've seen it all, and done it all, but this is where the wonderful modding comunity steps in. With hundreds of large game-changing mods one is never bored, and the core gameplay experience can be tweaked to anyone's liking.
I haven't played a game this engrossing in decades.

Deus Ex is a cyberpunk RPG with FPS elements... or is it the other way around? The game places you in the shoes of a nano-augmented U.N. super-soldier, fighting terrorism across the globe as you uncover conspiraces around you and secret underground bases literally everywhere. The story takes you through the dark alleyways of New York, the Paris catacombs, the cramped, neon quarters of Hong Kong and the white h- Oh, wait. The levels are huge, littered with bonus items and side-quests for the explorer, and even more context is added when you read the numerous newspapers, books and datacubes scattered around.
It's all about freedom of choice. You can go through the entire game without killing anyone, sneaking through each area and pacifying targets with non-lethal means, but you can also play Rambo, running and gunning down enemies with a vast array of customizable futuristic weapons. On the other hand, you could stay perched atop a rooftop and pick off targets with a sniper rifle, or try to smooth talk your way into privileged information. You can also choose whether to enter an enemy base through the front door (probably not a good idea), find an alternate entrance through air ducts, or bypass a locked rear entrance by finding the code or hacking the keypad.
The voice acting isn't great, the AI isn't terribly smart and some of the design choices were ill-advised (Swimming and environmental protection, anyone?), but they're easily overlooked. Graphically, it can seem a bit dated (It was made on the modified Unreal 1 engine, after all.), but this is easily remedied with the user-made HD texture pack, DirectX10 Renderer and ENB Series. Aesthetically though, it's gorgeous. It's a world of industrial decay, towering buildings, dark alleyways, a somber castle, an secret world under the city, a grayeard full of secrets, as well as some familiar settings (Hell's Kitchen, for instance, used a reference of the real-world location for its design)
Add to that a vast plethora of mods and multiplayer deathmatch/team modes and you've got quite a bit of staying power. Oh, yeah, and the music is awesome.
Upon release, this game received universal praise and earned top spots on countless "best games ever" lists, including PC Gamer's. To this day, whenever the game is mentioned, it's re-installed en masse. As revolutionary as Half-Life and highly influential, it's definitely worth a playthrough.

If you play strictly keyboard & mouse, AVOID AT ALL COSTS.
Default controls are WASD for movement, which you need to use in the menus. Arrow keys are completely ignored, as is the mouse.
Keyboard setup is handled so badly that it's practically guaranteed to screw up your controls so badly that you have to dig around in the game's files and delete the configuration. This is one of those "go down the list and assign every single command" kinds of setups. Escape is registerred as an input during this, presumably so you can immediately start screwing things up. If you get past that and are successfully inputting your controls, you will then notice that the movement commands are at the very bottom of the list. Some VERY LOGICAL alternatives people could use for movement are the arrow keys or the numpad's arrows. Except those aren't recognized by this game. So then you're stuck having to navigate menus with some random set of keys (or giving up and deleting the config. Again) until you can reconfigure them.
I've been encountering this kind of thing in a lot of games lately, and it seriously needs to stop. I don't care if a game "plays better" on a controller. That is no excuse to cripple the experience of keyboard users. When the menus alone are enough to cause a rage quit before the player has even gotten to the game itself, THAT IS A PROBLEM.

Currently stuck on the final stretch of the game thanks to a plethora of technical issues. This game is easily one of the worst ports I've played. KB+M support is exceptionally terrible, so a controller is 100% required. Next issue, the game is locked to 30fps. I was getting weird stuttering glitches from the outset, not frame drops per say, just completely freezing my screen while looping the same two frames. I have to tab out and in to fix this, and still don't know what causes it. It has slowly gotten more and more common as I progressed through the games 3 islands, it used to occur once every fight, now happens once every few seconds. I have tried verifying the game cache, to no avail. I am using Win10, running in Win7 compatability mode stops the stuttering issue, but seems to completely mess the frame rate randomly, crashing and freezing the game. Assets fail to load all the time currently, I can see through objects and enemies constantly disappear, leaving me swinging wildly into the air.
If you're somehow still interested in the game after the wall of technical issues above, it is an uninspired hack and slash game. You travel to different points, usually to rescue fellow Viking clan members, and then mount an assault on the islands major stronghold. It gets repetitive, you are forced to use the broken stealth, and combat sucks. However, I found the gameplay somewhat enjoyable for some reason, partly because its so simple and mindless you can just zone out while playing. The big battles are a nice spectacle, but do nothing to fix the games issues, and you'll get tired of them after the first one. I'd probably recommend this game if you could bypass the technical issues, but sadly it seems that you cannot.
