Just finished playing this game on win10. And seeing this game was published by Sega I expected a lot of bugs, but didn't really experience any. Exept for one. Going to the dragon's eye view the screen can go "tilt". Going to desktop and back into the game through alt-tab fixed it every time.
Other then that this game was enjoyable even though it has many rough edges. You start in a small settlement and have to build up an army. The game was pretty lineair and walked you straight from point A to B in a logical and cleanly designed fashion. This makes the experience quite relaxing, but also predictable and repetitive. You go around freeing settlements and tied up vikings in order to increase your army. The culmination at the end of completing each map makes it all worth while however.
As a reward for the grind you can see it was all worth something. The battles feel big and need some patience. You can see catapuls and summoned dragons in action. When you take over the city it is your turn to occupy and use it as the next forward base of operations. This too will show that your army and support from people is growing as your progress.
Still the battles themselves are not challenging in the least and functions very roughly. Having to gather rage in order to perform combo's takes away the flow of battle at times. While in the combo you can't stop it and use a block/evasive action resulting in the occasion stunlock by opponents.
It is a rough. mediocre game with some interesting ideas. People looking for a challenge won't find it here. The story is fairly standard. Still worth a try for a casual entertaining walktrhough. If you take your time this game is finished entirely in about 15hours of play.

Great metroid style game.  Thoroughly enjoyed pretty much all of it, the controls are mostly good, power ups were fun and interesting, and enemies and environments decently varied. Trying to jump past them once you land is an exercise is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.  Story was pretty good, not ground breaking, but well delivered. A very strange surreal FPS beat-em-up. Short length, could be played through in its entirety in one sitting, which is perfectly fine in this case. Combat is complex enough to allow for reflex based reactions and fights, but simplsitic enough to where if you can't grasp that, simple stick and moving can win the day too.
The entire game's art direction is creative and altogether "Weird", but everything feels weird for a reason - even if that reason is never actually explained to you.
While there are some snags to gameplay (being forced to circle strafe "big" enemies to hit them with a club is simply boring, and you do it a good number of times.), it's not a long enough game for it to drag. It answers just enough questions while opening up more, but still feels like it can stand on its own.
It's short enough to be an easy recommendation for anyone who likes short, relatively simple action games, or has a taste at all for the weird.

I don't do reviews a whole lot, I tend to let stuff speak for itself. Buuuut this one is really, really good.
The gameplay is well done; even when things get crazy and you're fighting an entire space station at once - it still responds well and if you play right you'll win through, skill-wise.
It's also got multiple upgrade paths; from remote control to turning the station aganst yur enemies in alarm waves, or benig a big, blasty juggernaut, and they're all done well and suited to the playstyles.
There's plenty of secrets to find, and exploring isn't just go room to room, it's exploring each room to try to find the scret within.
Puzzles are there, too; some optional and some not.
The upgrades and RPG parts have 'tough choice' selection which is really good; there's not a lot of useless options when picking out your skills, but a lot of competing options on hwo to move forward.
The story and characters are great; the cutscenes with them even better, the voices are well done and integrated, not distracting, and the overall theme and ambience of the game ties together really well. The plot is definitely trope-savvy, and it'll dodge your predictions a lot. ;3
The side-missions and alternate events are all fun, too.
And it's replayable! Not even the newgame+, but you have alternate play modes like Survival which plays like a very different experience.
Anyhow. Highly recommended.

Despite the tiny amount of time listed in Steam that I have played, I bought this game eight years ago and for around six or so of those years it was the most common game I played. It have watched its development (successes and blunders) all along, and the newest update adding in Workshop support is an amazingly great thing. The 2D sprites with physics on each individual bit of pixel and sprite debris, the fully destructible environment, the jumping control between bodies, the building bunkers and fortifications to hold back the onslaught, or the calling in wave after wave of reinforcements to raid and destroy the AI's brain are all great fun by themselves. What really made Cortex Command great was the prolific modding community on the games website, and now that Cortex Command finally has Steam Workshop integration it will be far easier for the masses to see the best of the work of the great modders.

PROS
-First of my favourite part of this game- local coop- This gmae allows up to four human palyers, with xbox controllers, in nearly ever mission, and can also have a A.I team in there. The primary reason I got this game, and kept it, was for this features flawless implementation.

Also, at the begining of some missions, you have acsess to the entire libary of content to build a customized bunker, that can stretch the entire map. The actors can be customized with every weapon of the game, but overloading them will slow them down, so you have to find the right balance. If the current selection of items is still to small for you, then there is the
-Mods- You can fight space nazis with space marines. Enough said.
-Gamplay- I'm not denying this game has some issues that need fixed, but this game palys flawlessly in most cases. some movment looks unnatural sure, but at the end of the day, this  gmae is a working mix of world map campaign, squad based , terraria like mining, base building,destuctible enviroment multiplayer shooter. AS much as I love it,, these features also make it a potential
CON(S)
-Complexity- AS some of my friends who are used to simple shooters like COD said, thsi game is a little complex. Although I think the dozens of diffrent gamepaly elements are as streamlinned as possible, the game still takes a bit of gettign used to. Which brigns me to the second con..

-Clipping issues- As a game with fully destructible enviroments, actors trying to get out of the palyer build catacombs some times get indefinatly stuck on on peices of terrain, but this can be fixed with a quick zap of a digger.

An innovative and refreshing Fantasy RPG that does not take itself seriously.
Magicka is an RPG in the spirit of Gauntlet, except there is only one class: Wizard.
In this reality, Wizards possess infinite power and do not run out of Mana - you only need to worry about running out of Health.
It can be played solo or with up to four players.
Multitudes of Robes with different abilties to choose from for everyone's own preferred playstyle.
Each character possesses a Staff and a Side Weapon (Knife, Sword, Gun).
Being a Wizard on the up-and-up, you are still learning, so you must explore to collect Tomes which contain different Magicks.
These Magicks contain the necessary element combinations to perform incredible conjurings of powerful efficaciousness.
It will take practice, it will take skill. You will die...alot. You will kill your friends...alot.
The journey ahead is filled with foes big and small, ferocious and...world conquering. But the journey ahead is also an enigma - you must write your own destiny...rise above the challenges and become the most powerful Wizard in all The Land!
11/10

Apparently I have a love/hate relationship with this game. I want to give it a good review because I like the simple but well-written story, the beautiful scenery and level design, the great soundtrack and the fact that one guy designed this game as his pet project. It really is an impressive feat, but as a videogame, it is extremely frustrating because of the most basic flaws holding it back.
First, the biggest pros: Despite all the warning signs, this game isn't geared towards furries, and that made me happy. It's an enjoyable RPG whether you're into that stuff or hopefully not. Also, MYSTERIOUS WALL CHICKEN is the funniest thing I've seen in a while.
Anyways, onto the real review. This is a 2D platformer game in which your character is a master swordsman, but he cannot turn around while attacking, and also wears banana peels as shoes. Seriously, why the hell would you make a 2D platformer where you cannot change directions when attacking, especially when you're constantly surrounded by enemies on both sides? The combat is fast-paced and fluid, yet I often find myself facing the wrong direction and unable to turn. Unresponsive controls are a sure way to make your game suck. Also, double jumping is really fickle and won't always work, which is great when you finally reach the top of that obstacle course only to have the game ignore your space-bar at the last second.
The slightest nudge forward sends your character skidding ten feet. Seriously? This is a platformer game which often requires you to have pinpoint accuracy when jumping and landing. For me, I always make the landing, then go sliding off the other end because this gameplay is god awful. Also, good luck getting hit by even a single environmental hazard, which will stun you and knock you back 30 ft, usually right into another hazard which will immediately do the same thing when you finally get up after a nap. Absolutely unfair.
I've changed this review from positive to negative a few times already. I honestly like the game, but I also can't play for more than five minutes without screaming at my character for doing the wrong thing. Dust is entertaining if you play casually, but its handling and response keep it from being a true gem. All that being said, the creator obviously has talent, and I hope he continues to release more in the future.

After 1,369 hours I think it's time I finally review Garry's Mod.
------------------------------------
You know, it isn't so easy to review a game like this. It's so free-form. As the description put it, there are no aims or goals. At all. There is simply a menu, the q menu, prop menu, tool menu, whatever you want to call it. You bring it up. You spawn a block. You throw it. You spawn more blocks, and an enemy. You throw blocks at an enemy. Then you start piling up those blocks to build something. Then throw that thing at an enemy. And then you open up multiplayer...
I first delved into Gmod a long, long time ago with a former friend. It was on sale (although I'd gladly pay the full price) so I picked it up. He had been telling me to get it for a while, and I'd finally joined in on this. We hopped on a Jailbreak server, ExoTerra, and started to play. After an hour or so my internet crashed for reasons unknown to this day. Reluctant to quit the game, I started up single player. Most players would have started with that, but as I had purchased Gmod to play online the single player aspect was merely a side thought to me. It still is, in a way. I always find even sandbox more enjoyable with friends. As time went on I got more and more engrossed in ExoTerra, eventually joining their forums and checking out their other server, DarkRP. I've stuck with ExoTerra as staff on both servers (until DarkRP shut down, then I just stayed with Jailbreak, which has slowly lost players) to this day. Without that friend, without Garry's Mod, I would never have met this group of people with whom I've shared the better part of the last two years with. I don't think I can put a price on that experience. Oh and yes, ExoTerra is still alive, at least at the time of writing this.
is their forum site, check it out if you want.
I'm still having trouble trying to display the amount of content in Gmod. The sheer number of workshop addons in even a single category dwarfs that of entire games. You'll probably never run out of things to do, addons to install, gamemodes to play. I sure haven't. It's my most played game on Steam, and I doubt another could re-create the experiences I've had here.
------------------------------------
I guess I should describe each of the most popular gamemodes, since there's really no other way to describe such a free-form game.
Standing for Dark Role Play, DarkRP is a role playing game, of course. You can be a police officer, a theif, a hobo, or anything you want really, as long as the server has a class for it. You can build your homes, raid the Police Department for money, get put in jail, print some money, mug people, and more. This gamemode has no limits. Although it does seem to be overrun with idiot little kids running around screaming RDM (Random DeathMatch, killing people for no in-character reason) and causing issues. The gamemode has become kinda bad over time, best stay away unless you find a nice server.
You've probably played this in other games like Counter Strike. A team, prisoners, is controlled by another team, guards. The prisoner team tries to either escape or kill the guard team, and the guards choose a warden (usually by F4 at the beginning of the round) to dictate what games the prisoners play that day. Prisoners can win LR (Last Request) by winning these games (colloquially known as "days") and will generally be able to choose what the next round's game is or choose DR (Death Request), where they can choose to fight guards or be killed in a special way. It's weird, yeah.
If you've ever watched a YouTuber play Gmod, it was probably this game. You, as Kleiner in a T-pose (the "old man") try to disguise yourself as different items (props) in order to avoid being caught and killed by the seekers. Health scales based on size, with the largest usually being a vending machine with 200 HP or similar. You aren't a professional at this game until you win as Kleiner in an obvious spot.
In this gamemode, everyone is a terrorist. A handful of players are chosen to be "Traitors" (Or Ts) who are sent to kill all of the other players. They can set off special traps designed to kill the other players, or attempt to kill them outright. One or two players are "Detectives" with special skills to find and kill the Ts. Everyone else is innocent (innos), they have weapons but no special powers. Ts look like innos (people looking at them see the "Innocent" tag, except for other Ts), only the Detectives are obvious in their role. Ts can never be Detectives, or vice versa.
Those are the big, popular gamemodes. There are many, many more than that. You could scroll through the multiplayer gamemode list (Oh yeah, did I mention that servers are grouped by gamemode? Very useful) for a long time and still be seeing new stuff.
------------------------------------
Pros
+ Unlimited possibilities
+ Literally just a giant sandbox with mod support
+ A plethora of mods to choose from
Neutral
-+ Graphics are lackluster, but don't impede gameplay
Cons
- Audio quality isn't very good (expensive mics don't sound so high-end)
- Errors galore if you don't have Counter-Strike: Source
------------------------------------
TL; DR
Garry's Mod is a giant sandbox in which you can do whatever you want. There are tons of online servers and too many mods to count, so you'll never be bored of this game. The graphics aren't the greatest thing, but are pretty decent I'd say. Just make sure you have Counter-Strike: Source or you'll have errors around every corner on most servers.
After all of this years, I finally play this game in my PC with updated graphics. So nostalgic, 11/10 in all aspects. Single player experience at it finest.

Dark Parables is one of these series with many games in it, in the world of casual gaming. Curse of the Briar Rose is one of the four (or five?) developed by Blue Tea Games, before the series was given to another studios. I've played one of the recent entries and I can see the improvements.
Curse of Briar Rose is the tale of Sleeping Beauty, though you're a Fairy Tale detective, going from fairy tales places to another. In this case, you're sent to a town where Briar Rose/Sleeping Beauty is rumored to be sleeping since a thousand years, despite the prince managing to lift a part of the curse. Right now, vines are invading and it's a sign that the curse is stronger and that the Evil Godmother is ready to come back.
I liked the plot, it's not really the problem in this game. It's interesting to be a detective exploring either the tales or the aftermath.
My main problem is the gameplay. I'm so used to the modern one that I felt that Briar Rose was totally a step back... and it has a reason: Curse of Briar Rose was released years ago. Here, you find items in different locations but the majority of them are in hidden objects scenes. That's my problem here: it's only find parts of objects, with a picture of them. Those are often hard to spot, either because they're too small or they're blending with the background. After a while, it was really boring. It's just frustrating. As for the puzzles, while they're only a few, they're often the same. Another problem for me is the lack of map to fasten the travel. Also, while the "Inspect" feature is nice to help you to find where to go, by moments, I found myself stuck because I didn't know where to go. In other words, it wasn't always clear where to go for using a specific item. Indeed, the Inspect feature is only there to show where hidden objects scenes are available. In other words, if you didn't pay attention entirerly to locations, you're just lost.
The graphics are decent though I was under the impression to have a grainy screen, which made me take some distance with the atmosphere of the game. The soundtrack is nice.
Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose is really showing its age and the gameplay isn't the most interesting and isn't even well balanced. While the plot is good, I found myself bored and stuck. I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone wanting to discover the genre, it's just for the hardcore players. And even for them, it might not satisfy them.

Just finished my playthrough of F.E.A.R and it was a wild ride. Very solid first person shooter elements, game mechanics, AI, music, sound and of course the horror element combine to form an excellent game.
This game is 12 years old (as of 2017) but has aged very well. I couldn’t imagine playing this back in 2005! F.E.A.R is thick with atmosphere and an overall sense of creepiness. I don’t want to call them jump scares, but the game uses multiple unexpected moments with great timing to get a good jolt out of you. I jumped and shouted several words out loud while playing.
At its core, this is a horror first person shooter. You have multiple guns and grenades to use. Also, there is a time shift mechanic that lets you temporarily slow down everything so you can adjust and take out an entire room of bad guys without getting hit. I initially found myself not using it much, but as the game progresses you rely on it almost all the time. There are 2 types of “collectibles” or stat boosts. Max health increase and longer time shift duration. These are permanent and found in some tighter spaces across the levels. It rewards exploring, which is always nice.
Ambiance and music are very well done. They add so much to the game and without it, the atmosphere would totally be lost.
The AI is fantastic and one of the best I’ve seen. Again, for 2005 this is exceptional. Enemies are smart and will find different ways to get to you. They’ll flank you, toss grenades, hide and melee you. It’s done in a natural way and is fairly unpredictable how the AI will act. Using time shift and catching them off guard was something I really enjoyed doing and makes you feel like a badass.
I didn’t find myself getting into the story, for whatever reason. It just didn’t connect with me. Also, it does feel a bit repetitive and very familiar after the first few levels. Enemy variety is lacking here.
I had to use the “DirectInput FPS Fix 0.2” as noted on PCGamingWiki or else my framerate would tank and go into the low 20’s. Using this fix solved that issue though. I would definitely recommend reading the page on PCGamingWiki about this game.
+60fps
+Creepy atmosphere
+Good scares
+Fantastic AI
+Graphics, sounds/music
+Time-shift mechanic
+Auto and manual quick save/load
+Had to use DirectInput FPS Fix
+Story wasn’t too interesting
+Repetitive
+Flashlight drains too quickly
+Only carry 3 weapons

I wrote a review almost 5 years ago for a Steam badge. But, I don't think a sloppy, lazy, short review does it justice. So, I would like to fix that.
Deus Ex is among the few that shaped the way first-person shooters have become now. It merged the genre with RPG elements to give the players choices to play the game. And, in the near-future dystopia, where every conspiracy is true (Alex Jones was right all along!), every choice determines the future.
Deus Ex has been around for over 15 years. In gaming years, that's the same age as a WWII veteran. The graphics by today's standards are ugly, but at the time, they were cutting edge. Using the Unreal Engine, the dark, bleak world could be presented in polygons rather than pixels. In fact, the blocky graphics helps the shabby and lifeless environment.
There is nothing breathtaking about the scenery because the world is dying, and what you see is a hollow skeleton of a refitted past. The buildings look like any other building today on the outside. There is no futuristic architecture or artwork in the ruins of the modern age. You will find those inside the inconspicuous buildings that are actually New World Order corporate bases. There is a clear visible divide between the haves and the have-nots.
The music is the weakest asset of the game. It's futuristic techno that seems to fit any other science fiction game. It's nothing to write home about. The only song I clearly remember is the main theme, which is pretty good.
The controls are pretty standard. If you have played other games from that time, such as Half-Life or other Unreal Engine games, you can jump right in and play. They are simple and easy to do. Darksydephil can't make any excuses for the controls here.
The brave, new world that Deus Ex introduces to FPS gamers is choice. Finally, a game where you have objectives rather than the insatiable thirst for destruction. Your character can be augmented and modified to fit a certain play style. For example, you can be a gun-blazing tank, or a silent sniper, or a sneaky agent. There is no wrong way to play, and not every solution is the easiest one. Choose wisely how you want to move the plot.
Speaking of plot, it's very simple in a complex world. The world is being consumed by a pandemic virus. J. C. Denton, a UN counter-terrorist, slowly uncovers the secret behind the, "Gray Death". Suddenly, he finds himself a fugitive terrorist out to stop the silent coup d'etat.
Adding RPG elements to a first person shooter is nothing new, even in 2000. However, Deus Ex finds the right balance between action and RPG. Thus, it changed the way FPS games were seen. It didn't have to be DOOM, or Wolfenstein 3D, or Duke Nukem. You didn't have to shoot everything up. In fact, many situations call for a more subtle method. This game brought strategy to a simple-minded genre. It required more to beat the game. Put the chain gun down already.
It's a great balance of two types, which makes it very fun. You can experiment different ways of gameplay. You can challenge yourself by setting personal goals, such as not killing anyone. The replayability factor is high. In fact, just thinking and writing about it makes me want to play again.
Deus Ex is one of the classics, and an example of a good game. It's revolutionary and now cheap. Buy it and try it out. It's aged very well and better than many of the newer games out there.

Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose is a solid hidden object game with an interesting twist on the classic tale of Sleeping Beauty. This game also holds the promise of a continue of a longer story arc through each Dark Parable game, so they may have to be played in order if you want to  follow that.
Story aside, the gameplay is a little different from most hidden object games. There are plenty of hidden object scenes to go around (at least three per chapter, I think!), however instead of finding a random list of objects in the scene, you find pieces that will combine to make an object needed in order to progress. It makes for interesting finding, although it can become a little repeatitive and sometimes pieces can be a little too well hidden.
As for the other key gameplay mechanic of hidden object games, i.e. puzzles, Curse of Briar Rose has some interesting ones. The puzzles were fairly diverse, and different from many of the one's I had personally seen before. Some even had multiple stages, or phases to go through before completion. All in all, I never really wanted to skip the puzzles, which is always a plus.
Now, what about graphics and music? Graphics-wise, the game is pretty. The scenes very pretty, and generally fit the fairytale feel of the game. As for the music, it was also quite nice, setting the tone and mood easily.
What's also nice is the game comes with a little bonus content. A strategy guide you can access while in the game, an extra chapter to play, and things such as wallpapers and extra puzzles to unlock at the very end.
The only negetive things I can think to say is that the lack of a map made it a little hard to navigate sometimes, and that again, some objects were just a little too hidden.
Overall, Dark Parables: Curse of Briar Rose is a great game, easily earning an 8/10 from me, and I recommend you give it a try.

Hired by a couple of "intellectuals" to break and enter a facility that mainly deals in AI solutions after hearing about a completely new form of AI, Ghost is hired through a contact and sent to a space station which holds more than just answers....
Gameplay: 9/10
Solid entry in the metroidvania genre albeit a tad low on the branching paths and exploratory options. Generally well done environment and great looking artwork. Power ups and progression is properly spread out, uniquely done in it's own way and gives a great overall feel of the game.
Story: 7/10
Starts off great, but drones off a bit later on. Still a solid way of conveying the message and gets it across properly, but some of the earlier gameplay is superior in terms of actually telling the story, albeit through exploration or narrative. Fantastic cutscenes at some point, but overall a bit lackluster in some areas.
Artistry / Musical score: 8/10. Solid soundtrack, well done audio, great sound effects and beatiful map detailing sets this apart from many other titles in the genre. Has a very very solid castlevania feel to it in terms of music and some of the items you find during the game. Great work overall ;)
Overall: 8/10.
A very very solid entry in a long standing genre that pleases fans and newcomers alike. The developer's older game "Unepic" is also a solid framework to describe this one, but overall it's enough refreshing ideas and new gimmicks to make it not feel like a base copypaste of an existing game.
Would absolutely reccomend it for fans of the genre and people looking for high quality platformer action in general.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a fantastic sidescrolling action RPG, and I want more of it.
Some would classify DustAET as a metroidvania. I personally disagree, as there are not terribly many upgrades. You basically start the game with all the combat abilities you'll ever need, leaving only a few new movement abilities to be acquired as you play. I played DustAET hoping to scratch a metroidvania itch that was left only barely scratched. To me, a good metroidvania gives you upgrades that let you find more upgrades (if that makes any sense), and rewards you for finding optional upgrades with more power. DustAET's upgrades primarily let you progress the story, and most of the optional treasure you can find feels largely insignificant.
That doesn't mean the game isn't immensely fun, though. In the end, DustAET isn't a game about finding metroidvania-style upgrades. It's a game about fighting a group of monsters, kicking butt, and having loads of fun doing it. The combat just feels great. There are tons of options for clocking, blocking, weaving, and cleaving your way to victory, and all of them are open to you from the beginning.
On top of that, if you can get past the occasionally-cringey dialogue, there's an interesting story to be told too.

As advertised Zeno Clash is something of a rarity i computer games those days, an artistic/surealistic game that is actually good. The setting is as strange as it get, you're a denizen in a strange colourfull dada'ish universe with strange unpredictable beings. As the protagonist you're being hunted by members of your tribe for some untold crime.
The story progress through linear events where you usually get attacked or have to attack others beings, usually with your fists in order to continue your journey. The raw brutality of those handfight with strange creatures in even stranger surroundings make the whole game an even weirder experience. The gameplay is anything but easy but it's fair and with some patience and practice you can actually get good at it. There is some exploration and you will meet many strange creatures and environments , those are great to experience , the music and sound is really good too and fit well in the surreal surroundings
The beauty with Zeno Clash is that despite being an artistic experience in itself, the creators of the game put some real good gameplay and a great mystery plot which come nicely together in the end. In those days were games are getting more and more prosaic in style, it's refreshing to play something that feels out of the ordinary, the creators dared to create a completly alien and beautiful world that would defy our sences.
The only games I could compare this to, would be Commander Blood or Lost Eden from the 90s, old but amazing games set in universes where you felt anything could happen. I got the same sence of awe when I played Zeno Clash, not many game give me this feeling anymore and I wish there were more of those.

I'm not sure I can accurately describe how much I respect this game.  And alright, I'll say it, I LOVE this game.  Or to be more accurate, I am ADDICTED to this game.  I want to say I hate it's brutal unforgiving difficulty (especially after you hit the last treasure room and you get the poop or some equally useless item and yes there are more useless items than the poop), but in all reality, it is it's randomness and roguelike nature that made me fall in love with it.  The enemies are incredibly varied for a game style that is so simplistic and yet beautiful.  The story, captivating to the point that it has spawned HUNDREDS of theories on what the hell is really going on in Isaac's nightmarish world.  This is truly a once in a lifetime type of game in how magnificent it is and how well it keeps dragging you back in until you've beaten EVERYTHING.
You beat Mom?  Good job!  But did you really kill her?

Great game for fans of extremely fast paced and hectic action games. it's somewhere between quick time event, turn based (you have to wait to use/refresh skills) and real time (your skill resources constantly replenish and the "round-time" you can act constantly ticks away).
Sadly the combination is made in a terrible way.
You often just stand there unable to do nothing while the enemy beats you down or even kills you.
Only a few attacks you can actually avoid via quick time events.
If you select Blocking on your turn, it only lasts a turn, but in real time. So the second it runs out the enemy attacks you and you get hit. Making it in most cases useless.
Or you are using kai skills but not the target fast enough, the enemy might just interrupt you.
Keeping you basically in an inaction/stun lock...
To summarize it forces you into turns, without the advantage to be able to plan turns.
It uses quick time events, but mostly only for attacks. Only rarely for defence which makes you often just stand there and get beat for no reason. (especially in the frequent 3vs1 scenarios)
And the real time part forces you to stand there to wait until your resources are regenerated while the enemy beats you.
While at the same time stresses you out that you have to do your actions fast, just to wait another 10 seconds without doing anything...
Without the combat it would be a nice game. But this way you just get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off after 30mins of play and you have to take a break...

Joe Dever's Lone Wolf is quite a unique game. Based off of an author's choose-your-own-adventure novels which were popular in the 1990s, it is a game with its own unique story in which you choose the methods you deal with hurdles, enemies, and adventuring. Before I get into the review, let me say this: some reviews have stated to only buy this if you are a fan of the novels. Personally, I'd never even heard of Joe Dever or his Lone Wolf series until buying this game, but I would have been interested in the books as a little girl if I'd known of them. I enjoyed this game, and I was not a fan, though I do enjoy reading and choose-your-own-adventure type stories. If you like those two as well, read on.
Lone Wolf puts you in the shoes of a man known as...well, Lone Wolf. You are a protector of a place called Sommerlund. An attack has wiped out most of a village and it's up to you to figure out why and to seek justice for the people. You choose your character build by asking a number of questions which will set you up with unique abilities and stats, which will give you different ways to deal with situations down the line. Then, the story begins. For the most part, you will be reading what happens between fights, lock-picking, and other choices. Is the story any good? Personally, I thought it was just okay. It certainly wasn't anything new or unique, and there was nothing here to pull me in and convince me to go out and buy Joe Dever's books (though due to his recent passing, many of his books are available now for free online for those who are interested). I also spotted quite a few grammatical/spelling errors throughout, so I suppose the story lacked an editor. However, it was interesting enough to keep me playing. The story here was probably my least favorite thing about the game, and there was one character in particular I found infuriating. Leandra is a side character that pops up quite often in the story and I could not stand her. She's always messing things up for you and spitting resentment at you despite your actions, and I couldn't help but hope her brashness would get her killed despite the story/game telling me I should care for her. I didn't like her character at all, and the story's insistence that I should certainly worked against it.
Much has been said about the combat of this game. You'll either love it or hate it. I'm not a huge fan of QTEs in games because I find them lazy, but I thought Lone Wolf pulled them off quite well. One could technically complete the game with just the mouse, so this is a good game to play if you feel like an RPG but you're also feeling lazy. QTEs make up the majority of battle sequences, but what keeps the fighting from getting dull is an action timer of sorts which requires you to choose your actions depending on how much stamina/Kai power you have before the enemy's turn comes along. The fights in this game certainly aren't a cakewalk, though it wasn't very challenging until Act 2. There is a severe difficulty spike in Act 2 that came out of nowhere, but the game offers you various ways to surpass this (lower difficulty, restart battle, restart checkpoint, etc.). I enjoyed the battles in this a great deal overall.
Throughout your journey you will visit different locations, get a variety of loot, and you can even upgrade your weapons and armor over time. It's a relatively short game (it took me just under 13 hours for one playthrough, though choice-making opens this up for multiple playthroughs if you wish it). Thus, don't expect any crafting systems that are too involved, or a great variety of loot. As for the design issues of the game that many have pointed out, the only confusion for me stemmed from the menu system. The majority of the game is set in a book, where you read along a page to the left and have something else open to your right (inventory, map, quests, etc.). Sometimes to go "back" to what you were doing (to the map, for example, if you decided to check your inventory first) you have to reopen it. I also found that it's really hard to go back if you get stuck. That difficulty spike I mentioned earlier? I tried to restart the chapter to rearrange the things I brought with me into battle, and found that it basically just started the battle over again instead. So sometimes things aren't particularly clear, but this is not a complex game. Any confusion is quickly cleared up because you only have so many options available to you.
Overall, I enjoyed this game a great deal. It was a fun romp through a fantasy world that was unfamiliar to me, and while I did wish for a greater variety of enemies and locales, the small scope of the game did not allow for it. I have heard that there was a possible sequel in the works that Joe Dever was working on before his death. If that comes out, I would probably support it if Leandra did not make an appearance. Lone Wolf is a really unique game that I'm glad I bought, and I think most people would enjoy this if you're looking for a quick and casual RPG to play between more complicated games that tells a complete story. I'd give Lone Wolf a 7/10.

This first otome visual novel from roseVeRte features a female protagonist Yukina Kudou, a student attending Serizawa High School with her best friend Nao and a fellow classmate Youji Kataoka. At the school, Yukina became the assistant to the school principal and her foster father Kouichi Serizawa with a strange request to become Youji's girlfriend and report on Youji's actions to Kouichi. Over a period of 3 months, Yukina (and the player) will manage her studies and relationship with Youji and Kouichi by listening to gossip, studying, monitoring Youji, helping Kouichi and resting. Yukina may develop a relationship with Youji or with Kouichi which could lead to a love, good or bad ending and might shed some light on Yukina and each character's past as well as their motivations and true intentions.
The game has an in-game link to a guide on roseVeRte's website to help players in reaching all endings and get all achievements, plenty of save slots to allow different gameplay and dialogue choices to be made during the game, Yukina's skill gauge and heart icons appearing in each character's portrait to help players with the stat management part of the game and the option to skip and fast-forward any part of the game. Background music and overall game presentation are great after factoring in chibis for each of the main characters, animated snowflakes and appropriate background music to match most settings and characters. Highly recommended when at discount or in bundle offer as it takes less than 10 hours to reach all endings and unlock all CGs and achievements.

So my review is exclusively based on my personal experience during this game, that i've played for the first time.
From what i can tell, i felt very satisfied with trying this small, but great title.
Starting from how the game is structured, i find that's truly amazing, really innovative and addictive.
Personally i've always loved games where plot it's influenced by various choices made by us.
Actually i don't know how strongly the choices influence Lone Wolf's story, a new run should be done in order to verify that, however i doubt that choices will make a big difference.
In any case, this style of writing accompanied by these different decisions, it's unique.
I really appreciated the gameplay, it reminds me a lot of Child Of Light (actually the opposite, since Child has been developed later than Lone Wolf).
The main difference in the combat system between Child and Lone, is that in Lone you can't predict enemies' turns, making the gameplay more spicy.
An important fact, the plot can be enjoyed without knowing the previous works of Joe Dever. It's really smooth, finely nuanced and cared, and truly addictive. I appreciated the narrative from all points of view, very well done.
At this point the graphics can take second place, this kind of title doesn't aim to good graphics.
For how the game is structured, the design is more than satisfying.
What can i say, a fantasy world influenced by our choices in which we assume total control of the battlefield.. everything is fascinating. Just play this game already!

[ITA] Ho ricevuto questo gioco gratuitamente tramite i soliti siti che regalano chiavi a caso. Sono rimasto veramente stupito che ogni tanto regalino anche dei giochi veramente ben fatti, anche se il 90% delle volte è sempre spazzatura, utili solo per le carte collezionabili.
Detto questo, sono completamente estraneo al mondo di Joe Dever, pertanto non conosco nessuno dei suoi "librigame". La mia recensione quindi si basa esclusivamente sull'esperienza provata in questo gioco per la prima volta, non collegandola quindi al mondo fantasy dell'autore.
Per quel che mi riguarda, sono veramente rimasto soddisfatto dopo aver provato questo piccolo, ma grande titolo.
Partiamo innanzitutto da come è strutturato l'intero gioco. Trovo che sia veramente eccezionale, assolutamente coinvolgente e innovativo. Personalmente ho sempre amato i giochi nei quali lo sviluppo della trama è condizionata dalle nostre scelte.
Ora non sò quanto effettivamente le scelte condizionino pesantemente la trama di Lone Wolf, bisognerebbe iniziare una seconda run per verificare ciò, tuttavia dubito che possano fortemente cambiarla.
In ogni caso questo stile narrativo, accompagnato dalle numerosi scelte che staranno al giocatore, è unico.

A core tenet of Lone Wolf, and something I have always loved about it, is that good choices in Kai powers and wise story decisions should allow you to finish the adventure even if your character is a weak combatant.  It's a sentiment that prefaces every single published Lone Wolf book.
And it is a sentiment that this game entirely lacks.
It is not just that combat is unavoidable.  That was often the case in the books as well, both at the end of the story and at significant plot points within each story.  In this game, combat is used to gate nearly every story segment.  Sometimes you are given a choice of strategies that may include eliminating or avoiding the enemies by cunning or use of Kai powers, after which you are then forced to fight those enemies in the awful combat engine anyway.
The combat mechanics are tedious and obtuse, and combat involves a lot of sitting through long unskippable animations, even when you have no ability to react.  There is little variation in the type or quantity of the enemies.  If it's not more damn giaks, it's giaks and drakkarim, or drakkarim in shiny armor.  And the reward for finishing a combat is generally a few pages of text and then more combat.
This game does not understand the core appeal of the world it pretends to be a part of.  It isn't worth your money or your time.

Most people describe this game as a metroidvania. It's one of the more popular tags for it and the main reason I bought it. Ghost 1.0 really isn't a metroidvania game though. It's more like a linear level based platformer. Sure all the areas are connected, but besides teleporting back to shops there's no real reason to return. The typical game loop goes:
There are some movement upgrades you can unlock in your skill tree, but they dont really allow access to any new areas or items, and aren't necessary to progress. Most weapons and upgrades are bought in shops.
There are secrets in Ghost, quite a lot actually, almost every room has one. The process to make each secret appear is pretty random though, and there's never environment hints on what to do. Some of the kinds of things you have to do are:
It gets pretty tedious doing this for every room. And the rewards are usually only some money or a weak healing item.
So Ghost 1.0 doesn't really check the metroidvania boxes for me. How is it as a platformer? For the most part pretty good! The movement is precise. The boss fights are fun. There's lots of different weapons you can buy, so there should be something that fits your playstyle. Although they are kinda expensive to buy and upgrade, so it's likely you wont wanna give up your earlier fully upgraded weapons.
The story is good, if a little predictable. The graphics are nice, and they have fun little 90's style cut scenes. This fits really well with the cheesy(but enjoyable) voice acting.
So why dont I recommend this game? Two reasons:
One, the developers like to troll the player. Some boxes drop bombs instead of money. Deaths are often used as a way to teach a concept or just for "fun". One particularly annoying example
. Every time you die you lose ALL your money (and items depending on difficulty). This is so frustrating because a lot of your upgrades have to be bought in shops. Try and spend your cash early and often, but some things are expensive so you have to save for them.
Two, The lab area. About halfway through the game your fun shooty-jumpy game is replaced with a puzzle section requiring super precise timing and movements. BTW make any mistakes you die! Start over from the beginning! Most times you can possess other robots, but some of the puzzles you have to do yourself. So you die, lose all your money, have to walk aaaaaaallll the way back from the last save room. I almost quit when this was reintroduced near the end of the game. Fortunately that section has an option to completely skip from the game menu. (
)
If you're a platformer-shooter fan you might like this game. But if you're looking for a metroidvania, I recommend something like Axiom Verge instead.

Just finished beating this game and I can't wait to complete the video series of it on my channel to show it off and hopefully get more people to play it. This is a fantastic Metroidvania style game that manages to hit a sweet spot on challenging and rewarding. The game almost never feels unfair, and the few times it does its usually because there's a trick to it that makes things click. Its hard while still making every victory feel satisfying and encouraging the player.
Aside from the tight and well-tuned gameplay, the writing is excellent and really makes you bond with the characters. I found myself eagerly awaiting the next cutscene to see what interactions would come up next. Some of them are simply amazing and utterly brilliant and had my girlfriend and I laughing out loud. To put a point on it, I was sad to see the game end knowing that would close the book on these guys. And this is a new IP, so its not like I had an entire series to grow to love these characters. That's a sign of excellent character crafting for sure.
The music is generally unobtrusive while still serving its purpose and usually decent, but there's a couple tracks in particular that stand out as very catchy and enjoyable to listen to. The main theme, of course, in its triumphant melody, but also the music for the "Chunker" area and the final boss come to immediate mind for their appropriateness for the situations.
Overall I can't recommend this game enough to anyone who's a fan of the genre. Tight controls, beautiful graphics that have a wonderful comic-esque aesthetic, a good soundtrack, an engaging story, and lots of wit and personality make this one a winner that can easily contend with the big titles for your money. I'd love to see a sequel, but sadly (though satisfyingly) the game wraps up everything in this one package so I don't see how a sequel could work. What are you waiting for? Get it and have some fun!
EDIT: Almost forgot, I've never played UnEpic as it didn't seem particularly appealing to me. I want to point out that after finishing this game, I fully intend to buy and play UnEpic at some point. That's how much I enjoyed this game, I want to see what else the dev has produced. How's that for a recommendation?

We devised a strategy to kill that monstrosity, one would check the camera and the other would stand watch. To conclude this long review off I will just say this; The game looks pretty extensive but it's actually really linear and monotonous. If we got bored in 40 minutes imagine the boredom of playing for hours trying to chip at his high health bar. The game is really bad and you should wait to get out of early access before buying this sad excuse of a game that is cowering behind games such as slender and the rake.

This is a story all about how Ace Wilder's life got twist turned upside down, so I'd like you to take a moment and take a deep breath and tell you how Manic this game can get!
Aces Wild is a crazy fast paced brawler that shows you no mercy.  It's tough as nails and it knows it, forcing you to fight and get better bit by bit.  Each level introduces new mechanics that show off the depth of the combat system. From breaking shields to aerial combat, dodging, and timing movements just right, the game shines the most once you learn the combat well enough to be plowing through the hordes of enemies that are flung at you.  The enemies range from standard ninjas to robot sentries, to brawlers and valkyries and NINJA DOGS, that's right ninja dogs!  You have to learn to adapt on the fly or you will be taken out fast even by the most basic of enemies.
The game is frantic with enemies spawning out of nowhere and taking you by surprise.  The bosses are all really well designed and each one has a unique fighting style. They are not easy to take down but it makes it oh so satisfying once you finally get em with a charged up final blow!  It's not terribly long, but that's expected for most brawler games, short and tough! If you're an old school brawler fan or just want a challenge, this game will have you shouting "BRING IT!" while gripping your controller (which I highly recommend to use)! - 8.5/10

I went into Paladins knowing nearly nothing about it. I had no clue if it would be good, bad or a compleate rip-off of TF2 or overwatch. That being said, I have had a lot fun with Paladins and it has far surpassed my expectectations.
For starters, it is a very begginer friendly game. It starts you off with a good selection of champions to play as and unlocking new champions and loadouts is very reaeasonable using the in game currency. Gameplay never seems to slow and each map seems to have just the right amount of bottleneck areas to keep the game from finishing too quickly.
Paladins loadout system, while at first can be a little complicated, has a lot of depth and strategy to it. Paladins also has some of the best cosmedic items i've seen in any game.
Sure, you can pay to win but you can also unlock everything at a pretty fast rate without paying a dime. 85 hours in and I almost have everything I want unlocked.
Constant updates, new game modes and maps being tested, more champions on the way, good patchnotes and more. From what I can tell Hi-rez studio is picking up their slack and listening to the comunity.
There are still bugs and server issues but that's why the game is still in Beta.
I would recomend giving this game a try and if you don't like it, remeber, it's free.

Ever since Master of Orion 2 I've waited for a worthy successor to the 4x genre, and after numerous failures and utter dissapointments (from MoO3 up until Beyond Earth) the candidate was finally released and in the different genre altogether - grand strategy and not a turn based game at all.
The game absolutly shines; exploration is terrific, quest-based scripting works well, empire managment is easy and satisfying, graphics are gorgeous, music is haunting and I am always left wanting for more.
Where the game lacks is the (current) lack of more detailed combat and inter-species diplomacy, but we are reassured by Paradox these will be addressed shortly in the 1.3 patch. Furthermore there is no spying at all, however I'm certain this aspect will also whow up sooner than later in a form of a DLC (which is a shame since spying should have been in there since day 1).
After all is said and done, over 300hours in game have left me with a feeling that I've seen it all, and done it all, but this is where the wonderful modding comunity steps in. With hundreds of large game-changing mods one is never bored, and the core gameplay experience can be tweaked to anyone's liking.
I haven't played a game this engrossing in decades.

I was excited when I first heard about this. I was a huge fan of the original Sierra AGI GoldRush from the 80's.
When I saw screenshots, I was surprised they looked unfinished and ordinary, but thought, well I'll give it a chance.
Well they weren't unfinished. They were the final images. This game is terrible. There is virtually no improvement from the original. The graphics are truly abysmal.
Remember the game Little Big Adventure(Twinsen's Adventure)? It was released in 1994, 6 years after Gold Rush. The games are nothing alike, however LBA had fantastic graphics for the time. Although, the backdrops had no lighting and were rather static, the characters were rendered in real time, as opposed to pre-rendered sprites.
This game, had it come out in 1994,  21 years ago, would have been lauded as equally good as LBA. This game has pre-rendered backgrounds, but I'm not sure what graphics package was used to make them. They have zero lighting, and the texture-mapping on objects appears to be flat and unrealistic. The characters and other animated parts are ALL pre-rendered sprites. It is almost impossible to believe that this game came out in 2015.
The trees look like they're straight from the default settings on a tree generator program, or some stock 3d library tree that's been duplicated throughout. There are so many 'curved' objects in which you can see the facets on the object. These are pre-rendered facets. Why? Haven't they heard of bump mapping, or normal mapping? Or, since it's pre-rendered why not just turn the detail up and leave the renderer on overnight?
There has been little artistic license taken to improve on the original screens. I am sure the artist(s) have put in at least a little effort into the graphics for this game, but surely at one point someone stepped back and realised how terrible it looks. I really can't understand how, looking at the credits, a team of over 20 people never once thought "is this really an improvement over the original game?"
The game itself is rather buggy, and counter-intuitive. The voice acting is robotic and stale. I don't have anything nice to say about this game.
If you're after some nostalgic Sierra adventures, take a look at some of the games made with AGS, such as Heroine's Quest or the AGDI Kings Quest remakes.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is an incredibly huge improvement on the first game, with greatly enhanced graphics, combat system, English voice acting, and story. Like its predecessor it is based on the Witcher short stories and novels by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski.
The story picks up about one month after the first game ended. The player once again takes control of Geralt of Rivia, a human that was genetically mutated to be better at killing monsters, or otherwise known as a witcher. The game starts out with Geralt in a prison cell being interrogated by a figure of authority that he seems to know from somewhere. Spoilers from the prologue and last cutscene of the first game follow.
I did not especially enjoy the first Witcher game and had to push myself to finish it, but it was the exact opposite case with this one. It was a joy to go through each quest and explore the world and I couldn't wait to play more every day.

If you're "old", buy this game for a couple of hours of nostalgia.
If you're young, buy this game to get a sense of what games were like long ago. Turn on the original parser for a minute. Then tell your father you're happy to live in the future, thank you very much.
Either way, with the updated graphics and interface it's a solid adventure game you both can enjoy.

I was always curious why this game has only "mixed" rating on Steam. And after I finally played it, it's even bigger mystery to me. This game is awesome! Well true, it has some bugs, but if you're an FF fan, these will not bother you at all.
But first things first.
FFIV was my first "numbered" Final Fantasy game that I played. And it was already 2002 back then. Since then I finished that part a couple of times (on SNES, PSX, and NDS). It surely is not my favorite part, not even top 5, but I really liked it, and true - I'm a little bit sentimental about it. But I was always afraid of playing the sequel. Why? Because Square Enix don't know how to make good sequels... And, honestly, I preferred to play other games than going back to the SNES era graphics (as the first FFIV:AF came out on PSP, not counting the mobile phones made in/for Japan). But then this version appeared on Steam... a couple years have passed, and I finally decided to give it a try.
And what can I say - Square Enix CAN make good sequels! This is a great sequel! It has everything a sequel needs: the same characters, the same battle system, the same world, the same monsters. And new story! And that's all there is to it! You hear me SE? I'm glad that the After Years is not about Rosa, Rydia and Porom acting as Charlie's Angels, changing their dresses and acting stupid... Surprisingly, particularly none of the main characters changed that much since the original story. True, the characters from FFIV were presented as deeply as those in FFVI and onward, but still. Of course, the story itself is not a masterpiece. Hell, it's even very far from being one. But that's not the point. While I was playing this game I really felt like I was playing an old, SNES-like Final Fantasy game. This is where it all began for me, the love for FF franchise. This love thing is nowadays long gone, but I really had a great time. I didn't have so much fun playing FF game since I've played FFX. And that was, like... more than 14 years ago.
By the way, it's not like this game has all the thing the old one had besides new story. There are new characters, a couple of new dungeons and bosses, new Band techniques used during fights (great stuff, helped me a lot in beating the game). And as far as new characters are concerned - we now have over 20 characters to choose from! Sure, half of them are pretty much useless, but that's not the point. If I'm not mistaken, there is no other FF game with so many playable characters! And taking all Square games into consideration... maybe only Chrono Cross had more. This is nice and surely makes you want to try different characters for another run.
Game is quite... hardish sometimes, but definitely not as hard as the original. The great thing is (for me) that even if you die, you don't have to start from the last save point. It works almost like FFXIII - you die, try again. You start from the last "checkpoint", be it the last won battle, or entry point to a new level/floor/dungeon. Well, looking back at SNES-times you will probably say: "games are now too easy" or "this is for babies". This is what I used to say a couple of years ago. But now when one works, has his own family and doesn't have that much time to play games - this solution is just perfect!
"What about the bugs" you ask? Well, there are some issues with sound (summoning Shiva), text in dialogues, and the game itself crashed 3 or more times. Sure, if I were to pay over €15 I would be mad. But since I bought this game years after its release and paid around €5, that's acceptable ;p
Some of you whine that a lot of original/PSP stuff was removed. And what was that? Never-ending, boring dungeons for grinding with super-hyper bosses that required from you to level up to 99 lv? Well... good ;p I never bothered with these. And this is another thing SE likes to do - release old FF for n-th time on n-th console and add loooong boring dungeons with tough bosses. Nah, I'll pass. I'm glad that I almost didn't have to do any grinding here. Only once: when it occurred that Porom can use Dualcast. I had to level her up and fire Rosa from the main squad :) I'm not sure, but I probably didn't even reach the 60th level with any of my characters...
Ok, let me finish this here. Who reads these things anyway, especially when it comes for the older games? This is also unlikely for me to write a review for me, but I really wanted to, as this game deserves much better attention and praise than it gets! You're an old-school FF/jRPG fan? Haven't played it yet? So what are you waiting for? Go!

Never before have I wanted to give a middle-thumbs for a game as much as I do now. Cortex Command is an incredibly depressing game. It's a beautiful brainchild of a passionate person or people who just did not want to polish their ideas. They game has been in development about eight years now, and it's still in a miserable state. It's horribly bug ridden, there are amazingly careless and obvious mistakes and errors, there's huge balance issues and very little depth, and it's stagnated for a ridiculous amount of time. This game is going nowhere. It's a perpetual prototype, seemingly never to be fixed or improved. A prototype with game-breaking bugs, including the overworld map not fitting on the screen, or fullscreen causing immense lag, or you just getting stuck in a wall all the time. Not to mention the game has prolonged lagging episodes constantly.
But what a fun prototype it can be. The game is at times incredibly tense as you try to find an opening to shoot while desperately trying to avoid having any bit of you out in the open, and the game is at times hilarious as drop pods go astray and crash into a squad of troops. It is perfectly viable to win by dropping a crate of crabs on the enemy brain's head. They game is incredibly silly, but also extremely engaging. It takes a lot of effort to take down some of the enemies, and it feels very rewarding when you manage to do so. The base game has incredibly potential.
Let's talk about the actual game for a second. It's a 2D shooter with strategy elements. It's very hard to compare, there's really nothing like it. You have your typical base building aspects; you want a unit or two mining for gold, yet you also want a few armed units hanging around defending your brain/HQ. Most of the time you're be controlling a single offensive unit of some sort, kitted out to your liking. You have to make sure your brain lives, and the enemy's brain dies.
It's set in multiple scenarios. There are a few separate missions, including a horde/defense mode and a few assualt based modes. There's also a campaign mode, where you will capture points and build bases on them, then try to take over the opponent's bases. Although, that mode suffers from the previously mentioned glitch concerning the overworld map, making it so you cannot see and select some of the base building points, making it impossible to win. And that's it. You got about five missions and a frankly boring and repetitive campaign mode and that's it. There are a few nice mods that add some, but it's just a bit more icing atop an inch-tall cake. You ought experience everything the base game in about four hours, you can add probably add another four to six with mods. It depends how much you can stomach before getting bored.
The game has a very robust physics engine which allows you to contort into all sorts of hilarious positions, but it is also incredibly clunky. The menues are a mess, the characters are extremely slow, and you will accidentally kill yourself in hysterical yet infuriating ways. This is a good and bad thing. At first it's novel and interesting, then it's incredibly frustrating. Then it's a bit easier, then it grows fairly boring. There is a huge arsenal of weapons, but a lot of them feel the same, and a lot of them are somewhat disinteresting. Again, the base game is there, and it's great, but there is absolutely no filling, and there is bare minimum content. Your enjoyment of the game will depend entirely on how much you can put up with repitition and how far the bare basics of the gameplay can carry you.
In the end, I cannot recommend Cortex Command at the asking price of twenty dollars. That's simply too expensive for so little content and polish. It's also a game that I don't entirely feel comfortable supporting, as it's eight years in development yet still contains crippling bugs. It really feels like the developers just didn't want to bother polishing their initial ideas, they didn't want to do the boring parts. It's like an unedited paper, they just wanted to jolt down all their interesting thoughts and conclusions but they didn't want to spend time making it presentable to an audience. Such a shame.
On sale, you might want to consider it. It's got a few laughs and fun moments between the frustration of the brief experience, and it has a lot of toys for the more imaginative players. If you like weird 2D shooters with comically spasmic physics engines with some resource management, wait for a fifty percent sale bringing it down to ten dollars. If you're not interested in that or you can't stand major bugs or you need significant motivation besides gameplay, avoid it like the plague. Also, don't bet on this game ever being finished, or even improving significantly. Eight years of dead air does not bode well.

From the maker of UnEpic comes another funny, Metroid-vania style game with futuristic story.
You need the following ingredients to get Ghost 1.0:
* Metriod-vania genre
* Sci-fi story with robots and guns
* Humor
* Add extra measure of story
* Add a "previously on..." vid whenever the player comes back to the game after turning it off
* tight game controls
* Solid graphics that are a cross between a 16 - 32 bit stylings
* And just because you can add all the geeky references to classic Sci-fi movies / games like Storm Troopers and Starcraft without saying it overly to avoid copyright issues and cease and desist notices.
* Bake in development for roughly 1 year until you hit the initial price point of $12.99.
While various other reviewers harp on the game barely touching on "deep" issues like who Ghost is and etc.  This is not one of those reviews.  At the heart of Ghost 1.0 is a story that is pulled from a lot of "geeky" things that people who enjoy Sci-fi like to see played with and explored.  The humor in Ghost 1.0 treats these items in a very tongue-in-cheek.  Don't look for a video game story to deeply wrestle with things discussed in 'Blade Runner'.
If you want or need this, go take a college level English course that talks about the "Angel in the Attic".  If they talk about topic or it is in the syllabus, you know you are in the right place.  A irreverent game is not the place to find this.
That being said...
Synopsis:
Ghost 1.0 is another Metriod-vania game from @unepic_fan aka franfistro.  Franfistro builds on the model established in UnEpic for developing Metriod-vania game with more story and humor mixed with a Sci-fi flavor.
Pros:
* Great use of the Metroid-vania genre
* Good story with great use of humor.  I am still laughing over parts of it.  (And yes, I have finished the game)
* The unique use of "previously on Ghost 1.0..." vids of recent story to remind you of where you are at.  Such a great touch!
* Controls - solid and very responsive
* Graphics - perfect for the approach
* Well supported by the Dev who is in touch with his community.
Cons:
* I couldn't even get my X360 controller to work with Ghost 1.0.  I imagine that Franfistro will probably address in a patch.  Still played well on the keyboard.  Default key layout worked well with the game.
* (I'm being really picky on this one) There were leftover / unused item slots in the Inventory panels.  This left me with the impression that I was missing items.  I could only confirm I had everything by googling on it.

It's strange to think that I first played Final Fantasy VII 20 years ago. This game, more than any other, has special meaning for me. I took the PSX version with me everywhere, and made sure I had a PS2 with backwards compatibility for it. I started a tradition of playing through the game every time I moved somewhere new, which happened quite a lot. FFVII was a familiar friend amidst scary new settings.
I became intimately close with those first 10 hours or so in Midgar. And then to some extent, all of Disc 1. I ultimately beat the game maybe 5-6 times, but started it many, many times more than that. On my most thorough playthrough I morphed enemies with stat increases to get everyone in my party maxed not only in level to 99, but in every stat I could to 255. I shutter to think what I could've accomplished with my life in the same number of hours it took to do that. But at the time it seemed worth it.
This PC port holds up surprisingly well in some areas and truly awfully in others. First, the graphics: the cell shaded 3D characters - particularly the battle versions - are still quite nice. It's super odd to me as a modern audience that they change so much throughout. Tiny, stunted figures in some cases, stretched out elegant ones in others. Wouldn't it have been less work to just pick one? I'm sure the original hardware limitations at the time had something to do with these odd choices, but if you look at an anime like Bleach they do it there too, so maybe it's just a stylistic choice common to Japanese media.
The pre-rendered backgrounds, on the other hand, are god awful. Why didn't they keep the original un-rendered assets so they could release a high definition texture pack? It seems like it would've been a trivial upgrade that would've paid major dividends.
The sound and music are still iconic. Still excellent. I have no idea how they accomplished it at the time with only midis.
The controls are terribly translated to the computer though. This game was designed solely for a controller. A keyboard is a poor substitute they never considered.
The story actually makes way more sense now than I remember it did originally. Maybe it's because I'm older, maybe it's because there's been time for the public at large to analyze it and figure everything out. I'm not sure, but I regardless I wish they made more games with stories and characters like this nowadays.
Despite its age and flaws I still feel the strong pull of nostalgia here. I'll admit that it's maybe not the best game ever made at this point considering some modern contenders, but it's my personal favorite game of all time.
If I ever loved a game, I loved Final Fantasy VII.

The 2D beat-up genre was a giant during the 8 and 16 bit generations as well as dominating arcades with their quarter munching gameplay and cooperative game design. With the decline of arcades and the birth of new genres in 3d, the popularity of beat 'em ups waned, making way for new gaming zeitgeists. In recent years the 2D beat-em up has settled for reboots of classics with little success, luckily the love for the genre burns in the hearts of indie developers and with this, Aces Wild Manic Brawling Action comes to life. Does this beat 'em up deliver a first round knock out punch or does it throw the towel?
Taking control of the title character Aces Wild, who must participate in this year's Maximus Circuit in an attempt to preserve the lands held by the Wilder Family. His brother Rex has struck a deal with key entrants of the tournament to ensure his victory so he can sell the lands for a hefty sum. In classic beat 'em up tradition, the story stops there allowing you to pummle your way through the games stages without narrative interruption.
Aces Wild's obvious key focus is it's stylized fast paced aerial combat. The controls consist of a light and heavy attack which are linked to the wild meter located at the top left corner of the screen. The meter fills up with every light attack landed increasing the potency of all your attacks. It's also used for health recovery, and charged attacks. This simple idea creates a system in which managing your wild meter become crucial. You'll find yourself debating on whether to use it for a quick heal, full on charge attack or conserving it just a bit longer for an array of potent light attacks. It's becomes a game of it's own that I was very impressed with, seeing as how simple it was. The three selectable character also bring a distinct combat style to the table, each with their unique skill set. If you find yourself in a bind consider a new route by selecting another character.
The combat is a bitter sweet. While it is mechanically solid, the level design and enemy encounters undermine it's strengths. One minute you'll feel like you're part of a knuckle sandwich catering service and the next you'll find yourself beaten, battered and tossed out on your♥♥♥♥♥like an unruly patron at a biker bar. This often becomes a one sided affair in the later stages when the screen is cluttered with enemies, and one missed dodge results in ten enemy hits. A handful of sword, fists and draggers to the face is a high price to pay for missing one dodge in a cluttered an chaotic melee where sometimes the greatest challenge is keeping track of where your character is among the action. Enemies moves don't necessarily evolve either, spamming becomes their game and it becomes extremely irritating when the difficulty is ramped up by cluttering the screen with enemies instead of providing a clever mix of foes that complement one another's attacks and patterns.
Boss battles continue the trend of being frustrating. Like their lesser counterparts, they have a bit of a penchant for spamming the same attacks again and again creating very narrow windows in which to land attacks. Small mistake and missed dodges are also punished severely. Earlier bosses are formidable at first but quickly become a joke as you learn their patterns. Later encounters ramp up completely taking much of the fun away as they become tedious and ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. Knowing what to do is one thing but succeeding is another when everything consuming the screen seems to be at the right spot to put a hurting on you. All is slightly remedied though, as you can select any stage whenever, infinite lives, and the instant respawn with full health after a loss. Still, consider having a pillow at arms reach to smack around when anger consumes you.
Leaderboards have recently been added for those looking to ascend them and local mutiplayer is available if you and friend want to tackle the challenge as a team. Co-op play isn't all that exciting though, other then adding a second player on screen the game is exactly the same. If played on a small screen the zooming in and out of the screen can be a pain, making it even more difficult to keep up with what is going on. Unless you have a large monitor and two controllers at hand consider passing on this feature.
Aces Wild channels the style of late 90's Capcom fighting games and side scrolling titles with the interface and the character design, but is a bit lacking when it comes to detail. Many of the environments feel lifeless and static. There are few interactive objects. Generally, stages are constructed with backdrop layered with platforms that are crisp and clean but lacking in personality or style. A more dynamic environment could easily add another layer to the static world of Aces Wild and pay better homage to a genre where using objects in the environment as weapons has been a long standing staple. There's also a dearth of detail missing throughout all the characters with little to no animation involved. Fortunately, the soundtrack is well done delivering some fantastic 16bit tracks and sounds.
The foundation of a great game are definitely here but the overall experience becomes a bit repetitive as the variation in enemies and environment do little to evolve along the way. Aces Wild is a tough game with some infuriating segments, there is no escaping the anger along the ride, but it's the nature of the beast. If it gets a sequel, an upgrade system is an obvious request, along with some improved visuals. Aces Wild Manic Brawling Action is a large dose of nostalgia for a great price, if you're up for a beat-em up and a challenge pick it up when you have the urge. But remember, keep a pillow at arms reach.

A game, that at the time of release, was considered by many to be the greatest game ever created. This was the first turn based RPG I played, sometime around 1997 IIRC. I remember thinking "I hate this taking turns fighting crap", and I did at the time. What sold me on the game, and RPG's in geneal, was the fact you could talk to NPC's who all seemed to have their own lives and purposes in the world.
From then a life long love with RPG's was born, and as I got older I began to enjoy turn based combat.
There's not much I can say that hasn't already been said about this game, and I may be repeating what others have said here, but I will tell you the reasons I think this game is still (one of) the greatest game(s) of all time.
1. Compelling story. I consider The Last of Us (even though I'm exclusive PC player) to be the greatest game ever created, but the story is pretty simple. Final Fantasy still has the best told story in video games IMO.
2. Compelling characters. There's not a single character in this game that you won't find yourself caring about. It also has possibly the most iconic villain in all of video game history, Sephiroth. Doesn't hurt that his name is bad♥♥♥♥♥too.
3. Music. Nubuo Uematsu IMO is on the same level as classical music writers like Beethoven and Mozart, and I am not being sarcastic. This game has some of the best music in any video game ever.
4. Unlike other JRPGs, like Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky, FF7 has a sense of danger. Of conflict. You know right away that things aren't going to all work out in the end. Bad things are going to happen.
Overall, all these years later, even with the outdated graphics, this game is still a perfect 10.

First impressions:
Aces Wild is a straight-up “beat up everything in your path” game, with some completely ridiculous fighting mechanics.
When I say ridiculous, I mean it. You’re able to continually punch and kick while remaining motionless in air, and you can even fly if you tried. Most enemies are easy to beat, but some, including what I thought to be a doge-like dog, are really difficult to defeat if there’s no combo going. The more rapidly you attack, the higher your combo, allowing more damage to be dealt.
Aces Wild makes use of arcade-style graphics, but with a simplistic style to them. Almost like a cartoon, actually. The game is a side-scroller, so once you find yourself in a battle, all enemies must be defeated before moving on.
Overall, the game feels really good to play. The satisfaction of wiping out dozens of on-screen enemies at once is awesome. The game may be difficult at parts, but it definitely deserves my recommendation.
