Reading all the negative reviews for this game is a bit disheartening so I thought I would do my best to give it a positive review, as I liked it overall.  I'll give a bit of advanced warning now so no one wastes their time reading this review.
If you are not a fan of visual novels, dating sims, stat raising games, etc., then I advise not to read any further.  I'm giving a bit of a heads-up since those who are not fans of the above genres will probably
be interested in this game.
Now on to the review:
dUpLicity~Beyond the Lies is both a stat raising and visual novel game, which makes it somewhat unique.  It's rare to find a game that has both of these aspects, as it is either usually just stat raising (with narrative dispersed here and there) or a visual novel where the player makes choices that affect the gameplay.  The first half of the game is stat raising and upon starting it, there are two dateable options.  Deciding which stats to raise will determine which of the guy's paths you'll go on but be warned...If you don't make the necessary stat requirements, you won't be able to continue on a path.
Now I have to admit that the stat raising aspect is a bit of a challenge and it is hard to get on a path without a walkthrough.  Fortunately, there is a walkthrough available via the developer's official website.
The second half of the game is the visual novel aspect.  Upon entering a guy's path, you get to learn more about the guy himself and possibly about Yukina, the main character, as well.  Depending on the choices you make from there, you can either get good or bad endings with each guy.
Once the guys' paths have been unlocked and completed, more options are available.  There is a "true" path in which you can learn more about Yukina's origins.  Once you get to the VN aspect of that path, you can decide whether to make choices that favor one of the two guys that are made available at the beginning.
However, the game doesn't end there.  As you play through, you'll meet a "mysterious boy" but you don't get to know him until the option to go on his path is unlocked.  Of course, this doesn't happen until after you complete the "true" path.  As you play on the mystery boy's path, you'll discover who he really is and that his path is the true one.  (For spoiler purposes, I won't reveal what that is here.)
Basically, that's what the game is about.  Now to critique certain aspects of the game:
The storyline was intriguing.  I found myself wanting to play more as I got on a guy's path although I did find it a little grinding in the stat raising part to get there.  Although the writing was proofread, I did find mistakes here and there so I think this aspect could be improved upon.
As for the art, it's in the anime style which I happen to like.  Although it is usually the case for VNs, I know that not everyone will like this art style.  To each his/her own, I suppose.  However, there is a nice CG gallery in the Extras section in the main menu and it was nice to see all of the CGs I unlocked as I played.
Also, I liked the Extras section overall.  In addition to the CG gallery, you can see how many endings there are to unlock as well as the ending videos when you unlock a good or true path.  I like these aspects in a VN but I suppose they won't matter so much for others.
As for the Steam release, I'm glad that the developer was able to add trading cards.  I would have liked for there to be Steam achievements as well, since they would highly motivate me to play so I can get them all.  I'm hoping that they might be added in a future release.
So yeah, I liked the game overall and congrats to the developer on releasing the game on Steam.  ^^

I'm glad the game looks like it took some amount of effort to make, because many RPGMaker games are very shallow and fall in the same mistakes. Unfortunately, Journey to Lunoto is no different to them. But I applaud the developer for actually finishing a game and getting it up on Steam. In my opinion, I just couldn't slog through it any longer. So, here are my reasons!
1) There's a huge reliance on RTP materials for... everything. Correct me if I'm wrong, but this is the impression I got from the start. Of course, when used effectively, the RTP (stock assets used in RPGMaker) can blend in better and be used to a developer's advantage. It just doesn't here, because it leads me onto my next point:
2) The maps are very bland and bare. If they're not, then they're usually sample maps - or slightly more visually interesting ones. It doesn't detract from the fact that they weren't pleasant to look at.
3) There's some strange performance issue when selecting to save your game... It takes a while for the engine to process that. I've had some experience with MV, and it isn't this slow to save your game. So I wonder what could be causing it. Nevertheless, it does make the overall experience more of a chore than a hobby.
4) The game as a whole feels unpolished because of the reasons I listed above. When I was battling the dragon, the dragon sprite clipped with the whole party. That's just a clear oversight that could be easily fixed if the developer tested the game properly.
5) Every time an NPC said "I've updated your quest log" or "check your quest log" without saying anything in regards to what they want the party to do, felt very detached. I wasn't immersed at all.
6) Now, this one isn't a complaint, but more of a curiosty - why is the game 2GB big? Are RPGMaker MV games getting this big now, or did something happen when packaging the game?
So... yup. This game feels more like a prototype of what it could be... a huge world filled with sidequests and a present storyline, perhaps? Anyway, I do know that I am only 20mins through the game but because of my negative first impression I don't think I'll be playing it anymore.

Very straightforward RPG game which takes about 5 hours to finish. The gameplay is linear without any side quests (you just follow the main story quest line) and the RPG part is rather basic (permanent party, no elements, no buffs and statuses etc.), so I would say this game is actually perfect for kids as their first RPG (and of course everyone else who is fine with simple RPG game).
Although the game is listed as finished (and story wise it really is finished), I recommend you to think about it as an early access game - several maps are very basic and there are some bugs as well, but as you can see from the patches, author works on finishing and fixing these things. Generally, for the most enjoyable experience and to avoid possible problems, I recomend to follow the instructions from the quests and do not enter the areas where the quest does not send you yet. Another problem you may encounter is delay between when you choose Save and when the window with saved games appears - it takes so long that on my first save I thought the game crashed - but just wait and the window will appear (I have not seen this problem in any other RPG Maker game). And regarding saving one more warning - letting Steam to upgrade the game to patch 0.2 wiped all my saved slots, so until you finish your game, it is wise not to upgrade.
Overall, I liked the game - the story is good (although you will have to wait for it until about 70 % of the game, when the gameplay slightly changes), art and music is nice, there is great feeling of progress as you play and it is generally apparent that author gave the game lots of time and love. If you like simple RPG games, I recommend it.

Zup Zero: 1043 achievements, 37 minutes

This game appears to be an homage to Metroid. Female protagonist collecting powerups, fighting bosses, and exploring a large area to uncover information? It should be obvious within 10 minutes of starting the game.
It falls a bit short of the Metroid 'standard', but is good enough to earn a recommendation from me. With that out of the way, here comes a torrent of criticism. (Possible spoilers ahead)
The voice acting isn't good. The animation in the cutscenes is bad. The story lacks details and flips between serious and humorous too much. The final boss involves a deus ex machina.
Near the beginning of the game, the characters discuss how none of them would be a good video game protagonist because of the three, one is fat, one is black, and one is female, and everyone knows only a muscular white man can be a video game protagonist. This is a thinly veiled criticism of mainstream gaming trends, but manages to come off as self aggrandizing on the part of the writers.
From the middle to the end of the game, the characters frequently discuss whether or not androids are conscious, and whether they deserve human rights. You expect this to play into the story heavily because the player can see that Ghost is a digital ghost "possessing" an android chassis. But the ending completely sidesteps the whole argument, even going so far as to have the characters express vindication that a computer really can't be conscious.
This actually offends me. Firstly, I would never make a story deeply involve such a philosophical argument as "can machines be conscious", and then not resolve it within the context of the story. Dodging it like this is cowardly.
Second, One of the characters actually makes arguments for the possibility of machine consciousness. Then by the end, he agrees that it was never possible. So the writing even contradicts itself.
Third, the story is in a sci-fi setting, a genre which deals largely with the "what-if"s and "could-be"s of our future. For the ending of this game to then state that one of the genre's favorite speculation material - True Artificial Intelligence - can't exist? It doesn't merely go against storytelling convention, it's a spit in the face of any sci-fi enthusiast who happens to play this game.

A 2D beat em up that plays more like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta than Streets of Rage or Final Fight. The action is faster, the characters can move across the screen in a flash, and you can have 10 enemies randomly appear poised to attack.
The crux of the game is balancing your use of your 'Wild' gauge and not dying. As you attack enemies or are attacked your 'Wild' gauge builds up. Past a certain point you can use 'Panic' mode, which depletes the gauge but restores health. Or you can charge up your attacks and inflict some serious damage; you can use up the entire gauge for a single charged attack if you wish. As you attack and build up your gauge, your rank goes up which makes your attacks stronger, but your enemies also become stronger. You want to stay alive as long as possible to continously rank up; using Panic lowers your rank.
The game is pretty fun; but its also pretty simplistic. Gameplay boils down to mashing the attack button and is really more about balancing gauge use and keeping your score up. It's status as an indie title shows: there are 5 level backgrounds in total and the enemy variety is minimal. Your characters have a limited variety of moves and unlike titles within the same genre, like Muramasa (fantastic game, btw) or Double Dragon Neon (BUY IT NOW), you don't get to customize your repertoire of moves and you're pretty much stuck with the same move set. Which would be alright if it were still 1993.
Overall the game is pretty fun, though, but it could use more polish (variety, upgrades, more varied levels). It's pretty damn bare bones as it is, so why the recommendation? Because it doesn't do anything wrong, it just doesn't do enough of it. I can SEE where the appeal might be and I can SEE where the fun might lie, but as it stands it could use more polish and more variety. There's nothing wrong with it as it is, it just doesn't do enough to draw me in and didn't warrant my attention.
5/10:meeehhh. Also, a 5 isn't an automatic ''♥♥♥♥ this title'' in this scenario. A 5 means alright; it isn't an atrocious score. I recommend the title if you can get it under 10 bux; 5=alright. Not a must-have, but alright if you're into the genre and are into the game system and mechanics.

Did you like Final Fantasy IV?
Are you curious to how the characters are getting on after the defeat of Zeromus?
Well, fast forward seventeen years later, and we find out!
Honestly, if you thought FF4's ending was perfect the way it was, or if you didn't care about the cast that much, you aren't going to get a lot out of this. Not only that, but quite a few bosses are repeated. I remember when in a quest involving a certain pair of twincasting siblings, we had to slay a monster that died very early in the story of the original game and going "wait, what? didn't Cecil and friends kill that all ready?" It wasn't explained if that was just a typical species of monster in either game, so I found it really confusing. Many characters will even say "this feels like before". And, yeah, it really does. Everything feels the way it did in the 3D remake of FF4.
Like, the battles. They're still pretty darn slow.
And the movement. It's kinda clunky and slow.
BUT if you didn't mind that, then you won't mind taking the plunge back onto the Blue Planet and seeing some old friends again... and meeting some new ones. There's a lot to choose from! Like, those dolls you once fought as a boss in the Dwarven Castle! And those faceless guards and faceless monks escorting the royal party members around. Huh. Weird. BUT BUT you get to see Kain finally face his inner darkness! Now that's worth seeing, right?! Yeah, totally, if you like Kain. If you don't care about him, then it'll be hard to be invested in it... or understanding his inner pain to begin with. You really should play the original game before playing this.
Do I like the game? Heck yes I love this game. But not because the gameplay is spectacular or because the writing is inspired. It... kinda isn't. It reads like a fanfiction. But I love this game! Why? I'm invested in these characters and I have been literally since I started playing RPGs and Final Fantasy.
Can I tell you to buy it? Ehhhhhhhhhhhh. Under certain circumstances. And those circumstances are: are you willing to deal with clunky gameplay to see these characters after their initial adventure is over? Do you love this world so much that you'll endure to see them through it? If you are, buy it. If you aren't, but you still care about these characters, check it out on PSP. If you don't care about any of that, then don't waste your money.
Kain is my favorite Final Fantasy character. I played this game to see him through his quest. That's my reason. But I can admit this game is far, FAR from perfect.

Also some optional choices present in the Wii- and PSP-Versions of this game were removed and the game forces you into the best choice (without extra work). Usually not a bad thing as these tended to be a bit tedious to do right, but some people like choices.
Graphics are okay. Definitely not better than FF4 here on steam is. The new areas in fact seemed somewhat blurry, like they did not put in the effort to clean them up properly for higher resolutions.
Cut Content: This version of The After Years does not include the challenge dungeons the Wii and PSP versions have. Also they removed the bonus bosses during the Final Dungeon that referenced Final Fantasy games 1,2,3,5 and 6. Which is a shame but does not change much story-wise. In fact the Final Dungeon appeared too long on the PSP, for the impatient this might actually a plus.
What weights worse is how they altered other areas of the Final Dungeon. Instead of designing the new areas they just copy-pasted old areas from FF4, without explanation.
I had a few crashes during the game but the game'S autosave feature put me right back to where it happened. So that is acceptable
Overall it is a lazy port of a decent-to-good game. If you have no other places to get this game or just enjoy grinding achievements, or just want ot complete your sets this is a totally acceptable game that is well worth buying while it is discounted. I don't think it is quite worth the full price. But overall it is a game worth playing.
But personally I recommend the PSP-version if you have a PSP or Vita over this. If you can get the Final Fantasy 4 Complete Collection for PSP get that one instead unless you are averse to sprite games.

Summary:  10/10 - possibly the greatest game ever made...even after being extremely dated.
You will read a lot of reviews that say "revolutionized the genre" or "changed how games were made forever".  Unfortuantely I couldn't disagree more.  Ever since I was that 15 year old boy, stuck in my room for a month, being sick - and experienced the most incredible story ever told; I have yet to discover the feelings this game tickled within the depths of my soul, from any game to date.
Now with that said... it will be very hard for a lot of people today to get past the squared hooves for hands, the ugly pixilated background textures, and even the music (as great as it is) is all MIDI beeps and boops.  But if you can get past that initial shock and allow yourself to be immersed - you will suddenly see beauty and perfection instead of pixilated garbage.  This is especially true for the music... because it is on another level.  It's will cast a spell over you and draw you deep into this world.  It's quite hard to explain....you just have to try it yourself.
The story is what sets this game so far above others of it's kind.  The dialog is at times completely incohearant and ridiculous - yet it makes the characters come alive in a very unique way.  But a story isn't enough to keep me coming back 20 years later - so what makes this game so addictive?  Why am I finding myself chosing to play this over the other top games I recently bought?  It's the progression.  It's beyond perfect.  Something I have dearly missed in this new age of gaming is the attention to difficuly and balance.  You will probably die in the first boss fight of the game, and you might die a heck of a lot more.  Even if you are really good at RPG's.  You have to bring your A game to every decision you make in FF7.  What developers don't understand anymore (even the ones that made this game) is that people don't get bored because of graphics or flashy systems...... they put a game down because they don't feel like they (as the player) matter at all.  Games play themselves these days and it's downright pathetic.  You might even have to take notes and draw maps in FF7, and you will be shocked at how long it takes to get 100% completion.

It will make RPG lovers worship the lore, and doodle pictures of Aeris in notebooks (or name your cat after her in my case lol).  If you haven't played this game yet - consider yourself lucky.  Because experiencing this for the first time has the power to change your life.  It will make you cry more than once - and for more than one reason.

Since lots of people want to compare this game with Overwatch I'll give reasons why this game is superior to overwatch:
- Cheaper:
Huh? What? I thought this was F2P, and yes that is correct. However, if you'd like to unlock all and FUTURE champions, all you need to pay is $20USD right now... That's right an optional $20 to unlock all current and FUTURE champions game vs a $60 B2P game. Yeah I know which is the better deal
- Faster paced:
Overwatch tends to have a lot of time wasted running from spawn to the objective. Paladins has made this less of an issue with mounts, which are used only when you're in your spawn room. This means there's less time travelling and more time actually being in the action. Oh and let's not forget the shorter spawn times which, by the time you've finished watching the killcam, you're alive again.
- Not an Overheal game:
Supports are a great addition to the team, but aren't so broken that you won't be able to do anything against the person that's being healed. Introducing Catuerise, a skill that you can buy which decreases healing received by 30%/60%/90%. And supports aren't a passive, excluded genre either. All healing abilities are CD based, so there's only burst healing, and all supports have proper weapons. Part of the action yet still supporting the team.
- Diversity:
Every champion has the ability to design their own deck, which is basically using cards which specialises certain skills, such as CD reduction, more knockback, etc. This makes it so your champion actually plays the way you want, rather than having to work around the things you dislike about them. As previously mentioned, there's also skills which further let's you specialise your champion in-game, which helps against enemy composition and situations.
- Fair time to kill:
There is only 2 champions in the game that can 1 shot you. Both are on ultimates and one of them requires a certain card to actually do so.  So no more insta sniped by widowmaker or FB + FTH by McCree again!
- No stupid gimmicks:
Did you ever 1v1 someone, bring them low, only for them to run over a HP kit and win the fight? Well there's no HP kits in this game, instead if you stay out of combat for a moment, you start to regenerate quickly. This means no more 6 people sitting on 1 health kit because no one wants to go support (which is fair, why should people feel forced to play something they don't like).
If none of the points above convinces you, then maybe sticking to Overfrustration is more of your game. But it's free, so why not give it a try anyway.

My personal favorite Final Fantasy, as it changes all the ideas of how a Final Fantasy game works. The enemies in the world scale with your level, so you can finish the game anywhere from level 6 to level 99 and the difficulty adapts to your level. The magic system has been replaced with the 'Draw" and 'Junction' systems. You can draw from enemies to stock different types of magic, then you can either use the magic or junction it to stats to increase your power. As an example, you can junction 'Death' magic to a character's attack and it will allow a chance for the enemy to be afflicted with the death ability, killing them instantly.
The graphics are outdated at this point, but at the time they were revolutionary. If you can get past the bumps in the story and the forced plot twists, you are in for an epic adventure with hundreds of hours of gameplay.
The hidden gem in this game is Triple Triad. You collect cards from various NPCs and enemies and play a card game that is amazingly addictive.
Note that I am currently replaying the game on steam, originally I played the 5 disc CD-ROM version on Windows XP, followed by the Playstation Classics version on PSP, so my playtime will not reflect the hundreds of hours I spent on the game.

R.I.P Mr Dever.  I recently found out he passed away in late 2016 and felt that I just had to get this game for old times sake.  Been a fan of the Lone Wolf series since my teenage years and watching Youtube gameplay of the game it felt like a gamebook brought to life to a screen.
I played this game to the end and it feels like a proper old school Lone Wolf gamebook with interactive quicktime elements.  I wish there are more games like this in the market.
Pros:
1) it really feels like an interactive book with proper writing.  Have to use your imagination.  People may not be used to this in a modern game if they don't like reading.
2) fun gameplay with good RPG elements.  Fun if at times unbalanced combat (more on this later).
3) a lot of choices.  Branching storylines.  The powers you pick and your stats greatly affect gameplay, which leads to replayability.
4) Nice puzzle minigames.  These range from simple to somewhat challenging.  Your choice of a Kai power enables an option to assist the cube puzzles.
Cons:
1) the uneven difficulty in combat as you progress in the story.  The game throws you into your first combat and it's either sink or swim.  Chances are you will die often before figuring out the mechanics to overcome certain enemies.  Even then you will still die because you simply don't know the correct order of using your skills and powers.
For example, sometimes the optimal choice is to save your Kai powers for more difficult enemies in the next round but the game does not give an indication of how many enemies you will fight.  You may have slain a couple of low level critters before an elite soldier steps up to confront you while your powers are on cooldown, meaning that your options are limited and leaving you open to be attacked.  For some combat it takes a couple of tries using trial and error of different combinations before you can succeed.
Eventually Lone Wolf became so powerful that he can take down several Drakkarim without being hit a single time.
2) Although I have only done one playthrough, it seems like some powers may be a more optimal choice over others.  E.G. how can you forgo Mindblast/Mindshield when you know certain enemies perform psychic attacks?
3) Dare I say, a bit too much combat?  I seems like Lone Wolf has slaughtered a whole batallion of soldiers when the story ended.
4) There could have been more variety of enemies.  Where is the Helghast?
TLDR:  Old school gamebook series brought to life on a tablet/PC.  Don't play if you don't like reading and using your imagination.

I stumbled over this game in a sale and I am absolutely content to have bought and played it.
It is kind of a different RPG, which lives through the written narative which unfolds as you play the game.
You cant chose a character, you play as the last Kai-Lord (a worshipper of the God Kai, who has bestowed great (magical) powers to his followers) that is left after their monastry has been overrun. Which powers you have you determine in the beginning of the game, there are good tutorials on the character creation so I wont refer to it any further. You have a powerful sword, the Sommerswerd, that is capable of dealing great damage to your foes. Those powers are needed, because you will meet powerful foes aswell and tactic and timing play a good part in fighting.
While the main story is written and holds at points where you can make choices to use certain abilities or the way the next fight will take place, your choices have consequences, resulting in advantage or disadvantage, victory or death.
Graphics, animated graphics or will loosen up the story. You can navigate to different places on the map, though you dont have much choices, since the story follows a more or less linear story, and you cant go back: the story is devided in 4 acts and you only can move to places you have been before in the same act.
Fighting itself is divided in turns according to a fading energy-meter which has to refill to be able to act again. You can chose to use the sommerswerd, sword and shield (or any other weapon you chose), throwing missiles or magic skills which also have a cooldown timer until your action-energy has run out. Again your choices matter in the fight. The fight takes places in an animated 3D fight. Your skills grow in power with more freequent use (and unlock an additional effect).
As it seems it is a remake of some gaming series that I didnt know. Although unfamiliar with that background-story, the good storytelling dragged me into the lore and the story. By chance I took a good set of skills (i liked healing, mind over matter, animal kinship and sixth sense, which really can prove helpful in some tasks), and played through the main story in 14-15 hours on a normal difficulty (which proves good to get to know the game-style)
Although the story is linear, so there is no great open world, no characters to chose, repeated fighting (once you have your set of skills) and especially a repeating and narrow sound track, I really liked the story and the way it was realized in the game. Having meaningful choices, influencing the gameplay and sometimes the story, resolving minigames and especially finding the right fighting tactics was fun to me and absolutely outweigh the negative points.
I really can recommend this games for players that like to dive into a narrative, that like language and reading and solving problems and that are interested in playing a different kind of RPG.

So i bought this game on a whim thinking that it would be a game that i would play and forget about in a short amount of time, oh how wrong i was. I had never heard of the Lone Wolf adventure stiry before so this game opened up my mind to a whole new world. Having just beaten the game, i will  list what i beleve are the pros and cons of the game for me.
Some replayability.
Pros:
Great Story where your choices do matter.
Great Turn-based combat system where your choices right befoer combat can either be advantageous or disadvantageous to you.
Creative writing that draws you into the character.
Variety of enemies that are unique in their own aspect.
QTE's add a bit of a challenge to the game.
There are physics for turning the pages, awesome touch to the game that adds character to the game.
Intro and outro cutscenes to battle go from story book to animated and vice versa which is just awesome and is exactly how i would imagine characters from a book coming to life.
If you are having trouble with the shianti puzles, you can take the health damage and just continue on with your day.
Now for the Cons:
While the enemies are unique, combat gets boring after awhile if you have to grind (which you do on hard)
The Shianti puzzles are an interesting aspect, but are extremely difficult to solve. Also wish there was some more consequences to failing the puzzles other than just health loss, i felt like i was cheating just taking the hp damage at times with no other repercusions.
The inventory and crafting system are a little awkward at times.
I felt like while upgrading armor and weapons helped a little bit, i would have liked for a more noticable difference between leather Kai armour and Kai plate armour.
Overall, i give this game a 9/10 and it has easily made it's way onto my top 10. I for one am going to go look into the rest of the Lone Wolf stories after this.

The animation is largely superb, barring that of the town NPCs, who appear very clearly to have their limbs rigged to a skeleton instead of uniquely animated.  The music, too, is quite nice and fits the atmosphere well with its various piano arrangements, but Dust: an Elysian Tale's combat is where the game truly shines.  Said combat is combo-heavy, both when grounded and mid-air, and bears a strong resemblance to what can be found in Capcom's Devil May Cry series, albeit on a 2D plane.  There is also a strong metroidvania element, but without a dense, labyrinthine structure to get frustratingly lost within, and I found the voice acting to be satisfying from all performers, especially Kimlinh Tran (who is perhaps more well-known for her work as Ms. Fortune in Skullgirls).  I won't spoil the story here, though it isn't particularly complex, but I will say that I was applauding as the credits rolled.  Dust: an Elysian Tale is truly one of my favorite titles on Steam, and is likely well worth your time.

When I first grabbed the game, I was expecting so much more. I had watched videos and done a little bit of research, and the game simply looked amazing for what it was. A unique side scrolling take on RTS.
When I actually got to hop in the game however, things went bad fast.
First off, learning the controls, even with the assistance of the tutorial was a pain. They only explain the bare minimum in how you can switch out to other units under your influence, and how to control them on a basic level. They tell you nothing of how you're supposed to actually use the unit, or how to activate its various AI scripts and what they actually do. The UI is bare minimum, you have to dig and test everything out on your own just to figure out things that should be presented directly, or have better in game descriptions.
While actually controlling your units, you'll find they are slow and terribly clunky. Even the faster/lighter units feel that way, and there's simply no way around. Heavy units are a literal nightmare to move around the map. With heavier units you'll find it almost impossible to reach certain areas, forcing you to use easily killed light units for everything, and only equipping them with the absolute bare minimum to assault the enemy. Attempting to use the AI scripts usually just forces them to saunter off to their deaths, they end up firing into the air blindly or never returning fire, while the enemy computer controlled units decimate your forces from half a mile away with a pistol.
While all the equipment and units you can call down are interesting, you'll find yourself most times just calling down basic units due to the cost to protect yourself, while the opponent seems to have near infinite resources he can call on. Even when you have a ton of money it seems to run out in seconds, where there's seem to have no end, even on the easier settings. That and the fact you'll notice the enemy AI is quite crafty in going after your controller unit/brain. Assassinating him from impossible angles, or simply just scuicide bum rushing you, while your idiot AI forces stand there and watch slack jawed, even is they are on sentry/defense mode.
There are a number of mods out there that can expand the gameplay, adding modes, areas, new factions and weapons and other things. Some of them are quite excellent, and it's to bad there was such a great modding community for this game, but the developer half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥it for about 10 years. Yep, that's right. This game was 10 years in development before seeing a "full" version launch. Looking at the game now you'd probably be wondering where the full version is. It feels much more like a late alpha build, or very early beta.
Like I said, it's such a shame there was such a passionate modding community, their talents and time went to waste on a devolper and his half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥game, when the modders could have put their attentions elsewhere and made something amazing in a game people actually care about.
If you can get the game for dirt cheap on sale for like 90% off go for it. Simply to check it out, and see "what could have been". The potential you can see in videos and in the game itself is amazing. But, the deveolper simply never capitilized on it, and now it sits as pretty much abandonware, festering here on Steam, where the deveolper is still asking money for a dead and rotting corpse of a product he will never patch, update, touch, or even look at again.
If the source code gets released, and others pick it up and do something with it, the results might just be amazing. So keep your eyes open if or when that happens.
Until then, stay away from this festering pile of abandonware garbage.

First of all I would like to preface this by saying that I really like FFIV and after replaying FFI I got the urge to try after years for the first time. I want to like it, and i suspect i will, but not this version.
This game has certain glaring issues that each on their own would make me question if it is worth buying. In combination with eachother this is certainly on the avoid list. The fact that it's a mobile port results in it having (by FF standards) a fairly ugly ui, and quite poor pixelated graphics (same quality as the DS version). The opening cutscene also plays a set ammount of time regardless of when you press the button to skip to the next chatbox, leaving you to look at a mouth opening and closing for 4-5 seconds before it again displays a one line textbox and another 4-5 seconds of flapping mouth. However graphical and cutscene issues aside it also suffers from some technical issues.
First of all is the fact that it is locked to 30 fps with 15 in battles, but it also has a terrible launcher that refuses to register controller button presses (in my case a 8bitdo NES30/SFC30), so if you plan on using this with a non xbox controller you might want to double check that you can rebind the controller before the refund period expires.
If you are interested in playing this i would suggest the FFIV: Complete Collection for PSP/Vita, the graphics is in my opinion better (somewhat high quality sprites as opposed to a somewhat low quality 3D models) with what i gather is quite a bit of extra content and you also get IV and Interlude.

In the Dead of Night is a fairly generic and somewhat uninspired TD.  The RTS elements are extremely minimal as you manage a group of villagers to gather various resources, build towers and construct them.  The towers are very limited and suffer from a lack of creativity as the first three traps are simply different spike traps built from the three resources in the game.  The game play can feel slow and repetative even after only the first day of a level.
From a technical stand point this game suffers from a few glaring issues.  The most basic of them is that the graphics will wow no one who has played a game made after 2000 yet despite what should be a very very low demand engine the optimization appears non-existant as the game will stutter and lag during fairly small enemy waves; long story short if my rig can handle Cry engine there is no way this game should lag.
The possibly most offending part of this game is the pure lack of polish to the menu/playing interface.  Many click boxes do not line up to their respective buttons or appear to be missing completely, with basically 3 interface interaction between start to finish on placing a tower that means you have to deal with 3 menus/interfaces each of which is full of missing or misplaced click boxes, it's tedious and frustrating.
The story idea is interesting but I've played better built free flash games than this mess.

This game is almost insultingly mediocre. Nevermind the abysmal framerate, nevermind the aggressively linear "dungeons", nevermind the weird cut scenes that are animated as if they have voice acting but lack voice acting and leave the characters mutely flapping their mouths.
Where to begin? I would say if you loved FF4 like I do, don't give this thing a second look. The primary problem is there's so much simply copied over from FF4. The music is wonderful because it's from FF4, for example, except for the one and only new track I've noticed in the game, which is a muddy nonsense-fire of annoying bells. Most of the monsters are the same, if shuffled to different areas with adjusted stats.
Rydia's theme from FF4 is used for one of the new characters, rather than giving her a theme of her own. That is a hideous misuse, to me. Speaking of Rydia, if this game takes place a decade (at least) after FF4, why does she still look like she's 17 or so? Why does she act like a teenager? If she's spent much time in the summoned land, she should be significantly older, right?
Why are my parties so often made up of "Black Mage" and "White Mage" or, good lord, "Monks A, B, and C"? Why is the siege on Fabul from FF4 repeated with almost no alterations? It's like they took the same game code and just swapped a few characters and dialog lines.
The difference in Square at the time this garbage fire was made is incredibly apparent. You've got mysterious, nearly silent overpowered characters showing up, endless cut scenes strung together by a minute or two of corridor-running, multiple nameless characters showing up (one of them even rocking Sephiroth hair) and a plot made ridiculously convoluted by an asinine episodic structure that never allows the player to get fully engaged in what's going on.
Why does a forest dungeon have cave dungeon music? I finished Ceodore's tale (god, I hate Ceodore), Rydia's tale (Rydia being my favorite character from FF4, it's odd her tale is almost entirely about Luca, who looks just ridiculous), and partway through Yang's tale, I just felt like I was being trolled. Why do I need flashbacks about Yang's pregnant wife? How many times in this game does the argument, "I'm coming with you!" "No you're not!" "I am and here's why!" "Fine, I'll protect you!" play out? I swear it happened three times between the same two characters within twenty minutes of Yang's tale.
I got this in the bundle, meaning I paid about eight bucks for it and holy crap do I feel sorry for anyone who paid even Steam's full price for this. This is poorly written fan-fiction with absolutely no soul. Thank god they didn't pull this stunt with FF6.

Story...
Meh. FFIV is a SNES game at heart. The world is tiny, there's maybe 100 actual citizens living on the whole planet. The monster are somewhat randomly drawn or based on monsters from previous games, and are generally designated their strength based on which area they are located in. The main problem with the story in TAY, is that it tries to create a real world from videogame mechanics. As a result, they say things that are somewhat real world accurate but make no sense in the context of the videogame, or they do things in the game that kinda contradict what they say.
This is one area that new FF games always focus on, long winded stories, with a lot of cut scenes and dialogue. I think they tried to borrow this story telling style from modern FF games and apply it to an older title. Instead of a interesting story, we just end up with 20 minutes of "cut scenes", where you need to keep pushing A, and jumping from character to character. Because FFIV was never really designed to make sense with real world principals, trying to make a logical world out of the game just ends up being way to much back story and unneccesary explinations for everything.
Gameplay...
So ignoring the fight mechanics for now, the game itself really lacks in some ways. The first is obviously the tales mechanic. I assume this was designed for the original release of the game, but jumping around from character to character is just annoying. I would have much prefered a single, simple and consistent story line. Way to many cut scenes, and ultimately they are not long enough to really level up your character.
The tales themselves are also not great. You find yourself with a lot of extra no-name characters that are pointless to gear or level up. You know they won't be around for long, so you try to rush through parts of the game just to get rid of them and get a real character again. You need to go through dungeons numerous times, back and forth, often the same dungeon from FF IV, sometimes with 1 character. You seem to just go places for the sake of doing something in TAY, where as the original always pushed you forward to the next location. This makes the tales especially repetative. Even the final dungeon is essentially just a series of parts of previous dungeons. It's a little disappointing when even the parts of the game that are supposed to be new, are just rehashed from the original. It feels lazy.
The fighting mechanics are also all over the place. Especially newer enemies, you find yourself generally dealing with mix groups of original enemies that vary wildly in strength, or weak enemies with a mechanic or low HP and high damage. Many monsters will take 24-50% of your health in a single attack, you'll find yourself just blasting away trash monsters with powerful spells just to end the fight quickly, especially when you only have 1 or 2 characters to crawl through a massive dungeon 2 or 3 times. You can kinda alliviate this with the moon phases, but the mechanic seems a bit added on.
The last tale is easily the best, but the character change mechanic in this game seems really primative compared to even the original FF VI. There is no simple way to remove gear from all characters. At no point in time does the game require you form 2 teams either, so with the exception of some character requirements for specific fights, you have very little reason not to just pick 5 and stick with it.
Video...Sound...Music...etc
The graphics are OK. Some people won't like the FPS cap at 15, but you can tell the game speed is tied to the refresh rate. Autobattle essentially doubles the frame rate. I personally find the characters a bit too cartoony looking in the DS remakes, but the monsters look good. I feel the graphics in the FFIII remake are much less jagged and smoother than this game. Music/sound is basically ripped from IV, the new boss theme is kinda cool though.
Is this game good? It's OK. If you like IV, it's probably worth a play if you enjoyed grinding that game. Just be prepared to including phoenix downs in your strategy.
I think I would have prefered a game that took place 100 or 1000 years later, with some familiar environments but ultimately seperated from the original story. It's a good concept, and I enjoy the SNES FF games, but this just feels rushed.

The genre and the trailer is pretty self explanatory. This is like an old school beat-em up/brawler game. It may remind you of games like Streets of Rage, Golden Axe, River City Ransom, Comix Zone, Double Dragon, Battletoads.......
This is a very satisfying game if you let yourself get to know it. It's a simple design with a detailed gameplay experience. The controls are simple and so is your goal. The experience, however, WILL challenge you. It demands all of your skill... anything less and you will be punished. This is a high paced action game that throws a lot of obstacles in your face (and all at once in some cases). It will intimidate you, frustrate you, and mock you... but in the end you may feel a sense of proudness and badass-ery when you clear that stage and/or boss, even after dying numerous times.
Even after beating it, which I honestly wasn't sure I was going to be able to do, I still find myself coming back to it because even after becoming better at the game I'm still challenged by it (in a mostly fun way). There's even a few more masochistic difficulty levels for the die hards out there. The gameplay feels fresh every time I play it because I try to play better than last time for the sake of personal achievement. To me this equals a game that was well done.
This game also has an awesome soundtrack to go with smashing up your enemies. Can't really say more than that.
8/10 is what I'd say. Buy it.

I played this game quite a bit by now, 50+ hours.
Current patch is 1.2 (Asimov)
--------
+ Accessible
>> I had a much easier time learning this game rather than when I tried HoI / EU4 (without success...)
+ Great initial impact and early game
>> Cool research technologies (albeit the choices are RNG, which is sometimes irritating) and exploration with science vessels.
+ GREAT soundtrack
>> My most favourite thing about the game, I listen to it almost daily
+ Mod support
--------
~ Average aesthethics
>> Nothing special here, the game looks fine for what it is but not outstandingly so.
--------
- Unbalanced weapon types
>> I can't find a reason to use ballistic weapons, they do only a tiny extra bit of  DPS than lasers which provide huge armor penetration bonuses instead. Missiles are hard countered by defense points.
- Lack of mid-endgame content
>> Aside a few events at late game, there's not much going on and it quickly turns into a grind. Eventually most technologies get researched, exploration is pretty much done and there's little to do
- Zero tactical decisions during ship battles
>> You can't give orders for, say, focus certain enemy ships or engage in particular manoeuvers
- AI is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
>> Consistently irrational behaviour from AI throughout the whole game.
A few examples:
1) Getting randomly kicked from alliances / federations for no apparent reason, even when you're saving your allies' asses.
2) Someone refused a trade deal where I was simply giving away some extra resources for nothing in return.
3) Sector AI is absolutely terrible. Even with plenty of resources (10k minerals / 5k energy) it fails to completely upgrade spaceports, even leaving some planets with just a lvl 1, which forces the player to do it manually. Same goes for spaceport modules.
- Performance
>> The game seems to mostly utilise 1-2 cores... mid-late game can become quite sluggish, with a 4690K / R9 290 / 16GB / SSD I was often dipping in 20s / 30s (using max time speed)
- UI is a mess
>> Plenty of things in the UI could be improved (on top of my head, upgrading individual land armies has to be done 1 by 1 and is ATROCIOUS, quick-upgrading spaceports / adding modules from the planet list tab is not allowed.
Also, the ship designer could use some love (copy / pasting designs to quickly make small variants, shortcuts to upgrade / downgrade a piece of equipment ...)
- Refineries / boosters
>> 100% personal opinion, but I hate the way spaceport refinery modules work.
They provide great bonuses to the ships built in spaceports where such modules are built, provided you own the strategic resources necessary to build them.
The bonuses are huge (like +50% armor, +10% damage...), but existing ships built BEFORE the modules were added cannot be upgraded.
That means that you're often delaying construction of ships if you know you can get a refinery in the near future, and also avoiding building ships in other spaceports, where such modules cannot be built for lack of resources.
--------
Conclusion: a game with a good first impression and potential but plagued with plenty of issues regarding AI, UI, balance.

To describe what Stellaris is in the most brief way possible it's basically what Civilization: Beyond Earth should have been. I feel like this game is the perfect mix between a Paradox strategy game and a Civilization game so what I've seen so far in my limited time of game play is a great platform for a revolutionary title. I say platform for a number of reasons.
Pros:
- AMAZING SOUNDTRACK
- Gorgeous visuals
- RTS type combat
- Complex game play but easy to master compared to other Paradox titles
- Helpful tutorial
- Workshop/Mod support
- Pretty good optimization
- Customizable races and ships (to an extent)
- Very Very VERY large in-game world (maximum world size is 1000 solar systems)
Cons:
- Game gets repetitive in the mid to end game
- AI is relatively poor in regards to diplomacy and self management
- Combat needs to be more complex compared to just spamming as many units as possible
- System map gets cluttered as the game progresses which reduces fps and just hurts to watch
From my time playing so far these are the things I picked up on. I feel like if you like Paradox or Civilization games you will enjoy this game. Paradox tends to support their games for a very long time so I believe most these issues will be ironed out eventually.

Not only was Deus Ex ahead of it's time, it remains innovative even to this day. At first glance, it appears to be an old FPS with graphics that could only benevolently be described as outdated. However, after giving the first level a shot, it becomes apparent that this game had more to offer.
The levels are multi-layered. There are multiple possible pathways so you don't always have to go from point A to point B. Stealth is an option with features including enemy LOS (didn't expect that in a game this old), patrol paths, group awareness, objects to hide around, and things like hidden corridors.
Enemies aren't limited to humans and individual limbs can be strategically targeted. That includes you. Being shot in the leg will slow you down. Lose both and you'll be crawling.
At least some of the decisions you make will influence the future.
At such a cheap price, it's at least worth giving it a shot.

If you're considering getting this game, chances are you've either played the 3D version of FFIV and are considering this sequel, or you're considering getting both in a bundle, as I did. Well, if you've played the 3D version of FFIV, this game is virtually identical to it in terms of gameplay. You'll be getting the same vehicles, using the same characters with a few new ones, the same spells, the same items with a few new ones, fighting the same enemies and even some of the same bosses. One might debate that this is true of a lot of sequels, and that's a valid point. However, please read the other reviews for this game. Let any reviewer's rational statements about the gameplay stand as a testament for you to understand how this is practically the same game. The only real difference in terms of gameplay is you get a few new characters that aren't very interesting from what I've seen, and there are combined attacks called "Bands." I will admit the last bit is pretty nice, but it's not worth buying the game for one new legitimate combat feature over FFIV.
The dungeon maps in FFIV were my favorite feature that didn't exist on the SNES version of the game. The maps filled in as you explored them, and there was a percentage counter. You got a little so-so reward item or three for hitting 100% on each map, and this system also ensured that you could find all the hidden areas on a map, while not revealing where they were, or giving little hints by spotting a distant wall edge on the map. It even marked chests on your map before you opened them. I loved this map system, and the maps are in The After Years, except every feature I just listed about the maps is not there in this sequel. The map is complete with no treasure chests marked. That's all. Nothing fills in as you explore, nothing interesting, nada. I was greatly disappointed in this change.
Remember the world map of FFIV? From what I've seen in the first two chapters I played, it is identical. The beginning of the game puts an airship landed on the map that wasn't there before, and that's where the changes end. You know where everything is already, and all about the places you're going to. That's not terrible, but takes wonderment out of exploring.

I've seen...I believe 2 new dungeons in what I've played so far, and both were just so-so and uninteresting. The majority of your time with this game, you will be going through the same dungeons, with the exact same layouts. Some chests may have been moved, but since the secret passages are still in place, they basically
to put the chests in those spots or it would look weird. Rather than having new, man or dwarf-made tunnels, new sections of prior dungeons opened up with only momentary excursions into old ground, and new structures, the game just sends you through the same dungeons with the same floor plans. This is pretty unforgivable in my book.
Seeing a pattern here? Yeah, everything is almost identical in the towns, too. To be fair, though, it's been about 15 years in the game world, and in such a setting, it's not unreasonable for towns to be largely the same. People stand in different spots, and houses have a few new residents. I never saw a new town, though, and that's kinda absurd, considering the world was saved and monsters became less frequent. Population should've boomed following the end of the chaos and war, with new towns popping up. However, that would've required effort to actually create for the game.
FFIV has some amazing music in my opinion. If you liked it, that same music is back. I believe there are a few new songs, but I cannot recall any of them, but can easily recall many of the other tunes in FF games including FFIV. Be prepared for the same songs that played on all the same maps, of course.  Just listen to the soundtrack on Youtube instead of putting down money for this sequel.
I haven't completed the game, but played most of two chapters and have just looked through a plot synopsis for the other major events. This game repeats several story beats far too similarly to FFIV itself. For instance, in FFIV, the king of Baron is acting suspicious like he might be evil. Same here. In FFIV, you get a black mage and a white mage in your party upon talking to someone in the building the elder is in. Same here. The good guys and bad guys are trying to get crystals? Same here. One character defeats his evil doppelganger and becomes a holy version of himself in FFIV. Same here. A large group of identical "people" are on the moon in the first one. Same here, but different people. The list goes on. This is shameless and I didn't believe the other reviews before I bought this mess.
Did you see Star Wars Episode VII The Force Awakens and think "Yeah, they did a few too many things that A New Hope did?" I know I did, even though I kinda like the film over all. However, FFIV The After Years doesn't even have the decency of looking like a new game that has a few plot similarities. Instead, they basically cut FFIV into pieces and rearranged them, repeating much of the plot from the original FFIV, along with the same old characters and almost the same gameplay, with a few new things here and there that just weren't worth it.
If you're like me, you'll think this game sounds good and ignore the reviews. I assure you I read them and knew this was supposed to suck, and despite thinking I would prove my peers wrong, I was the only one ending up looking like a fool. I don't know if this is the worst direct sequel FF game or not...I've played all of them, but I can say that this game is
the
direct sequel to a Final Fantasy game, and it shows in its poor quality. I could not keep playing this game out of sheer boredom and disgust at the lazy cash-grab that it is. I highly recommend avoiding this game, but FFIV itself (not The After Years) is good.

This is easily the worst Final Fantasy game I've ever been on (and I've been on pretty much all of them, including Dirge of Cerberus). First, the characters. There are a couple of decent characters that are new to this game. The rest are almost unendinly crap and have no decent skills or stats to offer to the table at all. The returning characters have not developed at all and are essentially just doing exactly the same stuff they were after the end of the first game. Well Rosa and Cecil have had a kid, that's about it. If you were hoping some interesting new developments would happen with the characters or something that would tie up some of your questions from FFIV, well you can forget about that as well. It's basically just the same old crap that happened on FFIV all over again.
The way they've split it up into "tales" sounds exciting, but in reality what it means is the actual decent characters (y'know, the ones you will actually want to play as during the endgame) are all split up, meaning that their battle teams have to be padded out with the aforementioned crap characters, and even some generic NPC type characters that are never seen or heard of again after their tale is finished. The end result is having to EXP grind for about a billion different random characters just to get one decent battle team at the end of it all. Not to mention none of the money or equipment carries over from previous tales, so you've got to start that again as well.
Apart from that, there are a couple of differences in gameplay from FFIV. Firstly, you've got this moon phase business, which basically just boosts and limits the damage/effect of certain abilities depending on the phase of the moon. Interesting idea, but doesn't exactly make much of a difference in reality. The other thing is that the whole command thing where you could set commands to materia or whatever they were called and change your auto-battle command is now a thing of the past. Instead, you've got this thing called "band" abilities, which are basically like overdrive abilities but they only work between 2 people and use up a load of MP. Plus they're for the most part not even very good.
So yeah, crap gameplay, crap story, crap character development. Why am I still playing this game? Well pretty much my only motivation to continue this game is the antagonist, who is the most murderable facsist little Hitler Youth ♥♥♥♥♥ of a character you could possibly imagine. I mean I have never in my life come across a videogame character that I want to brutally murder in the most painful way possible as this little arrogant cow. So that is certainly a tick in Square Enix's favour that they managed to come up with one of the most antagonistic antagonists I've ever had the misfortune of experiencing. Just a shame they couldn't have done it for a game that was actually decent in the first place.

Sidescrolling action at its finest - this game comes highly recommended, especially for the price. I haven't played it for long, but I've enjoyed every minute of it's button-mashing action. I grew up enjoying many a cartoon-looking side scroller, and this one not only delivers in the nostalgia department, there's definitely lots of fun to be had for newbies.
The game looks like it should have been made in the 90s, but this isn't a bad thing. Genuinely good arcade games have been scarce of late, especially the side scroll, button mashing, high scoring sort. Games like Cadillacs and Dinosaurs and Final Fight were hits because of the ridiculous number of enemies you had to beat down until your fingers hurt and the insane boss fights. This game is no exception.
The action is smooth, comboing enemies into all corners of the screen is fun, and if you're worried it's too easy, don't. If you're like me, you'll go down a few times, but still want to come back for another round. You can also adjust the difficulty, so you're never short of a challenge. Each time I play I get a better feel for it, so after an hour or so you'll settle into a rythm, dodging ninjas and counter attacking until your wild meter is nice and full.
Kudos to the game creators! They've got a hit here. It still feels like it needs a little refinement or more detail but it's good as it is. I'd give it a solid 8/10 - a must buy.
Make sure your controller (or keyboard) can take the hammering. You're going to want to keep that Wild meter full for the extra damage, flashy effects and ricocheting enemies ;)

I initially got this game thinking it would be like FF4, good story, decent gameplay, bit of a challenge, this game though is just as if someone recycled FF4, and here's why.
Gameplay: Just like FF1-FF9, really not much to explain, not that long a game and it's cut into 10 different stories, fairly slow gameplay though and not entirely fun
Story: As said before, recycled from FF4, a few differences (like no voiced cutscenes), but not entirely enjoyable, one of the weaker FF games, overstays its welcome from an early point
How it runs: Doesn't use to many reasources, runs as well as you'd expect, maybe better, if it does crash, it commonly quicksaves
Difficulty: More a test of how patient you are over anything, requires a fair deal of farming to do certain things, not entirely fun, a few annoying difficulty spikes in the last few stories
Music: Few new tracks, most of it's recycled from FF4, and the new tracks aren't entirely "good"
Overall, I would not reccomend this game unless you love the FF series, or just FF4 in general, overall, it isn't to great.

I playtested this, bought it on Humble Store, and now am playing and loving Aces Wild on Steam. Since its Humble Store release I've spent dozens and dozens of hours playing, and my time with this game is far from over.
The controls are easy to pickup but are incredibly precise. You can do crazy combos and fly around the screen with your aerial-powered fighter using a minimal amount of buttons.
The game is challenging but fair. Cliche statement, yes, but true in the case of Aces Wild. Nothing that the game throws at you is outside is unbeatable if you've got the skill.
Do you want a score-attack focused game without those annoying unlockables or DLC? All the content in Aces Wild is available to play from the get go. Do you want to jump straight to the final boss on hardest difficulty? Go for it! It's all good!
Lastly, and possibly what Aces Wild does best, is how much you can simply improve playing the game and how rewarding that feels. The skill ceiling in Aces Wild is absurdly high, and playing through the five difficulties gives a gradual learning curve instead of creating brick walls to bash your head on. Soon enough you'll be flying through dozens if not hundreds of attacks each minute, crashing your fists/swords against enemies so hard *it kills everything nearby*
In short, this game is incredibly challenging, incredibly deep, and incredibly great. GO WILD!!

OK, this game is awesome.  On the surface it seems like a very simplistic iPad tap and manage game, but you have to have an imagination when you play to fully appreciate it.  You have the moral dillemnas, do you enslave a populace, or do you let them try to regulate their own political system of governance?  What about lesser lifeforms and pre-warp civilizations, what about then?  Do you let them live on their own, do you scan them and learn anthropology passivley, do you try to "uplift" them and integrate them into your own workforce, do you completely purge them from your resources, or worse yet, enslave them and send them to the mines?  That little bit won me over.  It ignites the Star Trek geek in me.  Are you the Federation, the Cardassians or are you some godlike precurser race viewed by them as gods?  Hey we're just "wormhole aliens" but if you want to see us as gods, then by all the means, add to our empire!  The combat system reminds me of a cross between Settlers and Deadlock 2.  You have the military might? send them in and a brief standoff occurs.  You win or lose.  They may send more at your borders, so be prepared to defend them.  Military is wasted inside your borders.  Lots of little popup mini-quests like pirates or heretic spawn within your borders, so have an inside fleet to deal with those.  For the most part it's the simple age-old empire building of gather resources, build militaryl, defend and build and conquer.  But what I love mosst about this game are the random events and the micromanagement.  Kind of like Civilization III, but with a sector by sector grid of battles vs. the wider spread of ships and such.  Some lets me down, some feels more fun.  It's a fun game in any sense.  What I DO wish, is that there were more victory conditions than mere expansionism and conquest.  I play this game, and I wish I could be more peaceful and mercantile.  I wish I could meet other races and form a federation.  As it stands (and I may be wrong since I just bought it a day ago) is that you build power and sieze it.  I want to be the good guy and uplift civilizations, make them my own, and I want to hash out alliances and trade empires, build more than destroy.  That's my only beef with this game, it seems too straightforward kill them all, ala Settlers 7.

Let's put this in context, okay? This game seems to draw heavy inspiration from the Flight Unlimited games of the late 90's, whose main feature was free-flight. No combat, no missions -- just flying around and taking in the beautifully rendered (for the time period) 3-D topography. I loved those games.
Fast forward to today: this early access title is sure to be misunderstood out of context, especially if you're looking for a flashy flight simulator or air-combat shooter. That was never the point with Flight Unlimited, and seems to not be the main feature with Flight Unlimited 2K18. Instead, we get a spiritual successor to those games, albeit with a few tweaks. There are several missions this time around (I particularly enjoyed the Alcatraz fly-by and prisoner extraction), and it seems the devs are hoping to make multiplayer dogfight mode happen. That's all good and well, but it will clearly take some time because what is there now is pretty basic.
I have hope, though! The controls are initially unclear and take some getting used to, most of the 3-D objects are ghostly window dressing, and some of the airplane engines produce the most annoying white noise I've ever endured. However! I do not regret purchasing this title, and will be checking back on it regularly, hoping to see the developers' vision come to fruition.

Jack said pretty much everything about this game:

You might have heard about Lone Wolf a long time ago, back when books were only on paper. It was also part of the pretty interesting genre of Choose Your Own Adventure that made you play a game while reading, perfect to get kids interested. I was pretty surprised to see a Lone Wolf video game, almost 25 years after I enjoyed some of those books.
The game itself is a mobile port but it's actually pretty solid, it would not look like a mobile game if you removed those touchscreen controls. Everything is using the mouse like if it was your finger but it's really responsive and forgiving. Not once did I felt like I was playing a mobile game.
The game is pretty unique, at its core it is an rpg with stats, abilities and inventory but it comes in two parts. The book is like a Visual Novel, a lot of text, some choices and very rare quick time events with some of those choices. Then there is the battle portion of the game where you use motions and clicks to battles some enemies. There are also two quick minigames, lockpicking and a puzzle cube. The book visuals are pretty sharp and stylished then the battle graphics are colorful and pretty detailed for a 15$ mobile port.
The book portion is pretty linear, sometimes you have two or three paths but in the end they will all lead to the same end. There are multiple choices that affect the text but often also the battles, you might be able to skip a battle, start one with enemies on fire or with less enemies for example. Some of those choices are also limited by the abilities you picked at the character creation so it add a good amount of replayability while the story will still mostly be the same but with some different events.
The battles are hit or miss. Depending on your character build you can have pretty close fights or you can have very unfair fight where you die in 5 seconds without having time to do any action or where you annihilate the enemies before they can act. It is very random but, to be fair, the books where also pretty random with battles using a random number table. I won't go into too much detail about the battle mechanic since the game gives tutorial prompts but it's pretty much all quick time event except some abilities without any prompt. You have a decent amount of time to do those prompt so it does not require lightning fast reflexes but messing up one prompt can mean losing a battle. There are no penalties to losing battles except the time lost because you can simply replay the battle as many time as you want, and you might need to do for some bosses or if you play on Hard.
As for the story itself, it is separated in 4 acts, all with pretty different areas and at least one new enemy type each. Lone Wolf was inspired by Dungeon and Dragon so it will feel familiar if you are used to this type of fantasy. Most of the story is about getting from point A to point B evading or killing monsters, looting stuff and with two or three npc to interact with per act. It is a dark story, you can't save everyone and some of those choices can be pretty mean. Lone Wolf is an already developped character so you can't be evil and act any way you want but, while he is a hero, he is not totally good and actually pretty grey. I guess you could compare it to the Paragon and Renegade system in Mass Effect.
Overall, if you can get past the pretty random filled battle system, it is a great game that is a very well though interpretation of the gamebooks genre. Sadly, Joe Dever passed away recently so it might be the last for Lone Wolf but they could use this system for other stories.

Flight Unlimited 2K18 is a barebones flight simulator that offers little engaging gameplay and misleads consumers through shady/illegal marketing tactics.
This game is very simple in concept and execution. You fly a variety of aircraft and have specific objectives to complete. These objectives seem to only be taking off, flying to specific locations and then landing the plane. The other mode available is free fly in which you simply choose a plane and fly it.
Now in essence that’s what most flight simulation games are. You fly planes around and have a chill time. This one is just incredibly boring to play. The planes handle poorly, the audio is ear-exploding and there is little engaging gameplay at all.
There is no tutorial in the game, it starts you in the air and you need to figure things out for yourself. The game doesn’t even go to the main menu until you complete the first mission.
The game looks bad, even by flight simulator and mobile port standards. The majority of the ground is simply an incredibly pixelated flat map. You can actually land on pretty much anything, including a residential house because it’s just 2D.
Taking off with the planes seems to be almost broken with the keyboard and mouse. The plans will sit there for a while until all of a sudden they go at full speed.
I’m trying to figure out what else to say about the gameplay here but there is honestly just not much of it at all. Definitely not enough to warrant the $16.00 CAD price.
The series was originally on mobile and it seems like most of the assets were ported over for this game. The developer has been trying to pass either this, or a very similar version of the game through Greenlight. They originally tried to get Flight Unlimited 2K17 on Steam by using the trailers for their previous game Flight Unlimited 2K16. It’s all very shady and confusing.
Speaking of shady let’s talk about the developer.
Flight Unlimited as a series was under a different company back in the 1990’s and then briefly published by EA. This developer got the rights to the trademark it seems but has no connection to the original series.
The developer has been caught listing the game with PEGI and ESRB ratings even though there are no listings through either group for any of their Flight Unlimited games. They are wrongfully listing these ratings and have not gone through the ratings board.
The use of “2K18” in the title of the game may also be infringing on the trademark of Take-Two and 2K Games. 2K Games uses 2K17, 2K18, et cetera as a way to label the yearly release of their sports titles. The terminology is almost certainly copyrighted by them and the use of it in Flight Unlimited could be misleading for potential consumers.
Finally, the developer has been deleting negative threads in the Steam forums for the game. This is common these days but nonetheless shady and dishonest as a practice and needs to be mentioned.
Overall, Flight Unlimited 2K18 is a boring, ugly and shady game that you should probably avoid.

Cortex Command is a strange beast.  It is, without a doubt, not quite finished, and unfortunately it's likely it never will be.  The single player campaign is functional, but sparse, and a quick look at the scenario menu makes it obvious a dozen ideas and features never saw the light of day.
Nonetheless, the game shows its worth in the multiplayer.  It has fully functional splitscreen--a rare treat for a PC game--and it's in the gleeful chaos of a multiplayer scenario with a friend or two that the game becomes truly fun.  I've spent countless hours with friends building ridiculous, convoluted bases, defending them against hordes of enemies and whooping and gasping at every particularly visceral headshot or burning dropship obliterating everything in its path.  The physics are modeled exquisitely, every pixel destructable and every thrust of an engine or recoil of a rifle having a visible impact on the characters and surroundings.  In the thick of a survival scenario with troops and bombs raining down all over your bunker, drones dragging themselves around on broken legs, craters being blasted in the turf by overloaded rockets crash landing, and missiles and bullets whizzing in every direction while you scream at player 2 "Oh god there's like thirty guys on the left", it is wonderful, insane anarchy.
There are also a truly impressive number of mods available, so if you want to be Master Chief taking on an army of orcs with a tuba that shoots miniature suns, well, you can.  My recommendation is mod Cortex Command to the gills, invite your buddies over, get really drunk and scream incoherently as your base explodes around you.  You'll have a blast.

You play as Ghat, a man on the run alongside a friend and accused of murdering a creature called "Father-Mother". It sounds like an interesting story, and while the story itself and what actually takes place is good, the writing and the voice acting are not all that great and it detracts from what would otherwise be a decent tale.
However, the graphics and gameplay both make up for these issue. The game is beautiful looking with a unique looking world with beautiful skies and landscapes, and you'll never see the same thing twice so you're never bored with what you see. This is good, as the game is played entirely from a first person perspective.
The game is best described as a beat em up, as you progress, face hordes of enemies, and progress to the next segment. You don't learn new moves or upgrades as you go, but that is fine as you do well with what the game gives you. It's solid with blocks, dodges, punches, kicks, and throws along with hand to hand weaponry and guns. It's hard to be bored as you progress the game's campaign. There are four levels of difficulty, with my playthrough happening on Hard but there is also Easy, Normal, and Extreme. Hard mode presented a great challenge and it took about eight hours to get through it. Once you're done, there is a set of challenges to go through with a fixed difficulty to try your hand at.
It's a beautiful, brutal, knock you down your♥♥♥♥♥recommendation. Give it a shot.
