Ghost 1.0 is a puzzle platformer with metroidvania elements, does it do enough to invade our minds or has no soul of its own like its protagonist. Let’s find out :
Ghost 1.0 puts you in the shoes of ghost, a robot tasked with infiltrating The Nakamura Space Station. Nakamura is a generic evil company which is trying to take over the world with the use of human like robots. The story is as basic as it gets. Ghost gets in a transport vehicle to get in Nakamura castle and is being commanded by two guys. While initially, it seems that Ghost 1.0 will be a stealth game, mostly from its name and its starting missions.
In the very beginning, Ghost is told to get pass a guard by using stealth and no loud noises. She drops down when the guard is facing away, jump up again and starts to run away towards the door when the guard spots her and tells her to stop, she turns around, shoots him and then open the door. When the guys ask her what she was doing, she replies “Stealth”.
This segment sums the stealth portion of the game, it is only there so you can say that the game has stealth, but is actually non-existent. Ghost blows up everything she comes in her part and in the process gains various upgrades and abilities. She has a gun which recharges its bullets itself, a power through which she can control enemy robots and turrets and some others. When ghost dies, she resurrects by creating a 3D model of herself in a 3D modelling machine. This resurrection theory is not only true for ghost, as the turrets also build themselves back with the help of small mechanical bugs.
This becomes frustrating really quickly as the speed with which the turrets resurrects is not fair. You get to the other side of the room to complete your objective and the robots are back. It takes mere seconds for the bugs to come out of their hiding and building the turrets again. You can shoot these bugs but that doesn’t stop more from coming out. Early levels when Ghost is not  equipped and upgraded properly, it is easy for any player to rage quit the game and never look at it again which is a shame as Ghost slowly does build up to make a surprisingly pleasurable gameplay experience.
The Space station itself is divided into various zones and are unlocked by using various keycards. That is the only metroidvania element present here, as whatever door you couldn’t unlock now would need a keycard which you will find later on. These do not require any abilities or anything else other than the keycards. Difficulty ramps up pretty quickly and the game is pretty difficult even on the easiest difficulty.
There is a good amount of enemy types available and all of them require thinking before going head on against them. There are two game types available: Classic and Survival. Classic is the mode where you lose your items when you died and start from where you saved. Survival mode plays more like a roguelike where you are granted various powerups and lose everything when you die. These two modes are a fun distraction from each other and in survival mode, it sometimes felt like Rogue Legacy, which is a great compliment.
Despite a few highlights here and there, the overall visual design of Ghost 1.0 is pretty generic. There were some unique enemy designs but from the comic style static cutscenes to the Nakamura Space Station itself, it all felt like a fairly basic platformer. Visuals can really elevate a game to another level, like Ori and the Blind forest but it’s a shame that Ghost 1.0 doesn’t do that. Even the colour palette is very basic and the colours don’t pop as much as they should.
For a indie game, the voice acting is surprisingly good. Ghost sounds like a generic robot but her two hacker companions have a lot more life in them. The Soundtrack itself is pretty good and compliments the cyberpunk theme of the game pretty well. What visuals don’t do for ghost, soundtrack manages to balance it by some really solid sound design.
Ghost 1.0 is a game which will test you patience, a lot. It is very frustrating in the early stages and takes time to get going. When it does get going though, it can be a pretty fun time killer to sink your time in. The backtracking involved is not great but does provide some additional gameplay hours for the completionist gamers. It is nothing exceptional and is overly ambitious at times but it still makes for a very good experience.

I'll recommend this because the atmosphere from the sound and graphics is spot on. It's like a missing part of SOMA, in that you can explore, and retreat to your small vehicle for minimal safety, and yet feel just as vulnerable. It was a world I wanted to explore.
Unfortunately there are rough edges that kept chipping away at my fun. Hopefully they'll all be improved with time so I can come back for another attempt.
1. At the start you have to choose between Story or Survival - I wasn't clear on the differences, and what might be removed from one. Would story mode be simplistic, with no threat? Would survival mode have the story stripped out? Yet I assume once you start with one mode you are stuck with it, and won't know if you are missing out.
2. I hated the interface and controls. It seemed like the mouse was disabled - there was no pointer to use it in menus, or the in-game controls and puzzles.
The game has fixed keyboard controls (WASD, but the tooltip looked more like the arrow keys). I have no problem with WASD being a default, but since I am uncomfortable with it it became an extra barrier for me. Please, all game devs - let players bind keys however they want! I was fumbling for the X key or F key or left control, and was just getting frustrated. If I could have set up controls how I wanted this wouldn't have happened.
Other control issues: you can't use the scrollwheel alone to toggle through your inventory - you have to press CTRL then use the scrollwheel. Clunky.
The interface for your systems was likewise confusing, how to switch between items. I managed to choose something in a menu (upgrades, I think) but tried all the keys and mouse buttons and couldn't work out how to get back to choose another option like Artifacts. The only way seemed to be to quit out of the game and reload it.
And yet, after using WASD for movement, I came to a button puzzle that used the arrow keys instead. It's all a bit of an  unintuitive mess for me. Being able to redefine things would have helped.
3. The one time I died in my small adventure was when I ran out of oxygen. It's badly implemented for three reasons. Firstly, the oxygen meter looked like I had three tanks. I assumed when the bar ran out a tank would disappear and the bar would refill. No, the three tanks are just decorative, you only have one bar. Secondly I was warned to get back to my sub because my oxygen was low - presumably my radio friend monitoring systems and being helpful. Except when he gave the warning I was too far to get back in time - I died just before I reached the sub. If you build in warnings, at least make sure they trigger when it is still possible to act on them. Thirdly it's bizarre that the oxygen tanks run out so quickly. They are teeny. Worse, the second they run out, you die. In real life you would have at least an extra 30 seconds of action. But no, my character wasn't gasping or breathing with difficulty - she went from normal, to dead, in a second or two. Even ten seconds of holding my breath and I would have made it to the sub in time. Actually, since the tanks are so small, why can't you carry them in your belt like the other small round items (first aid kits, repairs etc)? If you pick one up the previous one is destroyed (even if full). Despite the extremely hazardous environment your character refuses to even carry a spare when she finds one.
4. Occasional clipping problems - usually items from chests falling through the chest and becoming unreachable, or clipping through a large cargo canister wall. Since the items might mean life or death, it can be annoying to die from a bug. Likewise the flares you follow are invisible - just red light and steam, but no actual flare, as if they clipped through the ground.
5. There is an aquajet you can use for getting around quickly. Sadly I found it to be cumbersome to use, due to the controls, and the fact that I couldn't view my scanner and use it at the same time. Since the aquajet doesn't even have a spare oxygen tank under the seat it was more irritating than fun.
6. My game ended when I had the objective to "find the final submarine". I had found it, and swam around it, but on reloading that objective remained. Presumably it was because you had to solve a puzzle to open a chest, but I had to give up. During two sessions I tackled the puzzle numerous times, and could never get all the buttons to light up. A YouTube video seemed to get stuck on that bit so I couldn't see the solution. I went to a help guide but the only tip I found was "read the logs"; I did that twice, none seemed to mention how to solve this puzzle. Maybe I'd missed a log earlier. At this point I explored a bit then stopped playing, because it is one of those games where you often can't move on until a scripted event occurs, triggered by something else you do or see. It left me mildly frustrated that a squad of diving soldiers (or whatever) would choose to look a crate by building a puzzle into it. Just seems a bit far-fetched. On the other hand, it worked. I couldn't get into it. I uninstalled eventually.
Still, I would like to come back one day and play again, see if I get further, hopefully when a few of the issues above have been fixed in patches. I'll reiterate: the atmosphere is brilliant. I played in the dark with headphones on. I enjoyed my couple of hours in the game on the whole, and it is promising. A bit more polish and it could become a go-to game for those who like slower-paced creepy horror explorers, soaking up a chilling atmosphere. It's almost there now.

Good:
-Nice open world level design with full 3D movement.
-Good, albeit limited, voice acting consisting mostly of two characters.
-Great story and world building for an indie game. it really makes you want to push on until the end.
-Great pacing of the story and introduction of gameplay mechanics and new tech.
Neutral:
-Graphics: they're fine for an indie game but don't expect it to look like The Witcher 3.
-Performance: I've had no issues with my 970 but other reviewers have, so keep that in mind.
-No hand holding: This is open 3D underwater world. While there are markers, that generally show you where to go so do not expect a Dead Space like line that literally shows you the path. And since it isn't a linear corridor shooter, there's a lot of room to get lost. It's more challenging than other games but definitely doable.
Cons:
-Lack of polish and bugs, although the dev is working on it.
-Not much customization: graphics options and keybinding settings are pretty limited.
Summary/What to Expect:
I see too many comparissons to Soma or Subnautica which I don't think is fair and could disappoint some people. I'd say Iron Fish is more like Firewatch (or other walking simulators) but underwater. You're alone underwater but in radio contact with your superior who helps you as you navigate the 3D underwater world and uncover the mystery. But unlike other walking simulators, there are a fair amount of gameplay elements, puzzles, and you can easily die. You can also mess badly enough that you need to restart and the world isn't linear so you could easily get lost.
I'm about 4 hours in (ignore the 22+ hours I have on record since I play a bit then alt-tab out) and love the setting, characters, atmosphere, and how the game gradually intensifies the mystery and spookiness. It isn't 100% polished but it's overall very well done for an indie game. The dev clearly has passion for this game and has communicated quickly with people on the discussions page. So if you're looking for a story rich, first person, exploration/walking sim hybrid in an underwater setting, this is the game for you.

Nothing but a cash-in trying to appeal to nostalgia: There is nothing new here, or at least nothing new that matters. The story is nearly identical to the original game, though even well into the final dungeon you have no idea who the antagonist really is.
Other than the introduction of Ceodore and Ursula and some minor characters from FF4 becoming somewhat more important, it's the same crew. And enemies. And bosses. And locations. Well, obviously you would revisit locations, right? It is the same world after all. But after seeing the underground waterway five times, it really hits home how lame this is.
Despite the fact that the game was originally released one episode at a time, there is no plot development until the final chapters, and even then it is limited to a twist-that-isn't-a-twist. Instead, each character's chapter involves them clawing their way from around level 10 to about 30, then in Chapter 10 you find out they're all still horribly underleveled anyway. That's ok though, because only a few of the characters will actually matter.
The one new element to the game is the Lunar Phase system, the cycle of which increases one and decreases one of the four types of actions' effectiveness - attack, white magic, black magic, and special actions (Edge's ninja tricks, Yang's kick, etc.). At first, it seems like this would cause you to think carefully about your strategy depending on what phase the moon is currently in, but since you don't choose your own party until Chapter 10, you always get stuck with a setup that is objectively good or objectively bad. Why would you NOT just sleep through a new moon in Yang's tale, during which your party of nothing but monks has their attack power crippled?
Also, the moon phases affect characters on the moon as well (that's not a spoiler, there's a "Lunarians tale" chapter). Huh?

What a wondeful experience. F.E.A.R. is a FPS shooter with twitch based and somewhat horror based shooting. Still holding up in 2017 even after 12 years on the market, the game allows for sub-linear open levels of play and freedom with shooting gameplay that would rival some of even todays standards.
You play the game as a nameless soldier called 'Pointman' whose tasked with an ultimate goal of finding the games antagonist 'Paxten Fettel' and his hundreds of telepathically controlled units that he now controls (he went rogue or something.). Along the way, you will encounter the para-normal child 'Alma' who's pretty much there for no other reason than to scare/creep you out it seems.
There's so much more to the story but I'll keep this spoiler free as possible. The story is fine however the way it is presented throughout using phone messages, laptop computers (against, just voice messages) and very few lines of dialoge from any NPC makes it very.. uneven. If I recall, everything except the beginning and end scenes is played from the eyes of the 'Pointman' in a first person view and certain scripted events can be missed if not in the right place/time.
Gameplay is fantastic. My first playthrough was on Hard, clocking in at 12 hours with pure keyboard/mouse. The core gameplay relys on shooting, scavenging and very little else other than pushing the action key on buttons or messages. There's a couple other sections like turret control and dreams worlds but there just didn't seem enough variety of objectives.
For what there was, oh man. Obviously, the main aspect is combat. Right off the bat you are introduced to Reflex (I think it's called that?) mode which slows down time and gives you an advantage over your enemies while quickly draining and slowly refilling in the background. This is probably the best looking bullet time looking effect I've seen in any video game title.
The game focuses heavily on corridor shooting. Very rarely will you be in open areas but it still happens occasionally. One of my gripes with the game is that level design is.. so bland. Recalling my 12 hours after credits I can only seem to remember (truthfully); office buildings, construction sites inside office buildings, a parking garage, abandoned office buildings like places and dream world on fire hallways. And that took me a second to think about. I got the the point of getting lost a few times in the game because I couldn't tell certain rooms from rooms. And there's lot of rooms.
The game is open linear structured broken into segments/levels. You'll always be exploring and going forward but get lost or a need to rebacktrack and you can actually go return to the beginning of a level. On the way, healthkits, messages, ammo/weapons and health/reflex boosters must all be found. The game is healthpack based and armor based.
Enemy variety was also a disappointment. Without spoiling anything, you will fight; soldiers, turrets, flying robot things, invisible ninja soldiers, ghosts, robots and bigger robots. This sounds like a lot which it is, however 95% of the game is focused of soldier warfare and I do not recall more than 2 types of 'soldier'. The 2nd kind which is only a stronger, recolored and textured 'soldier' is found only on the last 2 chapters.
What balances this (somewhat) is the fantastic AI. This is truly one of the best enemy intelligences I have seen is a game period, no exaggeration. You rarely take on less that 3 guys at once. They always work and comunicate as squads. They will flank, take cover and make cover, help/drag other comrades to safety .. just amazing work here. No battle will ever function the same and it's not just like they are aimbots or anything (far from it, just good work), they act so realisticly.
Weapons are varied as well. There's a good amount of them if you go by situational standards. Dual pistols, shotgun, smg, assault rifle, battle rifle, rocket launcer and a few others I won't spoil but they are pretty cool and unique thereselves. Each gun looks and sounds amazing and each one has a specific role. Considering the Pointman can only carry 3 weapons of his choice at one time, they must be chosed wisely. Ammo is sort of scare playing on higher difficulties and I had a chance, or rather, actually had to use each weapon individually throughout the game.
You also have a few types of explosives and a couple cool looking melee attacks that are easy to perform.
Effects are beautiful here. Particle effects run wild with sparks bounding and flying across the environments. Smoke will fill up small corridors (literally), blood sprays and enemies lose limbs (or just explode!) in mists, fire blurs the screen from it's heat and every bit of this looks so much better in Reflex mode. The graphics hold up quite well here. Textures are still reasonable. The lighting effects manage to provide a believable atmosphere and you will be getting used to the dark. It just gets rather old seeing the same bland office buildings over and over and over.
Performance wise, the game ran rather smoothly after using the 'Logitech Mouse/Keyboard fix' I found on Google. I played on Max settings, no FXAA and Soft Shadows OFF. I recieved perfect limited 60FPS on a AMD12 6Gig ram and an integrated card Laptop. The requirements are not high at all and any computer newer than 5 years old should be able to run it smoothly.
In all, F.E.A.R. is an amazing title that has survived (so far!) the test of 12 years and holds up rather well. Gameplay wise, Monolith had everything going for this game that just suffers from drab level design and lacking story that tries to be told but best left to Wikipedia after the credits. Still the coolest slow motion of any game and best AI I've yet to find, I paid $9.99US Dollars for F.E.A.R. and both it's expansion I have yet to try. Well worth my money.

Ahh... Final Fantasy VIII. The great divider. Some people love it, some people hate it, some people
hate it.
Final Fantasy VII and VIII were the first (and for many years, the only) Final Fantasy games released on the PC. This version is very similar, and likely based on, the original PC port released in 2000. Final Fantasy VIII was the first in the series for me, I played it near to its PC release, when I was 17, and have since finished it about 9 or 10 times. It is not a great game, but it's not bad, by any stretch of the imagination. It has flaws, but as a complete package, it's a very enjoyable experience.
Most of the criticism for this game comes from the kitschy story and the terrible implementation of the Junction system; specifically, the Draw system. This review will cover those systems.
On paper, the Junction system is phenomenal; and it completes the process Final Fantasy VII began with Materia affecting character stats. Simply put, the Junction system allows you to directly link a spell to a character stat. Life magic linked to your HP stat will give you more health, and strong magic such as Triple or Ultima will provide huge bonuses to various other stats.
The system really shines in its Status and Elemental Attack and Defence junctions, which allow you to link a Status spell (such as Sleep, Drain and Blind) and an Elemental spell (such as Fire, Water and Holy) to your weapon attacks and defence:
Linking Fire to your elemental defence will reduce the damage you take from fire spells. Linking higher level spells, such as Fira and Firaga will reduce the damage you take further and eventually even allow you to absorb that damage. As you'd expect, linking Fire to your elemental attack will cause your attacks to deal fire damage, which is a big advantage against monsters weak to fire.
Similarly, linking a Status spell, such as Sleep to your status defence will reduce the likelihood of being affected by that status effect; and eventually, will negate it completely. And naturally, linking a Status spell to your status attack, will cause your attacks to have a chance to afflict the enemy with that effect. This, by the way, also applies to the Death spell, which has a chance to one-shot a non-boss monster.
Holy hell, what a remarkable level of customization! Amazing, right?!
Not quite.
On its own, it is a great system. Unfortunately, it's not on its own. It is joined by the Draw system; which deviated dramatically from the series' norm and drew (get it?) most of the criticism leveled at the game. Prior to (and since) Final Fantasy VIII, magic spells in the series had a cost of MP - that is, mana. Spells were permanently learned (for the most part), a character had a pool of MP, and each spell cost a certain amount. Not so in this game. Final Fantasy VIII's spells existed in a large, but finite, inventory and each of your characters was able to stock 100 of a spell.
Obtaining these spells required you to extract - or "Draw" - them from your enemies. Stronger enemies yielded stronger spells. And the type of enemy you fought affected the kinds of spells it possessed - for example, enemies in snowy regions were likely to have the Ice spell and its variants on it, aquatic enemies had Water, and so on. Add to this the fact that your characters' magic stat affects the amount of magic you are able to retrieve in any given Draw action. It is entirely possible for you to spend more than an hour drawing between 1 and 5 spells each time. On each character. Three times.
The option to synthesize these spells from various items dropped by enemies, as well as quest rewards and cards from the card minigame is available; but it's fairly clear that enemies were intended as the main source of most spells.
And the grind begins.
Final Fantasy is not a series foreign to grinding, in most other games in the series, this is implemented as the traditional grind for XP and levels; but as those are fixed in Final Fantasy VIII (every single level requires 1000 XP), the grind was shifted to the acquisition of magic.
OK... So far, it's not so bad... Grind is always a thing...
Ah, but what I have yet to mention, however, is that the quantity of the magic you link to your stats affects them directly. The less of a spell you have, the less effective it is. And if you follow along the logic, you'll come to the conclusion that the magic you link - ostensibly, the strongest magic you have - are the ones you are
Yep. I can't remember the last time I actually used a spell in combat.
And so, the other shoe drops. Magic, which is one of Final Fantasy's most recognizable aspects and, arguably, quintessential to the nature of the series, is effectively removed from the combat system.
That sounds terrible, doesn't it? Nah, it's not as grim as all that. You get used to it, and the rest of the game absolutely makes up for it. Final Fantasy VIII is not a bad game, it's even a good game. The art is great for its time, the cinematics are awesome and the story is a bit juvenile - maybe a bit more than your average Final Fantasy (or highschool anime for that matter) - but if you're into that, then you'll enjoy it quite a bit. As I have.

There are not many games these days that you can play at a leisurely pace while you drink your cup of java or tea with the other hand. Lone Wolf sets that exact pace, but maintains the right to shove its foot up your rear if you decide to venture in on a higher difficulty.
Lone Wolf is entirely about your styles and choices that you make as you play, and it gives you the feeling that your decision do matter and do alter your path through the adventure from the very beginning, up to and including when you are selecting your skills and starting weaponry. The decisions impact the scenarios you experience just the same as those old "choose your own adventure" style game-books that have been all but forgotten.
The main brunt of gameplay is spent reading the book and turning the pages, or if you're like me, taking time to look at and appreciate the beautiful art designs that are spread throughout the entirety of the game. In between reading (and putting your rusty imagination to proper and good use) you'll find yourself with a lockpicking situation similar to that of The Elder Scrolls series, and my personal favorite, the Shianti Cube puzzles. Neither of these are particularly difficult, but they do an excellent job of keeping with the theme that this game has from the start: making you use your brain instead of mindlessly clicking or mashing buttons.
Combat scenes are a transition from the pages and into 3D graphics, and with them comes the addition of a light strategic turn-based system with QTE sequences spotted throughout each attack; there are just enough little circles and arrows to keep you from becoming a mindless drone as you click through attacks, like in more traditional turn based RPGs.
Lone Wolf is an older game, of course, but not old enough to lose what charm it had to offer since the beginning. If you can bring yourself to not whine or complain about harmless QTEs and you are willing to spend time reading and appreciating artwork as well as an enchanting choose-your-own-path style story, this game will not  let you down in capturing the original spirit of the series it is based on.
Perhaps you'll go buy one of the books afterwards.

First, let me say this: I have played this game on Android. So, while my Steam account shows not that much time I have beaten the game on Android. So yes I do know what I'm talking about.
I so highly recommend this to everyone. More so to those who are fans of the books. I've read up to book 12 in the Lone Wolf book series.. The game takes place, I'd say, between book 4 and 5. I say that because it mentions that your the Fryearl or something like that (governor of the land). It sticks really close to how the books are and how it was done, even down to what's going on in the books. There's even mention of the Shainti wizard tribe from the Grey Star book series.
As a huge fan of the book series when I was a kid to teen years I really enjoyed this game. It is Lone Wolf turned into a book/video game all the way.
There are 4 books. Each book contains 4 Chapters if I remember right.
Choices matter and your choices do effect what happens in later books. Some people show up in later books.
Collect items. Items are the same as in the books. Potion of Laumspur and such. They even put in Potion of Ether which I thought was a nice touch. The special items never can be traded or sold (at least not that I came across anyway). Named items like rings and necklaces doesn't come into play either but is nice because it reminds you who gave it to you. For example: You meet Banadon in the Lone Wolf book 1. He gives you the Crystal Star Pendent. Later in Book 5 it ask if you have said item on hand. You do, you know who Banadon. You don't, the book acts as if you never met him even though you did. This doesn't matter in the game. You either know the person or you don't.
Armor and weapons take damage over the course of combat. You do find people to repair said items. Armor and weapons can also be upgraded as well. Sommerswerd is there with 3 special attacks. Instint kills are done with the Sommerswerd.
Combat is done in real time turns. By this I mean you have a timer bar that ticks down while you attack. Your attacks take up so much of your attack bar (endurance). When you run out of endurance you wait for you timer to tick down. Blocking an attack ends your turn right away no matter what. As your timer fills up your endurance fills up as well. Attacks with knives, crossbow, and Abilities does not use endurance.
Choice of 3 weapons, axe, sword, and mace. Each weapon has 3 attacks. Dual weapon or weapon and shield. When dual weapon welding your off hand weapon is used to block, stun, or bleed damage the enemy.Off hand weapon does weapon damage. Dual weapon use in the books never happened but in the Lone Wolf magizine club, I think, Joe Dever did mention that you can use in the books with a negitive to hit. Or it may have been  brought up on the Project Aeon site. I can't remember. It's on the site mentioned though. Shield is used to block, stun, or bleed damage though when hitting an enemy isn't high you get a bonus to block attacks. Side weapons are throwing daggers (3 attacks) or crossbow (3 different attacks) which can be done all in 1 attack.
You get to choose 4 abilities out of 8. Mind blast and mindshielf are combined as 1 skill. Mindblast damages and stuns target. Mindshield is an auto ability. There is Healing, Tracking and Hunting are combined into 1 skill which is used to heal in combat. Weapon skill gives bonus to hit, damage, and something else I think. Animal Kinship calls a wolf during combat to help. MInd Over Matter gives the choice throw an object in the background at enemies. Sixth Sense gives you a chance to dodge enemeies attacks and counterstrike. Camouflage makes it so that they can't attack you and something else. Can't remember. Abilities do come into play while reading. All abilities can be used in combat, obviously.
The stats are Strength, Dexterity, and Kia power. These come into play while reading and in combat. Kai power is to use you abilities in combat. Strength is used for damage and health. Dexterity is used to dodge and block. Said stats are color coded and those stats used while reading increase that stat at the end of the chapter. Abilities used increase Kai power.
Enemies are also taken straight from the books as well. Each are just as powerful or weak just like in the book. Sadly, as with books 1-4 there's not a lot of variation of enemies though each book has 1 or 2 new ones.
The pictures are done really well and have a cool loop animation to them. There's not too many but the ones that are there are really cool.
Theres an extra section for background info on lands, characters, enemies, etc, as well as a gallery for looking at the enemies in poses and even the locations of combat. You can spin the camera around the combat locations. The gallery was not part of android so this was a really cool addition to the game.

In short, pass this one.
To give myself credibility: I have been playing games for the last thirty (yes, 30) years. I started with Commodore 64, continued to PC. My main focus is single player (SP) games, so I mainly focus on that. Oh, and I am an engineer with an MBA. Enough self promotion.
I am an avid fan of real time strategy (RTS) games. When Act of War came out in 2005, it was a fresh outlook for RTS mechanics. The graphics were the most advanced of its time, except Age of Empires 3. The story was interesting, and cutscenes were top notch. It was a serious modern warfare RTS game, unlike the too fantastic Red Alert 3. It introduced prisoner concept, of which I have never seen in another game yet.
Act of Aggression is the successor of that game. But it is not.
See, Act of Aggression is too much like Wargame European Escalation, which tried to be like World in Conflict. From the games I mentioned, Conflict > Escalation >> Aggression. Problem is, the traditional base building RTS is not suitable for engines that has been produced for baseless RTS. You need choke points, defensive areas for base building. And you need urban warfare, always moving battle line for baseless. So, when you try to combine both, it is a mess.
OK, enough history lesson. Let's focus on what does this game do best:
Hmmm.....nothing. Yeah, sorry but nothing.
Resource system is problematic as the trucks for your refineries actually have to come back to your base. There is no indication on efficiency, like how many trucks do I need? When I produced the max for each refinery, most of them just waited for the production to end. Capturing the prisoners is still a good income source, coming for AoW. But, your soldiers just sit idle when you give the order. Only one soldier tries to arrest all of the prisoners, which should have been looked upon. A ten person group should handle arresting ten prisoners without giving them individual commands. Another thing is the power structure, I couldn't find the shortcut or key for powering down my structures when there is a shortage. Such a button has been in effect since the advent of RTS genre. Another button is repair. Where the hell is it? So, in general, user interface (UI) is a mess. There is no attack move, as long as I can see. Only upside is the units are capable of firing on the go.
Music used in the game is terrible, repeating techno. Look, if you want to be Red Alert, understand the beauty of the interaction between the game and the music. Red Alert has been a tank skirmish. A hard rock tone is actually sitting well with the overall gameplay. Here, nothing! There is no connection between the units and the music. Soundeffects are also in trouble. When my units go over an obstacle and there is an explosion, there is no sound that follows the action.
Where to start? It just starts without any concrete explanation, with static pictures talking nonsense. Writing is bad, acting is bad, cutscenes are bad. Even the loading screens are terrible.
The strongest suit of Act of War was its fresh graphical overhaul with respect to RTS games of its time. Unfortunately, AoA doesn't fill any shoes. Units are so small and indistinguishable from each other, you mainly got lost on what is going on. The icons that appear when you choose the units disappear when you are group selecting. Bases are lifeless.
This game looks like it is still at its alpha stage, with a good six months is required to make it what it should have been. What makes me sad is, I believe developers haven't played the original game, and didn't understand what made it such an underdog. Act of War should have been in a better place, and Act of Aggression should have been the game that reminded us that.
2/10
Final word: I hope developer will learn from its mistakes, and revitalized this series. It is a missed chance.

I actually like this game alot. The original that is, I never played the rebooted edition and not even sure why they bothered making that. From what I read it's seriously dumbed down.
Positive things:
----------------
Infantry:
It's an rts which infantry plays a big role.  Each of the three factions has multiple air and land units that can transport infantry and Chimera and US have aircraft that can transport vehicles aswell. Infantry can garrision buildings and also enter buildings occupied by hostile infantry to clear them (you don't actually see the fights inside buildings). You can basically have urban infantry warfare, advance building by building, something i liked about CnC 3, but it's better in this game. It's good for those like myself, who like (role)playing a bit in RTS games, instead of just rushing to defeat the enemy. You can load infantry in an apc and/or humvee and send out a patrol, then capture and hold a certain zone in the city, secure an LZ, send in more units by helis etc.. Wish it had naval units aswell.
Realistic and varied  units:
Some units are a bit futuristic, but not unrealistic. The relative sizes of the units  are correct aswell. I like that alot more that for example the ridiculous/cartoonish units in Red Alert 3 or Starcraft.
There are alot of different units and each side is completely unique. All units are based on real world military vehicles or on scrapped prototype and planned vehicles. PAK-FA, F-22, Su-47 Berkut, Abrams, different Stryker versions, Comanche, Apache etc. Chimera and Cartel have a combination of international units.
Scouts & Artillery:
You can have (stealth) scouts spot for your artillery. Makes for interesting gameplay combined with the urban warfare and bombers and helis.
GI Joe vs Cobra (and maybe GDI vs NOD):
The US and Chimera are basically GI Joe, Chimera is UN military so a bit like GDI. Cartel is Cobra. (I read that in someone else's review and that's part of the reason why I bought it)
US is regular military. Chimera is a mix of regular military and stealth. Cartel relies heavily on stealth/surprise element. In the last mission of the Chimera campaign u control both Chimera and US forces.
Individual infantry:
Most infantry units are also individuals, not squads (except mortars/grenadiers, which come in pairs. I never liked the squads in other games. If I want squads, I'll make them myself.
- Maps are large enough:
I hate RTS' with tiny maps.
Negative:
----------
-Planes run out of fuel too fast so if u want a constant air patrol u need to send them way too often. They should also be more controllable, and perhaps actually land at the airfield, like in CnC3. Apparetntly in the reboot version they're totally uncontrollable (one of the reasons i never booted that version), not sure who thought that was a better idea ...
- You cannot deselect units (afaik) by clicking the map or pressing escape or whatever. You always have one unit (or building) selected, unless that unit dies.
- When infantry exits a vehicle, the infantry is automatically selected instead of the vehicle. I had many times where I wanted to send the carrier back home to pick up more infantry, but instead i notice the infantry running towards the base ...
- The units are hightlighted when selected, not just with a healtbar above them, but with shiny colored/glow aroudn them. Immersion breaking to me.
- Zooming out goes to tactical overview (or whatever it's called) too fast. You cannot admire the pretty units from a larger distance in regular view. I ended up playing in tactical overview most of the time in missions, until I establshed a tight defensive perimeter around my base.
- Helicopters cannot land (would just be cool if the could, like in Wargame: Red Dragon)
- No naval units
- Sometimes the game crashes

some people might not get the importance of mods in this game,you shouldn't expect to have a lot of fun with this game if you dont play with mods on, because they add so much content and interesting scenarios to the game.
in my honest opinion, it's a pretty good game, you'll probably get a few laughs and good times out of it, also seeing as how you can play with buddies split-screen, but you will definately also rage at it once in a while.
here's the website of the devs and where you'll find the mods (mods are in the fan forums section);
i'll list a couple that people should definately check out if they want to play this game here;
there are two kinds of mods that you'll find in the fan forums; mods and scenes. scenes are general scenarios, such as a base assault or an entirely redone campaign. mods are, well, mods. factions, weapons, you name it. someone even made a filter to make the game dark and gritty, and someone made tiberium from command and conquer.
-Mods-
Warhammer 40K imperium of man: a massive mod that adds pretty damn overpowered soldiers and weapons into the game, but not so op that it's no fun to play them, you can feel very powerful with the soldiers, but they're not indestructible, and they're fairly expensive. one thing i should note is that with the soldiers with jetpacks you can do a dash in the direction your mouse is pointing by pressing shift+up.
there's additional instructions for how to make the individual factions other than the standard blue space marines available on the forum page.
Unitec: *note: it's very important that you download the 1.05 compatible version that weegee posted on page 136 of the thread. otherwise it wont work, unless you're using an older version of the game.*
the unitec mod is really amazing, it adds 3 inredible factions into the game which each have a big variety of weapons to use, it's really incredible how much this mod has to offer. i'd like to note that you can enable hidden weapons in
and change the ones you dont see in the in-game menu to either 1 or 0 (depending on what it's already set to)
Darkstorm: very cool mod with quite a few interesting devices that will light your enemies ablaze (the fire on them will light other units that walk into them on fire as well) or freeze enemies to death. the warhammer mod uses this fire mechanic as in their mod as well.
SAW: you should really just take a look at the thread, the artwork that's been done of this is incredible, and it's fairly satisfying to use as well.
Kettenkrad's wehrmacht: this mod. this. mod. it's nazi and absolutely fabulous. i've seen tanks and artillery as well in this mod, but i think they were in earlier versions of it. it's worth a try to install earlier versions of it and see if they still work. i'd also like to post and additional mod for this one, since it fits very, very well. yes indeed, 'tis undead hitler. (none's post)
-Scenes-
ssl assault: if you're bored of the good ol' bunker breaches, this is a brand new, easy to install scene which introduces 3 new ones (not under bunker breach, but under a new one called ssl assault 1-3) the first two of which being assaults against the coalition with no counterattacks, and the third being an attack against techion with a lot of counterattack once you reach exit the first building you go into.
Cortex Shock: HOLY COW THIS IS GOOD, i almost forgot this one, it's an adventure scenario that puts you through various fairly hard levels, get your game face on for this one. there is some mod compatibility in this, but it'll be better explained on the mod page.
SHIELD: Under Siege: this is a scene that requires the Unitec mod i listed, it's a fantastic campaign with 14 levels that each has unique oblectives and hardcore gameplay, very very fun, but be careful not to lose your units, you will instantly lose. the mod is discontinued, but there should be enough content to make anyone happy. i very much recommend getting this mod.
Prison Escape 1-3: i really think you should just start playing this without any other words from me. 3 fantastic missions with an incredible feat of scripting at the end.
Unmapped Lands 2: this scene is very simple to play, but it can also get very long the longer you play, because the AI gets so much gold that he simply never runs out when he's attacking you. there's a manual in the thread for how to play the games.
and that's it. i hope you enjoy playing with mods, since i certaintly have done. there's a bunch more mods on the forums that you can find, but i'll leave it there.

Dust is an amazing accomplishment. The game was created by one developer who did all the art and programming over 4 years.
However, while this does give you a new perspective on the game, that still doesn’t and shouldn’t make it safe from criticism in areas where it fell short for me.
My initial hour or so was a pleasant experience. The environment seemed stylistic, the game ran well on my low end PC and had a diverse selection of features to make the game more accessible. The UI, even if it did look like an RPGMaker preset, was smooth and responsive with tactile sound effects for feedback. The soundtrack was nothing outstanding but did work well for setting the mood.
I had high hopes for how the metroidvania elements would play into improving and expanding what was a responsive combat system while perhaps also adding more diverse movement elements for platforming and enhanced mobility during fights.
Unfortunately, beyond the first hour the combat hardly changes. You retain the same ‘full X attack’, two ‘X into Y at some point’ and transition to air/ground combos. You get more overpowered attacks for Fidget that encourage sloppier gameplay. Mashing X in the right direction momentarily between fits of spamming Y+B to damage and stun everything on screen becomes an unbeatable strategy. There’s no incentive/punishment for more precise combat. In fact, the game rewards you with xp bonuses for the more hits during a combo and nothing racks up points like zapping everything on screen. My expectations for and anticipation of more dynamic gameplay throughout the game were subverted, disappointingly so especially considering the game’s inspirations.
Environments, while detailed, are way too expansive visually repeat themselves constantly and leading Dust to produce long, unmemorable hallways. You walk as slow as turtle and are constantly stopped by enemies and dialog. You can midair Y past some enemies, but if there are any near the screen’s exit, you’ll have to kick them around for a while before you can move on.
When you do get hit you take a surprising amount of damage. This means you’ll be spending the majority of your money on a crap ton of healing items for the rare occasion when you stop mashing X into Y+B and get punished. You can equip some regeneration but +2 health every second does nothing to help my 1000 health pool.
Enemies change up visually but never feel any different as you’ll be carelessly flying around and indiscriminately zapping everyone. Maybe sometimes there’ll be a dude who needs to be zapped first cause they eat up your health, but the way you defeat these punching bags never changes.
The only real exception is with the introduction of the ‘3 hit kill counter-only’ guy who exists to remind you about parrying half way through the game (a system that you’ll, at most, accidentally use). Parrying by itself feels shaky and every encounter with this enemy will eat up a fair amount of your healing items. Then the guy just disappears for the rest game.
There are only a few upgrades throughout Dust. Beside the Midair Y, that is unlocked early on, the upgrades do little to change up combat.
Even as a metroidvania enthusiast, I found the backtracking felt slow, intolerable and primarily pointless. ‘Quicktime event chests’ net you money, for buying health or, infrequently, better equipment, or materials for crafting items (something I never felt the need to do).
Even without seeking out secrets, you always have plenty of money or keys. There are no obstacles that require grinding to be overcome. Moving from place to place is so slow and enemies always remain a cake walk so I never felt the completionist, stat-collecting or explorative rush to motivate me to check out old/optional areas.
Although it rarely happened to me, the consumable nature of keys puts you at risk for bumping into a chest, having no keys, and then having to just remember to lug yourself back there. I imagine that this would’ve been a more direct issue if I wasn’t already wholly disinterested in retracing my steps.
There are teleport stones but they’re
for moving from a save point to the world map, are consumable and cost a fortune earlier on. This could have easily saved the tedium of backtracking if each save point provided a skip over the prolonged, repetitive hallways of meaningless enemies.
The graveyard area makes this
apparent with no teleportation to save you from a long 15 minute trip up and back to each of the 3 objectives. This area also fervently engenders lackadaisical gameplay. It’s riddled with group after group of harmless zombies with large health pools and wizards that can only be beaten by fidget’s lightning (which does little direct damage), providing arduous and redundant gameplay and promoting the mindless mashing.
While I can’t personally get behind the artstyle, animations on Dust himself are as smooth as butter and help amplify the responsiveness of combat. Honestly, this was the game’s saving grace and is why I stuck with it for as long as I did. Dust is fun to control.
It’s hard to imagine one guy doing all the art assets because there are a lot here and even a few full animated cutscenes. Environmental themes are produced well but the overall anthropomorphic animal design and the character portraits are largely shabby. Enemies and NPCs are animated limb-by-limb and create a stiff unit that reminds me of Bookworm Adventures 2 and appears unpolished but is typically undetectable during action.
The story was is paint-by-number simple and something I wasn’t remotely interested in from the beginning. Thankfully you can skip through dialog relatively quickly and there is even a skip scene button in the pause screen that I unfortunately failed to notice until basically where I stopped playing.
Voice actors, while convincing, play roles of character stereotypes that were hard to listen to. In game, there are so many moments where you see a thing and the game stops and has the 3 protagonists make a quip or say, “Oh, look. A thing”. These distractions took me out of the experience and made me more restless to reach objectives that I began to care about even less.
When I saw that the game was rated overwhelmingly positive on steam, I found myself genuinely confused. So much so that I watch ‘let’s plays’ to see if I was playing the game wrong.
I think it’s fantastic that one dude found an idea that he liked and spent 4 years on a single passion project making what was his perfect game. It seems that a lot of people share his vision and Dust certain deserves plenty of attention for that. I’m disappointed that I couldn’t find a way to love Dust as well.
I cannot recommend Dust, although, my experience does seems to be an outlier.

I never cared much for F.E.A.R. . All I knew about it was that it had the The Ring girl and you could slow time like The Matrix, and those two things never really interested me anyways since they just seemed like gimmicks that were cashing in on what was popular at the time.
So it came quite as a shock that I managed to find one of the best FPS games I have ever played here. Preconceptions can be deceiving so it seems, who knew?
For a game released all the way back in 2005, im amazed at how well it holds up today in the technical department. The physics and particle effects are some of the best I have ever seen in a shooter, and the way they increase the positive feedback from the gameplay is great and ultimately what makes the game.
And the slowing down mechanic only enhances it. Entering a room and dispatching every single enemy in the span of 5 seconds and bringing the game back to normal speed never gets old. The room will be filled with blood, bullet holes, lights swinging back and forth and smoke all over the place, giving you this immense feeling of satisfaction and empowerment.
Its also great that the enemies have really good AI and will constantly try to flank  get the drop on you, and the game has a way of tricking you into believing they act like humans by having them have conversations between squads in relation to your actions. Most of that dialogue is simply a way of disguising the AI, since the enemies actions never really matches what they are saying, but it goes a long way to immerse you into the game and increase your suspension of disbelief.
The weapons are also fantastic, they all have this absurd kick to them that makes killing the enemies incredibly rewarding, and it only gets better as the game progresses, giving you even more ridiculous overpowered guns that will either desintegrate or explode your enemies. Enemies react very realistic to being shot, and by slowing down time you can really see how a bullet hitting on their shoulder, for example, makes them move as you would expect them to.
It never got old unloading a shotgun at point blank on an enemy face with time slowed down.
You would think the slowing down time mechanic would make you feel overpowered, but the game balances that well by making you die very easily if not behind cover and in normal time. So the combat loop of this game ends up making you feel like a monster just annihilating everyone before they can even react and leaving a trail of destruction behind you.

To complement this amazing gameplay, you also have the brilliant level design. You will spend most of your time moving through builidings, offices and factories, and while those environments may seem a bit boring, they are completely elevated by the qualitiy of their routes.
You see, there is always more than one way of approaching a combat segment, the levels tend to be circular, where there is always at least two paths leading to the same spot. This not only provides some really fun moments of hide and sek between you and the enemies, but it also always leaves you a bit tense turning your back to a spot that might just have an enemy trying to get the drop on you.
If there is something FPSs should take from F.E.A.R., its the level design, just some of the best I have seen in a long time.
The presentation is also fantastic. The pace of the game is broken up by horror segments, where you you will have to move through dark corridors and empty building structures. This is all elevated by the lighting system of the game that still holds up, creating some really great shadows, and the realistic environments only enhance the uneasyness.
As for the horror itself, I have to say I found it more endearing than scary, but this is mainly due to the time the game was released, since most of its tricks are cliche by now. But they are good tricks, dont get me wrong and I did have fun getting startled by some of them, its just that they are really tame by today's standards. One thing I have to commend the game, is that the jump scares dont have the obnoxious high pitch sound meant to make you jump so I appreciate that.
Hilariously, I found myself getting more spooked with combat situations that would either surprise me by introducing a new type of threat or by the creative way the enemies would approach me.
The soundtrack is great, having that Half Life feel where it kicks into high gear when the moment calls for it, turning certain situations into a scene straight out of an action movie.
The story itself while managing to get you invested is very by the numbers and the game has a way of trying to make a big deal out of what I think is a very straightforward plot, and some of its twists and revelations were a bit eye rolling inducing, but it was all in good fun and it was never intrusive.Its understandable, being a game of 2005.
My biggest gripe with the game however has to be the way it decides to end the game. You would expect that the last moments of a visceral FPS like this would be to throw everything and the kitchen sink at you, bringing every enemy type at the same time and giving you every weapon you could carry to give you one last final showdown.
But nope, the last two chapters are dedicated to the horror component, having you just follow some hallways killing some weird paranormal ghosts that cause minimal damage to you, just so the plot can be served to you.
It really left a bad taste in my mouth, and it was a severe case of blue balls.
Final veridict, play this game. It deserves more love than it gets, this is one of great FPS games of its time, and I think alot of devs would benefit from taking a look at how a shooter is ♥♥♥♥ing done.

If you recognize "Lone Wolf" or Joe Dever, you'll have a good idea of what to expect. For the uninitiated, Lone Wolf is based on a series of choose-your-own adventure gamebooks of the same name. The game's story is told primarily through text, with the occasional animated illustration and cutscene. Battle takes place in 3D space, featuring varied settings. RPG features allow you to customize your character's skills, growth, and loadout as you see fit.
This game is not a "standard" RPG, having more in common with a visual novel (or gamebook). Combat is based on quick-time events. The higher difficulties can be surprisingly brutal. It's a port from mobile, and it's not exactly cheap. In short, it's not for everyone.
However, if you like what you see, it's a fun adventure. If you can, try getting it on mobile (or on sale), but the port is enjoyable.
P.S. Last I checked, the mobile version lets you play part 1 for free, so try that out to get a feel of the game.

+polished and pleasant graphic presentation, which pays great attention to details
+plenty of choice&consequence moments
+great overall atmosphere and sense of immersion
+lockpicking is a real thing
+the good ol' rewarding feeling of accomplishment
+it's a Joe Dever's Lone Wolf story.. yo, so 80s!
On a side note: personally I was quite pleased to find out this has been developed by an italian team. Wouldn't mama be proud? <3
-the massive amount of QTEs; not only they're at the core of the combat mechanics, but they're also basically everywhere else
-repetitiveness: you're going to face tons of Giak trolls in the beginning before you meet your first 'different' enemy, and even then nothing really improves on the diversity front
-redundancy: some actions will trigger almost always the same response: yet another troll fight..
-Cube puzzles: totally unnecessary, as they add nothing to the story or to your personal enjoyment, but further annoyance
-not a great deal of originality: if I weren't nostalgic of the genre I would have probably dismissed the whole thing as a trite re-hash of something already read/seen times and times again, but this wouldn't really be a con for 'new' players I guess
-clichés: as stated above, we all heard the story of the lonesome hero with a superpowerful sword who also happens to be lord of something - while the female character, when it's not a cold-blooded badass ♥♥♥♥♥, ends up weeping on your shoulder or moping around in a cellar door waiting to be rescued
-difficulty spikes: some early fights are quite hard to beat unless you resort to 'easy mode', or if you're prepared to try them again for 2-3 times - which is not that funny considering how repetitive they are
Overall, I'd recommend the game only to the true patient ones out there: it's not a bad game, it's actually entertaining for the most part, but it requires to be dealt with.

It's the same game as FF4. 17 years later they couldn't figure out how to advance the story so they just copied the same story and added fan fiction romances to show that time had lapsed. FF4 wasn't some masterpiece, but it did have some nice plot twists for its time: my brother is the villain, I'm a bad guy and I need to find redemption to be a good guy. This was the 90's it was cheesy. It was fine. Decades later they pull the same cheesy clichés that have been used a billion times in stories just to remind you of events from the previous game.
It's episodic so you see how everyone gets together, but the way it's presented makes you feel as if you're playing the same opening every time only to lead to "Hey, this has happened before...". Not to mention how you have to level up your allies every-single-♥♥♥♥ing-time whenever you start a new tale because while you're level 10 or 15 they're like level 1 or 5.
And I got a huge issue with Edward's Tale and a other tales. I had to go through the Underground Waterway five times. FIVE TIMES! How do you own a kingdom that's a "hub of commerce, not of war" yet not have a port for ships to dock so you can trade and negotiate with other kingdoms? Blimps are even available in this world. Why does a kingdom reliant on trade and diplomacy need to go through the same cave on another part of the continent AT LEAST FIVE TIMES TO ADVANCE THE PLOT just to be able to interact with the outside world? How did the director approve reusing the same dungeon 5 times? They had Ceodore climb up and down a mountain but I can't climb over the Underground Waterway?
The story finds any excuse to go through the Underground Waterway
On top of that, I had to listen to this song for 2 hours straight, throughout the game like 4-5 hours.
It's enough to drive a person insane. I was so frustrated with Edward's tale that I didn't even have to mute the game, my body forced itself to block this song from registering as sound as a defense mechanism to keep me safe.
Lastly, the moon phases are a new addition that ended up being a bad idea with good intentions. Depending on the moon type, weapons/skills/white magic/black magic damage gets doubled, stay normal, or get halved. This is entirely useless because throughout the game because each tale is focused on one or two characters of a specific monotype. If you get your specific damage halved you can just sleep in the Inn or use a Tent/Cottage until you get the right moon phase, so it ends up just being a nuisance. This is pretty good, provided you know what you're getting into.
Lone Wolf was a series of fantasy gamebooks written by Joe Dever in the 80s. Since then the books have been reprinted a few times in various languages, and have even been made available for free with the author's consent on
. If this is not immediately made apparent further down this apologetic review, I loved these books and I'm quite pleased to see their universe transition into video game form. Rather than being an adaptation of one of the books, this game is an original story taking place somewhere between books 3 and 4.
Originally a mobile game, this PC port is still mostly a gamebook with QTE-based combats thrown in, meaning there's more reading than action in there - so if you're waiting for a full-fledged RPG you're going to be seriously disappointed. However, as an expanded gamebook, it works pretty well, and that's coming from someone who usually despises QTEs.
The writing is on par with the original books (which is to be expected, since Dever wrote the game's script as well), and the gameplay has a lot of similarities as well. You get to make choices along the way which alter the events of the story, though the instant game overs from the books are far less common here. One of the interesting features the books had were the skills you could select at the beginning (among an assortment of classic ranger stuff like tracking, hiding, talking to animals, and the famous ranger core-skills, telekinesis and psionic blasts), with corresponding skillchecks throughout the story. The books provided a random number table to pinpoint in case the reader didn't have a D10 to resolve the skillchecks (combat worked more or less the same way). The exact same skills are back in this game, but here you have to resolve them with QTEs, which when you think about it is not very different from trying to frantically pin numbers from some table with a pen.
Combat is mostly real-time with pause and QTEs as well (except in Hard, where it's real-time with nope enemies can still attack you when you think), but you'll also have to manage the character's stamina, attacks cooldowns, and debuffs. Classic post-2010 RPG stuff, the devs probably liked their Dark Souls and Witchers, but the combats flow nicely and it's all that counts. These combats are numerous, though enemy variety is extremely low (5 different enemies with a couple variants, including bosses, throughout the game), but I had no problems with it since it mimics the books pretty well - in the first couple books you fought plenty of Giaks, Drakkarim and Vordaks (the same enemies you find in this game). Some encounters can be quite hard, I had a few run-ins with Gourgaz where they basically one-shot me in the first 5 seconds, but here again, bonus points for book fidelity, where Gourgaz were one-shotting [illegitimate offspring - thanks wordfilter] as well.
The adventure is quite long for a gamebook, definitely longer than the later books of the series anyway (which, as far as gamebooks go, were already huge bricks), it took me a dozen hours to finish it and I'll probably play it again to try alternate paths and builds, so there is quite a bit of playtime-to-be here.
My only major complaints are the artsyle, which really screams 2010s (once again, Dark Souls and Witcher got there before, but it's not
a major complaint anyway), while Gary Chalk's original illustrations had a distinctly British and somewhat goofy flair that is not present there. But it's somewhat close to the Mongoose reprints' covers (barring Lone Wolf's ridiculous sideburns and edgy victory poses, but they provided well-needed hilarity moments in an overall grim story), so at least it doesn't come out of nowhere. Oh, there's also the economy, which makes absolutely no sense and is really as far from the books as you can get (this one actually
a major complaint). Gone are the days of the 5 GP for a sword, 3 for a healing potion, here you'll be shelling dozens of coins to sharpen the edge of a blade. Now
did break the spell of the good old days, but it didn't stop me from enjoying the game anyway.
So, to sum it up.
+ Great fidelity to the source material
+ Good length, with added replayability
+ Nice extras (in-game menus, PDF artbook, OST)
- Low enemy variety
- Repetitive gameplay (which I didn't mind)
- Mediocre economy and crafting mechanics
- Lots of farming needed in harder difficulties
7/10 if you're a fan of the series (I'd even say 8, but I have a tendency to overrate things, especially anything Lone Wolf-related), 5/10 otherwise - you won't find much here unless you're willing to go out of your way to learn about this series.

This game is an experience, just like its successor The Witcher III: The Wild Hunt. This game has a spectacular, inclusive story that makes you just want to devour it all at once. It's engaging and fun, while at the same time being graphically gorgeous and exciting.
The combat is pleasantly smooth, and easy to execute. Sometimes, using objects other than your swords can be tedious, but in all honesty, it really doesn’t affect the overall feel of battle. The AI provides a decent amount of challenge at all difficulty levels.
Geralt of Rivia is an interesting character to play. He has a surprising amount of personality for an emotionless monster-hunter. Geralt’s antics and overall demeanor make the game pleasant and funny. Sometimes the snarky and sarcastic humor that laces this game is so smart it’s easy to miss, other times it’s in your face and hilarious.
The Witcher II: Assassins of Kings does not feel like a game released in 2011. This game has the ability feel as well put together as a current blockbuster game, while still feeling original and unique. There are hundreds of games like it, but not even one of them can compare to it.
Honestly, this game—like the Witcher III—is a delight to play. One could play these games for hours. CD Projekt really does know how to make a remarkable game.
This is recommended to anyone who loves fantasy, sarcastic humor, medieval themes—or really, to anyone who just wants to have a good time.

I'll break it down for ya.
1 part Shadowrun
1 part Megaman
1 part Metroid
1 part Castlevania
The game is fun, slick, and highly polished. The voice actors are top notch (I'm lookin at you Miri Shalyn!) and very quirky (thats a good thing). Music is well done, and suits each zone of the Nakamura station nicely. One feature I'm especially fond of is HOW your save game is loaded. When you hit "Continue" it plays a recap of recent cutscenes as though it were from a previous episode of a tv show/anime. This is preceded by Miri (aka Ghost in the game) saying "Previously, on Ghost 1.0" before going into the cutscene bits.
Anyway, moving on. There are LOADS of interesting alternate weapons, and even more passive power-up items that stay with you. You have guns galore, of every type. You have several kinds of drones that stick with you and fight. There are deflector shields, cloaking devices, and lots more. If you seek them all out before going to end-game, Ghost will be a killing machine. The game is full of what the developer terms "Geeks" which are easter-egg items that are hidden in rooms which alter parts of the game without impacting gameplay. For instance, the "Moria" geek will make your minimap look like an old-school roguelike version of the map until you toggle the geek back off. If you are a completionist, there is PLENTY to hunt for, believe me.
Another interesting aspect of the game is that your character, Ghost, is an AI (or is she? maybe so, maybe not.) that can digitally possess other robots by leaving her body/chasis, then flying in her "ghost form" and taking over theirs. Some levels require some very precise use of this trick to advance. There is also one part, I won't tell you where, that lets you beat an unwinnible fight by being clever with that ability...
The story is good, much like the Shadowrun storylines. Big, shadowy corporations doing shady things, your team operating in a criminal and techie underworld to get things done, whether for profit or a just cause. Cloak and dagger espionage. All that good stuff. In my opinion, there is HUGE potential for more storyline. I mean the game has a lengthy one with twists and turns, and while satisfying, it can be considered just a prologue for an even bigger story, or a series of smaller ones. Hm, maybe I just want more. *laughs*
I give it a 9/10. Great game for your money, and lots of replay if you want to hunt down all the hidden goodies or play the Survival mode once you beat Classic.
Buy it folks, its worth it!

I enjoyed UnEpic, so I was pretty interested in Ghost 1.0, despite some of the early negative reviews. Unfortunately the reviews are arguably on point, and while technically competent, the game fails to engage the player on any level. I freely admit I only completed the game to justify my purchase, and because I am a completionist ♥♥♥♥♥ (sex industry worker, as Steam doesn't like that word).
The plot is bland, and lacking closure in parts, most of the characters aren't very interesting or developed. I'd critique the juvenile writing, but anyone who played UnEpic should have come to this title expecting that sort of dialogue. Combat is busy to the point that you sometimes lose track of what's going on, which is why the game has an option titled "make cursor more visible" which turns your targeting reticle into a giant blazing cross of blue fury that stretches across 1/4 of the screen. The platforming feels clumsy until you buy all the mobility upgrades for Ghost, at which point it's simply adequate.
The real bone of contention for me was the problem of "soul" secrets in the game. Most of these, early in the game, unlock some much-appreciated upgrades for your character or currency to purchase upgrades, but the logic behind the secrets is bizarre at best, counter-intuitive at worst. With tasks like "destroy the droids, then the mines, then the floor turret, then the roof turret, IN THAT ORDER ONLY", to "save and exit to the main menu, then continue", the majority have to be googled to figure out. Are these optional? Definitely. But as someone who enjoys unlocking all the upgrades in their games, this was positively mind-numbing for me. Even with an unlocked ability to *sometimes* be shown a vague hint where *something* needs to be done, I'd still be at a loss as to what that task was for 90% of the secrets. There's no logic. There's no fun challenge. It's just bizarre, arbitrary bullcrap.
And finally, this game is a flawed Metroidvania in one important regard: certain areas are inaccessible until you acquire items to unlock them, but ALL of those items in this game are keycards, not items or abilities. A pretty poor representation of a Metroidvania by most standards.
I don't enjoy ragging on games made by indie developers, but I feel obligated to warn people like myself who enjoyed the creator's previous work: If you want to support the developer, buy a second copy of UnEpic for a friend. You'll get more satisfaction from that than you will playing Ghost 1.0.

I love it.

It's the video game version of those direct-to-video Disney sequels to beloved animated movies but  It doesn't even reach the Return of Jafar level of quality.
I'm only on Episode 4 of 10 and I can pretty much tell the game isn't about to improve anytime soon.  Nostalgia isn't enough to recommend a boring, fanfic story with tedious gameplay mechanics.
Most of the game involves you redoing things you did in FFIV but in a different order and different characters.  You literally fight all the same boss battles again, often in the exact same location.  If you were hoping to see what happens 17 years after FFIV ended, it's really not that much.  The world is basically the exact same only now you occasionally play as carbon-copies of the original characters, usually their children.  The story in FFIV was always pretty simple but it at least felt like a plot you could follow where characters had consistent motivations. Zeno Clash is a unique game in its genre : a first person fighter - beat-them-all set in a tribal punk fantasy world. You play as Ghat all along his journey exiled from his tribe through the end of the world. Helped by his sister he will face many opponents and dangers to survive along his exile : that will includes many brothers and sisters of his own Father-Mother (an hermaphrodite creature) as well as a hired head-hunter, the Corwid of the Free's tribe and many critters.
But Ghat isn't weak at all, quite the contrary, he is really strong despite his thin shape. He also learned how-to fight with Metamoq the chief of Corwid of the Free. So he knows how to fight using his fists or melee or gun weapons.
The game features levels, meaning that there is no at lot to explore but there are many brawls and fights to come through. Despite that, there are many new environments and concepts to make the game quite interesting. Also each level are independent meaning that weapons you had at the end of a level won't be transferred to the next level. (Unless the bombs are but I'm not sure) So as you understood each level as its own weapons, enemies and fruits in specific places. The game consists in exploring (a little) and fighting/brawling waves of foes and bosses. The HUD is very simple : you got your own portrait with your health and stamina bars. Every time you run or prepare a strong attack you use stamina which will be restored slowly. And don't be afraid for your health bar running low, there are always some fruits that give you some health back as well as some checkpoint that restore you whole health ! The HUD show you also the remaining bombs you got.
Adding to the story mode there is also a challenge mode. Challenges take place in a tower, split in two area : the top and the bottom. If you are going in the top you are going to fight many foes on each level using the given weapons or not (you can brawl instead most of the time) to reach the top level which include the story boss as well as many foes at the same time ! If you are going at the bottom, you'll need to fight foes and make you way below by jumping platform by platform using bombs if needed to break a whole platform to make a hole. But don't forget to take care of every foe cause you won't go deeper until you dealt with all of them. So you can push them all in the pit below but you'll need to face all the survivors at the end. Also when you'll go deeper you'll encounter golden enemies which are more powerful and tougher. Each level can be played independently so it's not a real survival game. At the end of each challenge you'll be in the leaderboard with the time you've made and the remaining health. So you can compete with your friends on steam.
That's not all : you have also 70 Zeno Clash characters and foes patterns for Garry's Mod.
I would really recommend this game !
(*): A very uncommon issue happened to me in the Corvid of the Free forest : after I've beat up every foe the game keep playing without occurring the next wave. But after waiting / moving several minutes the next wave appeared.
(#): I would say almost every achievement can be backtracked and several of them are kept while making another playthrough or replaying some levels. Only one "difficult" achievement requires you to play the whole story from the beginning to the end using weapons when you really need to. There are a lot of information on steam or elsewhere that explains when you need to use weapons or not. If you used one by mistake you can still kill yourself and try the current level but if you forgot to this playthrough will not count.
