As with most old PC games - where they've been re-released to modern systems through digital retailers without receiving any optimisation - I had to go through the motions of setting compatibility modes and downloading third-party patches before the game would launch. Once I had made the achievement of reaching the main screen I had to reset almost all of the keybindings, as they just weren't up to standard.
At first I noticed that F.E.A.R. really shows its age: the animations are quite wooden, especially with the main player's arms (seriously, this is something on-screen for the entirety of the game and they're as stiff as planks). The UI scaling is completely out of whack for larger resolutions, I can barely read the subtitles. It's like trying to read an 8pt font on a 50 inch monitor.
I know this is common in FPS games but having the camera located in the player's chest makes me feel a little like like Tom Cruise on the set of his next major blockbuster. I believe this has also caused problems during firefights as enemies will aim at my head, and be able to hit me while I'm crouched, even though it appears that I'm behind cover. This issue persists through the ages, even appearing in games such as PAYDAY 2.
I'm uncertain as to what technicality is causing frame-rate issues while enabling slo-mo but activating v-sync in the graphic options has improved this greatly. I can now use slo-mo without the screen stuttering like crazy. There are still a number of issues, such as the camera flying through geometry during short cut-scenes. There was also one instance where enemies were able to shoot through walls from across the map, luckily this was a once-off occurrence.
The physics engine is great, it's extremely satisfying to blast enemies and see their ragdolled bodies flying through the air, especially in slow motion. The only problem with this is that the physics is applied to so many environmental objects that I feel is unnecessary, such as cans and general rubbish, which can sometimes cause these objects to spasm violently when they're stepped on by the player.
Whilst the graphics of F.E.A.R. don't particularly hold up, the game is over 10 years old as of writing, I found that the lighting and physics are still something to be admired. Even modern games still can't achieve this level of quality. Enemy spawn positions can be odd at times, where a number of soldiers will spawn right in front of my eyes on a single point. Despite the oddity it became convenient since a single, well-placed shotgun blast can take out 2-3 at once.
Everything, from the physics, the silent protagonist, and the level and sound design - especially of the enemies when they communicate - all remind me heavily of Half-Life 2 but I found that the A.I. in F.E.A.R. is much more intelligent and unpredictable. They would often outflank me, draw me into a bottleneck, and manoeuvre in such a way that I'd end up missing them only to end up dead. There are also certain special enemies that remind me of BioShock's splicers and Big Daddy's, although their appearances are short-lived.
Even though I love linear games I found F.E.A.R. to be far too linear, it's a straight up corridor shooter without much flavour. I also found the game to be very, very dark. I'd often run into walls or closed doors when my flashlight had run out of power.
There is a poor amount of variety when it comes to weapons and an even smaller pool of ammunition to go with them. I would often end up running out of ammo for my preferred weapon (pistol) very quickly. For some reason there is a seemingly unlimited amount of ammunition for the shotgun so I mostly relied on that when my other guns ran dry. I don't particularly appreciate there being a limit on having only three weapons at a time when there is already such a small variety of guns to choose from, I don't see why I can't just hold all of them for the sake of convenience. It's the same with the torch, why allow it to run flat if its recharge time is only a matter of seconds. I found these mechanics to be quite silly and limiting when their implementation was obviously to create some artificial difficulty and basic resource management system. It's a nuisance.
There isn't much to say for the sound design and soundtrack, it's all very ambient and atmospheric.
As for gameplay, it feels like I'm performing the same task over and over again... I'll enter an area, there will be a security lock-down happening, I'll be given the task to deactivate the security system and/or traps and then progress to next area... to be met by further security systems that must be deactivated in order to raise some gates, or activate elevators. To break up this monotony I'll be rewarded by either discovering a civilian or by being reunited with my team. All this progress I've made is soon wiped clean as I take two steps back and have to make up all that lost progress by scaling elevator shafts or taking back alleys. If I'm lucky I'll be extracted by another helicopter. The budget for disposable helicopters must be immense as each chopper somehow manages find itself in compromising situations and soon destroyed. As well as my soldier buddies always seeming to be sidetracked or incapacitated so that I'm forced to take the role as a one-man-army of the hour type hero. It starts becoming a little bit ridiculous and annoying, story-wise.
I do wish there was more focus on the supernatural elements and cut-scenes as they were very sparse, and the small amounts of interesting encounters that did happen weren't enough to break up the monotonous pacing of the story and gameplay. I found the slo-mo system to be a huge crutch for me, without it I was very easily overwhelmed by enemies. I actually feel like the player takes a higher amount of damage without it.
There was a point where the game's difficulty ramped up excessively where resources, such as med-kits and grenades, became much more scarce. Where before I had been able to hoard 10 med-kits at a time and keep a full supply of explosives, I was soon whittled down to nothing for long lengths and at the same time I was expected to handle hordes of special enemies. It soon became too much for me to bear.
Don't get me wrong, F.E.A.R. is a very atmospheric and nice looking game, especially for its time. It's simply not a very exciting or memorable experience, devoid of personality, so much so that I had to force myself to continue playing. I could no longer suspend my disbelief with all of the immersion breaking issues I came across.
I've resorted to using cheat codes for unlimited ammo and health so that I can experience the story and continue on with the expansions and later sequels.

Ech, I don't know how to rate this. It's a pretty experience type thing akin to Journey on the playstation. It's pretty obvious Journey is a massive influence right down to aesthetic style and audio choices but somehow they just drop short of hitting so many high notes that made Journey great.
For a start there's very little interaction, which isn't too much of an issue as the game is short but it does sometimes give the game a bit of an illusory nature where you feel like it'd be best serving as a background. I also generally found that the movement never quite hits a satisfying peak like in Journey. The movement always feels sluggish and off, even with heavy utilization of the weirdly limited boost (why does it even have a limit?). The visuals are very pretty but the game doesn't really use much variance in them and when it does it doesn't use them in a way that has any emotional clout. Due to the water thin story this isn't really like Journey where the environments have an emotional atmosphere it's instead just like "Oh, a different underwater place, cool.". The story telling is also lacking, though there isn't much of a story any way it's still very poorly conveyed, it's a mix of too vague and too irrelevant. Non-verbal story telling can be good but without enough effort no connection is made with the player. I'm just gonna finish by saying whilst the music seems well done it once again suffers from poor placement or lack of emotional impact. Instead it's just nice orchestra music, well everything that isn't heavy on voices, the voice parts of the ochestra are frustratingly off-key and often too loud, just turning the music into meaningless noise.
So yeah, as you can tell, I think it's not perfect. However I am going to recommend this still as it's entertaining enough for a short trip (buy it on sale though) and the only thing close to Journey on PC. So yeah. Cool.

I purchased a few of the Lone Wolf books from a second hand bookstore, when I was in my teens. I loved the idea of a Choose Your Own Adventure style book with RPG elements. I played through the few books I had many times. They have always held a special place in my memory and I tried to turn my own child onto the books, when he was of an age to be interested. So yeah, this game played on my nostalgic memories and had won my favor before I even started a game.
The game gave me no technical issues whatsoever. It looks great, has a great soundtrack and of course, a great story line. It was very easy to get into. It uses so few resources that I was able to play it on my rapidly aging laptop and still looks great! My only complaint would be with the combat system. While you can plan a strategy for combat, there is an element of luck, as there was with the book series. However, when you enter combat and haven't been able to make a single move before the enemy dispatches you, I can't begin to tell you how frustrating that is. I had to repeat a fight with some middle level enemies four times, before they made a move that allowed me to make a move in my own favor.
So, this game is addicting, solid and fun. It can be incredibly frustrating at times, but the only reason it is frustrating is because I am so hooked and really want to progress in it. I love progressing in the game and I hope they will make more.

I have to say, i ♥♥♥♥ing love this game, though admittedly my basis here will be greatly influenced by the fact that i play with a lot of mods, which isnt neccesarily a bad thing, but some systems like for example Sectors, i just dont have experience with because i just dont use them due to mods. I was actually pretty apprehensive about buying the game, and who can blame me? Look at other paradox games like CK2 and try and tell me those are great easy to jump into games. I decided to buy the game after watching a few episodes of the Blorg playthrough (Resistance is impolite). They have on youtube. Its a great way to get an idea of how the game progresses from the beginning onwards. The game starts with you in a single system, as a species of myriad origin, having just unlocked your first FTL method. These can be Warp, slow but unrestricted, Hyperlanes, fast but restricted, and Wormholes, extremely fast and with decent range, but has a minor annoyance of having to build wormhole stations. You start with a few corvettes and a science ship along with a minor income level for minerals and energy credits and a small amount of researching ability and the game progresses from there.
Customizability is fabulous, Design bird people that hate everyone who's alien and are willing to defend their lands with military might. Or design these people as a peaceful theocracy who build federations and grand alliances to protect themselves through allies.(More on this later) I thoroughly enjoy this aspect of the game and its made replayability fun, atleast for me.
Gameplay is mostly managing cities, your people and to a lesser extent your policies, You also have chances to get rare technologies which can be incredibly strong or miraculously mediocre. Thankfully the vast majority of all technologies are well worth researching, Lasers especially are a joy to behold in battles watching huge swathes of ships cut an explosive path through opposing fleets is a joy to see. But you will spend most your time managing your respective leaders of your civ, and depending on your goverment type, elections. I personally due to no sectors spend a bit more time micromanaging my cities, as once you get more than 10+ planets it really is something you are just doing ALL the time, and other things like wars are just distractions from this. But thats how i prefer these games.
Politics to be frank for me, were a little dissapointing. the Trust system, atleast for me never really held any meaning for me because i tend to play extremely aggressive empires. nobody ever ends up trusting me in the game(NOBODY) and im generally in a situation where its Me versus the world. But again that is just how i play, for a more peaceful player the systems probably fine, i just dont have that experience.
Steam workshop support is fabulous for the longevity of the game, as mods for lots of different things, from empire colors to Flag emblems and beyond are made for the game. Also the glorious Exterminatus from the WH40k universe can be brought in. Sign the death warrant of an entire world, and consign a billlion souls to oblivion. Its awesome and i cant wait to check every few days to see what new upcoming idea modders have come up with. Its great and i can honestly say i cant imagine the game without this as it allows for so much silly♥♥♥♥♥♥to be in Stellaris as well as more serious and respectable mods.
Stellaris's greatest qualities in my opinion are its Customizability, both in game for various empires, as custom made ones are allowed, and in the Workshop support to modify the rules and boundaries of the game. The battles are enjoyable but really its a hand off affair, which can be good or bad depending on your point of view. Overall if your new to Grand Strategy i think this would be a great way to enter it, but if your into more in-depth games, like CK2, i might suggest skipping it. For most people though i think Stellaris is worth its purchase price, However if you are really on the fence for the game id suggest waiting for a sale. Paradox usually have great sales on steam and it would be an absolute steal if you got it for 20$.

Call of Duty: Black Ops was released in 2010. It can be played in single player mode as well as Multiplayer Mode and Zombies: Multiplayer Mode, both of which are immensely fun. Having played it to 100% completion on the PS3 already, I can't give it any higher praise. Only games that I think are fantastic do I bother putting in the kind of effort to achieve 100%. You play as Alex Mason, a soldier who is being held and interrogated, as you progress through various black ops Mason went on over several years. I can't go into more detail without spoilers, so I will leave it at that.
Call of Duty: Black Ops, plays the same way previous titles in the Call of Duty franchise, so if you like that style, Black Ops won't disappoint. Multiplayer is actually rather fun with Black Ops, as is Zombies Mode, where you can play on several Maps and must survive waves of zombies with a team of other players. Call of Duty: Black Ops has went on to be successful enough to spawn 2 sequels, which I have not yet had the chance to play, but that does speak volumes of how popular the game was and still is. If you like first person action/shooters, Black Ops is a must play.

Zeno Clash is a very interesting First Person Brawler, in which you play as Ghat, one of the many children of the strange FatherMother, who, after killing FatherMother, is chased out of town by his own brothers and sisters. The game's story starts right after FatherMother's murder, but there's also flashback sequences when Ghat tells his friend Deadra about the events that lead to him killing FatherMother.
Now, let's talk about the gameplay. As I mentioned above, it's a First Person Brawler, which means that for most of the game you'll be fighting with your fists. There's weapons, too, and areas in which you're required to use them, but for most of the game, it's a lot more satisfying to simply punch your way out. Progression is fairly linear, you'll go from point A to point B, fighting enemies in the middle, with some cutscenes here and there adding more story. Don't take that as a negative, though! It works fine enough for this game.
The game also has a challenge mode, unlocked through story progression, with two distinct types: tower and pit. In the Tower challenge levels, you'll fight through five floors, each one filled with different enemies, and you must reach the top in the shortest amout of time possible, while losing very little health; even then, if you do lose some health in a floor, you'll gain some of it back for the next one. The Pit challenge levels have you going down a pit, trying to reach the bottom without killing yourself (if you drop from too high, you'll die), while some enemies try to fight you.
I guess I should talk about the art style, which is quite unique; you'll find a world filled with bizarre environments and creatures; even some of the most "normal" characters, like Ghat or Deadra, have their bits of weirdness. And the soundtrack is excellent, I should say, with some really good tracks playing during the fight sequences. All of this adds to making Zeno Clash a really good game.
Of course, not everything is positive; even though I enjoyed the game a lot, it seems to have some issues with hit detection: sometimes I would attack an enemy thinking that my fist would hit them, only to hit thin air, while in other cases, believing to be out of reach, some enemies have managed to hit me. Even then, this isn't noticeable for most of the game.
So, to conclude, I can say I recommend Zeno Clash.

I have not played a huge amount of FEAR yet, but I have done some research and feel I need to make something clear for buyers of this game
This is not a horror-combat game, this is a game where you kill lots and lots of soldiers and every thirty minutes something mildly scary happens and then you go back to killing soldiers for another 30 minutes or so. The only fear in F.E.A.R are badly made, cheap jumpscares that would only "Terrify" someone who has never played a horror game before, I mean, if youve ever run away from a wasp, you have experienced more horror than fear offers.
I am not trying to diss the game here, but I will say that the fear community manages to be more "Fanatical" than the mind controlled soldiers that are at the center of this game. I started with fear three, barely a horror game, and was told "Nah, man, fear 1 is the scary one" So i tried it.
The honest to god truth is, when this game came out, it probably was pretty scary to those who played it, especially as kids. The honest to god truth is that this original fear game will at best make you jump one time. Even the few jumpscares are badly made, and can be seen coming from around corners, as in, you see the static monster or person and then shoot at it, nothing happens, you realize its for a cutscene, and have to stroll into its "Grab range" to initiate the cutscene.
At the end of the day, a  fanatical fear fan (Not all are this bad) will tell you the series is super horror, some kind of amazing entity that pulls off horror in ways no other game has. This is complete crap, this is a good first person shooter with a horror themed story, max payne style bullet time (Why is that in a horror game anyway?) and most of the game comprises you moving through tunnels, offices, and ships to find a cutscene thats supposed to be scary then repeat. You will not fight many, if any, monsters.
Do not buy this game expecting it to live up to its name, it simply does not. Call me desensitized, but even as a kid in 2005 I dont think this would have scared me, and it defenitely doesnt today.
Again, this is not meant to bash fear, this is meant to cut through all the crap put out by the fanatics that put this rather typical FPS game onto a pedestal along with other horror icons like silent hill, and the simple fact is this game doesnt even hold a candle to great horror games. A good shooter, horror story, and that's the package, end of story.
Buy for nostalgia, buy for a good shooter, do not buy for killing paranormal monsters or being scared, simply doesnt happen.

Note : Review only covers the single player
I liked Act of War, I thought it was a very interesting RTS, so when I saw that Act of Aggression was a successor to the series I got interested quick.
So as said in the note I have only played the single player campaign and messed around in a couple of skirmishes, therefor I did not really play the Reboot at all.
So core gameplay is very much like Act of War, you build up a base and you attack the enemy with a wonderful array of death and destruction. The POW system also makes a return giving you another rout for gaining resources. To elaborate on the POW system; When you kill an enemy unit there is a chance they will either be wounded in the case of infantry, or the crew will escape the vehicle in the case of vehicles. You are able to capture these with your infantry that give you an immediate cash bonus for capturing an enemy combatant, but if you own a prison building will be stored in the building that will begin generating resources for you. Each faction has alternate ways of collecting the main games 3 resources and most of these revolve around the prison system.
The resources system is also an interesting take, you manage 3 resources that are categorised by what tier they are used in. You have your base resource, Oil (or money I call it) which is used to build basic units and buildings and can be easily obtained via oil fields, capturing enemy prisoners and can be over time via your HQ or special buildings. The second resource in Aluminium. This is used to create mid tier units and structures as well as purchase the vast majority of upgrades for units. Aluminium can be mined from seperate nodes on the map, but if you are unable to claim, or the resources have run out, you have other options avalible to you to generate your own. For instance, the US faction can exchange a single POW for a nice chunk of aluminium while other factions can construct a building that gives them a slow but constant income of aluminium over time. The final resource is rare earth which is used in end game units and upgrades. This resource is usually very rare and is only ever obtained (and used) in small amounts. again like with aluminium each faction has a method of obtaining this resource without having to mine it.
In terms of the factions themselves you have a reflection of the 3 factions from act of war. The chimera faction is the mirror of Task Force Tallon and is a very addaptable force but lacks any focused hard hitting units like the other factions do. The US millitary is a robust force with easy to understand units that are good at what they do, but are not flexible when it comes to a changing situation. The final faction is the cartel, taking over from the consortium of Act of War, They specialise in stealth and high tech units that bring a good mix of hard hitting firepower and versitility in their unit roster, but usually at a high cost.
The campaign, from what I can tell does not seem to have a difficulty setting and this can become a bit of a problem as the game can become very punishing very quickly. A main theme in many of the campaign missions is the opposing forces ability to construct units regardless of their supply sittuation leading to many campaign missions quickly overwhelming a resource starved player. Another issue is with ballancing in some of the units in the game. While many units are well thought through and balanced there are some true crackers thats make your cringe at the sight of them. once such unit is what I saw labeled as a "Land Battleship" which is essentially an artillery unit with a rediculous range, firepower and armour that can go toe to toe with main battle tanks and simply sweep them away. While in skirmish this is not an issue due to this unit requiring a large amount of rare earth, in the campaign however the AI don't seem to care and send these badboys like nobodys buisiness at you.
an issue that seems to also plague the game is how unit will automaticly attack any enemy building that they are in range of. This makes it extremely irritating if you are intending to capture an enemy building and your nearby units are constantly pouring shells into it. There is a hold fire function that stops this however if the unit is attacked this breaks the hold fire mode, meaning once it has killed it's attacker it will go back to automaticly attacking the enemy building that you are attempting to capture.
Overall, I really liked this game. In a market that is made up of exclusivly multiplayer focused cut and paste RTS games with no thought put into anybody wanting a single player mode, This is a very fun and interesting game reminicant of the older command and conquer games and I would recommend this if you can pick it up at around the £10 - 15 mark (or about $20)
Seriously though, ♥♥♥♥ the final chimera mission. That♥♥♥♥♥♥is hard.

I'm so torn on this game. It's illustrated super well and the aesthetic is great. The combat is smooth and enjoyable. The music is nice. The main character is very well animated.
However, there are issues that seem almost contradictory to the positives about the game. For example:
-The combat is satisfying, and in that the counter/parry move is very satisfying to perform, but the timing for the counter is overly-strict and feels inconsistent with the enemy animations at times.
-Another thing is, while the main character is very well animated, every other character and almost every creature looks like their animations are from a flash game (this isn't really visible in still screenshots). They look like they're just very obvious limbs with hinges at the elbows etc. Even the main character's animations turn HORRIBLE in the very last scene of the game. There was also the weird jarring fact that one character (just one, and not the main character either. a rather minor one) had a 3D model when he speaks in dialogue. Just some random cel shaded guy while everyone else is 2D... There's also, again, one single enemy type only at the end that is 3D, again it's just an insignificant enemy.
-The art in the game is all very well drawn, but the character portraits in dialogue scenes are lower quality than the rest of the game's art, and also very obviously stretched bigger than they should be.
-The story is decent and some voices are well done, but others are terrible and I can't stand the main character's voice or the way he talks. That, mixed with the terrible animations of everyone but Dust, really takes me out of the story constantly.
-Secrets and puzzles are nice, but they seem overused here. I get that it's a metroid-vania, but you run past SO MANY things that you have to come back for later. It made it feel like padding out the game at some point.
-Frankly I can't say that I have sufficient technical knowledge about this kind of thing to have authority, but there also were a lot of things that bugged me with the balance of the game. Some enemies felt like they hit too hard/had too much health compared to the player. The further you get into the game the more healing items felt way off when it comes to price/healing ratio. I believe the best healing item I saw was for 300hp, when I had 1800... On top of that, 300hp is like 1-2 hits from the higher enemies. And I probably could have bought like 25 of those tops if I had spent ALL of my money. Then at the same time there are certain items that feel super OP toward the end. My magic abilities went from low-damage but useful for crowd control, to by far my strongest attacks VERY quickly and suddenly toward the end. My "Fidget" stat went from around 250 to over 3800 in just the last couple hours of the game from some new items I got. And none of those items were things I had to grind for, while at the same time the last armor piece I saw was just an incremental upgrade from the previous one, but I would have had to grind just to get the materials to forge it. The whole item system seems off balance. I also never needed the vast majority of the materials and blueprints I picked up.
Overall, I wish I could give it an "indifferent" rather than up or down. If you can look past those things, I'd recommend it, however I personally felt like I was having to force myself to keep going several times. I honestly can't even decide if I would say I enjoyed the game or not overall. It's just so jarring to have some aspects be really well done, but at the same time have those same aspects be done so poorly at the same time in other areas (e.g. animations, art, etc). Based on the fact that I don't think I would have played it if I had known how I'd feel about all these things from the start, I think I'm going to have to give it a pass.

ABZÛ, conceived (among others) by the people who brought us Journey, is absolutely breathtaking. There is just something fascinating and captivating about the sprawling life hidden from our sight beneath the surface of the ocean; and this game lets you experience it first hand, in all of its incomparable and often even indescribable beauty. ABZÛ succeeds in bringing about a sense of harmony, serenity and tranquility; all rare feelings rare when playing a videogame. These uncommon emotions are then even further amplified by the genious work of Austin Wintory who managed to create and unforgettable soundtrack adapting to your behaviour and progressing along with your discoveries, thus crwning the overall contemplative ambience. And yet, ABZÛ brings more to the table than a simple opportunity to relax (and even meditate) while observing the wonders of nature: for if you pay attention and start observing the structures occasionally surrounding you during your explorations of the ocean bed, it may even provide a brilliant cautionary tale.
TO SUM UP: Whatever your opinion of indie games is, you should think about getting ABZÛ. Seriously. Buy it. Install it. Play it. Experience it. Question it. Question everything. Think about it. Then play it again; and then think some more.

After Max Payne combined Hong Kong Action with noir - an odd combo, but one that worked - another developer tried their hand at a Hong Kong Action hybrid. This time with an even stranger genre: horror.  It works, but the spooks are more of the themepark variety. You hallucinate, see some creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥ move on. Only on a few occasions are you forced to shoot your gun at something coming towards you, which isn't much of a challenge. But it's nice to have an atmospheric game where you're not crapping your pants because you're being chased by some hellish monster or a damn xenomorph. You're just haunted by a little girl who appears to spook you when you go around corners then vanishes. It's managable for wimps like me.
It's the slow-mo bullet-time FPS action where the real threat is at, and it's great. A lot has been said about the FEAR AI, which is damn good, always on the move, outflanking you, sometimes sneakily hiding in corners. I just feel that most of the claustrophobic environments, with the exception of some ingeniously designed office spaces that loop in on eachother, don't really bring the most out of the AI. The warehouses and underground secret labs do little to test the AIs on their ability to move their way around to murder you. Looks like most of the budget went to the middle of the game, where you're moving your way up an office skyscraper, featuring the best level design, in terms of gameplay as well as aesthetics. The rest of the levels pale in comparison.
Still, give this game a shot if you want John Woo mixed with Japanese horror. It's visceral action with great gamefeel, great gore, environmental damage as well as exaggerated physics and particle effects. Still looks pretty good despite being a decade old by now.

I was always a fan of FF4, back in the SNES days. When they made this sequel to it, albeit with the modern 3D graphic polygon style, I felt it was worth the price. Well...
I hate to say it, but this game isn't much fun and it isn't designed any better than someone's starter game on RPGmaker. The paths are linear, recycled, and it's mainly just a rehash of just about everything from FF4, from the plot to the dungeons.
Notably, the fight balance is just awful. You get pre-designed teams that consist of FF4 characters and relatively disinteresting new characters, but the problem comes down to it that the team compositions just stink. For example, the twins from FF4, Palom and Porom, each get their own story episode in this. And apparently they thought it was a great idea to pair mages with other mages, leaving your team in these annoying glass cannon scenarious where lucky hits basically end your adventure and there's nothing you can do but reload and hope it doesn't happen again. And I'm not talking about boss fights, but basic encounters. The enemy's speed for turns is this game is ridiculous. I notice they get about 1.5 to 2 attack actions for every one of mine. Why do basic enemies need to be this quick? Couple this with the fact you almost never have full groups (FF4's combat system worked in that everyone was different and it was almost always a 5 man group) and you're basically playing long dull scenarios with a broken party design.
Crummy battle system aside, the game is just boring. Outside of the team up attacks of the band system, this is just cobbled together left overs of what was a better first title. It doesn't even do FF4 lore any justice. Rydia gets her summon spells removed by the plot so she's just a generic black mage. Porom's story is more about the people around her, than much about herself. And the best one... they turned the dwarf king's daughter into a ganguro girl who doesn't look anything like her people or anyone else in the world. Huh?? These design decisions are nonsensical.
This is a really weak entry in the FF series and it doesn't work any front. The tight forced perspective and the ugly polygon graphics don't do it any favors either. You can easily find better indie RPGs for five dollars or less on here. This painfully generic title has nothing going for it beyond the FF brand slapped onto it. It's a lazy cash grab game that should be avoided and nothing more.

I'd like to consider myself something of a critic in regards to JRPGs, as far too many have stereotypically bland plots, environments, and characters. If you can't tell it apart from its predecessors in regards to gameplay, it's not worth a good review, or any comment for that matter. That's why I had to stick up for this one, especially since FF4, this game's prequel, was markedly less interesting.
For one, the episodic nature of the game (not in the present-day sense of splitting up games needlessly into multiple cashgrabby installments) gives the story surprising depth. Each character is cast as a protagonist in their own 'tale', left to interpret and respond to the overall game's events differently. They have their own strengths, challenges, and settings that make adapting enjoyably difficult. And to make it all worthwhile, in the endgame you can reselect your favorite combinations to take on the final struggles.
The combat system saw a subtle revamp that considerably smoothed gameplay compared to FF4. The newgame+ feature was also buffed enough to give the game actual replay value, and for once you got the refreshing feeling that nothing was truly missable.
It's definitely worth at least a single playthrough anyway, and experience with the first game is not required as many of the main plot points relevant to After Years are covered in cutscenes.

Hardcore tactics game - not recommended for players looking for a more casual experience (e.g. the newer XCOM games). Micromanagement of units is heavy, down to posture and walking speed, but the game is a real-time with pause for giving orders one, so it is manageable.
This game shares its engine with 7.62 High Caliber; if you haven't played that game before, I'll just say that it's like the Silent Storm games but slightly more complex on one side but the environments aren't as destructable as in Silent Storm.
The story, as far as I could grasp it (from what I played plus some let's plays and what little I read about the novel) is set on an alternate 1990s where the USSR splits and falls into absolute chaos (as opposed to the partial chaos that happened there in the 90s) and a multinational force (led by the US) steps in as peacekeepers but ultimately stay as occupants. The protagonist is a guy trying to hoard supplies and survive, and you make a few pals along the way and fortify your apartment block.
Pros:
-A believable story about societal collapse where you don't try to save the world - just you, your family and friends.
-Hardcore tactics! Luck doesn't matter as much as proper tactics.
-You get to learn a bit of Russian, since it's got Russian voiceovers w/English subtitles. Beware that some of the swearing is minced (e.g., "Blin!" instead of "♥♥♥♥♥!").
-Graphics are nice for its time and scope.
Cons:
-Camera angles can be a bit of a pain at times, especially when you walk into buildings (moreso in multi-storey buildings).
-Controls are a bit complex - if you only play every now and then, you may want to revisit the tutorial (which is rather lengthy and deadlier than usual as far as tutorials go).

This game was a surprise, havent heard of it before (traded another game for this one) and I though it was awesome.
This game is a perfect mix of a book and game. While the narrative sets the mood and lets you use you imagination the gameplay illustrates the story better and adds an interactive part with actual skill and planning involved
Honestly, this is how gaming visual novels should be done, not just the lazy "make one choice now" that almost all anime visual novels do (there are few exceptions that actually do have an RPG or strategy element), or the tell tale style (they are awesome at story telling, but its more of an interactive movie than a game really).
But it does have some weaknesses, story does not change too much from your choises, so you will likely do only one gameplay unless you are a completionist. At some points it can feel a bit grindy if you are trying to max your skills or items.
There is certain unfairness when you start the game with no previous experience, as it makes you choose the skils to use during the full game, without you knowing how effective they are and selecting your stongest stat (int, vit or dex) without knowing which fits you best, this could lead to you having a very unbalanced char without noticing and being forced to restart the game or lowering the difficulty since you keep losing the same battle over and over again without being able to go back to the map to be a bit more prepared for it.
Also, keep in mind that the "Lone Wolf" series is a gaming fantasy novel with focus on teenage males, with the main idea being that the reader puts himself in the role of the main character.  And as expected the main character is this overpowered, chick magnet, super smart, knows how to do everything, angsty, cant do no wrong, legendary race hero so... yeah some reading parts are a bit cringey as you can imagine, specially the ones where he interacts with the female lead.
Still, great game, would love to see more games of the same style or a sequel to this.

I desperately want to change my review to "Recommend," but in its current state (7/10/2016, ver. 1.2.1) Stellaris is one gigantic cocktease of a 4x game. I have played through the game four times, but cannot bring myself to continue the most recent playthrough.
Quite simply, the time required to play a single game is not proportionate with how basic a lot of the systems are: from combat to colonization to diplomacy to trade to research, everything feels like a placeholder for a more complex version of itself. If I'm going to sink 20+ hours into a single playthrough, I should be discovering and struggling with new things the whole way through, but once I reach the midgame the game basically plays itself: build auto-designed battleships, colonize my planets, divide into sectors, upgrade my buildings, declare war to slowly chew away at my neighbors, and eventually kill the endgame menace (which is not guaranteed to show up). The game is exciting at the beginning but never expands its mechanics to match its scale.
Maybe Paradox will release patches/DLC to flesh out all of these systems, but as it is the game ends up playing in a very straightforward manner that is disappointing given the scope. For example, Sins of the Solar Empire had a more engaging lategame due to multiple win cons and competitive enemies. As it is, even playing Stellaris as a sandbox is boring because of bland enemy interactions (trade or declare war, that's about it).
As it is, I'll fire it up again when it receives a major patch/DLC, or when a full-conversion 40k mod exists, at which point I'll re-evaluate my review. Until then, I would recommend that people wait on this game.

There are tons of options for how to play this game. Each level has different threads to follow, and is playable in different ways. For example, you can choose to pursue methods of stealth or use brute force. Your behavior is noted by other characters and changes how you interact with them. Sometimes your actions affect their fates as well. But unlike other games of this vein, it's hard to tell, even after consequences have occurred, which choice was the "morally right" choice. You just make a choice and have to live with it, and follow through until the end of the game. You'll be asking yourself what the designers made to be the "right" and "wrong" choice, but in the end you have to choose who you want to be and act accordingly. In that way, Deus Ex is more true to life than many other games. Aside from that, it's just a lot of fun. It's a classic for a reason-- I most definitely recommend it!

Quick Summary: Zeno Clash is built on the Half Life 2 Source engine, so that should give you an idea what to expect in terms of graphics and hardware requirements. However in gameplay and art style the games are completely different. I gave Zeno Clash a try because my video card crapped out a while back and I wanted to try something less hardware intensive while I waited for a replacement. It was a fun game, but it’s definitely not for everyone.
First off, note that the world of Zeno Clash is weird and alien while seeming like it could possibly be a post-apocalyptic Earth (it’s not). The “people” speak English but mix in strange words and phrases like it was an adaptation of a novel. Many citizens of this world are also a mix, of human and animal. Some of the people you’ll encounter are fully human while others look like bird men, elephant men, or just completely original beasts. The environment is sort of stone age with some odd guns/crossbows/magic thrown in (fish guns?). You play a human looking dude named Ghat who for some reason is being chased down by his former brothers and sisters. You and your one friend in the world are on a quest to bring justice to the children of Father/Mother (the main antagonist) even as these children fight you every step of the way.
While I mentioned guns earlier, the game is mostly melee fighting, and you’ll need to get comfortable dodging and blocking blows from enemies, sometimes simultaneously from different sides.  The guns are mostly weak pea shooters but can be helpful if you get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off from trading punches with a bunch of cheaters. Unlike kung-fu movies, these guys like to all attack at the same time. There is some variety in enemy types, but they’re mostly the same fighting style with character appearances. It’s the really big dudes that you need to watch out for.
Pros:
+Weird story that keeps you thinking. You’ll probably spend a bunch of the time trying to figure out what’s going on, and what happened leading to Ghat’s predicament.
+The melee fighting system is fun, though challenging since you’re playing in First Person Shooter perspective and can only really concentrate on one guy at a time.
Cons:
-The graphics are rather dated, since the game is pretty old
-There’s no “easy mode” for people who just want to experience the story. The game’s difficulty can be brutal for new players at certain point. The challenge levels seem more frustrating than they’re worth, especially when you’re forced to fight a whole group at once, and your “target lock” messes with your repositioning efforts.
Overall, if you’ve run out of games to play or just want to try something weird, you can do a lot worse than Zeno Clash.

I have like/hate relationship with this game, resulting in positive, but very cautious recommendation.
Ghost 1.0 feels very ambitious in many places, which I commend and support wholehearthly, but there are some blind spots that show up very often in design, story, art and gameplay, ultimately making the game take a serious hit.
Story is really a weakest part of the game. It's not the worst story ever, since main characters are likeable, but the all other elements seem to be duct taped. Pacing is schizophrenic, bombarding you with cutscenes with (reasonably good) exposition early on, after which everything is put into halt. Aside from the main "twist" there is like to no intersting plot moments at all, making whole supporting cast insignificant and dull. Humor fails flat most of the time, with lots of unfitting referential humor and jokes that overstate their welcome. I recall that I only laughed once in the game from a clever joke. Whole main trio's voice acting is decent, with any other character sounding extremely unprofessional.
The base gameplay consist of you exploring the space station and trashing robots with various weapons. Exploration is fine, but the most hidden secrets use the "souls" system. It is sometimes completely idiotic, requiring you to do seemingly random task, without telling you exactly what to do. Combat is also sound, with good gamepad controls and satisfying shooting, but the overreliance on kill-rooms in form of alarms shows how the design is ultimately a little bit too shallow to flesh out interesting set pieces and level designs. Whenever game tries to mix things up with the gameplay, it falls short throwing tedious, disguised puzzles as an answer. In result, both Labs and Rescue Mission levels are really tiring and not as good as the rest of the game.
I must give to the devs that they got in some interesting innovation in form of two completely different game modes. They change gameplay structure significantly, resulting in game's high replay value and a reason the play it at least twice. The Classic Mode looks like Metroidvania, but it only takes an open-ended level structure as a base. For example, there are no gamechanging upgrades that open new areas. You still get improvements for your robot and while they are mostly useful, they don't change the style of play that much. Survival mode is the real innovation, mixing the classic formula mentioned above with upgrade acquisition in vain of Binding of Issac or Risk of Rain. While story advances regardless of your skill and deaths, more you stay alive, then more difficult the game becomes and more ridiculously powerful your character gets. Die and you reset the difficulty to level 1 and lose most upgrades. Great idea and great execution.
Art and music is good, but I'm ultimately disappointed with it. Locals and areas become really stale after a while with lack of variety. Music score seems to have some really nice ideas here and there, but they aren't really realized enough, leaving some seemingly good tunes not as engaging or memorable as they were planned to be.
The soundtrack really mimics the state of the whole game. It's a decent title, with effort put into it, but something doesn't really click here. I would be really happy to ignore many of the title's faults, like in many other games I reviewed very positively. However, in the comparison, the core gameplay and structure isn't really consistently good enough to make me turn a blind eye on the faults. Then the game was at its best, I couldn't stop playing it, but the moment something slipped, the positivity started to fade.
I ultimately give it a positive recommendation, because good parts of Ghost 1.0 are still there and you really get a bank for your buck content wise. It's really shame that this content isn't really polished enough to be really outstanding.

If you enjoyed Final Fantasy 4, you'll probably get a nice nostalgia high from playing through this "sequel."  The music is preserved beautifully, and the feeling of the original seeps through. The graphics have been updated, and follow the similar design of the other remakes that appeared on the 3ds and PC ports.
The playthrough is episodic, and provides a very quick journey through each of the characters realms.  Even the characters seems to retain the sense of humor they had from the first game, while introducing new children and followers that serve as the protagonists in the new game.
The game suffers from a few flaws on the PC, notably controller issues which saw my cursor scrolling uncontrollably. The refresh rate of the graphics appears very low when played in Big Picture, though its not nearly as noticeable on the smaller screens.  The interface is classic, which can also be read as "cumbersome."  The dungeons appear to be traversed quickly, but it could have always been that way and I'm not remembering correctly.
Overral, I am enjoying the game, but a lot of that is due to having Final Fantasy 4 as my favorite of the series.

This game really makes me wish for some sort of a Neutral Rating on Steam reviews. It's not great, but it's not terrible either. I ultimately decided to give it a positive rating because I want players to focus on the good (which it has loads of) and not the bad (just a few things). Ultimately, it's Steam. If a game has questionable ratings/reviews that make you hold off on taking the plunge and purchasing the game, just wait for a sale. They happen pretty often. With that said, let's move on!
Final Fantasy IV: The After Years is a continuation/sequel to Final Fantasy IV that was originally released as a downloadable title for the Nintendo Wii. Since then it's had a few other releases on various platforms. Taking place 17 years after the events of Final Fantasy IV, it's a great sequel, although it has some major pacing issues. The majority of the game feels like a huge slog, and it really takes a lot of patience to get through. However, once you make it to the last couple of chapters (called Tales), the story payout is huge and the game really starts to shine.
==========
This game is much the same as FFIV, however it is episodic. Not episodic like TellTale Games titles, but more like it plays out in chapters. Each chapter (Tale) centers on a different character and the other characters they join up with, and in the very last Tale they all unite into one huge group that you are able to choose from to tackle the last sections of the game. The biggest draw of this game is the continuation of the story from IV and how each of the original characters has changed and moved on. Some of them have had children, and other characters that crop up are completely new.
The After Years utilizes the same battle system as IV, and it works wonderfully. Don't fix what isn't broke, right? Aside from the pacing issue I mentioned, my only other problem with The After Years is that it's missing a sizeable amount of content from previous versions. Final Fantasy IV Complete for the PSP (includes FF4, FF4 Interlude, and FF4: The After Years) had Challenge Dungeons at the end of EVERY Tale, and over a dozen extra cameo bosses in the final dungeon of the last Tale. While the Challenge Dungeons weren't too too much, and just served as a more efficient way to level your characters in preparation for the last Tale, the extra cameo bosses are a huge loss. The fights featured bosses from other entries in the series, such as the 4 fiends from FF1 (Lich, Tiamat, Marilith, and Kraken), and these fights were a lot of fun. They could probably throw up a patch to add these if they really wanted to, or even add them as DLC, but it's most likely not going to happen.
Another complaint is that most of the game is going through the same areas found in FFIV multiple times. And while this is true, they are all tied into the story to an extent. Each time you run through them with a different set of characters you'll run into different events (as well as refilled and different treasures!!).
A new feature The After Years utilizes is the Moon Phase System. The Moon has 4 distinct phases, and each phase affects certain abilities directly by changing their attack power or effectiveness...which can drastically alter the difficulty of battles. Some rare monsters also only appear during certain Moon phases.
==========
Featuring the same 3D graphics as FFIV (they both use the same engine), The After Years looks just as good as its predecessor. This is an upgrade from the 2D graphics the PSP version featured. The new characters that were added look just as good as the original characters as well.
==========
Frequent readers of mine have probably figured out that I love video game music, and that I like pointing out particularly good tracks in a game's soundtrack. The After Years has one particular track that stands out to me thats used in particular battles against a certain foe.
Amazing. Most of the game reuses tracks from FFIV, but it adds a few new tracks that were composed by Junya Nakano. While different from Uematsu, Nakano has managed to pump out a few memorable tracks that really stand out and fit the game very well. The track above, in particular, manages to capture the wrongness and desperation of the situations it plays in PERFECTLY, and I cannot praise him enough for that.
==========
The After Years runs on the same engine as FFIV, and as such runs more or less the same. FPS isn't a huge issue for an older classic game like this, and I did not encounter any game-breaking bugs or glitches. I played with a controller the whole time and found it very comfortable. Not much to say here.
==========
One of the extremely rare sequels in the franchise, Final Fantasy IV: The After Years delivers a great continuation to a beloved story, although it does suffer from a couple of glaring problems with the gameplay itself. Despite this, fans will undoubtedly find something here to enjoy even if it takes some work and a lot of patience to reach. If you have never played The After Years before but have played FFIV and would like to see what happened to the beloved characters, this would be a great version to try out. If you've played or already own the PSP FFIV collection...stick with that one.

This is a review of the game when I reached Act 2 Chapter 2, so this review is my initial impression of the game. Obviously it can change, but I figured I'd do a first-impressions review because this game strikes me as a journey-not-the-destination type of game. I made this review short because this game is very straight forward and there's nothing special to talk about.
Oh boy, this is one flawed gem of a game. What's that? I'm recommending it? Yeah, a game can even be severely flawed and still worth a shot. So, this game is a video-game adaption of a series of adventure game books(similar to the CYOA style books that were very popular in the 80s/90s, although I think this series is exactly that) by Joe Dever, who presumably also helped make the game. I am not and have never been hugely into books as a favourite pass time but adventure books have always intrigued me, so to see a game that effectively plays like reading a book with huge interactivity(for example, the combat) is nice. If you don't want to read my whole review, the gist is that it's a very decent game so far but the combat is very flawed, specifically in RNG aspects.
First off, the story. The story is just as you'd expect from a adventure-book-turned-video-game. I'd actually put it on the same shelf as The Witcher in terms of depth, specifically in the form of its codex and its writing (it is, after all, played like a book). As for the main character? Well, he really strikes me as a "Geralt-esque" character, is how I would describe him. So, your character, who is the last of his kind due to a obligatory massacre, goes to his fiefdom of which he is the lord of to find that it has been besieged and he has to save the day. There's a lot more to it than that but I'm not going to spoil anything. Tthe story may seem pretty bland but I can tell you that the story goes very slowly and isn't rushed at all, which means it has a lot of detail and work put into it.
The graphics are actually pretty good, and on my potato-computer it runs amazingly with most settings on, albeit in windowed mode. The character model itself is very well done and so are the models for the enemies. The book pages are  very well done as well and actually immersed me quite a few times, to the point that I just wanted to read the book pages and that's it. The only thing I can complain about is the lighting on some backgrounds interferes with certain QTE(explained later) icons.
The character-creation is pretty neat. You can choose your combat style (sword, axe, and mace) as well as your dominant stat (Strength, intelligence, or dexterity). You can also choose three(3) skills that are both usable in combat(buffs) and as options when making a decision in dialogue. For example, a group of enemies are caught taking a pee-break. You can use your dexterity to sneak around and shoot an arrow through their brains, or you can use your mind-over-matter ability and throw an object at them. Fun! Certain options give certain benefits, but they can also cause harm. For example, you can choose to ram open a door in one choice and it results in two out of three enemies being stunned in the following battle but in another scenario... Let's just say being brutish isn't always the best choice. There is no levelling either, persay. Your stats improve ever chapter in an act depending on the actions you performed, so if you want a lot of strength, presumably you would work towards making strength-based choices, but this also means you don't *have to* make certain actions. You can spice it up, especially since all of the stats are important (and improve your Kai energy requires you to make Kai choices, so spice it up a bit!). I believe the combat style(or your currently equiped weapon(s), since you can duel wield) that you choose also changes the attack abilities available to you.
Gameplay is a bit odd, in my opinion. Cut this short, there's several parts to the gameplay : Reading the book/story progression, turn-based combat that relies on QTE(mouse or keyboard options available) actions to determine if you hit or dodge etc, and a lock-picking minigame that is pretty much the bethesda format. There may be more but those are the ones introduced up to Act 2 so far. The book-reading segments are pretty much your book-reading segments, story progression. These segments also include making certain choices (e.g., using a skill or attribute to deal with a situation, either benefiting you or stabbing you in the back) which, suprisingly, actually feel like they matter because... They do. The lock-picking segment is *literally* the popular bethesda lockpicking. I don't even know if it originated from them, but that's what it's associated with. You move the lockpick around, see if you can force the lock, adjust if needed, and voila. Anyways, the turn-based combat is actually where this game falls quite a bit. I'm not going to go into detail but the entirety of the combat is QTE. Want to use your combat attack on this enemy? Better hit all three QTES! Want to parry this attack? QTE! Now, I'm actually misleading you quite a bit. The part that makes this *UNBEARABLE* is that your chance to hit/dodge is a %. Yes, it's a percentage. You can literally SEE this as your dodge value is a %. What does this mean? It means that to make the game "balanced", you have random chance, aka RNG, alongside you on your journey to decided whether not you're a brain-dead zombie or an acrobatic lightning bolt. Let's get one thing straight - RNG is artificial difficulty. It's not fair in any sense unless it's a strict 50-50 chance and it doesn't leave the results up to the player and their skill. You are absolutely at the mercy of chance, and most of the time the chance isn't even 50-50 but if you've ever taken a data-management course, you'd know that it's never garunteed to be a strict 10/20 hits if you have a 50% to hit. That's only the *chance* to hit, not the number of times you will hit. Now, this also applies to the enemies in that you can randomly miss *AND* randomly be countered by the enemies. It's such an infuriating design choice that really makes most of the combat complete chance. I did the same battle THREE(3) times and the first two times was me getting countered constantly and rarely ever dodging but on the third try, I was dodging like crazy and getting hit after hit in, and I didn't feel accomplished at all. I felt cheated. What makes it worse is that with a shield activated, you can go into a defense stance that lasts until your turn ends, but it has a cooldown meaning you only get a short break from the RNG. It's actually why I like action-RPGs more than anything else because skill is actually a factor in those. Aside from that rant, there are buffs you can cast which depend on your initally chosen skills and then there's your magic which you cast via your Sommerswerd(your magic claymore, basically). Finally, you can have ranged weapons which work amazingly well as end-of-turn weapons in that the only thing required to use them is turn time and the ammo(examples of such are throwing daggers and crossbow bolts). All of this is severely held back by the how often enemies tend to attack (more than you overall) and how much damage they are able to deal(especially a specifically heavy-infantry-type enemy later on) and of course the RNG. That's really the gist of how the combat works and it's VERY flawed, to say the least, but it also has a lot of potential.
So... That's my first-impression review of this game. I'm not going to quit it, mostly because I'm too enthralled by the writing and the story but the combat - OH LORDY, THE COMBAT. It's horrible. I just cannot and will not EVER praise RNG or accept it as good design. Get it on sale and it's a decent buy.
Feedback is wanted! I want to get better at writing reviews.
TL;DR - Gist is that it's a very decent game so far but the combat is VER flawed, specifically in RNG amd QTE aspects.

This game runs likes it has never been looked at by a Quality Assurance department. It's just a mess. Menus lag and stutter randomly, it's unstable as all hell and crashes at the slightest provocation, and even the installation process is buggered.
But who cares right? We're all RTS players here. We only care about gameplay.
And the gameplay is ok. The bases take up most of your screen around midgame, farming resources is simple as can be, moving troops is kinda a pain because they handle and move like garbage, but fights have a lot of weight to them.
Theres depth (some) where you can capture enemy soliders, and your tanks and vehicles will take damage from running over things like cars, oil tanks, etc. Pathfinding is nice, since vehicles will use roads naturally - and infantry are fast enough to not be vehicle fast but still respectably speedy. Upgrades feel meaningful.
Its just not good though.
The design may be pretty, the look and feel is ok, but the play is garbage. You'll spend 20 minutes building up a reasonable fighting force, only to have most of it die in a 2 second skirmish. Units die incredibly fast, since every weapon hits hard and most heavily armored tanks can only take 4 hits tops. Aircraft zip in and out of the battlefield, so you can't really rely on them to be a sustained prescence. They also die and kill fast too, so aircraft battles are underwhelming.
Movement around the map is terrible as well. The maps all feel just too small, but at the same time getting troops anywhere in something resembling a formation is a pain. And it just runs HORRIBLY. I'm talking missing mouse clicks every 2 seconds. I'm talking frequent unexplainable crashes. Things of that nature.
Its just not good. And it runs like absolute rubbish. Seriously, who in their right mind thought this was a finished game?

I got this game in a bundle awhile back and just recently got around to playing it.
This is a first person fighting game with a unique art style. Another reviewer referred to it as "Stonepunk", and I feel that is an appropriate description.
The first part of the game was interesting with the blend of first person fighting and gunplay, but by the end of the game I was more than ready to be done with it. The story and characters are mediocre at best, and the game is quite short. The combat, which starts out relatively fun, degenerates into a repetitive slugfest with you constantly getting overwhelmed by more enemies than you can keep track of (including snipers) and it simply ends up being not fun by the end.
On top of that, the combat controls were glitchy and didn't always register, and there's some major issues with enemies being invincible during most animations and your character getting stuck in a corner and taking a ton of damage. The icing on the cake is the baffling control decision to have the block/dodge key also throw your weapon, which makes fights with certain types of enemies far more difficult/annoying than they should be since the only way to harm them is with a melee weapon, but they almost always block your attacks if you're in front of them. You basically have to sprint in a circle around them (and they still hit you half the time from angles you wouldn't expect, and do a ton of damage) when you should be able to dodge and counterattack (they can do it to you, why can't you return the favor?).
Overall, when this game works, it's a satisfying first person brawler, but when it doesn't it is one of the most frustrating and annoying games I've played in awhile. While not a completely terrible game, it has enough issues and little enough content (you fight against the same dozen or so characters over and over again in the course of the game) that I can't really recommend it unless you got it for next to nothing in a bundle like I did.

1) "It's short."
Well, yes. Yes, it is.
2) "You lose all your money when you die!"
Yes you do. It's literally the ONLY penalty for dying in classic mode. You can farm for more money. This was a necessary design to keep things lively.
3) "The controls are..."
Nope. They're awesome. And customizable. Maybe there used to be some problems but if so, they've been fixed. Brings me to...
4) "The developers are..."
Lemme just stop you right there: the developer is AWESOME. Franfistro (did I spell that right?) has kept on the pulse of these threads and provided several modifications/tweaks as requested by the players. A "skip rescue mission" option was even added for those who didn't like that part of the game. So really can't complain there. I only hope they'll add a new game + option because I want to keep playing until my fingers bleed.
5) "The game's too easy/it's too hard..."
You people are never happy. It isn't Dark Souls, and it isn't solitaire, alright? If anything it's Dex. Which is fine because I freaking LOVE Dex.
It's just plain fun.

Having bought a steam controller recently, I decided to revisit this old favourite and refresh my memory of the experience.
And it's just as good as it always was.
The story is incredibly well written. Despite knowing how it ends, I still choked up a little at the final cutscene. Not only that, but all characters are entertaining in their own ways. Fidget is one of the best sidekicks I've had while playing a game.
The visuals are still as beautiful as they were before. Everything is vididly detailed and the weather effects helps complete the feeling of the world you're playing being a living, breathing thing. The levels are built intricately, with each puzzle made all the more  satisfying when you finally solve it. In true Metroidvania style, you'll need to come back to certain sections later once you have the neccesary ability.
Combat flows fluently and, when done well enough and with plenty of enemies, can result in massive, satisfying combos. Add in Fidget's ability and you'll be dealling some major damage.
The music is very fitting no matter the situation or environment. Whether you're making your way through darkened caverns or you're in the thick of a large-scale battle, it always fits.
Finally, the controls. Having played both with the keyboard and a steam controller, I'd definitely recommend the controller. That way, you're not getting your hands mixed up during combat.
Overall;
This is hands down one of the best Metroidvania games you will find on Steam. If you want to get into this genre, play this game first as an impressive example of what lays in store.
TL;DR
This game is awesome. Get it.

The official Sequel to the classic Final Fantasy IV (1991) set 17 years after the events in the original game. Originally released on the wii in episodic format. You would play each part or "tale" following one of the many characters, all of which follow the same story leading to a climax in which everyone will reunite to save the world yet again.
The release on ios & steam was tossed on the cutting board and sadly it loses most of it's charm in the process. Challenge dungeons that ended each tale were removed from this version. Which leaves you very underdeveloped and geared by the time you reach the final chapter. In episodic format they encouraged you to farm until the next tale was released to the public. But instead of adding a fix they just decided to cut them from this version.
The second huge disappointment from the steam release is after playing nearly 30 hours through the 9 character tales. You enter the final stages of the game, In which if you have watched any trailers for the game you will see the many many bosses and optional bosses that the game offered you to challenge. In the original release you could fight 12-15 optional bosses in the final dungeons. Which encouraged you to level your party to max level. Some of those included past final fantasy bosses such as Lich (FF1) Kraken (FF1) even Ultima weapon (FF6). All of these have been removed from the game, leaving the final dungeon quite barren.
A good handful of achievements from this game are also luck based and require you to literally farm for potentially hundreds of hours for items that are obsolete and not necessary since the optional content was all removed.
So even after all that, I leave the game with a positive review only because of the nostalgic strings it pulls, I enjoyed my playthough. But if you want to experience the game in it's entirety I suggest you purchase a copy of Final Fantasy IV The Complete Collection on PSP or Vita.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers here to share my thoughts on F.E.A.R by Monolith Productions and Sierra Entertainment. I didn’t receive a copy of this game for review this time around. I purchased a boxed copy and then a digital copy ages ago and I wanted to write this review after completing the game.
FEAR was originally released on PC on October 18, 2005 with Playstation 3 and Xbox 360 versions arriving on October 31, 2006 (360) and April 24, 2007 (PS3). For today’s review we’re covering the PC release. The game originally released on CD-Roms (The version I own) but a DVD (Director’s Cut) version was later released which included many bonus features including a Dark Horse comic book, a series of Live Action Vignettes, and a Making of FEAR/Developer’s Commentary documentaries.
In the commentary video Producer Chris Hewitt revealed that there was an entire car chase level which they had worked on for 2 months before removing from the game because it didn’t come out right. He also mentions that there were originally 2 villains; Fettel and Conrad Krieg. The two of them were eventually combined into one enemy with Fettel wearing Krieg’s jacket.
There were two expansion packs titled Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate but these were developed by TimeGate Studios and released on October 24, 2006 and November 2007 respectively. There were also two sequels to the game; FEAR 2: Project Origin and FEAR 3. The game also originally released with multiplayer as well but has since been shut down due to Gamespy’s closure in 2012.
Now that our history lesson is over we can begin talking about the game itself!
FEAR is a psychological, horror, first-person shooter that puts you in control of a new member of the First Encounter Assault and Recon unit that specializes in dealing with supernatural threats. Your mission is to locate a man named Paxton Fettel and kill him at any cost. Over the course of the game you’ll travel to various locations around the city in search of Fettel and to uncover what’s going on. Eventually you begin learning about a research program called Project Origin and it’s none too pretty.
One of my favorite parts of this game is easily the gunplay - which is fast, fluid and a ton of fun. Our unnamed hero has the ability to slow down time (which is really just moving faster than people can register) to take down enemies and escape hairy situations. The game features various types of weapons which are based on real world weapons like assault Rifles and shotguns. There’re also some unique weapons too including one that shoots railway spikes and another that fires particle beams. You can also choose to go full on melee if you so choose and you can unleash some pretty devastating punches and kicks.
Another thing I really enjoyed about the game is the enemy AI which is incredibly smart so long as you’re not playing on easy difficulty. Enemies will hide behind cover, work with their teammates and will often try to flank you in order to kill you. They also have superb melee skills and if they get close to you they’ll unleash the hurt. They’ll also try to use grenades to flush you out from cover as well. The game can get pretty intense.
The game’s graphics have held up incredibly well over the years as well. It still has some absolutely gorgeous lighting/shadowing and the particle effects from ricocheting bullets are still incredibly awesome. Bullets leave deep holes in walls which also increases immersion and shows the destructive power of the weapons.  The sound effects hold up pretty well as well and lends to the superb atmosphere.
The horror elements didn’t work on me simply because I don’t find games scary, but there was a pretty good balance between the horror and action. There was also one section of the game that was lacking in horror elements but the rest of it was quite good.
Overall, FEAR has been an incredibly fun experience and one I gladly recommend if you haven’t played it yet. It’s not a very long game by any means (I beat it in 6 hours) but it has some excellent gunplay, a great balance between horror/action and it’s quite gorgeous to boot.
Thanks a lot for taking the time to watch my video and read my review folks. I’d greatly appreciate if you could give them both a share or like. Also, be sure to subscribe to my channel for future videos!
Happy gaming folks! - Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) out!

I have some pretty mixed emotions about this game. On one hand I consider it to be one of the best scifi themed 4x grand strategy games ever made. On the other hand the sheer amount of bugs and crashes I have experiencd within the last two weeks have been unreal. Most of the time I cant even get the game to start without having serious portions of the game either missing or looking half finalized and grainy. When I can get it to play correctly, I have experienced 16 hard crashes, five of those times where the game would completely restart my computer, and countless other minor bugs that I have seen in the game. As I said this is a pretty damn good game when everything is working correctly. For me however it has only worked correctly 1/4 of the times I have logged into play. This has all been further agitated by the release of 1.2. Paradox get to working on fixing this because as of now I feel I have waisted money on this game. Much optimization and work is still needed. For now dont waste your money, wait until winter for them to get some serious updates posted.
Update: Okay so I found the reason for all of the Crap I experienced when I first bought the game. It is a graphics option called Multi-Sampling. Unless you are running this game on a top line rig with specs to rival a supercomputer then set the level to 0 or else you will probably experience what I experienced before I scoured the internet for this knowledge. Now that I have finally been able to play through two full games without any bugs or crashes I can say I agree with the majority of players in saying that middle to late game are boring as hell. You will sit there micromanaging for Decades in game time until one of the three crisises occur to where you shall soon be bum rushed unless your fleet has a power level in the higher tens of thousands . Diplomacy is lackluster as you can barely form aliances (amongst other things) with other species and when you do it really has no impact on interstellar politics. I would recomend this game only to those who can stand long periods of micromanaging without wanting to throw things against the wall. For the majority of those who do not have the patience for such a feat, I would wait unitl Paradox adds serious content through future patches.
Update : So a year has passed since this review was originally posted and many patches have released since the dreaded 1.2.1. Now with a full expansion behind its belt and much deeper fleshing out of the middle and late game, I can finally say that this game is worth your money. As you can see from the hours played icon I ADORE this game. As a med student in his 3rd year of school I have very limited free time in my dorm and any time I can get away from friends and loved ones, I am leading my miltaristic/xenophobic/spiritualistic horde of space flora on a purge through the known galaxy. Most definently would purge again.
