I loved back in past Joe Dever's Lone Wolf Game Books a lot, but i think they were much better than this game.
I had great expectations from this game but my fears were confirmed when i tried the fighting sections...
About the lore and the story nothing to say, it's like the old Lone Wolf i remember, but the real pain happens when you meet an enemy.
First thing, in the old books, when you was facing an enemy it was most often a 1 vs 1, while here, in the videogame, almost always is you vs 3 enemies together in a sort of Turn Based like (it's not 100% turn based but is very similar) fight, almost always ends up with you dead forced to restart the fight again and again till some luck not goes to your side, yes because the fights are totally random with the chances you get smashed hard at beginning or you can dodge the first attack, giving you more opportunities to survive.
I  resisted for some chapters but more you go deep with the story more the difficulty increases and i did not find any special items that helped me to become much stronger than what i was at the beginning, so the combat system and toughness and number of the enemies make this game , at high levels, very very frustrating and nearly impossible to progress in some point.
So my final vote is positive cause i was used to love Lone wolf when i was young and the fashion of the character still works also in this game, but sadly the combat system and the not balanced difficulty at Hard ruined the real fun for this game that could have been much better.
Recommended to the old fans of the books only, most of them would probably be forced to play this game at lower difficulty.

Having finished the game in about 18 hours I have to say that it was very satisfying, even if unusual to me, experience. It being my first contact with "make you own story" books, I found it at first a bit confusing (being used to save-load systems being commited to a choice was for a while stressful), but it quickly passed.
What can I say about the game itself? The story is pretty basic, but the branching emergent stories make a difference, your skills actually matter for the story in big ways, unlike most RPGs, so it can be fun replaying it once or twice, just to see what happens.
When the game gives us a bit more active role, it's clearly a smart-device port, its QTE events are a clear proof of that, and so are the visuals, which while nice considering the game's origin, fall squarely into early 2000s from a PC gamer's perspective. The combat can get repetitive, and on later levels quite easy, usually (especially when you pick Healing and Weaponskill as some of your specialties), it's quite fast and requires a slight tactical approach in planning the order of attacks performed and cooldown management.
In general, I recommend this game to all who don't mind reading their games, don't mind subpar graphics, and like straightforward, heroic adventures with a lot of room for different outcomes.

The biggest flaw in my opinion is the sector-system where you need to divide your empire into sectors and give them over to a AI governor that is inept and does not appear to know what it is doing.
Luckily there are mods to fix that (I found one that removed the need to keep sectors and never played without it again) and even more mods to make the game more fun ... because ... Quarians in Star Destroyers are fun! ^_^
Combat is another thing that could use some improvement since, even when this is a grand strategy game and the important part is the empire building and not combat, some ways to influence the happenings on the tactical level would be very welcomed.
But for a space based grand strategy game Stellaris is possibly still the best out there and I think it will become bigger and better with every DLC appearing. That is what I hope because the game also has a big glaring problem. I have never finsihed a game because at a point the empire grows so big and strong that I swept away all opposition, stomped out the end-game crisises without really any effort and integrated numerous species into my big happy empire. At this point there is no challenge anymore, nothing that my fleet could get rid of and nothing that would really keep my interest in seeing the game all the way to it's finish.
So the biggest joy ended up being restarting and playing again. what I did several times because it is still lots of fun to do it.
So yes, I still recommend it but it is far from a 10/10 score sort of game.

I picked this game up, rather at random, during a time of bored wandering across the net.
Boy, was I suprised at what I found. I haven't been a big player of 2D sidescrollers, but this one had me hooked from the beginning.
The characters are funny, well voiced, and there was a point early on in the game where I literally fell out of my chair, and rolled on the floor, I was laughing so hard. The game has it's moments of humor, as well as seriousness. The story really drew me in, when the game was approaching the climax of the story, I could not put it down.
The gameplay is also solid. It can be challenging, and on a couple occasions, was frustrating, but on classic mode, you don't lose much when dying, and you can just go again. Once you get lots of power ups, there is little that can threaten you. And some of those power ups or perks, lead to hilarity. My favorite is the scrap perk, where enemy robots sent after you during an alarm faze are nothing but a pair of legs running around like a headless chicken. It cracked me up every time I saw it.
When the game was over, and the ending had finished playing, I was left weak in the knees from the experience. That's a good thing.
I would definitely recommend this. It's a good price, and the experience is, frankly, worth more than the asking price. Not that I'm complaining about the low price.

Ghost 1.0 is a very desirable futuristic metroidvania that stays more true to the formula than most other games in that genre. You play Ghost, a character capable of taking control of robots, on a seemingly improvised mission to fulfill a request made by two nerds (Jacker and Boogan) who seek to understand the secret behind a new model of android that seems all too realistic.
The majority of the game takes place on the Nakamura space station which is almost like a living creature made robotic with its layout and self-repairing systems. Every room you clear out will have little robots rushing in to rebuild turrets and drop capsules bringing replacement units. Even the non-combative elements of the station will summon legions of soldier robots to attack you if they see you as a threat. This added a lot to the feel of being inside of a self-repairing space station in addition to giving the player an impetus to move on to the next room.
As you would expect, the gameplay in Ghost 1.0 is among your typical metroidvania faire so I won’t go much into that. Aiming is a bit different however, since you have a bit of a dual stick feel to your “move and shoot” and instead of having to face your target the whole time you can move in one direction and fire in another.  You get a variety of weapons and armor upgrades that can be purchased or found throughout your exploits on the space station, as one would expect, and several specialized items exist to counteract threats found in specific areas.
One interesting thing the game adds is the not-so-documented ‘Souls’ system. Every room has some sort of interesting challenge or hard to reach location that, when reached or achieved, releases a bunch of glowing souls into the room. Collecting all of the souls will net you a reward ranging from an upgrade to your max ammo, health, or just a bunch of cubes. Finding out what exactly unlocks the souls for each room is a bit of an exercise in experimentation and not every soul location is obvious or even unlockable, depending on your progress in the game. Fortunately, it seems like the rewards are pooled per sector and you need only gather souls until the game starts giving you cubes as rewards, instead of upgrades, indicating a “tapped out” area (that was my experience at least!).
Ghost 1.0 is the kind of game that challenges you to adjust your standards about a genre. Sure, it has a few SJW-esque elements (mostly involving jacker the neckbeard and ghost) but none of these are so damning that they would keep me from enjoying the game. The rest of the game is absolutely solid and actually very fun and worth the 19 hours I put into it. I would recommend this game even at full price, pick it up and see for yourself!

Zeno Clash is a stage=based first-person brawler with occasional shooting segments, in contrast with many first-person shooters that have occasional brawling segments.  The player must use an arsenal of punches, kicks, and throws--along with the occasional club or primative firearm--in a robust combat system that requires proper positioning and timing in addition to good awareness of the surroundings, as the player is outmatched 3 to 1 in every fight if not worse, and the opponents are just as strong as them.  All this is set in a visually rich world that borrows from many ancient and tribal cultures, creating a unique immersive experience.
Approximate Length:  5-6 hours.  Additional arena challenges add a few more hours.
PROS
(+) World & character design is creative and genre-defying
(+) Accomodates a variety of combat playstyles
(+) Difficulty is well-balanced and punishes mistakes appropriately
CONS
(-) Enemy AI is simplistic and can easily be exploited
(-) Stages are often flat and open with minimal obstacles
(-) Plot is disjointed and many things are left unexplained
(-) Suffers from sporadic game lag even at low settings
OVERALL:  Zeno Clash is a "weird" game, in setting, character design, story, and even in the base concept of a first-person brawler.  Weird games are a good thing; it shows that game designers are being creative and testing the limits of what a game is, or what it can be.  However, for all its creativiity Zeno Clash falls just short of a positive experience.  The combat system is enjoyable, but simplistic arenas and simplistic enemies that value quantity over quality quickly make it tedious, and the points it wins with its inventive setting are taken away by the fact that it ultimately does very little with it.

In Zeno Clash, you play as Ghat who is part of a 'family' by this strange creature known as Father-Mother. During the beginning of the game, things won't be very clear except that the supposed brothers and sisters that are a part of this family accuse you of killing Father-Mother. More is revealed as you progress in the game and you eventually find out the truth. Personally, I won't go into further details about the story to avoid spoilers.
The gameplay is very unique in such a way that you don't often see this genre...This game plays in a first person perspective but your use of combat isn't through weapons (there is ranged weapons in the game, but you won't always be using them) instead, you use your fists to beat the ever living crap out of whoever stands in your way. You can lock on to your enemies and switch between which can be handy for quickly knowing when to defend or attack. At some areas of the game, your fists alone won't be reliable enough to hurt some enemies as some of them can vary from big enemies who charge at you and can knock you over resulting in some nasty damage or you have creatures that spit crap at you. So what do you do when it comes down to that? You use weapons! You can pick up some unique looking weapons that help from dual welded bone like pistols to a crossbow that fires skulls that explode upon impact with your enemies or you can have a bone sledgehammer that can deal massive damage to your enemies as you charge your swing.
The level design is incredibly trippy but that's likely what the developers were going for as the world of Zeno Clash is incredibly unreal and is full of plenty of strange yet pretty scenary.
Zeno Clash also has a unique tower mode which you unlock levels of as you progress through the main story. In the tower mode, you are inside a tower killing every enemy in the room to progress higher into the tower and you also also put against a time which shows how long you take. The timer isn't all too important as its just to put you against your friends to see who's faster at the level. As you progress, you'll meet all the different enemies you have met throughout the main game and in some rooms, you will have weapons that you can use or disarm from your enemies. But in the later levels there will also be room hazards that can be useful for killing your enemies in one fell swoop but be careful! As if you aren't, you can also be killed quickly.
All in all, Zeno Clash is a incredibly fun game where you beat the crap out of people and I recommend checking it out if you're looking to punch in some faces! Plus, if you buy it and own Garry's Mod, you'll get all the models from the game!

You know when people say: "It's a classic, it's great."?
That's this game. This game is a classic (In a good way.). I played the MP beta years ago, instantly bought a copy, lost my copy, bought it on Steam some 7 years ago, restarted it multiple times through those years but never finished the expansions until just recently and after all those years, this game is STILL absolutely amazing. Way ahead of it's time, gameplay is tight as can be and does not feel like a 12 year old game unlike a lot of other games from the same period. So while it is a classic, it doesn't look or feel like it's very old at all.
The sound design in this game especially with EAX enabled is astounding, just astounding.
Almost everything in the environment in destructible and physics based including great ragdoll physics and dismemberment/gibbing. The real time dynamic lighting was way ahead of it's time. Even shell casings cast their own shadows, Point Man casts his own shadow and HAS LEGS. Something I WISH more FPS devs would do. After you see your legs in-game, you'll have a hard time going back to games where you're a floating torso. The super simple melee system in this game is amazing too, so are almost all the weapons.
Explosions and certain particles all cast their own dynamic light. This game was also one of the first games to support soft shadows, a technology that smooths shadow edges depending on their distance from the object casting the shadow. All of this from a game that is now almost 12 years old. Monolith was the KING of FPS games. This game also has TONS of high resolution textures, you can make out addresses and stuff on tiny little postal letters with ease. Although they're all just Monolith easter eggs anyways.
A.I. as many others have said, is great. Enemies will rush, flank and flush you out of cover. They will make plans to gank you and their reflexes are top notch. Enemies can be surprised, you can stealth kill by meleeing them if they're unalerted but there are some issues with the AI such as them being TOO quick to draw weapons on you/spot you too easily and being damn near dead silent when walking around, if you do not have EAX enabled that is, with it enabled footsteps are audible but still kind of quiet while yours are ear piercingly loud which will lead to them/you accidentally bumping into you/them A LOT. They'll also fire at you while running away and it's hit and miss if they'll hit you. A single enemy can take you down pretty easily and some enemies are way too good at range, you'll get hit by every shot of their massive spread fire auto assault rifle randomly. The sneaky special mercs are horrible, easily the worst enemy in the game (PM XP Only), harder to kill than any other enemy (Aside from mechs.) and they can take you down in a split second and they're so fast that they'll get right up in your face and take you down to nothing while you stand there not being able to do much, so keep your distance, they also have a wall flip where they throw three grenades at you, this can insta-kill you, as, if you get hit one grenade can and will set off the other two, three grenades are more than enough to kill you even on Moderate difficulty. Enemies can also shoot you through walls/objects sometimes, it's really strange but it happens a bit.
People say the story sucks, well I say suck it. This game has a great blend of horror, action and sci-fi and manages to keep itself grounded while containing an interesting story that's not over convoluted. While F.E.A.R. 3 tries to explain things, it ends up making a ton of plot holes, the expansions of this game also cause the same problem BUT they could be canon, they aren't though and that was deliberate from Monolith as they had F2 in production and had plans for a third game that was completely different from the one we got since the publisher owned the rights to the game they gave Day One Games the right to do whatever they wanted to do with it. While F.E.A.R. 3 isn't a horrible game, it's a really well done FPS game but the story doesn't follow F1 properly at all. F2 is a direct sequel and it's fun, not as fun as this one, but still really fun and DOES follow Monolith's actual story since it was actually from them.
The only thing bad I have to say about this game aside from some AI issues is that there are no options for aim holding, ie, holding mouse2 to aim and letting go puts the weapon back to hip fire, don't know if there's a way to mod that in at all either.
All and all, this game is amazing. Absolutely one of my top favorite series and singular games. I'd recommend it to any fan of FPS games. There was so much more that I wanted to say about one of my all time favorite games but Steam has a character limit. I probably literally wrote a small novel, only to have hit the Steam character limit a quarter of the way through pasting it, sadly.
This game also holds special place in my heart for another reason, it was the second game I ever modded without any help, first game was Far Cry. It was always fun messing with the Arch files. ;)
Still one of my favorites.

I love FFVII - I spent literally months playing this as a teen, and despite not being the best in the Final Fantasy series, and being hailed as a higher budget, less good vremake of FFVI, it still holds a special place in my heart. All of that aside, this PC port has got a few neat additions, overall smoothing out the experience of playing FFVII on your PC - this was a selling point for me due to my nostalgia connection, but nostalgia only gets you so far.
Being based on a port Eidos made in th 90s, the graphics in the PC remake are inconsistent. With blurry, low resolution pre-rendered backgrounds, and character models rendered at full res, we're left with the characters standing out like a sore thumb, an issue that wasn't present in the low-def original. There are new glitches that have been introduced by accident in the conversion, and generally the open world gameplay has aged pretty badly when compared to fully 2D games of a similar generation. It's a bit of a mess, and frankly, I have mixed feelings about the need for this re-release at all, even for newcomers. The whole experience leaves alot to be desired, which is a shame for modern audiences. Maybe just wait until Square release the proper FF7 remake, unless you are super keen on the OG.

I should preface this review with the acknowledgement that I am an avid fan of all the FF games, and FFIV, FFVI and FFX all hold a special place in my heart.  I think they are some of the most powerful stories ever told, and some of the most enjoyable and well-made games that I've had the pleasure to dump hours of my life into.  I have hardly gone a single year of my life since these games came out without re-playing them.  I love them that much.
Which is why I had such high hopes for this game... Unfortunately, it feels too much like a cash-grab by Square-Enix.  All the familiar characters are there, all the familiar places, but they didn't bother to come up with a story beyond, "Hey, you know all the stuff that happened years ago?  It's happening again!"  Ugh...  This would be bearable if it weren't such a *tedious* game to play.  Even with auto-battle on and the fastest battle settings, grinding through four or more hours per tale to get, "Yep, the Tower of Babil is back" is kind of a slap in the face to players.  Grinding was acceptable in the original games because one felt a sense of progression.  There is a humungous difference between being at level one and level twenty; not so much in this game.  Every level up is such a microscopic improvement to your character that you have to gain 25-30 levels to even be competetive against the bosses at the end of each tale (read: not get killed by their first attack).  Rydia's tale has been particularly painful to play, as you are not given anyone with the ability to heal, making you rely on potions for dungeons that beat the crap out of you until you are above the mid-twenties in level.  This game really feels like a job, which is just sad.

Players can explore the world previously seen in Final Fantasy IV two decades later, unraveling a mystery told through the intertwining stories of a familiar cast of characters. Prince Ceodore has enlisted in the airship fleet known as the Red Wings, eager to meet the expectations demanded of his blood and station. Yet once more another moon has appeared in the sky, and with it vast hordes of monsters intent on destruction. The brief peace enjoyed by the Blue Planet now stands threatened under the shadow of impending catastrophe.
Final Fantasy IV: The After Years is based on the epic quest of the 2009 release of FF IV: The After, but enhances the experience with an all-new 3D graphical presentation.

After playing this game yet again after playing it on the Wii, I once again realized why I disliked this game so much.  Oh where to begin.
First off, I've played every version of FFIV out there (I still have my original SNES cart!) with the exception of the PSP complete collection edition (Which is just the GBA version of FFIV, which I have played, and the Wii version of After Years, which I have on my Wii and some interlude chapter that takes place between the end of FFIV and the After Years, which I could care less about).  I also played the After Years on the Wii, and the only chapter I did not buy at the time was Yang's.
To start, I really do not understand why people are mad at the removal of the bonus dungeons.  The bonus dungeons only purpose was filler in between chapters, because when the game originally came out, we had to wait a month or so between chapters.  So what did we do?  Farm stuff!  There is no point to the dungeons when all the chapters are available unless you really wanted to farm for Admantite.  So this did not bother me.
What bothered me was the complete recycle of the FFIV's story.  Considering that FFIV ended pretty well on it's own, I was really shocked that a sequel was announced.  And curious too.
The After Year's story could be summed up like this;  Take FFIV's original plot, throw it in a blender, add in a few of the main hero's kids plus the dwarf princess and a few ninjas, and bam.  You have After Years.  Almost every thing that happens in the After Years has happened in the main game.  From someone getting Desert Fever to fighting Mombomb to a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor redemption plot that reflected Cecil's redemption from the original.  And we top off with a big reveal that almost mirrors the horrible Star Ocean 3 reveal.
What the heck happened to the designs of some characters too!?  Why is Rydia running around in a leotard all of a sudden?  What the heck happened to Porom!?  So much freaking pink!  And what's with Rosa's robes too???  Definitely liked the original designs of the characters better, especially Rydia's.
Gameplay wise, it's only okay.  This version is easier than the Wii version.  I rarely had to grind in chapters, though the last chapter, you'll definitely have to grind, especially if you want characters that may be lagging behind in levels.  The Bands are a nice set up, but half the time, I rarely used them.   Summons and Black Magic and certain character's abilities I found worked just as well.
The Moon phase is a neat idea, but is easy exploitable and you can work around it by abusing tents.  Depending on your setup or an upcoming boss, a moon phase is better than another, but again, easy to work in with tent abuse.  The only way this doesn't work is a balanced party, and even then, it's not that much of a deal.
This game really needed the VA FFIV for the DS did, but Square got lazy and gave us the phone port, which had no VA.  Not a deal breaker, but it looks weird in the intro.
I am kinda disappointed but not surprised that a lot of the bonus bosses were taken out.  Though really, the bonus bosses were really only there as a nod to older FFs.  Not a deal breaker for me.
Overall, if you absolutely have to play the After Years, get the PSP version.  If you're an old school FFIV fan though who enjoyed the original story, stay away from the After Years in general.  It spits on the original story, and this is coming from someone whose favorite character in the original story was Kain (There's a reason for me saying that, but I wanted to keep this review spoiler free.  Then again, if you played the original game, you are spoiled for the game anyways).  Just stick to FFIV and pretend the After Years doesn't exist.

So, Stellaris. I absolutely adore this game. Since it's release, it has only improved. The more I play this game, the more I enjoy it, and I haven't even thought about modding yet. Being a total space nerd, this game is perfect for me.
It does have some weak points, though by the time of update 1.5, most of these have been resolved. My main concern would currently be with AI behavior, but the game is looking better than ever, good time to buy it together with the Utopia expansion!
Stellaris is about creating and controlling an interstellar empire, building mining stations and colonizing planets to grow your empire and compete with the other empires in the galaxy, either against AI or friends in multiplayer. In the late game, intergalatic invaders might even strike to take control!
The game is very diverse, and with the ethic, government and newly added civic system, new ways can always be found to play the game. Want to play as a Fanatical Purifier to conquer the galaxy and purge dozens of alien species? Want to be a huge Megacorporation cooperating and trading with other empires to achieve power? Want to be an Isolationist Xenophobe Monarchy, claiming massive amount of space and avoiding all contact with other empires? It's all possible in Stellaris, with many more ways to play the game, be creative!
If you like Sci-Fi or Strategy games, I would highly recommend Stellaris. If you can get it on sale that's definitely the best, but the price is still fair for the amount of entertainment you get.
Just a warning, it can get a bit addictive. Once you've started a session there are so many things to do all the time, it's hard to stop again :)
Now, go play it, go in blind if you can! It's an exciting learning experience!

Despite its technical and gameplay flaws, such as the broken default camera settings (easily fixed by turning up sensitivity and move speed), tedious loot-gathering and occasional glitches potentially spoiling the fun, Man of Prey (aka Marauder) offers a captivating, tense, and usually rewarding squad-based strategy experience for those willing to put up with its quirks. The storyline is a neat perspective not seen often by western audiences, the soundtrack sets the tone well, gunplay is satisfying once the player conquers the challenge of the interface itself, with simple but effective RPG elements carrying the game's progression well enough to be invested in your character's builds and weapon loadouts. Considering its modest price, Marauder is definitely worth a play for fans of the genre or people who get enjoyment out of games that lack a certain level of polish but present a distinctive experience for the patient.

First off, the process of making your actual empire or choosing from one of the pre-made ones is in of itself and incredibly satisfying experience. Instead of relegating you to predertimed stats for each 'species' or portrait, the game allows you to determine what your species is actually capable of.
Nataurally I made my glorious starship-troopers ripoff federation, this time maade up of actual alien apes.
Within seconds you are greeted by your AI instructor who gives you a greeting based upon your government type, asking for what level of assistance you would like proferred. Immediately I noticed the quest system, and before this I had a history of disliking games with quest sytems but.....
This quest system WORKS. It doesn't feel scripted or intrusive, and I feel that it actually increases the level of immersion. In your typical sci-fi strategy, the whole RP or national crises that would arise were often cold logical wars over predetermined resources, with a very artificial feel.
In Stellaris, the quests feel as though they are things that aren't just shoved in your face for a tutorial or credits, they are as much a part of the lore of your playthrough as anything. For example, my military republic ape people got a quest where they had to retrieve old sub-light sattelites before the dirty xenos got them. I won't spoil it, but the questline is MUCH more complex than you might be led to believe by the initial prompt.
In other words, You can practically have your own in-depth space opera, and with modding, have it feature any species you could dream of.

+: At the time I had no idea who the guy making this was, I just heard it was a good roguelike-like and bought it on a whim. Quite possibly one of the best random unresearched purchases I have ever made.
+: While the story isn't great, the atmosphere and characters are actually really well done - the game creates a very dark feel that most games don't really match actually I think. It isn't very overt about it but if you think about what is actually going on in the game and everything around it, it's pretty grim.
+: The music is terrific.
+: The gameplay mechanics are really well done and while quite a bit of the game is random, due to the nature of the mechanics being kind of a top down shooter roguelike thing, you never really feel like you lost because of the randomness but rather because you made mistakes.
+: The DLC is cheap and extremely good and it adds a ton of content for the price that it is.
+: I enjoy running around as a naked baby.
-: It's a Flash game so the graphics are nothing to write home about and even if you have a super computer this game will drop tons of frames at the worst times.
-: While the DLC is extremely good, it also changes the game in some ways that make it harder if you're entering the game brand new with it on. I would recommend disabling the DLC in Steam until you clear the game once, then enable the DLC.

It's becoming harder and harder to create an interesting game, something that engages an audience for a length of time for them to follow through to the end: bundle games offering loads of different styles, sheer wealth of unplayed games in a Steam library, new flavour of two minute noodles at Coles. What Ghost 1.0 offers is what I found in games like Transistor and Bastion: a fun gameplay style that not only offered a cohesive gaming experience, but a story that went with it also.
Ghost 1.0 is a Metroidvania style game at its essence, with players embarking on a mission that you want to complete. Upgrades and power ups are offered along the way and are almost necessary for some areas to complete. However, the voice acting of not only the protagonists and portagonist support, but the antagonists I felt melded into the wealth of the experience that is offered here.
Sure it has its flaws, but no game is perfect; the development team however are proactive and listen to bug reports as well as feedback making it a smooth experience for players as best as they can. They themselves are their harshest critic as they wish for their prooduct to be as robust as possible.
For me this filled a hole I was missing since putting Rogue Legacy down, and with its story, voice acting, gameplay and mechanics I thoroughly enjoyed the experience. I highly recommend this to anyone looking for something challenging as you won't be disappointed. I look forward to the next installment, as well as what the developers have on offer.

No. Just, no. Absolutely nothing in this game makes any damn sense. The most mind-boggling thing so far is how this has a rating of 85%.
The visuals are interesting, and the music reminds me of Diablo at times, but then that's about it. The voice acting is atrocious, the gameplay is severely lacking and repetative, and I'm not even sure if there's an actual story, despite their efforts.
There's only so much an indie or 'non A+++' game can get away with before you have to stop treating it like a child's kindergarten project, giving it A's for effort. The one time I thought the game was going to do something interesting, or reveal what the actual plot was about, and it just immediately shoehorns you into a boss fight - the same exact one that you've already done half way through the game. That's all that ever happens; cutscene, pointless fight. Cutscene, pointless fight. Do you get to do anything to advance the plot? Explore? Manage an inventory (re: choose what weapon to carry around with)? No. Every 'level' or whatever you want to call it will choose how you will start the fight, that means it will either take away anything you were carrying at the time, or give you a random weapon and make absolutely zero effort on explaining why this happens.
The majority of the game, you have a companion... but does she do anything to be even remotely helpful? No. During one of the boss fights that has no rhyme or reason (like much of the game), this character perches herself up on a vantage point with a rifle, and what does she do? SHOOTS THE CRABS SKUTTLING AROUND... I'M DEAD SERIOUS. All she ever does is gets up on a vantage point, and does virtually nothing. You can hear her shooting at times, but at what, I have no idea.
For the first hour or so, I kept asking myself... why did I get this game? And then, the question turned into: what the hell is this game even trying to do? I don't understand how or why this game has a sequel. I really don't. I forced myself to play through to see what the hub-bub was about, and was just as disappointed at the end as I was at the start. Easily the longest, least-deserving 3 1/2 hours of my life.
A game needs more than interesting visuals and a 'well, they tried' attitude to warrant being as popular and highly praised as this one is. Please avoid at all costs, even if that cost is $1.99. It's not worth it.

Gameplay:
You can normal punch, strong punch, block and dodge. You can also do some advanced techniques like a super strong punch, a rushed elbow hit, and if you block then press your normal punch or strong punch button you can land a devastating quick kick. It's pretty simple. There are also weapons that have a small "magazine" (the best gun I found had 3 shots before I had to reload). You mostly walk in a straight line.  It is kind of dreamlike because even though it is linear many of the things from point A to B are cut out. For example in one part you are in the forest and then 5 minutes later (after a fight) you are in the coast. The gameplay is simple but fun.
Story:
Without giving too much away: Ghat murders Father-Mother (the name implies everything). He is on the run and his girlfriend (Deadra) tags along cause I don’t know. You get many flashbacks that tell more of the story and you try to piece it together. He refuses to tell his girlfriend Father-Mother's secret (why he killed it). This game is kind of weird. See a couple of the screenshots and you will see what I mean. The world looks twisted and colorful as do the characters. People are weird and some talk in riddles. You definitely will be laughing at some points in the game.
Definitely get it. The story mode is short but you also get a challenge mode. I believe there is an SDK for this game but I haven’t come across any mods.

This game is beautiful. I was looking for something to relax from the usuals (PUBG, CS: GO, etc.), and saw this. I love the simplistic art style that reminds me of Breath of the Wild, and in this setting the devs nailed it. The other creatures and interactables you come across in gameplay are simple, but beautifully crafted adding to that art style, and interact with the player in a way I've never seen before. The lighting and soundtrack work in perfect harmony and always keep you interested. The game could be warm and colorful, and then quickly switch to be dark and mysterious which keeps the player interested.
The game gives you ZERO context for anything, which in my opinion is pefect because none of the puzzles in the game take very much effort at all, and I think having to go through pages of reading in a game like this wouldn't fit the style at all. To me this game is the perfect relaxing tool, and not having to put much effort into it is nice. You can sit back and just enjoy the game for what it is.
The game its self is rather linear, and sometimes repetative, BUT I never once felt bored playing through it because I was so busy exploring my new surroundings. Every new area feels unique and is fun to explore (which I usually did for a couple of minutes before doing the actual objective). The last segement of the game is SUPER satisfying, and I probably spend about 20 minutes just messing around seeing what would happen if I did this or that.
Negatives:
-Slightly linear/repetative feel.   MINOR ISSUE
-For a very brief period your character gets to go on land, and I thought that was a bit awkward, but of course that isn't
supposed to be the focus of the game.   MINOR ISSUE
-Fps was usually around 60, but whenever I went into a LARGE school of fish my frames would usually drop to around 30
(I left the default graphics how they were).   MINOR ISSUE
-Keyboard controls were just a tiny bit wonky at first, but I got used to them pretty quick, and it was all good (Should
have gone controller).   MINOR ISSUE
-Length - I finished this game in about 2.5 hours just going through and messing around with what I was interested in. I
did NOT go through and try to find every single object in the game (there are collectable things of sorts which you can
go through and find) which would have made the experience longer. It was perfectly fine for me becuase I only paid
$5.99 for it, but I could see some people having more issues with the full price.

With over 30 hours under the belt, and still haven't completed the game (At the final section now), I thought it would be a great time to review.
The story is set 17 years after the events of Final Fantasy IV, where the main cast has moved on, got a new life, the usual. The peace is broken when the previously defeated evil of the Moon has returned above the Blue Planet once more...Ok, seems good so far. Chapters are used for gameplay, with each main character and a suporting cast with them. This can be a little off-putting for some players of Final Fantasy, as you will not get free exploration in these tales. It's very straight lined for you, and the only 'optional' exploration would be to wander various dungeons in said tales. I personally enjoyed this feature, however, it did soon come with a flaw. The tales of each character... They're not really an original story. It seems SE sat down and thought: 'Hey, Final Fantasy X-2 was good. We made a trilogy from Final Fantasy XIII. Why not sequel the only game we've remade about 500 times! Success guaranteed!'
The story might as well have just been Final Fantasy IV all over again, as most of the Tales seem to just copy the events from the previous game. This was a little depressing, as you would expect a new original story. That's not to say the story isn't a good playthrough, as it did have some good cliffhangers and reveals. But in my personal opinion, the story only started to get GOOD at Chapter 8 (Kain's Tale). And then, it just decided to go back down hill. Upon hitting Chapter 10 (Final Tale), the game recycled Final Fantasy bosses. I mean, sure, they COULD have given more background on WHY they appeared, but no. It just seemed like a way to fill in the space between Point A to B.
Personally, I would recommend this game, as I have enjoyed it, despite it's lacking orginal storyline plot. On the other hand, I would say buy with caution. If you loved Final Fantasy IV, then you will most likely enjoy this game.
As a quick note, take note of how many times one character must yell someones name. I mean seriously, it seems like 60% of the script just involved people yelling 'Cecil!'.
A short but deep experience, to repeat whenever you feel like meditating: recommended!

Aperion’s previous game, 7.62 High Calibre, was a real-time open world tactical RPG, heavily inspired by the Jagged Alliance series. While rather buggy and with a boring storyline, its complex simulationist combat and highly detailed “gun porn” conquered quite a few devout fans.
Marauder, also known as Men of Prey in Europe, is instead a linear, story-driven game, based on a book series by the same name from Russian author Berkem Al Atomi. The game places you in the boots of Akhmetzyanov, a common man trying to survive an alternate-history Russia where the government collapsed, anarchy reigns and the US is invading.
Don’t expect a pleasant game. Ahkmet himself is neither a virtuous paragon nor a noble-hearted anti-hero – just a man trying to survive with his wife, at any cost. You will fight militias, rogue cops, raiders and cannibals, but also desperate, starved neighbors trying to take some of your precious food.
Marauder’s combat perfectly reinforces its harsh atmosphere. The unique real-time with pause system from High Calibre is still here, if slightly streamlined. Every action takes a set time to be performed, and each has its pros and cons. The shotgun is a sure kill at close range, but it takes 0.42 seconds to ready it, while a pistol-wielding enemy can fire in just 0.08 seconds. You must take that into account in order to survive.

While I usually prefer turn-based tactical games, Marauder’s intense and nerve-wrecking battles make great use of the game’s elaborate real-time system.  To add to the challenge, Ahkmet can only see what’s in front of him and must otherwise rely on hearing to guess the enemy’s position. This is further accentuated by the game’s overwhelming odds, pitting you alone against dozens of looters or a full elite military squad with nothing but a rifle, some mines and your wits.
The game keeps the extensive and highly detailed armory found in High Calibre, with almost a hundred weapons, and adds a few more RPG mechanics to the formula, such as character creation, a skill tree and lockpicking. You’ll also get up to three companions as the plot advances, allowing for more complex tactics.
Sadly, Marauder is extremely linear. Besides the main story, you’ll only be able to visit a bazaar, do a couple of side-quests and have one-line conversation with a handful of NPCs. And the dialogs are all in Russian, with poorly translated English subtitles.
Rough, challenging and intense, Marauder is an unique low budget tactical RPG. Its bleak story, harsh setting, high difficulty and complex combat are a sure treat to cold-blooded tactical enthusiasts.
PS: I strongly recommend to manually edit the game’s config files. That way you can unlock higher resolutions and better camera controls.

TL;DR Very fun at the start, but gets tiresome as the game goes on, and falls short in the late game.
Stellaris is an exciting new release from Paradox. It offers new aspects of strategy games including civilization ethics, unique species, traits, and preferences. Along with it is a very interesting technology tree, as well as currencies that you must balance to get the most out of (and strategic resources that add flavour to the game). The game requires patience, strategy and planning, as well as micro-management.
The game is exciting from the beginning. You are launched into a galaxy which you have no knowledge of. Your quest for the aquisition of resources is presented along with the opportunity to explore new star systems, and perhaps discover that you are not alone in the universe as it once seemed. The more you explore, the larger the galaxy begins to appear, and new opportunities arise.
However, after putting in enough time and effort, the game begins to become a grind. You have achieved your goals of creating a utopia for your people, or becoming a force within the galaxy to be reckoned with.. But you have not completed the game yet and you're looking for a way to find closure. So you check your victory conditions and see that you have no choice but to control 40% of the galaxy (A normal galaxy is 600 stars, which each have their own number of planets) or eliminate every other nation, and you realise.. Whew, this is going to take longer than you thought. Hours, days, maybe weeks real-time.
Unless you're really determined to see a victory screen, which itself is not really a reward (No achievement, or bonus), it's not really worth pursuing a late game goal, counter to your own intuition. As a side note, the tech-tree at first is fascinating, but with a descent amount of play-time you realise it's very homogenous in the end. (It never really ends, just small perks that you can keep researching and are cummulative)
Despite the lacking late-game playability, this game is really interesting and exciting. You really feel immersed as a new galactic civilisation, and discovering new and interesting things as you play keeps you wanting to play more. As a space simulation, this game is excellent. Real-time space battles are a beauty to watch as well.
On the whole, a very enjoyable, but short-lived experience. 8/10

If you remotely enjoy side-scrollers, metroidvania, platformer games - you owe it to yourself to play Dust.

The characters are very well designed and Fidget, a sidekick that follows the main character Dust is the cutest thing I've seen in a game with how she's made and the voiceactor that was chosen for her.
The gameplay is a side scrolling hack & slash which I'm not noramlly a fan of but with the large amount of mobility your playable character has you don't feel like you're being held back with movement. You do only have the same weapon from the start of the game and once you find a tactic you find best you'll just keep using it for the rest of the game, only changing every now and again when an enemy only really gets affected by certain attacks. While you can get upgrades for your health and damage they tend to not feel that they change things that much.
What's really the draw for this game though is the story and I don't want to spoil anything but I'll just tell you that for me personally I played through this game quite a few times because I loved the characters and got attached to them and wanted to help them through their struggles and although it can be serious at times it still can make me chuckle at times with the writing.
This is one of the best PC games you can think of getting, and at this price its a steal for the quality, being so good compared to AAA games that might only last a few hours with no soul or life to it. This is full of life and fun, get this game.

This is a hardcore tactics/battle sim/RPG set in postapocalyptic Russia. The graphics can be described as 'functional' by today standards, but attention to detail in graphics and gameplay and is immense. For example, you can see spent casings and MG belt links on the ground after firing a heavy MG. The gameplay is similar to game predecessors 7.62 and Brigade E5, it is pausable real time where 0.15 secs difference between aiming may mean death for a more sloppy character. These games offer the most realistic modern tactical engagement simulation I know.
The story of the game is based on a very grim and tragic book with the same title about civil war and chaos, where you can be killed for a can of fish. It's full of  violence, includes famine, slavery and even mentions cannibalism, so I definitely won't recommend this title to kids or teenagers. On the other hand, it makes you play to learn what will happen next and to right the wrongs, much more captivating than a usual game story.
Worth every cent you pay! Beautiful artwork, a feels kicking story and fun colorful combat with a punishing difficulty setting if you are into that.

The commuinty-made translation to English is far from perfect, but it works well enough to give you the gist of what is going on. But I must be honest, I preferred to listen to the dialogue in Russian rather than read the (sometimes puzzling) English subititles.
In short -- definitely worth playing if you like challenging, tactical squad-level games. But bear in mind the handful of annoying recurring bugs!

An amazing RPG experience. I
finished the game a second time. To fully appreciate this game, you HAVE to play it twice: Once with Roche's path, and the second time with Iorveth.
Witcher 2 is vast, the maps are beautiful, and the characters are well-developed. Every single character in this game has so much personality. You can't walk past the townsfolk without them sneering at you, or giving you their opinion on things. And oh do they have things to say! Everyone has strong opinions on everything, and I love it,
The script feels fluid, and it does a good job of making you feel like a complete outsider (which Geralt happens to be). Each line of dialogue has been crafted with care, and
- a rare achievement for a game that takes ~30 hours to finish once.
The dwarves are fun to hang with, the elves are pure class, the sorceresses are beautifully designed - but for me the most adorable characters in this game are the ..wait for it.. trolls! You spend all of 5 minutes with them. They look like how vomit tastes, and yet this game managed to make me adore them. The females are strong too, and the romance is handled pretty well - this game will make more sense if you happen to be a functioning adult, well versed in interpersonal relationships.
The political arc in this game does feel a bit drawn out (it's just plot device). I found it difficult to care about any ruler (except Saskia), but perhaps the game was purposely trying to make me dislike them. It would've been more interesting were the male rulers given more complexity and better judgement. The in-camp politics was way more stimulating than the overarching plot.
Graphics are nice even by today's standards. Gameplay is top notch, especially if you're playing with an Xbox controller.
To conclude, this game is an absolute must-have for anyone who cares about videogame storyteling.

A well thought out adventure game. Stunning hand drawn environments, quality voice acting and animation mixed with a high level of polish make the game a pleasure to play through.
The game switches between 2 different characters as you roll through the story. Definitely geared toward the younger generation in terms of difficulty and story arc. All puzzles are logical and there is a built in hint system to basically give you the answer if you ever get stuck. Most of the time the screen will only have 5 or less hot spots to interact with and you'll only be carrying a few items  at a time.
But let's discuss the main issue which is the game length. You'll be able to complete the game in under 2 hrs (give or take). For the price it's going to annoy some people as there is plenty of games out there which you can sink hundreds of hours into for half the price. I'm giving it the thumbs up on the basis of the game being quality over quantity and understanding trying to push out a new IP (with this level of art quality) to a niche audience must be a huge risk. At times I did feel so much more could have been done with the world they built (adding more voice lines, more hotspots to interact with, more items to use, more characters etc.) but they have shipped a well made product that doesn't end in a cliffhanger with you needing to wait and pay for act 2. It is a finished game, and functions well as a short compact experience. I'm sure production in some areas needed to be cut to meet deadlines but at the end of the day I want to support studios that are willing to take the risk to bring a game like this out. How else are we going to get more of them? Granted my gaming budget is alright, so I can afford to purchase a game like this and not feel bad about the price. If you are tight for money and really value your bang for buck, I'd reccommend waiting for a sale to help bring your game time expectations in line. Replay value is pretty minimal unfortunately.
Apart from that, all achievement popped. You can't skip dialogue or cutscenes which will annoy some people who read fast and don't care to wait. I can't really fault anything else as I did not experience any glitches/bus/crashes. Worth a look if you're into this type of game.

Metroid meets Shadow Complex meets rogue-like in this enjoyable platformer. You control Ghost with the ability to possess any robot on will. Your main body is what'll stay with you throughout the course of the game, but you can whenever you want jump out to take control over enemies or neutrals. And the game requires you to do so outside of just combat, to solve some of the game's many puzzles.
There are a throng of powerups and they even made a skilltree. With various difficulty levels you can randomize your experience even more, but it's mostly the loot that's seeded more. Since Ghost 1.0 also mixes rogue-like things into the game, you'll lose all of your belongings when you die. Thankfully you can recover some of your items by returning to your corpse, Dark Souls-style, but not all items are returned to you.
The story is okay enough. You're told to infiltrate the Nakamura space station to get the schematics for the Naka, robots that have become so sophisticated some sane people are fearing it is just a matter of time before it'll revolt and tearing humanity a new one.
Ghost 1.0 is unique on enough on its own, and the dialogue is for the most time very serviceable. There are some tongue in cheek moments that balance on cringeworthy, but you have to hand it to them that they've made a game with soul and aren't afraid to roll with it. If you like Metroid-vania type games like Shadow Complex, you'll probably be very satisfied with what's on offer here.

I've played about 2 full games now where a group of two others and myself have successfully captured Bigfoot.  The first time through was quite fun. The Cameras seem completely useless.  They are a really cool idea, but there's simply too few of them to actually make them useful.  The map is pretty large and Bigfoot gets around so quickly that by the time you see him on one camera there's no way to find him again.
Traps seem like a cool idea but again don't seem to work all that well.  In the two hunts, we've only been able to get Bigfoot to run into a trap one time and it was just by coincidence that he ran right over it.
Flares are kinda cool but not really necessary either.

As a fun party type game to play with two others give the game a go.  It's fun and will keep everyone on edge for the first game or two.  Don't expect to get a ton of the game in terms of countless hours of gameplay.  In its current state, it is just simply not that game. Ghost 1.0 is a "metroidvania" style platformer, but in "survival mode" (the default, and in my opinion better, of the two modes) it is very different from any metroidvania I've played before, and brings a lot of interesting innovations of its own. The alarm-raising mechanic makes for surprisingly interesting strategic decisions, and the death mechanics are particularly refined, including some great innovations that I haven't seen in any similar game before (The quasi-savepoints before bosses are an incredibly nice feature. I hope more games borrow that mechanic in the future.)
Aesthetically, it's got very well-drawn art across the board, from the character sprites to the cutscenes to the level backgrounds and so forth. The music and sound effect are both quite nice in my opinion. Unusually for an indie game, the writing and the overall story are both excellent. Even more unusually, the voice acting is so good that it's actually noticable when the actors occasionally flub a line-- which I only noticed two or three times over the course of the entire game.
In short, this is actually a pretty strong contender for my favorite game of the year. I'm as surprised as anyone by that. It's definitely worth full price, go buy it now.

This game is not just about looking around though, and there is a nice implicit story to follow. It is not the most memorable ever, but it serves the game right and succeeds in being both engaging and intriguing. The story will mostly be built in your head, but that's what's fun about it: it all leaves place to the imagination. In the end though, I'd not recommend the game for someone mainly interested in the story, or even in the gameplay: it appeals to people who want a soothing game centered around observation. If going to a giant aquarium and watching the fishes, rays and jellyfishes excited you as a kid, you're likely to love ABZU.

If you live 4x and don't have anything on the go right now; worth it. If you're mid some other 4x game that you love - wait a little longer for some more kink fixing.

If you loved the original FF4, you will love The After Years. If you haven't played FF4, finish it first before starting The After Years.
The After Years is most of all a nostalgia trip to 20 years ago, and those of us fortunate enough to have played FF4 back in the early 90's will shed tears of joy playing this game and reliving those golden memories. The storyline folds masterfully together, although not everyone will appreciate breaking it into multiple tales and having to level from scratch every time around. And in that vein, a word of caution is in place: nightmares about Underground Waterway may occur!
The PC port, as mentioned by other reviewers, lacks some content that's present on PSP and WiiWare versions, but if they are out of reach for you the PC version holds its ground just fine. There are a few dialogue hiccups, and twice the game simply has crashed upon entering battle, but thanks to the autosave feature you can pick up right from where things went wrong. Multiple save slots per tale (as opposed to 3 slots for the whole game) is also a very welcome feature.
If FF4 is a 10/10 game for me, The After Years deserves a 9½/10. Highly recommended for fans of SNES era JRPGs.

I want to start by saying that I really, REALLY wanted to like this game--and for the first few hours, I really did! Final Fantasy IV was my first (main series) FF game, and therefore one of my favorites. I hadn't played the After Years because I didn't have a system or phone capable of playing it, so I was excited when it was announced on Steam and even pre-ordered it.
There are quite a few things I do really enjoy about the game, but unfortunately the flaws outweigh the positives.
As you know, this game has an episodic format. I like how you'll play through each character's own tale--you get to piece together events plaguing the world from each character's perspective. This makes the game's plot intriguing, as you'll want to know "how did this character end up there?!" at the climax of each scenario. And because each character has ample time in the spotlight, they're fleshed out more this time around than the original game. For example, I found Palom and Porom to be much more interesting in this game than FF4, as you get to see how they've grown and changed--and learn about their respective insecurities as much as their ambitions. As others have said, the plot is pretty much fan-fiction tier--but the characterization and development, I think, is really good.
There is a problem with the episodic format, though: a good 75% of the game is exposition. While it's great to watch events from so many perspectives, and is certainly interesting at the start of the game, 10 hours in you'll be thinking "okay, but where will this all LEAD to?" Once you reach the climax of someone's tale, it ends--which means starting fresh with a new character elseware. While characters will unite later--MUCH later--you spend the majority of the game feeling as though you aren't actually progressing.
I wish they paced the plot differently: have the first 3 or so tales be expositon, the next few "in the middle" of it all, then the last few being a little more climactic. But instead, you play maybe 8 tales that are all happening at the same time before you can progress through the timeline/plot.
Also, and this might be a spoiler! You don't actually learn anything very significant, plot-wise, until the very end. I'll save you the trouble by saying the antagonist is generic, has no compelling backstory, and you won't learn the enemy's motive until seconds before the final fight. I don't mind that the plot is fanfiction-y, but I do mind that there just isn't a real payoff at the end.
And then there's the dungeons. At first, I didn't mind that almost all the dungeons are recycled from FF4. In fact, I kind of like that they didn't change the world too much; after reading others' reviews, I decided to think of this more as an "expansion" than a sequel, knowing that the world would be mostly untouched but with new scenarios. You might care much more than I do about the recycled dungeons, but you probably already know about that.
What I didn't know, and what made this game ultimately frustrating, is that within this game alone you will go through certain dungeons over and over and over. I can't tell you how many times they make you go through the underwater passageway--5 or 6, with 3 of those in Edward's tale alone (and back to back, too!). There's also the Lunar Subterraine, but I won't talk about that too much since it might be spoilery to--but let's just say you'll have the layout of that memorized by the time you're finished playing as well. Taking stuff from FF4 and putting it in this game was ok enough, but the way this game makes you do the same exact tasks over and over as different characters (or within the same tale) is unforgiveable and lazy.
The endgame is also incredibly grindy. Once you're able to form a party with all the characters you've played as, you'll find that they're terribly underleveled, even though they were leveled fine in their respective tales. Grinding + the endless rehashing you'll find in the final dungeon makes this game difficult to win--not because enemies are too tough, but because you'll simply become too bored to want to go any further. It becomes very clear by the end of the game how a great deal of it exists to drag out the length, rather than deliver any interesting playing experience.
Some little "pro" points:
+ I loved the bands feature, which adds an extra little thing to battles while also making characters' relationships more interesting.
+ The lunar phases were a neat idea, though I'm not sure they made much of a difference--though I could be wrong.
+ You'll have different parties in different tales, which means you're always expected to come up with new strategies. For example, you might not have a healer in one tale. Or maybe you have no magic user at all. This might seem annoying, but it can be good to switch things up.
Little "cons":
+ Because you begin as a new, low-level character at the start of each tale, you'll spend a good chunk of the game only being able to attack or use the lowest-leveled magic. I spent most of the game with "auto battle" on, because you simply don't have many choices in fights, since no one really has good abilities. And you can imagine that the enemies in the first half or so of every tale are pushovers until the endgame.

Hit and Miss:

- Opening chests are pretty fun, though I think they could be more interesting with added difficulty.
Cons:
- Skills are limited, and the fighting mechanics are uninteresting.
- The game could use some balancing. Money was an issue in the beginning, but I had a ton of cash in the middle of the game. Keeping the health bar healthy was a real struggle at the start as well.
- Despite having fast travel, I found myself moving more than I needed to.
Overall, the storyline was the greatest reason for me to finish this game, even when the game wasn't that fun. It was a story well-told, and I was sad that it had ended with a bit of a rush. Still, this game was something special. I'd give it an 8.5/10!

Witcher 2 is vast, the maps are beautiful, and the characters are well-developed. Every single character in this game has so much personality. The script feels fluid, and it does a good job of making you feel like a complete outsider (which Geralt happens to be). Each line of dialogue has been crafted with care, and
- a rare achievement for a game that takes ~30 hours to finish once.
The dwarves are fun to hang with, the elves are pure class, the sorceresses are beautifully designed - but for me the most adorable characters in this game are the ..wait for it.. trolls! You spend all of 5 minutes with them. They look like how vomit tastes, and yet this game managed to make me adore them. The females are strong too, and the romance is handled pretty well - this game will make more sense if you happen to be a functioning adult, well versed in interpersonal relationships.
The political arc in this game does feel a bit drawn out (it's just plot device). I found it difficult to care about any ruler (except Saskia), but perhaps the game was purposely trying to make me dislike them. It would've been more interesting were the male rulers given more complexity and better judgement. The in-camp politics was way more stimulating than the overarching plot.
Graphics are nice even by today's standards. Gameplay is top notch, especially if you're playing with an Xbox controller.
To conclude, this game is an absolute must-have for anyone who cares about videogame storyteling.

Well, the short answer is yeah, it was pretty decent. More detailed rambling follows:
First of all, as The After Years is a sequel for Final Fantasy IV, I will assume that you have played at least some release of the original. Otherwise you might want to consider getting that one first.
The After Years is set 17 years after the events of Final Fantasy IV. Story starts with Ceodore, son of Cecil and Rosa, leaving the town of Baron for training. Meanwhile, Baron and various other locations are invaded by a mysterious girl who is after each nation's crystals for an unknown reason.
What is unique about The After Years compared to any other Final Fantasy game is that story is actually told through ten separate Tales, each told from different character's point of view. As the game progresses, these separate stories start to gradually connect with each other and the main story starts to get clearer. I actually quite liked this way of doing things because it was something different from what I was used to with other Final Fantasy games. The story and writing in The After Years are also actually fairly good, and in my opinion actually better than in Final Fantasy IV.
Along with the original cast of Final Fantasy IV, The After Years introduces a fairly huge roster of new characters, and many of those new characters are actually quite likeable and well written. Many old familiar characters such as Kain, Edward, Parom, and Polom (hey, those two are 22 and not 5 now!) also receive more welcome character development.
Admittedly when an RPG has such a huge character roster as The After Years does, there is almost bound to be some throwaway stock characters, such as bunch of ninjas from Edge's Tale in the After Years.
With the addition of Band abilities, skills performed with two or more characters together, the combat system of The After Years is your same old turn-based ATB gauge system you know from many other Final Fantasy games, so there is really nothing more to say about it. It's good, just don't expect any huge changes to the original like you might have seen in Final Fantasy X-2 for example.
What about the port and cut content? Well, the Steam release is a quick Android port. What this means is that you are still stuck with your 30 FPS (and 15 FPS in combat, just like in the Steam release of Final Fantasy IV), uglier UI, and missing content when compared to Wii and PSP releases of the game. Visually it looks like a PS1 era game, which honestly is something I personally don't really mind but I realize that there are people for whom that is a problem.
Missing content includes challenge dungeons for different characters and an extended final dungeon with cameo bosses from other Final Fantasy games. While this is regrettable, I must say that even the current final dungeon drags on so darn long and frankly, I was quite sick of it towards the end, so I was just glad that it was not an even longer version of it. But it is still missing content and especially people who have played that content before will most likely miss it if they decided to pick up the game here.
So, did I like it? Well, yeah, I did. While not perfect, The After Years does lot of things right and it was fairly enjoyable. However, while I liked it, I never got that "Oh man, this game is amazing!" feeling I usually get when I pick up a Final Fantasy, and I can't really pinpoint why that was the case. Maybe it is because it still felt like your same old Final Fantasy IV and therefore really didn't feel like a whole new game, aside from the story.
Would I recommend the game? Well, yes, but only if you are either a huge fan of Final Fantasy IV and really want more of the same or if you have played every other Final Fantasy game available on the platforms you own and really want more. If you just want a Final Fantasy game, or any JRPG, to play, pretty much every other Final Fantasy game available on Steam for roughly the same prize would probably be a better choice than this one. Not that The After Years would be a bad game, it is just that there are better games available out there.

After completing this game, I felt compelled to leave a review. This is a classic, hand-drawn 2D point and click adventure games (much to the likes of monkey island, full throttle, deponia series, broken sword, etc) and these kind of games are almost extinct due to the higher demand for action packed 3D games like call of duty, battlefield, GTA, as such. This game does not disappoint its genre. It has a good, solid, adventurous plot, it's well-written, the game's quality is excellent (in terms of graphics, programing, music, sound, etc) and does not resemble a low budget and low quality game, despite the low asking price of the game. And personally, I really like how the game isn't overly complicated or practically impossible to figure out the puzzles/solutions without referring to a walkthrough, such as those classic adventure games that I mentioned above. This type of gameplay is no longer very practical (I'm looking at you: Thimbleweed park. lol) in this new era of gaming generation (whereby the only way you can solve most of the puzzles is to try everything you have in your inventory on everything around you everywhere you go). I'm glad I can finish the game without referring to any walkthrough, though I use the in-game hints once in a while.
So, to sum up, if you're an avid point and click adventure gamer, you really shouldn't pass this by. It's a must-play title. A rare gem that's really hard to come by nowadays. If you're not an adventure gamer as such, you may or you may not like this title, depending on your personal preferences. But I really do urge you to give it a chance. It's a really good change of scenery among all those 3D action packed games and it wont take up much of your time. I manage to complete it within 2 hours.
As for the downside of the game, as mentioned above, it's really short. I estimate it will take about 2 to 4 hours average for anyone to finish this game.

This game definitely won't be for everyone, but I've been totally hooked since I bought it.  Be warned straight away, that the game is half book, half RPG combat/inventory management, and I mean that literally (you spend much of your time turning pages in a virtual book and reading).  It's based on the Lone Wolf CYOA books, and stays true to that formula for the most part.   Half of the game is simply reading the progressing story and making decisions on how to handle situations.  I will say that it's not nearly as difficult or high stakes as the original Lone Wolf books were, as most encounters can be handled whichever way you decide to go.  The other half of the game is a turn based / real-time hybrid RPG combat system (kind of like Final Fantasy 6/7 or Chrono Trigger, except with multiple actions available in one turn), which is surprisingly fun.  The difficulty seems to be balanced perfectly on normal difficulty (at least for myself), which keeps it engaging, though the combat can be a bit repetitive with a lack of variety of different enemies and only one party member.
If the idea of combining a CYOA book with a well balanced, fun, but slightly repetitive RPG combat system sounds interesting to you, check it out.  The writing isn't amazing, but it isn't terrible.  The art is cool, but limited.  The music is similarly nice, but very limited...in the end though, the real fun of the game for me is in making your own decisions as you roleplay your character, and the tough but fair combat.

Truly one of the last good CoD games.
The time that it's set in is great, it's like the perfect mix between legacy military combat and technology. It's a shame that more wasn't done in this cold war era. The zombies was great too, maps like Ascension and Call of the Dead were some of my favorite maps in the whole of the Zombies timeline. They were simple, well designed and the gimmicks and Easter eggs they contained were in-depth and great!
The multiplayer also had some quite abstract, but well executed ideas, I liked the currency system first of all, it was different and it gave you a reason to play other than just to level up, you could earn more money which could be spend on new calling cards and attachments for weapons or even just new weapons themselves. Also, if you wanted to, you could try your luck in gambling, interesting game modes like “Gungame” and “One in the Chamber” were a great way to compete to win other people's money, I remember losing like 10,000 points on one of the high stakes modes and I was gutted, I actually cared about it, which is something I can't say for more recent Call of Duty titles, they lack innovation, I mean sure, you can call all of this future jetpack s*** innovation but really all it does is detract from the experience, the future is overdone and boring, I liked playing the campaigns in Call of Duty games because they took you to conflicts that happened in the past and created a story based around said conflicts, when you take things into the future all you do is make it generic and uninteresting. Who cares what happens in some futuristic fictional war that will never happen? I sure don't.
In summary, I like Call of Duty: Black Ops because of its use of recent history, you get to see places like Vietnam during the war and I think that's real swell. Also most of the multiplayer maps were based around areas that had seen conflict during the past at some point, which gave it a good historical feeling. I do think that this is the last game so far in the CoD series to do this (I've played every one apart from Ghosts), and I just wish that the devs at Treyarch and IW would take my criticisms into consideration, I know they won't, but it would be really nice to see a return to the basics next time it's CoD season.

The weapons are also quite fun to use and vary enough that you won't get bored using the same ones over and over. The only weakness in the combat was the boss' and big enemies. The story is interesting and actually made me want to find out what happened and the ending feels very rewarding.

This is the newest addition to Steam's library of metroidvanias. It is an indie game with a focus more on the castlevania gameplay and the metroid setting and atmophere. It is made by the maker of unepic and as such the game is expectedly loaded with geek culture references. My feel on the game is a bit mixed and I will elaborate on why:
The good:
- The graphics: The graphics are absolutely superb, great lighting, great attention to detail, excellent smooth framerate which is rare with 2D games these days thanks to the crappiness of the unity engine.
- The sounds: The sound quality is great
- The music: The music is absolutely great, I personally liked the tutorial music the most
- The story: The story is deep and engaging, a lot of thought went into it and the cutscenes are great.
- Replayability: Due to the multiple difficulty levels, variety of items, and two available gamemodes to pick, the game offers a lot of replayability
- The price: For the gameplay time, graphics, sound and other content offered, this game is fairly priced.
The bad:
- The name: Ghost 1.0 is an abysmal name for a video game, almost as bad as action fighter. The name is so bad that metacritic didn't even create a page for this game.
- The level design: The design tends to be quite poor at times with damage in many times damage being unavoidable or jumps being awkward or other problems.
- infinite damage tick: There is no limit to how quickly damage can be done, in certain cases it can make quick work of your armor and kill you fast even though your health is full, this is especially problematic with turrets.
- The compromise: The game offers two modes of playing the game, classic metroidvania style and roguelike style. Both come with serious pitfalls. The classic mode allows you to keep your items if you die in exchange for offering you only a small sample of all the weapons and items in the game during a full run. Roguelike mode offers you a huge variety of items in a run, but they are all taken from you should you die. Also in roguelike mode, the difficulty goes significantly up.
- The voice acting: oh boy... the voice acting of the characters other than the three main characters is so bad.
All in all, this game is recommended to fans of metroidvanias and fans of roguelikes, but I don't recommend it for anyone else.
