The story is great - in the great tradition of classic game book romantic fantasy hokum, but you know what you're getting! The interface itself is beautiful, really nice and brilliant (although obviously a translation from a touch-screen/mobile device... don't be lazy, make it be PC specific!). The simple artwork animations do an amazing job of helping to invigorate the text and add to it. I cannot fault any of this - however amongst all this greatness there an utter and complete let down within the awful fighting mechanism.
1) It feels like a JRPG - I know this is marmite, and I'm on the hate side of this. Does anyone actually like this rubbish mechanism? Anyone? You do? Why? Maybe you can expla... oh nostalgia... ok, so is there anything ACTUALLY good about it? No? Didn't think so... shall we all get over this nonsense and finally move on?
2) They happen an awful lot and Lone Wolf seems completely ill-prepared and completely out-matched, it's a miracle he makes it through any battle. Also, so much randomness... again a fail-over over from JRPGs... at some point people will look back and go "You know those Final Fantasy games came out at the same time as Planescape: Torment and Baldurs Gate and were immensely lame in comparison... why are we still copying them?" Well... I don't know why anyone wanted to copy them instead of PT and BG in the first place, but who knows... maybe the dumbed down/random infuriating and thus dull reloading/restarting is for some people in the world that have nothing better to do. I however, want a game that has play-tested, balanced, and isn't JRPG. I'm sure even the patience of a Saint would be tried and have him throwing a controller around in frustration.
3) All icons have cooldown on them... er... I have a cooldown on basic Attack/Defend? WHAT THE DICKINS?!?
Who thought that was a good idea? Find them and give them a good slapping with a large wet fish.
4) I have next to no endurance, and i'm completely useless without any of it... and it takes endurance to drink an edurance potion... er... ok... we'll chalk this one up on "Dumb Ideas".
5) And the worse part of combat is the idiot waves his arm around often obscuring the ranged combat icon making it inaccessible. And when you can't always use basic icons over and over (cooldown - on the defend icon... duh) This kind of flaw is even more unforgivable.
So, there's a great game here, that I would love to play, it would need the awful fighting mechanics to be ripped out and replaced with something less utterly appalling.

So, Stellaris. I absolutely adore this game. Since it's release, it has only improved. The more I play this game, the more I enjoy it, and I haven't even thought about modding yet. Being a total space nerd, this game is perfect for me.
It does have some weak points, though by the time of update 1.5, most of these have been resolved. My main concern would currently be with AI behavior, but the game is looking better than ever, good time to buy it together with the Utopia expansion!
Stellaris is about creating and controlling an interstellar empire, building mining stations and colonizing planets to grow your empire and compete with the other empires in the galaxy, either against AI or friends in multiplayer. In the late game, intergalatic invaders might even strike to take control!
The game is very diverse, and with the ethic, government and newly added civic system, new ways can always be found to play the game. Want to play as a Fanatical Purifier to conquer the galaxy and purge dozens of alien species? Want to be a huge Megacorporation cooperating and trading with other empires to achieve power? Want to be an Isolationist Xenophobe Monarchy, claiming massive amount of space and avoiding all contact with other empires? It's all possible in Stellaris, with many more ways to play the game, be creative!
If you like Sci-Fi or Strategy games, I would highly recommend Stellaris. If you can get it on sale that's definitely the best, but the price is still fair for the amount of entertainment you get.
Just a warning, it can get a bit addictive. Once you've started a session there are so many things to do all the time, it's hard to stop again :)
Now, go play it, go in blind if you can! It's an exciting learning experience!

Zeno Clash is, and definitely feels like a 10$ game. There's fun to be had here, but not enough to justify a purchase price of over 5$. Absolutely a game that favors style over substance.
Pros:
+ Unique and twisted artstyle
+ Fascinating concept for a game
+ Great soundtrack and beefy sound effects
+ Makes you want the drugs the devs were smoking
+ Pretty funny from time to time
+ Overall PC performance is great
Cons:
- The combat is alright (when it actually works), but it just feels... unresponsive and clunky. Managing more than two enemies at once is practically impossible, because each enemy requires a specific move/dodge for each individual attack, but the game only registers blocks from one enemy. What this means is that you'll be trying to block three incoming attacks, the game will think you're trying to block only one, while the other two land their punches and drain your health. It forces you to A: Run in circles around them and go for fast attacks like a headless chicken, or B: Use a gun (wich also sucks, but I'll get to that later). Fighting several enemies at the same time is just not fun (a melee combat game like Condemned did crowd control right). Mix that with some enemies wich use some really annoying tactics and moves and the fact that the game often thinks you want to kick instead of punch (wich can get you killed, and also some guy though mapping several attacks to one button was a smart idea), the combat just becomes mediocre at best.
- I've played short games, I've played REALLY short games and then I've played zeno clash, wich lasted about 2,5 hours...
- The story is not nearly as deep as advertized. Don't expect much from it
- Practically the most linear game I've ever played, the entire game is a slightly disguised corridor
- The shooting (yes, there are ranged weapons in the game) is underwhelming at best, but sadly what you'll spend most of your time doing, since fighting multiple blokes in hand to hand combat is a pain in the butt
- The bosses (even the final boss) are copy pasted at least twice, and they quickly get boring
- I got such a bad headache from playing this! You know why? Because there's no f#*!ing FOV slider!
I can't really reccomend it unless you REALLY enjoy twisted artstyles, or you want a game to play while hitting the bong.

, also known as Man of Prey, is a title which has a very soft spot in my gamer heart. There are some minor bugs, the story cutscenes are constantly freezing on modern systems and some ethical elements in the story indeed leave you behind with a raised eyebrow.
But if you've got a thing for turnbased strategy games like
or Marauder's spiritual predecessors
or
, then this game is totally for you. Because of its appealing post-apocalyptic setting even fans of
or the
series may take a look at this game.
The story, based on the same-named novel by Russian writer Berkem al Atomi, keeps you hooked for about 30 hours and is pretty unique. You control Akhmet, a Russian muslim and former army sapper, through the outskirts of a deserted city south of the Ural mountains. After a Russian political approach to NATO and the west, the US Army invades Russia under the pretext of a Peacekeeper Mission. The huge country therefore falls into chaos and soon anarchy spreads out. Akhmet and his lovely wife must now try to survive through this indeed chaotic cluster♥♥♥♥. As the game title already suggests, Akhmet does so in looting and fighting off bandits, stray dogs, corrupt policemen and even foreign soldiers. Interestingly Akhmet is not a
in the proper sense. He doesn't really care for the wellbeing of other dwellers or to bring justice all over the city. He only takes care of his family and its survival - whatever the cost. Soon he begins to fortify his apartment block against enemy raids...
Like in 7,62 High Calibre you control Akhmet from above and you can pause the game at all times. While the game is paused you can plan your next moves and give Akhmet (and later his companions) commands. Rather than taking away Action Points like in Jagged Alliance 2, all your actions require a certain amount of seconds, which will be counted down as soon as you un-pause the game. This gameplay element, called the Smart Pause Mode, may take a while to get used to it but works perfectly as soon as you progress. Once you also get your proper equipment the combat sequences are a blast - I've seldomly cheered so much while Vitek, our pro sniper in the team, scores another yet perfect headshot from hundreds of yards away. On top of that there is also a fancy skill system and upgradable character parameters. After levelling up you can invest points in better accuracy, stamina, barter skills or whatever comes in handy. The inventory, also similar to the one from the S.T.A.L.K.E.R.  series, is pretty simple and self-explanatory. In the Bazaar, the local city market, you can trade further equipment and even upgrade your weapons. Also note that, similiar to the Metro series, the local main currency in Marauder are 5.45x39mm cartridges, colloquially called «fives».
Even if all this suggests that Marauder is an open-world game, it sadly isn't. In fact the game is pretty linear and you move from one section to another while regularly returning to your house and the Bazaar. I wish the developers would had implemented more city sections back then, but even then it's an already quite immersive world.

The fluffiest tail & best Hack & Slash game I've played so far.
You play as Dust, a furry feller with amnesia, with his sidekick, Fidget, a flying female Nimbat. (Just as useful as a Fidget-spinner)
His quest is to regain his memory and save the world - Doing so will save multiple lives, but kill just as many. Actually you'll probably kill more monsters, since this is a Hack&Slash game with endless spawns of creatures to slay.
The story is great, and most of the sidequests blends well in with the main story.
The story is a mystery right up till the end, since Dust has amnesia. - However don't put this into the average amnesia hero/heroin story, where you have
The combat-system works fluently, with a lot of combos to make. Spam the keyboard and have fun.
There's also a big variety of enemies, and enemy abilities for a Hack&Slash game. Play it on the hardest mode where they one-hit kills you.
The scenery and especially backgounds are beautiful - Sometimes you can see the layers, but it's rare - The graphic is done well with smooth cutscenes & fighting effects.
Hand-drawn, just saying.
The music is powerful and you really don't get tired of it. I spend 35 hours ingame, and still return to Youtube for the soundtrack.
Different tracks for different areas, which really suits each "world", and the battlemusic is as epic as a firebreathing Pink Fairy Armadillo
Sidequests and eastereggs are in a huge abundance.
They blend well in with the story and are so enjoyable that you really need to explore every nook and cranny. Which you still do since you unlock small parts in visited areas as you gain new abilities.
However if you don't like returning to an area 2-3 times to discover 100% you won't like this grind-game.
The combat might seem repetitive - But that's to be expected, monsters respawn in areas, and you need to revisit most areas 2-3 times.
I beat this game on the normal and hardest difficulty, so it holds some replay-value, but of course it's less enjoyable when you know the story.
However if you're the type to bond with characters and get emotional, this will just be like re-reading a good book over and over again.
Slow start. It takes a little for the story and gameplay to really kick off. I actually got bored in the beginning and tried getting started 4 times on a span of half a year before I really gave it some time and attention.
Overall a solid game.
The mechanics work well with the combat-movement system, great visuals, good story and nice music.
Give it some time to really get started, and you won't even have to be a furry-fandom to enjoy this.

First off, the process of making your actual empire or choosing from one of the pre-made ones is in of itself and incredibly satisfying experience. Instead of relegating you to predertimed stats for each 'species' or portrait, the game allows you to determine what your species is actually capable of.
Nataurally I made my glorious starship-troopers ripoff federation, this time maade up of actual alien apes.
Within seconds you are greeted by your AI instructor who gives you a greeting based upon your government type, asking for what level of assistance you would like proferred. Immediately I noticed the quest system, and before this I had a history of disliking games with quest sytems but.....
This quest system WORKS. It doesn't feel scripted or intrusive, and I feel that it actually increases the level of immersion. In your typical sci-fi strategy, the whole RP or national crises that would arise were often cold logical wars over predetermined resources, with a very artificial feel.
In Stellaris, the quests feel as though they are things that aren't just shoved in your face for a tutorial or credits, they are as much a part of the lore of your playthrough as anything. For example, my military republic ape people got a quest where they had to retrieve old sub-light sattelites before the dirty xenos got them. I won't spoil it, but the questline is MUCH more complex than you might be led to believe by the initial prompt.
In other words, You can practically have your own in-depth space opera, and with modding, have it feature any species you could dream of.
Combat is simple yet effective and fluid. Story is a little basic, but I liked it so meh.

It takes audacity to make a half finished game, get bad reviews for it, make a trailer making fun of the people who left the bad reviews, and not improve on anything that people criticized.
Cortex Command is probably the first game online that I became starry-eyed over, I bought it before it was on steam and sat on it thinking "this is really incomplete, but boy it's going to be great one day!". That day never came.
This came before early access but still feels like it's a hastily put together early access title. It has this nostalgic "old PC freeware" polish to it that I do like, but the core features of the game being blatantly over-promising similar to newer titles creates a jarring experience where the player feels the negatives of both without the positives of either. You have a ton of half finished amazing (but over-optimistic for the scope of the game, admittedly) ideas that are disappointingly hollow, combined with clunky and frustrating controls that leave you feeling powerless.
Don't bother.

There has to be some appeal to the idea that one person taking out a group of bad guys in style is 'A grade' material for a lot of different kinds of media, whether it be movies or games. The thrill of one highly trained operative taking on the world never gets old, and being in the shoes of one is better. Video games are a perfect way to put the player in the spot and what better way to do this then in F.E.A.R.
now F.E.A.R is what you get if you combine "the raid" with "the ring", a beautiful ballet of♥♥♥♥♥kicking action with themes of the supernatural. It has some good set pieces and level design even if it's linear, the levels are still wide enough for experimentation. But let's get down to the details.

The core gameplay is based on close quarter shooting and the use of your reflexes. The reflexes aspect make the game go into slow motion for making more accurate shots and better judgment in areas around you. The reflexes are really well designed and might I say this, if shooting a guy then grabbing his gun in mid air to shoot at another  guy doesn't appeal to you then you probably should stop reading this. It even lets you see the special effects differently then what you would see without the reflexes, like Explosions warping the area around them. The guns in this game are pretty amazing if not overdone on purpose. It may not make sense that a sub-machine gun with an mp5 mag have 50 rounds and a fire rate the same as a mini-gun but that's the whole point.  Oh yeah and even the way you kill people can be cool as well. Especially the shotgun that shreds people into piecies, and a particle smasher that literally turns enemies into skeletons
I also have to say that the AI are really smart, they give orders to each other during battle and try to get the drop on the player in ways that the player would never guess. They even work with each other to flank and get to better positions to stop the player dead. I played this on hard and if I didn't have reflexes I would have never beaten the game.
In summary the whole thing is suppose to be a stupid but enjoyable action game that doesn't take itself too seriously, (well maybe the story). Don't think too hard about why a flying kick does more damage than a gunshot to the head, it's all for mechanics sake to make an enjoyable game without ruining it for the story.

Now if you have been reading this and you read the words "well maybe the story" I'll tell you right now that it's interesting, but not amazing. The story goes that you are an operative of F.E.A.R  and have to stop an army of psychedelic cloned soldiers that can communicate telepathically. Avoiding the games obvious moral
the game tries to be like bioshock in the twist of the story, but is delivered very poorly. It even tries to do the horror elements but with most twits, (including me) its actually quite hard to scare someone who's behind a monitor especially playing as a guy who can take care of himself in an end of world scenario. But don't ignore the game for the story, do it for the gameplay, that what the developers were trying to do.

There is not really much to say about the negatives in this game, Unless you call the mixed feelings of the story negative. Well a couple I could really think of is the characters. In one scene you meet up with a lady operative and one of the nameless F.E.A.R soldiers who's with her and all join up in a room with the ceiling drenched in blood. She wasn't even scared about it, including the git with her and I thought they were literally clones in disguise. But no that was her and it's never brought up again.
So the character building is bad except for the fat guy wearing a flower shirt and the antagonist. If the story was given to Bioware they would push this under the carpet and make a good story, probably with an option to bone one of the team members.
but the biggest one there is, is that theres no mission select, and take it from me. If you want to replay the missions,
, you'll thank me later.
It's a really good first person action game and I could also go on to the music and physics in the game to make more positive remarks but know this. If taking down a team of soldiers with the skill and accuracy of a hopped up cs:go player on adrenaline shots is appealing then go play this. It's cheap, it even has two expansion packs and a lot of hours of content to play and I cannot recommend it enough. If fighting is not your thing and you want a good story or tackle a situation differently, go play deus ex or the old thief series.
If nothing I said is appealing then go outside because you are clearly someone's who takes to much advice from fox news.

Initially purchased this because I had played the Wiiware version to completion some time ago, and with my console now dead wanted to return to the FF franchise in general.
Positives
1) The story, as far as I've gotten, is for the most part unchanged up to the first visit to Mysidia. A good thing, they're selling this mostly off nostalgia after all.
2) The Band system went a little deeper with bands increasing in strength with continued usage. A nice quirk but not something I delved too deeply into before anyway.
3) We do see the original FF4 cast once the prologue is concluded. Again, nostalgia sales
That said there are a few negatives...
1) Graphics: while not usually a graphical snob this seems to use the same engine as the FF4 DS remake, which was released a few years back, And those weren't top level back then. Yes it makes it playable on a potato but screams of getting the most money for the least effort possible.
2) Sound:  Voice acting present in the DS FF4 and it's re-release on steam is conspicuous by it's absence, this combined with the cut out of background music in 3/4 scenes already leaves text boxes and the click of keys as the only way of being immersed, FF games are renowned for their music so this is disappointing.
3) Controls/Gameplay: I put these together because otherwise I'd repeat myself, the core gameplay is unchanged the ATB system returns with a vengeance and is as gripping as before, but there are no mouse controls. At all. Menus both battle and otherwise are entirely controlled with directional button commands. I don't own a controller for PC yet, though one is on order but I like to play my PC games on my PC not as a glorified console.
On the whole I'll likely finish the game because I loved the original version I played but if you are looking for games that stand up against modern competition? look elsewhere.

Metagaming is becoming an important niche and I am glad that a somewhat popular mobile game is finally arriving on Steam, to introduce itself to a much wider audience on PCs. I’m talking of Draw Your Game, naturally. Free to play, along with annoying ads and waiting times on Android & iOS, now quite trouble-free on the PC platform after a single purchase and already featuring over a dozen custom levels from creative players. It’s the personification of replay value within indie gaming. The Steam debut for Zero One, yet they successfully ported their sleeper hit.
The story is orbiting around you, the player and potential content creator. You get to make your own “story” in Draw Your Game, just as the name suggest so eloquently. In case you’re like me (anti-talent when it comes to drawing/painting or playing a musical instrument) you can rest assured that this title still features nearly 100 skillfully crafted levels. Short and sweet, yet some will test your patience and reflexes like I’ve come to expect from any noteworthy platformer. This open-ended narrative structure is subject to quite a lot of interpretation. Each person can think of something entirely different in regards to Draw Your Game. Common ground is represented by the fun factor and huge potential for replayability through custom levels.
Same as the mobile versions, the PC variant is also powered by the Unity Engine. Fonts and textures scale perfectly, even if you’re playing at 4K resolution while the frame rate shall never suffer from drops. A unique feature which you don’t see everyday in platformers, is the option to rapidly switch from 2D to 3D perspectives within the leves themselves. I can only recall seeing this option in the Evoland series, but its wasn’t as seamless as the transition in Draw Your Game. Once I “discovered” the 3D switch, I never went back to 2D unless I wanted to compare the graphical fidelity between dimensions.
Nothing spectacular yet it certainly was more enjoyable than the sound assets we’re treated to, in most indie platformer cases. Obviously no voice acting, since those stick figures and drawn avatars aren’t very chatty. At all.
There are 99 official levels so far. Seven for each of the first 14 seasons and a final one for the 15th. Apart from the different visual style, Draw Your Game did remind me of BADLAND: Game of the Year Edition’s gameplay flexibility and the freedom to create new custom stages. At least on the mobile versions since on PC BADLAND, that has yet to happen. But I digress. The title I’m reviewing today is as open as a book and allows all its players to dip their toes in a little amateur drawing session. Or skilled, if they just happened to be really determined to project their own vision within Draw Your Game. It may not even be that time consuming, yet I prefer to judge this title for its official levels.
Interesting choice, to further separate the stages into “seasons”. Since I never played the mobile version (I seldom play on my smarthphone) I can only imagine that it must have been a thorough work-in-progress. At least the dev team waited long enough for the Steam edition, until they had a lot of quality content to justify the price tag. They didn’t just release a handful of levels along with an Early Access label. I respect that. So what are the objectives, apart from the charm of creating your own game levels from converted drawings? Well the stick figures and subsequent avatars which represent either miniaturized animals or fictional characters, have to either traverse a level from one end to another or touch/reach certain blue objects as fast as they can.
Each level has a rating and a maximum of three stars can be achieved per stage. The reward system in the form of coins, seems to be a nearly irrelevant legacy from the mobile versions which relied on them to “speed things up” or perhaps employed an in-game store? I won’t even bother checking this out and I shall refrain from expressing my thoughts relating to microtransactions. I’m sure you can guess them anyway. As mentioned, Blue is an objective or helper or sorts. Green signals a trampoline-like object (what’s  a platformer, without epic platform jumping?) and as expected, Red is a foe which upon touch, hinders your efforts and forces a level restart. Basic chromatic rules and the white backgrounds do provide an adequate contrast to the black borders which limit the extent of the level itself.
Despite a small install size, I’d say that the game certainly has a lot to show for it. The Achievements seem easy enough to unlock and the very fact that you can always download a new custome stage after you’re done with the official ones, adds significant value to this unconventional platformer. Whether you play it in 2D or 3D, draw and adapt your own ideas or test out the proven levels forged by others, one thing is clear: Draw Your Game is a fun and relaxing experience.
+ Steam Achievements.
+ Plenty of official levels to play already.
+ Huge potential for user-created content.
+ Interesting switch between 2D/3D perspectives.
- Gameplay “legacy” from its mobile counterparts.
- No Steam Trading Cards.

If you purchase/obtain this game or own it on Steam without the patch, please download the free
mod available from Steam. It upgrades the graphics, makes the textures MUCH higher-resolution, fixes bugs, and generally and specifically in other ways makes
a much more modern experience without removing the charm of the original game. Even old-timers like me appreciate the improvements and those younger gamers who can't stomach the old graphics or controls of the original game will find DX:REVISION much more palatable. Yeah, there's still text to read. Yeah, there are still more ways to complete each level than you're probably thought of yet. Yeah, this depicts a future time when all conspiracy theories are part of reality, just like the original DX did.
The only thing that would make it better without a complete rewrite is the original fold-out paper pack-ins from the boxed game.
Some people in 2011 have a problem with DX from 2000 because it used the Unreal 1 engine and the sky/ground textures are low-resolution. I didn't have a problem with that because, if I were playing as if I were JC Denton, I wouldn't waste time looking at distant city lights mapped onto the skybox. Having them visible at all was a bonus.
I thought it was awesome; I've played through it many, many times since the first release. I still hear the Hong Kong music in my head when I think about it because I've spent so many hours over the years running back and forth through that portion of the game. Heh. After I got a 3DFX card and was able to see the 3D-accelerated version's enhanced effects (Ooh! Shiny floors at UNATCO HQ, and I can play in a higher res than 320x240 / 512x384!), replaying was just that much more fun! Choosing different paths, favoring different factions, playing to the different endings, etc., gave DX a LOT of replayability, and the game is never too long!

If you're looking for an RPG with a ton of customization, unique skills, epic graphics, and other frills in the modern era of RPGs - this is not that game.
If, however, you adore the FF4 Storyline, have a huge amount of nostalgia for the game, or simply want to relive how you felt in the 90s when you played the game back on a cartridge - give this game a try.
This game can pretty much be summed up in a nutshell as Fan Service to those people who loved the original FF4.  There are moments in the game where you'll say "Oh - I remember that!", or you'll remember secret chests from the original game that have been painstakingly replaced in the sequel; a reward for FF4 veterans.
The combat system and abilities are essentially the same from the original game, so don't expect to see any amazing breakthroughs or revolutions in gameplay.  This game is a homage to the late NES/Early SNES style of RPG; and it faithfully recreates that feeling.

.Story.
This is a world where technology is incredibly advanced. There are androids, the Naka, which are so technologically advanced that they are able to learn and do anything.
You are Ghost, a special agent with the power to possess any robot. You’ve been hired by two nerds in order to steal the AI source code for the Nakamura bots.
Mission commence.
The story is told via cut scenes that are fully voice acted and slightly animated. You’ll be given bits of story as you explore the Nakamura’s innards and also for completing tasks such as gathering pieces of key cards. More on that later.
.Gameplay.
I have a lot to say here. Bottom line: the gameplay is smooth and responsive and the power up aspects are very well put together. They make the punishing difficulty a little more palatable while also spicing up normal gameplay in clever and quirky ways that just make you feel powerful.
You use WASD to move and your mouse to aim and shoot. Space bar allows you to jump and the numerical keys 1-4 allow you to use the items assigned to your hot bar. You can dodge roll if you first crouch with S and then press either A,D or, CTRL.
You can also exit your chassis via R, which allows you to float around in your ghost form. If you get close to any other robot, you can possess them by pressing R again. Be careful, however, because enemies will sense that their allies have been possessed and will immediately move to destroy your borrowed form. This is used to solve a variety of puzzles and, after you’ve added some skill points to the Ghost skill tree, you can do cool things like stun the enemy.
The Skill Tree is one of my favourite part of the game. There are five possible categories to improve: Chassis (your primary robot), Boogan (technical improvements), Jacker (hacking improvements) Ghost (improvements to your Ghost form), and Nakamura (improvements that affect the environment).
-Chassis—These skills add to your combat prowess, including but not limited to double jumps,
-Boogan—These skills add nifty traits like the ability to see enemy HP.
-Jacker—These skills help you during the alarms (you can trigger alarms to face waves of enemies and are rewarded with energy cubes after defeating them).
-Ghost—These skills allow your Ghost form to move faster and have additional effects on the robots you possess.
-Nakamura—These skills change aspects of the ship, including what you find in shops, rewards gotten from alarms, how many enemies can be found, etc.
There are four tiers, each of which you can unlock by placing enough points into the tier before it (5, 10, and 15 respectively with the first tier being unlocked automatically. There's also an overall benefit for each tier.
Pickups include:
-Items, which are one-time use. You can recharge them at shops by paying Energy Cubes, the in-game currency.
-Powerups, which can be enable and disabled, add effects to your base attacks and movement
-Weapons and secondary weapons, which can be bought or found.
-Upgrades, which are passive and always active. These can also be bought or rewarded by drops after collecting all of the soul fragments in a room.
-Geeks, which change up the way the game looks or reacts without changing core gameplay. For example, the Tarzan Geek makes your character howl like Tarzan when zip lining.
But back to the main game.
The ship is divided into interconnected rooms in which you’ll find enemies and/or puzzles. You can clear out rooms or run through them—your choice. You’re only required to fight if you trip an alarm, which will result in waves of enemies. After the waves are cleared, you’re rewarded with Energy Cubes, which can be used in stores to purchase upgrades, weapons, and consumable items as well as charges for those consumable items.
*Consumables stack when collected, so you can use them as many times as you have copies.
In typical metroidvania style, you face a giant boss at the end of the zone. And these baddies are tough as nails, so expect to retry a few times. After defeating the boss, you move onto the next zone and begin collecting a card key with higher security clearance (and more pieces to collect). Rinse, wash, and repeat to progress.
.Atmosphere.
The game looks great. It feels futuristic from the glowing neon effects of the machinery to the robotic enemies that you’ll face. The bots chatter amongst themselves and they’ll sometimes say funny things about your power (“If I get possessed, promise you’ll shoot me) which is a nice touch. There are also little
The music is phenomenal—the kind of upbeat, electronic tunes that one would associate with the futuristic vibe the game is going for. The kind of music you can bob your head to as you navigate the treacherous innards of the ship.
*You can buy the soundtrack separately, which is very reasonably priced at 3.99. Worth every cent.
.Longevity.
There are two game modes: classic and survival.
-Classic: This is the pure metroidvania approach. When you save at the 3D printers, all of your items—including power ups and upgrades—are saved as well. Upon dying, you only lose the items that haven’t been saved. The game also scales as you progress rather than based on the passage of time. Finally, in classic mode you are in total control of your loadout.
-Survival: This is the rogue-like option in which you lose everything upon death. In this mode the run gets harder the longer you survive rather than scaling with your progress through the game. You also spawn in with a random loadout that you build upon rather than with a clean slate.
I played classic and am at (according to the game) 37% of my playthrough with 5 hours under my belt. I suck at this type of game, but that should give you an idea of how much time you’ll spend with this game. I still have a bunch of upgrades and power ups to collect and I’m close to facing the second boss.
.Pros and Cons.
.Bottom Line.
Ghost 1.0 is a blast and it’s accessible to a multitude of skill levels. Even if you aren’t great at metroidvanias, I urge you to try this one: not only does it look great and perform well, it also has a multitude of power ups and secondary weapons that make playing a joy.
I am genuinely enjoying my time with Ghost 1.0 and I’m eager to see what the story holds for Ghost and the silly duo of hapless tech geeks that hired her.

While the game has good graphics (For a Playstation game), and one of the best soundtracks in the series, I can't really Reccomend this game for any other reason.
While the first disc of the game is Alright, the quality of the game just chugs afterwards.
The gameplay features some backwards mechanics, such as enemy scaling, in which enemies level up with you, but the problem is that in the end, that feature will punish you for grinding. Limit breaks can be spammed with the Aura spell or if your character is at low health, so not healing is rewarded. And the Draw system allows you to get some insanely high stats by just immobilizing the enemy and casting draw. Magic becomes less of an offensive/Support option and more of equipment with the Junction system, which will punish you for using your Magic (Assuming you don't Draw more)
The story becomes an absolute trainwreck after Disc 1, with an incredibly forced and sappy love story, and very confusing time shenanigans. The most interesting Characters are only playable for small portions of the game, and the flashbacks amount to very little by the end of the game. In an RPG, a genre traditionally based around story, this game is probably the weakest in the franchise, only ahead of Final Fantasy I and III.
All in all, I can only reccomend this game to Diehard Final Fantasy Fans, if you want fun gameplay, stick to FFVII, and if you want a good story, go to FFIX.

This is about the journey; not the endgame. Enjoy the stunning beauty and contemplate the story's meaning.
I went in with the wrong mindset. I was ready for boss fights or something like Subnautica, and I was annoyed that there wasn't much to do. About 2/3 of the way through, I realized my mistakes.
My suggestion is to take your time and hit the Shift and Space buttons often.  Explore everything.  Touch the wildlife.  Have fun gliding gracefully with no worries about oxygen or energy consumption.  It isn't a race.  You won't die.
I liked that this wasn't pretentious like EA tends to be with their realistic cinematics ("Hey, look at me!  I can make this long boring bus ride look real!" *cough Lifeisstrange *cough*).  The artistic creativity of ABZU flowed flawlessly throughout every part of the game.  My usual motion sickness didn't bother me.  I felt connected to the characters and environment.  There was just enough fantasy/sci-fi/mystery to balance it out.  It's an unconventional game but worth the price and time.

I had actually put this game on the backburner for a few years and had mostly forgotten about it until cleaning out my backlog. I finally decided to pick it up and was reminded of the really interesting and well-designed fantasy world that originally had interested me. And then I was reminded of some of the most ponderous and awkward combat in gaming.
It's not much of a shooter, so I'll just say there's an endless supply of ammo for ranged weapons, but damage is typically pokey and reloading slows your character's movements to a crawl. Couple this with the same button for blocking being the THROW YOUR WEAPON AS FAR AWAY AS POSSIBLE (even with melee weapons), you can see how this gets ridiculous.
There are a wide variety of moves at your disposal, which is engaging, all of them activated in combos or by aiming higher or lower in relation to your enemies. Despite this, enemies will often phase through many of them while carrying out their own combat animations. The game locks melee weapons level with the ground, which is a bit disorienting when trying to get your bearing, and it locks your empty hands during unarmed combat within a 45 degree angle that makes it difficult to aim attacks toward larger enemies.
Moving too close to an enemy auto-locks you into engaging them, which can only be broken by running backward. Supposedly this is an aspect of the game's difficulty, but taking on multiple enemies who auto-lock you into one-on-one combat gets immediately frustrating when the most functional method of combat is just flinging fists. Furthermore, locking onto enemies makes it nearly impossible for you to aim to the left or right of them, which prevents most of your defensive techniques.
Later on, you'll learn counterattacks and deflection, but the window of activation for any of these is both bizarre and variable by enemy. In one instance you'll have to deflect on your enemy's wind-up. For another enemy, it'll be right before it hits you. Good luck guessing which is which. Also, activating counterattack is fairly finicky by design, since it's coded that enemies can sometimes ignore/dodge a successful counterattack based on arbitrary conditions.
All in all, it's an interesting experiment in game design but the parts never quite congeal into a likeable whole.

This is the epitome of 2D action platformers to me. The fact that you can choose to play it as a rogue-like, or in a classic linear playthrough mode is just brilliant. It's got some RPG elements, along with utterly gorgeous pixel-art style graphics. The voice-acting is actually on-point (not gonna lie, that surprised me) with some good banter between the characters.
The gameplay doesn't pull any punches either - it's not a casual shooter. The 3 core difficulty modes offer enough variance too, so that it's not just a ±0.01% damage spread or the likes. There are appreciable changes in the number of bots, and how the game plays out. There are even "insane" skills available in the standard skill-tree that will make the game harder if you choose them!
You also don't need to worry long-term about ammo, as it regenerates. However there are still a limited number of charges that each weapon will hold. So there's still a challenge there in the heat of battle, but you don't need to worry about back-tracking through 5 empty levels to get an ammo pickup. This really helps to keep the pace of the game going.
You can buy certain upgrades for your weapons (as well as earning them through certain "hidden" gameplay elements), as well as purchasing secondary weapons - you can have 3 secondaries equipped at a time to cycle through, as well as your primary weapon. Again, there's some great variety here; beam weapons, shotguns, shield guns, mine-layers, bot-spawners.
You can also earn and/or buy upgrades for your character. There are purchased passive addons that can be toggled at-will (weapon bonuses, helper bots, shields, etc), permanent character upgrades that are unlocked through gameplay (HP increases, ammo reserve bonuses, etc) and primary items that are activated via a hotbar (health regen, item magnet, ammo regen, EMP bursts etc).
The single downside in this entire game as I see it, is how sparse these primary items are. You can buy them at shops, but they're relatively expensive and the shop will only have one of them at a time. Some of the shops (though not all) will allow you to restock items you've previously purchased, and you can earn some lower-level items through some of the "hidden" gameplay mechanics. However, you still end up too worried to use them up most of the time because of how rare they are.
With that said though, this game is ultimately immense fun. It's been brilliantly crafted with great attention to detail and user-interaction; something that even a great many AAA games seem to overlook these days.

I think this might be the closest thing to a perfect example of 'Game As Art' I have ever played.
It is thought provoking. It evoked real emotion - joy, happiness, even sorrow. It asks us questions. It gives us answers. It is a journey. It tells a story.
It is just so beautiful.
All this while giving you the freedom to explore as much or as little as you desire, and providing no shortage of clever, unobtrusive hints to help guide you on your way. All the subtle attention to detail makes it all so much better. All the little things they did just right - animal behaviors, how they swim, interact with eachother, and with you. The simple, intuitive controls. The sweeping orchestral sound track weaving a tapestry of sound all around it. The almost seamless progression from one place to the next one, and how it all ties together.
The game is not perfect. It struggled at times to display full 4k at frame rates exceeding 30fps. Sometimes the controls feel wonky. Animals don't always interact perfectly with their environment, breaking the immersion. The story only takes a few hours to play through. These are all very minor gripes.
If you feel like taking a journey, exploring, or just playing something that will help you relax, this is a game for you. If you value the idea that games can be art, this game is a Must Play.

It has a quirky sense of humour, hours of fun in the story, hours more in challenge mode trying to beat waves of enemies, the ability to play multiplayer with just one copy of the game if you have a computer controller or Xbox PC adapter, and then not very expensive DLCs that add hours more fun. I’m not a Trekkie, but if you can imagine William Shatner reading those words at the start of a new game of Stellaris, continue reading.
Stellaris is, for Paradox, a new beginning in a long curriculum of strategy games. They have change Earth for the Galaxy and they have done a good game where you can invest a lot of hours just in your first game with your custom race. At the moment of this review, I have played for 33 hours just with my first race and I have seen 1/3 of the galaxy and contacted with just 6 other races.
There were some bugs at the previous versions that are fixed and the most common problem is that there are not enough events at mid-end game, but with mods this is not a real problem. Because the mod community is very active in this game.
The game, like vanilla, is pretty good: choose race, play with it just at the beginning of space era and start exploring the galaxy with your ships in one of the 3 types of engines you can travel through the galaxy: Warp, like Star Trek. Hyperjump, like Endless space.  And wormholes, like Farscape. Then, first contact with a new galactic empire, politics, alliance, war…
All this appears in it’s right moment and you don’t get bored.
But it’s really with mods, allowed and promoted by Paradox, that this game really shines: Do you want to play like Klingons, with their ships models and warp adapted to Star trek rules (3 days of cd instead of 20), fighting to Romulans, Feds and Borg?
. To play like the Tau’ri of Stargate?
. Or navigate through the space searching for Arrakis like an Atreides?
Change your ships, colors, music, rules, hud, planets, races… all you can imagine, is possible, so this game is in fact, a lot of games inside just one.
I could say more, but these points are the most important. If you like what you have read you will be in love with this game, guiding your race…

If I was not a die hard fan of Act of War, I'd give this a BAD review. I am only giving a positive review because I want the devs to make the next game in the series and do better.
Unlike the original Act of War, this one is too difficult on default difficulty. The game is very fast paced, trying to throw enemies at you from all directions and expecting you to respond quickly without actually explaining how the base building mechanics work, how units work, etc. Yes, there is a tutorial, but it is very limited.
While you try to learn by trial and error, the AI mercilessly pounds you into submission not letting you relax and breathe even for a second. There are no difficulty settings. There is only one difficulty, the default one, which is way too hard! Most missions are TIMED. Do this before the time runs out! Do that in 40 minutes or less! Destroy this in 30 min, destroy that in 30 min! You cannot take your time, explore what your units can do, build up a force and attack. You have to constantly struggle. The idea is for you to constantly build small attack forces and throw them in, hoping they will have good effect.
The story is sort of convoluted, and yet not too original or interesting. Some of the characters are very generic and forgettable. The story doesn't make me care and I just want to skip through all the "blah blah" to get to the action. The original Act of War was at least somewhat better, story wise.
Soundtrack is pretty generic and lame and doesn't really convey the feeling of conflict or war.
The saving grace of this game is the action. Units look great, the firefights are awesome, and the sound effects are adequate. No other RTS has such detailed projectile animations maybe short of "Wargame" series. The MLRS salvo is a joy to look at every time. Helicopters are awesome as well as planes. There are a myriad of awesome upgrades and abilities.
The end result is a weird convocation of overwhelming negatives fighting with some very strong positives so basically my honest opinion is something like 50/50. I am glad I paid twelve bucks. I wouldn't pay a penny more.

This is a pretty good game. I would end my review there but this game deserves it.
I never experienced FFVII as a kid, as my PlayStation broke and I never bothered to have it replaced. Had I known about this game I would've begged for another PS or tried to repair it myself.
I learned about this game over a few years of browsing YouTube and talking with some friends. I had tons of story elements spoiled for me, but it didn't matter as I played it. I'm actually glad it was spoiled because I understood certain aspects much more--probably more so if I went in blind. If you haven't wanted to buy this game because the story was spoiled for you, don't let that stop you.
The graphics... are somewhat dated, in my opinion, but there are some moments that were really great. I think of the train scene during Midgar and the final cutscenes. The best part is the music. You could probably skip playing this game and just listen to the music. Okay, as for actual gameplay, it's satisfying. The most enjoyable moments are ridiculous summons and moves that are pulled off. (If you've never heard of Super Nova, don't look it up, play the game til' the end. It's worth the wait for that one move.)
Any gripes? The keyboard layout stinks, so use a controller instead. Also, random encounters are the bane of every RPG player. You might get lost at certain parts if you don't talk with the NPC's for help, so a guide might be needed. Actually, if you want the best experience, you'll want to use a guide. Certain bosses for the main story can be ridiculous, so expect a lot of grinding. Although, if you level up too much, the bosses are jokes.
Honestly, those are nitpicks, since the rest of the game is great. Buy it now for full price! Or, if my gripes concern you, get it on sale.

If you purchase/obtain this game or own it on Steam without the patch, please download the free
mod available from Steam. It upgrades the graphics, makes the textures MUCH higher-resolution, fixes bugs, and generally and specifically in other ways makes
a much more modern experience without removing the charm of the original game. Even old-timers like me appreciate the improvements and those younger gamers who can't stomach the old graphics or controls of the original game will find DX:REVISION much more palatable. Yeah, there's still text to read. Yeah, there are still more ways to complete each level than you're probably thought of yet. Yeah, this depicts a future time when all conspiracy theories are part of reality, just like the original DX did.
The only thing that would make it better without a complete rewrite is the original fold-out paper pack-ins from the boxed game.
Some people in 2011 have a problem with DX from 2000 because it used the Unreal 1 engine and the sky/ground textures are low-resolution. I didn't have a problem with that because, if I were playing as if I were JC Denton, I wouldn't waste time looking at distant city lights mapped onto the skybox. Having them visible at all was a bonus.
I thought it was awesome; I've played through it many, many times since the first release. I still hear the Hong Kong music in my head when I think about it because I've spent so many hours over the years running back and forth through that portion of the game. Heh. After I got a 3DFX card and was able to see the 3D-accelerated version's enhanced effects (Ooh! Shiny floors at UNATCO HQ, and I can play in a higher res than 320x240 / 512x384!), replaying was just that much more fun! Choosing different paths, favoring different factions, playing to the different endings, etc., gave DX a LOT of replayability, and the game is never too long!

When you buy this game there's something you should know, it's buggy and feels unfinished. I got the game on a sale, and it's totally worth the $2.49. $10 is on the verge of being too expensive for such an unpolished game. And the translation from Russian is plain horrible. That being said, and if you are able to overlook those facts, it's a really interesting game.
You play as Akhmet, this Muslim crazy Russian Unabomber with balls as big as the great USSR, trying to survive as a marauder when the NATO invades Russia.
It's based on a book that I haven't read, so the story line is all new to me. So far, the game is challenging for many reasons. It's pretty easy to die, which makes it realistic and fun, and the translation is just horrible.
The biggest problem, as mentioned before, is the translation. Because of this, sometimes it's unclear what you are supposed to do. But it's also part of it's charm. You have no clue what are they saying, but the subtitles are ridiculous and laughable. Good Laughable.
You are called by many names by other characters, but by far my favorite is "beard".
"Hey, beard! Entrance ain't free. Gimme a five!"
Dealing with the traders is a constant source of laughter:
"Are you ill, my friend?"
"What the ♥♥♥♥ are you?"
"I'm a doctor. Was a surgeon in the hospital before, and doing the same here. Name's Gennady. So what bothers you?"
"I'm as strong as an ox. But pills could be useful. You have something for sale?"
Akhmet is cocky, but because he can. He's the soviet Muslim Chuck Norris. It feels like they just added the language to make it more bad♥♥♥♥♥ as there is NO REASON to be rude to this poor guy. Other characters use all kinds of profanities as well, just for the sake of it.
Afer the missions you go home back to your nagging wife. You are a lethal weapon with a heart of gold. All the killing you do, you do it to provide. That includes killing hobos and starving neighbors if they get on your way.
The game plays like many other tactical games, with a pause trigger that brings the game to a halt when an event requires your attention (No active task, enemy spotted, enemy heard, relevant object on your field of view, etc).
It has RPG elements, especially in character leveling, where you can choose perks and specializations. There's some dialog options, but that's about it.
The AI seems pretty weak. So far I've been able to use doors and let them come to take care of most of them. As long as they don't come in mobs, it's pretty simple to get a slug through their chests. But it's always more fun to go on the hunt with your big iron balls and show them who's boss.
The levels are kinda small but they really immerse you in the game world.
Overall, worth trying it out...for the right price.

Dust is a beautiful game, with obvious care taken into character designs and movements. A hack n slash platformer, the simple combos and strikes feel statisfying with a gradual increase in difficulty as the game progresses.
Pros:
-Characters are lovable and dialogue is fun
-Story is good, all commonly used tropes yet it still feels fresh and interesting
-There are four aspects to upgrade, so you can more or less customize your build. I put most of my upgrades into attack and special attacks, so my play style was combos on combos to avoid being hit, since one hit could knock me down to half or even kill me
-Short enough of a game that you don't feel like you have to put in a ton of time, yet long enough that its a concise story
Cons:
-Save points are strategetically placed, which means on some levels it is a couple of rooms before you find another one. I found the mountains to be particularly difficult with this and was constantly running from encounters to prevent myself from dying
Neutral:
- Some people like this, others don't; Usually a fatal hit doesn't kill you right away, but brings you down to 1HP. This gives you time to heal before the enemy attacks again. I consider this a pro because I'm not a hardcore player and I have slow reaction time, so I have a chance to heal before I die.
I highly recommend Dust!

This was a great game! I loved it all the way through. I have to admit when I heard that you had pretty much the same weapon the entire game only with some augments to said weapon, I thought it was gonna be a bland game but it was far from it.
First, let's get through some positives. The graphics are amazing. I normally keep graphics as something I talk about later but damn, its presentation was beautiful. I mean every frame of every movement was beautifully animated. Plus I love how they also animated the backgrounds as well. Its not something I'd say is new in games but the effort was still very much appreciated. Next, I like how smooth the controls are. In a MetroidVania game such as this, there will be moments where it will go from a clear room to an instant barrage of enemies in the next so clear, easy controls are always a must in these kinds of games. That's another thing about it, the progression of difficulty never felt like it took a giant leap like other games I've played recently like Guacamelee or Ducktales: Remastered. The progression here was natural. The story, the acting, they're all right. Not great and not really a lot of stand out performances but they weren't bad either. I'll admit, the twist that comes later in the story was actually quite interesting. It kind of show itself in small parts throughout the game where you can make this decision or that decision.
Now, the negatives. The whole decision making aspect is not really made a giant part of the game's story except for small parts here and there. If it were played into more, I think it would have made the twist more impactful. Another is that this game seems to crash when on my old Mac system. It worked fine prior but once it got to the final boss battle and cutscene, the game would instantly crash. The people in the forums did their best to help but nothing. I only got to see the ending once I got my new Windows laptop for Christmas lol. So this is really only a game meant to be played on Windows for less issues but even then I heard some Windows users had the same problems I did.
Final verdict: GET IT! Great game with only technical issues really holding me back from getting it. The whole decision making thing can be put aside because overall, the game is just fun to play and pick up. If you can do that, then it's definitely worth a look.

A very fun and well-polished Metroidvania style game. Ghost 1.0 lets you play as a female cyborg infiltrating a space station and engage in every aspect of what you'd expect from a Metroidvania title - non-linear exploration, powerups and equipment, and so on.
The gameplay is a smooth ride. The combat is fun, the controls are great, enemies pose a good challenge, and the level design is well done. You are even able to leave your cyborg body as a ghost and possess other machines, which forms the basis of many of the game's puzzles. I really enjoyed all the puzzles the game had as they were intuitive and made sense in the context. In addition to all the combat and puzzles, you acquire skill points throughout the game, which allow you to gain passive upgrades of your choice. The game also has a tonne of different secondary weapons (which you need to buy in the in-game shops), each of which adds spice to combat and lets you tackle on the challenges with a different flavour.
It's a little bit slow at the start, because dying causes you to lose all the collectible cubes that act as money, meaning the more you die, the less you are able to upgrade, which forces you to grind. Gladly this gets smoothened out in latter stages of the game as you gain upgrades that allow you to start with some cubes upon respawn.
The game has stunningly beautiful visuals, which give each level their own unique feel, and the music is also fun to listen to. There are also plenty of cutscenes with fun dialogue conversations between the main character and the two hacker guys who are on the line helping you. Their personalities have been developed very well and the humour gives the game a nice light-hearted flavour.
Although the overarching story isn't mindblowing, it is still a fun ride. I especially like how when you come back to the game, it gives you a 'Previously on Ghost 1.0...' and brings you up to speed on the most recent events. I thought it was a great touch and isn't something I've seen in any game before. Everything in the game creates immersion, such as dying is all normal in the game world and your cyborg simply gets re-printed with 3D printers. Sometimes you even get cutscenes and dialogue during some deaths, such as one which even hinted at a solution for me to try. It's all executed very well and with great presentation.
There is only one part of the game that I absolutely detested and which seems to be disliked by many other players too. Without giving away any spoilers, the part happens in late game and completely pulls you out of the main space station map, removes all your upgrades and weapons temporarily, and takes you to a whole new area to do a very linear and frustrating stealth infiltration platforming section which forces you to be extremely precise with your timing and jumps. EDIT: This part of the game has now become skippable. The dev has been very attentive to player feedback in the community hub and making necessary adjustments to make the game as fun as possible, which is always a huge plus in my books.
In general, I would highly recommend the game to anyone who likes Metroidvanias or 2D platformers in general. The game is of a very high standard for its modest price.

Ghost 1.0 is a metroidvania rougelike developed by people with a good sense of humor. Only about an hour or so in with 18% of the map explored and I am feeling things I have only felt since the last 2D metroid I played, which was fusion so many years ago.
While Nintendo may have forgotten people love these types of games, the developers of Ghost 1.0 put polish and creativity behind their take on a genre that is loved by many.
First things first: when starting out, you will need a controller unless you are a keyboard wizard. This is because you can freely aim and shoot while moving in another direction using the right analogue stick. "Ghost" moves swiftly and controls beautifully when she is in her android body and outside of it as well.
The greatest feature for navigating or even scouting ahead is using Ghost's ability to leave her battle chassis and take over an enemy or worker android body. You can eliminate foes, collect energy for the purchase of weapons, and solve puzzles this way.
Everything is very intuitive, the game plays like a dream, and I am wondering how I missed out on this excellent game.
If you loved or still love Metroidvania type games or Metroid style games in general this game will be worth your time.

Heh, so this thing is getting panned by critics pretty hard and I'm kinda surprised at that.
I am a casual trash solo RTS player. I have neither the time nor inclination to jump into a PvP environment on what is essentially an extremely complicated chess set that you have to manage economics on... so perhaps the criticisms for multiplayer are completely warranted, I wouldn't know.
Campaign and skirmish however... heck, I love this game. Perhaps it wouldn't hold up as a streamlined competitive environment, as a system in which players prove their superiority over each other... I love it the same way I did my action figures and Micro Machines when I was a kid.
It's commonly compared to C&C: Generals, and I can see why, but honestly it pulls more of a vibe from Command & Conquer (1995.. C&C 1 I suppose you could call it). The low-res newscasts, the pumping techno soundtrack, the five minutes in the future setting, the teeensy tiny infantry.  Which brings me to my next point;
This probably doesn't make an effect on 90% of Steam users, being all jaded by modern graphics, but I thought the level of detail in the scenery was awesome. (Granted, there are a lot of really well made RTS's out now for proper fans of the genre). Having every single block of suburbia modeled to perfection (and then plowing through it with tanks), fulfills some almost-buried 8 year old power fantasy of mine.
In fact I probably shouldn't admit it, but given the fact that most of this game's maps are representing anytown USA (instead of some war torn hamlet or wilderness), the backgrounds are rather bright and cheerful... and to be perfectly frank the Cartel is almost a copy paste of Cobra, in my mind this is the Sunbow-era GI-Joe game Hasbro will never ever give us...

HOLY JESUS BEAUTIFUL GAME. The seascapes are gorgeous and have so many creatures for you to discover. The music really drives the game and along with vibrant colors and lighting, the game conveys so much despite there being no dialogue. Overall, the feels you experience during your journey make this game definitely worth your while. Try playing it with moody lighting.

You get to blow space pirates up. In space.
Welcome to Stellaris. The year is 2200 and your species has just discovered Faster than Light travel. It is time to spread out your influence across the galaxy. You meet a group of xenophobes next door, and they immediately invade you because you're like, invading their personal space. So you counterinvade them and enslave them all. Your new space allies are a bit skeptical that you just exterminated an entire race of intelligent space-goers, but what can they do? Break their alliance and declare war on a superpowered human player? You can't even remember the name of the empire you just crushed, and you certainly don't care about your weak allies either.
Let's talk the cons first:
Stellaris suffers from a lack of personality, especially when compared to Paradox's other historical strategy games. This is a problem with 4X Games as a whole, so it wouldn't be fair to compare it to their other games, one of which is literally about characters with personalities, however, I often find myself feeling lost in a space full of weird-looking humans who aside from appearance, are barely alien at all.
Gameplay wise, strategy and diplomacy are suffering a lot in this game. It is very barebones, even for a 4X game, and diplomacy can be chalked up to, if other empire is a xenophobe, they won't like you and won't make trade deals with you. If other empire is not a xeonphobe, do some trading. Trading with what? The only real resources you have are plentiful and universal; other empires often don't have anything worth trading that isn't a spare energy bank for when you build up a gigantic space fleet and can't support it all on your own. Speaking of space fleets, combat is very lackluster, as what often happens is the nation with the biggest doomstack wins. 1 big battle and the war is over. Done.
Pros: There is a lot of potential in this game. All of the things I listed above can be easily fixed in patches, and there are patches coming out already that look to address some of the major complaints that people have with this game. There is a lot of individual empire customization too, and you can tailor the galaxy's size to your making. If you have an imagination (I don't when it comes to sci-fi), you can easily fill in the personality gaps with stories if you can keep track of all the names in the galaxy.
Plus, what's not to love about setting up custom empires and watching Space Nazis and Space Communists duke it out amongst man-eating mullosks?
In conclusion: A bit barebones at the moment, but there is an excellent foundation for improvement in the future.

Act of Aggression (Reboot) is seriously worth consideration if you are looking for something Similar to Red Alert 2 which is  better than Red Alert 3.
Act of Aggression has a steep learning curve and is extremely unforgiving.  The game might be slow paced at first, but make any tactical error or bad build order choice early on and it will haunt you relentlessly.  Initally the game was not much fun to play at all, but gradually as the play mechanics and general nuances became more familiar the game became more fun to play.
The AI in skirmish mode can be downright brutal (even at the "Very Easy" setting) and expect to lose the first few matches horribly.
This game sits somewhere in the middle ground between C&C Red Alert 3 and Company of Heroes 2.  While not as good as Red Alert 2 Act of Aggression is sadly the closest thing you can play if you are running windows 10.
Alternative games to look at include:
Command and Conquer 3
Command and Conquer 3 Kanes Wrath
Dawn of War
Dawn of War 2
Age of Mythology
Age of Empires 2
Rise of Nations 2
Rise of Legends
Warcraft 2
Warcraft 3
Starcraft
Starcraft 2
All things considered Act of Agression is a reasonable game but is far from perfect.  The game has really good graphics and decent sound effects.  The music is reasonable but not as iconic or memorable as the thumping tracks on Red Alert 2.
Players who are willing to climb the steep learning curve and invest a few hours will be rewarded with a fun and challenging gaming experience.  While the game does not warant consideration at full price, it is certainly worth getting when it is on special or offered at a good discount.

Marauder, aka "Man of Prey", can be best described as Jagged Alliance/Frozen Synapse  meets Homefront transplanted to Russia. You play Ahmed, a former Red Army soldier, now retired just trying to eek out a living. The local army have deserted in the face of advancing NATO "peacekeepers". As a "marauder", Ahmed will be looting the local warehouses, deal with any one who gets in his way, loot any useful items (including clothing, weapons, and other items that can be useful) sell and trade items, and basically survive and perhaps, find a way to get rid of the invaders.
At its heart, Marauder is a turn-based tactical combat sim with simultaneous move phases. When not in combat, you may move about the map freely, looking for boxes to open or smash for loot inside (some locked boxes have to be forced). Enemies nearby triggers combat mode, where you plan your move, (kneel/crouch, aim this direction, hasty shot, for example) each of which takes a certain amount of time, and you only have so much in a single turn. Enemies will do the same. And if you manage to see each other, then they will shoot, and so on, based on complex combat formula such as weapon condition, relative movement, luck, and so on.
The game is EXTREMELY difficult until you understand the combat mechanics, and how to setup ambushes properly so you take minimal damage (or none) in the combat phases, as well as knowing where the loot are. I think I have died about 15-20 times just in the end of the first mission (where you, with a shotgun and maybe a pistol, encounter three army deserters with pistols)  because I kept getting flanked or not doing the ambush right. But once you do, you felt as if you accomplished something.
If you like your tactical games with a challenge, get Marauder (i.e. Man of Prey).

To truly appreciate Dust: An Elysian Tail, one has to absolutely read up on the development of this game. It is not wrong to give full credit to the creator, Dean Dodrill, for this remarkable game. Granted, the voice acting, music and sound design were provided for by the individual voice talents and by HyperDuck SoundWorks, but absolutely everything else (the conceptualisation of the idea; the art; the animation; the programming; the game mechanics and gameplay; the majority of the story; the publishing; the advertising; the sourcing of capital and funding) are all done by just Dean Dodrill alone! Having actually studied and dabbled in 2D and 3D animation myself, I salute Mr. Dodrill for having the perseverence of seeing this project through in its entirety. Truly, it is a feat of incredible talent that a rare few possess in this day and age. This was a journey that took three and a half years to complete, with the end result being a game that was borne from a labour of love and passion, and it shows!

text: I remember the early 2000s, my dad turned an under the stair pantry into a small ply-wood computer room. I was a young boy maybe 5-ish and i would sit on my dads knee and watch him play games. I would watch him play WoW, Day of Defeat and most importantly Garrys Mod. He loved Sandbox and I would watch him LAN his work friends and build kooky contraptions. Fast forward from then to a couple years and im playing GMod all the time on my dads computer, im building contraptions and getting banned for being an annoying squeaker (thats where I got my user name). Fast forward to 5 years ago and I get a Steam account for the very sole purpose of buying GMod, I never intended to get other games it just happened. Now its 2014 and ive meet my still best friend on a middle school field trip. I wanted someone to play GMod with so I asked him to get a Steam account. He was once athlete now turned full blown gamer and we still play GMod all the time. Fast forward to now and when people see my hours played they know I am The One with No Life. Why GMod is still relevent is that literally you can do anything. When I load it up I still get the excited chill that I had in that computer room. GMod has always been a staple in Steam, everybody owns it. Its a game you can play with friends, by yourself, you can shoot movies and direct competitions. It means a lot to my childhood but unlike legos and Christmas you dont really grow out of it. I still find myself starting a game to go♥♥♥♥♥♥around. Im pretty sure everyone on Steam already owns GMod but if you dont I cant recommend it enough. Your friends who play games probably own it too so you are missing out on a lot of fun.

Ghost 1.0 is almost certainly one of the best Metroidvanias on Steam, a game with massive scope, professional graphics and full VO among other things. Despite being an indie game it feels like it could easily be a title published by CAPCOM. Easily worth the MSRP if you have interest in Mega Man or Metroid style 2D games.
The only thing that didn't sit well with me are the very lengthy laser puzzle sections. Sometimes they are more frustrating than fun. Still fulfilling to beat, but a lot of puzzles demand extreme precision with no room for error. I can easily see people raging because they are forced into various very difficult puzzles when they just want to be exploring and shooting stuff.
The plot is surprisingly good, and contains many semi-animated cutscenes and radio chatter. I feel like the pacing was slightly strange - at times there can be a ton of back and forth and at others you are in silence for the length of a level... but for the most part it goes above and beyond most indie games.
I thought that Doogan had the best VO out of the main characters. Ghost has a very cute voice, but at times she can sound too friendly for someone who's supposed to be an operative.
All in all the game's incredible and I think that it was a total steal for the sale price I got it for. Buy it as the devs deserve the money.

This game does the adventure book style of games very well, the writing is original and well done. I didn't think there would be a lot of content consideing the game is based on books, however it managed to entertain me with a 20 hour play through and a story that spans over many maps. As could be seen in the game's trailers, it mixes in turn based combat scenes and some event-driving mini games such as the lock picking  to enrich the experience beyond simply reading a book and making choices, which I think is a nice touch and makes the game more interesting and playable. The music is subtle, which doesn't seem like an important thing at first, but having played some other game-book inspired games with blaring music that just serves to distract me from my reading, it is important to have a good appropriate score to play to your game..
It's an rpg which follows the typical strength-agility-intelligence attribute archetypes which each has a use in several aspects of the game, however it doesn't fix you to the predictable and boring stereotypes you often see associated to each.  (such as, intelligence typically being an attribute reserved for wizards who only do things such as cast spells and be wise, etc.) Rather, your chosen attribute gives you a headstart for making choices of that type easier to be successful, your choices increase your attribute scores when it comes to levelling up, giving the gamer much more freedom to play how they like in my opinion. The combat is ok, it is turn based and made interesting with qte-type events to determine some dodges and hits.
I thotoughly enjoyed this game and would recommend it to anybody who is interested in a story and making choices with consequences.

I'm not going to go into best games or best Final Fantasies, but I've played a whole slew of games with great stories or sparkling reviews over the years and very, very few have made an impact anywhere close to this. Final Fantasy VIII is, without a doubt, a must play for all gamers and anyone who wishes to experience great depth of storytelling and gameplay. I can't recommend this enough, and I've told so many friends already.
However, it is not for those wanting an evening of mindnumbing shiny lights to forget and walk away from. It is a long game and requires thought, for both the gameplay and the story. It also requires it's share of 90's style game management skills. If this is a learning curve, stick with it, you'll get it and still have plenty of game to go.
I'd recommend not using the game boosters though unless you've already played all the way through once or you have a REALLY casual relationship with good games and fine art. Seriously, they take you out of the game too much and cheapen the experience. This game rewards perserverance and draws in curiousity.
Play it if you like Final Fantasy, love story games, or need to see a part of gaming history. Oh and get a good controller too, one with full synergy with Windows. You'll thank me later.
