This game stayed in my library unplayed for a lot longer than I'd care to admit. If I'd known how much I'd enjoy it, I would have played it sooner.
Off the bat, I'll say this game really isn't for everyone. There's no combat and the few puzzles there are are very simple. There is no dialogue, save from whale song, dolphin chatter, and various assorted marine noises. Even the story itself must be pieced together on your own by observing ancient murals and drawing your own conclusions. No books, scrolls or scattered notes to put the lore together.
It's a swimming simulator at heart, but it's a beautiful one. The fish move realistically. They scatter when you swim into a school, the octopus on the ocean floor scuttle into shelter when you draw close -- and so do other critters like sea anemones and garden eels. The ocean is well populated, and everything feels alive. I didn't see any fish swim through each other, or clip through objects.
Hats off to the devs on this one; the little details stand out. Seaweed and plants move and sway when you swim near or through, moving around your character rather than being static. Swimming along the sandy ocean floor can kick up little clouds of sand behind you, and a couple whale pods even had juveniles swimming alongside the adults.
Riding animals is a joy, and breaching them out of water is a blast. Although, if you ride a predator species, they're generally more inclined to take you along for a (non-graphic) hunting trip instead of swimming precisely where you'd like.
There are collectable shells scattered throughout, and little pink pools that release additional animals into that area. In addition to that are "meditation points", where you can sit and view the area. Once unlocked, you can visit those points whenever you like, including from the menu.
It's very much like a modern version of the old aquarium screensavers; relaxing and soothing. You could probably even let it play while studying, or getting some reading done; the scenery and animals are different enough between each point that it shouldn't grow old too fast, and it will automatically move to a new fish every so often, so you aren't seeing the same shark, anchovy or squid for too long.
The only significant drawback I had with this game was that the controls were rather floaty (pun intentional). To some degree, that should be expected since you're playing underwater, but occasionally I found myself struggling not to turn too far in one direction, failing, and veering off course entirely. This was all with a controller -- I imagine keyboard and mouse, while still playable, would be a bit more frustrating. Once you get used to the controls, they're fairly easy, but may need a bit of wrangling at times.
Overall, 9/10, would visit Atlantis and break pyramids again.

I've played this game all the way from the time when it was still being released by episodic on iOS. The gameplay certainly is different from what one may be used to if one has played the original gamebooks. I was surprised at first, but eventually find that this is quite a refreshing way to explore the world of Lone Wolf.
Artwork is absolutely gorgeous! Loved seeing Lone Wolf actually portrayed in his full glory for the first time ever, albeit still in his early years as a Kai Lord. The transition from paper to 3D and back is a great touch. Battle backgrounds are varied according the player's location when attacked.
The soundtrack is pretty good as well, well suited for the environment and events. They add to the mystique, danger, sorrow of whichever fortunate, or unfortunate event that occurred in the game world.
Battles require players to understand the mechanism and adapt to something completely different from the gamebooks. It also may seem repetitive, but personally, I feel that it's unavoidable for a game of this caliber. The freedom of movement and random battles aim to help the player to get used to fighting a certain enemy, gain items and gold, as well as provide the player with the ability to have some control over moving in an area. It allows the player to break free from the typical gamebook linearity where they must perform certain XYZ actions at a specific time, and no other (i.e. purchase from merchants. or training skills).
A lot of balancing changes have been made to the battle system since it was first released. I find it quite well balanced compared to initial release. Some battle elements appear to be random, unfair and hard, but if one played the original gamebooks properly (i.e. without cheating), one may find themselves on the verge of death or dying quite often as well.
Not a fan of QTEs, but I feel that this game has it done right for the general user. They are doable as long as the player remembers what QTE action is required for which combat skill. The QTEs are fixed for almost every battle action, and events (as long as you can memorize the QTEs every event in the game). The controls are intuitive for the mouse, and does not impose strict directional movements on the player (i.e. the swipe does not have to be a definite 45 degree semi-circular movement to be executed).
Statistics can rise depending on the actions the player decides to take during an event. Repeated usage of weapon skills will eventually lead to an additional bonus for that particular skill. Crafting to improve weapons, armours and certain items are a welcome surprise. (I only miss my Sommersack from the iOS). There are some puzzles in the game to give variety, but not that much that it takes too much from the gameplay.
This is certainly an interesting way to breath life into a gamebook, what with many other companies already creating digital gamebooks that adhere more or less to the standards of a paperback (i.e. dice-rolling, turn to page ###).
Sure, it's not perfect (seriously, what is?), but a truly excellent work from both the original creator of Lone Wolf, and the developer of this game.

I know I have a lot of hours on record for not recommending a game, but I have finally admitted to myself that this game is so overcomplicated simply for the sake of being overcomplicated, and it really dampens the experience.
To start, this game is incredibly limiting in how it let's the player play. If you want to have an empire that has the materialist ethic then you lose the ability to research the Psi Jump Drive, and therefore lose the ability to spawn one of the three end game events. You aren't able to control more than 5-7 planets at a time, and if you try to control more you receive a -33% penalty to all your resources that'll almost always put you in the negative. You cannot remove pops unless you play as a collectivist or xenophobe, meaning if you have a rowdy species you don't want you have no way of dealing with them unless you spend precious trait points on one of two ethics. But if you are a collectivist or a xenophobe, you'll get a penalty from neighoring nations that may disagree with your line of thought. If you at any point go to war with another species, you will get a "threat" penalty from all empires, and they will more than likely close their borders to you. Meaning if you attack an empire that's harrassing other empires, those empires then begin to hate you instead, which makes no sense! This game is so limiting in how it plays, with no real way to customize the maps that it loses all fun.
Then in patch 1.2, they removed embassies, which was one of the best ways to build relationships with other empires, and replaced it with non aggression packs. Not only do non aggressions provide less positive influence, but once you break a non aggression pack you have to wait an in game decade to be able to declare war on said nation. Embassies were a far better way to run things, and they were simply removed from the game for a far more complicated, and punishing mechaninc in non aggression and defensive pacts.
But that isn't even the worst part, the worst part of the game is influence. The one, extreme bottleneck that limits pretty much everything. Influence is used in almost all functions in the game, and if you don't have enough then you are prevented from doing most things, like colonizing planets, or listing edicts to help unruly pops, or simply being friendly with another nation. There aren't that many ways to gain influence, except for one building you may build (only once) and becoming rivals with empires, beyond that there is the occasional tech that helps but nothing more. Things like non aggression pacts and Frontier Outposts (which puts systems in your empires borders) use far more influence monthly than they are worth. This is easily the most frustrating part of the game.
There are mods and console commands that help some of it, but they are few and far between, and the mods that are available are hardly kept updated with the new patches that come out sporadically and are either far imbalanced or just don't work at all. This game at it's base is a good idea, but it is so poorly implemented that i cannot recommend it. Hopefully people out there like it more than I did but as it stands this is not a game that i would recommend.

I love the Lone Wolf books.  I saw them for the first time when I was really young, and I was enthralled by the amazing world Joe Dever created.  With just one book, 'Flight from the Dark', I was hooked on the adventures of Lone Wolf, last of the Kai Lords, as he fought the Darklords of Helgedad and the forces of the god of darkness, Naar.
Joe Dever does not disappoint with this game.  The writing, world building and feel of the story is a perfect match to the old CYOA books.  From the first moments of the game, you feel like you really are Lone Wolf, the last hope for Sommerlund.
It's an absolute travesty that this fantastic writing is ruined by positively garbage game design.  All of the problems in this game revolve around combat which, incidentally, was one of the biggest stumbling points in the original book series.  In the book series, it was because Dever had to write around the player potentially having the Infinity +1 Sword (The Sommerswerd).  In this game, it is because the designers couldn't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to make a fighting system that relied on something other than RNG and confusion.
The game has four chapters.  The first two, it is worth noting, are fantastic.  The combat is simple and to the point.  Enemies can hit decently hard, but you are well equipped to handle them and supplies are plentiful.  It isn't that the games design is better at this point, it is that the flaws are easier to overlook.  Combat will rarely be fatal, even if it takes a turn for the worse, and this keeps the player moving through the story, which is the real meat of the game.
The final boss of the second chapter is where things start to get really rough.  The enemy will go first, deals massive damage, and has a chance to stun you.  If you are stunned in this opening salvo, you WILL die before getting a chance to act at all.  The chance of this happening isn't too high, but it is still there, and most players will see it at least once, if not more.
From then on, the game pulls no punches, in the worst ways possible.  Random encounters are BOSS level mobs, which make it easier to just reload an old save then to deal with the pointless slugfest.  Enemy monsters are filled with 'Rapid Clicking QTEs', which seem to be used for almost everything in the game.  Early on, you'd take some damage or screw an attack up if you failed.  Now?  Dead if you mess it up.
I got sick and tired of it and just installed an auto clicker.  And even with that, it only makes the combat slightly LESS unfair.  You WILL die, many times, to swarms of foes before you can possibly react.  100% to dead before you can do anything, even if you were defending.  Adding onto everything else, the enemy is not held to the same mechanical rules that the player is.
Lone Wolf can act during his own 'phase'.  When his timer runs out, he cannot act for a bit, and then the cycle repeats.  The enemy has no such difficulty.  They can attack whenever they wish, your phase or not.  They can attack the millisecond your defenses drop (and often will) and hit with DoT effects that deal huge chunks of your health (similar DoTs are nearly scratch damage to them).
The original books were about controlling conflict.  You weren't an army slaying warrior, so you were supposed to be clever about how you engaged in fights.  This game not only forgot that, but went the other way and puts you into bland, annoying and uninteresting combat CONSTANTLY.
If you want a good story, I can recommend this game.  But I'd advise you to play Chapter 1 and 2 on Normal, then slam it down to Easy to just burn through the rest of the story without the BS.  There's no reason to give yourself a migrane over "Difficulty by Frustration."

When Paradox first announced Stellaris last year, I found myself asking if, in an already crowded category, we really needed another space strategy game. Now, after spending more than a week with the final product I have my answer.
No, we don’t need another space strategy game. Not now, at least. What we need is more Stellaris.
It’s a fantastic platform, a capable, flexible sandbox that's customizable inside and out. Would you like to play as a race of bird-like creatures who can only colonize dry, rocky desert worlds and prefer a collectivist society that worships technology? Then maybe try your hand at a ruling science directorate, an oligarchy of eggheads elected every 50 years. Perhaps next time around you'd like to conjure up a society of floating, spore-like creatures who are fanatic, warlike xenophobes. If that's the case, you can explore the challenges of managing a military republic with a five-year election cycle. For completionists looking to experience everything the game has to offer, expect many challenging campaign playthroughs. This year I have sampled every 4x game out there. Take a look at my library.
Stellaris takes home the gold medal this year.

I'd never heard of Lone Wolf 24 hours ago. I paid $7.49 for this game, and it was beyond worth it. I've played just under thirty minutes. This game feels great. You get to create a customized character in minutes, those choices immediately affect the story you are reading and the combat you will face. The story events are between old school text based adventures and quick time events. It blends your decisions with your actions beautifully. The turn based combat doesn't let you walk away. You have limited time and resources to take actions, so you need to make snap decisions. To be effective you need to stay calm and focused. This makes the combat thrilling, and did I mention this game looks pretty too. The way they blend art from the book into the combat sequences is stunning. The graphics aren't what you would see on a next gen console, but they look good. As far as animation is concerned, I have to say they nailed it. From throwing knives to having your chest slashed open, the models move fluidly. I definitely recommend picking Lone Wolf up if you have $10 to spare.
Edit: Now that I have almost ten hours under my belt, I would like to expand this review a little bit. I started another character because I didn't see how it was possible to survive without certain skills. Turns out I was wrong. You can definitely take whatever starting skills you are interested in trying. Sometimes enemies will wreck your day. When it happens, you may not even get to defend yourself because it is absolutely possible to become stun locked. It isn't likely, and because the game uses a random element, it is also completely possible for you to dodge every attack in a fight. You will probably die a couple of times during a fight that you are prepared for due to bad luck. It makes it far more rewarding when you try again and slaughter your enemies. If you really get stuck, the game even has the option to drop the difficulty a step when you retry. I should also talk about replay value after making a second character. It's okay. If you choose different skills at the beginning of the game, and you try taking another path through each of the obstacles in the game, then it isn't too repetitive. Many of the fights will be the same or nearly the same unless you had the option to avoid one completely. When you know what you are doing, you can definitely work through the fights faster, and it feels like you are accomplishing something rather than grinding because the story actually moves as you cut down your enemies. I can't say how long a run through this campaign should take. I just set the game on hard, turned off hints, and charged into the fray.

A fun side scrolling hack and slash game with great voice work and a solid storyline. Categories typically get a base score, followed by pros and cons.
Graphics: 8/10
==========
Most graphics appear to be hand drawn with some 3D work thrown in here and there. It comes together, for the most part, pretty darn well. There are a few nit picky things that bother me (such as the shadows on some of the drawings, they don't look natural), but on the whole, they look great. +8
Sound: 9/10
=========
A game where I separate sound and music. The sounds effects are great for the most part but not outstanding. +7
Voice acting is pretty damn good. I'm happy to see the work that went into it. +2
Music: 10/10
=========
Jesus the music in this game is unbelievable. Every track in every world fits great with the given setting and sounds fantastic. The battle music especially is just soooo damn good. 10 out of freaking 10. +10
Story: 7/10
========
You are Dust. You have woken up in some random forest and your memory is gone. All that's around you is a talking sword and the guardian of said sword. Lets go get our memory back. +6
Final battle itself is fantastic. +2
The antagonist could stand to be bit more evil. -1
Gameplay: 9/10
===========
Oh lawd the gameplay. Yeah, it's a fast paced hack and slash side scroller with great moves, new abilities as you progress, craftable equipment, healing items, and level ups where you can distribute new stat points. There are various quests you can take part in to get new gear and more XP. +7
The whirlwind attack is bloody fantastic. Combining it with the Thunder you get later in the game is always a joy. +1
Difficulty modes are fun and fair (I played on Tough. It was fairly tough). +1
Throughout my (2nd technically) playthrough, I didn't do a single side quest. I'm extremely happy this game doesn't force the side questing upon you in order to continue the game (whether it be because you're not strong enough, and need to do side questing to get strong enough, or a side questing tutorial). +1
The jump between stat points with each given level is far too outrageous and exponential. This goes for items as well. Level one you'll get like 10 more attack power, then level 2 will give you 50 more. This is too great of a leap and made areas far too easy only after gaining a couple levels. -1
Overall: 8.6/10 (43/50 = 0.86)
=====================

Marauder: Man of Prey is a Russian game with a high difficulty level (not impossible, but I still recommend saving often), brutal and realistic combat, light RPG elements (you can level up and train your skills), loads of loot (including various weapons and their attachments, ammo, gear, explosives, food, tools, cigarettes etc) and a grim storyline based on a book with a setting that reminds me of Tom Clancy's stuff (if Tom Clancy was Russian).
As an old Jagged Alliance and UFO: Enemy Unknown player, I felt right at home with this game, even if it is RTwP instead of Turn-Based. It's a bit rough around the edges, with some bugs here and there, and the English translation is not very good, but I've been enjoying Marauder's intense battles and bleak Russian post-apocalyptic atmosphere immensely. The player character, a Russian Tatar called Akhmet, is not a regular hero. Actually he is more of an anti-hero, and not a very nice guy. Akhmet is not an evil man, but he is rather crude and his motives are mostly selfish. He will do almost anything to ensure his and his wife's survival. I really like this about him, as it makes him feel like a more realistic character, considering the setting where it's basically "every man for himself".
The graphics are dated, but good enough for me, and I like the small details like different gear changing the character's appearance and the gun's actually showing their attachments like scopes, lasers and silencers in the game.
Highly recommended for people who like games like Jagged Alliance 2 and Silent Storm. Just remember it is not a turn-based game. If you have problems with the game's videos freezing, find the game's LP from LPArchive to see the translated videos.
Edit: Some reviews are complaining about the extremely sluggish camera controls. I had a problem with this too, until I realized you can make the camera controls more sensitive from the options menu. Do that and controlling the camera will be easier. There are still some annoyances like trouble getting the camera through doorways or windows etc., but if that happens, just double click on Akhmet's portrait and the camera should take you to him (if you are far enough from him).

It's a highly recommended buy, though with many restrictions and prerequisites. Yeah, game-is-not-for-everyone's-tastes.
First, you should really like squad-tactics games like Jagged Alliance, Silent Storm or 7.62 and DON'T BE a graphics freak who wants everything in 16:9 with 60fps. Game's a bit dated, see? And still, it can be successfully compared by gameplay options even with latest tactics games. That slow-paced genre never was too hard about graphics. Physics, mechanics - that's a prime, but high resolutions... meh.
Second, be ready for glitches. Game and engine developers now either dead or missing, so there is no help in asking for patches. Although for the most part, game is running okay, except for cutscenes.
Third and last is about moral - it's a game where a desperate man doing everything to survive, so if you like playing knights in white armor, that's surely a wrong game. Try "The Shining Force", maybe?
Now, what's it all about? Well, it's a game based on the book "Marauder", bestselling in Russia, which were telling a story about a smooth and easy diplomatic victory of NATO forces. Russia is no more, sold to "West world" by some puppets and oligarchs, with "all included". Some cities like Moscow and Saint-Petersburg remains almost the same - just to decoy everything else that is going on in the once-a-great-country. And what is going there? Every big force in former state like paramilitary formations, or even some villages coalitions is methodically observed and negated by NATO "peacemakers". They called "mistresses" there, in sado-mazo sense, meaning they are masters and natives are slaves... Russkies are living in ruins of cities, without energy, fuel, water, food supplies. Anarchy and "homo homini lupus est" rule is prior for everyone. Our "hero" Ahmed, with the collapse of the state, is off to search for every piece of scrap he can use or sell, marauding and killing for own survival. Oh, grim apocalyptic future! Maybe it's close by already. I mean, look at eastern Ukraine...
Anyway, although this game is constructed pretty linear, right along with the book plot, there is a little twist in the end, for which I'm so fond to this game. While in the book a protagonist fled away when his city was about to be "purified", in game we have a chance to strike back. To kill a slave in yourself! That's grand, really. Like killing Hitler or defending Alamo on your own.
I'm spending all that much space revealing you the story, because it's the ♥♥♥♥♥iest part in the game. Not a story itself, but the way of its telling. Cutscenes are bugged, I don't know anyone who could see it all without glitch. More to that, translation from russian to english were surely made by Promt software, or something like that. Those who answered for translation, should be burned alive, since they were lazy enough to bungle even with a tutorial!
Okay, if you were able to read that all and still thinking "why I should buy it?", like I said from start - it's a good tactical game, highest evolution of Apeiron engine, knowing by "Brigade E5" and "7.62" games. Buy it with 75% discount, sell cards - and maybe you will have upper hand at the end of a deal, gaining more than spend.
9/10 successful missions. The sapper makes only one mistake.
PS: to turn on camera rotation in game fix "camera sensitiveness" setting from zero to twenty, at least. And maybe it will be wise to turn on "windows xp" compatibility with "e8.exe". Peace, people.

Marauder is a surprisingly fun game, it feels like Stalker meets Jagged Alliance, which makes for a great setting. The story so far is decent enough, the combat is excellent, and the graphics are pleasently nice looking.
The only real problem with the game is it's a little buggy from time to time, and the translation could've used more time put into it (Honestly, we were lucky to get anything at all). But overall, it's a damn fine game.
This is the crowning jewel of Apeiron, I really liked the concepts in their previous games, but couldn't get past the clunky interfaces, buggyness, and general unpolish. Marauder fixes all these problems, and just feels...Good. They really got their♥♥♥♥♥♥together for this game.
So yeah, highly recommend it to anyone who's into squad based tactical strategy games.

From the emotional feel you get from talking to the townsfolk, digging through Dust's past, Bonding with fidget as you traverse the lands locating hidden content and items... to chopping through hordes of enemies, combo chaining, and fighting insaine bosses, This game has a little something for everyone.
The Story was enticing and continuously keeping me on the edge of my seat to see what would happen next. Keeping a steady (and wisely applied) flow of short triggered interactions with your partner, Fidget, to the long and in depth cutscenes that apeared from time to time. Talking with the townsfolk and having choices as to your responces made the story imersive in every way.
The animation style was memorable and alwasy pleasing to look at. And you don't necessarily have to be into the "Furry Fandom" to enjoy these characters. Everything from the environment around you to the character animations is done with utter beauty.
OVER ALL... the game is a remarkable work of art. Check out IGN's Review to get a better look at the overall details, but I personallly would recomend this game to many gamers.

I don't feel like it's as good as all the reviews over the years have made it out to be, but it's still a fantastic game.
I wouldn't classify it as the "BESSSSSSSST GAAAAAAAAAAAAAME EVURRRRRRRRRRRRRRRRRRRR" but it's still an immensely satisfying game.
The mouse is a bit weird in the Steam version, and if you're using a monitor with a high resolution, you may have to toy around with the settings; I started it up and had t he game look a giant one colour blob.
Save often. Save frequently. The game never really seems to do it for you. I can't stress that enough. I played for about 90 minutes one day, sneaking around as I'm known to do, completing objectives, and then bam, one shot kill by an environmental hazard. I didn't play for about 2 days after that.
BUT STUPID WHINING GRIPES ASIDE Deus Ex is a really superb game. My word of advice would be to "not believe the hype". It's good, but (I feel) not the proverbial "Best. Game. Ever".
It doesn't feel complete, and it's not bug-free, but get  this sucker on sale and you should be worth your money.
